- A lightweight, incremental repo intelligence skill. Walks a repository, analyzes each file, and stores the results in the the internal context hub `file-analysis` library via MCP tools. Does **not** write any files to the analyzed repo. [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- You want a quick, searchable per-file index of any repo without running the full repo-bootstrapper [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- You want to understand what a specific file does without reading the whole codebase [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- You want to find which files handle authentication, routing, database access, etc. across a repo [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- You want to re-run the analysis after changing some files and only re-process what changed [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- `mdb_context_hub` must be running (HTTP on `127.0.0.1:3939`). The skill uses these tools: [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- `tam_get_file_analysis_state` — load previous file hashes for the repo [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- `tam_save_file_analysis` — save a single file's analysis entry [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- `tam_save_file_analysis_state` — persist updated hashes after the run [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- `tam_list_file_analyses` — browse results after analysis [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- `tam_search_file_analyses` — find files by keyword across all summaries [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- `tam_delete_repo_file_analyses` — wipe a repo's data and start fresh [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- -- [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- Before analyzing anything, classify every file into one of four buckets. Process them in order: **skip → meta → high-signal → standard**. [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- Do not call `tam_save_file_analysis` for any file matching these patterns: [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- These files contain high-value prose that should be preserved largely intact as the `summary`. Truncate at ~8 KB if the file is very long. [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- Patterns (matched against filename or relative path): [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- `README*` (README.md, README.rst, README.txt, etc.) [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- `CONTRIBUTING*` [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- `ARCHITECTURE*`, `DESIGN*`, `OVERVIEW*` [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- `CLAUDE.md` [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- `LICENSE*` (store as-is; mark purpose `"docs"`) [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- `docs/*.md` and `docs/**/*.md` (top-level docs folder) [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- Any `.md` file in the **repo root** that is not in the SKIP list [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- Use these field values: [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- `purpose: "docs"` [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- `summary`: full file content (up to 8 KB; if longer, include first 4 KB + `"... [truncated]"`) [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- `tags`: `["meta", "documentation"]` plus one of `["readme"]`, `["license"]`, `["contributing"]`, `["architecture"]` as appropriate [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- `exports`: `[]` [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- `dependencies`: `[]` [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- These files justify 3–5 sentence summaries and complete export/dependency lists. [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- Entry points: `index.*`, `main.*`, `app.*`, `server.*`, `__main__.py`, `cli.*`, `run.*` [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- Service/business logic: `*.service.*`, `*.controller.*`, `*.handler.*`, `*.router.*`, `*.middleware.*`, `*.resolver.*`, `*.provider.*` [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- Core models/schemas: `*.model.*`, `*.schema.*`, `*.entity.*`, `*.domain.*` [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- Any file **over 200 lines** of non-test source code [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- Files referenced by 3+ other files (if you can tell from imports) [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- For high-signal files: [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- Write 3–5 sentence summaries covering: what it does, the key algorithm or pattern used, and any important side-effects or invariants [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- List all named and default exports [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- List all significant dependencies (external packages + key internal imports) [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- Add a `"high-signal"` tag [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- All remaining source files. Write 1–3 sentence summaries. List key exports and dependencies only. [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- -- [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- Accept the repo path from the user or infer it from the working directory. Resolve to an absolute path. This becomes `repoPath` for all tool calls. [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- repoPath=$(pwd)   # or take from user [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- **Do not proceed with a full analysis on an archived repo** — it wastes time and pollutes the library with stale data. [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- Check for archival using any available signal: [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- gh repo view "$(git -C "$repoPath" remote get-url origin 2>/dev/null | sed 's|.*github.com[:/]\(.*\)\.git|\1|;s|.*github.com[:/]\(.*\)|\1|')" \ [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- -json isArchived --jq '.isArchived' 2>/dev/null [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- ls "$repoPath/ARCHIVED" "$repoPath/.archived" "$repoPath/DEPRECATED" 2>/dev/null [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- grep -i "archived\|deprecated\|no longer maintained" "$repoPath/README.md" 2>/dev/null | head -3 [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- If the repo is determined to be archived: [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- Print: `⚠️  Repo appears to be archived. Skipping analysis to avoid storing stale data.` [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- Offer the user two options: **(a)** abort, or **(b)** continue anyway with a `"archived"` tag appended to all stored entries. [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- If the user chooses (b), proceed with all steps and add `"archived"` to every file's `tags` array. [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- If the user chooses (a) or gives no response, stop here. [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- Call `tam_get_file_analysis_state` with `repoPath`. The response is: [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- { "repoPath": "...", "lastRun": "<ISO or null>", "files": { "src/foo.ts": { "hash": "...", "analyzedAt": "..." } } } [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- Store this as `previousState`. If `lastRun` is null, this is a first run. [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- Enumerate all files using: [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- find "$repoPath" -type f \ [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- not -path "*/.git/*" \ [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- not -path "*/node_modules/*" \ [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- not -path "*/.next/*" \ [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- not -path "*/dist/*" \ [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- not -path "*/build/*" \ [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- not -path "*/__pycache__/*" \ [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- not -path "*/.venv/*" \ [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- not -path "*/vendor/*" \ [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- not -path "*/.idea/*" \ [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- not -path "*/.vscode/*" \ [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- For each file, compute its SHA-256 hash: [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- shasum -a 256 "$filePath" | cut -d' ' -f1  # macOS [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- sha256sum "$filePath" | cut -d' ' -f1       # Linux [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- Before doing any analysis, classify each file into one of: [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- `skip` — matches any SKIP pattern (see table above) [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- `meta` — matches any META pattern [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- `high-signal` — matches any HIGH-SIGNAL pattern [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- `standard` — everything else that isn't skipped [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- Print the category counts before starting analysis: [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- skip:        N files  (not stored) [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- meta:        N files  (stored verbatim) [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- high-signal: N files  (deep analysis) [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- standard:    N files  (concise analysis) [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- For each file in the `meta`, `high-signal`, and `standard` buckets, compare its hash against `previousState.files[relPath]?.hash`. [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- **New file** (not in state): analyze [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- **Changed file** (hash differs): analyze [src: repo-file-analyzer]
- **Unchanged file** (hash matches): skip — do NOT call `tam_save_file_analysis` for it [src: repo-file-analyzer]

- ETE (Environment for Tree Exploration) is a Python toolkit for phylogenetic and hierarchical tree analysis. Core use cases: tree I/O and manipulation, evolutionary event detection, NCBI taxonomy integration, visualization, and clustering analysis. [src: scientific-pkg-etetoolkit]
- Use for: loading/pruning/rerooting/traversing Newick/NHX/PhyloXML trees; detecting evolutionary events (duplication, speciation) and identifying orthologs/paralogs; NCBI taxonomy queries, lineage retrieval, tree annotation; tree visualization (PDF/SVG/PNG) with custom NodeStyle/Faces/layout functions; Robinson-Foulds comparison; ClusterTree heatmaps. [src: scientific-pkg-etetoolkit]
- **When not to use:** generating sequence alignments, running inference tools (IQ-TREE, RAxML), or general bioinformatics not involving tree structures. [src: scientific-pkg-etetoolkit]

- **Web API** — HTTP RPC at `https://slack.com/api/METHOD.name`. NOT REST. [src: slack-dev]
- **Events API** — Slack POSTs events to your URL when things happen. Requires URL verification challenge. [src: slack-dev]
- **Socket Mode** — WebSocket-based alternative to Events API. No public URL needed. [src: slack-dev]
- **Block Kit** — JSON schema for rich UI in messages, modals, and Home tab. [src: slack-dev]
- **Interactive Components** — Buttons, select menus, modals. Slack POSTs interaction payloads to your app. [src: slack-dev]
- **Slash Commands** — `/command` invocations. Slack POSTs form data to your URL. [src: slack-dev]
- POST https://slack.com/api/METHOD [src: slack-dev]
- Authorization: Bearer xoxb-TOKEN [src: slack-dev]
- Content-Type: application/json [src: slack-dev]
- Response: { "ok": true, "error": "...", ...fields } [src: slack-dev]
- **Always check `ok: true` before using response data.** [src: slack-dev]

- `error-summary` - For multiple errors, show summary at top with anchor links to each field (WCAG) [src: ui-ux-pro-max]

- `destructive-emphasis` - Destructive actions use semantic danger color (red) and are visually separated from primary actions (HIG, MD) [src: ui-ux-pro-max]

- `timeout-feedback` - Request timeout must show clear feedback with retry option (MD) [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- `bottom-nav-limit` - Bottom navigation max 5 items; use labels with icons (Material Design) [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- `drawer-usage` - Use drawer/sidebar for secondary navigation, not primary actions (Material Design) [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- `back-behavior` - Back navigation must be predictable and consistent; preserve scroll/state (Apple HIG, MD) [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- `deep-linking` - All key screens must be reachable via deep link / URL for sharing and notifications (Apple HIG, MD) [src: ui-ux-pro-max]

- -- [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Before delivering UI code, verify these items: [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Scope notice: This checklist is for App UI (iOS/Android/React Native/Flutter). [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] No emojis used as icons (use SVG instead) [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] All icons come from a consistent icon family and style [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] Official brand assets are used with correct proportions and clear space [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] Pressed-state visuals do not shift layout bounds or cause jitter [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] Semantic theme tokens are used consistently (no ad-hoc per-screen hardcoded colors) [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] All tappable elements provide clear pressed feedback (ripple/opacity/elevation) [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] Touch targets meet minimum size (>=44x44pt iOS, >=48x48dp Android) [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] Micro-interaction timing stays in the 150-300ms range with native-feeling easing [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] Disabled states are visually clear and non-interactive [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] Screen reader focus order matches visual order, and interactive labels are descriptive [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] Gesture regions avoid nested/conflicting interactions (tap/drag/back-swipe conflicts) [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] Primary text contrast >=4.5:1 in both light and dark mode [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] Secondary text contrast >=3:1 in both light and dark mode [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] Dividers/borders and interaction states are distinguishable in both modes [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] Modal/drawer scrim opacity is strong enough to preserve foreground legibility (typically 40-60% black) [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] Both themes are tested before delivery (not inferred from a single theme) [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] Safe areas are respected for headers, tab bars, and bottom CTA bars [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] Scroll content is not hidden behind fixed/sticky bars [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] Verified on small phone, large phone, and tablet (portrait + landscape) [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] Horizontal insets/gutters adapt correctly by device size and orientation [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] 4/8dp spacing rhythm is maintained across component, section, and page levels [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] Long-form text measure remains readable on larger devices (no edge-to-edge paragraphs) [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] All meaningful images/icons have accessibility labels [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] Form fields have labels, hints, and clear error messages [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] Color is not the only indicator [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] Reduced motion and dynamic text size are supported without layout breakage [src: ui-ux-pro-max]
- Link: [ ] Accessibility traits/roles/states (selected, disabled, expanded) are announced correctly [src: ui-ux-pro-max]

- **Event model, delegation, teardown, and abortable listeners:** MDN docs for `addEventListener`, `removeEventListener`, `AbortController`, `Event.target`, `Event.currentTarget`, `Element.closest`, and `Event.composedPath()` ([MDN addEventListener](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/EventTarget/addEventListener), [MDN removeEventListener](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/EventTarget/removeEventListener), [MDN AbortController](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController), [MDN Event.target](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Event/target), [MDN Event.currentTarget](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Event/currentTarget), [MDN Element.closest](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/closest), [MDN Event.composedPath](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Event/composedPath)). [src: vanilla-js-ui-reviewer]
- **Safe DOM updates and structure:** MDN docs for `textContent`, `innerHTML`, `replaceChildren`, `appendChild`, `DocumentFragment`, and semantic HTML elements like `button`, `main`, `nav`, `section`, `ul`, and `li` ([MDN textContent](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Node/textContent), [MDN innerHTML](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/innerHTML), [MDN replaceChildren](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/replaceChildren), [MDN appendChild](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Node/appendChild), [MDN DocumentFragment](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/DocumentFragment), [MDN button](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/button)). [src: vanilla-js-ui-reviewer]
- **Focus, keyboard behavior, and modal/widget semantics:** MDN docs for `focus()`, `activeElement`, `tabIndex`, `:focus-visible`, `dialog`, `inert`, and keyboard-navigable widgets, plus APG dialog/tabs/accordion/menu/treeview patterns and WCAG understanding docs for focus order and name/role/value ([MDN focus](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLElement/focus), [MDN activeElement](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document/activeElement), [MDN tabIndex](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLElement/tabIndex), [MDN :focus-visible](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/:focus-visible), [MDN dialog](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/dialog), [MDN inert](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Global_attributes/inert), [MDN keyboard-navigable JavaScript widgets](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/Guides/Keyboard-navigable_JavaScript_widgets), [APG keyboard interface](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/practices/keyboard-interface/), [APG dialog modal](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/dialog-modal/), [WCAG focus order understanding](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/focus-order.html), [WCAG name role value understanding](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/name-role-value.html)). [src: vanilla-js-ui-reviewer]
- **Performance guidance:** web.dev docs for DOM size/interactivity and layout thrashing ([web.dev DOM size and interactivity](https://web.dev/articles/dom-size-and-interactivity), [web.dev avoid layout thrashing](https://web.dev/avoid-large-complex-layouts-and-layout-thrashing/)). [src: vanilla-js-ui-reviewer]
- **Repo-specific framing:** `extensions/aggregaytor/sidepanel/panel.js`, `panel.html`, `panel.css`, and popup files. [src: vanilla-js-ui-reviewer]
- **Prefer native semantic elements before custom widget code.** Native buttons, lists, landmarks, and dialogs usually beat hand-rolled `div` patterns ([MDN button](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/button), [MDN main](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/main), [MDN nav](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/nav)). [src: vanilla-js-ui-reviewer]
- **Use event delegation intentionally.** Review `target`, `currentTarget`, `closest()`, and composed-path assumptions together; many plain-JS UI bugs are mis-targeting bugs ([MDN Event.target](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Event/target), [MDN Element.closest](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/closest)). [src: vanilla-js-ui-reviewer]
- **Use `textContent` for text and treat `innerHTML` as a security/perf review hotspot.** HTML-string rendering deserves explicit trust/sanitization scrutiny ([MDN textContent](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Node/textContent), [MDN innerHTML](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/innerHTML)). [src: vanilla-js-ui-reviewer]
- **Review focus and keyboard behavior together.** A UI is not accessible if it looks right but traps, loses, or hides focus ([APG keyboard interface](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/practices/keyboard-interface/), [WCAG focus order understanding](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/focus-order.html)). [src: vanilla-js-ui-reviewer]
- **Prefer one-off or abortable listeners/observers/timers over immortal globals.** Large vanilla UIs often leak work through forgotten listeners or polling ([MDN addEventListener](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/EventTarget/addEventListener), [MDN AbortController](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController)). [src: vanilla-js-ui-reviewer]
- **Batch DOM reads before writes and be suspicious of large always-on sweeps.** DOM size and layout churn affect responsiveness directly ([web.dev DOM size and interactivity](https://web.dev/articles/dom-size-and-interactivity), [web.dev avoid layout thrashing](https://web.dev/avoid-large-complex-layouts-and-layout-thrashing/)). [src: vanilla-js-ui-reviewer]
- **Start with structure and semantics.** Identify landmarks, major sections, lists, headings, and interactive controls. [src: vanilla-js-ui-reviewer]
- **Map event ownership.** Review direct listeners vs delegated listeners, how targets are resolved, and whether teardown exists ([MDN addEventListener](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/EventTarget/addEventListener), [MDN removeEventListener](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/EventTarget/removeEventListener)). [src: vanilla-js-ui-reviewer]
- **Audit DOM mutation surfaces.** Check for `innerHTML`, repeated full rerenders, and excessive polling or mutation-driven churn ([MDN innerHTML](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/innerHTML), [web.dev avoid layout thrashing](https://web.dev/avoid-large-complex-layouts-and-layout-thrashing/)). [src: vanilla-js-ui-reviewer]
- **Audit focus and keyboard flows.** Check initial focus, focus restoration, visible focus, tab order, and expected key bindings for custom widgets ([APG keyboard interface](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/practices/keyboard-interface/)). [src: vanilla-js-ui-reviewer]
- **Audit modal and composite-widget behavior.** Review dialog semantics, inert/background blocking, roving tabindex, `aria-selected`, `aria-expanded`, and state synchronization ([APG dialog modal](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/dialog-modal/), [MDN inert](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Global_attributes/inert)). [src: vanilla-js-ui-reviewer]
- **Audit runtime work.** Review DOM size, repeated selectors, polling intervals, and layout-sensitive code for likely INP/responsiveness regressions ([web.dev DOM size and interactivity](https://web.dev/articles/dom-size-and-interactivity)). [src: vanilla-js-ui-reviewer]
- Prefer **native controls and landmarks** over ARIA-heavy generic containers where HTML already models the concept ([MDN button](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/button)). [src: vanilla-js-ui-reviewer]
- Keep **state, labels, and ARIA attributes synchronized**; a widget with stale `aria-expanded` or `aria-selected` is a real bug, not polish. [src: vanilla-js-ui-reviewer]
- Use **abortable listeners and explicit teardown** to keep long-lived panels from accumulating dead work ([MDN AbortController](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController)). [src: vanilla-js-ui-reviewer]
- Review **periodic DOM sweeps and mutation observers** for visibility gating, debounce, and selector scope to avoid unnecessary CPU in an always-open sidepanel ([web.dev DOM size and interactivity](https://web.dev/articles/dom-size-and-interactivity)). [src: vanilla-js-ui-reviewer]
- For this repo specifically, favor patterns that fit the existing **large vanilla-JS sidepanel** rather than framework assumptions; readability, teardown, and semantic correctness matter more than framework-style abstractions. [src: vanilla-js-ui-reviewer]
- APG patterns apply primarily when custom widgets are truly necessary; do not force a complex ARIA pattern where a native element would be simpler. [src: vanilla-js-ui-reviewer]
- Performance guidance here is directional; confirm suspected hot paths with actual profiling when a review needs confidence. [src: vanilla-js-ui-reviewer]
- Some plain-JS UIs intentionally mix direct listeners, delegated listeners, and timers. The review question is whether that mix is controlled and comprehensible, not whether it is framework-like. [src: vanilla-js-ui-reviewer]

- license: Complete terms in LICENSE.txt [src: webapp-testing]
- -- [src: webapp-testing]
- To test local web applications, write native Python Playwright scripts. [src: webapp-testing]
- **Helper Scripts Available**: [src: webapp-testing]
- `scripts/with_server.py` - Manages server lifecycle (supports multiple servers) [src: webapp-testing]
- **Always run scripts with `--help` first** to see usage. DO NOT read the source until you try running the script first and find that a customized solution is abslutely necessary. These scripts can be very large and thus pollute your context window. They exist to be called directly as black-box scripts rather than ingested into your context window. [src: webapp-testing]
- User task → Is it static HTML? [src: webapp-testing]
- ├─ Yes → Read HTML file directly to identify selectors [src: webapp-testing]
- │         ├─ Success → Write Playwright script using selectors [src: webapp-testing]
- │         └─ Fails/Incomplete → Treat as dynamic (below) [src: webapp-testing]
- └─ No (dynamic webapp) → Is the server already running? [src: webapp-testing]
- ├─ No → Run: python scripts/with_server.py --help [src: webapp-testing]
- │        Then use the helper + write simplified Playwright script [src: webapp-testing]
- └─ Yes → Reconnaissance-then-action: [src: webapp-testing]
- Navigate and wait for networkidle [src: webapp-testing]
- Take screenshot or inspect DOM [src: webapp-testing]
- Identify selectors from rendered state [src: webapp-testing]
- Execute actions with discovered selectors [src: webapp-testing]
- To start a server, run `--help` first, then use the helper: [src: webapp-testing]
- python scripts/with_server.py --server "npm run dev" --port 5173 -- python your_automation.py [src: webapp-testing]
- **Multiple servers (e.g., backend + frontend):** [src: webapp-testing]
- python scripts/with_server.py \ [src: webapp-testing]
- -server "cd backend && python server.py" --port 3000 \ [src: webapp-testing]
- -server "cd frontend && npm run dev" --port 5173 \ [src: webapp-testing]
- - python your_automation.py [src: webapp-testing]
- To create an automation script, include only Playwright logic (servers are managed automatically): [src: webapp-testing]
- from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright [src: webapp-testing]
- with sync_playwright() as p: [src: webapp-testing]
- browser = p.chromium.launch(headless=True) # Always launch chromium in headless mode [src: webapp-testing]
- page = browser.new_page() [src: webapp-testing]
- page.goto('http://localhost:5173') # Server already running and ready [src: webapp-testing]
- page.wait_for_load_state('networkidle') # CRITICAL: Wait for JS to execute [src: webapp-testing]
- **Inspect rendered DOM**: [src: webapp-testing]
- page.screenshot(path='/tmp/inspect.png', full_page=True) [src: webapp-testing]
- content = page.content() [src: webapp-testing]
- page.locator('button').all() [src: webapp-testing]
- **Identify selectors** from inspection results [src: webapp-testing]
- **Execute actions** using discovered selectors [src: webapp-testing]
- ❌ **Don't** inspect the DOM before waiting for `networkidle` on dynamic apps [src: webapp-testing]
- ✅ **Do** wait for `page.wait_for_load_state('networkidle')` before inspection [src: webapp-testing]
- **Use bundled scripts as black boxes** - To accomplish a task, consider whether one of the scripts available in `scripts/` can help. These scripts handle common, complex workflows reliably without cluttering the context window. Use `--help` to see usage, then invoke directly. [src: webapp-testing]
- Use `sync_playwright()` for synchronous scripts [src: webapp-testing]
- Always close the browser when done [src: webapp-testing]
- Use descriptive selectors: `text=`, `role=`, CSS selectors, or IDs [src: webapp-testing]
- Add appropriate waits: `page.wait_for_selector()` or `page.wait_for_timeout()` [src: webapp-testing]

- Reference for technical, business, and report writing. Deep treatments of every craft concept live in `references/advanced-craft.md` and the per-topic files in the Sub-skill routing table below. Load the matching reference when the user needs depth beyond the core rules in this skill. [src: writing-expert]
- **Output is correct when:** the delivered document (a) opens with the bottom line if BLUF applies, (b) contains zero Tier 1 terms, (c) matches the audience register in the Tone Calibration table, and (d) addresses the user's stated goal without adding unrequested content. Apply the Tier 1 ban list to your own prose as well as to the user's document. [src: writing-expert]
- Activate when the user: [src: writing-expert]
- Asks to write, draft, or improve any prose document (report, summary, email, runbook, architecture doc, proposal, meeting minutes) [src: writing-expert]
- Needs help with document structure, tone, or formatting [src: writing-expert]
- Wants a status report, QBR, account review, executive summary, or post-mortem [src: writing-expert]
- Asks about writing frameworks (BLUF, Pyramid Principle, SCQA, STAR, Minto) [src: writing-expert]
- Wants to eliminate AI-sounding prose or improve human voice [src: writing-expert]
- Needs to calibrate tone for different audiences (executive vs developer vs customer) [src: writing-expert]
- Asks about data storytelling or dashboard-to-prose conversion [src: writing-expert]
- Wants markdown formatting guidance (headings, tables, lists, code blocks) [src: writing-expert]
- Has an ambiguous "make this better" request — triage by asking: audience, document type, and primary goal (clarity / tone / structure) [src: writing-expert]
- Route to a sibling hub instead when the user needs: [src: writing-expert]

- **Executive / business / persuasion** — one-pagers, OKRs, pitch decks, proposals, speeches, public speaking, founder letters, whitepapers, case studies → `executive-comms` [src: writing-expert]
- **Marketing / PR / external comms** — sales copy, press releases, crisis PR, newsletters, op-eds, launch narratives, audio scripts, NPS/support replies → `content-and-marketing-writing` [src: writing-expert]
- **Career / academic / legal / formal** — resumes, cover letters, job descriptions, performance reviews, academic/citation writing, legal-adjacent prose, policy, surveys → `career-and-formal-writing` [src: writing-expert]
- **AI-voice cleanup of an existing draft** → `kill-the-ai-ism` [src: writing-expert]

- This hub consolidates 18 prose-craft sub-skills plus a deep-craft reference as on-demand reference files. When a task matches a row, **Read the listed `references/<name>.md` before deep answers** — do not rely on this table alone for depth. [src: writing-expert]
- **BLUF (Bottom Line Up Front)** — Lead with the conclusion. Put the most important information in the first sentence. Supporting details follow in decreasing importance. [src: writing-expert]
- **One idea per paragraph** — Each paragraph makes exactly one point. The first sentence states it; the rest support it. [src: writing-expert]
- **Active voice by default** — "The team deployed the fix" not "The fix was deployed by the team." Passive voice only when the actor is unknown or irrelevant. [src: writing-expert]
- **Concrete over abstract** — "Latency increased from 50ms to 340ms" not "Performance degraded significantly." [src: writing-expert]
- **No AI-isms** — Apply the full Tier 1 ban list below. Chatbot tics (`certainly`, `I hope this helps`, `Let's dive in`) are Tier 3 tells — delete on sight. [src: writing-expert]
- **Preserve facts** — Never substitute, paraphrase, or fabricate numbers, names, dates, or technical claims from the input. If a claim is unclear, flag it rather than rewrite it. [src: writing-expert]
- **Confirm before rewriting** — Before editing any document over 100 words, ask at most one compound question: "Who is the audience, what's the primary goal (clarity / tone / structure / AI-ism removal), and is there a length target?" — unless all three are already stated. For from-scratch requests (no existing document), ask: topic, audience, and desired length before drafting. [src: writing-expert]
- **Self-check before delivery** — Scan every output for Tier 1 terms and Tier 3 chatbot tics before responding. Remove any found. Confirm the document opens with the bottom line if BLUF applies. Re-read the output against the user's stated goal to confirm it answers what was asked, not a related-but-different question. [src: writing-expert]
- One-sentence bottom line [src: writing-expert]
- Key metrics (3–5 numbers that tell the story) [src: writing-expert]
- What changed since last report (delta-focused) [src: writing-expert]
- Risks / blockers (max 3) [src: writing-expert]
- Recommended actions with owners and dates [src: writing-expert]
- Summary (what happened, duration, impact — 2–3 sentences) [src: writing-expert]
- Timeline (bullet list with timestamps) [src: writing-expert]
- Root cause (specific, technical, no blame) [src: writing-expert]
- Contributing factors [src: writing-expert]
- Remediation actions (with owners, dates, status) [src: writing-expert]
- Lessons learned [src: writing-expert]
- Purpose (one sentence: when to use this) [src: writing-expert]
- Prerequisites (tools, access, permissions) [src: writing-expert]
- Steps (numbered, imperative mood, one action per step) [src: writing-expert]
- Verification (how to confirm each step worked) [src: writing-expert]
- Rollback (how to undo if things go wrong) [src: writing-expert]

- Completed this period (bullet list) [src: writing-expert]

- Blocked / at risk (with mitigation) [src: writing-expert]
- Next period plan [src: writing-expert]

- Proposed solution [src: writing-expert]
- Alternatives considered (with one-line rationale for rejecting each) [src: writing-expert]
- Cost and timeline [src: writing-expert]
- Risks and mitigations [src: writing-expert]
- Recommendation [src: writing-expert]
- Decisions made (numbered) → action items (owner + date) → open questions. Skip discussion recap — only decisions and actions matter. [src: writing-expert]
- For types not above (RCA letters, press releases, cover letters, change announcements), apply the closest template and note the adaptation: "Using Incident Post-Mortem structure for RCA letter — sections 3–5 map directly." [src: writing-expert]
- harness, foster, resonate, ecosystem, journey, empower, unlock, drive (metaphorical), transform, innovative, dynamic, significant [src: writing-expert]
- Em dashes used as sentence separators in prose (target: ≤1 per 500 words for AI-ism detection; the craft rule for polished human prose is ≤1 per 100 words — see Em-dash discipline in the craft section; structural use in headings and table separators is exempt) [src: writing-expert]
- Uniform paragraph/sentence lengths — vary between 1 and 5 sentences [src: writing-expert]
- Formulaic openings ("In the world of...", "When it comes to...", "In an era of...") [src: writing-expert]
- Hedge-stacking ("could potentially", "may eventually", "might arguably") [src: writing-expert]
- Generic conclusions ("In conclusion, X remains a Y") [src: writing-expert]
- Chatbot tics ("I hope this helps!", "Let me know if...", "Certainly!", "Let's dive in!") [src: writing-expert]
- Tier 1 replacements are mandatory in all contexts. Tier 2 and Tier 3 strictness varies: [src: writing-expert]
- Every sentence's subject should carry old (given) information; its predicate should carry new information. Violations make text feel jumpy. [src: writing-expert]
- Bad: "Many companies use containers. Containers are the unit that..." [src: writing-expert]
- Good: "Many companies use containers. These containers package..." [src: writing-expert]
- Apply when: text feels choppy or each sentence opens a new topic. [src: writing-expert]
- A topic sentence at the start signals the point; a buried lede forces the reader to extract it. Default to topic-sentence-first for business and technical writing; buried-lede is acceptable in narrative writing for surprise. [src: writing-expert]
- Bad: 5-sentence paragraph where the actual claim is sentence 5. [src: writing-expert]
- Good: Sentence 1 makes the claim; sentences 2–5 support it. [src: writing-expert]
- Apply when: paragraphs feel like they bury the point. [src: writing-expert]
- A nominalization turns a verb into a noun ("perform a calculation", "make a decision"). Replace with the verb form ("calculate", "decide"). [src: writing-expert]
- Bad: "We made the decision to perform an investigation." [src: writing-expert]
- Good: "We decided to investigate." [src: writing-expert]
- Apply when: scanning verbs and finding "perform", "conduct", "make", "do" + noun. [src: writing-expert]
- Every paragraph should answer "so what?" — explicitly or implicitly. Read each paragraph and ask "so what?"; if there's no answer, cut. [src: writing-expert]
- Bad: "MongoDB uses a document model. Documents live in collections. Collections live in databases." (three facts, no point) [src: writing-expert]
- Good: "MongoDB's document model stores related data together, eliminating the joins that slow relational queries." [src: writing-expert]
- Apply when: a paragraph feels like throat-clearing or filler. [src: writing-expert]
- Acknowledge the opposing view before stating yours. Shows consideration and disarms pushback. [src: writing-expert]
- Bad: "We should use X." (no acknowledgement of objections) [src: writing-expert]
- Good: "Yes, Y has lower latency. But Y costs 3x more, and our SLO is met with X." [src: writing-expert]
- Apply when: writing persuasive prose anticipating disagreement. [src: writing-expert]
- A headline tells the reader the conclusion; a subhead tells them the topic. Use headlines in business writing (claim-first), subheads in reference docs (topic-first). [src: writing-expert]
- Headline: "Renewal at risk: TechCorp's CSAT dropped 30 points in Q3" [src: writing-expert]
- Subhead: "TechCorp renewal status" [src: writing-expert]
- Apply when: writing scannable content. [src: writing-expert]
- For full exec-summary structure see `## Document Type Templates → Executive Summary` above. [src: writing-expert]
- **TL;DR:** ~1 paragraph, top of long documents, the conclusion. [src: writing-expert]
- **Abstract:** ~150–300 words, formal documents, summarizes methods and findings. [src: writing-expert]
- **Executive summary:** ~1 page, business documents, the decision context + ask. [src: writing-expert]
- Pick one; don't stack all three. [src: writing-expert]
- **Inline (parenthetical):** "(Williams, 1990, p. 50)" — APA-style, common in academic writing. [src: writing-expert]
- **Footnotes:** numbered superscripts at the bottom of each page — common in legal/journalism. [src: writing-expert]
- **Endnotes:** numbered superscripts gathered at the end — common in books. [src: writing-expert]
- **Markdown link references:** `[claim][1]` with `[1]: https://...` — common in technical writing. [src: writing-expert]
- Pick one and hold it throughout the document. [src: writing-expert]
- **Hyphen (-):** compound modifiers ("data-driven"), prefixes ("non-trivial"). [src: writing-expert]
- **En-dash (–):** ranges ("pages 5–10"), connections between equals ("New York–London flight"). [src: writing-expert]
- **Em-dash (—):** parenthetical asides — like this — or to set off a strong break. [src: writing-expert]
- AI-written prose over-uses em-dashes. Target ≤1 per 100 words in human prose. [src: writing-expert]
- Three items lands harder than two or four. "Veni, vidi, vici." For business writing: lists of 3 feel complete; lists of 2 feel incomplete; lists of 4+ feel like a dump. [src: writing-expert]
- Apply when: choosing how many examples to include. [src: writing-expert]
- Every bullet should start the same way: all noun phrases, all verb phrases, or all complete sentences. Do not mix. [src: writing-expert]
- Bad: "- Increased CSAT\n- Reduce churn risk\n- The team is happier" [src: writing-expert]
- Good: "- Increased CSAT by 15 points\n- Reduced churn risk by 30%\n- Improved team morale (Q3 survey)" [src: writing-expert]
- Apply when: writing any bulleted list. [src: writing-expert]

- description: "Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. - Atlas Cloud Backup is the default backup mechanism for M10+ dedicated clusters. It uses the **cloud provider's native disk-snapshot capabilities** (AWS EBS / Azure Managed Disks / GCP Persistent Disk), so snapshots are incremental at the block level — fast to take, fast to restore. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Each tier has its own retention period and snapshot time (UTC). The default backup policy uses 18:00 UTC and four active tiers (hourly, daily, weekly, monthly). [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- When two policy items would generate the same snapshot, Atlas associates the snapshot with the policy item with the **longest retention** — you do not pay twice for the same snapshot. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- atlas backups snapshots create \ [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- -clusterName myCluster \ [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- -desc "pre-schema-migration $(date -u +%FT%TZ)" \ [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- -retentionInDays 30 [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Rule of thumb: take an on-demand snapshot **before** any destructive or schema-changing operation, and **wait until it completes** before performing the change. Atlas refuses a second on-demand snapshot while one is `queued` or `inProgress`. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Atlas creates snapshot storage volumes in the **same region as the cluster's current primary**. Maintenance events or cloud-provider events that elect a new primary can move the snapshot storage volume — see Section 9. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- -- [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Continuous Cloud Backup adds **oplog tailing** on top of standard snapshots so you can restore to any second within a configured PIT window — not just to the moments when snapshots were taken. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Atlas takes scheduled snapshots per the cloud-backup policy. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Atlas continuously copies the cluster's oplog into S3 (or the equivalent object store) for the duration of the PIT window. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- On restore, Atlas mounts the most recent snapshot **before** the target time, then replays the oplog forward to the target. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Date & Time** target: 1-minute precision (RPO ≈ 1 minute) [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Oplog Timestamp** target: 1-second precision (use when you need to land just before a specific operation, e.g., right before a destructive `updateMany`) [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- The PIT window is configurable (commonly 24 hours to 7 days). Within the window, you can restore to any moment. Outside the window, you fall back to the nearest snapshot. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- PIT is billed on **oplog storage volume** in addition to snapshot storage: [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Longer PIT window → larger oplog footprint → higher monthly cost [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Write-heavy clusters generate larger oplogs than read-heavy clusters [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Backups list price starts at **$0.14/GB/month** for snapshot storage; oplog storage is billed against the same per-GB rate in the highest-priority region [src: mongodb-backup-restore]

- "https://cloud.mongodb.com/api/atlas/v2/groups/$PROJECT_ID/clusters/$CLUSTER/backup/schedule" \ [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- -data '{ "useOrgAndGroupNamesInExportPrefix": true, [src: mongodb-backup-restore]

- "referenceMinuteOfHour": 0, [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- "restoreWindowDays": 7 }' [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- `restoreWindowDays` is the PIT window in days. Set it to match your RPO target — e.g., RPO = 24 h → `restoreWindowDays: 1`; RPO = 7 days → `restoreWindowDays: 7`. Do not set it to "as long as possible" — every additional day costs real money in oplog storage. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- -- [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Queryable Backups let you **run reads against a backup snapshot without restoring it to a live cluster**. The snapshot is mounted as a read-only deployment that accepts standard MongoDB queries. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Forensics**: when did the bad write happen? Query several snapshots in a row to bisect the corruption window. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Targeted recovery**: pull a single document or collection out of a 2 TB snapshot without provisioning a 2 TB restore cluster. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Audit / compliance**: prove what data existed at a regulatory checkpoint without disturbing production. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Pick the right PIT target**: query consecutive snapshots to find the last clean state before restoring with PIT to that moment. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Read-only — no writes, no index builds, no aggregation `$out`/`$merge`. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Performance is **not** comparable to a live cluster; treat it as cold storage with a query interface. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Available on Atlas (dedicated M10+) and Ops Manager / Cloud Manager. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Open the snapshot in the Atlas UI → Backup → Snapshots → Query [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Atlas spins up a queryable backup deployment (takes 1-5 min) [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Connect via the provided connection string (uses standard mongo URI + temp creds) [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Run reads; the deployment auto-tears-down after idle timeout [src: mongodb-backup-restore]

- A Backup Compliance Policy makes backups **WORM (Write Once Read Many)** at the **organization level** — it applies to every project and cluster in the org. Once enabled, no Atlas user — regardless of role — can shorten retention, disable backups, or delete snapshots before they expire. See Section 11 for the complete deep reference including API, compliance frameworks, and pitfalls. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Minimum retention floors** for each policy tier (hourly/daily/weekly/monthly/yearly). [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **PIT window minimum** — operators cannot shrink it. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Snapshot copy protection** — copies cannot be deleted before retention expires. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Encryption at Rest with Customer Key Management** can be required; non-encrypted clusters fail compliance. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Once enabled, the policy can only be disabled by a **designated security contact** completing an out-of-band email verification with MongoDB Support (typically 3–5 business days processing time). This is intentional: an attacker who steals an Atlas admin credential cannot quickly turn off backups before exfiltrating data. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Atlas encrypts all snapshot blocks with **AES-256** in the cloud provider's object store (S3 / Azure Blob / GCS). If you enable Customer Key Management, snapshots are wrapped with your KMS-held CMK on top of the provider key, giving you the ability to revoke decryption by revoking the key. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]

- By default, Atlas stores snapshots in the **same region as the current primary**. For DR, copy them to one or more secondary regions. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Each snapshot copy policy item attaches to one of the five frequency tiers and names a target region. Atlas copies snapshots **asynchronously** after the primary snapshot completes — typical copy lag is **15-60 minutes**. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- You can copy specific snapshots (e.g., only weekly + monthly + yearly to a cheap DR region) rather than every snapshot in a tier. This reduces cross-region data transfer cost. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- If you set Point-in-Time Restore = On for a snapshot copy policy item, Atlas also copies **oplog segments** to that region. After a primary-region outage, you can restore PIT directly from the DR region. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- If snapshots are copied to **every region** in a multi-region cluster, Atlas can do a **direct-attach restore** (fast, no streaming). [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Otherwise Atlas does a **streaming restore** across regions — measurably slower (often 2-3x), and bandwidth-billed. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]

- The runbook **is** the disaster recovery plan. If it lives only in an engineer's head, you do not have a plan. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]

- There is a documented interaction between long-running snapshot operations and replica-set events that can make snapshots **appear** to block primary promotion. The symptom: a primary step-down or maintenance window is queued behind an in-flight snapshot or snapshot-copy operation, and the cluster appears stuck. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Atlas creates snapshot storage volumes in the **same region as the current primary**. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Events that move the primary (maintenance, cloud-provider event, manual `replSetStepDown`) can require Atlas to move or re-create the snapshot storage volume. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- An in-flight snapshot or snapshot copy cannot be cleanly migrated mid-flight; Atlas waits for completion before the election logic finishes the handoff. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- The user-visible effect: "we tried to step down to do a maintenance window, but it's been pending for 40 minutes." The cluster is healthy; the snapshot pipeline is the long pole. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Before planned maintenance** (version upgrade, instance resize, region change): check `atlas backups snapshots list --status inProgress` and **wait for completion** before triggering the change. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Before a major version upgrade**: take an on-demand snapshot and wait for it to finish before launching the upgrade — the docs explicitly call this out. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **If you see a stuck step-down**: do not force-kill it. Check Atlas Activity Feed for an in-flight snapshot or cross-region copy; let it finish. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **For repeat customers with this symptom**: schedule maintenance windows **outside** the snapshot frequency tier that runs most often (e.g., if hourly snapshots run at :00, schedule maintenance at :30). [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- atlas backups snapshots list --clusterName myCluster \ [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- -status inProgress,queued [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Anything returned here will gate primary-mutating operations. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- The TS Tools case file shows this exact pattern: customer perceived "snapshots blocking primary promotion" during a maintenance window. Resolution was operational (sequence the maintenance after snapshot completion), not a code defect. Document this in the customer's runbook so the next on-call engineer doesn't escalate. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]

- Backups answer "restore data **to a point in time**". When the operator actually needs to **move data between two live clusters** — Atlas Live Migration, cluster-to-cluster sync, or any cutover with sub-minute downtime — the right tool is `mongosync`, not mongodump/mongorestore or `$out`. Load the `mongosync` skill when the task involves continuous CDC between two MongoDB clusters, `includeNamespaces`/`excludeNamespaces` filtering, the IDLE/RUNNING/PAUSED/COMMITTING/COMMITTED state machine, reverse sync for rollback, or oplog window sizing to avoid `ChangeStreamHistoryLost`. This skill (`mongodb-backup-restore`) stays focused on snapshot, PIT recovery, queryable backup, and dump/restore tooling. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- -- [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- A Backup Compliance Policy (BCP) is an **irrevocable, org-level governance control** that enforces minimum backup retention floors, prevents snapshot deletion, and applies WORM (Write Once Read Many) semantics to all backup data under its scope. Unlike a per-project backup policy (which any Project Owner can modify), BCP is set at the **Organization level** and, once activated, cannot be modified or disabled by any Atlas user — including Org Owners — without explicit intervention from **MongoDB Atlas Support**. This is by design: an attacker or rogue admin who compromises Atlas credentials cannot deactivate backup protection before exfiltrating or destroying data. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- BCP is Atlas's answer to regulated workload requirements (HIPAA, PCI DSS, SOC 2, GDPR) that demand tamper-evident, immutable retention — not just a policy that exists on paper but one that is enforced at the control-plane level. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- -- [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Required role:** Organization Owner. Project-level roles are insufficient; the toggle lives in the org-level settings panel, not in a project. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Location in Atlas UI:** [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Organization → Settings → Backup Compliance Policy [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Or navigate directly to: `cloud.mongodb.com/v2#/org/{orgId}/settings/backupCompliance` [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Configuration parameters:** [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Org Owner configures the BCP parameters. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Atlas sends a **confirmation email** to the Org Owner's registered email address. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- The Org Owner must click the confirmation link within the TTL window. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- BCP becomes active. From this point on, the settings are locked at the control-plane level. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- This two-step email confirmation exists so that BCP cannot be silently enabled by a compromised session cookie — the actual mailbox must be accessible. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- -- [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Once active, BCP prevents the following operations at every project under the org: [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Snapshot deletion:** [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Users cannot manually delete any snapshot whose age is less than the BCP minimum retention floor. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- The "Delete" button is grayed out / returns a 409 for in-compliance snapshots. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Snapshots that already exceeded their retention window expire normally — BCP does not make every snapshot immortal, only enforces the floor. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Backup policy modification:** [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- No project can reduce its snapshot retention schedule below the BCP minimums. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Attempts to `PATCH /backup/schedule` with shorter retention return a 403 referencing the compliance policy. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Projects **can** increase retention above the BCP floor (more protection is allowed; less is not). [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Backup cannot be turned off for any cluster while BCP is active on the org. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- The "Pause/Disable Backup" option is hidden in the UI and blocked in the API. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Cluster **deletion** is also affected — see pitfall section below. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **PIT window reduction:** [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- The `restoreWindowDays` cannot be set below the BCP minimum PIT window. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Hourly snapshots required by BCP cannot be removed from the policy schedule. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Encryption at Rest / EaR (if required by BCP):** [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Clusters without Encryption at Rest (EaR) with Customer Key Management configured fail a compliance check surfaced in the Atlas UI's Backup Compliance Status view. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Atlas does not automatically enable EaR — the cluster is flagged; the operator must remediate. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- -- [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- BCP can require a **minimum PIT window**, which means: [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Every cluster under the org must have Continuous Cloud Backup enabled. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- The configured `restoreWindowDays` must be ≥ the BCP minimum (e.g., 7 days). [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Reducing `restoreWindowDays` below the BCP minimum via API returns an error. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **How to read PITR status in the Atlas UI:** [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Navigate to Cluster → Backup → Backup Policy. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- The "Continuous Cloud Backup" toggle shows "On" with the configured window in days. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- A BCP badge appears next to the retention controls that are locked by the policy. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **How to read PITR status via API:** [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- curl --user "$PUB_KEY:$PRIV_KEY" --digest \ [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- "https://cloud.mongodb.com/api/atlas/v2/groups/$PROJECT_ID/clusters/$CLUSTER/backup/schedule" [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- The response includes `"restoreWindowDays"` and a `"copySettings"` array. If BCP is active, a `GET /groups/{groupId}/backupCompliancePolicy` call returns the org-level minimums that gate all modifications. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- -- [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Retrieve current compliance policy:** [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- GET /api/atlas/v2/groups/{groupId}/backupCompliancePolicy [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- "authorizedEmail": "security@example.com", [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- "copyProtectionEnabled": true, [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- "encryptionAtRestEnabled": true, [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- "onDemandPolicyItem": { [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- "frequencyType": "ondemand", [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- "retentionUnit": "days", [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- "projectId": "<projectId>", [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- "restoreWindowDays": 7, [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- "scheduledPolicyItems": [ [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- { "frequencyType": "hourly",  "retentionUnit": "hours",  "retentionValue": 12, "frequencyInterval": 6 }, [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- { "frequencyType": "daily",   "retentionUnit": "days",   "retentionValue": 7  }, [src: mongodb-backup-restore]

- **Update compliance policy (restricted — BCP blocks *loosening* of existing locks):** [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- PATCH /api/atlas/v2/groups/{groupId}/backupCompliancePolicy [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- > Note: PATCH can only **increase** retention values or **add** new constraints (making the policy stricter). Any attempt to reduce a retention parameter below the currently-active BCP minimum is rejected with a 409. To loosen any constraint, a MongoDB Support ticket is required. After initial activation, the `authorizedEmail` field identifies the designated security contact for Support-side modifications. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Required permission for API calls:** `Project Backup Manager` or higher on the target project. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Atlas CLI equivalent:** [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- atlas backups compliancePolicy enable \ [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- -authorizedUserEmail security@example.com \ [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- -authorizedUserFirstName Security \ [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- -authorizedUserLastName Lead \ [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- -projectId $PROJECT_ID [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- atlas backups compliancePolicy describe --projectId $PROJECT_ID [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- -- [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Once activated, BCP can only be relaxed through an Atlas Support ticket. No self-service path exists — this is a compliance guarantee, not a UX oversight. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Open a P2 or P3 support ticket via `support.mongodb.com` with subject line indicating "Backup Compliance Policy modification request." [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- In the ticket body include: [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Organization ID (`orgId`) [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Current BCP configuration (GET response above) [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Desired new configuration with specific parameters to change [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Business justification (auditors / legal may review this) [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Verification that the requester is the current Org Owner or authorized security contact [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- MongoDB Support verifies the identity of the requestor against the `authorizedEmail` on the BCP record via out-of-band communication (phone call or secondary email confirmation). [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Support modifies the compliance policy in the control plane on behalf of the org. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **SLA:** BCP modification requests are not treated as break/fix incidents. Typical processing time is **3–5 business days** under standard SLA; P1 escalations may be faster but require documented emergency justification. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **What cannot be changed retroactively:** [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Snapshots that were retained under the old BCP minimum **cannot** be deleted even after BCP is relaxed to a shorter retention. Those snapshots must age out naturally per their original policy item retention. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- If BCP required EaR and a cluster was flagged non-compliant, the compliance flag persists until EaR is actually enabled — removing the BCP requirement does not retroactively clear flags. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- -- [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Atlas Backup Compliance Status view:** [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Organization → Backup Compliance → Compliance Status shows a per-project compliance posture dashboard. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Green (compliant): every cluster meets the BCP minimums. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Yellow (warning): a cluster was created before BCP was enabled and has not yet been brought into compliance. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Red (non-compliant): a cluster violates a hard BCP requirement (e.g., EaR disabled when BCP requires it). [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- -- [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Enabling BCP without testing the restore process first.** [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- BCP prevents you from cleaning up failed or partial test restores whose snapshots fall within the retention window. If your quarterly restore test creates a 2 TB cluster that you want to delete after testing, you cannot delete the cluster's snapshots before they age out. Always test restores in a **separate Atlas project** that you do not intend to place under BCP, then enable BCP on your production org after the restore process is validated. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Setting the retention window too short, then needing Support to extend it.** [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Many customers under-set the minimum (e.g., 7-day daily retention) thinking they can always extend later, only to discover a compliance audit requires 30-day minimum. "Extending" via Support is straightforward — but requires the same 3–5 business day SLA. Set retention to the regulatory requirement at activation, not the operational default. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Not excluding dev/test clusters from BCP scope.** [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- BCP applies at the org level — every cluster in every project under the org is subject to it. Ephemeral development clusters accumulate snapshots they cannot delete, burning backup storage costs. Pattern: use a **separate Atlas org** for dev/test with no BCP; use the production org (with BCP) only for production and staging. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **BCP preventing rapid cluster deletion for cost savings.** [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- A cluster with BCP-protected snapshots **cannot be terminated immediately**. Terminating the cluster stops new snapshots but the cluster's backup data is retained for the full BCP retention window. The cluster appears as "Terminated" but backup storage continues to accrue costs until all protected snapshots expire. Factor BCP snapshot retention costs into total cluster ownership cost. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Confusing "org-level BCP" with "project-level backup policy."** [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Project-level backup policies set the frequency and retention for snapshots — these are editable by Project Owners unless constrained by BCP. BCP is the org-level floor that constrains every project's policy. Many operators enable a project-level policy and assume that equals BCP protection. It does not; a malicious or mistaken Project Owner can still reduce or disable a project-level policy. Only org-level BCP is tamper-resistant. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- **Assuming BCP covers snapshot copies in DR regions.** [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- If you have cross-region snapshot copies enabled, BCP's `copyProtectionEnabled: true` flag extends WORM protection to the copies. If `copyProtectionEnabled` is `false` (the default for existing BCP configurations pre-2024), snapshot copies in DR regions **can still be deleted**. Verify `copyProtectionEnabled` is `true` in your BCP configuration if you rely on DR copies for compliance. [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- -- [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Do not enable BCP if any of the following are true — resolve the condition first or accept the permanent consequence: [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- Use this checklist before enabling BCP on a production org: [src: mongodb-backup-restore]
- <!-- Provenance: reference under the `mongodb-operations-expert` hub. Mirrored from ~/.claude/skills/mongodb-operations-expert/references/mongodb-upgrade-paths.md by scripts/persist-spoke.mjs. --> [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Operational reference for MongoDB major-version upgrades on self-managed deployments. Covers the supported version sequence, Feature Compatibility Version (FCV) lifecycle, rolling replica-set and sharded-cluster procedures, driver matrices, pre-/post-upgrade verification, and the common failure modes that show up in real customer upgrades. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Active customer context (2026): **Goldman Sachs "Cookie" 7.0 → 8.0** and **Straight-to-8 self-managed** initiatives. Both rely on every section below being correct. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Planning, scoping, or sequencing any MongoDB major-version upgrade (especially 7.0 → 8.0 or multi-hop from 4.4 / 5.0 / 6.0). [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Drafting or reviewing an upgrade runbook, change ticket, or maintenance-window plan. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Designing the FCV pin / unpin schedule and the binary-downgrade rollback window. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Diagnosing an upgrade-related incident (driver mismatch, FCV refusal, mongos skew, cold-cache regression, PSA stepdown failure). [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Coaching a customer DBA team through their first 8.0 rollout. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Producing post-event sign-off artefacts (Error Envelope, metric snapshots, customer sign-off). [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Atlas-managed upgrades driven entirely through the Atlas UI — point at `mongodb-atlas-expert` references/mongodb-atlas-managed-upgrades.md instead (this skill covers Atlas-specific FCV pin behaviour but not the auto-upgrade cadence, maintenance windows, or 7.0->8.0 Atlas-only gotchas covered there). [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Patch-revision upgrades within a major (e.g., 8.0.3 → 8.0.10) when no FCV change is needed — the procedure is the same rolling pattern minus FCV, and is documented inline only as a reference. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Driver-internal questions unrelated to server upgrades — point at the driver-specific skill (`mongodb-drivers-k8s`, etc.). [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Schema migration or aggregation changes — use `mongodb-migration-patterns` or `mongodb-aggregation-pipeline`. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Backup / restore design — use `mongodb-backup-restore`. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]

[src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- `mongodb-atlas-expert` — Atlas UI flows, Atlas-managed FCV pin window, Atlas-only safety rails. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
