- -- [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- MongoDB enforces **strictly sequential major-version upgrades**. You cannot skip a major release on a single cluster. The supported sequence today is: [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- 4  →  5.0  →  6.0  →  7.0  →  8.0 [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Each arrow above is one full upgrade cycle: bump binaries → wait for cluster to stabilize → set FCV → only then start the next hop. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- To upgrade to **8.0**, every member must already be on a **7.0** binary with `featureCompatibilityVersion: "7.0"`. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- To upgrade to **7.0**, every member must be on **6.0** with FCV `"6.0"`. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- The same chain holds for 5.0 ← 4.4. You cannot jump 5.0 → 7.0 or 6.0 → 8.0. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Patch-level (revision) upgrades within a major (e.g., `8.0.3 → 8.0.10`) are unrestricted and use the same rolling pattern but never require FCV changes. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- "Straight-to-8" is a customer-facing label for **rapid sequential** upgrades on the same cluster, not a literal skip. The pattern compresses the 4.4 → 8.0 ladder into a small number of well-rehearsed maintenance windows by: [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Doing back-to-back **binary-only** upgrades through 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 with the **FCV held at the source version** for each hop (so each hop remains downgrade-eligible until validation). [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Validating workload + drivers between hops, but **deferring `setFeatureCompatibilityVersion`** until the cluster is sitting on the 8.0 binary set with all health and driver tests passing. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Pinning FCV to `"7.0"` before the 7.0 → 8.0 hop so you retain a full 4-week binary-downgrade window from 8.0 back to 7.0 if 8.0 misbehaves under production load. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Straight-to-8 is **not** a documented MongoDB product feature — it is an operational rollout pattern. The supported upgrade matrix is unchanged: 4.4 → 5.0 → 6.0 → 7.0 → 8.0. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- db.version();                                            // binary [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- db.adminCommand({ getParameter: 1, featureCompatibilityVersion: 1 });  // FCV [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- If FCV lags binary by more than one major version (e.g., binary 7.0 with FCV `"5.0"`), **stop**. You must walk FCV forward one hop at a time before any further binary change. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- -- [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- FCV is the gate between **binary upgrade** and **feature activation**. It exists so customers can roll new binaries first, verify stability, then opt into the new on-disk and protocol features once they are confident no downgrade is needed. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- FCV is **separate from binary version**. `db.version()` returns the binary; `featureCompatibilityVersion` is its own admin parameter. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- After upgrading every node's binary to N, the FCV remains `"N-1"` until you explicitly run `setFeatureCompatibilityVersion`. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- New backwards-incompatible features (queryable encryption range queries, new index types, resharding of time-series in 8.0.10+, etc.) **stay disabled** while FCV is on the older value. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- `setFeatureCompatibilityVersion` requires `confirm: true` starting in 7.0 and remains required in 8.0: [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- db.adminCommand({ setFeatureCompatibilityVersion: "8.0", confirm: true }); [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Downgrade requires the inverse: FCV must be moved back **first**, then binaries. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Once binaries are at N and FCV is still `"N-1"`, you can **binary-downgrade** to N-1 safely. This is the "preservation window". [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Self-managed**: the preservation window is open as long as you keep FCV pinned and no backward-incompatible features have been used. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Atlas-managed**: FCV pinning is bounded to a **4-week window** from the pin date. Atlas auto-unpins on the next maintenance window after expiry; once unpinned, FCV is auto-upgraded to match the binary and the rollback path closes (this is the Atlas "Point of No Return"). [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Self-managed customers should mirror the 4-week discipline as a policy even though no automation enforces it — long-pinned FCV blocks feature adoption and leaves the cluster perpetually "half-upgraded." [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- After binary upgrade, run **without** advancing FCV for a deliberate burn-in (1–4 weeks is typical). Only set FCV to the new value when: [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Driver upgrades have been deployed and steady-state for 7+ days. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- No production incidents traced to the new binary. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Backup verification on the new binaries succeeded. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- The application owner has explicitly signed off on irreversibility. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- -- [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- The rolling upgrade contract: at any moment, the replica set retains a writable primary and a majority of voters. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Secondaries**, one at a time. Shut down `mongod`, swap the binary, restart. Wait for the node to return to `SECONDARY` (it may transit `STARTUP2` or `RECOVERING` first — this is normal). **Do not** start the next node until `rs.status()` shows the current one back in `SECONDARY`. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Arbiters** (if any). Arbiters are stateless and have priority 0 by default. Upgrade them at any point after the secondaries but before the primary. Treat them like a tiny secondary: stop, swap, start, confirm `ARBITER` state. **Do not** make the arbiter the last node — its election votes matter when the primary steps down. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Primary, last.** Connect `mongosh` to the primary and run: [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- rs.stepDown();   // default freeze: 60s on 6.0+, 120s on older versions [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Stepping down is preferable to a hard shutdown because it triggers a clean election. Then upgrade the now-secondary former primary. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Median election time with default settings is **~10–12 seconds**. Plan for a brief write outage when the primary steps down. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Election priority is configurable per node via `members[n].priority`. Setting your preferred upgrade-last node to high priority before stepDown gives you a predictable post-upgrade primary. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- `electionTimeoutMillis` (default 10s) controls how long secondaries wait before calling an election. Some customers lower this in pre-upgrade maintenance windows to **5000ms** to compress outage, then revert post-upgrade. Document and review with the customer — it changes failover semantics in production. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Arbiters cannot become primary and hold no data, so they do **not** require FCV considerations on upgrade. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Three-node replica sets with one arbiter (PSA topology) are the most fragile during rolling upgrades because losing the data secondary while the primary is stepping down leaves no eligible primary. Recommend customers move arbiters off PSA topologies before any major upgrade. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- -- [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Sharded clusters have three component classes — config servers, shards, mongos — and the upgrade ordering is **strict**. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Pre-step 0 — Disable the balancer** before any binary change: [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- sh.isBalancerRunning();   // confirm "false" [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Then walk the tiers in this strict order: [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Config server replica set** (CSRS). Apply the rolling replica-set procedure (Section 3) to the config servers. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Shards** next. For each shard (replica set), repeat the rolling procedure. Upgrade least-critical shards first if possible — most v8 sharded upgrade incidents originate in the shard phase, and walking from least to most critical limits blast radius. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **`mongos`** routers last. mongos is stateless, so you can drain connections and restart them in parallel groups. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Post-step — Re-enable balancer**, then **set FCV** only after all three tiers are upgraded and stable: [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- db.adminCommand({ setFeatureCompatibilityVersion: "8.0", confirm: true }); [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- A `mongos` running version M can **only** talk to mongods with FCV ≤ M. Concretely: a 7.0 mongos cannot connect to a sharded cluster whose FCV has been advanced to `"8.0"`. It **can** connect to an 8.0 cluster that is still pinned at FCV `"7.0"`. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Mixed-version mongos pools are tolerated **during** the upgrade window but should not be left in production beyond the maintenance event. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Config servers must be on the same or newer version as the shards. Never let a shard run a newer binary than its config server. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- If your cluster uses the **config shard** topology (config server doubling as a data shard, introduced in 7.0), you must run `transitionToDedicatedConfigServer` before downgrading FCV below 8.0. There is no equivalent path forward — this is a downgrade-only gate. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- -- [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- A driver mismatch is the most common day-1 production incident after a server upgrade. The driver must support the target server version **before** binaries change. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- `retryWrites=true` is **default** on 4.2+ drivers; do not disable it for upgrade convenience. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- `retryReads=true` is default on 4.0+ drivers. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- During a primary stepdown, an in-flight write with `retryWrites=true` is automatically retried against the new primary once the driver's server selection timeout (default 30s) discovers the new topology. This is why a clean `rs.stepDown()` is preferable to `kill -9` — kill-9 invalidates connection state in ways that break some retry paths. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- For **5.x Java drivers**, `MongoClientSettings` exposes finer-grained `serverApi` and `serverSelectionTimeout`. Default is fine for upgrades. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Node.js**: driver 6.x supports MongoDB 8.0. Driver 5.x maxes at 7.0. Always confirm against `mongodb` package `peerDependencies` vs the connected server. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Python (PyMongo)**: 4.7+ for 7.0, **4.9+** for 8.0. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **C# / .NET**: 2.28+ for 7.0, **3.0+** for 8.0. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Go**: 1.13+ for 7.0, **1.17+** for 8.0. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- The canonical matrix lives at `https://www.mongodb.com/docs/drivers/` — verify there for the exact patch level before any production upgrade. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- -- [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Run these checks before touching binaries. Missing any one of them is how upgrades fail in the middle of the maintenance window. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **All nodes on the prerequisite version**, FCV matches: [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- db.adminCommand({ getParameter: 1, featureCompatibilityVersion: 1 }); [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **No in-flight index builds**: [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- db.currentOp({ "command.createIndexes": { $exists: true } }); [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- db.currentOp({ msg: /Index Build/ }); [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- An interrupted index build leaves the collection in `unfinished` state. Either let the build complete or `dropIndex` and restart it after the upgrade. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Change-stream consumers are resumable**: confirm every consumer is storing `_id` (resume token) durably so it can resume past the maintenance window. If oplog rolls beyond the last-seen token during upgrade, the consumer must do a full reseed — surface this risk to the customer in writing. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Oplog window** comfortably exceeds expected maintenance duration: [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- rs.printReplicationInfo();   // shows oplog length [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Aim for **≥ 4× the expected maintenance window** (e.g., 4-hour oplog for a 1-hour upgrade). If short, raise oplog size before upgrade with `replSetResizeOplog`. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Backup verified, not just taken**. Restore the latest snapshot into a scratch cluster and run a smoke query. Untested backups are not backups. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Driver compatibility deployed**. Drivers should be on the target-server-compatible version for at least 7 days before the upgrade. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Replica lag < 5 seconds** on every secondary: [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- rs.printSecondaryReplicationInfo(); [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Disk free space**: at minimum 25% headroom. WiredTiger needs room for the new on-disk format files even when FCV is held. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Compatibility scan**: review the target version's "Compatibility Changes" doc and grep the application for any removed/deprecated command names (e.g., `$listLocalSessions` semantics, `geoNear` aggregation pipeline equivalents). [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Starting in **MongoDB 8.0**, the **commit quorum** specifies how many nodes must be **ready to finish** the index build before the primary commits, while the **write concern** specifies how many nodes must **replicate the commit oplog entry** before the command returns success. This is a semantic change vs. 7.0 and earlier. If your application sets `commitQuorum` explicitly, audit those calls. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Default `commitQuorum` is `votingMembers` (all voting data-bearing members). Lowering it (e.g., `majority`) can prevent index builds from stalling on a lagging secondary during the upgrade window. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- -- [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- The rollback path depends entirely on **whether FCV was pinned before the upgrade**. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- `setFeatureCompatibilityVersion` with the new version **is** the Point of No Return for the rollback window. Once executed and confirmed, the FCV gate closes: [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- On **Atlas**, the 4-week pin window starts at FCV pin time. After expiry, Atlas auto-advances FCV at the next maintenance window — explicit and visible in the Atlas UI. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- On **self-managed**, there is no automation. Operator discipline is the only enforcement. Add the burn-in calendar reminder to your runbook. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Detect regression (latency, error rate, missing feature support in application). [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Confirm FCV state. If FCV is still `"N-1"`: [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Apply rolling **binary downgrade** in reverse order: primary last for replica sets; mongos → shards → config servers for sharded clusters. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- If FCV has been advanced: [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Audit for use of new-version-only features. Atlas indexes that depend on new operators, new index types, sharded time-series with reshardCollection, etc. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- If clean, run `setFeatureCompatibilityVersion: "N-1", confirm: true`. If features are in use, open a Premium Support case before touching anything. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Document the rollback as a near-miss event regardless of whether downgrade succeeded. The data is the most valuable input for the next upgrade. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- -- [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Status**: known operational gap, manual SOP, **not** documented in upstream MongoDB upgrade procedures. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Goldman Sachs "Cookie" cluster upgrades from 7.0 → 8.0 exposed a recurring symptom: secondaries that come back online after the binary swap return to `SECONDARY` state quickly, but their **WiredTiger block cache is cold**. When the load balancer (or a stepDown on the primary) shifts read traffic onto a freshly upgraded secondary, query latency spikes 10–100× until the cache rewarms. For latency-sensitive workloads (Cookie's read SLA is sub-10ms p99), this looks like a production incident. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- The WiredTiger cache is in-process memory; it always starts empty after `mongod` restart and warms naturally with traffic. Standard MongoDB guidance is "let it warm". For most workloads that is fine. For low-latency, predictable-workload customers it is **not** fine — the natural warm-up takes minutes and the latency degradation is customer-visible. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- This is the pattern Goldman Sachs operators developed. There is no automated tool from MongoDB. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- After binary swap and `SECONDARY` state, **hold the node out of routing** (e.g., `hidden: true, priority: 0`, or remove from driver readPreference rotation). [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Run a **scripted touch query workload** that mimics the production read pattern — typically a parallel sweep over the most-frequently-accessed indexes (covered queries against the hot collections), constrained to a small key range so the OS cache and WT cache fill in a controlled order. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Monitor cache pressure with: [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- db.serverStatus().wiredTiger.cache; [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Watch `bytes currently in the cache` and `pages read into cache` — when growth flattens, warm-up is complete. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Reset `hidden: false` (or re-add to routing rotation) only after the cache fills to ~70% of `cacheSizeGB` and p99 latency from the touch workload matches pre-upgrade baseline. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- This SOP is a documentation and tooling gap. The TAM team should propose: [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- A documented "pre-warming after rolling upgrade" appendix in the upgrade tutorial. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- A built-in `cacheWarmup` admin command that walks the hot indexes for the calling user — opt-in, time-boxed, and observable via `currentOp`. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Until then, the manual SOP above is the supported pattern for latency-critical customers. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- -- [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- An upgrade is a **scheduled maintenance event**, not a deploy. TAM-owned upgrades follow a three-phase template with explicit sign-offs. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Driver compatibility verified and deployed (Section 5). [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- All pre-upgrade checks (Section 6) green and documented. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Backup tested via restore (not just taken). [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Customer change ticket approved with explicit start/end timestamps. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Rollback decision matrix (Section 7) attached to the change ticket. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- On-call rotation: TAM + MongoDB Premium Support + customer DBA, contact tree pre-shared. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Communication template ready: customer status page, internal Slack channel, exec summary email. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Single change owner (DRI) running the runbook step-by-step. Every step gets a timestamped status post in the shared channel. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Health gates between each component group (after every secondary, after primary, after each shard, after mongos pool). [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Error Envelope** logged in real time. Every non-fatal warning gets: [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Timestamp [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Component (mongod hostname, mongos node, driver, etc.) [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Error text verbatim [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Decision: continue / pause / rollback [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Sign-off by DRI [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- If the Error Envelope accumulates more than one **unexplained** entry, the default decision is **pause**, not push through. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Application smoke tests (read, write, change-stream, aggregation, index builds). [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Driver-level smoke tests — each app team confirms they can connect, read, write, listen. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Metrics baseline restored: p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, replication lag, oplog window. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Burn-in monitoring window opens (1–4 weeks before FCV advance). [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Customer sign-off captured in writing, attached to the change ticket. Without sign-off the event is **not** closed even if the binaries are upgraded. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Post-event review within 5 business days: what worked, what surprised us, what changes the runbook for the next upgrade. Append to the customer's `customer-files/.../upgrade-history.md`. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- A complete upgrade event produces: [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- The change ticket with start/end timestamps and DRI. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- The runbook as executed (mark each step with timestamp + initials). [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- The Error Envelope log. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Pre- and post-event metric snapshots (latency, lag, oplog). [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Customer sign-off (email or ticket reply). [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Post-event review document. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Anything less and the event is not auditable. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- -- [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- The recurring failure modes, ranked by frequency from real customer post-mortems: [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Symptom**: application throws connection errors immediately after the primary steps down, or after the cluster is fully on the new binary. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Root cause**: driver was not updated to a server-compatible version before the upgrade. Common in environments where multiple application teams share a database — one team upgrades, ten others discover they can't connect. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Driver upgrade as a **mandatory** pre-step, completed 7+ days before binary upgrade. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Connection-string validation across all app teams. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Audit `currentOp().clientMetadata.driver.version` on the cluster before upgrade to enumerate every driver version in production. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Symptom**: customer wants to roll back after the upgrade because of unrelated production incident; rollback path is closed. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Root cause**: operator (or Atlas auto-unpin) advanced FCV before the burn-in window completed. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Burn-in window written into the runbook with explicit calendar dates. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Atlas customers: track FCV pin expiration in the customer's GS docs. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Self-managed: review FCV state at every weekly cadence call until burn-in expires; do not advance silently. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Symptom**: secondary returns to `RECOVERING` and never reaches `SECONDARY`, or `replSetReconfig` rejects the new member set because of inconsistent indexes. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Root cause**: an in-flight index build was interrupted by the binary swap, leaving the collection in an inconsistent state across members. Or, the new version changed default index behavior (e.g., 4.2 → 4.4 wildcard index, 7.0 → 8.0 commit-quorum semantics). [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Pre-upgrade check: no `currentOp` matching index build (Section 6). [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Post-upgrade: scan each member for inconsistent indexes: [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- db.runCommand({ listIndexes: "<coll>" }); [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Compare across primary and secondaries. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Use the official MongoDB **Shard Index Inconsistent Script** for sharded clusters. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Symptom**: queries fail intermittently with `IncompatibleServerVersion` or routing errors after partial upgrade. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Root cause**: mongos pool contains a mix of N-1 and N binaries while FCV has been advanced to N, or shards on mixed versions. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Strict component-order discipline (Section 4): config → shards → mongos → FCV. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Health gate after the **last** mongos restart, before any FCV change. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Verify all mongos versions match: [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- db.adminCommand({ listShards: 1 });  // run on each mongos [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Symptom**: during the upgrade of the data secondary in a Primary-Secondary-Arbiter (PSA) topology, the primary steps down and cannot find a majority for a new election. Cluster is read-only. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Root cause**: PSA only has two data-bearing voters. While the secondary is offline for upgrade, the primary alone cannot achieve majority for any write that requires `w: majority`, and the arbiter cannot help. If the primary then steps down, the cluster has no eligible primary until the secondary returns. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Pre-upgrade: convert PSA to PSS (three data-bearing voters) before the major upgrade. This is the single most impactful PSA recommendation TAMs can make. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- If conversion is impossible, do **not** combine the secondary upgrade with the primary upgrade in the same window — leave 24+ hours between them. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Symptom**: secondary returns from upgrade and immediately enters full initial sync because its lag exceeded the oplog window. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Root cause**: maintenance ran longer than expected; oplog size was sized for steady-state replication lag, not for a multi-hour maintenance window. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Section 6 oplog window check. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Resize oplog **upward** as a pre-upgrade step: [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- db.adminCommand({ replSetResizeOplog: 1, size: 102400 });   // 100 GB [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- Restore oplog size post-burn-in if disk pressure requires it. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Symptom**: post-upgrade p99 read latency spikes for minutes after each rolling upgrade step. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Root cause**: WiredTiger cache reset on `mongod` restart; default warm-up is uncontrolled. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- **Mitigation**: pre-warming SOP from Section 8. Document gap; advocate for upstream tooling. [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]
- -- [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]

- db.adminCommand({ replSetResizeOplog: 1, size: 102400 }); [src: mongodb-upgrade-paths]

- Stages execute left-to-right; each stage receives the document stream from the previous [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- stage. Order matters enormously for performance (see Section 4). [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]

- -- [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- MongoDB performs a hash-lookup on the foreign collection for each input document. [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- **Always index the `foreignField`** — without an index MongoDB scans the entire [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- foreign collection per input document (an O(N×M) table scan). [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- One important footgun: if the `as` field name already exists on the input document, [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- **it is silently overwritten**. Choose an `as` name that does not collide. [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- // Join orders → customers on orders.customerId = customers._id [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- db.orders.aggregate([ [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- localField: "customerId", [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- as: "customer"          // ⚠ silently overwrites if "customer" already exists [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- // $lookup always returns an array; unwrap for 1-to-1 cardinality [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- { $unwind: { path: "$customer", preserveNullAndEmptyArrays: true } } [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- Required index on the foreign side: [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- db.customers.createIndex({ _id: 1 })   // _id index already exists [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- db.customers.createIndex({ email: 1 }) // create explicitly for any other join field [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- Use when you need filtering beyond a simple equality, or when joining on multiple fields. [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- `let` binds local document variables; reference them inside the sub-pipeline with `$$varName`. [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- db.orders.aggregate([ [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- let: { orderSku: "$sku", orderQty: "$quantity" }, [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- // Both $match conditions can use the bound variables via $expr [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- { $eq: ["$sku", "$$orderSku"] }, [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- { $gte: ["$stock", "$$orderQty"] } [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- { $project: { name: 1, price: 1, _id: 0 } } [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- Index every `foreignField` (or the first field in the sub-pipeline `$match`). [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- Place `$match` **inside** the sub-pipeline to push filtering before the join materialises. [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- Avoid interleaving `$unwind` → `$lookup` → `$unwind`; chain all lookups, then unwind. [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- On sharded clusters, joining a **sharded** foreign collection is supported (MongoDB 5.1+), [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- but each input document fans out to every shard holding the foreign collection [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- (scatter-gather). Co-locate the collections on the same shard key, or use Atlas Data [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- Federation, to avoid the fan-out. [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]

- `$out` atomically replaces the target collection after the full pipeline completes. [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- Use for nightly full rebuilds where brief stale reads are acceptable. [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]

- { $out: "daily_event_summary" } [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- Target must be in the **same database** unless using `{ db, coll }` object form (4.4+). [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- Reads see the old collection until the atomic swap completes. [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- `$merge` (introduced in **4.2**) writes into an existing collection with [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- per-document conflict control. Ideal for incrementally updating materialized views. [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]

- Each pipeline **stage** is limited to **100 MB of RAM** (raised from 32 MB in 4.4). [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- Stages most likely to hit this: `$sort`, `$group`, `$bucket`, `$setWindowFields`. [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- When the limit is exceeded, MongoDB aborts with: [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- MongoServerError: $sort used too much RAM. Memory limit: 104857600 bytes. [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- Pass allowDiskUse:true to opt in to writing spill files. [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]

- Atlas tiers: `allowDiskUse` is **disabled on M0/M2/M5** (shared) tiers; requires M10+. [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]

- When running aggregation pipelines against **time series collections** (MongoDB 5.0+), the following behaviors differ from regular collections: [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- **Bucket-level pruning:** The query planner uses `control.min`/`control.max` metadata on internal buckets to skip entire buckets that don't match time-range or metaField predicates. Always place `$match` on the `metaField` and `timeField` as the **first stage** to maximise pruning. [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- **$densify / $fill on time series:** `$densify` `partitionByFields` supports dotted paths into `metaField` sub-fields but not measurement fields. For measurement field partitioning, use `$addFields` to promote the field before `$densify`. [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- **$setWindowFields performance:** Window functions do not push down through bucket storage. A tight `$match` before `$setWindowFields` is critical — without it, MongoDB unpacks and scans all buckets. [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- **$dateTrunc for downsampling:** Use `$dateTrunc` with `binSize` to downsample raw measurements into fixed time buckets (hourly/daily OHLCV, hourly averages). It is more efficient than `$dateToString` + `$group` for time-bucket aggregations. [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- **$out to time series (MongoDB 7.0.3+):** `$out` can write directly into a time series collection. `$merge` into a time series collection is not supported — use `$out` instead. [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- **Cannot use `distinct()` on time series** — use `$group` with a supporting metaField compound index instead. [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- For full time series aggregation patterns including IoT multi-sensor, financial OHLCV, gap-fill dashboards, and working set sizing, see `mongodb-time-series`. [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]

- **`mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep`** — deep-dive reference for high-value stages: `$lookup` (equality, pipeline-with-let, Atlas Search), `$graphLookup` (recursive joins, tree/BOM patterns), `$facet` (16 MB ceiling, pagination idiom), `$bucket`/`$bucketAuto` (Renard / POWERSOF2 granularity), `$merge`/`$out` (materialized-view refresh, idempotency), `$setWindowFields` (rank, shift, derivative, integral), `$densify`/`$fill` (gap filling), `$unionWith`, plus 100 MB-per-stage memory limits, `allowDiskUse`, and `explain("executionStats")` spill detection. [src: mongodb-aggregation-pipeline]
- **`mongodb-operations-expert` (references/mongodb-spark-connector.md)** — when an aggregation pipeline runs as part of a Spark/Databricks job. The connector accepts the same MQL aggregation pipeline syntax via the `aggregation.pipeline` read option, and Catalyst pushes Spark filters/projections/limit down by prepending `$match`/`$project`/`$limit` stages to the user-supplied pipeline. Pipeline tuning rules from this skill (index-backed `$match` first, `$project` early, `allowDiskUse` for large `$sort`/`$group`) apply identically. Use the Spark connector reference when the pipeline result becomes a DataFrame for downstream Spark work; stay in this skill for pipelines that run only inside the Mongo cluster. - **Migrating without pilot testing:** Always test with a non-critical collection first [src: mongodb-migration-patterns]
- **Not sizing oplog for migration duration:** If migration takes > oplog window, migration restarts from scratch [src: mongodb-migration-patterns]
- **Underestimating initial sync time:** 1 TB at 100 MB/s = ~3 hours; plan for 2-3x actual transfer time [src: mongodb-migration-patterns]
- **Not testing application compatibility before cutover:** Atlas has different defaults (w: majority, retryWrites: true, TLS required) [src: mongodb-migration-patterns]
- **Ignoring DBA user differences:** Create all required database users in Atlas before cutover [src: mongodb-migration-patterns]
- **Single-attempt cutover with no rollback plan:** Keep source live for 48 hours post-cutover [src: mongodb-migration-patterns]

- <!-- Provenance: reference under the `mongodb-operations-expert` hub. Mirrored from ~/.claude/skills/mongodb-operations-expert/references/mongodb-cost-optimization.md by scripts/persist-spoke.mjs. --> [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Expert guidance on reducing MongoDB Atlas spend while maintaining performance SLAs. Applicable to all Atlas dedicated cluster tiers (M10–M700+). Real-world context: this skill was developed in part to support a $300k cost optimization target for enterprise Atlas deployments. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **In scope:** Atlas dedicated clusters (M10 and above), replica sets, sharded clusters, backup, network egress, index storage, and committed-use pricing. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Out of scope:** Atlas Serverless and Atlas Flex clusters use per-operation and range-based pricing models that differ fundamentally from instance-based pricing. Cost guidance for Serverless and Flex requires separate analysis — this skill does not cover them. Atlas App Services (triggers, Data API) costs are also excluded. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- -- [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Use this table to prioritize effort. Detail for each lever is in the numbered sections below. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- -- [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Right-sizing is an iterative process, not a one-time event. Atlas clusters are over-provisioned by default because teams size for peak-of-peak and never revisit. Most production clusters run at <40% CPU and <60% RAM utilization on average. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Sustained CPU < 60%**: healthy headroom. If sustained CPU consistently sits below 30%, the cluster is a candidate for one tier down. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **P99 CPU < 80%**: spikes above 80% during batch windows are acceptable if they are brief and predictable. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **CPU steal > 5%** on M10/M20 clusters: signal that the underlying host is saturated; consider moving up one tier to get more dedicated compute headroom. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Working set fit**: the most critical metric. If the Atlas "Page Faults" metric (in Metrics → Cache) shows sustained page faults, your working set has outgrown RAM. Size up until page faults are near zero. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Cache utilization > 90%**: investigate query patterns first (indexes, projections, covered queries) before adding RAM. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Target 70–85% cache utilization** as a healthy steady state. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Monitor "Disk IOPS" in Atlas Metrics. If IOPS consistently approach the tier's provisioned limit, consider scaling up or switching to Provisioned IOPS storage (NVMe or custom IOPS). [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- For write-heavy workloads, watch "Disk Queue Depth" — values above 1 sustained indicate I/O saturation. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Pull 30-day P50/P95/P99 CPU, memory cache utilization, and IOPS from Atlas Metrics or Data Explorer. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Identify the busiest 3-hour window in the week (typically Monday morning or end-of-month batch). [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Simulate one tier down: will P95 CPU stay below 75%? Will working set still fit? [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- For RS primaries, validate oplog window stays above 24 hours after downsizing (oplog window shrinks with smaller disks). [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Apply the change via Atlas UI rolling restart (Atlas changes secondaries first, then the primary automatically via election). Watch metrics for 24 hours after the rolling restart completes before declaring success. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Consolidating several under-utilized M30 clusters onto fewer M50 clusters often saves more than tier reduction alone. Evaluate multi-tenant cluster patterns (separate databases per tenant) when per-cluster overhead exceeds actual workload cost. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- -- [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- OLTP workloads with moderate write rates (< 3,000 sustained IOPS). [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Analytical or reporting workloads. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Development, staging, and QA environments — always use standard here. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Majority of M30–M60 production clusters that are not latency-sensitive. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Write-heavy workloads where disk queue depth consistently exceeds 1. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- When you need deterministic IOPS SLA for compliance (fintech, healthcare). [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Clusters where you can't size disk larger (data volume constraint) but need more IOPS. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Cost break-even: provisioned IOPS becomes cost-effective only when you need > 3,000 IOPS from a disk that would otherwise require scaling the cluster tier. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Hot data caches (Okta session store, rate-limiting counters, real-time leaderboards). [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- When working set exceeds 500 GB and cache miss latency is unacceptable. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Note: NVMe local disks are not network-attached persistent storage — if an individual node fails, WiredTiger data on that node must be rebuilt by initial sync from a healthy peer. Atlas manages this automatically, but it means the replica set must stay healthy (never lose quorum) or recovery time increases significantly. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Audit provisioned IOPS allocations quarterly.** Teams frequently provision 10,000 IOPS for a cluster consuming 800. Move over-provisioned io1 clusters to GP3 with IOPS matching actual P95 usage + 30% headroom. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- -- [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Atlas Compute Autoscaling (available M10+, enabled per cluster) monitors CPU and memory, then scales up or down one tier at a time. It does not skip tiers. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- CPU utilization > 75% for 1 hour (or shorter sustained window depending on tier). [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- OR cache dirty bytes approaching capacity. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Scale-up is immediate (rolling restart, no downtime for RS). [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- CPU utilization < 50% for the trailing 24 hours. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- The 24-hour delay is intentional — Atlas will not oscillate. Reduce to 12 hours only if your workload has predictable weekly patterns (e.g., weekday-only traffic). [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Opt in** for: non-production clusters, single-region analytics clusters, clusters with variable batch workloads. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Opt out** for: sharded clusters (autoscaling applies per shard — coordinate with capacity planning), clusters with strict latency SLAs where a rolling restart during a scale event is disruptive, M0/M2/M5 free/shared tiers (autoscaling not available on shared infrastructure). [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Atlas Project Activity Feed logs every scale event. Set a budget alert at 110% of current spend to catch unexpected autoscale-up events. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- -- [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Atlas triggers disk autoscaling when disk utilization reaches **90% of provisioned storage**. The disk is expanded by approximately 25% (rounded to the next billing increment). [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- By the time Atlas fires the autoscale event and the expansion completes, the cluster can momentarily spike above 90%, causing the `WiredTiger` storage engine to stall writes. For high-write clusters, configure the disk alert at **85%** to give yourself a 2–4 hour window to intervene manually. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Configure in Atlas UI → Project → Alerts → Add Alert: [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Condition**: Disk Utilization > 85% [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Notification channels**: PagerDuty + Slack channel [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Evaluation window**: 5 minutes [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Manual scaling** is preferred for predictable growth patterns (data archival, known ingest schedules). Avoids unexpected storage cost jumps. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Auto scaling** is appropriate when ingest rate is variable and unpredictable. Set a maximum disk size cap in cluster configuration to avoid runaway expansion. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Atlas does not automatically compact reclaimed disk space after large deletes. Use `compact` command during maintenance windows on secondaries, then primary, to reclaim space. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- After TTL index deletes or large bulk-delete operations, compaction can recover 30–60% of disk, avoiding an autoscale event. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- -- [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Atlas charges for backup storage separately from cluster storage. Snapshot storage list price starts at approximately $0.14/GB-month (varies by cloud provider and region; see `references/mongodb-backup-restore.md` for the same figure). Snapshots are incremental after the first, so realized cost is typically well under the full dataset size times that rate. Continuous (PIT) backups add overhead for oplog tailing. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Default Atlas backup policies are often set to 7 daily + 4 weekly + 12 monthly + 2 yearly. For non-production environments, this is severe overkill. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Recommended retention by environment:** [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Applying minimal retention to staging/dev/QA clusters alone can reduce backup spend by 20–40% for organizations with many non-prod clusters. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Queryable backups** (Backup Query) allow running read queries against a snapshot without restoring. They incur an additional charge per hour the queryable session is active. Terminate sessions immediately after use — stale queryable backup sessions are a common surprise charge. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Continuous backups** (Point-in-Time Restore, PITR) require oplog storage in addition to snapshots. For clusters with high write rates, oplog storage can equal or exceed base snapshot storage. PITR is essential for production; disable it on all non-production clusters. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Atlas charges cloud provider data transfer rates for cross-region snapshot copies. Example: us-east-1 → eu-west-1 snapshot copy on AWS costs ~$0.02/GB in egress. For a 2 TB cluster with weekly cross-region backup copies, this is ~$40/week ($2,080/year) in egress alone, before storage. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Optimization:** Use cross-region backup only for your most critical production clusters. For DR, consider whether a replica set spanning regions (geo-distributed RS) eliminates the need for cross-region backup copies. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- -- [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Intra-region, same VPC/peering**: traffic between your application VPC and Atlas via VPC peering in the same cloud region is free on AWS and GCP (standard peering rules). This is the target architecture. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Private Link / Private Endpoint within the same region**: free for data transfer; you pay for the endpoint hour only. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Cross-region data transfer**: any data that crosses cloud provider region boundaries is charged at the provider's inter-region rate (~$0.02/GB on AWS, similar on GCP/Azure). [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Internet egress (no peering)**: clusters accessed over the public internet are charged at provider internet egress rates (~$0.09/GB on AWS). This is the most expensive path and should be eliminated in production. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Atlas Data Federation**: egress from Atlas Data Federation to S3 or external storage layers has its own pricing. Review federation query patterns. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- When Atlas is purchased through AWS Marketplace (or GCP/Azure Marketplace), egress charges from Atlas to compute in the same cloud are often offset by Marketplace agreements. Verify with your MongoDB sales rep whether your Marketplace agreement includes egress credits. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Co-locate application and Atlas cluster in the same region. Mismatched regions are the single largest source of unplanned egress costs. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Use VPC peering or Private Link everywhere — eliminate public endpoint usage. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Minimize cross-shard scatter queries in sharded clusters (scatter-gather reads data from all shards, multiplying egress if shards span regions). [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Atlas Charts and Atlas Data Federation running cross-region against production clusters generate egress at query time. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- -- [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- MongoDB offers committed-use pricing (similar to cloud provider reserved instances) through multi-year Atlas contracts. Discounts range from 15–35% depending on commitment term and volume: [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- 1-year commitment: ~15% discount [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- 2-year commitment: ~25% discount [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- 3-year commitment: ~30–35% discount [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- AWS, GCP, and Azure Marketplace support Private Offer agreements where MongoDB can negotiate custom pricing with volume commitments. These are distinct from on-demand Marketplace rates and are typically accessed through MongoDB's enterprise sales team. Private Offers can bundle: [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Atlas cluster usage [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Atlas Search (Lucene-powered) [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Atlas Stream Processing [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Professional services [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- For AWS customers with an existing AWS EDP agreement, Atlas Marketplace spend can count toward your EDP commitment and receive EDP discounts. This stacks with any MongoDB-level committed-use discount. Validate with both your AWS account team and MongoDB sales rep. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Key question to ask:** "Does my Atlas Marketplace spend count toward my AWS EDP draw-down, and is there a private offer available that reduces the per-unit rate further?" [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Annual Atlas spend > $100k: dedicated Technical Account Manager and discount eligibility. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Annual Atlas spend > $250k: committed-use discount almost always warranted. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- At Okta's $300k cost optimization target: combination of right-sizing + committed-use renegotiation + Marketplace private offer is the typical playbook. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- -- [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Pausing a cluster in Atlas stops all compute charges (you continue to pay for storage). Atlas M0 (free) clusters are excluded; M10+ clusters can be paused via UI or API. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- For a paused cluster, you pay storage cost only — typically 5–15% of the running cluster cost. A paused M30 cluster ($0.54/hour compute) saves ~$389/month, paying only ~$20–40/month in storage. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Cluster resume takes 1–5 minutes (Atlas provisions the compute instances, mounts storage, initiates replica set election). Plan for this in CI/CD pipelines that spin up on-demand. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Use Atlas API + a cron job or Atlas Scheduled Triggers to automate pause/resume for non-production clusters: [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- curl --digest -u "$PUBLIC_KEY:$PRIVATE_KEY" \ [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- X PATCH "https://cloud.mongodb.com/api/atlas/v2/groups/$PROJECT_ID/clusters/$CLUSTER_NAME" \ [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- H "Content-Type: application/json" \ [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- d '{"paused": true}' [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- curl --digest -u "$PUBLIC_KEY:$PRIVATE_KEY" \ [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- X PATCH "https://cloud.mongodb.com/api/atlas/v2/groups/$PROJECT_ID/clusters/$CLUSTER_NAME" \ [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- H "Content-Type: application/json" \ [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- d '{"paused": false}' [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Pause: weekdays 8pm local time [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Resume: weekdays 7am local time [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Pause all weekend (Friday 8pm → Monday 7am) [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Savings: ~65% of compute hours eliminated [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Clusters with active Atlas Search indexes cannot be paused (as of Atlas 7.x). [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Clusters paused for more than 60 days are automatically resumed by Atlas (to prevent indefinitely stale configs). Set a calendar reminder or monitoring alert if long-term pause is intended. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Paused clusters still run scheduled Atlas triggers and Atlas Charts queries — review and disable these before pausing. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- -- [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Every index consumes disk storage, which is included in your cluster's storage billing. For large collections, indexes can represent 20–50% of total disk usage. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Teams frequently create indexes during development and never prune them. Common patterns: [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- ESR (Equality, Sort, Range) indexes created separately instead of as compound indexes. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Indexes created for a feature that was never launched or was retired. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Redundant prefix indexes: `{a:1}` when `{a:1, b:1}` already exists (the compound covers the single-field case). [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Text indexes on every string field "just in case." [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- In Atlas Data Explorer or mongosh: [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- // Per-index sizes for a collection [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- db.myCollection.aggregate([ [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- // Storage sizes including indexes [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- db.myCollection.stats({ indexDetails: true }) [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- // Full database storage breakdown [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- db.runCommand({ dbStats: 1, scale: 1024 * 1024 }) [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Atlas Metrics also exposes "Index Size" at the cluster level in the Storage metrics group. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- // $indexStats tracks accesses since last restart [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- db.myCollection.aggregate([ [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- { $match: { "accesses.ops": { $lt: 100 } } },  // low access count [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- { $sort: { "accesses.ops": 1 } } [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- For Atlas clusters, use Atlas Performance Advisor — it surfaces "Redundant Indexes" and "Unused Indexes" recommendations automatically. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Identify candidate unused index via `$indexStats` over a 14-day window (catch monthly jobs). [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Hide the index first: `db.collection.hideIndex("index_name")` — hidden indexes are maintained but not used by the query planner. Monitor for 1–2 weeks. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- If no degradation observed, drop: `db.collection.dropIndex("index_name")`. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- For large indexes (> 10 GB), expect an immediate disk space reduction after compaction. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- -- [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Navigate to Atlas Organization → Billing to see: [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Invoices**: line-item breakdown by project and cluster. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Cost Explorer** (Atlas Advanced): filter by project, cluster, service type (compute, storage, backup, data transfer) across date ranges. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Usage details CSV export**: machine-readable daily usage for offline analysis. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Atlas supports resource tags on projects and clusters. Align tags with your cloud provider's tagging taxonomy for cost allocation: [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Environment: production | staging | development | qa [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Team: platform | data-engineering | product-backend [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Application: user-auth | analytics | search [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Tags flow through to Marketplace bills and can be used in cloud provider Cost Explorer for consolidated reporting. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Set Atlas budget alerts at the organization and project levels: [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Organization budget alert**: 90% and 110% of monthly budget. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Per-project alert**: for projects with known spend floors; alert at 120% of 3-month average. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Alert destinations: email, PagerDuty, Slack webhook. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Use the Atlas API to pull daily cost data and feed it to a cost anomaly tool (AWS Cost Anomaly Detection if using Marketplace, or a custom time-series alert). A 20% day-over-day spike in a project's cost is worth investigating — common causes are autoscale-up events, runaway Data Federation queries, or accidentally un-paused dev clusters. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- For accounts > $10k/month Atlas spend, establish a monthly review: [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Pull invoice line items, sort by cost descending. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Identify top 5 clusters by cost — are they appropriately sized? [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Review autoscaling events in Activity Feed. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Check for orphaned clusters (no connections in 30 days per Atlas access logs). [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Validate backup retention policies match current policy. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- -- [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- This is a customer-defined classification, not an Atlas-native concept. Align with your SRE or platform team's existing tier model. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Don't gold-plate Tier 2**: a common mistake is running internal dashboards and analytics clusters at Tier 1 specs "because it's easy." An M30 with a 3-day daily snapshot is almost always sufficient for internal tools. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Separate clusters by tier**: avoid co-mingling Tier 0 and Tier 2 workloads on the same cluster (multi-tenancy) — a noisy Tier 2 workload can degrade Tier 0 performance. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Tier 2 pause savings**: if you have 20 Tier 2 clusters at M20 average, pausing them 65% of the time saves ~$5,000–$8,000/month. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- For an account targeting $300k in savings: [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Audit all clusters: classify into T0/T1/T2. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Right-size T1 clusters (likely 20–40% of spend, 40% reduction = $30–60k savings). [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Pause T2 clusters off-hours (~$60–80k savings if significant T2 footprint). [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Negotiate committed-use discount on remaining T0/T1 spend (~15–25% = $60–120k savings). [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Prune backup retention on T1/T2 (~$20–30k savings). [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Total: $170–290k annualized, reaching or exceeding the $300k target with combined levers. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- -- [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Pattern**: Team provisions io1 storage with 10,000 IOPS "to be safe" for a cluster consuming 600 IOPS at P95. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Detection**: Atlas Metrics → Disk IOPS → compare provisioned vs actual over 30 days. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Fix**: Switch to GP3 storage, set IOPS to `actual_P95 * 1.5` (minimum 3,000 for GP3). [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Savings**: Can be 50–70% of storage cost for over-provisioned io1 clusters. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Pattern**: M80 cluster purchased for a projected workload peak that never materialized. Team inherited it and never questioned the spec. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Detection**: 30-day CPU P95 < 30% AND page faults near zero AND disk utilization < 50%. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Fix**: Rolling tier-down via Atlas UI. Start one tier at a time, validate, continue. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Savings**: Each tier step is roughly 40–60% cost reduction. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Pattern**: Both continuous backups (PITR) and aggressive snapshot retention enabled on dev/staging clusters. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Detection**: Atlas Billing → filter by "Backup" service type — compare backup cost vs compute cost per cluster. Backup > 30% of cluster cost is a red flag for non-production. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Fix**: Disable PITR on staging; reduce to 1-day daily retention for dev clusters. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Pattern**: Cluster created for a proof-of-concept 18 months ago. PoC ended, cluster never deleted. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Detection**: Atlas Data Explorer or `listClusters` API → filter for clusters with zero connections in the past 30 days via Atlas access logs. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Fix**: Confirm with application team, take final snapshot, delete cluster. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Pattern**: Atlas Data Federation configured to query S3 data on-demand. A scheduled report or misconfigured dashboard runs full-collection scans every 5 minutes. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Detection**: Atlas Billing → Data Federation line items spiking. Atlas Data Federation logs show query frequency. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Fix**: Add query result caching, reduce schedule frequency, add `$match` filters to reduce data scanned. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Pattern**: 3-region global cluster deployed "for availability" on an internal analytics workload that has no international users. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Detection**: Atlas cluster topology → global write distribution map → low write/read volume outside primary region. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Fix**: Convert to single-region RS with appropriate tier. 3-region global clusters are 3× the base compute cost. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Pattern**: Atlas Search (Lucene) indexes deployed on collections that are no longer queried via Atlas Search (application switched to a different search path). [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Detection**: Atlas Search Index list → check `queryCount` via Atlas Search metrics. Search indexes on large collections add meaningful storage overhead. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- **Fix**: Drop unused Search indexes via Atlas UI → Search → Indexes. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]

- *Cross-pollinated from `mongodb-atlas-flex-serverless` — researched 2026-05-28.* [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Flex is the entry-level paid Atlas tier ($8–$30/month hard cap) that replaced M2/M5 shared clusters and Serverless instances (EOL: January 22, 2026). It is the most cost-efficient option for development, staging, and low-traffic production workloads. [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Ops/sec tiered, billed hourly prorated — $8 base (100 ops/sec, 5 GB), caps at $30/month at 500 ops/sec [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- No per-document billing (unlike the deprecated Serverless RPU model) [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- No runaway billing: $30/month is the absolute maximum regardless of load spikes [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Private Endpoints / VPC Peering required (security policy) [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- PITR backup required (compliance) [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- BYOK encryption at rest required [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Data > 5 GB [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Connections > 500 [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Ops/sec > 500 sustained [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]
- Atlas Vector Search going to production (resource contention on Flex) [src: mongodb-cost-optimization]

- Request Private Endpoint in Atlas UI/API: `POST /api/atlas/v2/groups/{groupId}/privateEndpoint/azure/endpointService` [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- Atlas creates Azure Private Link Service backed by Standard Load Balancer [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- Azure creates NIC in your subnet with private IP [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- Status sequence: `Creating → Available` [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- Private DNS Zone `<cluster-id>.mongodb.net` with A records pointing to private endpoint NIC IP. Zone must be linked to every VNet needing resolution. [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- Connection string: `mongodb+srv://cluster0-pl-0.<cluster-id>.mongodb.net` [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]

- is_manual_connection           = true [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- resource "mongodbatlas_privatelink_endpoint_service" "atlas" { [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- project_id          = var.atlas_project_id [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- private_link_id     = mongodbatlas_privatelink_endpoint.atlas.id [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]

- **Legacy (deprecated Apr 30 2027):** `_pl-` prefix; 50 IP addresses per region; 50 forwarding rules [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- **Port-Mapped (current):** `_psc-` prefix; 1 IP address; 1 forwarding rule; requires `portMappingEnabled: true` [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- Cloud DNS private zone. Allow TCP 27017 + high ports (1024-65535) through VPC firewall rules for SRV connection strings. [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- **3-node across 2 clouds (HA across clouds):** [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- Primary: AWS US_EAST_1 [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- Secondary: GCP EASTERN_US [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- Secondary: Azure EASTUS [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- **Write-concern latency:** W:majority in multi-cloud = at least one write acknowledged from another cloud. Cross-cloud RTT typically 10-50ms. Use `wtimeoutMS` to prevent write stalls. [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- **Read preference:** Route reads to local secondary with `readPreference: nearest` + `maxStalenessSeconds`. [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- Primary cloud (AWS): 3 electable nodes [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- DR cloud (Azure/GCP): 1-2 non-electable nodes (priority=0) or hidden secondaries [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- Hidden secondary in DR cloud: receives replication without being elected [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- Failover: promote DR nodes by changing priority [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- **RPO:** Near-zero (replication lag typically <1 second for healthy cluster) [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- **RTO:** 10-30 seconds for automatic election after primary failure [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- Cross-cloud data transfer incurs egress charges: [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- AWS→GCP: ~$0.08/GB (US East) [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- AWS→Azure: ~$0.08/GB (US East) [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- GCP→AWS: ~$0.08/GB (US Central) [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- For a 3-replica-set with 10 GB/day replication across clouds: ~$0.80/day in egress costs. [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- **Mitigation:** Keep primary and majority of nodes in lowest-cost cloud. Use hidden secondaries in DR cloud to limit replication traffic. [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- Atlas purchased via Azure Marketplace counts toward Microsoft Azure Consumption Commitment (MACC). Direct MongoDB invoices are NOT MACC-eligible. [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- **MACC-eligible purchases:** Atlas cluster compute/storage, Advanced Security, Dedicated Search Nodes, Stream Processing. [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- **Azure Native MongoDB (ANM):** First-party Azure resource in Azure Portal. Billing on Azure invoice (MACC-eligible). Generally at feature parity with standard Atlas. [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- GCP Marketplace Atlas purchases are EDP (Estimated Discount Program) eligible. GCP startup credits can be stacked. Committed use via GCP CUD contracts. [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- MongoDB is an AWS ISV Accelerate partner. Atlas clusters on AWS can qualify for AWS partner funding for customer migrations. [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- MongoDB Atlas is an Azure Preferred Solution. Purchases via Marketplace impact partner competency and incentive credits. [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- MongoDB participates in Google for Startups Cloud Program. Atlas credits available for eligible startups. [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- **Multi-cloud without read preference tuning:** Default `primary` read preference sends all reads cross-cloud → high latency. Set `readPreference: nearest`. [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- **Majority writes in high-latency multi-cloud setups without wtimeoutMS:** Writes can block indefinitely if cross-cloud replication stalls. Always set `wtimeoutMS`. [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- **Using VNet peering instead of Private Link for new Azure deployments:** Private Link is recommended and simpler (no IP overlap constraints). [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- **Legacy GCP PSC endpoints without migration plan:** Must migrate to port-mapped before April 30, 2027. [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
- **Forgetting cross-cloud egress costs in TCO analysis:** Multi-cloud replication incurs ~$0.08/GB egress. [src: mongodb-atlas-multicloud]
