- <!-- Provenance: reference under the `mongodb-expert` hub. Mirrored from ~/.claude/skills/mongodb-expert/references/mongodb-indexes-deep.md by scripts/persist-spoke.mjs. --> [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Reference for every MongoDB index type, ordering strategies, build mechanics, [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- and production anti-patterns. Use this alongside `explain()` output when diagnosing query plans. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- > **Audience:** MongoDB developers and DBAs working on query optimization, schema design, or [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- > production index management. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Single-field  : { field: 1 } [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Compound      : { eq1: 1, eq2: 1, sortField: -1, rangeField: 1 }  ← ESR order [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Multikey      : automatic when field is array; no parallel arrays in compound [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Partial       : { field: 1 }, { partialFilterExpression: { status: "active" } } [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Sparse        : { field: 1 }, { sparse: true }  ← prefer partial instead [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- TTL           : { dateField: 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: N } [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Text          : { field: "text" }  / { "$**": "text" } [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Wildcard      : { "$**": 1 }  / { "sub.$**": 1 } [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Hashed        : { _id: "hashed" }  ← even distribution shard key [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- 2dsphere      : { location: "2dsphere" }  ← GeoJSON [lng, lat] [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Unique        : { field: 1 }, { unique: true } [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Unique+Partial: { field: 1 }, { unique: true, partialFilterExpression: {...} } [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Hidden        : createIndex(..., { hidden: true })  ← test removal without drop [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Sections: §1 Single-field · §2 Compound/ESR · §3 Multikey · §4 Partial · §5 Sparse · [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- §6 TTL · §7 Text · §8 Wildcard · §9 Hashed · §10 2dsphere · §11 Unique · [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- §12 Intersection · §13 Build Strategies · §14 Selectivity & Covering · [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- §15 Hidden Indexes · §16 hint() & Forcing · §17 Anti-Patterns [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- -- [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- The most common index type. MongoDB automatically creates a unique index on `_id`. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Ascending index on a single field [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.orders.createIndex({ customerId: 1 }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Descending — functionally equivalent for single-field indexes [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // (MongoDB traverses B-tree in either direction) [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.orders.createIndex({ createdAt: -1 }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Explicit _id index already exists; do not recreate it [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // db.orders.createIndex({ _id: 1 }); // no-op [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- **When single-field is enough:** [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Query filters only one field with high selectivity (e.g., UUID, email). [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Sort is on the same field as the filter and no range condition is involved. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Write throughput is a concern — every extra index adds write overhead. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- **Ascending vs descending matters** only for compound indexes. For a solo field, both [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- directions serve equality and range queries equally well. Direction only becomes load-bearing [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- when combining fields in a compound index (see §2) or when serving sort-heavy queries where [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- the sort order must align with the index direction. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- -- [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Compound indexes cover multiple fields in a declared order. **Order is everything.** [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Place fields in this sequence to maximize the index's usefulness: [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- **E**quality predicates first — fields compared with `$eq` or `$in` (point lookups). [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- **S**ort fields next — fields in the `sort()` clause, preserving their direction. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- **R**ange fields last — fields with `$gt`, `$lt`, `$gte`, `$lte`, `$ne`, `$nin`, regex. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Query: find active orders for a customer, sort by date, filter price range [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- { status: "active", customerId: "abc123", price: { $gte: 50, $lte: 200 } } [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- ).sort({ createdAt: -1 }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // ESR compound index: [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Equality: status, customerId [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Sort:     createdAt (descending matches the sort direction) [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.orders.createIndex({ [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Any prefix of a compound index can serve queries on that prefix alone: [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.users.createIndex({ country: 1, state: 1, city: 1 }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Serves: { country } queries [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Serves: { country, state } queries [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Serves: { country, state, city } queries [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Does NOT serve: { state } or { city } queries alone [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- A single compound index replaces multiple single-field indexes when queries consistently [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- filter on prefix subsets. Avoid creating redundant `{ country: 1 }` if the compound exists. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- For compound indexes that serve sorts, each field's direction in the index must match the [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- sort direction **or** every field's direction must be reversed: [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.events.createIndex({ category: 1, ts: -1 }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // .sort({ category: 1, ts: -1 })   ✅ exact match [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // .sort({ category: -1, ts: 1 })   ✅ full inversion [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // .sort({ category: 1, ts: 1 })    ❌ COLLSCAN or in-memory sort [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- -- [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- MongoDB automatically creates a **multikey index** when any indexed field contains an array. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Each array element gets its own index entry. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Documents have shape: { tags: ["mongodb", "indexing", "performance"] } [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.articles.createIndex({ tags: 1 }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // MongoDB creates one entry per element — "mongodb", "indexing", "performance" all get entries. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Works with array of subdocuments too [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // { scores: [{ subject: "math", grade: 90 }, { subject: "english", grade: 85 }] } [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.students.createIndex({ "scores.grade": 1 }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- When a query has predicates on an array field, MongoDB intersects multikey bounds: [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // { $elemMatch: { $gte: 70, $lte: 90 } } — bounds applied to the SAME element [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.students.find({ scores: { $elemMatch: { $gte: 70, $lte: 90 } } }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // { scores: { $gte: 70 } }, { scores: { $lte: 90 } } — separate bounds, may produce false positives [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // that are filtered during FETCH stage [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- A compound index **cannot** index two fields that are both arrays in the same document: [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Document: { a: [1,2], b: [3,4] } [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.col.createIndex({ a: 1, b: 1 }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // ❌ MongoServerError: cannot index parallel arrays [b] [a] [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // MongoDB rejects document insertion OR the index build fails [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Design around this: embed the array relationship inside a single subdocument array field. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- -- [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- A partial index only indexes documents that match a `partialFilterExpression`. This is the [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- preferred modern alternative to sparse indexes. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Only index orders that are "pending" — ignores completed and cancelled orders [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.orders.createIndex( [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- { customerId: 1, createdAt: -1 }, [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- { partialFilterExpression: { status: "pending" } } [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- **Requirements:** queries that use a partial index must include the filter expression [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- (or a superset of it) in their predicate, otherwise MongoDB will not use the index. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Will use the index — query matches the partialFilterExpression [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.orders.find({ customerId: "abc", status: "pending" }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Will NOT use the index — status is absent from query filter [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.orders.find({ customerId: "abc" }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- A partial index on 10% of documents is ~90% smaller than a full index, with proportionally [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- faster builds, lower memory pressure, and reduced write amplification. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- -- [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- A sparse index omits documents where the indexed field does not exist (or is `null`). [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.users.createIndex({ phoneNumber: 1 }, { sparse: true }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Documents without phoneNumber are excluded from the index [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- **When to prefer sparse:** you must support MongoDB < 3.2 (partial indexes require 3.2+) [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- or need a quick "skip nulls" index without a filter expression. For MongoDB 3.2+, use partial. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- **Gotcha:** a sparse index will not be used for queries that include a sort on the sparse [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- field unless the query predicate also restricts that field to non-null values. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- -- [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- TTL (Time-To-Live) indexes let MongoDB automatically delete documents after a specified [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- number of seconds past a date field. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Expire session documents 30 minutes after their createdAt timestamp [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.sessions.createIndex( [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- { expireAfterSeconds: 1800 } [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Expire at an absolute date stored in the document (set expireAfterSeconds: 0) [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Document: { expireAt: ISODate("2026-06-01T00:00:00Z") } [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- { expireAfterSeconds: 0 } [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- The indexed field must be a **BSON Date** type or an array of Date values. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- If the field is an array, the earliest (minimum) date is used for expiration. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Documents are deleted by a background task that runs **every 60 seconds** — do not [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- rely on sub-minute precision. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- TTL indexes cannot be compound indexes. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- TTL indexes cannot be created on capped collections. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- index: { keyPattern: { createdAt: 1 }, expireAfterSeconds: 3600 } [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- On Atlas, TTL deletions count against your oplog and IOPS budget. For high-volume [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- expiration, consider sharding on the TTL field so deletions are distributed. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- -- [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Text indexes tokenize string content, apply language-specific stemming, and support [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- the `$text` / `$search` query operator. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.articles.createIndex({ body: "text" }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Multiple fields with weights (higher weight = more relevant in score) [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.articles.createIndex( [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- { title: "text", body: "text", tags: "text" }, [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- { weights: { title: 10, tags: 5, body: 1 }, default_language: "english" } [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Wildcard text index — all string fields [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.articles.createIndex({ "$**": "text" }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.articles.find({ $text: { $search: "mongodb indexing" } }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.articles.find({ $text: { $search: "\"compound index\"" } }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.articles.find({ $text: { $search: "indexes -sharding" } }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Sort by relevance score [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- { $text: { $search: "performance" } }, [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- { score: { $meta: "textScore" } } [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- ).sort({ score: { $meta: "textScore" } }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Only **one text index** per collection is allowed. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- -- [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Wildcard indexes use `$**` to index all fields (or a projection subset) in a document, [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- useful for workloads with unpredictable or polymorphic field sets. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Index every field in every document [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.catalog.createIndex({ "$**": 1 }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Index only fields under "attributes" subtree [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.catalog.createIndex({ "attributes.$**": 1 }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Wildcard projection — include specific fields, exclude others [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.catalog.createIndex( [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- { wildcardProjection: { "attributes": 1, "metadata": 1 } } [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Compound wildcard index (MongoDB 7.0+) [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Fixed prefix fields + wildcard suffix [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.catalog.createIndex({ category: 1, "attributes.$**": 1 }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Each leaf field in a document generates a separate index entry. A document with [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- `{ a: 1, b: { c: 2, d: 3 } }` produces entries for `a`, `b.c`, and `b.d`. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Cannot replace a compound index for queries filtering multiple specific fields — [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- the planner will only use the wildcard index for **one field** per query. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Wildcard indexes are always **sparse** (missing fields are not indexed). [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Multikey semantics apply — arrays create multiple entries. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- `_id` is excluded by default; include explicitly in `wildcardProjection`. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- -- [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Hashed indexes store a hash of the field value rather than the value itself. They are [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- primarily used as shard keys for even data distribution. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Create a hashed index on _id (common shard key pattern) [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.events.createIndex({ _id: "hashed" }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- sh.shardCollection("mydb.events", { _id: "hashed" }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Support **equality queries only** — range queries (`$gt`, `$lt`) cannot use hashed indexes. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Hash is computed deterministically; queries with `$eq` resolve to one hash bucket. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- A hashed index on `_id` distributes writes evenly across shards, avoiding hotspots. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- **Compound hashed shard keys (MongoDB 4.4+):** a shard key may combine a range prefix [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- with one hashed component — e.g., `{ country: 1, _id: "hashed" }` — giving locality on [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- the range field while distributing the hash field evenly. Only **one** field in a shard key [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- may be hashed; you cannot hash two fields in the same key. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Do not use hashed indexes for range-heavy workloads — switch to ranged sharding instead. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Equality queries work fine [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.events.find({ _id: ObjectId("...") });  // uses hashed index [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Range query — full shard scatter [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.events.find({ _id: { $gt: ObjectId("...") } });  // COLLSCAN on each shard [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- -- [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- 2dsphere indexes support queries on GeoJSON geometry objects and legacy coordinate pairs [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- on a spherical Earth model. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // GeoJSON document shape [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // { location: { type: "Point", coordinates: [lng, lat] } } [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.places.createIndex({ location: "2dsphere" }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Compound with 2dsphere [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.places.createIndex({ category: 1, location: "2dsphere" }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // $geoNear — nearest points (requires 2dsphere index) [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.places.aggregate([ [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- near: { type: "Point", coordinates: [-73.9857, 40.7484] }, [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- distanceField: "dist.calculated", [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- maxDistance: 5000,           // meters [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- query: { category: "restaurant" } [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // $geoWithin — points inside a polygon [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- coordinates: [[ [-74, 40], [-73, 40], [-73, 41], [-74, 41], [-74, 40] ]] [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // $nearSphere — near a point, sorted by distance [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- $geometry: { type: "Point", coordinates: [-73.9857, 40.7484] }, [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- `Point`, `LineString`, `Polygon`, `MultiPoint`, `MultiLineString`, `MultiPolygon`, [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- `GeometryCollection`. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Coordinates are `[longitude, latitude]` (GeoJSON order — opposite of most map UIs). [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- 2dsphere supports Big Polygon (> 180°). Legacy `2d` indexes (flat earth) do not. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- `$geoNear` must be the **first stage** in an aggregation pipeline. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- -- [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Unique indexes enforce that no two documents share the same value for the indexed field(s). [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.users.createIndex({ email: 1 }, { unique: true }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Compound unique — combination must be unique, individual fields need not be [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.teamMembers.createIndex({ teamId: 1, userId: 1 }, { unique: true }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Partial unique — uniqueness only among documents matching the filter [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // (allows multiple docs with null email, but unique among those with email) [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.users.createIndex( [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- partialFilterExpression: { email: { $exists: true } } [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- A sparse unique index allows multiple documents to **omit** the field entirely while [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- enforcing uniqueness among those that have it. Partial unique is more expressive. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.users.createIndex({ phoneNumber: 1 }, { unique: true, sparse: true }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- MongoServerError: E11000 duplicate key error collection: mydb.users index: email_1 [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- dup key: { email: "user@example.com" } [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Handle with `{ upsert: true }` + `$setOnInsert` pattern, or use `writeConcern` + retry logic [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- for optimistic-concurrency scenarios. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- -- [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- MongoDB can combine two separate indexes at query time to satisfy a query that filters [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- on two different fields — without a compound index. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Two single-field indexes [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.orders.createIndex({ status: 1 }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.orders.createIndex({ customerId: 1 }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Query may trigger intersection [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.orders.find({ status: "pending", customerId: "abc" }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // explain() IXSCAN on each, then AND_SORTED or AND_HASH stage [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- MongoDB's query planner will choose intersection only when it estimates it to be faster [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- than either single index alone. In practice, a well-designed compound index almost always [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- outperforms intersection. Use `explain("executionStats")` to verify. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- **Index intersection does not work for sort.** If a query needs to sort, a compound index [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- covering equality + sort is required. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- -- [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Since 4.2, all index builds use a **hybrid** approach that replaced the old [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- foreground/background distinction: [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Takes an intent lock (not exclusive) during the bulk phase — reads and writes continue. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Briefly takes an exclusive lock at the start and end to set up/commit the index. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Progress is written to the oplog and replicated to secondaries automatically. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- > **`{ background: true }` is deprecated and ignored since MongoDB 4.2.** The option is [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- > accepted without error but has no effect — all builds now use the hybrid approach. Remove [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- > it from any legacy scripts to avoid confusion. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Default — hybrid build, replicated [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.orders.createIndex({ customerId: 1 }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // LEGACY (no-op since 4.2 — remove from new code): [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // db.orders.createIndex({ customerId: 1 }, { background: true }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Check build progress [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.currentOp({ op: "command", "command.createIndexes": { $exists: true } }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Kill a running build [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Rolling builds build the index on one member at a time (starting with secondaries), [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- avoiding the performance impact of a coordinated build: [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- **Manual rolling build steps:** [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Run `rs.freeze(300)` on the secondary to prevent it from calling elections during the procedure. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Remove it from the replica set with `rs.remove("<host:port>")`. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Restart `mongod` in standalone mode on a different port: `mongod --port 27217`. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Build the index: `db.collection.createIndex(...)` against the standalone instance. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Shut it down and restart as a replica set member; rejoin with `rs.add("<host:port>")`. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Repeat for each remaining secondary, then step down and reconfigure the primary. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- **Atlas rolling index:** [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- atlas api rollingIndex createRollingIndex \ [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- -projectId <projectId> \ [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- -clusterName <clusterName> \ [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- -key '{"field": "customerId", "type": "1"}' [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Rolling builds: lower performance impact, but reduced cluster resiliency during build. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Use when CPU > (N-1)/N-10% or WiredTiger cache fill > 90%. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Atlas provides in-UI index creation with rolling build toggle, performance advisor [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- recommendations, and redundant/unused index reporting. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- -- [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Selectivity measures what fraction of the collection an index scan must touch to answer a [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- query. **A highly selective index returns very few documents** (small fraction = high selectivity [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- = good). A low-selectivity index touches most of the collection, at which point a full [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- collection scan is often cheaper. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Estimate selectivity ratio [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- const total = db.orders.countDocuments(); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- const matching = db.orders.countDocuments({ status: "pending" }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- const ratio = matching / total; [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // ratio = 0.05 (5% of docs match) → high selectivity, index helps a lot [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // ratio = 0.80 (80% of docs match) → low selectivity, COLLSCAN may be faster [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- **Rule of thumb:** an index is beneficial when the ratio < ~20-30% of the collection. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Below that threshold, a collection scan is often faster due to document prefetching. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- A query is "covered" when all requested fields — both filter and projection — exist in [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- the index. MongoDB returns results **without touching the collection** (no FETCH stage). [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.users.createIndex({ country: 1, email: 1, name: 1 }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Covered query — all projected fields are in the index [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- { email: 1, name: 1, _id: 0 }   // _id must be explicitly excluded [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // explain() shows: "totalDocsExamined": 0, stage: "PROJECTION_COVERED" [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- **_id caveat:** `_id` is returned by default. If `_id` is not in the index, you must [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- exclude it with `_id: 0` to achieve a covering query. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.orders.find({ customerId: "abc" }).explain("executionStats"); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // executionStats.totalDocsExamined — 0 means covered [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // executionStats.totalKeysExamined — index entries scanned [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // executionStats.executionTimeMillis — wall time [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // winningPlan.stage — COLLSCAN, IXSCAN, FETCH, PROJECTION_COVERED [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // winningPlan.inputStage.indexName — which index was chosen [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- WiredTiger stores indexes in a B-tree. The working set of the index (frequently accessed [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- pages) should fit in the WiredTiger cache. Check: [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.orders.stats().indexSizes; [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // { "_id_": 12345, "customerId_1": 98765, ... } [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Indexes that do not fit in cache will cause disk I/O on every lookup — a common cause of [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- p99 latency spikes under load. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- -- [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Hidden indexes (MongoDB 4.4+) allow you to prevent the query planner from using an index [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- **without dropping it**. This lets you safely evaluate the impact of removing an index in [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- production before committing. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Hide an existing index — query planner ignores it immediately [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.orders.hideIndex("customerId_1"); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Create a new index already hidden (build it, but don't activate it yet) [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.orders.createIndex({ status: 1 }, { hidden: true }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Un-hide (re-activate) the index [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.orders.unhideIndex("status_1"); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Verify visibility — check "hidden" field in listIndexes output [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.orders.getIndexes(); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Hidden index shows: { ..., "hidden": true } [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Hide the candidate index with `hideIndex()`. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Monitor query performance for 24–72 hours (cover at least one full business cycle). [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Check `$indexStats` — confirm no queries are using the index. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- If performance is acceptable: drop it with `dropIndex()`. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- If performance degrades: `unhideIndex()` to restore instantly — no rebuild needed. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Hidden indexes still consume write overhead and storage — they are not free. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- `_id` index cannot be hidden. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Hidden indexes still count toward collection index limits — hiding is for testing removal impact, not for bypassing limits. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- -- [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Use `hint()` to override the query planner and force a specific index. Useful when the [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- planner makes a suboptimal choice or when testing index effectiveness. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Force by index key pattern [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.orders.find({ status: "pending" }).hint({ status: 1, createdAt: -1 }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Force by index name [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.orders.find({ status: "pending" }).hint("status_1_createdAt_-1"); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Force a collection scan (no index) [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.orders.find({ status: "pending" }).hint({ $natural: 1 }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- `hint()` bypasses the query planner entirely — if the hinted index does not contain the [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- query fields, MongoDB will still return correct results but may perform a full index scan [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- instead of an efficient point lookup, degrading performance. Always validate with `explain()` [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- after adding `hint()` to application code. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- > **Do not use `hint()` as a permanent fix.** If the planner consistently picks the wrong [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- > index, the root cause is usually a missing or mis-ordered compound index. Redesign the [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- > index using the ESR rule rather than patching with `hint()`. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- -- [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // List all indexes with access stats — run on each replica set member [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.orders.aggregate([{ $indexStats: {} }]); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Fields: name, host, accesses.ops (query count), accesses.since (reset timestamp) [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Zero-ops indexes that have existed for > 24h are candidates for removal [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Always check on secondaries too — replica sets may route reads differently [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Long-running update-heavy workloads can fragment B-tree pages. Use: [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.runCommand({ compact: "orders" }); [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // WARNING: Takes an exclusive lock on self-managed; avoid on primary [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Atlas: compact is triggered via Atlas UI or API without downtime [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- -- [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- Time series collections (MongoDB 5.0+) have a fundamentally different index model. **Use this section as a quick-reference when advising on indexes for a time series collection; defer to `mongodb-time-series` for full context.** [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- **Key differences from regular collection indexes:** [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- **Clustered range index (automatic):** MongoDB creates a compound clustered index on `(metaField, timeField)` automatically. This drives bucket-level pruning — queries that filter on `metaField` + `timeField` range use this index at the bucket level without needing an explicit secondary index. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- **Adding secondary indexes (compound pattern):** [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Best pattern: metaField sub-field first, timeField last [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.sensor_readings.createIndex({ "metadata.sensorId": 1, "timestamp": 1 }) [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- // Measurement field index (supported but rarely needed — bucket pruning handles time ranges) [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- db.sensor_readings.createIndex({ "metadata.location": 1, "temperature": 1 }) [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- **ESR rule still applies** to time series compound indexes on `metaField` sub-fields + measurement fields. Place equality fields first, sort fields second, range fields last. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]
- **TTL on time series** is set at collection level (`expireAfterSeconds` in `createCollection`) or modified via `collMod` — never via `createIndex`. Tiered TTL with `partialFilterExpression` on `metaField` is supported from MongoDB 7.0. [src: mongodb-indexes-deep]

- Comprehensive reference for monitoring MongoDB deployments — from Atlas built-in dashboards through third-party integrations, CLI tools, and low-level FTDC diagnostics. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **When to use this skill:** When answering questions about Atlas metrics, alert configuration, third-party monitoring integrations (Datadog, New Relic, Prometheus), FTDC diagnostics, slow query analysis, replication lag, connection pool behavior, or Atlas maintenance windows and planned operations. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **When not to use:** For Atlas Search index tuning (use `mongodb-search-ai`), Atlas cost optimization (use `mongodb-cost-optimization`), or backup/restore planning (use `mongodb-backup-restore`). [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Required roles for most monitoring operations:** `clusterMonitor` role on the `admin` database (self-managed), or Atlas `Project Read Only` / `Project Data Access Read Only` (Atlas UI). Third-party integrations (Datadog, Prometheus, New Relic) require Atlas `Project Owner` or `Organization Owner` to configure. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]

- -- [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Atlas provides real-time and historical metrics for every cluster tier M10 and above. Free/shared-tier clusters have reduced metric granularity (5-minute resolution vs. 1-minute for dedicated tiers). [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Opcounters** — insert, query, update, delete, getmore, command rates (ops/sec) [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **CPU / System** — process CPU, system CPU, I/O wait broken by read/write [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Memory** — resident, virtual, mapped, cache (WiredTiger block cache, dirty bytes) [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Disk I/O** — IOPS read/write, I/O utilization, disk queue depth [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Network** — bytes in/out, number of requests [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Connections** — current, available, total created [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Replication** — oplog window hours, replication headroom, replication lag per secondary [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Query targeting** — scanned/returned ratio (key indicator of missing indexes) [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Tickets** — WiredTiger concurrent read/write tickets in use vs. available [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Atlas dashboards are pre-built per cluster but allow: [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Pin metric charts to a custom "Metrics" view for side-by-side comparison across nodes [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Toggle between individual node view (per-host) and cluster aggregate view [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Adjust time range (1h, 8h, 24h, 48h, 1w, custom) [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Use the **Real-Time Performance Panel** (RTPP) for 1-second granularity on live traffic — available on M10+ in the Atlas UI under the cluster's **Real Time** tab [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- The RTPP shows: opcounters, read/write tickets, connections, network, logical size, and an interactive `currentOp` view showing the slowest in-flight operations per namespace. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- -- [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- > **Deep reference:** see `mongodb-ops-manager` for full coverage of App DB sizing/HA, Backup Daemon placement, automation goal-state, air-gap/Local Mode, Kubernetes Operator, federation, and Live Migration to Atlas. This section covers the monitoring agent surface only. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **MongoDB Ops Manager** is the on-premises deployment of MongoDB's management platform for teams running MongoDB in their own data centers or private clouds. **MongoDB Cloud Manager** is the hosted SaaS version of the same platform — it provides identical monitoring, automation, and backup capabilities without requiring you to host the Ops Manager application yourself. Both share the same agent architecture described below. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Runs as a daemon alongside your MongoDB processes [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Polls `serverStatus`, `replSetGetStatus`, `dbStats`, `collStats`, `currentOp` (filtered) at configurable intervals [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Stores time-series data in Ops Manager's own MongoDB backing store (separate from your application data) [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Sends alerts through Ops Manager's alert notification system — same alert types as Atlas [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Both platforms replicate Atlas-style metric dashboards inside the web UI. The topology view shows replica set health, node states (PRIMARY/SECONDARY/ARBITER), and replication lag per member. The **Hardware** tab surfaces CPU, disk IOPS, and memory at host level for correlation with MongoDB behavior. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- -- [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Project-level alerts** — apply to all clusters in a project (e.g., CPU > 80% on any node) [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Cluster-level alerts** — scoped to a specific cluster [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Billing alerts** — monthly spend thresholds, data transfer thresholds [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Set delay intervals** (e.g., "notify if condition persists for 5 minutes") to suppress transient spikes — CPU can spike briefly during flushes without being actionable [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **CPU alert baseline**: M10–M30 should alert at 75%; M50+ with sustained IOPS-heavy workloads often benefit from 85% thresholds with short delay [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Replication lag**: alert at 10–15 seconds for most OLTP workloads; 60 seconds for batch-heavy pipelines [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Oplog window**: never let it drop below 4 hours; alert at 48 hours to give time to investigate before backup windows are at risk [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Connection count**: alert at 80% of the cluster's `maxIncomingConnections`; calculate max from `db.adminCommand({getCmdLineOpts:1})` or Atlas connection string parameters [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]

- FTDC is MongoDB's always-on internal diagnostic system (enabled by default since MongoDB 3.2). It is the first artifact MongoDB Support requests for any performance investigation. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]

- **M0, M2, and M5 clusters do not support configurable maintenance windows.** Atlas manages all maintenance entirely, with no operator control over timing. These clusters may be restarted at any time. Upgrade to M10 or higher for maintenance window control. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- This is a common point of confusion — the project-level maintenance window setting applies only to dedicated-tier clusters (M10+). [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Atlas maintenance windows are configured at the **project level** and apply to all dedicated-tier (M10+) clusters within that project. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Location:** Atlas UI → **Project Settings** → **Maintenance Window** [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Default behavior:** When no custom window is configured, Atlas selects the window (commonly Tuesday 10:00–12:00 UTC for many regions). Configure an explicit window aligned with your lowest-traffic period for production workloads. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Configuring a custom window:** [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Choose day of week (Sunday through Saturday; Sunday=1 in the API/CLI, matching the integer table below) [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Choose start hour in UTC (0–23); the window is exactly 1 hour [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Changes take effect immediately and persist until cleared [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Important scope limitation:** Project-scoped, not per-cluster. To set different windows for dev vs. prod clusters, place them in separate Atlas projects. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Atlas CLI commands:** [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- atlas maintenanceWindows describe --projectId <projectId> [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- atlas maintenanceWindows update --dayOfWeek 1 --hourOfDay 2 --projectId <projectId> [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- atlas maintenanceWindows clear --projectId <projectId> [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Day-of-week values: Sunday=1, Monday=2, Tuesday=3, Wednesday=4, Thursday=5, Friday=6, Saturday=7. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Emergency security patches bypass the maintenance window entirely. Atlas notifies project and organization owners via email, but the window configuration does not constrain it. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Secondaries first** — one at a time, waiting for each to rejoin and catch up before proceeding. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Primary last** — triggers a replica set election. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Election window** — typically 10–30 seconds; writes temporarily unavailable, reads fall back to secondaries. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **mongos nodes (sharded clusters only)** — restarted last. Skip for replica-set-only deployments. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Application impact:** Drivers with retryable writes handle the election transparently. Applications without retryable writes may see one transient write failure. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Alert during maintenance:** The **"Primary election"** alert fires during every maintenance restart. Configure a lower-urgency channel for this alert type or correlate it with the maintenance window time. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Total duration:** 3-node replica set: 5–15 min. Sharded clusters: multiply per-shard restart time by shard count (30–60 min for large topologies). [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Deferral postpones by exactly **7 days**, once only per scheduled event [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- After one deferral, maintenance executes at the rescheduled time — no further deferral [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Critical security patches cannot be deferred** — attempting to defer returns an error [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- atlas maintenanceWindows defer --projectId <projectId> [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- POST /api/atlas/v2/groups/{groupId}/maintenanceWindow/defer [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- curl -u "{publicKey}:{privateKey}" --digest \ [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- "https://cloud.mongodb.com/api/atlas/v2/groups/{groupId}/maintenanceWindow" \ [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- H "Accept: application/vnd.atlas.2023-01-01+json" [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Response fields: `dayOfWeek` (1–7, absent if no custom window), `hourOfDay` (0–23 UTC), `startASAP` (maintenance queued for next opportunity), `autoDeferOnceEnabled`. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Same-day or next-day notice for critical CVEs; 24–48 hours for lower-severity updates [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Notifications sent to all Project Owners and Organization Owners [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Cannot be deferred; rolling restart procedure still used to minimize impact [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Monitor **Activity Feed** (Atlas UI → Project → Activity) for maintenance start/completion timestamps [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Why `serverSelectionTimeoutMS=30000` matters:** With 3000ms, a 12-second election causes `ServerSelectionTimeoutError` before the new primary is elected. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Post-election warm-up:** First queries to the new primary may be slower (30–60s) while connections re-establish and the WiredTiger cache warms. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Sequence: config server replica set (CSRS) → shard replica sets (sequentially) → mongos routers (parallel, stateless). [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Balancer:** suspended during maintenance; in-progress migrations complete, no new ones start. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Duration estimate:** per-shard restart time × shard count + CSRS + mongos. A 4-shard cluster at 10 min/shard ≈ 40–50 min for shards alone. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Replace all `[bracketed]` placeholders before sending. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Subject: Planned database maintenance — [Day, Month DD YYYY] [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Maintenance window: [Day of week, YYYY-MM-DD] [HH:MM]–[HH:MM] UTC [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Expected impact:    < 30 second connection interruption during primary election. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- No data loss will occur. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Action required:    None. Retryable writes handle this automatically. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Non-retryable operations may see one transient error. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Questions after [HH:MM] UTC: contact [support channel / Slack #channel]. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Placeholder guide:** `[HH:MM]–[HH:MM] UTC` = configured 1-hour window (e.g., "02:00–03:00 UTC"). Always include: specific UTC time window, < 30s impact (not full restart duration), explicit no-data-loss statement, retryable writes note, escalation path. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- <!-- Provenance: reference under the `mongodb-expert` hub. Mirrored from ~/.claude/skills/mongodb-expert/references/mongodb-geospatial.md by scripts/persist-spoke.mjs. --> [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- Use when designing or troubleshooting MongoDB geospatial queries, indexes, or data models. Covers GeoJSON storage, 2dsphere and 2d index types, proximity and containment operators ($near, $geoWithin, $geoNear, $geoIntersects), radius calculations, $lookup pipeline joins across spatial collections, and common anti-patterns. Apply this skill whenever a schema includes location fields, a query filters by distance or bounding region, or a $geoNear aggregation stage needs tuning. [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- -- [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- MongoDB natively stores and queries the GeoJSON spec. Every GeoJSON field is an embedded document with a `type` string and a `coordinates` array. **Longitude always comes before latitude** — the opposite of most mapping UIs. [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- // Point — single location [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- { type: "Point", coordinates: [-73.9857, 40.7484] }   // [lng, lat] [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- // LineString — ordered sequence of positions [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- // Polygon — closed ring; first and last coordinate must be equal [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- { type: "MultiPoint", coordinates: [[-73.98, 40.75], [-74.01, 40.71]] } [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- type: "MultiLineString", [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- type: "MultiPolygon", [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- // GeometryCollection — heterogeneous mix [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- type: "GeometryCollection", [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- { type: "Point",      coordinates: [-73.9857, 40.7484] }, [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- { type: "LineString", coordinates: [[-73.98, 40.75], [-74.00, 40.72]] } [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- Insert a document with a GeoJSON Point field: [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- db.places.insertOne({ [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- name: "Empire State Building", [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- location: { type: "Point", coordinates: [-73.9857, 40.7484] }, [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- -- [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- A **2dsphere** index supports queries on GeoJSON geometry computed over a sphere modelled on WGS84 (the same datum used by GPS). Version 3 has been the default since MongoDB 3.2; MongoDB 8.3+ defaults to version 4. It handles Points, LineStrings, and Polygons stored as GeoJSON and supports all geospatial query operators. [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- // Basic 2dsphere index on a GeoJSON field [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- db.places.createIndex({ location: "2dsphere" }); [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- // Compound index — location plus a scalar field [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- db.places.createIndex({ location: "2dsphere", category: 1 }); [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- // Check the index was created correctly [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- db.places.getIndexes(); [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- // → { "key": { "location": "2dsphere" }, "name": "location_2dsphere", "2dsphereIndexVersion": 3 } [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- // Specify index version explicitly (rarely needed) [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- db.places.createIndex({ location: "2dsphere" }, { "2dsphereIndexVersion": 3 }); [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- Handles wraparound at the anti-meridian (180° longitude) correctly. [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- Required by `$geoNear`, `$near`, `$nearSphere`, `$geoWithin` with `$centerSphere`. [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- 2dsphere indexes are **always sparse** (MongoDB ignores the `sparse` option). A document missing the geo field — or where it is `null` or an empty array — is not indexed, whether the index is standalone or compound. In a compound 2dsphere index, only the geo field determines whether a document is indexed. [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- -- [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- A **2d** index uses planar (flat-earth) geometry. It is a legacy index type intended for coordinate pairs stored as `[lng, lat]` arrays (not GeoJSON documents). Use it only when the coordinate space is genuinely flat (e.g., game maps, CAD drawings, grid systems) and spherical correction is not needed. [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- // Legacy coordinate pair stored as an array [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- db.legacy.insertOne({ name: "HQ", loc: [-73.98, 40.75] }); [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- db.legacy.createIndex({ loc: "2d" }); [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- // Optional: define the bounding box and granularity [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- db.legacy.createIndex({ loc: "2d" }, { min: -180, max: 180, bits: 26 }); [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- // $near on a 2d index — returns sorted by distance, Euclidean [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- db.legacy.find({ loc: { $near: [-73.98, 40.75], $maxDistance: 0.5 } }); [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- Limitations vs. 2dsphere: [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- No polygon-edge wraparound. [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- Distance unit is degrees, not metres. [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- Does not support GeoJSON input documents. [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- Cannot use `$geoNear` aggregation with `spherical: true`. [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- -- [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- `$geoNear` must be the **first stage** of an aggregation pipeline. It returns documents sorted by computed distance from a reference point and appends the distance value to each document under `distanceField`. A geospatial index is required; if multiple exist, specify `key`. [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- db.places.aggregate([ [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- near: { type: "Point", coordinates: [-73.9857, 40.7484] }, [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- distanceField: "dist.calculated",   // field added to output docs [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- maxDistance: 2000,                  // metres (spherical: true) [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- query: { category: "restaurant" },  // pre-filter before distance [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- spherical: true,                    // required for 2dsphere index [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- key: "location"                     // required when > 1 geo index exists [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- { $project: { name: 1, "dist.calculated": 1, _id: 0 } } [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- `distanceMultiplier` converts metres to another unit: [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- near: { type: "Point", coordinates: [-73.9857, 40.7484] }, [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- distanceField: "distKm", [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- distanceMultiplier: 0.001,   // metres → kilometres [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- `includeLocs` records the matched location field alongside distance: [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- { $geoNear: { ..., includeLocs: "matchedLocation", spherical: true } } [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- -- [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- `$geoWithin` finds documents whose geometry is **entirely contained within** a specified shape. It does not sort results and does not require a geospatial index (though an index improves performance significantly on large collections). [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- // Within a GeoJSON Polygon [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- // $centerSphere — circle on a sphere; radius in radians [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- // radians = distanceKm / 6378.1 [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- $centerSphere: [ [-73.9857, 40.7484], radiusKm / 6378.1 ] [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- // $box — planar rectangle (2d index only) [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- db.legacy.find({ loc: { $geoWithin: { $box: [[-74.1, 40.6], [-73.8, 40.9]] } } }); [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- // $polygon — planar polygon (2d index only) [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- db.legacy.find({ loc: { $geoWithin: { $polygon: [[-74, 40.7], [-73.9, 40.7], [-73.95, 40.85]] } } }); [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- -- [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- `$geoIntersects` finds documents whose GeoJSON geometry **intersects** — shares any point with — the query geometry. Useful for routes, delivery zones, and region overlap checks. Requires a 2dsphere index for good performance. [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- // Find all routes that pass through a query polygon [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- // Find zones that contain a specific point (point in polygon) [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- $geometry: { type: "Point", coordinates: [-73.9857, 40.7484] } [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- // Works with LineString query geometry too [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- coordinates: [[-74.0, 40.7], [-73.9, 40.8]] [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- -- [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- `$near` and `$nearSphere` are **query operators** (not aggregation stages). Both sort results by distance and **require a geospatial index**. They cannot be used inside `$or` or `$and` alongside other `$near`/`$nearSphere` expressions. [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- // $near with GeoJSON (requires 2dsphere index, metres) [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- $geometry: { type: "Point", coordinates: [-73.9857, 40.7484] }, [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- $maxDistance: 1500,   // metres [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- $minDistance: 100     // metres [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- // $nearSphere with GeoJSON (spherical interpretation, metres) [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- $geometry: { type: "Point", coordinates: [-73.9857, 40.7484] }, [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- // $near with legacy coordinate pair (2d index, degrees) [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- loc: { $near: [-73.98, 40.75], $maxDistance: 0.5 } [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- // Combine with additional filter fields [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- $geometry: { type: "Point", coordinates: [-73.9857, 40.7484] }, [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- **$near vs. $geoNear:** Use `$near` for a simple `.find()` that returns sorted documents. Use `$geoNear` when you need the distance value in the result, further pipeline stages, or more control (distanceMultiplier, query pre-filter, key selection). [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- -- [src: mongodb-geospatial]

- function kmToRadians(km) { return km / 6378.1; } [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- function milesToRadians(mi) { return mi / 3963.2; } [src: mongodb-geospatial]

- Geospatial query operators (`$geoIntersects`, `$geoWithin`, `$near`) are **query operators, not aggregation expression operators** — they cannot be used inside `$expr`. Inside a `$lookup` pipeline stage, place them directly inside `$match` against a field in the **joined** collection. The outer document's location must be supplied via `$geoNear` output or by denormalizing the coordinate. [src: mongodb-geospatial]

- // (most scalable; spatial work happens in the first stage against the driving collection) [src: mongodb-geospatial]

- near: { type: "Point", coordinates: [-73.9857, 40.7484] }, [src: mongodb-geospatial]

- localField: "zoneId",    // scalar ID pre-assigned at write time [src: mongodb-geospatial]

- db.orders.aggregate([ [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- $geometry: { type: "Point", coordinates: [-73.9857, 40.7484] } [src: mongodb-geospatial]

- boundary: { $geoIntersects: { $geometry: point } } [src: mongodb-geospatial]

- Performance considerations for geospatial $lookup: [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- `$geoIntersects` / `$geoWithin` inside a `$lookup` pipeline runs once per driving document; ensure a 2dsphere index on the joined collection's geometry field. [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- Add a `$match` with a bounding-box `$geoWithin` before `$lookup` to narrow candidates when the joined collection is large. [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- Denormalizing the zone or region ID at write time (Recommended pattern above) eliminates the per-row geo scan entirely and scales best. [src: mongodb-geospatial]
- For hot-path proximity queries at scale, consider Atlas Search `$search` with a `geoWithin` or `geoShape` filter, which uses a dedicated search index and avoids aggregation pipeline overhead. [src: mongodb-geospatial]

- Atlas Stream Processing (ASP) is a fully managed, Atlas-native stream processing engine that lets you build real-time data pipelines using MQL-compatible aggregation syntax — without operating separate Kafka Streams or Flink infrastructure. [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- Real-time alerting, IoT analytics, fraud detection [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- Near-real-time materialized views [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- CDC fan-out from MongoDB Atlas [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- Event-driven enrichment and transformation [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- **When NOT to use ASP:** [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- Batch re-processing of finite historical datasets → scheduled aggregation pipelines or Atlas Data Federation [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- Kafka Connect-only pipelines with no ASP involvement → mongodb-kafka-connector [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- Spark Structured Streaming → mongodb-spark-connector [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- Complex stateful ML inference requiring Flink [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- Sources (Kafka / Atlas Change Stream) [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- $source stage (connect to registry entry) [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- Pipeline stages ($match, $addFields, $lookup, $merge, etc.) [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- $emit stage (write to Atlas collection or Kafka topic) [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- Each **Stream Processor** is a named pipeline with exactly one `$source` and one `$emit`. Processors run continuously in the background. [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- Before writing processors, register connections to data sources/sinks: [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]

- Stream Processing Instances (SPIs) are priced per instance-hour: [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- Measure peak message rate × average message size [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- Add 2-3x headroom for burst [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- Windowed aggregations require more memory → prefer SP10+ for windowed pipelines [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- Multiple simultaneous processors share the SPI's capacity [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- ASP uses **event-time watermarks** for windowed processing: [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- { "$tumblingWindow": { [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- "interval": { "size": 5, "unit": "minute" }, [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- "watermark": { "field": "$eventTimestamp", "allowedLateness": { "size": 30, "unit": "second" } }, [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- `allowedLateness`: grace period for late-arriving events. Events arriving after the watermark + lateness are dropped to the DLQ. [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- // Check processor stats from mongosh connected to the Stream Processing instance [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]

- // Check consumer lag (Kafka source) [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- db.adminCommand({ "streams": "stats", "processor": "myProcessor" }) [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- **Key metrics in Atlas UI:** [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- Consumer lag (Kafka) — growing lag = processor can't keep up with source throughput [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- Error rate — check DLQ for failed events [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- Processing latency — end-to-end from source to emit [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- **Decision rule:** If you're already on Atlas and need real-time processing without operating infrastructure, use ASP. Use Kafka Connector when you need MongoDB as a source/sink in an existing Kafka ecosystem. Use Flink for complex stateful computation. [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- **Single SPI for all processing:** Separate high-priority from low-priority processors across different SPIs [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- **Windowed aggregation without watermarks:** Late events cause incorrect window results [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- **No DLQ configured:** Failed events are silently dropped without `$validate` + `allowedLateness` [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- **Growing consumer lag left unchecked:** Indicates SPI undersized for throughput; upgrade tier [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]
- **Using ASP for batch re-processing:** ASP is for continuous streams — use Data Federation for historical batch [src: mongodb-atlas-stream-processing]

- **`match` expression:** Pre-filters change events BEFORE the function is invoked. Filtered events do NOT count as billable requests. Use aggressive match expressions to reduce cost. [src: mongodb-atlas-triggers-functions]
- **`unordered: true`:** Events processed out of order (higher throughput but no ordering guarantee). Default `false` = in-order per document. [src: mongodb-atlas-triggers-functions]
- **`full_document: true`:** Includes the complete document after the change. Required to access document fields in the function. Adds ~10-20ms latency vs `false`. [src: mongodb-atlas-triggers-functions]
- **`full_document_before_change: true`:** Includes the document state before the change. Requires enabling preImages on the collection (`changeStreamPreAndPostImages: { enabled: true }`). [src: mongodb-atlas-triggers-functions]

- <!-- Provenance: reference under the `mongodb-expert` hub. Mirrored from ~/.claude/skills/mongodb-expert/references/mongodb-transactions.md by scripts/persist-spoke.mjs. --> [src: mongodb-transactions]
- -- [src: mongodb-transactions]
- MongoDB added multi-document ACID transactions in **4.0 (replica sets)** and extended them to **sharded clusters in 4.2**. Before 4.0, atomicity was limited to single-document operations (which remain the preferred approach for most use cases). [src: mongodb-transactions]
- **ACID guarantees provided:** [src: mongodb-transactions]
- **Atomicity** — all writes in the transaction commit together or all are rolled back [src: mongodb-transactions]
- **Consistency** — data is moved from one valid state to another; session-level causal consistency is maintained [src: mongodb-transactions]
- **Isolation** — snapshot isolation: the transaction sees a consistent snapshot of data as of the transaction start; no dirty reads, no non-repeatable reads [src: mongodb-transactions]
- **Durability** — committed data survives node failures when `w: "majority"` is used [src: mongodb-transactions]
- **Snapshot isolation** is the default isolation level since 4.0. Within a transaction, a client sees the data as it existed at transaction start, even if concurrent writers commit changes. This avoids dirty reads and non-repeatable reads but can cause write conflicts (two transactions modifying the same document — the second writer's commit or a read-write conflict will abort one of them). [src: mongodb-transactions]

- -- [src: mongodb-transactions]
- Since MongoDB 4.2, multi-document transactions work across shards using **two-phase commit (2PC)**. [src: mongodb-transactions]
- When a transaction touches multiple shards, the `mongos` router designates one of the participant shards as the **coordinator** (the shard that receives the first write). The coordinator: [src: mongodb-transactions]
- **Prepare phase** — sends `prepareTransaction` to all participant shards; each shard locks its data and votes yes/no [src: mongodb-transactions]
- **Commit phase** — if all shards vote yes, coordinator sends `commitTransaction` to all; if any vote no, sends `abortTransaction` [src: mongodb-transactions]
- The coordinator's decision is durable in `config.transactions` so recovery is possible after coordinator failure. [src: mongodb-transactions]
- // Sharded cluster transaction — same driver API; MongoDB routes internally [src: mongodb-transactions]
- const session = client.startSession(); [src: mongodb-transactions]
- await session.withTransaction(async (session) => { [src: mongodb-transactions]
- // orders collection on shard A, inventory on shard B [src: mongodb-transactions]
- const orders = client.db("shop").collection("orders"); [src: mongodb-transactions]
- const inventory = client.db("shop").collection("inventory"); [src: mongodb-transactions]
- await orders.insertOne( [src: mongodb-transactions]
- { _id: new ObjectId(), customerId: "c1", sku: "sku-99", qty: 2 }, [src: mongodb-transactions]

- { $inc: { available: -2 } }, [src: mongodb-transactions]
- }, { writeConcern: { w: "majority" } }); [src: mongodb-transactions]
- await session.endSession(); [src: mongodb-transactions]
- **Performance cost vs. replica set transactions:** [src: mongodb-transactions]
- 2PC adds at least one extra round-trip (prepare → commit) per participating shard [src: mongodb-transactions]
- Each shard holds WiredTiger write locks during the prepare phase [src: mongodb-transactions]
- Cross-shard transactions are 2–4× slower than replica set transactions under load [src: mongodb-transactions]
- Prefer co-locating transactional data on the same shard (zone sharding, compound shard keys) to avoid cross-shard transactions [src: mongodb-transactions]

- **Snapshot isolation detail:** [src: mongodb-transactions]
- MongoDB picks a `clusterTime` at transaction start as the snapshot point [src: mongodb-transactions]
- Reads within the transaction consistently see the state as of that clusterTime [src: mongodb-transactions]
- If the snapshot falls behind the oldest in-use WiredTiger snapshot, MongoDB will abort the transaction with `SnapshotTooOld` (increase `wiredTigerCacheSizeGB` or reduce long-running transactions) [src: mongodb-transactions]

- -- [src: mongodb-transactions]
- Write concern on a transaction applies at **commit time** — it controls how many replica set members must acknowledge the commit before the driver considers it successful. [src: mongodb-transactions]
- // Recommended production write concern [src: mongodb-transactions]
- session.startTransaction({ [src: mongodb-transactions]
- readConcern: { level: "snapshot" }, [src: mongodb-transactions]
- w: "majority",    // majority of voting members must acknowledge [src: mongodb-transactions]
- j: true,          // commit must be written to journal (fsync) [src: mongodb-transactions]
- wtimeout: 5000    // abort if majority ack not received within 5 seconds [src: mongodb-transactions]
- **Write concern levels:** [src: mongodb-transactions]
- **`j: true` (journaled):** [src: mongodb-transactions]
- Ensures the commit is written to the on-disk journal before returning success [src: mongodb-transactions]
- Protects against data loss from process crash (but not disk failure) [src: mongodb-transactions]

- No fixed cap on the number of operations (reads + writes) per transaction; the practical limit is oplog size and WiredTiger cache pressure (see below). - **Key characteristics:** [src: mongodb-atlas-charts]
- No driver required; reads directly from the cluster via Atlas data-access path [src: mongodb-atlas-charts]
- Real-time queries — each chart load triggers a live aggregation query [src: mongodb-atlas-charts]
- No separate cluster: reads from the cluster you designate as a data source [src: mongodb-atlas-charts]
- Sub-100ms live refresh → Grafana + Atlas monitoring panels [src: mongodb-atlas-charts]

- Complex cross-cluster joins → Atlas Data Federation + dedicated BI tool [src: mongodb-atlas-charts]
- Streaming / CDC visualization → Charts is not designed for event-stream display [src: mongodb-atlas-charts]

- **Federated data sources:** Atlas Data Federation can expose S3/Azure Blob/GCS/BigQuery. Federated queries are slower — avoid live-dashboard use cases requiring sub-second render times over S3-backed sources. [src: mongodb-atlas-charts]

- Atlas capacity planning covers four primary resources: RAM (working set), IOPS, storage, and connections. Getting these right prevents both over-provisioning (wasted cost) and under-provisioning (performance degradation). [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- The working set is the set of indexes + active document data that MongoDB keeps in WiredTiger cache. When the working set fits in RAM, queries are fast. When it doesn't, cache eviction causes disk I/O spikes. [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- **Rule of thumb:** Atlas WiredTiger cache = 50% of RAM − 1 GB. An M30 (8 GB RAM) provides ~3 GB of WiredTiger cache. [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- // mongosh: get index sizes [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- db.collection.stats().indexSizes [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- Object.entries(db.collection.stats().indexSizes) [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- .map(([name, size]) => ({ name, sizeMB: size / 1024 / 1024 })) [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- // Get collection size [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- db.collection.stats().size  // bytes of data [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- db.collection.stats().storageSize  // bytes on disk (compressed) [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- **Working set = frequently accessed document data + all active indexes** [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- Indexes must always be hot (in WiredTiger cache). If total index size > cache, performance degrades severely. [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- **Cache Utilization (%):** > 80% signals working set doesn't fit in RAM [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- **Page Faults:** > 0 steady-state = working set pressure; growing = critical [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- **WiredTiger Cache Dirty Bytes:** Consistently high = eviction pressure [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- **GP3 note:** All GP3 volumes provide 3000 IOPS baseline regardless of size. For higher IOPS, upgrade to NVMe-backed tiers (M60+) or enable Provisioned IOPS (significant cost increase). [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- IOPS demand = (write ops/sec × avg document size / 4 KB) × write amplification [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- Write amplification = typically 3-5x for WiredTiger (journaling + checkpoint + compression). [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- **Atlas metrics to watch:** [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- **Disk IOPS Utilization:** > 80% = IOPS exhaustion risk [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- **Disk Queue Depth:** > 1 = IOPS saturation [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- // Current rate of growth [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- db.runCommand({ dbStats: 1, scale: 1024 * 1024 })  // MB [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- // Track storageSize over time to get growth rate [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- // Atlas metric: "Disk Usage" — daily reading [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- storage at T+months = current_storage × (1 + monthly_growth_rate)^months [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- Add 25% headroom for index growth and temporary operations. [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- Atlas can auto-scale storage. Enable in cluster configuration → Autoscaling → Storage. Atlas automatically adds storage when utilization exceeds 90%. Note: storage autoscaling is one-directional (up only). [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- Oplog is a capped collection used for replication. Default size: 5% of available disk space (minimum 990 MB, maximum 50 GB). [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- **Oplog window** = how far back a secondary can fall behind before needing a full resync. [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- // Check oplog window [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- rs.printReplicationInfo() [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- // "oplog first event time" to "last event time" = current window [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- **Increase oplog** if: [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- Secondaries frequently fall behind (replication lag spikes) [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- Maintenance windows require > current oplog window [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- High write rate + slow secondaries [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- **Per-node limits:** The above are per-node limits. A 3-node replica set has 3× per-node connections available (reads can go to secondaries). [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- Client applications should use connection pooling. Default pool size in most drivers = 100 connections per MongoClient. [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- max_connections_needed = (application_instances × connection_pool_size) + 20% headroom [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- For serverless/Lambda: set `maxPoolSize: 5-10` per function to prevent connection floods. [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- Enable in cluster configuration → Autoscaling → Compute. [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- Atlas auto-scales up based on: [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- Average CPU > 75% over the past hour [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- Memory utilization > 90% [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- Atlas auto-scales down based on: [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- Average CPU < 25% over the past 24 hours [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- Configure min/max tier bounds to control costs. [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- Consider sharding when **ALL** of the following are true: [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- Single M60+ cluster is consistently maxed on CPU or IOPS [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- Working set won't fit in even the largest single Atlas tier [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- The workload has a natural shard key with good cardinality [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- **Do NOT shard prematurely:** Sharding adds operational complexity and scatter-gather query overhead. Exhaust vertical scaling options first. [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- Atlas Performance Advisor (M10+ only) automatically analyzes slow queries (> 100ms by default) and recommends indexes. [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- atlas clusters advancedSettings describe myCluster [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- atlas performanceAdvisor slowQueryLogs list --clusterName myCluster [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- atlas performanceAdvisor suggestedIndexes list --clusterName myCluster [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- **Sizing for peak without autoscaling:** Most apps have 5-10x peak-to-baseline ratios; use autoscaling [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- **Ignoring index memory:** Indexes must be hot; total index size often exceeds "active document" working set estimate [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- **Underestimating connection count in serverless environments:** Lambda × 100 connections/pool = connection flood [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- **Sizing storage on current data only:** Model 12-month projected growth + retention policies [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- **Choosing M10 for Vector Search in production:** mongot and mongod share resources; upgrade to M30+ with dedicated Search Nodes [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- **Not setting a connection pool max in containerized apps:** Each container starts 100 connections; multiply by container count [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- Link: [Atlas Cluster Sizing](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/scale-cluster/) [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- Link: [Atlas Autoscaling](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/cluster-autoscaling/) [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]
- Link: [Atlas Performance Advisor](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/performance-advisor/) [src: mongodb-capacity-planning]

- Two distinct approaches for SQL-based BI tool integration with MongoDB: [src: mongodb-bi-connector]

- **Atlas SQL Interface (current):** Managed service via Atlas Data Federation. Certified connectors for Tableau and Power BI. [src: mongodb-bi-connector]
