- <!-- Provenance: reference under the `mongodb-expert` hub. Mirrored from ~/.claude/skills/mongodb-expert/references/mongodb-time-series.md by scripts/persist-spoke.mjs. --> [src: mongodb-time-series]
- MongoDB Time Series Collections, introduced in MongoDB 5.0 (GA), are a specialized collection type optimized for time-stamped measurement data. They use an internal columnar storage format with automatic bucketing, delta encoding, and Zstd compression to achieve 50-90% storage reduction over regular collections while dramatically improving query performance for time-range access patterns. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Time series collections are the preferred choice over the manual bucket pattern for IoT sensor data, server metrics, financial tick data, application events, observability signals, and any domain where data is appended in timestamp order and queried by time range. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- > **Skill boundaries:** [src: mongodb-time-series]
- > - Use this skill (`mongodb-time-series`) for: collection creation options, bucket internals, TTL, time-series-specific index constraints, $densify/$fill/$dateTrunc/$setWindowFields in a time-series context, Atlas triggers/change-stream limitations, migration, sharding for time series, and performance sizing. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- > - Use `mongodb-aggregation-pipeline` for: general pipeline stage design, $lookup, $merge/$out to regular collections, explain profiling, memory/allowDiskUse tuning. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- > - Use `mongodb-schema-design` for: the manual bucket pattern, embedding vs referencing decisions, general IoT schema modeling without the native time series collection type. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- > - Use `mongodb-indexes-deep` for: ESR compound index design, partial/sparse/wildcard/text index types on regular collections. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Version timeline:** [src: mongodb-time-series]
- MongoDB 5.0: Initial release (create, insert, query, TTL, basic indexing) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- MongoDB 5.1: $densify aggregation stage [src: mongodb-time-series]
- MongoDB 5.2: Columnar compression format (major storage improvement) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- MongoDB 5.3: $fill aggregation stage [src: mongodb-time-series]
- MongoDB 6.0: partial index support with $or/$in/$geoWithin [src: mongodb-time-series]
- MongoDB 6.3: Custom bucketing parameters (`bucketMaxSpanSeconds`, `bucketRoundingSeconds`) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- MongoDB 7.0: $out can write to time series collections; TTL partial filter on metaField [src: mongodb-time-series]
- MongoDB 8.0: Block processing — direct write into column-compressed format (2-3x throughput, 10-20x cache reduction); timeField shard key deprecated [src: mongodb-time-series]
- MongoDB 8.3: timeField cannot start with `$`; creating `"_id_"` index returns error [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Atlas (2023+): Atlas Stream Processing introduced — time series collections can be a *sink* but not a `$source` (no change stream support) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [MongoDB Time Series Documentation](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries-collections/) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [MongoDB 8.0 Block Processing Blog](https://www.mongodb.com/company/blog/technical/key-enhancements-mongodb-8-0-block-processing) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [Columnar Storage Cost Savings Blog](https://www.mongodb.com/company/blog/technical/columnar-storage-time-series-collection-cost-savings) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- -- [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Time series collections are created with `db.createCollection()` using a `timeseries` subdocument. The `timeField` is the only required parameter; all others are optional but significantly affect performance. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- db.createCollection("sensor_readings", { [src: mongodb-time-series]
- timeField: "timestamp",        // REQUIRED: must be a Date field [src: mongodb-time-series]
- metaField: "metadata",         // OPTIONAL but strongly recommended [src: mongodb-time-series]
- granularity: "seconds",        // "seconds" | "minutes" | "hours" [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // MongoDB 6.3+: custom bucketing (overrides granularity) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- bucketMaxSpanSeconds: 3600, [src: mongodb-time-series]
- bucketRoundingSeconds: 3600, [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // MongoDB 5.0+: automatic TTL [src: mongodb-time-series]
- expireAfterSeconds: 2592000    // 30 days [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Parameter reference:** [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Granularity and bucket time spans:** [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Changing parameters after creation:** Use `collMod` to update `granularity`, `bucketMaxSpanSeconds`, `bucketRoundingSeconds`, and `expireAfterSeconds`. You can only **increase** bucket span, never decrease it. `timeField` and `metaField` are permanently immutable. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // Increase granularity (allowed) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- collMod: "sensor_readings", [src: mongodb-time-series]
- timeseries: { granularity: "minutes" } [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // Set custom bucketing (MongoDB 6.3+) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- collMod: "sensor_readings", [src: mongodb-time-series]
- bucketMaxSpanSeconds: 86400, [src: mongodb-time-series]
- bucketRoundingSeconds: 86400 [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [Time Series Considerations](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-considerations/) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [Create and Query Procedures v7.0](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v7.0/core/timeseries/timeseries-procedures/) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [Community: Granularity and metaField](https://www.mongodb.com/community/forums/t/timeseries-collections-in-mongodb-granularity-and-metafield/222943) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- -- [src: mongodb-time-series]
- MongoDB stores time series documents in internal `system.buckets.<collectionName>` bucket documents, not as individual BSON records. The view layer (`<collectionName>`) presents unpacked measurements to applications. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Bucket structure:** [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // Internal bucket document (system.buckets.sensor_readings) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- "_id": ObjectId("..."), [src: mongodb-time-series]
- "_id": ObjectId("..."), [src: mongodb-time-series]
- "timestamp": ISODate("2024-01-01T00:00:00.000Z"), [src: mongodb-time-series]
- "_id": ObjectId("..."), [src: mongodb-time-series]
- "timestamp": ISODate("2024-01-01T00:59:59.000Z"), [src: mongodb-time-series]
- "meta": { "sensorId": "A42", "location": "building-3" }, [src: mongodb-time-series]
- "timestamp": { "0": ISODate("..."), "1": ISODate("..."), ... }, [src: mongodb-time-series]
- "temperature": { "0": 18.2, "1": 18.5, ... }, [src: mongodb-time-series]
- "humidity": { "0": 61, "1": 62, ... } [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Bucket lifecycle:** [src: mongodb-time-series]
- A bucket is opened when the first measurement for a given `metaField` value arrives. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- A bucket is **closed** when it reaches either ~1,000 measurements OR ~125 KB, whichever comes first, or when the bucket's time span limit (determined by granularity) is exceeded. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Closed buckets are compressed and eligible for WiredTiger cache eviction. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Compression mechanisms (MongoDB 5.2+):** [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Column-oriented storage**: Values for each field (temperature, humidity, pressure) are stored together rather than per-document. This enables delta encoding and RLE to be applied across entire columns. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Delta encoding**: Stores the first value absolutely, then subsequent values as differences (`+0.1`, `-0.2`). Highly effective for monotonic timestamps and slowly changing sensor readings. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Run-Length Encoding (RLE)**: Repeated values (e.g., `status: "active"` for 1,000 measurements) stored as `(value, count)`. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Metadata deduplication**: Field names and BSON types stored once per bucket rather than per document. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Zstd block compression** (WiredTiger level): Applied on top of the already column-compressed data. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **MongoDB 8.0 block processing**: Documents are written directly into column-compressed format, eliminating the decompression-recompression cycle on write. This results in 2-3x write throughput improvement and 10-20x cache usage reduction compared to MongoDB 7.0 for time series workloads. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [Columnar Storage Blog](https://www.mongodb.com/company/blog/technical/columnar-storage-time-series-collection-cost-savings) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [Time Series Compression](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-compression/) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [High vs Low Ingestion Study](https://www.mongodb.com/company/blog/technical/a-practical-study-of-mongodb-time-series-bucket-behavior) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [MongoDB 8.0 Block Processing](https://dev.to/mongodb/supercharging-time-series-collections-key-enhancements-in-mongodb-80-with-block-processing-5b3i) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- -- [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Time series collections index at the bucket level, not the document level. The `control.min` and `control.max` values on each bucket function as a clustered range index that enables bucket-level pruning for time-range queries. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Default clustered index:** A clustered index on the `metaField` and `timeField` is automatically created. No explicit `_id` index is created (unlike regular collections). In MongoDB 5.0, only a single compound index on `metaField` + `timeField` was supported; secondary indexes on measurement fields were added in later versions. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- > **Skill boundary:** For general compound index design (ESR rule, multikey, partial, sparse, wildcard), use `mongodb-indexes-deep`. This section covers only time-series-specific index constraints and patterns. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Supported secondary index types:** [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Adding a compound secondary index:** [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // Index for queries filtering by sensor + time range [src: mongodb-time-series]
- db.sensor_readings.createIndex( [src: mongodb-time-series]
- { "metadata.sensorId": 1, "timestamp": 1 } [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // Index on measurement field (metaField sub-field + measurement) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- db.sensor_readings.createIndex( [src: mongodb-time-series]
- { "metadata.location": 1, "temperature": 1 } [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // TTL partial filter on metaField (MongoDB 7.0+) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- db.sensor_readings.createIndex( [src: mongodb-time-series]
- expireAfterSeconds: 86400, [src: mongodb-time-series]
- partialFilterExpression: { "metadata.tier": "free" } [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Key indexing constraints:** [src: mongodb-time-series]
- `partialFilterExpression` can only reference the `metaField` (not measurement fields). [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Unique indexes are not supported — duplicate prevention must be handled at the application layer or using `$match` + `$group` in aggregation. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Text indexes are not supported — consider Atlas Search for full-text needs. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- The `distinct()` command is not efficiently supported; use `$group` with a supporting compound index instead. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Query on object metaField — use sub-field dot notation:** [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // GOOD: queries a scalar sub-field [src: mongodb-time-series]
- db.sensor_readings.find({ "metadata.sensorId": "A42" }) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // BAD: queries the entire metaField object (no index benefit) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- db.sensor_readings.find({ metadata: { sensorId: "A42", location: "b3" } }) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [Time Series Indexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-index/) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [Add Secondary Indexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index/) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [Time Series Limitations](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-limitations/) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- -- [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Time series collections support bucket-granularity TTL via `expireAfterSeconds`. Unlike regular collection TTL indexes (which delete individual documents), TTL on time series collections deletes entire buckets once all measurements within the bucket are older than the threshold. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- db.createCollection("metrics", { [src: mongodb-time-series]
- granularity: "minutes", [src: mongodb-time-series]
- expireAfterSeconds: 604800   // 7 days [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Modify after creation (cannot use createIndex):** [src: mongodb-time-series]
- expireAfterSeconds: 2592000    // change to 30 days [src: mongodb-time-series]
- The background TTL task runs every 60 seconds. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- A bucket is deleted only when **all** measurements in that bucket have expired (i.e., `control.max.timestamp + expireAfterSeconds < now`). [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Because of bucket aggregation, actual deletion may be delayed by up to bucket-span + 60s after expiration. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- A bucket created with `granularity: "hours"` covering a 30-day span won't be deleted until all 30 days of measurements within it have expired. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Tiered TTL pattern (MongoDB 7.0+ with partial filter):** [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // Different retention for free vs. paid tier sensors [src: mongodb-time-series]
- db.metrics.createIndex( [src: mongodb-time-series]
- expireAfterSeconds: 86400,    // 1 day for free tier [src: mongodb-time-series]
- partialFilterExpression: { "host.tier": "free" } [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // Paid tier uses collection-level expireAfterSeconds (longer) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [TTL for Time Series](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-automatic-removal/) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [TTL Indexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-ttl/) [src: mongodb-time-series]

- MongoDB provides three specialized aggregation stages that are particularly valuable for time series analysis: [src: mongodb-time-series]
- > **Skill boundary — aggregation stages:** For general aggregation pipeline design ($lookup, $group, $merge, $out, explain profiling, memory limits), use `mongodb-aggregation-pipeline`. This section covers only time-series-optimized stages ($densify, $fill) and time-series-specific $setWindowFields usage. `$dateTrunc` (for downsampling into time buckets) is also covered here as it is the primary time-bucketing operator. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- `$dateTrunc` truncates a date to a specified granularity boundary. It is the canonical operator for downsampling raw measurements into fixed time buckets (minute candles, hourly rollups, daily aggregates). [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // Downsample 1-second ticks into 5-minute OHLCV bars [src: mongodb-time-series]
- db.equity_ticks.aggregate([ [src: mongodb-time-series]
- { $match: { "instrument.ticker": "AAPL" } }, [src: mongodb-time-series]
- ticker: "$instrument.ticker", [src: mongodb-time-series]
- bucket: { $dateTrunc: { date: "$tradeTime", unit: "minute", binSize: 5 } } [src: mongodb-time-series]
- open:   { $first: "$price" }, [src: mongodb-time-series]
- high:   { $max: "$price" }, [src: mongodb-time-series]
- low:    { $min: "$price" }, [src: mongodb-time-series]
- close:  { $last: "$price" }, [src: mongodb-time-series]
- volume: { $sum: "$quantity" } [src: mongodb-time-series]
- { $sort: { "_id.bucket": 1 } } [src: mongodb-time-series]
- The `binSize` parameter (MongoDB 5.0+) groups dates into multiples of the unit — e.g., `binSize: 5, unit: "minute"` snaps all timestamps to 5-minute boundaries. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Fills gaps in a time series by inserting synthetic documents at regular intervals where data is missing. Critical for dashboards and window function inputs that assume uniform spacing. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // Fill hourly gaps in weather data [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // NOTE: stationId here is a top-level field (the metaField itself, not a nested sub-field) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- db.weather.aggregate([ [src: mongodb-time-series]
- { $match: { "stationId": "WS-101" } }, [src: mongodb-time-series]
- partitionByFields: ["stationId"], [src: mongodb-time-series]
- ISODate("2024-01-01T00:00:00Z"), [src: mongodb-time-series]
- ISODate("2024-01-02T00:00:00Z") [src: mongodb-time-series]
- `"full"` — spans min to max across all documents in the collection. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- `"partition"` — spans min to max within each partition group. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- `[lower, upper]` — explicit range; lower inclusive, upper exclusive. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Populates `null` or missing fields in densified documents using interpolation or last-observed-carry-forward (LOCF). [src: mongodb-time-series]
- db.weather.aggregate([ [src: mongodb-time-series]
- { $densify: { field: "timestamp", range: { step: 1, unit: "hour", bounds: "full" } } }, [src: mongodb-time-series]
- sortBy: { "timestamp": 1 }, [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // partitionBy key names are arbitrary output labels, not field paths [src: mongodb-time-series]
- partitionBy: { "stationId": "$stationId" }, [src: mongodb-time-series]
- "temperature": { method: "linear" },     // linear interpolation between known values [src: mongodb-time-series]
- "status": { method: "locf" }              // carry last known value forward [src: mongodb-time-series]
- `"linear"` — calculates value proportionally between surrounding non-null values. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- `"locf"` (Last Observation Carried Forward) — repeats the last known non-null value. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Applies window functions over ordered partitions without collapsing documents (unlike `$group`). Enables rolling averages, cumulative sums, lag/lead comparisons, and rankings — all SQL-standard window function patterns. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- db.sensor_readings.aggregate([ [src: mongodb-time-series]
- partitionBy: "$metadata.sensorId", [src: mongodb-time-series]
- sortBy: { "timestamp": 1 }, [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // 5-minute rolling average [src: mongodb-time-series]
- $avg: "$temperature", [src: mongodb-time-series]
- window: { range: [-5, 0], unit: "minute" } [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // Cumulative sum since start of partition [src: mongodb-time-series]
- "cumulativeEnergy": { [src: mongodb-time-series]
- window: { documents: ["unbounded", "current"] } [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // Previous reading (lag) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- $shift: { output: "$temperature", by: -1, default: null } [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // Rank by temperature within window [src: mongodb-time-series]
- "tempRank": { $rank: {} } [src: mongodb-time-series]
- `documents`: `["unbounded", "current"]`, `[-N, M]` — count-based. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- `range`: `[-N, M]` with `unit` for time-based (ms, second, minute, hour, day, week, month, quarter, year). [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Important performance note:** Window functions on time series collections do not automatically push down through the bucket storage format. Use `$match` on `metaField` and `timeField` before `$setWindowFields` to minimize the scanned document set. [src: mongodb-time-series]

- Atlas Charts works natively with time series collections. The time-series-optimized aggregation engine (bucket-level pruning, columnar projection) applies to Charts queries automatically — no special configuration needed. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Use cases with Atlas Charts:** [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Real-time IoT sensor dashboards using time-range filters [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Environmental monitoring with rolling average overlays [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Infrastructure metrics with aggregated panels (mean, p95, max) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Financial dashboards showing OHLCV candlestick data [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Limitation:** Embedded charts querying time series collections with a high-cardinality `metaField` can generate expensive scatter-gather queries. Use time-range and `metaField` equality filters in the embedded chart filter to scope queries. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [Visualizing Atlas Data with Charts](https://www.mongodb.com/resources/products/platform/visualizing-your-data-with-atlas-charts) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [IoT + Atlas Charts Example](https://www.mongodb.com/developer/products/atlas/iot-mongodb-powering-time-series-analysis-household-power-consumption/) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Time series collections **do not support change streams** and therefore **cannot use Database Triggers**. The optimized bucket storage format does not emit per-document change events. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Workaround patterns:** [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Dual-write to a regular collection**: Write events to both a regular collection (for triggers) and a time series collection (for historical queries). The regular collection can be capped or have a short TTL. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Scheduled triggers**: Use scheduled Atlas triggers to run aggregations over the time series collection at regular intervals and emit derived events or aggregated results to another collection. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Atlas Stream Processing**: Use Kafka or Atlas Stream Processing `$source` stage to consume events before they enter the time series collection and react in real-time. Note: time series collections cannot serve as a `$source` in ASP. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [Community: Change Stream Workaround](https://www.mongodb.com/community/forums/t/mongodb-timeseries-change-stream-support-or-any-alternative/192106) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [Triggers Limitations](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers/limitations/) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Atlas Flex clusters (the replacement for M2/M5 and Serverless instances, as of January 2026) support time series collections as they run MongoDB 5.0+ wire protocol. However, Flex clusters have limitations compared to Dedicated clusters: [src: mongodb-time-series]
- No Continuous backup / Point-in-Time Restore (snapshots only) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- No cross-region replication [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Private Endpoints support is limited — verify current availability in the Atlas docs, as Flex private endpoint support has been expanding since 2025 [src: mongodb-time-series]
- For production time series workloads requiring PITR, guaranteed HA, or private networking, use Dedicated clusters (M10+). [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [Manage Flex Clusters](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/manage-flex-clusters/) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [Flex Migration Guide](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/flex-migration/) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- -- [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Sharding enables horizontal scaling for very high ingestion rates. Time series sharding has several important constraints that differ from regular collection sharding. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Shard key must contain only the `metaField`, sub-fields of `metaField`, or (deprecated) the `timeField`. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- `timeField` as a shard key component is **deprecated in MongoDB 8.0** because monotonically increasing values cause write hotspots on a single shard. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- `metaField` can be used as a ranged or hashed shard key. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Zone sharding is **not supported** for time series collections. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Recommended shard key patterns:** [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // Shard on metaField sub-field (range sharding — best for region-scoped queries) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- "iot.sensor_readings", [src: mongodb-time-series]
- { "metadata.region": 1 } [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // Hashed sharding on metaField (even distribution for high-cardinality deviceId) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- "iot.sensor_readings", [src: mongodb-time-series]
- { "metadata.deviceId": "hashed" } [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // Compound: region + deviceId (best balance for multi-region IoT) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- "iot.sensor_readings", [src: mongodb-time-series]
- { "metadata.region": 1, "metadata.deviceId": 1 } [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Anti-pattern — timeField-only shard key:** [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // BAD: All writes land on the shard holding the current time range [src: mongodb-time-series]
- sh.shardCollection("metrics.readings", { "timestamp": 1 }) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Pre-splitting:** If device groups or regions are known in advance, pre-split chunks before ingestion to avoid initial primary-shard hotspot. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [Shard a Time Series Collection](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-shard-collection/) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [Time Series Limitations — Sharding](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-limitations/) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- -- [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Unlike regular collections where the working set is the "hot" subset of documents, for time series the working set is primarily: [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Open buckets** (currently being written) — proportional to `metaField` cardinality. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Recently queried time ranges** — based on your typical query lookback window. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Open bucket RAM   = (unique metaField values) × (avg bucket size ~125 KB) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Recent query RAM  = (query lookback seconds / granularity bucket span seconds) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- × (unique metaField values) × (avg bucket size ~125 KB) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Granularity bucket span seconds reference: [src: mongodb-time-series]
- `seconds` granularity → 3,600 s (1 hour) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- `minutes` granularity → 86,400 s (24 hours) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- `hours`   granularity → 2,592,000 s (30 days) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Example (10,000 IoT sensors, `minutes` granularity = 86,400 s span, 1-hour lookback):** [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Open buckets  = 10,000 × 125 KB            = ~1.2 GB [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Recent queries = (3,600 / 86,400) × 10,000 × 125 KB = ~54 MB [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Total working set ≈ 1.3 GB [src: mongodb-time-series]
- (At `seconds` granularity the same 1-hour lookback covers exactly 1 bucket span, so recent-query RAM ≈ open-bucket RAM = ~1.2 GB — an important difference when choosing granularity.) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Recommendation:** Size WiredTiger cache (`storage.wiredTiger.engineConfig.cacheSizeGB`) at 50-60% of available RAM, targeting > 95% cache hit rate. Monitor `wiredTiger.cache.bytes currently in the cache` and `page faults` in Atlas metrics. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [Columnar Storage Cost Savings Blog](https://www.mongodb.com/company/blog/technical/columnar-storage-time-series-collection-cost-savings) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [Time Series Compression Docs](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-compression/) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [Bucket Behavior Study](https://www.mongodb.com/company/blog/technical/a-practical-study-of-mongodb-time-series-bucket-behavior) [src: mongodb-time-series]
- Link: [Medium: Storage Comparison](https://medium.com/codex/analyzing-data-storage-regular-collection-vs-time-series-collection-54532ade7088) [src: mongodb-time-series]

- Time series collections cannot update measurement fields. Use the versioning pattern to handle corrections: [src: mongodb-time-series]
- db.readings.insertOne({ [src: mongodb-time-series]
- timestamp: ISODate("2024-01-01T10:00:00Z"), [src: mongodb-time-series]
- metadata: { sensorId: "A1", version: 1, superseded: false }, [src: mongodb-time-series]
- temperature: 21.5   // original, possibly erroneous [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // Correction: insert new version, mark old as superseded via metaField update [src: mongodb-time-series]
- db.readings.insertOne({ [src: mongodb-time-series]
- timestamp: ISODate("2024-01-01T10:00:00Z"), [src: mongodb-time-series]
- metadata: { sensorId: "A1", version: 2, superseded: false }, [src: mongodb-time-series]
- temperature: 22.1   // corrected value [src: mongodb-time-series]
- db.readings.updateMany( [src: mongodb-time-series]
- { "metadata.sensorId": "A1", "metadata.version": 1 }, [src: mongodb-time-series]
- { $set: { "metadata.superseded": true } }   // only metaField updates allowed [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // Query always uses latest non-superseded version [src: mongodb-time-series]
- db.readings.aggregate([ [src: mongodb-time-series]
- { $match: { "metadata.superseded": false, "metadata.sensorId": "A1" } }, [src: mongodb-time-series]
- { $sort: { "timestamp": 1, "metadata.version": -1 } }, [src: mongodb-time-series]
- { $group: { _id: "$timestamp", doc: { $first: "$$ROOT" } } } [src: mongodb-time-series]

- **You cannot convert an existing collection in-place.** Migration always requires creating a new time series collection and copying data. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // Step 1: Rename existing collection as staging [src: mongodb-time-series]

- **Mismatch 1 — granularity too coarse (high-frequency data):** Setting `granularity: "hours"` for a sensor that reports every second means each bucket can remain open for up to 30 days before the *time* limit triggers a close. In practice, the *measurement-count* limit (~1,000 documents) is hit first (after ~17 minutes at 1/s), but this still produces far more bucket churn than needed and misrepresents the intended data cadence to the storage engine, degrading compression locality. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- **Mismatch 2 — granularity too fine (low-frequency data):** Setting `granularity: "seconds"` for a sensor that only reports once per hour means each bucket closes after 1 hour (time limit), typically containing only ~1 measurement. This destroys compression — you lose all the benefit of columnar storage across many measurements. [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // BAD for 1/second data: granularity implies 30-day lifecycle [src: mongodb-time-series]

- // BAD for 1/hour data: each bucket closes after 1 hour with ~1 document [src: mongodb-time-series]
- { granularity: "seconds" } [src: mongodb-time-series]
- // GOOD: match granularity to how often the same source sends data [src: mongodb-time-series]

- { granularity: "minutes" }   // 1–60 minute intervals [src: mongodb-time-series]

- MongoDB recommends Private Endpoints (Azure Private Link) for new deployments over VNet peering. [src: mongodb-atlas-azure]
- **Private Link DNS:** SRV connection string resolves to `pl-0-eastus2.<cluster-id>.mongodb.net` — an A record pointing to the NIC's private IP. Private DNS Zone `<cluster-id>.mongodb.net` must be linked to every VNet needing resolution. [src: mongodb-atlas-azure]
- **NSG Rules:** SRV connection strings use high ports (1024-65535), not just 27017. Allow TCP 1024-65535 outbound to private endpoint subnet. [src: mongodb-atlas-azure]
- **Hub-and-spoke:** Place private endpoint in hub VNet; use Azure Private DNS Resolver (managed, HA) instead of BIND forwarder VMs. Link Private DNS Zone to ALL VNets including spokes. [src: mongodb-atlas-azure]
- Human users SSO into Atlas database access using Entra ID credentials. Issuer URI: `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/v2.0`. [src: mongodb-atlas-azure]
- Azure Managed Identities and Service Principals authenticate to Atlas without passwords using short-lived OAuth 2.0 tokens. Issuer URI: `https://sts.windows.net/<tenant-id>/`. [src: mongodb-atlas-azure]
- Add label `azure.workload.identity/use: "true"` to pod. Create federated credential linking AKS OIDC issuer + service account + audience `api://AzureADTokenExchange`. [src: mongodb-atlas-azure]
- Atlas uses its own Azure Service Principal (`atlasAzureAppId: 9efedfcc-2eca-4b27-a613-0cad1e114cb7`). Grant it "Key Vault Crypto User" and "Reader" RBAC roles. [src: mongodb-atlas-azure]
- Use versionless key identifier (no trailing `/<version>`) so Atlas automatically uses the latest key version after rotation. [src: mongodb-atlas-azure]
- If AKV is inaccessible: running cluster continues (DEK cached in memory), but mongod will NOT restart. Create private endpoint for KV in EACH Atlas-deployed region. [src: mongodb-atlas-azure]
- Use `maxPoolSize: 5` (low pool for horizontal scaling). Cold starts create new connections. Do NOT store client in async context — use module-level singleton. [src: mongodb-atlas-azure]

- `callResetPasswordFunction()` is unauthenticated — always return `pending` for out-of-band verification [src: mongodb-atlas-app-services]
- Custom JWT: App Services always enforces 30-minute access token expiry regardless of JWT `exp` claim [src: mongodb-atlas-app-services]
- Permissions are defined per-collection. Role evaluation: first matching role wins (role order matters). If no role matches, the operation is denied entirely. System functions bypass all rules. [src: mongodb-atlas-app-services]
- Variables: `%%user.id`, `%%user.custom_data.<field>`, `%%root.<field>`, `%%environment.values.<name>` [src: mongodb-atlas-app-services]
- App Services schemas are JSON Schema (draft 4 + BSON extensions). Validates every write after the operation is computed but before commit. Key differences from mongod `$jsonSchema`: App Services validates post-operation; system functions bypass App Services schema. [src: mongodb-atlas-app-services]

- MongoDB Atlas Flex tier (GA: February 6, 2025) is the successor to both the shared tier (M2/M5) and the serverless tier. As of January 22, 2026, M2/M5 clusters and Serverless instances are end-of-life and no longer supported — all existing instances were automatically migrated. Flex is now the entry-level paid cluster in Atlas. [src: mongodb-atlas-flex-serverless]
- Ops-per-second tiered hourly model capped monthly — no per-document billing: [src: mongodb-atlas-flex-serverless]
- Base: 100 ops/sec + 5 GB storage → $8/month [src: mongodb-atlas-flex-serverless]
- 200 ops/sec → $15/month [src: mongodb-atlas-flex-serverless]
- 300 ops/sec → $21/month [src: mongodb-atlas-flex-serverless]
- 400 ops/sec → $26/month [src: mongodb-atlas-flex-serverless]
- 500 ops/sec → $30/month (hard cap — no runaway billing) [src: mongodb-atlas-flex-serverless]
- Billed hourly, prorated. Burst to 500 ops/sec for 1 hour does not cost $30. [src: mongodb-atlas-flex-serverless]
- **Key differences from Serverless:** Fixed-price cap (no unbounded billing), no cold starts, always warm. [src: mongodb-atlas-flex-serverless]

- PSC uses Cloud DNS private zones. Two options: [src: mongodb-atlas-gcp]
- **Private DNS zone** scoped to VPC (recommended) [src: mongodb-atlas-gcp]
- **DNS peering** from application VPC to the zone where PSC records exist [src: mongodb-atlas-gcp]
- For Shared VPC: DNS zone must be in the host project; application projects access via DNS peering. [src: mongodb-atlas-gcp]
- SRV DNS requirement: Allow TCP 27017 + high ports (1024-65535) through VPC firewall rules, as SRV records return per-node ports. [src: mongodb-atlas-gcp]

- Online Archive automatically moves documents matching an archival rule out of the live Atlas cluster into Atlas-managed object storage, while keeping those documents queryable through the cluster's FDI endpoint (transparent to the application). [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Dedicated cluster M10+ (not available on M0/Flex/Serverless) [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- MongoDB 5.0+ on the source cluster [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- "dateField": "createdAt", [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- "dateFormat": "ISODATE", [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- "expireAfterDays": 90 [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- `dateFormat` options: `"ISODATE"` (default ISODate), `"EPOCH_MILLISECONDS"`, `"EPOCH_SECONDS"` [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- "query": "{ \"status\": \"completed\", \"updatedAt\": { \"$lt\": {...} } }" [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Partition fields organize archived data into S3 prefix paths for efficient filtering. Critical for query performance. Choose fields commonly used in query filters: [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- { "fieldName": "region",     "order": 0 }, [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- { "fieldName": "createdAt",  "order": 1 }, [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- { "fieldName": "customerId", "order": 2 } [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Maximum 2 partition fields per archive rule [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- First field MUST match the `dateField` (for DATE criteria) or be the most selective filter field (for CUSTOM criteria) [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Order matters: highest-selectivity filter field should be first [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Supported partition pruning operators: `$eq`, `$gt`, `$lt`, `$gte`, `$lte`, `$ne`, `$in` [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Fields NOT in partitionFields trigger full archive scan when queried [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Runs every **5 minutes** [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Max throughput: **2 GB per 5-minute interval** [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Max file size: **100 MB per archive file** [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Documents deleted from live cluster AFTER successful write to object storage [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Schedule window: Archive jobs can be limited to off-hours to reduce production impact [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- When querying via the cluster's FDI endpoint: [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Recent data → live cluster (fast, indexed) [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Archived data → Online Archive object storage (slower, partition-based) [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Combined queries → both, results merged transparently [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Applications do not need to change query patterns after data is archived — same connection string, same MQL. [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- **$5/TB cost applies when QUERYING archived data.** Storage itself is much cheaper than cluster storage (NVMe/GP3). [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- **Minimum:** 10 MB per archive query (no benefit from very small queries). [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Archive data is immutable (append-only). To restore to the live cluster: [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- // Restore archived data back to the live cluster via $merge [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- db.archivedCollection.aggregate([ [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- { $match: { createdAt: { $gte: cutoffDate } } },   // Filter from archive [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- { $merge: { into: { db: "mydb", coll: "orders" }, // Rehydrate into live cluster [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- whenMatched: "keepExisting", [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- whenNotMatched: "insert" } } [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- **No updates/deletes on archived data:** Archive is immutable object storage; `updateMany` or `deleteMany` against archived documents will not affect them [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- **No Atlas Search on archived data:** Full-text `$search` doesn't work on archived data [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- **No indexes on archived data:** All archived queries use partition pruning only [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- **$sample not random:** Returns first N documents, not a statistical random sample [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- **No transactions crossing live+archive:** Cannot span a transaction across live and archived documents [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- **Maximum query timeout:** 6 hours (inherits from Data Federation limit) [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Check Atlas → Online Archive → [collection] → Activity tab for job status and errors [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Verify `dateField` name is exact (case-sensitive) and matches documents [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Confirm correct `dateFormat` — `ISODATE` requires actual ISODate values, not Unix epoch integers [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Confirm cluster tier is M10+ and MongoDB version 5.0+ [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Archive jobs process 2 GB per 5-minute window [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- If data accumulates faster than 2 GB/5 minutes, backlog will grow [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Mitigation: narrow the archive rule to reduce concurrent archiving volume, or contact MongoDB for higher throughput [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Partition fields not aligned with query filter → full archive scan [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Check `partitionFields` match the most common query filter fields [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Run `explain()` on the FDI endpoint to check `nPartitionsScanned` [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Archive storage costs appear on the Atlas invoice under Tools & Services → Online Archive. Query processing costs under Data Federation. Monitor in Atlas Billing → Current Invoice. [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- **Choosing partition fields that don't match query patterns:** Full archive scan on every query → high $5/TB cost [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- **Using CUSTOM criteria without an index on the filter field:** Archive job itself will do slow scans to find matching documents — add an index on filter fields [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- **Querying archived data without partition-aligned filters:** Always include a partition field in `$match` when querying archive [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- **Expecting consistency between live and archive:** Documents are copied to archive and then deleted from live — there is no transactional guarantee between the two [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- **Using Online Archive as a backup system:** Archive only stores the final document state at archival time — not a substitute for backup snapshots with PITR [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Link: [Online Archive Documentation](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/online-archive/) [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Link: [Configure an Online Archive](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/online-archive/configure-online-archive/) [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Link: [Query Archived Data](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/online-archive/query-online-archive/) [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- Link: [Online Archive Billing](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/billing/online-archive/) [src: mongodb-atlas-online-archive]
- **Ops Manager** is MongoDB's self-hosted management platform for on-premises MongoDB deployments. **Cloud Manager** is the hosted SaaS equivalent (no infrastructure to manage). Both provide: [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- **Automation:** Declarative goal-state management of MongoDB clusters (topology, version, config) [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- **Monitoring:** Real-time metrics, alerts, and dashboards [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- **Backup:** Continuous oplog-based backup with PITR [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- MongoDB Agent (runs on every DB host) [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- Ops Manager Application Server [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- ├─ App Database (MongoDB 6.0+ RS — Ops Manager state store) [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- ├─ Backup Daemon (runs backups, stores to blockstore/S3) [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- The App DB stores Ops Manager's own state. Sizing: [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- Small (< 50 MongoDB processes): 3-node RS, M10 equivalent (8 GB RAM) [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- Medium (50-500 processes): 3-node RS, M30 equivalent (32 GB RAM) [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- Large (500+ processes): 5-node RS or sharded cluster [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- **App DB HA:** Always use 3-node replica set. Single-node App DB = single point of failure for Ops Manager. [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- A single binary that handles automation, monitoring, and backup for all MongoDB processes on the host. [src: mongodb-ops-manager]

- Ops Manager maintains the desired topology in the **automation config** JSON. The Agent continuously reconciles actual state to match the goal state. [src: mongodb-ops-manager]

- Backup Daemon runs on a dedicated host. It: [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- Reads from oplog of source MongoDB (via agent) [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- Writes snapshots to configured store [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- Maintains PITR window by tailing the oplog [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- Place the Backup Daemon close to the data (low latency to both source MongoDB and snapshot store). [src: mongodb-ops-manager]

- Atlas uses a three-tier identity model: Organization → Project → Database. [src: mongodb-atlas-iam-rbac]
- Username + password. Most compatible. FIPS 140-2 compliant when using SHA-256. [src: mongodb-atlas-iam-rbac]
- Client certificate authentication. Two types: [src: mongodb-atlas-iam-rbac]
- **Atlas-managed:** Atlas generates and manages the CA; valid for up to 5 years (configurable) [src: mongodb-atlas-iam-rbac]
- **Customer-managed (LDAP):** Customer operates their own CA; Atlas validates against customer's CA [src: mongodb-atlas-iam-rbac]
- Passwordless auth using AWS credentials (IAM user, role, EC2 instance profile, IRSA, Lambda execution role). [src: mongodb-atlas-iam-rbac]
- Connection string: `authMechanism=MONGODB-AWS` [src: mongodb-atlas-iam-rbac]

- Workforce (human users) and Workload (apps/services) identity federation. [src: mongodb-atlas-iam-rbac]
- **Workforce OIDC:** Human users SSO into Atlas database access via Entra ID, Okta, Google Workspace, or any OIDC provider. [src: mongodb-atlas-iam-rbac]
- **Workload OIDC:** Applications authenticate without passwords using OIDC tokens from GCP, Azure, AWS, or any OIDC provider. [src: mongodb-atlas-iam-rbac]
- LDAP authentication and authorization supported in MongoDB 4.x–7.x. Deprecated in 8.0. Migrate to OIDC or X.509. [src: mongodb-atlas-iam-rbac]
- Replaces legacy Programmatic API Keys for machine-to-machine Atlas API access. [src: mongodb-atlas-iam-rbac]

- <!-- Provenance: reference under the `mongodb-expert` hub. Mirrored from ~/.claude/skills/mongodb-expert/references/mongodb-wiredtiger-internals.md by scripts/persist-spoke.mjs. --> [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- WiredTiger has been MongoDB's default storage engine since **3.2** (replacing MMAPv1). It is a B-tree backed, MVCC, copy-on-write engine with document-level concurrency, configurable in-memory cache, block-level compression, and a write-ahead journal. Everything below the document model — durability, concurrency, compression, eviction, checkpoints — is WiredTiger. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- This skill is the deep internals reference. For surface-level performance triage, see `mongodb-performance-troubleshooting`. For diagnostic packaging, see `atlas-diagnostics-expert`. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- -- [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- WiredTiger has a **hybrid architecture optimized for multi-core CPUs and large memory**: [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Application threads (mongod query/index ops) [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- +----------------------------------------------------------------+ [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- +--------|----------------|----------------|-----------|----------+ [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- v                v                v           v   versions [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- +----------------------------------------------------------------+ [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- +----------------------------------------------------------------+ [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- v                                            v [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- On-disk B-tree files                       Write-Ahead Log [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- (collection-*.wt, index-*.wt,              (journal/WiredTigerLog.*) [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- WiredTigerHS.wt, WiredTiger.wt) [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- **In-memory cache** — uncompressed B-tree pages. Working set lives here. Default size: `max(0.5 × (RAM − 1 GiB), 256 MiB)`. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- **Block manager** — translates pages to/from disk, owns checksums, compression, encryption, free-list. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- **OS filesystem cache** — holds compressed data blocks. Often roughly the same size as the WT cache (uncompressed) because of compression ratios. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- `mongod` exposes WiredTiger via a single `WT_CONNECTION` (per-process), holding one `WT_CACHE` struct and N `WT_SESSION` objects for application threads. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- -- [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- The cache size formula (since 3.4): `max(0.5 × (RAM − 1 GiB), 256 MiB)`, capped at **10 000 GiB**. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Override with one of (mutually exclusive): [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- cacheSizeGB: 32          # absolute size in GiB [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Or at the command line: `--wiredTigerCacheSizeGB 32` / `--wiredTigerCacheSizePct 60`. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- **Containers and cgroups**: WT's default sizing was historically based on **host** RAM. Always pin `cacheSizeGB` explicitly when running in a container with a memory limit, or you will OOM. Newer MongoDB versions detect cgroup limits in some configurations, but pinning is still safest. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- **Sizing rule of thumb (dedicated host)**: target ~50% of RAM for the WT cache and leave the rest for the OS filesystem cache plus mongod overhead (connections, plan cache, TCMalloc fragmentation). On shared hosts or multi-`mongod` deployments, reduce proportionally per instance. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Uncompressed B-tree pages for collections and indexes that were touched recently [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Dirty pages awaiting reconciliation [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Update structures (per-key linked lists of in-progress modifications) [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- The history store (recent MVCC versions) [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- WT session metadata, transaction structures [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- WiredTiger uses **two memory tiers**: [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- A common rule of thumb: leave ~50% of RAM for the OS filesystem cache. Setting `cacheSizeGB` too high starves the OS cache, increasing disk reads after a page is evicted from WT but before being purged from the FS cache. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- -- [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Eviction reclaims cache space by either dropping clean pages or reconciling dirty pages (writing them to the data file). Done well: invisible. Done poorly: the source of 80% of WiredTiger production pain. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- **One eviction server** thread — walks the B-trees in fairness order, finds candidates [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- **N eviction worker threads** — pop pages from queues and actually evict them [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- **Three queues**: two ordinary + one **urgent** queue (priority queue) [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- The server samples a portion of each B-tree, scores pages by access recency, takes the **one-third oldest** of evictable candidates, and pushes them onto the queues. This approximates an LRU policy — true LRU would be too expensive for a multi-million-page cache. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- The urgent queue holds pages flagged for forced eviction (sessions disabling eviction/splitting, large in-memory pages exceeding the maximum size, etc.). [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Additional thresholds (newer versions): [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- **Invariant**: `target < trigger` for every pair. The engine will refuse a config that violates this. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Normal mode: only background eviction workers do reconciliation. Pressure mode: when cache used ≥ `eviction_trigger` (or dirty ≥ `eviction_dirty_trigger`), **application threads must perform eviction before they're allowed to do their own work**. This shows up in `serverStatus()` as: [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- wiredTiger.cache.pages evicted by application threads > 0 [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- A non-zero value means writes are being throttled and latency is climbing. A persistent non-zero rate (per-second, derived from FTDC deltas) signals chronic under-sizing or under-threaded eviction. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Use `wiredTigerEngineRuntimeConfig` to change cache/eviction parameters **without restart**: [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- wiredTigerEngineRuntimeConfig: [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- "eviction=(threads_min=8,threads_max=12),eviction_target=75,eviction_trigger=90,eviction_dirty_target=5,eviction_dirty_trigger=15" [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Persist in `mongod.conf` under `setParameter:` (not `storage.wiredTiger`): [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- wiredTigerEngineRuntimeConfig: "eviction=(threads_min=8,threads_max=12)" [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- **Gotcha**: forum users have reported `db.adminCommand` with this parameter not taking effect on certain versions — verify with `db.serverStatus().wiredTiger` after applying, and prefer setting it in `mongod.conf` for sticky deployments. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- When a dirty page is evicted, WT performs **reconciliation**: [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Walk the in-memory page, collect committed values (newest visible to all readers) [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Build a new on-disk image with one entry per key (newest committed value) [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Push older committed versions to the **history store** (`WiredTigerHS.wt`) [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- If the resulting image exceeds the configured max page size, **split** into multiple pages [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Compress, checksum, write via the block manager [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- If page is small enough to merge with a neighbor on the next pass, leave a hint [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Reconciliation is the single most CPU-expensive operation in the engine. It's why: [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Hot pages with massive update lists pin the cache [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Long-running transactions inflate the history store [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Cache pressure under heavy write workloads is fundamentally a reconciliation throughput problem [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- -- [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- WiredTiger combines **checkpoints** (point-in-time consistent snapshots flushed to disk) and **a write-ahead log** (the journal). Recovery uses both. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Default interval: **60 seconds** (`storage.syncPeriodSecs`, or via `wiredTigerEngineRuntimeConfig` as `checkpoint=(wait=60)`) [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Alternative trigger: **2 GiB of journal accumulated since last checkpoint** [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- The checkpoint thread creates a consistent snapshot of all B-trees, writes new on-disk root pointers, and only after successful write does it consider the checkpoint complete [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Crash mid-checkpoint: the previous checkpoint stays valid; the new one is discarded [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Storage is **copy-on-write**: new pages are written to free space, then the root pointer is flipped — the old pages become free list candidates after the checkpoint completes [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Compressed with **snappy** by default. Configure via: [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- journalCompressor: zstd   # or snappy / zlib / none [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Files are pre-allocated 100 MB segments named `WiredTigerLog.<n>` under `dbPath/journal/` [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Records ≤ 128 bytes are **not** compressed (minimum log record size) [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Default flush cadence: every **100 ms** (group commit) — this is your data loss window in a crash [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- `j: true` write concern forces an immediate journal flush before acknowledging [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- `disableJournal=true` (NOT for replica-set members) skips the journal entirely [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Find the latest valid checkpoint in `WiredTiger.wt` [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Replay journal records from the checkpoint LSN forward [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- For each table, resolve outstanding transactions (commit or roll back per stable timestamp) [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Open `WT_CONNECTION`, expose to mongod [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- **Worst case data loss** in a clean crash (no replica set): up to **100 ms** of acknowledged writes from non-`j:true` clients. With `j:true`, zero. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- WiredTiger batches journal flushes via group commit. `--syncdelay` (or `storage.syncPeriodSecs`) controls the **checkpoint** cadence, not the journal flush. Many older blog posts conflate the two — be precise: [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- `syncPeriodSecs` (default 60) → checkpoint interval [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Journal flush → every 100 ms (hard-coded, plus `j:true` triggers) [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- -- [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- MongoDB layered **timestamp-based MVCC** on top of WiredTiger's transaction subsystem to support snapshot isolation, causal consistency, and `readConcern: "snapshot"`. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Every operation acquires a read snapshot at start. WT guarantees that the operation sees a consistent point-in-time view, regardless of concurrent writes. Readers never block writers; writers never block readers. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- WT exposes a small set of global timestamps: [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- The **pinned timestamp** is the crucial concept: even if MongoDB advances `oldest_timestamp`, an active long-running snapshot pins the floor and forces WT to keep history. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Introduced in 4.4 (replacing the old **lookaside file**). When reconciliation evicts a page with non-current committed versions, those older values **spill into the history store**. The current value stays in the data file. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- History store key format: `(table_id, record_id, start_timestamp, counter)` — i.e., one entry per old version, per key, per timestamp. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- The history store is itself a B-tree, lives in the cache, gets reconciled and evicted like any other table. Pages become reclaimable when **all rows on the page are obsolete** (no reader can see them, all are older than the pinned timestamp). [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- A snapshot pinned by a long transaction stalls cleanup: [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- All updates in the transaction's view must remain available → history store grows [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- All in-progress updates accumulate in update lists → cache pressure [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Reconciliation can't compress update lists into a single value [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Keep transactions short (MongoDB aborts multi-doc transactions after **60 s** by default, controlled by `transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds`) [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Set `minSnapshotHistoryWindowInSeconds` (default 300 s) sensibly — every second held forces history retention [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Watch `cache.history store on-disk size`, `cache.history store table updates inserted into history store`, and `transaction.read timestamp of the oldest active reader` in FTDC [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Don't run `mongodump` against a hot collection with a low `snapshotHistoryWindow` — it pins the snapshot [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- -- [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Three knobs, three layers. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- blockCompressor: zstd   # snappy (default) | zlib | zstd | none [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Regular collections: `snappy` [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Time-series collections (5.0+): `zstd` [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Journal: `snappy` [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Per-collection override at creation: [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- db.createCollection("archival_events", { [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- wiredTiger: { configString: "block_compressor=zlib" } [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Indexes use **prefix compression**: shared key prefixes are stored once. This is on by default and almost never worth turning off — it both saves space and speeds up scans (more keys per page). [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- prefixCompression: true   # default [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- journalCompressor: snappy   # default [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Records ≤ 128 bytes skip compression regardless. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- -- [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- The block manager owns the on-disk layout. Pages are the unit of I/O. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Larger pages → better compression ratio (more data per block), worse cache granularity. Smaller pages → vice versa. MongoDB ships sensible defaults; touch only with profiling evidence. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- When an application thread is updating a hot page and the in-memory size crosses `memory_page_max`, the thread is conscripted to **forcefully split** the page so reconciliation doesn't see an unbounded image. This shows up as elevated `cache.pages split during eviction`. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- When pages are written via copy-on-write, old extents become free-list candidates. The block manager tracks these for reuse. Periodic **compaction** (`db.runCommand({ compact: "<coll>" })`) consolidates free space — useful after big deletes, mostly irrelevant during steady-state operation. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- -- [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- WT enforces a hard cap on **concurrent storage-engine transactions**: read tickets and write tickets. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- **128** read tickets, **128** write tickets, per-node, fixed [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Configurable via `storageEngineConcurrentReadTransactions` and `storageEngineConcurrentWriteTransactions` [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Exhaustion: new operations queue, latency climbs [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- `db.serverStatus().wiredTiger.concurrentTransactions.{read,write}.available` shows current free tickets [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- MongoDB 7.0 introduced a **dynamic algorithm** that adjusts ticket counts based on observed throughput and contention. Defaults are lower than 128 during normal operation — this is intentional. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- db.serverStatus().queues.execution [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- //   read:  { in: 0, out: 0, totalTickets: 64 }, [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- //   write: { in: 0, out: 0, totalTickets: 64 } [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- **Manually setting** `storageEngineConcurrentReadTransactions` or `storageEngineConcurrentWriteTransactions` (or the older aliases `wiredTigerConcurrentReadTransactions` / `wiredTigerConcurrentWriteTransactions`) to a non-default value **disables the dynamic algorithm** on 7.0+. Don't override unless you have hard evidence of ticket starvation. Look at queue depth (`queues.execution.*.in`) not at `available` alone. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- WT uses **optimistic concurrency control**. Multiple writers can hit different documents simultaneously. Same-document concurrent writes → one wins, the other gets `WT_ROLLBACK` and MongoDB retries transparently. This is per-document, not per-collection — a fundamental advantage over MMAPv1's collection-level lock. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- -- [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- MongoDB Enterprise ships an alternative WT configuration with **no disk persistence**. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Data lives only in memory. No data files, no journal, no checkpoint. Restart = empty database. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Cache layer in front of a primary store [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Real-time analytics with TTL'd ephemeral data [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Test/CI environments that need MongoDB but not persistence [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Session storage [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Same MVCC, document concurrency, indexes, aggregation as on-disk WT [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Sustains higher write throughput (no journal/checkpoint cost) [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Can act as a replica-set secondary alongside on-disk primaries — but every secondary needs enough RAM [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- `WT_CACHE_FULL` errors are **explicit** and abort the operation (vs. on-disk where they'd just throttle) [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- -- [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- MongoDB Enterprise integrates encryption-at-rest at the WT block manager layer. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Default: **AES-256-CBC** via OpenSSL [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Linux only: also supports **AES-256-GCM** (authenticated encryption — strongly preferred) [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- The cipher is applied per-page after compression but before disk write [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Two options for the master key: [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- **KMIP**: integration with an external KMIP-compliant appliance (HashiCorp Vault Enterprise, Thales CipherTrust, Fortanix, etc.) [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Default protocol version 1.2; configurable to 1.0/1.1 with `security.kmip.useLegacyProtocol: true` [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- **Local keyfile**: read from a file on disk (test/dev only) [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- The master key encrypts per-database keys (DEKs). DEKs are stored in `WiredTiger.wt` and encrypted with the master key. Master-key rotation re-wraps DEKs without re-encrypting data. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Atlas always uses encryption-at-rest; cloud-provider key (CMK) integration via AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP KMS is available at the cluster level — that's BYOK over the same WiredTiger layer. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]

- Estimate **working set** — the set of pages touched in a typical hour. Often << total data. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Target: WT cache ≥ working set, with 20% headroom. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Leave ~50% of RAM for OS filesystem cache. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- On containers, **pin `cacheSizeGB`** to a value that respects the cgroup limit. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Don't blindly set `cacheSizePct: 80` — that leaves nothing for the rest of mongod (connections, plan cache, query operators, TCMalloc fragmentation) and nothing for the kernel. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Is cache used % > 80% sustained? [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- YES → potential under-sizing or working-set blow-up [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- NO  → maybe dirty pressure only [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Is dirty % > 5% sustained? [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- YES → reconciliation can't keep up: [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- a. Check eviction worker count vs. dirty pages backlog [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- b. Check disk write latency (FTDC: disk write time) [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- c. Check for long-running transactions (oldest active reader) [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Is pages evicted by application threads > 0? [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- YES → application threads are doing eviction, latency is climbing [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- → bump threads_min/threads_max [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- → consider larger cache [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- → look for write amplification (over-indexing, bad ESR) [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Is history store on-disk size growing unboundedly? [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- YES → long-running transactions or readers are pinning history [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- → query for active sessions, kill if needed [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- → audit mongodump, change streams, snapshot reads [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- → tighten minSnapshotHistoryWindowInSeconds [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]

- Use Atlas pre-warmed disks (newer tiers cache more of the working set) [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Don't restart all nodes at once [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- WiredTiger pages are checksummed (CRC32C by default); the block manager will reject a torn page on read with `WT_ERROR`. Symptoms: `corrupt WT page`, `checksum mismatch`, `WT_PANIC`, or mongod refusing to start. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- **Triage path** (in order of escalating risk): [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- **Stop the node** if it's still up — further writes can amplify damage [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- **Run `db.collection.validate({ full: true })`** on a healthy replica to confirm the issue is local to the affected node [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- **Re-sync from a healthy replica** (initial sync) — the safest path for a single-node corruption in a replica set [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- **`--repair`**: `mongod --repair --dbpath <dbPath>` — last-resort rewrite that drops any unrecoverable data. Always back up `dbPath/` before running. Repair does not preserve replica-set membership; the node must be re-added afterward. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- **`wt verify`**: low-level forensic check on individual `.wt` files using the standalone WT CLI tool (built from the WT source tree) [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- `WT_PANIC` is unrecoverable in-process. The node has to be restarted; if it panics again on startup, treat it as data-file corruption and follow the path above. Never run `--repair` on a node still serving traffic. [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Background index builds (post-4.2) hold uncommitted entries in the WiredTiger cache until commit. Symptoms during a build: [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Cache used % climbs and stays high [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Dirty % climbs [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- `serverStatus().wiredTiger.cache["bytes belonging to the cache overhead"]` grows [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Throttle with `maxIndexBuildMemoryUsageMegabytes` (default 200 MB per build) [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- Schedule large index builds in low-traffic windows [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]
- For very large collections, consider rolling index builds across replica-set members [src: mongodb-wiredtiger-internals]

- <!-- Provenance: reference under the `mongodb-expert` hub. Mirrored from ~/.claude/skills/mongodb-expert/references/mongodb-driver-internals.md by scripts/persist-spoke.mjs. --> [src: mongodb-driver-internals]
- This skill covers the internal mechanics of MongoDB official drivers — the wire-level behavior, state machines, retry policies, timeouts, and protocols that customers actually hit during incidents. It complements `mongodb-developer` (which covers the driver API surface) and `mongodb-drivers-k8s` (which covers Kubernetes-specific deployment). [src: mongodb-driver-internals]
- The content is sourced from the canonical [mongodb/specifications](https://github.com/mongodb/specifications) repository, which is the source of truth all official drivers implement against. [src: mongodb-driver-internals]
- Debugging **connection pool exhaustion** (`waitQueueTimeoutMS` exceeded, `MongoServerSelectionError: no available servers`, pool `PoolClearedEvent` storms) [src: mongodb-driver-internals]
- Diagnosing **failover behavior** on the driver side — what happens during an election, how SDAM detects topology changes, when retryable writes save the operation vs surface to the user [src: mongodb-driver-internals]
- Understanding **retry semantics** — what makes a write retryable, which errors carry the `RetryableWriteError` label, how `txnNumber` deduplicates [src: mongodb-driver-internals]
- Tracing **transaction failures** — `TransientTransactionError` and `UnknownTransactionCommitResult` labels, sharded transaction coordinator behavior, two-phase commit between coordinator and participant shards [src: mongodb-driver-internals]
- Understanding **causal consistency** — when `afterClusterTime` is sent, why `readConcern: majority` + `writeConcern: majority` is the only fully durable combination [src: mongodb-driver-internals]
- Tuning **timeouts** — `timeoutMS` (CSOT, unified) vs the legacy `socketTimeoutMS` / `connectTimeoutMS` / `serverSelectionTimeoutMS` / `waitQueueTimeoutMS` / `wTimeoutMS` / `maxTimeMS` matrix [src: mongodb-driver-internals]
- Diagnosing **DNS SRV** issues — `mongodb+srv://` resolution, SRV polling for sharded clusters, `srvMaxHosts`, TXT-record options [src: mongodb-driver-internals]
- Reviewing **TLS** configuration — `tlsCAFile`, `tlsCertificateKeyFile`, `tlsAllowInvalidCertificates` (anti-pattern), Atlas implicit TLS [src: mongodb-driver-internals]
- Explaining the **streaming `hello` protocol** vs legacy polling, FaaS-specific tuning (Lambda / Cloud Run), `heartbeatFrequencyMS` [src: mongodb-driver-internals]
- Choosing a **read preference** correctly — when `secondary` is wrong, why `secondaryPreferred` falls back to primary on tag-set miss but `secondary` errors, `localThresholdMS` latency window [src: mongodb-driver-internals]
- Differentiating **maxStalenessSeconds vs localThresholdMS vs hedged reads** vs operationCount load balancing for server selection [src: mongodb-driver-internals]
