- Before benchmarking, characterize the production workload so synthetic tests reflect reality. Benchmarking the wrong workload produces misleading results. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Profile production using `db.serverStatus().opcounters`. Take two samples separated by a known interval — mongosh does not have a built-in `sleep()`, so use a shell loop or run the command twice manually: [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- // Sample 1 — run this, wait 60 seconds, then run Sample 2 [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- const before = db.serverStatus().opcounters; [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- // ... wait 60 seconds ... [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- const after = db.serverStatus().opcounters; [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- const elapsed = 60; // seconds between samples [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- const readRate  = (after.query - before.query) / elapsed; [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- const writeRate = (after.insert + after.update + after.delete - [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- before.insert - before.update - before.delete) / elapsed; [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- print(`Reads/s: ${readRate.toFixed(0)}, Writes/s: ${writeRate.toFixed(0)}`); [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- print(`Read/write ratio: ${(readRate / writeRate).toFixed(1)}:1`); [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Alternatively, use `mongostat --rowcount 2 --sleep 60` from the shell to get two consecutive 60-second samples. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Sample the hot collection to understand document size: [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- db.orders.aggregate([ [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- { $sample: { size: 1000 } }, [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- { $project: { size: { $bsonSize: "$$ROOT" } } }, [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- avgBytes: { $avg: "$size" }, [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- p95Bytes: { $percentile: { input: "$size", p: [0.95], method: "approximate" } }, [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- maxBytes: { $max: "$size" } [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Document size directly affects WiredTiger cache efficiency. A 100KB average document means 10,000 documents fill 1GB of RAM. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- The working set is the subset of data (indexes + hot documents) that must fit in RAM for optimal performance. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- // Check if working set fits in cache [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- const status = db.serverStatus(); [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- const cacheUsed = status.wiredTiger.cache["bytes currently in the cache"]; [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- const cacheMax  = status.wiredTiger.cache["maximum bytes configured"]; [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- const readInto  = status.wiredTiger.cache["pages read into cache"]; [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- const evictions = status.wiredTiger.cache["unmodified pages evicted"]; [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- // High evictions relative to reads = working set exceeds cache [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- print(`Cache utilization: ${(cacheUsed/cacheMax*100).toFixed(1)}%`); [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- print(`Pages read into cache: ${readInto}, Unmodified pages evicted: ${evictions}`); [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- print(`Eviction ratio: ${(evictions/readInto*100).toFixed(1)}%`); [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Rule of thumb**: If `unmodified pages evicted` > 5% of `pages read into cache`, the working set does not fit in RAM and you will see cache-miss-driven I/O under load. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Low selectivity indexes (e.g., boolean field) waste cache space and slow writes without helping reads: [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- // Check index usage stats [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- db.orders.aggregate([{ $indexStats: {} }]) [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- // Focus on: accesses.ops (how often), since (last reset) [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Monotonically increasing `_id` (ObjectId) creates insertion hotspots on the rightmost shard/chunk. Use hashed shard keys or time-bucketed keys for even distribution in sharded clusters. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Estimate required connections: [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Required connections = (peak concurrent threads per app server) × (number of app servers) [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Each mongod in a 3-node replica set receives: maxPoolSize × number of app servers connections [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- -- [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- The Performance Advisor monitors all queries against the slow operations log (default threshold: 100ms, adjustable in Atlas UI). It analyzes query execution plans and identifies patterns where missing indexes cause full collection scans or large document examinations. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Availability**: M10 and above dedicated tiers only. Not available on shared (M0/M2/M5) tiers. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Analysis window options**: 1 hour, 24 hours, 7 days. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Recommendations are ranked by two scores: [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Impact**: High or Medium — based on total wasted bytes read across all queries matching that pattern [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Average Query Targeting**: Lower is better — ratio of keys examined to documents returned [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- The most actionable recommendations have **High impact + low query targeting**. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Suggested index: { customerId: 1, orderDate: -1 } [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Avg Query Targeting: 1842.3  <- Very bad (examining 1842x more docs than returned) [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Queries analyzed: 47 shapes [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- An `avgQueryTargeting` score above 10 indicates the query is examining far more data than it returns. Atlas considers queries with a score above 1000 high-priority. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Sampled data only**: Advisor analyzes queries exceeding the threshold — fast queries that run billions of times per day are invisible to it [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Atlas-only**: No equivalent for self-hosted (use `db.currentOp()` + `system.profile` instead) [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **No write overhead analysis**: A suggested compound index may improve reads but significantly slow writes on high-ingest collections — always test the suggested index under write load before applying in production [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Redundant indexes**: Advisor may suggest `{ a: 1, b: 1 }` when `{ a: 1, b: 1, c: 1 }` already exists [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Cannot suggest indexes for ctime timestamp format** — set timestamp format to `iso8601-utc` first [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- After running a benchmark, increase the Atlas slow query threshold to 0ms temporarily to capture all query shapes: [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Atlas UI → Cluster → Performance Advisor → Configure → Slow Query Threshold: Custom (0ms) [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- This surfaces patterns that complete quickly in isolation but degrade under load. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- -- [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- For a 3-node replica set with 4 app servers, each with `maxPoolSize=100`: [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **From one app server**: 100 × 3 = 300 outgoing connections [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **At each mongod**: 100 × 4 = 400 incoming connections [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Total across cluster**: 400 × 3 = 1,200 connections [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- MongoDB's `maxIncomingConnections` is very high by default (effectively unbounded on modern Linux), but the practical ceiling is OS file descriptor limits — typically 65,536 on default Linux configurations (`ulimit -n`). Atlas manages this automatically; self-hosted deployments must tune `ulimit` and `net.maxIncomingConnections` in `mongod.conf`. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Use a thread sweep to find the saturation point: [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Pool exhaustion symptoms**: [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- `waitQueueTimeoutMS` errors in driver logs [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- `db.serverStatus().connections.current` ≈ `maxPoolSize × replica-set-members` [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- p99 latency rises sharply while p50 stays stable (timeout-driven outliers) [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- // Critical OLTP operations (user-facing, <100ms SLA) [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- const criticalClient = new MongoClient(uri, { [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- waitQueueTimeoutMS: 1000,    // Fail fast — surface pool exhaustion quickly [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- connectTimeoutMS: 5000 [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- // Analytics / reporting operations (relaxed SLA) [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- // Note: readPreference must be specified in the URI or as a ReadPreference object, [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- // not as a bare string in the options object. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- const analyticsClient = new MongoClient( [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- uri + "?readPreference=secondaryPreferred", [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- waitQueueTimeoutMS: 30000   // Allow queuing for long-running aggregations [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- // Run this during benchmark to detect pool saturation [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- db.serverStatus().connections [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- //   current: 387,          <- active connections [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- //   available: 51413,      <- OS-level slots remaining [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- //   totalCreated: 412, [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- //   active: 156,           <- connections with in-flight operations [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- //   threadsAwaitingConnection: 0   <- queue depth (danger if > 0 consistently) [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- -- [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- // executionStats — what you actually ran [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- db.orders.find({ customerId: "C123", status: "pending" }) [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- .explain("executionStats") [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- // allPlansExecution — all plans considered (helps understand rejection) [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- db.orders.find({ customerId: "C123", status: "pending" }) [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- .explain("allPlansExecution") [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- // Bad: COLLSCAN — scans entire collection [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- "docsExamined": 2847392, [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- // Ratio = 60,583:1 — catastrophically inefficient [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- // Ratio = 1.09:1 — nearly optimal [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- // Optimal: Covered query (IXSCAN with no FETCH stage) [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- "stage": "PROJECTION_COVERED", [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- "inputStage": { "stage": "IXSCAN" } [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- // totalDocsExamined: 0 — data served entirely from index [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- queryTargetingRatio = totalKeysExamined / nReturned [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **1.0–2.0**: Excellent — index is highly selective [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **2.0–10.0**: Good — minor index key scanning overhead [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **10.0–100.0**: Investigate — consider compound index refinement [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **>100.0**: Poor — index may be wrong field order or low cardinality [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Run YCSB Workload C (read-only) before and after adding an index: [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- ./bin/ycsb run mongodb -P workloads/workloadc -threads 32 > baseline.txt [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- mongosh --eval 'db.orders.createIndex({ customerId: 1 })' [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- ./bin/ycsb run mongodb -P workloads/workloadc -threads 32 > after_index.txt [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- grep "Percentile99" baseline.txt after_index.txt [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- -- [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Measure everything, assume nothing.** A baseline is a frozen snapshot of system behavior under a defined workload. Without it, "improvement" is unmeasurable. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Match production data volume**: Use a dataset at least 10% of production size (ideally 100%). Benchmarking with 10,000 documents when production has 100M produces invalid results. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Match production schema and indexes**: Export production index definitions: [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- db.orders.getIndexes() [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Apply them to the benchmark cluster before running any tests. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Match document structure**: Use production-representative documents, not synthetic uniform data. Skewed field distributions, nested arrays, and large string fields all affect performance differently. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Warm the cache first**: Always run a "warm-up" pass before recording baseline numbers: [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- ./bin/ycsb run mongodb -P workloads/workloadc -p operationcount=200000 -threads 16 > /dev/null [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- ./bin/ycsb run mongodb -P workloads/workloadc -p operationcount=1000000 -threads 32 > baseline.txt [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Run for at least 30 minutes**: Short runs (< 5 minutes) miss WiredTiger checkpoint storms, TTL deletes, background compaction, and replication lag spikes. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Run at consistent times**: Atlas shared infrastructure can show 20–30% throughput variance between peak and off-peak hours. Run benchmarks at the same time of day across comparisons. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- To isolate the effect of a single change (new index, schema change, tier upgrade): [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Test A: baseline configuration, 30-minute run, record p50/p95/p99 + throughput [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Test B: same workload, same thread count, same data, 30-minute run [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Never change multiple variables between A and B. If you upgrade the tier AND add an index simultaneously, you cannot attribute the improvement. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- For latency comparisons: [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Run each configuration at least 3 times [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Report median of the 3 runs (not best) [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- If p99 varies by >15% across runs, investigate variance sources before declaring a winner [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- MongoDB's own benchmark specifications use 100 timing samples and take the median [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- -- [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Note: M0/M2/M5 are the true shared-tier clusters (free/low-cost, multi-tenant). M10+ are all dedicated. M10/M20 have lower vCPU allocations than M30+ but are not shared infrastructure. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- NVMe tiers (M40+) provide 5–10x higher I/O throughput vs standard SSDs. This only matters when the **working set does not fit in RAM**. If working set fits in WiredTiger cache (typically 50% of RAM), storage type is irrelevant for read latency. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Benchmark implication**: Benchmarks on M30 with warm cache and small working set may show similar latency to M50 NVMe. The NVMe advantage appears when: [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Working set > available RAM (cache misses hit disk) [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- High write throughput with large checkpoints [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Bulk insert/bulk delete operations [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Autoscaling can resize the cluster mid-benchmark, invalidating results. **Always disable autoscaling before benchmarking**: [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Atlas UI → Cluster → Edit → Auto-Scaling → Disable Cluster Tier Scaling [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Re-enable after benchmarking completes. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- For multi-region clusters, the dominant latency contributor is replication round-trip. With `writeConcern: majority`: [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- US-East to US-West electable secondary: ~70ms added to write latency [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- US-East to EU-West: ~100ms added to write latency [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Use `readPreference: nearest` to measure local vs. remote read latency difference [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- // Measure write latency with different write concerns [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- const t = Date.now(); [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- await collection.insertOne(doc, { writeConcern: { w: "majority" } }); [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- console.log(`majority write: ${Date.now() - t}ms`); [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- const t2 = Date.now(); [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- await collection.insertOne(doc, { writeConcern: { w: 1 } }); [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- console.log(`w:1 write: ${Date.now() - t2}ms`); [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- -- [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Production MongoDB runs with a warm WiredTiger cache. A cold-cache benchmark measures worst-case startup performance, not steady-state. Always warm the cache and discard the warm-up phase results. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Driver latency over loopback (~0.05ms) vs. real network (~0.5–5ms) can make a 10x difference on low-operation-count benchmarks. Always benchmark from a client on the same network segment as production (same VPC/VNet for Atlas). [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- YCSB default document size is 1KB (10 fields × ~100 bytes each). If production documents average 50KB (embedded arrays, large text fields), YCSB throughput numbers overstate performance by 10–50x. Override with: [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- p fieldlength=5000    # 5KB average field size [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- p fieldcount=20       # 20 fields per document [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- MongoDB WiredTiger is designed for concurrent access. Single-thread benchmarks understate throughput by 5–20x. Always test at production-representative concurrency levels (100+ concurrent connections is common for production apps). [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Running benchmarks without production indexes makes writes appear faster (no index maintenance overhead) and reads either deceptively fast (full scan over a warm small dataset) or slower (no index to accelerate lookups). Export index definitions and apply them to the benchmark cluster before running: [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- // Export from production [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- db.orders.getIndexes() [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- // Recreate each index on the benchmark cluster before any test run [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Benchmarks targeting only the primary with `writeConcern: w:1` do not reflect production replica sets using `writeConcern: majority`. The latency difference can be 2–10x. Always use the same write concern as production. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- When throughput stops increasing with more threads, it often means the **client** is saturated (CPU, network bandwidth, connection pool), not MongoDB. Verify by: [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Monitoring Atlas CPU (< 70% = MongoDB not the bottleneck) [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Checking driver-side queue depth (`threadsAwaitingConnection`) [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Adding more client machines [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- YCSB defaults to Zipfian distribution (a small number of hot keys receive most traffic — like a typical web app). If your production access pattern is truly uniform (every document accessed equally), the default overestimates cache hit rate and understates average latency. Match the distribution to your actual access pattern: [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- p requestdistribution=uniform    # All records equally likely [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- p requestdistribution=zipfian    # Default: hot records (power law) [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- p requestdistribution=latest     # Newest records most likely [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- WiredTiger performs checkpoints every 60 seconds by default. A 5-minute benchmark will include ~5 checkpoint events, which temporarily spike write latency. A 30-minute benchmark averages these out for a representative p99. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- AWS us-east-1 consistently outperforms AWS ap-southeast-1 for MongoDB Atlas benchmarks due to infrastructure generation differences. Always run baseline and comparison benchmarks in the same region. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- -- [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Always report as a table across thread counts, not just the best result: [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- The row where throughput plateaus and p99 spikes is the saturation point — the practical operating maximum for that configuration. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Executive summary** (1 slide): "M30 handles 13,400 ops/s at <30ms p99. M50 handles 22,100 ops/s at <30ms p99. Peak projected load of 18,000 ops/s requires M50." [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Methodology slide**: State exact tool, workload type, dataset size, thread count, Atlas tier, region, writeConcern. Without this, benchmarks are unverifiable. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Comparison table**: Before/after or tier A vs. tier B. Never present a single benchmark in isolation. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Resource utilization**: CPU and cache charts from Atlas Metrics during the benchmark window. High throughput at 90% CPU means no headroom; high throughput at 40% CPU means room to grow. [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Caveats**: State what the benchmark does NOT test (complex aggregations, transactions, multi-collection joins, production schema complexity). [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- Use Atlas Metrics during benchmark runs to correlate: [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Disk IOPS spikes** → checkpoint intervals or working set exceeds cache [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **CPU spikes** → aggregation pipelines, sort stages, full collection scans [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Network throughput** → may cap before MongoDB does (especially on M10/M20) [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- **Replication lag** → write concern `majority` latency inflation [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- For production performance sampling without a benchmark harness: [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- // Captures latency histograms for actual production traffic [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- db.orders.latencyStats({ histograms: true }) [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- // Returns read, write, commands latency buckets [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]
- // Compare p50/p99 before and after an index change [src: mongodb-performance-benchmarking]

- **Ops Manager** is MongoDB's self-hosted management platform for on-premises MongoDB deployments. **Cloud Manager** is the hosted SaaS equivalent (no infrastructure to manage). Both provide: [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- **Automation:** Declarative goal-state management of MongoDB clusters (topology, version, config) [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- **Monitoring:** Real-time metrics, alerts, and dashboards [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- **Backup:** Continuous oplog-based backup with PITR [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- MongoDB Agent (runs on every DB host) [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- Ops Manager Application Server [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- ├─ App Database (MongoDB 6.0+ RS — Ops Manager state store) [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- ├─ Backup Daemon (runs backups, stores to blockstore/S3) [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- The App DB stores Ops Manager's own state. Sizing: [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- Small (< 50 MongoDB processes): 3-node RS, M10 equivalent (8 GB RAM) [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- Medium (50-500 processes): 3-node RS, M30 equivalent (32 GB RAM) [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- Large (500+ processes): 5-node RS or sharded cluster [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- **App DB HA:** Always use 3-node replica set. Single-node App DB = single point of failure for Ops Manager. [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- A single binary that handles automation, monitoring, and backup for all MongoDB processes on the host. [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- curl -OL https://cloud.mongodb.com/download/agent/automation/mongodb-mms-automation-agent-xxx.x86_64.rpm [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- sudo rpm -ivh mongodb-mms-automation-agent-xxx.x86_64.rpm [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- sudo vi /etc/mongodb-mms/automation-agent.config [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- sudo systemctl start mongodb-mms-automation-agent [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- Ops Manager maintains the desired topology in the **automation config** JSON. The Agent continuously reconciles actual state to match the goal state. [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- **Example: Add a replica set via API** [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- curl -X PUT "https://ops-manager.example.com/api/public/v1.0/groups/{groupId}/automationConfig" \ [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- u "user:apikey" --digest \ [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- H "Content-Type: application/json" \ [src: mongodb-ops-manager]
- d @automation-config.json [src: mongodb-ops-manager]

- MongoDB Relational Migrator is a free GUI tool for migrating RDBMS schemas and data to MongoDB. [src: mongodb-migration-patterns]
- Oracle 11g+, MySQL 5.7+, PostgreSQL 11+, SQL Server 2016+, DB2 11.5+, Sybase/ASE 16.0+, YugabyteDB [src: mongodb-migration-patterns]
- **Embedded documents:** Denormalize related tables into embedded arrays/documents (recommended for 1:1 or bounded 1:many) [src: mongodb-migration-patterns]
- **Referenced documents:** Keep normalized references (for many:many or unbounded arrays) [src: mongodb-migration-patterns]
- Unique index violations in source → become duplicate documents [src: mongodb-migration-patterns]
- NULL handling: SQL NULL → MongoDB absence (not `null` by default) [src: mongodb-migration-patterns]
- DECIMAL precision: Map to Decimal128 for financial data (not Double) [src: mongodb-migration-patterns]
- Date/time columns: RDBMS timestamps → MongoDB Date with UTC conversion [src: mongodb-migration-patterns]
- **Snapshot only:** Full copy; requires application downtime during migration [src: mongodb-migration-patterns]
- **Snapshot + CDC:** Initial snapshot + ongoing change tracking; minimal downtime cutover [src: mongodb-migration-patterns]

- mongosync is MongoDB's official utility for continuous, real-time replication between two MongoDB clusters. It performs a full initial sync followed by change-stream-based CDC (no Kafka, no Debezium) and supports cutover with sub-minute downtime, reverse sync for rollback, and filtered namespace replication. mongosync powers Atlas Live Migration and Cluster-to-Cluster Sync. [src: mongosync]
- mongosync runs as a standalone Go binary outside of mongod/mongos. It opens connections to two clusters and moves data in two phases: [src: mongosync]
- **Initial sync** — mongosync reads collection data from the source cluster in parallel workers, applies inserts to the destination cluster, builds indexes, and tracks progress per-collection. [src: mongosync]
- **Change Event Application (CEA)** — once initial sync completes, mongosync tails the source via **change streams**, applies operations to the destination, and stays in lockstep until you commit or pause. mongosync does **not** read the oplog directly — it relies on the change-streams API. [src: mongosync]
- Because CDC runs over change streams, mongosync's resumability depends on the source oplog window. If un-applied operations age out of the source oplog, the change stream returns `ChangeStreamHistoryLost` and mongosync fails — see Section 6. [src: mongosync]
- **Replica set → replica set**: one mongosync instance. [src: mongosync]
- **Sharded → sharded**: run **one mongosync per shard** on the source. mongosync replicates individual shards in parallel from source to destination. [src: mongosync]
- **Replica set → sharded** and **sharded → replica set**: supported with a single mongosync for the all-to-one cases, with caveats; check the version-specific topology page. [src: mongosync]
- Both clusters must run MongoDB **6.0 or later** and share the **same major version** (mongosync also supports certain version-cross migrations — confirm against the version matrix for your mongosync release). [src: mongosync]
- For a production sync, MongoDB recommends a dedicated migration host with **at least 8 CPUs and 24 GB of RAM**. The host needs network reachability to both clusters and enough disk for logs and the local progress state. [src: mongosync]
- mongosync accepts CLI flags or a YAML/JSON config file via `--config`. The config file is the **production-grade path** because: [src: mongosync]
- Passwords on the command line are visible to `ps`, `top`, and audit logs. [src: mongosync]
- The config file can be reloaded mid-migration to change settings like `loadLevel`. [src: mongosync]
- > Cluster role (source vs destination) is **not** set on the binary — it's decided by the call to the `/api/v1/start` endpoint. The same mongosync process can be reversed; see Section 8. [src: mongosync]
- cluster0: "mongodb+srv://migrator:<password>@source.example.com/?authSource=admin" [src: mongosync]
- cluster1: "mongodb+srv://migrator:<password>@dest.example.com/?authSource=admin" [src: mongosync]
- logPath: "/var/log/mongosync" [src: mongosync]
- mongosync exposes an HTTP API on `127.0.0.1:27182` (default port). Key endpoints: [src: mongosync]
- "source": "cluster0", [src: mongosync]
- "destination": "cluster1", [src: mongosync]
- "enableUserWriteBlocking": true, [src: mongosync]
- "includeNamespaces": [ [src: mongosync]
- { "database": "sales", "collections": ["EMEA", "APAC"] }, [src: mongosync]
- { "database": "marketing" } [src: mongosync]
- `reversible:true` + `enableUserWriteBlocking:true` are **both required** to support reverse sync later. [src: mongosync]
- `enableUserWriteBlocking` tells mongosync to block writes on the destination during the sync so reverse sync remains safe. [src: mongosync]
- `includeNamespaces` and `excludeNamespaces` are mutually exclusive arrays of filter objects. Each object has a `database` and optionally a `collections` array. With no filter mongosync performs a **full cluster sync** (every non-system database/collection). [src: mongosync]
- "includeNamespaces": [ [src: mongosync]
- { "database": "sales", "collections": ["EMEA", "APAC"] }, [src: mongosync]
- { "database": "marketing" } [src: mongosync]
- This includes only `sales.EMEA`, `sales.APAC`, and every collection under `marketing`. [src: mongosync]
- Filter values can be regular expressions, so you can match many databases/collections at once: [src: mongosync]
- "includeNamespaces": [ [src: mongosync]
- { "database": "/^tenant_[0-9]+$/", "collections": ["/^orders.*/"] } [src: mongosync]
- `namespaceRemap` lets you rewrite the destination namespace, useful for tenant consolidation or rename-during-migration. The destination database and/or collection name can differ from the source. [src: mongosync]
- **You cannot change a filter on a running sync.** Stop mongosync, prepare the destination (drop any partially-synced collections), and start a new sync with the updated filter. There is no in-place filter edit. [src: mongosync]
- `local`, `config`, `admin` database internals (system collections). [src: mongosync]
- User credentials and roles — you must recreate roles/users on the destination. [src: mongosync]
- Any collection mongosync flags as "unsupported" for the version (e.g., certain time-series edge cases — check the FAQ for your release). [src: mongosync]
- mongosync writes progress and resume tokens to the **destination** cluster (in a metadata collection mongosync owns). That is why `resume` after a process crash works even on a brand-new mongosync host: the durable checkpoint lives next to the data. [src: mongosync]
- `resume` only works if mongosync is in PAUSED state (or the process was killed in RUNNING and you bring it back). [src: mongosync]
- After `resume`, mongosync may take **at least 2 minutes** before re-entering RUNNING — it re-validates the resume token and reopens the change stream. [src: mongosync]
- The resume token is a change-stream `_data` value. If the oplog has rolled past it, the change stream errors with `ChangeStreamHistoryLost` and the sync **cannot** resume — you must drop the destination and start over. [src: mongosync]
- Long pause + small source oplog → window exhausted. [src: mongosync]
- Destination collection dropped/altered while mongosync was paused. [src: mongosync]
- Filter change attempted (filters are immutable — see Section 3). [src: mongosync]
- mongosync ships four verification methods. Pick based on cluster shape and downtime budget. [src: mongosync]
- On by default for replica-set clusters. [src: mongosync]
- Runs in the background after initial sync, comparing documents on the destination as they are written. [src: mongosync]
- No locks, no extra downtime. [src: mongosync]
- `dbHash` MD5 over each collection on source vs destination. [src: mongosync]
- **Locks the cluster** for the duration of the hash — no writes can land. [src: mongosync]
- **Not available on sharded clusters**. [src: mongosync]
- Slow on large collections; precise. [src: mongosync]
- Cheapest method: `db.coll.countDocuments()` on both sides. [src: mongosync]
- **Only safe for insert-only workloads** — it cannot detect document drift from updates. [src: mongosync]
- Standalone open-source tool from MongoDB Labs. [src: mongosync]
- Connects to source and destination, compares documents/views/indexes. [src: mongosync]
- **Can run concurrently with mongosync** — no need to pause. [src: mongosync]
- The right choice for large, heavily-mutated, or sharded migrations. [src: mongosync]
- sharded cluster?           → migration-verifier [src: mongosync]
- replica set, low-mutation? → embedded verifier (default) is enough [src: mongosync]
- need cryptographic proof?  → dbHash, but pause writes first [src: mongosync]
- insert-only data?          → document counts [src: mongosync]
- Symptom: mongosync exits with `ChangeStreamHistoryLost` or similar — the source oplog rolled past mongosync's resume point. [src: mongosync]
- Initial sync taking too long on a high-write source. [src: mongosync]
- Long pause while CDC is suspended. [src: mongosync]
- Source oplog sized too small (default 5% of disk can be tiny on busy servers). [src: mongosync]
- **Pre-sync**: increase `oplogSizeMB` (or `replSetResizeOplog` with `minRetentionHours` > expected sync duration). [src: mongosync]
- **During sync**: scale up the mongosync host (more CPU/RAM) so CDC keeps up. [src: mongosync]
- **Post-failure**: drop destination collections and restart — there is no recovery once the oplog window is gone. [src: mongosync]
- Rule of thumb: set `minRetentionHours` to **2–3× the expected initial-sync duration plus any pause window**. [src: mongosync]
- mongosync retries transient network errors with exponential backoff. Sustained partitions cause mongosync to surface errors via `/progress` and eventually stop. Restart picks up from the last checkpoint **iff** the oplog window is still intact. [src: mongosync]
- mongosync replicates DDL via change events — collection creates, drops, index builds. It does **not** repair manual drift on the destination. If someone writes directly to the destination while a sync runs, you've corrupted the migration; restart from scratch. `enableUserWriteBlocking` on the destination is the guardrail. [src: mongosync]
- Check `/api/v1/progress` for `lagTimeSeconds`. [src: mongosync]
- Check destination index builds — slow index builds back up CDC. [src: mongosync]
- Check destination CPU/IOPS — `loadLevel` may be too high. [src: mongosync]
- `reversible` was not `true` at start. [src: mongosync]
- `enableUserWriteBlocking` was not `true`. [src: mongosync]
- Source and destination MongoDB **major versions differ**. [src: mongosync]
- Topologies differ (e.g., replica set vs sharded). [src: mongosync]
- Destination oplog rolled past the moment mongosync went `canWrite=true`. [src: mongosync]
- All three use the **same underlying mongosync engine**. The difference is the operating envelope: [src: mongosync]
- Need filtered sync, namespace remap, private link, or cross-version → **standalone mongosync**. [src: mongosync]
- Smaller cluster going into Atlas with public network → **Atlas Live Migration** (one-click). [src: mongosync]
- Long-lived ongoing replication between two clusters (DR, multi-region, active-passive) → **Cluster-to-Cluster Sync** (same binary, configured to never reach COMMITTED). [src: mongosync]
- mongosync is RUNNING with `lagTimeSeconds` low (sub-second on healthy networks). [src: mongosync]
- Quiesce application writes on the **source**. [src: mongosync]
- Call `POST /api/v1/commit`. [src: mongosync]
- mongosync moves to COMMITTING — drains remaining change events. [src: mongosync]
- mongosync reaches COMMITTED — final state. The destination is now authoritative. [src: mongosync]
- Flip application connection strings to the destination cluster. [src: mongosync]
- Healthy production cutovers complete in **under 60 seconds** because mongosync already had CDC caught up before `commit`. [src: mongosync]
- If the destination misbehaves post-cutover, you can flip the direction: [src: mongosync]
- `reversible:true` set at original start. [src: mongosync]
- `enableUserWriteBlocking:true` set at original start. [src: mongosync]
- Same major version on both clusters. [src: mongosync]
- Same topology (replica set ↔ replica set, or sharded ↔ sharded). [src: mongosync]
- The destination cluster's oplog has **not** rolled past the `canWrite=true` moment. [src: mongosync]
- After `reverse`, the original destination becomes source, and writes on the new source flow back to the original source. **Filtered Sync is not supported during reverse** — reverse syncs the full cluster. [src: mongosync]
- IDLE ──start──▶ RUNNING ──pause──▶ PAUSED ──resume──▶ RUNNING [src: mongosync]
- │                    │ [src: mongosync]
- │ commit             │ (auto from RUNNING/PAUSED) [src: mongosync]
- COMMITTING ──(auto)──▶ COMMITTED [src: mongosync]
- │ reverse (only with reversible=true) [src: mongosync]
- REVERSING ──(auto)──▶ RUNNING (reverse direction) [src: mongosync]
- State transitions are mostly API-driven; **COMMITTING→COMMITTED** and **REVERSING→RUNNING** are automatic. [src: mongosync]
- 1–4 scale. Default 3. [src: mongosync]
- Higher means more parallelism on both sides → faster initial sync, **more load on the destination**. [src: mongosync]
- Can be changed mid-sync by editing the config file and signaling mongosync. [src: mongosync]
- For sharded sources, run one mongosync instance per shard for true parallel copy. Coordinate them so they share the destination cluster's URI. [src: mongosync]
- Allocate 100 MB–1 GB of memory **per concurrent index build**. [src: mongosync]
- Keep total concurrent-index-build memory **under 20% of destination RAM**. [src: mongosync]
- mongosync defers some index builds until after initial sync to avoid contention. [src: mongosync]
- **Disable the balancer on the sharded destination** (`sh.stopBalancer()` / `balancerStop`) before starting the migration. The balancer fighting with mongosync inflates the migration window and can cause chunk-move-vs-CDC races. [src: mongosync]
- Increase migration host CPU/RAM if CDC lag grows. [src: mongosync]
- Increase source oplog window proactively for long initial syncs. [src: mongosync]
- Use connection pooling URIs (`maxPoolSize`, `socketTimeoutMS`) tuned for your cluster. [src: mongosync]
- mongosync inherits MongoDB's standard auth. For production: [src: mongosync]
- Use TLS for every connection — both `cluster0` and `cluster1` URIs should be `mongodb+srv` with TLS implied, or include `tls=true`. [src: mongosync]
- The mongosync host needs to trust the CA bundle for both clusters. Use the CA file via the URI parameter `tlsCAFile=`. [src: mongosync]
- mongod logs a warning if the presented certificate expires within 30 days — monitor cert expiry on the migration host as part of pre-flight checks. [src: mongosync]
- Authentication mechanism: `MONGODB-X509`. [src: mongosync]
- `authSource=$external` in the connection URI. [src: mongosync]
- The DN of the migration host's client certificate must exist as a user in `$external` on both clusters with sufficient privileges. [src: mongosync]
- The mongosync user on each cluster needs broad read/write across the synced namespaces plus: [src: mongosync]
- On source: read on every synced namespace, plus permission to open change streams. [src: mongosync]
- On destination: readWrite on every synced namespace, plus index creation, plus the metadata collections mongosync writes to. [src: mongosync]
- Atlas exposes a built-in role specifically for mongosync (`Atlas Admin` is sufficient but overpowered — use the documented minimal role set). [src: mongosync]
- Migration host inside a VPC with private link or VPC peering to both clusters when possible. [src: mongosync]
- Lock the mongosync HTTP API to `127.0.0.1` (default) — it has no built-in auth. [src: mongosync]
- If you must expose the API, front it with a TLS-terminating reverse proxy + auth. [src: mongosync]
- Both clusters on MongoDB 6.0+, same major version. [src: mongosync]
- Migration host with >= 8 CPU, >= 24 GB RAM, network access to both. [src: mongosync]
- Source oplog window >= 2-3x expected initial sync duration. [src: mongosync]
- Destination cluster sized to absorb both sync load and post-cutover production load. [src: mongosync]
- TLS + x.509 (or strong password auth) wired up on both URIs. [src: mongosync]
- Balancer disabled on sharded destination. [src: mongosync]
- Users/roles recreated on destination (mongosync does NOT migrate them). [src: mongosync]
- Config file (not CLI password) — secrets out of `ps`. [src: mongosync]
- `reversible: true` and `enableUserWriteBlocking: true` if rollback is required. [src: mongosync]
- Filters reviewed — `includeNamespaces`/`excludeNamespaces` (cannot be changed later). [src: mongosync]
- `loadLevel` chosen for destination capacity. [src: mongosync]
- Monitor `/api/v1/progress` for state + `lagTimeSeconds`. [src: mongosync]
- Watch source oplog window vs sync ETA. [src: mongosync]
- Run migration-verifier in parallel for sharded or high-mutation workloads. [src: mongosync]
- Quiesce source writes. [src: mongosync]
- `POST /commit`, wait for COMMITTED. [src: mongosync]
- Verify counts/hashes on destination. [src: mongosync]
- Flip app connection strings. [src: mongosync]
- Keep mongosync available for `reverse` until you're confident in the destination. [src: mongosync]

- `$lookup` performs an unsharded-style left outer join from the input [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- collection (the "local" side) to a foreign collection. The optimizer picks [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- between four physical operators based on input cardinality, index presence, [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]

- hundreds of thousands of documents as a red flag** — it scans the foreign [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- collection once per input document. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]

- The `as` field is always an array, even when at most one document matches. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- Add `{ $unwind: { path: "$stock", preserveNullAndEmptyArrays: true } }` to [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- flatten while keeping unmatched rows. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- If `localField` is an array, MongoDB matches **any element** of the array [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- against the scalar `foreignField` (no `$unwind` required since 3.4). [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- The foreign collection must live in the **same database**. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]

- Before MongoDB 5.1, `$lookup` could not target a sharded foreign collection. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- From 5.1 onward, sharded `$lookup` is supported but the optimizer routes [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]

- which can serialize throughput. Strategies: [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- Keep the foreign collection unsharded if it is small (a few hundred MB). [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- Use a covering index on the shard key so `$lookup` can target a single [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- For analytics, materialize via `$merge` to a denormalized collection. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- See `mongodb-schema-design` for the embed-vs-reference framework. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- **The `as` array grows large**: a `$lookup` that joins to a 50 000-document [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- parent will return a 50 000-element array per input document, which can [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- push the result over 16 MB. Use the pipeline form with `$match`/`$limit`, [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- or add a `$lookup`-then-`$unwind`-then-aggregate sequence. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- **Type mismatch silently returns empty arrays**: `localField` `ObjectId` [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- vs `foreignField` `string` will never match. Normalize types first or [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- use `$expr` with `$toObjectId` / `$toString`. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- **`$lookup` placed before `$match` loses pushdown**: if the post-lookup [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]

- the predicate is on a field that exists pre-lookup. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]

- `$densify` (5.1+) inserts synthetic documents to make a sequence dense [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- along a numeric or date field. The synthetic documents carry only the [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- densified field (and any partition fields); other fields are absent and [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]

- `"full"` — span the global min/max of the `field` across all input [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- documents (one synthetic sequence covers every partition). [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `"partition"` — span the min/max within each partition independently. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `[lower, upper]` — explicit literal bounds. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `unit` is required when `field` is a date and optional for numeric fields. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]

- Result: every device gets one document per hour from its earliest to its [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- latest reading. Missing hours appear as `{ deviceId, ts }` with no other [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- db.weeklySales.aggregate([ [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- partitionByFields: ["region"], [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- range: { step: 1, bounds: [1, 52] } [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- Use cases: tax periods, fiscal weeks, leaderboard rank slots — anywhere a [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- key is expected to be contiguous but real data has holes. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `$densify` does not modify existing documents; it only **adds** new ones. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- Inserted documents inherit only `partitionByFields` and the densified [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `field`. Use `$fill` next to populate value fields. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- If two existing documents collide with the same generated key, the [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- existing documents survive — `$densify` is a no-op for those positions. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `$densify` must precede operations that assume dense input [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- (`$setWindowFields` for moving averages, charts, time-aligned joins). [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- -- [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `$fill` (5.3+) sets a value for fields that are null or missing. It is [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- typically paired with `$densify` to fill in the synthetic gap rows, but [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- works on any pipeline. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- For `linear` and `locf`, you must supply `sortBy` so ordering is defined. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- partitionByFields: [ <field>, ... ],   // optional [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- partitionBy: <expression>,             // optional, exclusive with partitionByFields [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- sortBy: { <field>: 1|-1, ... },        // required for linear/locf [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- <field>: { method: "linear" }, [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- <field>: { method: "locf" }, [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- <field>: { value: <expression> } [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- The canonical pattern from the MongoDB blog: [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- db.storageRoom.aggregate([ [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]

- partitionByFields: ["room"], [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]

- `$linearFill` is also available as a window function inside [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `$setWindowFields`. Use the standalone `$fill` stage when you want a [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- self-contained gap-fill step; use `$linearFill` inside `$setWindowFields` [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- when you are already partitioning / sorting for other window operators. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- For `locf`, the first run of nulls before any non-null value remains [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- null — there is no value to carry forward. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- For `linear`, the same boundary rule applies and additionally: leading [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- and trailing nulls (before the first or after the last non-null) [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- remain null because interpolation requires two endpoints. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `$fill` only writes the **output** fields you specify. Other fields are [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `$fill`'s `partitionBy` / `partitionByFields` must match the upstream [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `$densify` partition keys, or you will see synthetic rows that never [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- -- [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `$unionWith` (4.4+) appends documents from another collection (and [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- optionally its own pipeline) to the running stream. It is MongoDB's [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- equivalent of SQL `UNION ALL`. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- { $unionWith: { coll: <name>, pipeline: [ ... ] } } [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- { $unionWith: <collectionName> } [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `pipeline` is optional and runs on the union'd collection's documents [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- before they are appended. The current pipeline's documents pass through [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- untouched and the union'd documents are appended **at this point in the [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- db.sales2024.aggregate([ [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- { $unionWith: { coll: "sales2025" } }, [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- { $unionWith: { coll: "sales2026" } }, [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- qty: { $sum: "$qty" }, [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- revenue: { $sum: "$total" } [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- { $sort: { revenue: -1 } } [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `$unionWith` includes duplicates. To deduplicate, follow it with `$group`: [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- db.suppliers.aggregate([ [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- { $project: { state: 1, _id: 0 } }, [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- { $unionWith: { coll: "warehouses", [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- pipeline: [ { $project: { state: 1, _id: 0 } } ] } }, [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- { $group: { _id: "$state" } } [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- All collections involved must be in the same database. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- The combined stream of documents may have heterogeneous shapes. Project [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- to a common shape before grouping or merging. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `$unionWith` cannot be used inside a multi-document transaction. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- Disallowed stages inside the inner `pipeline`: `$out`, `$merge`. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- Each collection scan inside `$unionWith` is independent — index it [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- appropriately if you push down a `$match`. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- **Sharded archive + hot collection**: union an archive collection with [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- the live collection for unified reporting. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- **Cross-tenant report**: union per-tenant collections (when the schema [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- forbids a single collection). [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- **Migration**: dual-read from old and new collections during cutover. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- **Heterogeneous corpora**: union "cases", "slack", "meetings" into a [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- single search/scoring pipeline. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- -- [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- Each blocking aggregation stage may use up to **100 MB of RAM** for its [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- in-memory state. Blocking stages include `$sort`, `$group`, `$bucket`, [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `$bucketAuto`, `$setWindowFields`, `$facet` (per branch), `$graphLookup`, [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- and `$lookup` (when buffering). [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- When a stage exceeds the limit: [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- **MongoDB 6.0+ with `allowDiskUseByDefault: true`** (the default for [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- Atlas / current community builds) — the stage spills to temporary [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- **`allowDiskUseByDefault: false`** — the stage errors out with [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `QueryExceededMemoryLimitNoDiskUseAllowed` unless the call explicitly [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- passes `allowDiskUse: true`. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- **Pre-6.0** — the stage always errors unless `allowDiskUse: true` is [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- set on the aggregation command. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- db.collection.aggregate(pipeline, { allowDiskUse: true }); [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- **Server**: `db.adminCommand({ setParameter: 1, allowDiskUseByDefault: true })` [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- **Atlas**: `allowDiskUseByDefault` is enabled by default; it can be [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- **Drivers**: `AggregateOptions.allowDiskUse(true)` (Java), [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `aggregate({ allowDiskUse: true })` (Node), `aggregate(..., allowDiskUse=True)` (Python). [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- db.collection.explain("executionStats").aggregate(pipeline); [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- Key signals in the output: [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `usedDisk: true` — at least one stage spilled to temporary files. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `spillFileSize` / `spilledBytes` / `spilledRecords` — magnitude of the [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- spill (newer versions). [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `executionTimeMillisEstimate` per stage — locate the slow stage. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `nReturned`, `totalKeysExamined`, `totalDocsExamined` — index health. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `$lookup.strategy` / `eqLookupStrategy` — [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `"IndexedLoopJoin"` (good), `"NestedLoopJoin"` (bad on large input), [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `"HashJoin"`, or `"DynamicIndexedLoopJoin"`. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- Every document at every stage must fit in 16 MB. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `$facet` output is **one document** containing every branch's array — [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- this is where the 16 MB ceiling hits hardest. Bound each branch. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `$group` with `$push` can blow up an array beyond 16 MB. Use [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `$accumulator` chunks, `$bucket` + `$group`, or write to a collection [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- with `$merge` instead of returning to the client. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- Pipelines that join with `$lookup` and then `$unwind` are fine; pipelines [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- that `$lookup` and then leave the joined array intact may overflow. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- The optimizer reorders stages where it can, but you should write [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- pipelines that already minimize the working set: [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `$match` first — filter early, ideally on an indexed field. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `$project` / `$unset` next — drop fields you do not need. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `$sort` before `$group` only if the sort is needed for output, and [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- only after the dataset is reduced. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `$lookup` / `$graphLookup` after pruning — every joined document [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- Terminal `$out` / `$merge` last. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- Stages run on each shard up to the first **split point** (a stage that [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- requires a global view, like `$group` without the shard key in `_id`, [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `$sort` over the full result, or `$facet`). [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- After the split point, intermediate results stream to the mongos (or [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- the merging shard) for the rest of the pipeline. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `$out` / `$merge` execute on the merging side; the target collection [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- may need to be unsharded or `$merge.on` must include the shard key. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]

- **`$lookup` without an index on `foreignField`** — turns every join [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- into an `O(N*M)` collection scan. Always index the foreign side. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- **`$graphLookup` without `maxDepth`** — unbounded recursion can hit the [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- 100 MB ceiling or, with disk spill, run for hours on dense graphs. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- **`$facet` branches without `$limit`** — easiest way to hit [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- `BSONObjectTooLarge`. Cap arrays in every branch. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- **`$merge` into the source collection** — risk of infinite loops if [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- the merge changes document size or shard key. Write to a separate [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- **`$out` to a sharded target** — unsupported on any version; `$out` cannot [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- write to a sharded collection. Use `$merge` when the destination is sharded. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- **`$setWindowFields` over one giant partition** — single-partition [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- window over millions of documents will spill. Add a `partitionBy` key [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- or split by tenant / day. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- **`$densify` without a following `$fill`** — produces ghost rows with [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- missing fields that downstream code may not expect. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- **`$unionWith` followed by a `$lookup`** — the join may need to scan [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- twice, once per input branch, without index pushdown for one side. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- **Pipelines that ignore `explain`** — without `executionStats`, you [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]
- cannot detect `usedDisk`, NestedLoopJoin, or unindexed sorts. [src: mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep]

- SRV records provide automatic host discovery and TLS defaults. Atlas always provides SRV URIs. The driver resolves DNS SRV and TXT records to discover all mongos/replica set members. [src: mongodb-developer]
- Always set `appName` so ops teams can trace connections in server logs. [src: mongodb-developer]
- Use SRV connection strings for Atlas and any DNS-seedlist deployment. [src: mongodb-developer]
- Never hard-code credentials; use environment variables or a secrets manager. [src: mongodb-developer]
- Set `compressors=zstd` for bandwidth-sensitive workloads (requires server and driver support). [src: mongodb-developer]
- For serverless functions (Lambda, Cloud Functions), set `maxPoolSize=1` and `maxIdleTimeMS=10000` to avoid connection exhaustion. [src: mongodb-developer]
- Set `retryWrites=true&retryReads=true` explicitly in shared URIs for clarity (both are default since 4.2). [src: mongodb-developer]
- -- [src: mongodb-developer]
- Each `MongoClient` maintains a pool of TCP connections **per server** (per replica set member or mongos). When your application requests an operation, the driver checks out a connection from the pool, executes the operation, and returns the connection. [src: mongodb-developer]
- Create a **single `MongoClient`** instance and share it across your application. The client is thread-safe (or goroutine-safe, or async-safe) in every official driver. Opening a new client per request is the most common pooling antipattern. [src: mongodb-developer]
- All drivers emit connection pool events for observability: [src: mongodb-developer]
- `connectionPoolCreated` / `connectionPoolClosed` [src: mongodb-developer]
- `connectionCreated` / `connectionClosed` [src: mongodb-developer]
- `connectionCheckedOut` / `connectionCheckedIn` [src: mongodb-developer]
- `connectionCheckOutFailed` / `connectionCheckOutStarted` [src: mongodb-developer]
- `connectionPoolCleared` [src: mongodb-developer]
- Subscribe to these events to track pool saturation, connection churn, and wait-queue depth. [src: mongodb-developer]

- Enabled by default since MongoDB 4.2. The driver automatically retries eligible write operations **exactly once** after a transient network error or a failover. [src: mongodb-developer]
- **Eligible operations**: `insertOne`, `updateOne`, `replaceOne`, `deleteOne`, `findOneAndUpdate`, `findOneAndReplace`, `findOneAndDelete`, `insertMany` (ordered or unordered), `bulkWrite` (ordered or unordered). [src: mongodb-developer]
- `updateMany`, `deleteMany` (not idempotent at the protocol level) [src: mongodb-developer]
- Writes with `w: 0` (unacknowledged) [src: mongodb-developer]
- Individual writes within an explicit transaction (the transaction itself is retried) [src: mongodb-developer]
- `RetryableWriteError` — the driver retries automatically [src: mongodb-developer]
- `NoWritesPerformed` (MongoDB 6.1+) — both attempts failed without writing; safe to retry at app layer [src: mongodb-developer]
- `TransientTransactionError` — retry the entire transaction [src: mongodb-developer]
- `UnknownTransactionCommitResult` — retry `commitTransaction()` [src: mongodb-developer]

- Use this checklist when reviewing any application that connects to MongoDB: [src: mongodb-developer]
- Link: [ ] **Single client instance** shared across the application [src: mongodb-developer]
- Link: [ ] **Connection string** uses SRV format for Atlas / DNS seedlist deployments [src: mongodb-developer]
- Link: [ ] **appName** set for observability [src: mongodb-developer]
- Link: [ ] **retryWrites** and **retryReads** enabled (default since 4.2) [src: mongodb-developer]
- Link: [ ] **Write concern** set to `majority` for durability [src: mongodb-developer]
- Link: [ ] **Read preference** matches the use case (primary for consistency, secondary for read scale) [src: mongodb-developer]
- Link: [ ] **maxPoolSize** right-sized for deployment environment [src: mongodb-developer]
- Link: [ ] **serverSelectionTimeoutMS** set to a reasonable value (not infinite) [src: mongodb-developer]
- Link: [ ] **Graceful shutdown** closes the client [src: mongodb-developer]
- Link: [ ] **Error handling** catches specific error types, not generic exceptions [src: mongodb-developer]
- Link: [ ] **Duplicate key errors** handled for idempotent operations [src: mongodb-developer]
- Link: [ ] **Transactions** use `withTransaction()` helper with automatic retry [src: mongodb-developer]
- Link: [ ] **Projections** used to limit returned fields [src: mongodb-developer]
- Link: [ ] **Indexes** cover query patterns (ESR rule) [src: mongodb-developer]
- Link: [ ] **maxTimeMS** set on long-running queries and aggregations [src: mongodb-developer]
- Link: [ ] **Change stream resume tokens** persisted for crash recovery [src: mongodb-developer]
- Link: [ ] **Monitoring events** wired to observability stack (pool events, command events, SDAM events) [src: mongodb-developer]

- Expert reference for the MongoDB Spark Connector V10+ (post-2022 rewrite) and its use inside Databricks. The connector is the canonical bridge between MongoDB (Atlas, self-managed, or Federated) and Apache Spark — both for offline analytics (batch DataFrame reads/writes) and real-time pipelines (Structured Streaming with change streams). This skill covers the full operating surface: setup, partitioning, pushdown, write semantics, streaming checkpoints, Databricks-specific wiring, and the failure patterns that bite production pipelines. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Designing or reviewing a MongoDB ↔ Spark/Databricks data pipeline. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Debugging a Spark Connector job that is slow, memory-bound, hitting skew, or failing schema inference. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Choosing between **Spark Connector**, **Kafka + Source Connector**, **Atlas Data Federation `$out`**, or **Delta Live Tables** for ingest. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Writing PySpark/Scala code that reads change streams into Delta Lake (CDC pipelines). [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Tuning partitioner choice, batch sizes, or connection pool sizing for high-volume reads. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Setting up Databricks cluster libraries, secret scopes, and Atlas network access (IP allowlist, VPC peering, PrivateLink). [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Migrating from V2.x (legacy `com.mongodb.spark.sql.DefaultSource`) to V10+ (`com.mongodb.spark.sql.connector.MongoTableProvider`). [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Questions about non-Spark MongoDB ingest (Kafka Connect alone) → `mongodb-kafka-connector`. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Aggregation pipeline syntax with no Spark involvement → `mongodb-aggregation-pipeline`. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Atlas Data Federation SQL queries without Spark → `mongodb-atlas-data-federation`. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Atlas Stream Processing pipelines that never leave MongoDB → `mongodb-atlas-stream-processing`. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Mongo change stream semantics without a Spark consumer → `mongodb-change-streams`. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]

- The connector has two lineages. Most production code in 2024+ should be on V10.x. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Package: `org.mongodb.spark:mongo-spark-connector_2.12:3.0.x` (3.x is V2 lineage despite the major-version look). [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Configures via `spark.mongodb.input.uri` / `spark.mongodb.output.uri`. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Pre-Spark-3.2 DataSourceV1 API. Less efficient pushdown. No first-class Structured Streaming. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Maven: `org.mongodb.spark:mongo-spark-connector_2.12:10.x.y` (Scala 2.12) or `_2.13:10.x.y` (Scala 2.13). [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Rebuilt on Spark 3 DataSourceV2 API — first-class catalog, batch, and streaming sources. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Configures via `spark.mongodb.read.*` / `spark.mongodb.write.*` namespaces. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Version compatibility: [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- 10.0.x: Spark 3.1+ [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- 10.1.x: Spark Connect support, schema inference improvements [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- 10.3.x: Spark 3.3 / 3.4 / 3.5; AutoBucketPartitioner introduced [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- 10.4.x: streaming write microbatch mode [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- 10.5.x: AutoBucketPartitioner is default; Atlas Data Federation supported [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- 10.6.x: Scala 2.13 builds; further Spark 3.5+ hardening [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Match the runtime's Scala major version exactly. Mismatched Scala fails at startup with `NoClassDefFoundError: scala/Product$class`. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- V10.1 added Spark Connect compatibility, enabling the connector to run inside Databricks Serverless SQL warehouses. Driver-side logic (schema inference, partitioning) runs on the connect server. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- V10 uses `spark.mongodb.connection.uri`, `spark.mongodb.read.*`, `spark.mongodb.write.*`. Three application scopes (last wins): SparkSession (`spark.conf.set`), DataFrame reader/writer `.option()` (drop the prefix), per-operation `.options({...})`. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- **Document convention:** all `.option()` calls in examples use the short key form (no `spark.mongodb.` prefix). All `spark.conf.set` calls use the full prefix. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- df = (spark.read.format("mongodb") [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- .option("connection.uri", uri) [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- .option("database", "sales").option("collection", "orders") [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Always supply explicit schema for production; inference samples 1000 docs by default and adds 30–120s startup. Use `aggregation.pipeline` to pre-filter server-side — single biggest read-performance knob. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Catalyst pushes `.filter`, `.select`, `.limit` (V10.1+), and column order down as `$match`, `$project`, `$limit` stages prepended to the user pipeline. UDFs, joins between Mongo DataFrames, and Spark-side aggregations do NOT push down. Verify with `.explain(True)` and check `PushedFilters`. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- **`AutoBucketPartitioner`** (default 10.5+): `$bucketAuto`-based, distribution-aware. Best general default. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- **`SamplePartitioner`**: `$gte`/`$lt` ranges on one field. Lowest overhead when single indexed field exists. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- **`PaginateBySizePartitioner`**: `$skip`/`$limit`-based. Use for small/medium collections without indexed partition field. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- **`PaginateIntoPartitionsPartitioner`**: target a fixed partition count. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- **`ShardedPartitioner`**: chunk-aware. Avoid on MongoDB 6.0+ where sharding starts with one large chunk that doesn't auto-split until the balancer triggers. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- `partition.size` default rule: [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Docs <1KB → 128MB [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- 1–100KB → 64MB (default) [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- >100KB or arrays >1MB → 32MB [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Atlas Data Federation supports AutoBucket/Sample/PaginateBySize since 10.5. AWS DocumentDB needs SamplePartitioner or SinglePartitionPartitioner (no `collStats`). [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Sample size default 1000; raise via `inferSchema.sampleSize`. Type promotion: Int32 ∪ Int64 → LongType, any ∪ String → StringType, mixed Date/String → DataException. Prefer explicit `StructType` for determinism, startup speed, sparse-field control. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- `operationType`: `insert` (not idempotent), `update` (`$set` on listed fields), `replace` (full document). `upsertDocument=true` (default) creates if no match. `idFieldList` defines the match filter — index the composite key. `maxBatchSize` default 512; lower for large docs. `writeConcern.w` default 1; use `majority` for transactional sinks. `mode("overwrite")` drops the collection — non-transactional. Prefer `append + replace + idFieldList` for idempotent overwrite. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]

- Spark's `checkpointLocation` stores the resume token. Failure mode: `ChangeStreamHistoryLost` if checkpoint older than oplog window. Atlas oplog windows are tier and workload dependent — verify via Atlas → Metrics → Replica Set Status. M10/M20 dev clusters often show 1–6 hours under load; M30+ typically 24+ hours. Extend with Oplog Min Retention Hours. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- For windowed aggregations, extract event-time from `fullDocument` and apply `.withWatermark()`. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Streaming sink is at-least-once. Make effectively exactly-once via `operationType=update`/`replace` with stable `idFieldList`. `outputMode("append")` for most pipelines; `update` only with upsert support; `complete` only for small aggregates. 10.4 added microbatch mode. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- **Library install**: Maven (`org.mongodb.spark:mongo-spark-connector_2.12:10.5.0`) or JAR upload. Match Scala to runtime. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- **Driver conflicts**: `IllegalAccessError` from competing mongodb-driver-sync versions; use the shaded uber-jar. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- **Secret scopes**: `dbutils.secrets.get(scope="atlas", key="connection_uri")`. Databricks-backed, Azure Key Vault-backed, or AWS Secrets Manager via init script. Avoid `spark.conf.set` for secrets (shows in Spark UI Environment). [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- **Network access**: IP allowlist (dev), VPC peering (same cloud/region), PrivateLink/Private Endpoint (production cross-account). [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- **Init scripts**: place connector config in `/databricks/driver/conf/00-mongo.conf` with `{{secrets/...}}` placeholders. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- **Delta Lake bronze/silver/gold**: `readStream` from Mongo → Delta bronze → silver (deduplicated) → gold (aggregated). [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- **DLT**: no native MongoDB source; wrap connector in `@dlt.table`. Kafka + DLT often preferred for production CDC. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Decision matrix (✓ fit, ✗ poor fit, △ conditional): [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Pre-filter at the source via `aggregation.pipeline` ($match server-side). [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Supply explicit schema. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Choose the right partitioner; size partitions 32–128MB. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Index read filters and `idFieldList`. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Tune `maxPoolSize`: `min(executors × cores, 80% of Atlas-tier connection limit)`. Atlas limits: M10 1500, M30 3000, M40 6000, M60+ 18000–32000. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Match Spark partition count to MongoDB parallelism (shards or secondary readers). [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- `readPreference=secondary` for read-heavy reporting; never for writes. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- `maxBatchSize`: 100 for large docs, 1024 for tiny. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- `writeConcern=1` for fast loads; `majority` for transactional sinks. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- Monitor Spark UI + Atlas metrics together (ops/sec, connections, ticket queue). [src: mongodb-spark-connector]
- `com.mongodb.spark.sql.DefaultSource` → `mongodb`. `input.uri`/`output.uri` → `connection.uri` + `read.database`/`read.collection`. `MongoSamplePartitioner` → `com.mongodb.spark.sql.connector.read.partitioner.SamplePartitioner`. `replaceDocument=true` → `operationType=replace`. The two namespaces coexist; migrate job-by-job with parallel verification. [src: mongodb-spark-connector]

- Comprehensive reference for MongoDB Atlas Search — the Lucene-based full-text search engine embedded in Atlas. Covers the full lifecycle from index design through query construction, relevance tuning, and production deployment. Explicitly excludes Vector Search (`$vectorSearch`); see [[mongodb-search-ai]] for hybrid and semantic patterns. [src: mongodb-atlas-search]
- Building full-text search features: search bars, typeahead, faceted filtering [src: mongodb-atlas-search]
- Relevance-ranked results with BM25 scoring [src: mongodb-atlas-search]
- Complex text queries: phrase, fuzzy, wildcard, regex, proximity [src: mongodb-atlas-search]
- Faceted navigation (e-commerce filters, category counts) [src: mongodb-atlas-search]
- Autocomplete / search-as-you-type [src: mongodb-atlas-search]
- Multi-language content with language-specific analyzers [src: mongodb-atlas-search]
- Rich scoring control: boost, decay, function score [src: mongodb-atlas-search]
- **Cluster tier requirement:** Atlas Search requires **M10 or higher**. Not available on M0 (free), M2, or M5 shared-tier clusters. [src: mongodb-atlas-search]
- **Do NOT use Atlas Search when:** [src: mongodb-atlas-search]
- You need immediate consistency — indexes are eventually consistent via change streams [src: mongodb-atlas-search]
- Exact-match on a handful of fields — standard B-tree compound indexes are faster [src: mongodb-atlas-search]
- The collection is very small (< 10k docs) and a `$regex` scan is fast enough [src: mongodb-atlas-search]
- See the full SKILL.md at ~/.claude/skills/mongodb-atlas-search/SKILL.md for complete operator reference, analyzer tables, anti-patterns, scoring, facets, autocomplete, and search node guidance. [src: mongodb-atlas-search]
