It provides visual tools for querying, aggregating, analyzing, and managing MongoDB data without requiring command-line expertise, while still exposing an embedded mongosh shell for power users. Current stable release: **1.49.8** (May 27, 2026). [src: mongodb-compass]
- User asks how to use, configure, or troubleshoot MongoDB Compass [src: mongodb-compass]
- Questions about schema analysis, explain plans, aggregation pipeline building, or index management in a GUI context [src: mongodb-compass]
- Advising on Compass editions for restricted or air-gapped environments [src: mongodb-compass]
- Evaluating query performance visually via explain plan trees [src: mongodb-compass]
- Using NLQ / AI-powered query generation in Compass [src: mongodb-compass]
- Compass plugin development or extensibility questions [src: mongodb-compass]

- -- [src: mongodb-compass]
- Compass ships in **two active editions** (Readonly Edition is being deprecated): [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Compass (Full)**: The standard edition with all features including AI-powered NLQ, automatic updates, and telemetry. Free and source-available. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Compass Isolated Edition**: Designed for air-gapped or high-security environments. All network connections except the MongoDB server are blocked — no telemetry, no AI features, no auto-update checks, no additional firewall configuration required. Use when data residency or network egress policies prohibit external calls. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Compass Readonly Edition (DEPRECATED)**: Historically limited to read operations. Will be removed in a future release. To achieve read-only behavior in the current edition: [src: mongodb-compass]
- Assign users the built-in `read` role at the database level in MongoDB. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Enable the `readOnly` option in Compass Settings. [src: mongodb-compass]
- > Warning: The `readOnly` Compass setting only hides write-operation UI elements; it does not enforce restrictions at the driver level for shell commands typed in the embedded mongosh. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Compass provides a visual connection form that builds connection strings without manual URI syntax knowledge: [src: mongodb-compass]
- **General tab**: hostname, port, authentication (username/password, X.509, LDAP, Kerberos, AWS IAM, OIDC) [src: mongodb-compass]
- **TLS/SSL tab**: CA certificate, client certificate/key, allow invalid hostnames [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Proxy/SSH tab**: SOCKS5 proxy, SSH tunnel configuration [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Advanced tab**: replica set name, read preference, authentication database, server selection timeout, `directConnection` flag [src: mongodb-compass]
- The built connection string is displayed and editable directly for power users who prefer URI syntax. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Save any connection as a **favorite** for quick access: [src: mongodb-compass]
- Favorites always appear at the top of the connections sidebar. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Each favorite can be assigned a **color label**. When connected, that color becomes the background of all tabs belonging to that connection — making it immediately clear which environment (dev/staging/prod) you are on. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Favorites can be edited (name, color, credentials) from the connections sidebar context menu (⋯ icon). [src: mongodb-compass]
- Favorites are stored with credentials in the OS keychain (macOS Keychain / Windows Credential Manager / GNOME Keyring on Linux). [src: mongodb-compass]
- Import/export favorites via JSON for team sharing or backup. [src: mongodb-compass]
- As of v1.44.5, you can edit name, color, and favorite status while actively connected. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Since Compass 1.36+, you can connect to multiple MongoDB deployments simultaneously in separate tabs, each color-coded by their favorite label. [src: mongodb-compass]

- -- [src: mongodb-compass]
- The **Schema tab** infers the shape of a collection by sampling documents and presenting interactive visualizations of field types, value distributions, and cardinality — without writing any code. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Default sample size: **1,000 documents** drawn using MongoDB's `$sample` aggregation operator. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Sampling works over the **entire collection** or a **filtered subset** when a query is entered in the query bar. [src: mongodb-compass]
- A random, non-replacement sample is used; results approximate full-dataset analysis for most distributions. [src: mongodb-compass]
- To increase the sample size beyond 1,000, go to **Compass Settings → General** and change the **"Sample Size"** field (default 1000). The query bar's **Options → MAX TIME MS** controls the query execution timeout (default 60,000 ms) — a separate setting that does not affect sample size. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Compass shows a warning when the collection has > 1,000 documents, indicating results reflect only the sampled subset. [src: mongodb-compass]
- For each field, Compass shows: [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Single data type**: type name with min/max/mean statistics. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Multiple data types**: percentage breakdown pie/bar (e.g., 20% int32, 80% string) — useful for spotting type inconsistencies in schemaless collections. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Missing/undefined**: percentage of documents that do not contain the field at all — critical for identifying optional vs. required fields. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Nested documents and arrays**: expandable to show nested field analysis, plus min/max/average array lengths. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Clicking on chart values generates query filter predicates automatically: [src: mongodb-compass]
- Click a bar in a string histogram → adds `{"field": "value"}` to the query bar. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Click+drag over a numeric histogram range → adds `{"field": {$gte: X, $lte: Y}}`. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Draw a circle on a geo map → adds a `$geoWithin / $geometry` polygon filter. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Shift+click for multi-select; multiple fields combine with `$and`. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Data quality assessment**: spot missing fields, unexpected type mixing, outlier values. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Cardinality analysis**: determine selectivity before creating indexes. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Range identification**: find min/max for numeric bounds and TTL candidates. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Index candidate identification**: high-cardinality fields with frequent query patterns. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Data modeling validation**: verify that actual data conforms to intended schema. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Geographic data exploration**: visualize point distributions for location-based collections. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Use the **Schema Export** feature (linked from the Schema tab) to export the inferred schema as JSON for documentation, sharing with teams, or importing into other tools. [src: mongodb-compass]
- -- [src: mongodb-compass]
- The **Aggregations tab** provides a visual, stage-by-stage builder for MongoDB aggregation pipelines. Each stage displays a live preview of its output from sampled data, making it easy to iterate on complex transformations. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Stage View Mode** (default): Visual pipeline editor. Each stage appears as a card with: [src: mongodb-compass]
- Stage type dropdown [src: mongodb-compass]
- Stage configuration editor with syntax highlighting and autocomplete [src: mongodb-compass]
- Output preview panel showing up to 10 sampled documents from the stage's output [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Stage Wizard** (within Stage View): Click the wand icon to get templates for common stages: `$group`, `$lookup`, `$match`, `$project`, `$sort`. The wizard generates boilerplate code to fill in. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Focus Mode** (within Stage View): Edit one stage at a time with a full-height view showing Stage Input, editor, and Stage Output side by side. Ideal for complex or deeply nested stages. Keyboard shortcuts: `Cmd+Shift+A` (add stage after), `Cmd+Shift+B` (add stage before), `Cmd+Shift+9/0` (navigate between stages). [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Text View Mode**: Raw text editor accepting full pipeline JSON/EJSON syntax with real-time linting. Toggle the `</>` switch to enter this mode. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Add stage**: Click `+ Add Stage` at the bottom, or `+` above any existing stage card. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Toggle stage on/off**: Use the toggle switch on the stage card header to include/exclude a stage without deleting it — useful for A/B testing pipeline behavior. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Reorder stages**: Drag the stage card header to a new position. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Delete stage**: Click the trash icon on the stage card. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Resize stage editor**: Drag the stage card border to adjust width. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Each stage previews up to **10 randomly sampled documents** from the stage output. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Expand all fields with "Output Options" → "Expand all fields". [src: mongodb-compass]
- `$merge` and `$out` stages display a warning before execution since they modify collection data. [src: mongodb-compass]
- When connected to a MongoDB Atlas cluster, additional stages become available in the stage dropdown: [src: mongodb-compass]
- `$search` — Full-text Atlas Search [src: mongodb-compass]
- `$searchMeta` — Search metadata aggregation [src: mongodb-compass]
- Click the **Export to Language** button to generate application-ready code in: [src: mongodb-compass]
- JavaScript (Node.js), Python, Java, C# (.NET), Ruby, Go, Rust, PHP [src: mongodb-compass]
- The generated code includes the driver boilerplate (collection reference, pipeline array, cursor iteration) so it can be dropped directly into an application. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Save a pipeline**: Click the Save button to name and save the pipeline for later use. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Open saved pipelines**: Load previously saved pipelines from the pipeline list. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Saved pipelines are stored locally in Compass. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Tip: save in-progress pipelines before closing Compass; unsaved pipelines are lost on exit. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Click **Run** (top-right) to execute the pipeline against the collection. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Use **Export Aggregation Results** to save results as JSON or CSV. [src: mongodb-compass]
- -- [src: mongodb-compass]
- The **Explain Plan** (accessible from both the Documents query bar and the Aggregation Pipeline Builder) visualizes how MongoDB executes a query or pipeline, helping identify performance bottlenecks. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Visual Tree View** (default): Each execution stage appears as a clickable node in a hierarchical tree. Click any node to see detailed execution statistics for that stage. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Raw Output View**: The full explain document shown as formatted JSON — equivalent to running `db.collection.explain("executionStats")` in the shell. [src: mongodb-compass]
- > Note: Visual Tree view is **not available** for vector search queries; use Raw Output view instead. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Execution time** (ms), **Returned documents** (nReturned), **Examined documents** (totalDocsExamined), **Examined index keys** (totalKeysExamined) [src: mongodb-compass]
- The ratio of examined to returned documents is the key efficiency signal. 1:1 is ideal; 1000:1 indicates a full-collection scan inefficiency. [src: mongodb-compass]
- For sharded collections: `SHARD_MERGE` node at top, per-shard sub-plans, winning plan per shard. Use Raw Output for the full `shards` array with per-shard `executionStats`. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Compass runs `executionStats` verbosity by default (executes the query). [src: mongodb-compass]
- Compass omits `$merge` and `$out` from pipeline explains. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Compass adds a `maxTimeMS` cap (configurable since v1.49.6). [src: mongodb-compass]
- The shell supports `allPlansExecution` verbosity; only available via Raw Output in Compass. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Run explain on a slow query. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Identify `COLLSCAN` (red) in the tree. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Note filter and sort fields. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Switch to Indexes tab (Section 5). [src: mongodb-compass]
- Create compound index: filter fields first, sort fields after. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Re-run explain → verify `IXSCAN` replaces `COLLSCAN`. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Check nReturned ≈ totalKeysExamined. [src: mongodb-compass]
- -- [src: mongodb-compass]
- > Usage statistics reflect only the connected node. For cluster-wide stats: `db.collection.aggregate([{$indexStats: {}}])`. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Index types per field: Ascending (1), Descending (-1), 2dsphere, Text. Add fields with `+` for compound indexes. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Hover → closed-eye icon → confirm. Hidden indexes exist and maintain writes but are invisible to the query planner — safe way to test impact before dropping. [src: mongodb-compass]
- > TTL indexes that are hidden continue to expire documents. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Click trash icon → enter exact index name → **Drop**. The `_id` index cannot be dropped. Never drop indexes on live production without first hiding them (see Section 12, Anti-Patterns). [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Zero-usage**: candidates for dropping (reset on every mongod restart — see §12.5). [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Redundant**: use `$indexStats` or Atlas Performance Advisor for prefix-redundancy detection. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Background operation on large collections; progress shown in Indexes tab. Do not disconnect or kill mongod during a build. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Do not create regular indexes on encrypted fields. Use `__safeContent__` for Queryable Encryption equality queries. [src: mongodb-compass]

- Query bar (filter, projection, sort, skip, limit, maxTimeMS, hint), three view modes, insert/export/count controls. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **List View** (default): Key-value pairs, expandable nested objects/arrays. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **JSON View**: Full EJSON rendering. Editing performs `findOneAndReplace` — replaces the entire document. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Table View**: Rows and columns; resizable columns (v1.49.0+). Editing performs `findOneAndUpdate` — modifies only changed fields. [src: mongodb-compass]
- > Critical: JSON view editing replaces the whole document. Use List or Table view for surgical field edits. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Double-click field → edit → checkmark to apply. List/Table view: `findOneAndUpdate` with `$set`. JSON view: `findOneAndReplace`. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **JSON Mode**: paste array or single object. **Field-by-Field Editor**: interactive BSON type selection. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Expandable inline in List view. ObjectIds auto-wrap when pasted (v1.49.0+). [src: mongodb-compass]
- `{field: 1}` include / `{field: 0}` exclude. Reduces noise and load time for large documents. [src: mongodb-compass]
- Checkboxes → **Delete Selected** → runs `deleteMany` on selected `_id` values. Irreversible. [src: mongodb-compass]
- The **Validation tab** (a separate tab adjacent to Documents, not inline editing) manages collection-level schema validation rules: [src: mongodb-compass]
- Supports `$jsonSchema` and MQL query operator syntax [src: mongodb-compass]
- `validationLevel`: `strict` (all inserts/updates) or `moderate` (new docs only) [src: mongodb-compass]
- `validationAction`: `error` (reject) or `warn` (accept with warning) [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Generate Rules**: auto-generates `$jsonSchema` from existing data [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Preview documents**: shows sample docs matching the validation expression [src: mongodb-compass]

- -- [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Anti-pattern**: Default `primary` read preference for schema analysis or explain plans on production. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Why it's harmful**: `$sample` and COLLSCAN explains compete with application workload on the primary. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Fix**: Set `readPreference=secondaryPreferred` in Advanced Connection Options. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Anti-pattern**: Sample size 100,000+ on limited-RAM machines. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Why it's harmful**: Large `$sample` loads many documents into Compass's Electron renderer process memory. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Fix**: Keep sample size 1,000–5,000; use query filters to narrow the subset instead. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Anti-pattern**: Explain on unfiltered `{}` against multi-million document collections. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Why it's harmful**: `executionStats` verbosity executes the query; COLLSCAN on large collections takes minutes. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Fix**: Add a narrow filter first. For planning-only analysis: `db.collection.explain("queryPlanner")` in shell. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Anti-pattern**: Idle Compass connections left open overnight or across weekends. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Why it's harmful**: Each connection counts against Atlas connection limits. As a rough guide: M0 ~500, M10 ~1,500, M20/M30 ~3,000 — verify current limits in the [Atlas connection limits documentation](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/faq/connection-changes/). [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Fix**: Disconnect when not in use; one connection per cluster per user. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Anti-pattern**: Using only the Usage column to decide which indexes to drop. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Why it's harmful**: Usage counters reset on every mongod restart. Monthly-use indexes show zero after a failover. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Fix**: Use `$indexStats` (includes `accesses.since`); cross-reference with Atlas Performance Advisor. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Anti-pattern**: Using JSON view for routine field-value edits. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Why it's harmful**: JSON view issues `findOneAndReplace`; accidentally removed fields are permanently deleted. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Fix**: Use List or Table view for surgical edits (`findOneAndUpdate`). [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Anti-pattern**: Creating regular indexes on QE-encrypted fields. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Why it's harmful**: Leaks frequency information about encrypted data. [src: mongodb-compass]
- **Fix**: Use `__safeContent__` fields or the dedicated QE index workflow. [src: mongodb-compass]

- Multi-tenancy in MongoDB means a single deployment serves multiple customers (tenants) while keeping their data logically or physically isolated. The right architecture depends on the number of tenants, their relative size, compliance requirements, and how much operational complexity you can absorb. [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]

- Choosing among shared-collection, database-per-tenant, or cluster-per-tenant isolation [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]

- Implementing RBAC, connection pooling, or row-level security for multi-tenant workloads [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- Automating tenant lifecycle with the Atlas Admin API [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- Diagnosing noisy-neighbor or cross-tenant data leakage bugs [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- Setting up Atlas Projects for billing chargeback [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- Single-tenant applications — no isolation patterns needed; use standard MongoDB schema design [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- On-premises deployments without Atlas — some patterns (Atlas Projects, Data Federation, Atlas App Services Rules) are Atlas-only [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- Fewer than ~5 tenants with no growth plans — operational overhead of isolation patterns exceeds the benefit [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- Internal tooling where all users belong to the same trust boundary [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- Need contractual isolation, dedicated throughput, or custom cloud region per tenant? [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- ├─ Yes → Model D: Separate Atlas Project per tenant [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- └─ No — How many tenants? [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- ├─ <100, stable, varied schemas → Model C: Separate database per tenant [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- ├─ Growing (100s–millions), uniform schemas → Model A: Shared collection [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- └─ Mixed tiers → Hybrid: A for SMB, C for mid-market, D for enterprise [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- -- [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- Tier 1 Enterprise → Model D [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- Tier 2 Mid-market → Model C [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- Tier 3 SMB/free → Model A [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- Meta-store maps tenantId → connection string, database, tier [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- -- [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- Always compound shard key with tenantId prefix: `{ tenantId: 1, _id: 1 }` [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- Zone sharding (MongoDB 6.0+): [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- sh.addShardToZone("shard-eu-west-1", "EU") [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]

- -- [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- Model C: one DB user per tenant scoped to their database only [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- Collection-level RBAC alone does NOT prevent cross-tenant document reads — must combine with app-layer filter injection [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- CSFLE: per-tenant DEK, one MongoClient per tenant, `autoEncryption.schemaMap` [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- QE: shared client possible, `autoEncryption.encryptedFieldsMap`, supports range queries [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- Atlas Cedar Resource Policies (2025): org-wide enforcement of MFA, public access blocks, project-scoped tenant API keys [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- -- [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- **Shared pool (Model A):** single MongoClient, maxPoolSize 100, all queries include tenantId [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- **Per-tenant LRU pool (CSFLE):** `lru-cache` with max:100, dispose closes evicted clients; maxPoolSize:5 per tenant; rule: LRU max × poolSize < cluster connection limit [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- **Lambda/serverless:** cache client in module scope outside handler; maxPoolSize:5, minPoolSize:0, maxIdleTimeMS:15000-30000; never call close() inside handler [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]
- **Atlas Serverless:** no pool config needed; scales to zero [src: mongodb-multi-tenancy]

- > **DEPRECATION NOTICE — Critical Context for All Readers** [src: mongodb-atlas-device-sdk]
- > On **September 9, 2024**, MongoDB announced the deprecation of Atlas Device Sync + Realm SDKs. The sync service (Atlas Device Sync) reached **end-of-life on September 30, 2025**. The local Realm database library continues as an open-source project, but SDK versions 20.x and later no longer support cloud synchronization. Users who need mobile-to-cloud sync must migrate to alternatives. [src: mongodb-atlas-device-sdk]
- > This skill documents the final architecture of the system because: (1) existing apps built on Realm/Device Sync still run in production and require support, (2) the Realm local database (without sync) is still viable open-source, and (3) the underlying patterns inform alternative architectures. All guidance is explicitly labeled by EOL status. [src: mongodb-atlas-device-sdk]
- -- [src: mongodb-atlas-device-sdk]
- Do not use this skill to guide **new greenfield project decisions**. Atlas Device Sync reached end-of-life on September 30, 2025 and is permanently shut down. Use this skill for: [src: mongodb-atlas-device-sdk]
- Supporting existing Realm/Device Sync production apps [src: mongodb-atlas-device-sdk]
- Advising on the EOL migration path for a current Realm customer [src: mongodb-atlas-device-sdk]
- Understanding the Realm local database (still viable open-source, sync-free) [src: mongodb-atlas-device-sdk]
- For new mobile sync architectures, redirect to alternatives: PowerSync, Couchbase Mobile, Ditto, or custom HTTP sync over Atlas. [src: mongodb-atlas-device-sdk]
- -- [src: mongodb-atlas-device-sdk]
- MongoDB Atlas Device SDK was the official rebrand of the Realm SDK in 2023, completing the migration of Realm (acquired by MongoDB in 2019) into the Atlas platform family. The system comprised two layers: [src: mongodb-atlas-device-sdk]
- **Realm local database** — an embedded, file-backed, reactive object store. Open-source (Apache 2.0). Continues to exist as a local database library without cloud sync. [src: mongodb-atlas-device-sdk]
- **Atlas Device Sync** — a managed sync service inside Atlas App Services that bridged the on-device Realm to a MongoDB Atlas cluster via a binary WebSocket protocol. **Shut down September 30, 2025.** [src: mongodb-atlas-device-sdk]
- **Atlas Edge Server** was a companion feature in public preview (May 2024) — a MongoDB process deployable at the edge (factory, retail, aircraft) that acted as an intermediate sync tier between device SDKs and Atlas. It was also deprecated before September 30, 2024. [src: mongodb-atlas-device-sdk]
- -- [src: mongodb-atlas-device-sdk]
- MongoDB maintained official SDKs for seven language/platform targets: [src: mongodb-atlas-device-sdk]

- Kotlin: `io.realm.kotlin` — `library-base` (local) + `library-sync` (Device Sync) [src: mongodb-atlas-device-sdk]

- Authoritative reference for MongoDB Atlas Analytics Nodes — the dedicated OLAP tier that separates analytical read workloads from operational OLTP traffic on Atlas dedicated clusters. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Explaining what analytics nodes are and how they differ from secondaries / hidden secondaries [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Configuring analytics nodes via Atlas UI, Admin API, Terraform, or AKO [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Routing queries to analytics nodes with `readPreference: secondary` + `readPreferenceTags=nodeType:ANALYTICS` [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Sizing analytics nodes for BI, reporting, and aggregation pipelines [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Connecting BI Connector, Atlas SQL Interface, Tableau, Power BI to analytics nodes [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Monitoring analytics node metrics, replication lag, and slow operations [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Estimating cost model for analytics node tiers vs. scaling the entire cluster [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Migrating from a manual hidden-secondary analytics pattern to official analytics nodes [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Explaining analytics node limitations (no elections, no writes, no primary promotion) [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Do not recommend adding analytics nodes when: [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- The cluster is M0, M2, M5, or Flex — analytics nodes require M10+. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Analytical queries are < 5% of total query volume and do not measurably impact operational latency — the cost of an extra node is not justified. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- The cluster already has dedicated read-only nodes (`readOnlySpecs`) sized and routed for the same analytical workload — adding analytics nodes would be redundant. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- The use case requires **write access** from the reporting tier — analytics nodes are strictly read-only. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- The customer needs **custom per-node indexes** (e.g., indexes only on the analytics node) — all indexes on Atlas nodes replicate from the primary; you cannot create analytics-only indexes without those same indexes existing on operational nodes, increasing write overhead cluster-wide. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- -- [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Analytics nodes are **dedicated read-only replica set members** provisioned in MongoDB Atlas specifically for analytical workloads (reporting, BI, aggregations, ETL). They occupy the same shard as the primary and operational secondaries, replicate the same data, but are entirely isolated from operational traffic through Atlas's pre-defined replica set tags. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Introduced in **2022**, analytics nodes are available on **M10 and larger dedicated clusters** only (not M0 Flex or shared-tier clusters). [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- A standard three-node Atlas replica set has: [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- 1 **primary** — accepts reads and writes [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- 2 **operational secondaries** — electable, serve operational reads [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Adding an analytics node creates a fourth (or more) member: [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **analytics node** — read-only, `priority: 0`, `votes: 0`, tagged `nodeType: ANALYTICS` [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Analytics nodes have **lower resource priority for oplog reads** than operational secondaries. This protects the oplog cursor on operational nodes and keeps their replication lag minimal, while analytics nodes may fall slightly behind during heavy write periods. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- A **hidden secondary** (priority: 0, hidden: true) is invisible to drivers and receives no reads from clients without custom routing. It is the traditional "roll your own" analytics isolation pattern and requires manual configuration of replica set member options and careful read-preference management. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- An **analytics node** is an Atlas-managed variant: it is **not hidden** (hidden: false), is automatically tagged by Atlas, and integrates with Atlas monitoring, the BI Connector, Atlas SQL Interface, and Atlas Data Federation without extra setup. You cannot manually create a hidden secondary in Atlas — analytics nodes are the supported replacement. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- A **read-only node** (`readOnlySpecs` in the API) is optimized for local reads in a geo-distributed cluster and tagged `nodeType: READ_ONLY`. It still receives the `workloadType: OPERATIONAL` tag, so operational read traffic can reach it. An analytics node never carries the `workloadType: OPERATIONAL` tag, guaranteeing true isolation from operational traffic. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **BI dashboards** (Tableau, Power BI, Metabase, Looker) hitting the cluster without affecting application latency [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **Reporting aggregations** — `$group`, `$lookup`, `$facet` pipelines that scan large collections [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **ETL export jobs** — bulk `find()` or aggregation-based exports to data lakes [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **Atlas Data Federation** queries that reference live Atlas collections [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **Atlas SQL Interface** (`mongoSQL`) queries from SQL-speaking tools [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **BI Connector for Atlas** (reaching EOL September 2026 — prefer Atlas SQL Interface for new projects) [src: mongodb-analytics-node]

- -- [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Atlas automatically assigns the following replica set tags to every analytics node: [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- workloadType: (not set — absent from analytics nodes) [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Operational nodes (electable and read-only) receive: [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- nodeType: ELECTABLE  (or READ_ONLY) [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- workloadType: OPERATIONAL [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- This dual-tag system allows drivers to precisely target one class or the other. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- mongodb+srv://<user>:<pass>@cluster0.example.mongodb.net/mydb [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- ?readPreference=secondary [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- &readPreferenceTags=nodeType:ANALYTICS [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- &readConcernLevel=local [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **`readPreference=secondary`** — reads only from secondaries; never falls back to the primary even if all tagged nodes are unavailable (returns an error instead). This is intentional: it prevents OLAP traffic from hitting the primary. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **`readPreferenceTags=nodeType:ANALYTICS`** — restricts the secondary pool to analytics nodes only. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **`readConcernLevel=local`** — required for sharded clusters to avoid returning orphaned documents. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- > **Warning:** Do NOT use `readPreference=secondaryPreferred` for analytics routing. `secondaryPreferred` falls back to the primary when no tagged secondaries are available, defeating workload isolation. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- mongodb+srv://<user>:<pass>@cluster0.example.mongodb.net/mydb [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- ?readPreference=secondary [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- &readPreferenceTags=nodeType:ANALYTICS [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- &readConcernLevel=local [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- First tag set `nodeType:ANALYTICS` — try analytics nodes first. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Second tag set `` (empty) — fall back to any available secondary if all analytics nodes are unavailable (e.g., during disk scale-down, initial sync, or NVMe tier changes). [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- This avoids read errors at the cost of occasionally hitting an operational secondary. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Add `workloadType:OPERATIONAL` tag to operational service connections: [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- mongodb+srv://<user>:<pass>@cluster0.example.mongodb.net/mydb [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- ?readPreference=secondary [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- &readPreferenceTags=workloadType:OPERATIONAL [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- &readConcernLevel=local [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Analytics nodes do **not** carry the `workloadType: OPERATIONAL` tag, so they are never selected by this tag set. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]

- -- [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- The **Atlas SQL Interface** (uses the MongoSQL dialect) routes queries to analytics nodes natively when analytics nodes are present in the cluster. It is the successor to the BI Connector for Atlas. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- > **EOL notice:** The MongoDB Connector for Business Intelligence for Atlas and on-premises reaches end-of-life and will no longer be supported after **September 2026**. Use Atlas SQL Interface for new projects. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Connect Power BI, Tableau, and other ODBC/JDBC tools to Atlas SQL Interface using the dedicated MongoDB Atlas SQL ODBC/JDBC drivers. The Atlas SQL Interface automatically prefers analytics nodes if they are available, directing OLAP SQL queries away from the primary. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- The MongoDB Connector for BI (`mongosqld`) supports analytics node routing via the `readPreference` and `readPreferenceTags` configuration options. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **Connection string for BI Connector → analytics nodes:** [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- mongodb+srv://<user>:<pass>@cluster.mongodb.net/db [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- ?readPreference=secondary [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- &readPreferenceTags=nodeType:ANALYTICS [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Set the BI Connector read preference to **Analytics** in the Atlas BI Connector settings panel. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **Why route BI Connector to analytics nodes:** [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Prevents Tableau/Power BI → `mongosqld` → MongoDB scan queries from competing with application write traffic on the primary. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- For multi-cloud clusters with BI Connector, routing to analytics nodes also **stabilizes the connection string** — if electable nodes fail over across cloud providers, the analytics node SRV host remains constant. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **Supported BI tools:** [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Tableau Desktop [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Microsoft Power BI Desktop (Windows, via Power Query connector) [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Qlik Sense [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- MySQL Workbench [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Excel (via ODBC DSN) [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- -- [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Atlas Data Federation (ADF) uses a distributed query engine to route queries across MongoDB Atlas clusters, Atlas Online Archive, and cloud object storage (S3, Azure Blob, GCS). [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **Routing ADF queries to analytics nodes:** ADF uses an elastic pool of query agents in the region nearest your data. For live Atlas cluster sources, ADF pushes down filtering and aggregation stages to the source when possible — which means the read issued against the Atlas cluster will use whatever read preference is configured in the ADF store. Large scans benefit from analytics nodes because the workload does not affect operational read/write latency. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- To route those reads to the analytics node, set `readPreference` in the ADF store configuration. In the Atlas UI federated database store JSON (or via the ADF API): [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- "name": "myAtlasStore", [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- "clusterName": "myCluster", [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- The outer `tagSets` array is tried in order: first try nodes tagged `nodeType: ANALYTICS`; if none are available, the inner empty array `[]` allows fallback to any secondary. This ensures federated `$lookup` operations and collection scans hit the analytics node rather than the primary or operational secondaries. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **Practical use cases with analytics nodes + ADF:** [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Joining live transactional data (from Atlas cluster via analytics node) with historical data from Atlas Online Archive or S3 [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Running `$lookup` aggregations across Atlas collections without impacting application performance [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Time-series reporting across the full data lifecycle (hot data in Atlas, cold data in archive/S3) [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- -- [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Since August 2022, analytics nodes can use a **different instance tier** from the operational (electable + read-only) nodes. This is the key differentiator from standard secondaries. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **Scale UP the analytics tier when:** [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Many concurrent BI users run dashboards simultaneously [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Aggregation pipelines require large in-memory sorts (`$sort` stage) that exceed available RAM [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Report queries scan large collections and benefit from faster I/O [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **Scale DOWN the analytics tier when:** [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Analytics usage is intermittent or limited to off-peak hours [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Reporting queries are simple and do not compete for memory [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Cost optimization is a priority (analytics workloads are secondary to OLTP) [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Use RAM-optimized (`R` series) tiers when aggregation pipelines frequently spill to disk due to the 100 MB in-memory sort limit (or when `allowDiskUse: true` is set). [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- NVMe-backed analytics nodes (M60 and above on AWS/Azure) provide low-latency sequential reads beneficial for: [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Collection scans over large datasets [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- `$group` with large cardinality keys [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- `$lookup` with large foreign collections [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **NVMe constraints for analytics nodes:** [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- If the Base Tier uses NVMe (e.g., M60 NVMe), the Analytics Tier must also be the same NVMe tier level. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- NVMe clusters cannot be paused. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Azure supports NVMe on M60, M80, M200, M300, M400, M600; GCP does not support NVMe clusters. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- If you size analytics nodes **significantly below** the base tier: [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Analytics nodes may develop persistent replication lag. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- In extreme cases, analytics nodes can fall off the **oplog window** and require a full initial sync. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Monitor replication lag metric in Atlas and set alerts (see Section 7). [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Analytics nodes **replicate all data from the primary** — they do not store a separate dataset. Storage capacity on the analytics node must be at least as large as the primary's data set. Storage settings must match across node types within a region when they are configured (disk_size_gb must be consistent). [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- -- [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- In the Atlas UI, analytics node metrics are available under **Metrics** on the cluster view. Select the analytics node host from the host selector dropdown to view node-specific metrics. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **Key metrics to monitor:** [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Enable the Atlas Query Profiler on the analytics node host to capture slow operations: [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- In Atlas, open the cluster and click the **Profiler** tab (or navigate to **Performance Advisor → Query Profiler**). [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Select the analytics node host from the host dropdown. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Set the slow operation threshold (default: 100 ms). [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Review the scatterplot of operation execution times. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- The Query Profiler captures up to the most recent **100,000 operations** and retains them for **7 days**. It shows: [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- `millis` — query execution time [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- `docsExamined` — documents scanned [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- `keysExamined` — index keys examined [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- `nReturned` — documents returned [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Missing index suggestions [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- The RTPP is available per-node in Atlas and shows live: [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Active operations on the analytics node [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Network I/O [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Replication lag on the analytics node vs. the primary [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Hottest collections (by scan rate) [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Use RTPP during load tests to verify analytics queries are hitting the analytics node (not the primary or operational secondaries). [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Configure these Atlas alerts specifically for analytics nodes: [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **Replication Oplog Window < 1 hour** — analytics node at risk of falling off oplog [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **Replication Lag > 120s** — analytics node lagging significantly; workload isolation may be degraded [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **System CPU > 90%** — analytics node overloaded; consider scaling up the analytics tier [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **Connections % > 80%** — connection pool exhaustion on analytics node [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **Disk Space Used % > 85%** — storage filling up on analytics node [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- -- [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Analytics nodes are billed at the **standard Atlas hourly rate** for their configured instance tier, **prorated per node**: [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Analytics node cost = analytics_tier_hourly_rate × node_count × hours_running [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- There is no premium or discount for analytics nodes vs. equivalent-tier operational nodes. An M40 analytics node costs the same per hour as an M40 electable node. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **Scenario: BI dashboard on M30 cluster without analytics nodes** [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Without analytics nodes, you would scale the entire cluster (primary + 2 secondaries) to M50 to handle concurrent BI queries without impacting application latency: [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Current cost:  3 × M30 nodes = 3 × $390/mo = $1,170/mo [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Scaled cost:   3 × M50 nodes = 3 × $1,450/mo = $4,350/mo  (+$3,180/mo) [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **With 1 analytics node at M50 tier:** [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Operational nodes: 3 × M30 = $1,170/mo  (unchanged) [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Analytics node:    1 × M50 = $1,450/mo [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Total:             $2,620/mo  (+$1,450/mo vs. baseline, saves $1,730/mo vs. full scale-up) [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Adding a single larger analytics node is significantly cheaper than scaling the entire cluster. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **When analytics nodes may NOT save money:** [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- If operational read traffic also needs scaling independently, full tier scale-up may be warranted. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- For very small clusters (M10) where a single analytics node is a major percentage of total cost. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- When analytics usage is so light it does not require a dedicated node at all. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Start analytics nodes at the same tier as base nodes. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Monitor `cpu.user` and `memory.resident` under peak analytics load. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Scale analytics tier up if CPU > 80% sustained; scale down if CPU < 20% sustained. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- For seasonal analytics (month-end reporting), consider programmatic tier changes via the Admin API to scale analytics nodes down between peaks. Note: clusters using NVMe storage cannot be paused — use tier downscaling instead. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- -- [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Before analytics nodes, teams would configure a priority-0, hidden secondary in a self-managed replica set: [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- // rs.reconfig() — self-managed replica sets only [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- { _id: 0, host: "primary:27017", priority: 2 }, [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- { _id: 1, host: "secondary1:27017", priority: 1 }, [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- { _id: 2, host: "secondary2:27017", priority: 1 }, [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- host: "analytics:27017", [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- votes: 0,        // non-voting [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- tags: { nodeType: "ANALYTICS" } [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- This pattern is **not available in Atlas** — Atlas manages replica set configuration automatically. Analytics nodes are the Atlas-managed equivalent. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **Add analytics nodes to your Atlas cluster** (UI, API, or Terraform — see Section 2). [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **Update read preference** in BI / reporting application connection strings: [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- If migrating from a **self-managed hidden secondary** with a custom tag (e.g., `nodeType: analytics_custom`), update both the tag name and add `readConcernLevel`: [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Before (self-managed, custom tag): [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- readPreference=secondary&readPreferenceTags=nodeType:analytics_custom [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- After (Atlas analytics node, Atlas pre-defined tag): [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- readPreference=secondary&readPreferenceTags=nodeType:ANALYTICS&readConcernLevel=local [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- If already using `nodeType:ANALYTICS` as your custom tag, only `readConcernLevel=local` needs to be added (for sharded clusters). Verify the exact tag name used in your existing replica set config before assuming no change is needed. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **Retire the manual hidden secondary** (if migrating from a self-managed cluster to Atlas). Atlas does not expose hidden secondaries; once your analytics nodes are provisioned and replication is confirmed healthy, decommission the old node. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **Configure BI Connector / Atlas SQL Interface** to use analytics read preference (see Section 4). [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **Verify routing** with the Real-Time Performance Panel: confirm queries appear under the analytics node host, not the primary or operational secondaries. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- **Set up monitoring and alerts** (see Section 7) — analytics nodes are separately monitored in Atlas, unlike hidden members which were less visible. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- -- [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Analytics nodes **cannot participate in elections** and **cannot become primary**. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- They are effectively `priority: 0`, `votes: 0` members from the replica set's perspective. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- A cluster's **availability (HA)** is not affected by analytics node count — only electable nodes count toward quorum. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- If all analytics nodes become unavailable, no HA impact occurs, but queries using `readPreference=secondary&readPreferenceTags=nodeType:ANALYTICS` will fail or fall back to empty tag set (if fallback is configured). [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Analytics nodes are **strictly read-only**. All write operations must target the primary. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Attempting to write directly to an analytics node's host will return a `NotWritablePrimary` error. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Analytics nodes are **only addressable** via `readPreference=secondary` (or `nearest`) **plus** `readPreferenceTags=nodeType:ANALYTICS`. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- They cannot serve requests for `readPreference=primary`, `primaryPreferred`, or untagged `secondary`/`nearest` reads. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- `secondaryPreferred` with analytics tags will route to the primary if analytics nodes are unavailable — avoid this for true isolation (use `secondary` instead). [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Analytics nodes require **M10 or larger dedicated clusters**. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Not available on M0 (free), M2, M5 (shared), or Flex clusters. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- If the base tier uses **NVMe-backed storage** (e.g., M60 NVMe), the analytics tier must be the **same tier level** (no mixing NVMe and non-NVMe). [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Mixing **General** and **Low-CPU** tier families between base and analytics nodes disables **disk auto-scaling**. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Storage (`disk_size_gb`) must remain consistent across node types within a region. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- No per-region maximum specifically for analytics nodes, but the cluster-wide limit is **50 total nodes** across all shards and regions (multi-region constraint). [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- For sharded clusters, the number of electable, read-only, and analytics nodes **must be the same across all shards**. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Analytics nodes **replicate all data from the primary** — they do not serve as a separate data tier or store different collections. Every byte in the operational cluster is also present on the analytics node. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Analytics nodes may become temporarily unavailable (0–10 minutes typically) during: [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Initial sync (after adding or resizing an analytics node) [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Disk scale-down operations [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- NVMe cluster tier changes [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- Always implement the **fallback empty tag set** in analytics connections to handle these windows gracefully. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]
- As of 2023, the MongoDB JDBC driver had a known bug where `readPreferenceTag` for analytics nodes in connection strings was ignored (GitHub issue #362 in `mongodb/mongo-jdbc-driver`). Check the driver changelog for your version before relying on JDBC-based routing to analytics nodes. Use the native MongoDB drivers (Java sync/async) when possible. [src: mongodb-analytics-node]

- MongoDB replication provides redundancy and high availability through **replica sets** -- groups of `mongod` processes that maintain the same data set. A replica set contains one primary member that receives all writes and one or more secondary members that replicate the primary's data asynchronously via the **oplog** (operations log). Replica sets are the foundation of MongoDB's data durability, fault tolerance, and read scaling strategy. [src: mongodb-replication]
- Key guarantees of a properly configured replica set: [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Automatic failover**: if the primary becomes unavailable, an election promotes a secondary to primary within ~12 seconds (median, with default settings). [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Data redundancy**: every data-bearing member holds a complete copy of the data set. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Read scaling**: applications can distribute reads across secondaries using read preferences. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Tunable consistency**: write concern and read concern let applications choose their durability and consistency guarantees per operation. [src: mongodb-replication]
- -- [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Primary**: The only member that accepts write operations. Records all writes to its oplog. At most one primary per replica set at any time. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Secondary**: Maintains an identical copy of the primary's data set by asynchronously applying operations from the primary's oplog. Can serve read operations when read preference allows it. Can be elected primary during failover. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Arbiter**: Participates in elections but holds no data. Provides a tiebreaking vote in even-member-count topologies. Must not run on the same system as primary or secondary members. Has exactly 1 election vote and a default priority of 0. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Hidden Members**: Must have `priority: 0`, so they cannot become primary. Excluded from default client read routing. Use for dedicated tasks: reporting queries, backups, analytics workloads. Only reachable by direct connection. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Delayed Members**: Maintain a time-delayed copy of the data (configured via `secondaryDelaySecs`). Must be hidden and should be non-voting. Serve as a defense against accidental data destruction -- the delayed copy preserves the state from N seconds ago. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Three-member replica set (P-S-S)**: One primary, two secondaries. Minimum recommended production topology. Tolerates one member failure while maintaining majority for elections and `w: "majority"` writes. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Primary-Secondary-Arbiter (P-S-A)**: Costs less but carries availability risk. If the sole data-bearing secondary goes down, `w: "majority"` writes fail. Avoid in sharded clusters. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Geographically distributed**: Place members across data centers. Ensure majority of voting members resides in the primary data center. [src: mongodb-replication]
- -- [src: mongodb-replication]
- Elections occur when: a new node is added; the set is initiated with `rs.initiate()`; maintenance commands run (`rs.stepDown()`, `rs.reconfig()`); secondaries lose connectivity to primary for longer than `electionTimeoutMillis` (default 10s); or the primary detects it can see only a minority of voting members. [src: mongodb-replication]
- MongoDB uses Raft-based consensus (pv1): heartbeats every 2 seconds; if no heartbeat within 10s member is marked inaccessible; candidate runs dry election first; first member to receive majority of votes becomes primary. [src: mongodb-replication]
- Higher-priority members call elections sooner. `priority: 0` members cannot become primary. [src: mongodb-replication]
- Maximum 7 voting members, up to 50 total members. [src: mongodb-replication]
- Non-voting members must have `priority: 0` and `votes: 0`. [src: mongodb-replication]
- -- [src: mongodb-replication]
- The oplog (`local.oplog.rs`) is a capped collection recording all write operations in idempotent format. Every member maintains its own oplog. Secondaries copy and apply entries from the primary's oplog. [src: mongodb-replication]
- The **oplog window** is the time between the newest and oldest oplog entry. A secondary that falls behind more than the oplog window must perform a full initial sync. [src: mongodb-replication]
- rs.printReplicationInfo()  // shows oplog size, time window, first/last timestamps [src: mongodb-replication]
- db.adminCommand({ replSetResizeOplog: 1, size: 10240 }) [src: mongodb-replication]
- db.adminCommand({ replSetResizeOplog: 1, minRetentionHours: 24 }) [src: mongodb-replication]
- -- [src: mongodb-replication]
- Write concern controls durability before the server acknowledges a write. [src: mongodb-replication]
- `j: true`: synced to on-disk journal before ack. [src: mongodb-replication]
- `j: false`: in-memory ack only. [src: mongodb-replication]
- With `w: "majority"`, controlled by `writeConcernMajorityJournalDefault` (default `true`). [src: mongodb-replication]
- Time limit (ms) for propagation. Does not undo applied writes on timeout. `0` = wait indefinitely. [src: mongodb-replication]
- MongoDB 5.0+: `{ w: "majority" }` for most deployments. Exception: P-S-A topologies default to `{ w: 1 }`. [src: mongodb-replication]
- Set at transaction level, not per-operation: [src: mongodb-replication]
- session.startTransaction({ writeConcern: { w: "majority" } }); [src: mongodb-replication]
- -- [src: mongodb-replication]
- `maxStalenessSeconds` (min 90s) excludes secondaries lagging beyond threshold. [src: mongodb-replication]
- -- [src: mongodb-replication]
- Strongest consistency                              Highest availability [src: mongodb-replication]
- linearizable --> majority --> snapshot --> local --> available [src: mongodb-replication]
- Use `rc: "majority"` + `wc: "majority"` for causal consistency. MongoDB sets `afterClusterTime` automatically in causally consistent sessions. See §17 for full coverage. [src: mongodb-replication]
- -- [src: mongodb-replication]
- A rollback reverts writes on a former primary when it rejoins after failover, when those writes had not replicated to a majority before the primary stepped down. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Recover-to-a-timestamp** (default, MongoDB 4.0+): reverts to consistent point, re-applies ops. No size limit. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Rollback via refetch** (legacy, only when `enableMajorityReadConcern=false`, fixed to `true` in 5.0+): limited to 300 MB. [src: mongodb-replication]
- bsondump <dbpath>/rollback/<collectionUUID>/removed.<timestamp>.bson [src: mongodb-replication]
- Use `{ w: "majority" }`. Enable journaling. Monitor replication lag. Avoid P-S-A topologies. [src: mongodb-replication]
- -- [src: mongodb-replication]
- rs.printReplicationInfo()           // oplog size and window [src: mongodb-replication]
- rs.printSecondaryReplicationInfo()  // per-secondary lag in seconds [src: mongodb-replication]
- rs.status()                         // full status, optimeDate per member [src: mongodb-replication]
- Common causes: slow disk I/O, secondary read overload, index builds, network congestion, large bulk writes, long transactions. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Flow control**: limits primary write rate to keep majority-committed lag under `flowControlTargetLagSeconds` (default 10s). [src: mongodb-replication]
- -- [src: mongodb-replication]
- Steps: database cloning → index building → oplog buffering → oplog application → SECONDARY state. [src: mongodb-replication]
- Ensure oplog window covers sync duration. Up to 10 retry attempts; 24h transient error window. [src: mongodb-replication]
- -- [src: mongodb-replication]
- Every change event has a resume token (`_id`). Use `resumeAfter` to resume from a token; `startAfter` to resume even after invalidate events. Tokens expire when oplog entry is truncated. [src: mongodb-replication]
- MongoDB 6.0+: `fullDocumentBeforeChange` and `fullDocument: 'updateLookup'` for pre/post images (requires `changeStreamPreAndPostImages` on collection). [src: mongodb-replication]

- Rolling maintenance: maintain secondaries first, then `rs.stepDown()` and maintain former primary. [src: mongodb-replication]

- -- [src: mongodb-replication]
- **`"local"`**: Returns the most recent data on the targeted node with no majority confirmation. On a secondary, data may not yet be replicated to a majority of members and could be rolled back if the current primary fails before replication completes. This is the default for find, aggregate, and getMore operations. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **`"available"`**: Identical to `"local"` on replica set members. On sharded clusters it diverges: reads are served directly from the shard that owns the chunk without consulting config servers for up-to-date routing metadata. During chunk migrations this can return orphaned documents. Avoid on sharded collections for any consistency-sensitive reads. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **`"majority"`**: Returns only data acknowledged by a majority of data-bearing voting members and written to the majority-committed oplog point. Guaranteed durable; will never be rolled back. Requires WiredTiger (only storage engine since MongoDB 5.0). [src: mongodb-replication]
- **`"linearizable"`**: Strongest single-document consistency guarantee. Reads block until the server confirms no write started before the read is still in-flight at a majority. Always targets the primary. Must be combined with `maxTimeMS`. Cannot be used with `$out`, `$merge`, or multi-document transactions. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **`"snapshot"`**: Returns data from a consistent snapshot of majority-committed data at a single point in time. Primarily used in multi-document transactions. When a transaction commits with `w: "majority"`, the snapshot guarantee is preserved end-to-end. [src: mongodb-replication]
- MongoDB maintains an internal **majority-committed optime** — the oplog timestamp up to which a majority of data-bearing voting members have confirmed replication. The primary advances this by computing the highest optime for which `floor(votingMembers/2)+1` members have reported an optime >= that value, every heartbeat cycle (~2s). [src: mongodb-replication]
- WiredTiger maintains an in-memory read snapshot pegged to the majority-committed optime. `"majority"` reads access this snapshot directly — they do not block writes and add negligible latency in steady state. [src: mongodb-replication]
- The interaction with `w: "majority"` write concern is tight: a write acknowledged at `w: "majority"` has by definition advanced the majority-commit point to at least its optime. A subsequent read with read concern `"majority"` (`rc: "majority"`) on any node will therefore see that write — this is the foundation of the causal consistency guarantee. (`rc:` is used as shorthand for "read concern level" throughout §16–17.) [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Choose `"linearizable"` when**: [src: mongodb-replication]
- You need the absolute freshest majority-committed data for a single document. [src: mongodb-replication]
- You are building a compare-and-swap or test-and-set operation. [src: mongodb-replication]
- Always pair with `maxTimeMS` to bound the blocking window. [src: mongodb-replication]
- const doc = await collection.findOne( [src: mongodb-replication]
- { readConcern: { level: 'linearizable' }, maxTimeMS: 5000 } [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Choose `"snapshot"` when**: [src: mongodb-replication]
- You need a consistent view across multiple documents or collections within a transaction. [src: mongodb-replication]
- You want point-in-time consistency without the primary-only restriction of `"linearizable"`. [src: mongodb-replication]
- const session = client.startSession(); [src: mongodb-replication]
- await session.startTransaction({ readConcern: { level: 'snapshot' }, writeConcern: { w: 'majority' } }); [src: mongodb-replication]
- const orders = await ordersCollection.find({}, { session }).toArray(); [src: mongodb-replication]
- const inventory = await inventoryCollection.find({}, { session }).toArray(); [src: mongodb-replication]
- await session.commitTransaction(); [src: mongodb-replication]
- await session.endSession(); [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Key difference**: `"linearizable"` waits for in-flight writes before responding (most current possible). `"snapshot"` reads from a fixed point in time and does not wait. [src: mongodb-replication]
- For sharded clusters, default to `"local"` or `"majority"`. `"available"` exists primarily as a performance optimization for non-sharded workloads. [src: mongodb-replication]

- Causal consistency guarantees that operations within a session (or across sessions sharing causal tokens) observe a logically consistent sequence of writes: [src: mongodb-replication]
- MongoDB implements causal consistency through two logical clocks in every server response: [src: mongodb-replication]
- **`$clusterTime`**: A hybrid logical clock (HLC) providing total ordering across the replica set. Every server response includes the current `$clusterTime`. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **`operationTime`**: The optime of the most recent operation in the session. Clients send it as `afterClusterTime` on the next read. [src: mongodb-replication]
- When a read is issued with `afterClusterTime: T`, the server waits until its majority-committed optime >= T before executing, ensuring the read sees all writes up to time T. [src: mongodb-replication]

- Every MongoDB operation uses a session, even if you do not create one explicitly. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Key implications**: [src: mongodb-replication]
- Implicit sessions provide no causal ordering guarantees between operations. [src: mongodb-replication]
- Explicit sessions maintain `clusterTime` and `operationTime` across all operations. [src: mongodb-replication]
- Multi-document transactions always require an explicit session. [src: mongodb-replication]
- Explicit sessions are lightweight — negligible cost for the duration of a request-response cycle. **Exception**: sessions with an active transaction hold a WiredTiger snapshot and should be kept short to avoid cache pressure (see §17.7). Always call `endSession()`. [src: mongodb-replication]
- Implicit sessions are fine for fire-and-forget writes where read-your-writes is not required. [src: mongodb-replication]

- MongoDB replication provides redundancy and high availability through **replica sets** -- groups of `mongod` processes that maintain the same data set. A replica set contains one primary member that receives all writes and one or more secondary members that replicate the primary's data asynchronously via the **oplog** (operations log). Replica sets are the foundation of MongoDB's data durability, fault tolerance, and read scaling strategy. [src: mongodb-replication]
- Key guarantees of a properly configured replica set: [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Automatic failover**: if the primary becomes unavailable, an election promotes a secondary to primary within ~12 seconds (median, with default settings). [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Data redundancy**: every data-bearing member holds a complete copy of the data set. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Read scaling**: applications can distribute reads across secondaries using read preferences. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Tunable consistency**: write concern and read concern let applications choose their durability and consistency guarantees per operation. [src: mongodb-replication]
- -- [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Primary**: The only member that accepts write operations. Records all writes to its oplog. At most one primary per replica set at any time. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Secondary**: Maintains an identical copy of the primary's data set by asynchronously applying operations from the primary's oplog. Can serve read operations when read preference allows it. Can be elected primary during failover. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Arbiter**: Participates in elections but holds no data. Provides a tiebreaking vote in even-member-count topologies. Must not run on the same system as primary or secondary members. Has exactly 1 election vote and a default priority of 0. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Hidden Members**: Must have `priority: 0`, so they cannot become primary. Excluded from default client read routing. Use for dedicated tasks: reporting queries, backups, analytics workloads. Only reachable by direct connection. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Delayed Members**: Maintain a time-delayed copy of the data (configured via `secondaryDelaySecs`). Must be hidden and should be non-voting. Serve as a defense against accidental data destruction -- the delayed copy preserves the state from N seconds ago. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Three-member replica set (P-S-S)**: One primary, two secondaries. Minimum recommended production topology. Tolerates one member failure while maintaining majority for elections and `w: "majority"` writes. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Primary-Secondary-Arbiter (P-S-A)**: Costs less but carries availability risk. If the sole data-bearing secondary goes down, `w: "majority"` writes fail. Avoid in sharded clusters. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Geographically distributed**: Place members across data centers. Ensure majority of voting members resides in the primary data center. [src: mongodb-replication]
- -- [src: mongodb-replication]
- Elections occur when: a new node is added; the set is initiated with `rs.initiate()`; maintenance commands run (`rs.stepDown()`, `rs.reconfig()`); secondaries lose connectivity to primary for longer than `electionTimeoutMillis` (default 10s); or the primary detects it can see only a minority of voting members. [src: mongodb-replication]
- MongoDB uses Raft-based consensus (pv1): heartbeats every 2 seconds; if no heartbeat within 10s member is marked inaccessible; candidate runs dry election first; first member to receive majority of votes becomes primary. [src: mongodb-replication]
- Higher-priority members call elections sooner. `priority: 0` members cannot become primary. [src: mongodb-replication]
- Maximum 7 voting members, up to 50 total members. [src: mongodb-replication]
- Non-voting members must have `priority: 0` and `votes: 0`. [src: mongodb-replication]
- -- [src: mongodb-replication]
- The oplog (`local.oplog.rs`) is a capped collection recording all write operations in idempotent format. Every member maintains its own oplog. Secondaries copy and apply entries from the primary's oplog. [src: mongodb-replication]
- The **oplog window** is the time between the newest and oldest oplog entry. A secondary that falls behind more than the oplog window must perform a full initial sync. [src: mongodb-replication]
- rs.printReplicationInfo()  // shows oplog size, time window, first/last timestamps [src: mongodb-replication]
- db.adminCommand({ replSetResizeOplog: 1, size: 10240 }) [src: mongodb-replication]
- db.adminCommand({ replSetResizeOplog: 1, minRetentionHours: 24 }) [src: mongodb-replication]
- -- [src: mongodb-replication]
- Write concern controls durability before the server acknowledges a write. [src: mongodb-replication]
- `j: true`: synced to on-disk journal before ack. [src: mongodb-replication]
- `j: false`: in-memory ack only. [src: mongodb-replication]
- With `w: "majority"`, controlled by `writeConcernMajorityJournalDefault` (default `true`). [src: mongodb-replication]
- Time limit (ms) for propagation. Does not undo applied writes on timeout. `0` = wait indefinitely. [src: mongodb-replication]
- MongoDB 5.0+: `{ w: "majority" }` for most deployments. Exception: P-S-A topologies default to `{ w: 1 }`. [src: mongodb-replication]
- Set at transaction level, not per-operation: [src: mongodb-replication]

- -- [src: mongodb-replication]
- `maxStalenessSeconds` (min 90s) excludes secondaries lagging beyond threshold. [src: mongodb-replication]
- -- [src: mongodb-replication]
- Strongest consistency                              Highest availability [src: mongodb-replication]
- linearizable --> majority --> snapshot --> local --> available [src: mongodb-replication]
- Use `rc: "majority"` + `wc: "majority"` for causal consistency. MongoDB sets `afterClusterTime` automatically in causally consistent sessions. See §17 for full coverage. [src: mongodb-replication]
- -- [src: mongodb-replication]
- A rollback reverts writes on a former primary when it rejoins after failover, when those writes had not replicated to a majority before the primary stepped down. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Recover-to-a-timestamp** (default, MongoDB 4.0+): reverts to consistent point, re-applies ops. No size limit. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Rollback via refetch** (legacy, only when `enableMajorityReadConcern=false`, fixed to `true` in 5.0+): limited to 300 MB. [src: mongodb-replication]
- bsondump <dbpath>/rollback/<collectionUUID>/removed.<timestamp>.bson [src: mongodb-replication]

- **`"local"`**: Returns the most recent data on the targeted node with no majority confirmation. On a secondary, data may not yet be replicated to a majority of members and could be rolled back if the current primary fails before replication completes. This is the default for find, aggregate, and getMore operations. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **`"available"`**: Identical to `"local"` on replica set members. On sharded clusters it diverges: reads are served directly from the shard that owns the chunk without consulting config servers for up-to-date routing metadata. During chunk migrations this can return orphaned documents. Avoid on sharded collections for any consistency-sensitive reads. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **`"majority"`**: Returns only data acknowledged by a majority of data-bearing voting members and written to the majority-committed oplog point. Guaranteed durable; will never be rolled back. Requires WiredTiger (only storage engine since MongoDB 5.0). [src: mongodb-replication]
- **`"linearizable"`**: Strongest single-document consistency guarantee. Reads block until the server confirms no write started before the read is still in-flight at a majority. Always targets the primary. Must be combined with `maxTimeMS`. Cannot be used with `$out`, `$merge`, or multi-document transactions. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **`"snapshot"`**: Returns data from a consistent snapshot of majority-committed data at a single point in time. Primarily used in multi-document transactions. When a transaction commits with `w: "majority"`, the snapshot guarantee is preserved end-to-end. [src: mongodb-replication]
- MongoDB maintains an internal **majority-committed optime** — the oplog timestamp up to which a majority of data-bearing voting members have confirmed replication. The primary advances this by computing the highest optime for which `floor(votingMembers/2)+1` members have reported an optime >= that value, every heartbeat cycle (~2s). [src: mongodb-replication]
- WiredTiger maintains an in-memory read snapshot pegged to the majority-committed optime. `"majority"` reads access this snapshot directly — they do not block writes and add negligible latency in steady state. [src: mongodb-replication]
- The interaction with `w: "majority"` write concern is tight: a write acknowledged at `w: "majority"` has by definition advanced the majority-commit point to at least its optime. A subsequent read with read concern `"majority"` (`rc: "majority"`) on any node will therefore see that write — this is the foundation of the causal consistency guarantee. (`rc:` is used as shorthand for "read concern level" throughout §16–17.) [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Choose `"linearizable"` when**: [src: mongodb-replication]
- You need the absolute freshest majority-committed data for a single document. [src: mongodb-replication]
- You are building a compare-and-swap or test-and-set operation. [src: mongodb-replication]
- Always pair with `maxTimeMS` to bound the blocking window. [src: mongodb-replication]
- const doc = await collection.findOne( [src: mongodb-replication]
- { readConcern: { level: 'linearizable' }, maxTimeMS: 5000 } [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Choose `"snapshot"` when**: [src: mongodb-replication]
- You need a consistent view across multiple documents or collections within a transaction. [src: mongodb-replication]
- You want point-in-time consistency without the primary-only restriction of `"linearizable"`. [src: mongodb-replication]
- const session = client.startSession(); [src: mongodb-replication]
- await session.startTransaction({ readConcern: { level: 'snapshot' }, writeConcern: { w: 'majority' } }); [src: mongodb-replication]
- const orders = await ordersCollection.find({}, { session }).toArray(); [src: mongodb-replication]
- const inventory = await inventoryCollection.find({}, { session }).toArray(); [src: mongodb-replication]
- await session.commitTransaction(); [src: mongodb-replication]
- await session.endSession(); [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Key difference**: `"linearizable"` waits for in-flight writes before responding (most current possible). `"snapshot"` reads from a fixed point in time and does not wait. [src: mongodb-replication]
- For sharded clusters, default to `"local"` or `"majority"`. `"available"` exists primarily as a performance optimization for non-sharded workloads. [src: mongodb-replication]

- **Key implications**: [src: mongodb-replication]
- Implicit sessions provide no causal ordering guarantees between operations. [src: mongodb-replication]
