- MongoDB replication provides redundancy and high availability through **replica sets** -- groups of `mongod` processes that maintain the same data set. A replica set contains one primary member that receives all writes and one or more secondary members that replicate the primary's data asynchronously via the **oplog** (operations log). Replica sets are the foundation of MongoDB's data durability, fault tolerance, and read scaling strategy. [src: mongodb-replication]
- Key guarantees of a properly configured replica set: [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Automatic failover**: if the primary becomes unavailable, an election promotes a secondary to primary within ~12 seconds (median, with default settings). [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Data redundancy**: every data-bearing member holds a complete copy of the data set. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Read scaling**: applications can distribute reads across secondaries using read preferences. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Tunable consistency**: write concern and read concern let applications choose their durability and consistency guarantees per operation. [src: mongodb-replication]
- -- [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Primary**: The only member that accepts write operations. Records all writes to its oplog. At most one primary per replica set at any time. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Secondary**: Maintains an identical copy of the primary's data set by asynchronously applying operations from the primary's oplog. Can serve read operations when read preference allows it. Can be elected primary during failover. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Arbiter**: Participates in elections but holds no data. Provides a tiebreaking vote in even-member-count topologies. Must not run on the same system as primary or secondary members. Has exactly 1 election vote and a default priority of 0. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Hidden Members**: Must have `priority: 0`, so they cannot become primary. Excluded from default client read routing. Use for dedicated tasks: reporting queries, backups, analytics workloads. Only reachable by direct connection. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Delayed Members**: Maintain a time-delayed copy of the data (configured via `secondaryDelaySecs`). Must be hidden and should be non-voting. Serve as a defense against accidental data destruction -- the delayed copy preserves the state from N seconds ago. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Three-member replica set (P-S-S)**: One primary, two secondaries. Minimum recommended production topology. Tolerates one member failure while maintaining majority for elections and `w: "majority"` writes. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Primary-Secondary-Arbiter (P-S-A)**: Costs less but carries availability risk. If the sole data-bearing secondary goes down, `w: "majority"` writes fail. Avoid in sharded clusters. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Geographically distributed**: Place members across data centers. Ensure majority of voting members resides in the primary data center. [src: mongodb-replication]
- -- [src: mongodb-replication]
- Elections occur when: a new node is added; the set is initiated with `rs.initiate()`; maintenance commands run (`rs.stepDown()`, `rs.reconfig()`); secondaries lose connectivity to primary for longer than `electionTimeoutMillis` (default 10s); or the primary detects it can see only a minority of voting members. [src: mongodb-replication]
- MongoDB uses Raft-based consensus (pv1): heartbeats every 2 seconds; if no heartbeat within 10s member is marked inaccessible; candidate runs dry election first; first member to receive majority of votes becomes primary. [src: mongodb-replication]
- Higher-priority members call elections sooner. `priority: 0` members cannot become primary. [src: mongodb-replication]
- Maximum 7 voting members, up to 50 total members. [src: mongodb-replication]
- Non-voting members must have `priority: 0` and `votes: 0`. [src: mongodb-replication]
- -- [src: mongodb-replication]
- The oplog (`local.oplog.rs`) is a capped collection recording all write operations in idempotent format. Every member maintains its own oplog. Secondaries copy and apply entries from the primary's oplog. [src: mongodb-replication]
- The **oplog window** is the time between the newest and oldest oplog entry. A secondary that falls behind more than the oplog window must perform a full initial sync. [src: mongodb-replication]
- rs.printReplicationInfo()  // shows oplog size, time window, first/last timestamps [src: mongodb-replication]
- db.adminCommand({ replSetResizeOplog: 1, size: 10240 }) [src: mongodb-replication]
- db.adminCommand({ replSetResizeOplog: 1, minRetentionHours: 24 }) [src: mongodb-replication]
- -- [src: mongodb-replication]
- Write concern controls durability before the server acknowledges a write. [src: mongodb-replication]
- `j: true`: synced to on-disk journal before ack. [src: mongodb-replication]
- `j: false`: in-memory ack only. [src: mongodb-replication]
- With `w: "majority"`, controlled by `writeConcernMajorityJournalDefault` (default `true`). [src: mongodb-replication]
- Time limit (ms) for propagation. Does not undo applied writes on timeout. `0` = wait indefinitely. [src: mongodb-replication]
- MongoDB 5.0+: `{ w: "majority" }` for most deployments. Exception: P-S-A topologies default to `{ w: 1 }`. [src: mongodb-replication]
- Set at transaction level, not per-operation: [src: mongodb-replication]

- -- [src: mongodb-replication]
- `maxStalenessSeconds` (min 90s) excludes secondaries lagging beyond threshold. [src: mongodb-replication]
- -- [src: mongodb-replication]
- Strongest consistency                              Highest availability [src: mongodb-replication]
- linearizable --> majority --> snapshot --> local --> available [src: mongodb-replication]
- Use `rc: "majority"` + `wc: "majority"` for causal consistency. MongoDB sets `afterClusterTime` automatically in causally consistent sessions. See §17 for full coverage. [src: mongodb-replication]
- -- [src: mongodb-replication]
- A rollback reverts writes on a former primary when it rejoins after failover, when those writes had not replicated to a majority before the primary stepped down. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Recover-to-a-timestamp** (default, MongoDB 4.0+): reverts to consistent point, re-applies ops. No size limit. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Rollback via refetch** (legacy, only when `enableMajorityReadConcern=false`, fixed to `true` in 5.0+): limited to 300 MB. [src: mongodb-replication]
- bsondump <dbpath>/rollback/<collectionUUID>/removed.<timestamp>.bson [src: mongodb-replication]
- Use `{ w: "majority" }`. Enable journaling. Monitor replication lag. Avoid P-S-A topologies. [src: mongodb-replication]

- **`"local"`**: Returns the most recent data on the targeted node with no majority confirmation. On a secondary, data may not yet be replicated to a majority of members and could be rolled back if the current primary fails before replication completes. This is the default for find, aggregate, and getMore operations. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **`"available"`**: Identical to `"local"` on replica set members. On sharded clusters it diverges: reads are served directly from the shard that owns the chunk without consulting config servers for up-to-date routing metadata. During chunk migrations this can return orphaned documents. Avoid on sharded collections for any consistency-sensitive reads. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **`"majority"`**: Returns only data acknowledged by a majority of data-bearing voting members and written to the majority-committed oplog point. Guaranteed durable; will never be rolled back. Requires WiredTiger (only storage engine since MongoDB 5.0). [src: mongodb-replication]
- **`"linearizable"`**: Strongest single-document consistency guarantee. Reads block until the server confirms no write started before the read is still in-flight at a majority. Always targets the primary. Must be combined with `maxTimeMS`. Cannot be used with `$out`, `$merge`, or multi-document transactions. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **`"snapshot"`**: Returns data from a consistent snapshot of majority-committed data at a single point in time. Primarily used in multi-document transactions. When a transaction commits with `w: "majority"`, the snapshot guarantee is preserved end-to-end. [src: mongodb-replication]
- MongoDB maintains an internal **majority-committed optime** — the oplog timestamp up to which a majority of data-bearing voting members have confirmed replication. The primary advances this by computing the highest optime for which `floor(votingMembers/2)+1` members have reported an optime >= that value, every heartbeat cycle (~2s). [src: mongodb-replication]
- WiredTiger maintains an in-memory read snapshot pegged to the majority-committed optime. `"majority"` reads access this snapshot directly — they do not block writes and add negligible latency in steady state. [src: mongodb-replication]
- The interaction with `w: "majority"` write concern is tight: a write acknowledged at `w: "majority"` has by definition advanced the majority-commit point to at least its optime. A subsequent read with read concern `"majority"` (`rc: "majority"`) on any node will therefore see that write — this is the foundation of the causal consistency guarantee. (`rc:` is used as shorthand for "read concern level" throughout §16–17.) [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Choose `"linearizable"` when**: [src: mongodb-replication]
- You need the absolute freshest majority-committed data for a single document. [src: mongodb-replication]
- You are building a compare-and-swap or test-and-set operation. [src: mongodb-replication]
- Always pair with `maxTimeMS` to bound the blocking window. [src: mongodb-replication]
- const doc = await collection.findOne( [src: mongodb-replication]
- { readConcern: { level: 'linearizable' }, maxTimeMS: 5000 } [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Choose `"snapshot"` when**: [src: mongodb-replication]
- You need a consistent view across multiple documents or collections within a transaction. [src: mongodb-replication]
- You want point-in-time consistency without the primary-only restriction of `"linearizable"`. [src: mongodb-replication]
- const session = client.startSession(); [src: mongodb-replication]
- await session.startTransaction({ readConcern: { level: 'snapshot' }, writeConcern: { w: 'majority' } }); [src: mongodb-replication]

- await session.endSession(); [src: mongodb-replication]
- **Key difference**: `"linearizable"` waits for in-flight writes before responding (most current possible). `"snapshot"` reads from a fixed point in time and does not wait. [src: mongodb-replication]

- Causal consistency guarantees that operations within a session (or across sessions sharing causal tokens) observe a logically consistent sequence of writes: [src: mongodb-replication]
- MongoDB implements causal consistency through two logical clocks in every server response: [src: mongodb-replication]
- **`$clusterTime`**: A hybrid logical clock (HLC) providing total ordering across the replica set. Every server response includes the current `$clusterTime`. [src: mongodb-replication]
- **`operationTime`**: The optime of the most recent operation in the session. Clients send it as `afterClusterTime` on the next read. [src: mongodb-replication]
- When a read is issued with `afterClusterTime: T`, the server waits until its majority-committed optime >= T before executing, ensuring the read sees all writes up to time T. [src: mongodb-replication]

- MongoDB Atlas Service Accounts are the **recommended programmatic authentication method** for the Atlas Administration API. Introduced in 2024 and reaching General Availability on April 2, 2025, they use the industry-standard **OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials flow** (machine-to-machine auth) to replace the legacy Programmatic API Key (PAK) / HTTP Digest approach. [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- A service account is a non-human identity used by applications, scripts, CI/CD pipelines, and infrastructure-as-code tools. It lives at the **organization level** in Atlas and can be granted access to one or more projects within that org. [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Use this skill to answer questions about, generate configurations for, or troubleshoot: [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Configuring programmatic access to the Atlas Admin API for any automation [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Setting up service accounts in Terraform, Atlas CLI, or CI/CD pipelines [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Rotating service account secrets with zero downtime [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Migrating an existing codebase from API key pairs to service accounts [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Designing least-privilege IAM for Atlas programmatic access [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Investigating audit logs for service account token issuance [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- **Not applicable for:** Reading or writing cluster data (documents, collections). Service accounts authenticate to the **Atlas Administration API only** — not the MongoDB data plane. For data-plane access use database users with SCRAM, X.509, or Workload Identity Federation. [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- **Usage guardrail:** When answering questions or generating configurations using this skill, only use the org roles, project roles, API endpoints, and event type names explicitly listed in this document. Do not invent role names, endpoint paths, or event type strings — Atlas rejects unknown values silently or with generic errors. [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- -- [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- **API Key Pairs (HTTP Digest):** [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Each request computes a hash of the request + nonce [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Nonce is short-lived and single-use [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- No bearer token; credentials are per-request [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- **Service Accounts (OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials):** [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Exchange `client_id` + `client_secret` for a Bearer JWT at the token endpoint [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Cache the token for up to ~55 minutes [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Present `Authorization: Bearer <token>` on every API call [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Re-exchange when token approaches expiry [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Legacy Terraform provider versions (< v1.15 that predate service account support) [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Third-party tools that have not yet adopted OAuth 2.0 for Atlas [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Atlas for Government environments (check docs for GA status) [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Cloud Manager (separate product — uses a different programmatic access model) [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- -- [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Creating a service account at the **organization level** requires the `Organization Owner` role. Adding a service account to a **project** requires the `Project Owner` role for that project. [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Go to [cloud.mongodb.com](https://cloud.mongodb.com) and select your organization [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- In the left sidebar click **Access Manager** → **Applications** [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Click the **Service Accounts** tab [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Click **Create Service Account** [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Fill in: [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- **Name** (1–64 characters, alphanumeric + `-_.,' `) [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- **Description** (1–250 characters) [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- **Organization Roles** — select one or more (see Section 4) [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- **Secret Expiry** — hours until the initial secret expires (8–8760 h) [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Click **Create** [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- **Copy the Client Secret immediately** — it is shown only once. Save to a secrets manager. [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Note the **Client ID** (format: `mdb_sa_id_<24-hex>`) [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- > **Bootstrap note:** To create the very first service account you need an existing credential with `Organization Owner` access — either an existing API key pair (HTTP Digest) or an authenticated Atlas session. Once you have one service account, you can use its Bearer token to manage others. [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]

- -- [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Secrets expire after a configured duration of **8 to 8760 hours** (8 hours to 365 days). When a secret nears expiry, Atlas triggers a **"Service Account Secrets are about to expire"** alert. [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- Multiple secrets can be active simultaneously on a single service account. This is the foundation for **zero-downtime rotation**. [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- **Generate a new secret** while the current one is still active [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- **Update all consumers** (applications, CI/CD secrets, IaC vars) with the new secret [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- **Verify** new secret works by running a test token exchange [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- **Revoke the old secret** — once revoked, the old secret immediately becomes invalid [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]
- > When you add a new secret, the old secret's expiry is shortened to a maximum of **7 days** from the new secret's creation (if the original expiry was farther away). Plan accordingly — don't delay consumer updates. [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]

- Select expiration duration → Click **Generate New** [src: mongodb-atlas-service-accounts]

- Comprehensive reference for monitoring MongoDB deployments — from Atlas built-in dashboards through third-party integrations, CLI tools, and low-level FTDC diagnostics. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **When to use this skill:** When answering questions about Atlas metrics, alert configuration, third-party monitoring integrations (Datadog, New Relic, Prometheus), FTDC diagnostics, slow query analysis, replication lag, connection pool behavior, or Atlas maintenance windows and planned operations. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **When not to use:** For Atlas Search index tuning (use `mongodb-search-ai`), Atlas cost optimization (use `mongodb-cost-optimization`), or backup/restore planning (use `mongodb-backup-restore`). [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Required roles for most monitoring operations:** `clusterMonitor` role on the `admin` database (self-managed), or Atlas `Project Read Only` / `Project Data Access Read Only` (Atlas UI). Third-party integrations (Datadog, Prometheus, New Relic) require Atlas `Project Owner` or `Organization Owner` to configure. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]

- Atlas provides real-time and historical metrics for every cluster tier M10 and above. Free/shared-tier clusters have reduced metric granularity (5-minute resolution vs. 1-minute for dedicated tiers). [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Opcounters** — insert, query, update, delete, getmore, command rates (ops/sec) [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **CPU / System** — process CPU, system CPU, I/O wait broken by read/write [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Memory** — resident, virtual, mapped, cache (WiredTiger block cache, dirty bytes) [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Disk I/O** — IOPS read/write, I/O utilization, disk queue depth [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Network** — bytes in/out, number of requests [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Connections** — current, available, total created [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Replication** — oplog window hours, replication headroom, replication lag per secondary [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Query targeting** — scanned/returned ratio (key indicator of missing indexes) [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Tickets** — WiredTiger concurrent read/write tickets in use vs. available [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]

- Pin metric charts to a custom "Metrics" view for side-by-side comparison across nodes [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Toggle between individual node view (per-host) and cluster aggregate view [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Adjust time range (1h, 8h, 24h, 48h, 1w, custom) [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]

- **MongoDB Ops Manager** is the on-premises deployment of MongoDB's management platform for teams running MongoDB in their own data centers or private clouds. **MongoDB Cloud Manager** is the hosted SaaS version of the same platform — it provides identical monitoring, automation, and backup capabilities without requiring you to host the Ops Manager application yourself. Both share the same agent architecture described below. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Runs as a daemon alongside your MongoDB processes [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Polls `serverStatus`, `replSetGetStatus`, `dbStats`, `collStats`, `currentOp` (filtered) at configurable intervals [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Stores time-series data in Ops Manager's own MongoDB backing store (separate from your application data) [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Sends alerts through Ops Manager's alert notification system — same alert types as Atlas [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Both platforms replicate Atlas-style metric dashboards inside the web UI. The topology view shows replica set health, node states (PRIMARY/SECONDARY/ARBITER), and replication lag per member. The **Hardware** tab surfaces CPU, disk IOPS, and memory at host level for correlation with MongoDB behavior. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]

- **Project-level alerts** — apply to all clusters in a project (e.g., CPU > 80% on any node) [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Cluster-level alerts** — scoped to a specific cluster [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Billing alerts** — monthly spend thresholds, data transfer thresholds [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Set delay intervals** (e.g., "notify if condition persists for 5 minutes") to suppress transient spikes — CPU can spike briefly during flushes without being actionable [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **CPU alert baseline**: M10–M30 should alert at 75%; M50+ with sustained IOPS-heavy workloads often benefit from 85% thresholds with short delay [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Replication lag**: alert at 10–15 seconds for most OLTP workloads; 60 seconds for batch-heavy pipelines [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Oplog window**: never let it drop below 4 hours; alert at 48 hours to give time to investigate before backup windows are at risk [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Connection count**: alert at 80% of the cluster's `maxIncomingConnections`; calculate max from `db.adminCommand({getCmdLineOpts:1})` or Atlas connection string parameters [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]

- FTDC is MongoDB's always-on internal diagnostic system (enabled by default since MongoDB 3.2). It is the first artifact MongoDB Support requests for any performance investigation. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Samples every second:** full `serverStatus`, `replSetGetStatus`, oplog metadata, system CPU/memory, WiredTiger internal stats. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Samples every 200ms:** lighter CPU/I/O subset for sub-second spike reconstruction. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Location:** `<dbPath>/diagnostic.data/` — files rotate at ~10 MB. Atlas retains FTDC automatically; for self-managed, copy the entire directory while `mongod` is live (safe — FTDC uses its own write path). [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Checkpoint stall? → WiredTiger checkpoint duration spike [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- CPU saturated? → system CPU counters at 100% [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Connection spike before incident? → `connections.current` time series [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Replication lag gradual or sudden? → `replSetGetStatus.members[].optimeDate` delta [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Cache eviction pressure? → cache dirty % over time [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]

- **M0, M2, and M5 clusters do not support configurable maintenance windows.** Atlas manages all maintenance entirely, with no operator control over timing. These clusters may be restarted at any time. Upgrade to M10 or higher for maintenance window control. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- This is a common point of confusion — the project-level maintenance window setting applies only to dedicated-tier clusters (M10+). [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Atlas maintenance windows are configured at the **project level** and apply to all dedicated-tier (M10+) clusters within that project. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Location:** Atlas UI → **Project Settings** → **Maintenance Window** [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Default behavior:** When no custom window is configured, Atlas selects the window (commonly Tuesday 10:00–12:00 UTC for many regions). Configure an explicit window aligned with your lowest-traffic period for production workloads. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Configuring a custom window:** [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Choose day of week (Sunday through Saturday; Sunday=1 in the API/CLI, matching the integer table below) [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Choose start hour in UTC (0–23); the window is exactly 1 hour [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Changes take effect immediately and persist until cleared [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Important scope limitation:** Project-scoped, not per-cluster. To set different windows for dev vs. prod clusters, place them in separate Atlas projects. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Atlas CLI commands:** [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- atlas maintenanceWindows describe --projectId <projectId> [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- atlas maintenanceWindows update --dayOfWeek 1 --hourOfDay 2 --projectId <projectId> [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- atlas maintenanceWindows clear --projectId <projectId> [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Day-of-week values: Sunday=1, Monday=2, Tuesday=3, Wednesday=4, Thursday=5, Friday=6, Saturday=7. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Emergency security patches bypass the maintenance window entirely. Atlas notifies project and organization owners via email, but the window configuration does not constrain it. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Secondaries first** — one at a time, waiting for each to rejoin and catch up before proceeding. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Primary last** — triggers a replica set election. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Election window** — typically 10–30 seconds; writes temporarily unavailable, reads fall back to secondaries. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **mongos nodes (sharded clusters only)** — restarted last. Skip for replica-set-only deployments. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Application impact:** Drivers with retryable writes handle the election transparently. Applications without retryable writes may see one transient write failure. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Alert during maintenance:** The **"Primary election"** alert fires during every maintenance restart. Configure a lower-urgency channel for this alert type or correlate it with the maintenance window time. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Total duration:** 3-node replica set: 5–15 min. Sharded clusters: multiply per-shard restart time by shard count (30–60 min for large topologies). [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Deferral postpones by exactly **7 days**, once only per scheduled event [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- After one deferral, maintenance executes at the rescheduled time — no further deferral [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Critical security patches cannot be deferred** — attempting to defer returns an error [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- atlas maintenanceWindows defer --projectId <projectId> [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- POST /api/atlas/v2/groups/{groupId}/maintenanceWindow/defer [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- curl -u "{publicKey}:{privateKey}" --digest \ [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- "https://cloud.mongodb.com/api/atlas/v2/groups/{groupId}/maintenanceWindow" \ [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- H "Accept: application/vnd.atlas.2023-01-01+json" [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Response fields: `dayOfWeek` (1–7, absent if no custom window), `hourOfDay` (0–23 UTC), `startASAP` (maintenance queued for next opportunity), `autoDeferOnceEnabled`. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Same-day or next-day notice for critical CVEs; 24–48 hours for lower-severity updates [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Notifications sent to all Project Owners and Organization Owners [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Cannot be deferred; rolling restart procedure still used to minimize impact [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Monitor **Activity Feed** (Atlas UI → Project → Activity) for maintenance start/completion timestamps [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Why `serverSelectionTimeoutMS=30000` matters:** With 3000ms, a 12-second election causes `ServerSelectionTimeoutError` before the new primary is elected. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Post-election warm-up:** First queries to the new primary may be slower (30–60s) while connections re-establish and the WiredTiger cache warms. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Sequence: config server replica set (CSRS) → shard replica sets (sequentially) → mongos routers (parallel, stateless). [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Balancer:** suspended during maintenance; in-progress migrations complete, no new ones start. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Duration estimate:** per-shard restart time × shard count + CSRS + mongos. A 4-shard cluster at 10 min/shard ≈ 40–50 min for shards alone. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Replace all `[bracketed]` placeholders before sending. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Subject: Planned database maintenance — [Day, Month DD YYYY] [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Maintenance window: [Day of week, YYYY-MM-DD] [HH:MM]–[HH:MM] UTC [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Expected impact:    < 30 second connection interruption during primary election. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- No data loss will occur. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Action required:    None. Retryable writes handle this automatically. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Non-retryable operations may see one transient error. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Questions after [HH:MM] UTC: contact [support channel / Slack #channel]. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- **Placeholder guide:** `[HH:MM]–[HH:MM] UTC` = configured 1-hour window (e.g., "02:00–03:00 UTC"). Always include: specific UTC time window, < 30s impact (not full restart duration), explicit no-data-loss statement, retryable writes note, escalation path. [src: mongodb-monitoring-observability]
- Atlas Federated Authentication implements **Federated Identity Management (FIM)** at the Atlas *organization* layer. Your identity provider (IdP) manages all credentials; Atlas acts as the SAML 2.0 Service Provider (SP). When a user logs in, their browser exchanges SAML assertions with the IdP instead of submitting MongoDB credentials directly. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- **Scope of federation**: One federation application can span multiple Atlas organizations under a single IdP, unified via the **Federation Management Console** (FMC). Federation covers **Atlas UI access only** — it does not control database-level user authentication. For OIDC workforce federation, X.509, SCRAM, or LDAP database auth, see [[mongodb-atlas-iam-rbac]]. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- > **SAML vs OIDC disambiguation**: This skill covers SAML 2.0 federation for Atlas *UI login* (org-level SSO). If the question is about authenticating *application workloads* to the Atlas database via an IdP, that is Workload/Workforce Identity Federation (OIDC) — a different feature documented in [[mongodb-atlas-iam-rbac]]. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- > **Guardrail**: Use only the API endpoint paths, attribute names, and URLs explicitly stated in this skill. Do not extrapolate or invent Atlas Admin API paths — verify any path not listed here against the [Atlas Admin API reference](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/api-resources-spec/) before use. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- The SP-initiated SAML flow: User visits cloud.mongodb.com → enters email → Atlas matches domain to IdP → sends AuthnRequest → IdP authenticates → issues signed SAML Response → Atlas validates assertion (signature, audience, timestamps) → extracts NameID/firstName/lastName/memberOf → creates/updates account (JIT) → applies role mappings → user lands in org. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- SP-initiated (most common) vs IdP-initiated (tile click in My Apps; requires RelayState = Atlas Login URL). Both flows supported. Federation disables direct Atlas credential login and Atlas-managed 2FA for users on mapped domains — configure MFA at IdP level. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- Full tutorials: Okta, Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD), Google Workspace, PingOne. Any SAML 2.0 IdP works (JumpCloud, OneLogin, Auth0, custom). [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- Create SAML 2.0 app in Okta with placeholder SSO URL/Audience URI [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]

- Attribute Statements: firstName=user.firstName, lastName=user.lastName; Group Attribute Statement: memberOf (Matches regex .*) [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- Update Atlas FMC IdP with real Okta Issuer URI and SSO URL [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- Add "MongoDB Atlas - SSO" from Entra gallery [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]

- Download Certificate (Base64) [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- Configure claims: email=user.userprincipalname, firstName=user.givenname, lastName=user.surname [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- Group claim: Security groups, Source=Group Id, customize name to "memberOf", Namespace blank, uncheck "Emit groups as role claims" [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- Configure IdP in Atlas FMC with Entra Login URL + Identifier → download Atlas metadata → upload to Entra (sets real ACS URL/Audience URI) [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- JIT enabled by default — no additional action needed [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- > **Critical**: With Entra ID Group Id source, enter group Object ID (GUID) in Atlas role mapping "Group Name" field, not display name. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- One federation can hold multiple Atlas orgs under one IdP. Each org connects to only one IdP. All orgs share the federation's domain verification pool. Link via FMC → Link Organizations → Configure Access → Connect Identity Provider. To change IdP: disconnect current first. Domain restriction per org: FMC → Organizations → Restrict Access by Domain (see Section 5). [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- At login: Atlas reads memberOf from assertion → looks up role mappings for each group in connected orgs → applies ALL matched roles (additive) → if user loses group membership, role removed at next login → if no maps + default role configured, assigns default → if no maps + no default, user has no roles but can still log in. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- Add mapping: FMC → Organizations → org → Manage Role Mappings → Create → enter Group Name (exact match, case-sensitive, max 200 chars; use GUID for Entra ID Group Id) → assign org roles → optionally assign project roles. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- Default role: FMC → Organizations → org → Default User Role. Typical: Organization Member. Constraint: cannot remove last Organization Owner mapping. When group mappings active, cannot manually edit per-user roles in Access Manager. Role sync is login-time only; SCIM (Section 8) enables real-time sync. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- Proves domain ownership before Atlas routes @domain users through IdP. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- Method A (DNS TXT Record — recommended): FMC → Add Domain → DNS Record → copy mongodb-site-verification=<32-char-string> → add to DNS → Verify. Propagation: minutes to hours. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- Method B (HTML File): Download mongodb-site-verification.html → host at https://host.domain/mongodb-site-verification.html → Verify → DELETE file after verification. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- After verification: FMC → Identity Providers → Edit → Associated Domains → select domain → Confirm. Without association, IdP shows as Inactive. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- Multiple IdPs per domain: Atlas routes to first configured IdP from web UI; use per-IdP Login URL to reach secondary. Delete domain: disassociate from all IdPs first. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- Restrict access by domain (org-level): FMC → Organizations → ellipsis → Restrict Access by Domain → On. New invitations restricted; existing users outside approved domains retain access. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- Bypass SAML Mode URL: per-IdP URL allowing Atlas credential login regardless of SSO. Enabled by default. To find: FMC → Identity Providers → click IdP entry → copy Bypass SAML Mode URL (do NOT toggle the switch just to find the URL — toggling changes the state). Disable in production once federation is validated; keep breakglass accounts instead. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- Breakglass accounts: Atlas Organization Owner accounts with email domain NOT mapped to any IdP (e.g., @admin.example.com), strong password in secrets manager, Atlas 2FA enabled. Use only during SSO outage. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- Federation lockout recovery: Contact MongoDB Support with org ID + proof of ownership. Process is slow — justify maintaining bypass-capable accounts. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- Restrict Membership to Federation: FMC → Advanced Settings → Restrict Membership On. Prevents federated users from joining/creating orgs outside the federation. Org Owners can still create orgs (auto-connected). [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- Atlas auto-creates user account on first successful SAML login. Enabled by default, no configuration needed. Works with all SAML IdPs. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- Required assertion attributes (case-sensitive): firstName (String), lastName (String), NameID/Subject (email format). For role mapping (not account creation): memberOf (multi-value string). [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- Entra ID attribute mapping: email→user.userprincipalname (or user.mail), firstName→user.givenname, lastName→user.surname, memberOf→Group Object IDs or display names. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- JIT vs SCIM: JIT creates on first login, no deprovisioning, login-time sync only, zero setup. SCIM provisions proactively, deprovisions on IdP removal, continuous group sync, requires IdP configuration. Enterprise with compliance needs: use both. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- SCIM 2.0 enables automated user lifecycle: create/update/deactivate events pushed from IdP to Atlas without login. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- Capabilities: user creation, deprovisioning (active=false → Atlas deactivates), group sync, attribute writeback (some IdPs). [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]

- Debugging order: (1) IdP-side logs (show raw SAML Response), (2) browser DevTools Network tab → POST to ACS URL → base64-decode SAMLResponse, (3) validate Issuer, Audience (must match Atlas SP Entity ID), NotBefore/NotOnOrAfter, NameID format+value, AttributeStatement names (memberOf, firstName, lastName), (4) Atlas Activity Feed. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- **Audience restriction mismatch**: Audience value doesn't match Atlas SP EntityID. Fix: download Atlas metadata XML → copy entityID → set as Audience URI in IdP exactly (no trailing slash, exact case). Entra ID: confirm real value replaced the temporary placeholder after metadata upload. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- **NameID format rejected**: Set Name ID Format to Unspecified in IdP. Atlas requires urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:unspecified or emailAddress. NameID value must be email matching Atlas username. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- **Clock skew**: Intermittent failures across regions. Ensure NTP on IdP servers. SAML library clockSkewMs tolerance: 180s typical, 300s max (security control). [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- **Group mapping not applying**: Capture SAML Response → check AttributeStatement for memberOf exact name. Entra ID: group claim name must be "memberOf", Namespace blank, "Emit groups as role claims" unchecked. Okta: Group Attribute Statement name exactly "memberOf". Atlas role mapping Group Name must exactly match assertion value (display name or GUID). [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- **Domain verification failing**: DNS propagation up to 48h; verify TXT record with dig TXT; HTML file must return HTTP 200 at https://host.domain/mongodb-site-verification.html (HTTPS required); TXT record on exact domain not subdomain. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- **Bypass user locked out**: Breakglass account domain was claimed. Fix: remap to unclaimed domain, disable bypass SAML mode (if accessible), or Atlas Support escalation. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- **Domain restriction too broad**: Claimed wrong domain (e.g., gmail.com). Fix: delete domain mapping, add correct narrow domain, re-verify. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- **Certificate expiry**: All logins fail. Fix: generate new cert from IdP → upload to Atlas FMC → test → remove old cert. Proactive: Atlas alert "IdP certificate about to expire" — configure ops notification; cert expiry visible in FMC IdP entry; rotate procedure: new cert in IdP → add to Atlas → verify login → remove old cert. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]
- **Wrong IdP redirect**: Domain mapped to multiple IdPs, Atlas routes to first. Fix: use per-IdP Login URL from FMC. [src: mongodb-atlas-federated-auth]

- This skill covers every facet of MongoDB connection strings — from the two URI formats (Standard and SRV) through every configurable option group. Use it when: [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Composing a connection string from scratch for Atlas, replica set, or standalone [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Debugging authentication failures (`authMechanism`, `authSource`, credential encoding) [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Configuring TLS for Atlas, mutual TLS, or self-hosted deployments [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Tuning connection pool behavior (`maxPoolSize`, `maxConnecting`, `waitQueueTimeoutMS`) [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Choosing the right read preference and understanding staleness [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Setting write/read concern guarantees for transactions or operations [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Enabling wire protocol compression to reduce bandwidth [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Understanding topology options (`replicaSet`, `directConnection`, `loadBalanced`) [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Using the new Client-Side Operations Timeout (`timeoutMS` / CSOT) [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Handling driver-specific quirks across Node.js, Python, Java, and Go [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **Quick rule of thumb:** When in doubt, use the SRV format (`mongodb+srv://`) for Atlas and DNS-managed replica sets. Use the standard format (`mongodb://`) for self-hosted, localhost, or when you need direct port control. [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- -- [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- mongodb://[username:password@]host1[:port1][,host2[:port2],...][/[defaultauthdb][?options]] [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **Single standalone:** [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- mongodb://localhost:27017/mydb [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **Authenticated standalone:** [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- mongodb://alice:s%40feP%40ss@localhost:27017/mydb?authSource=admin [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **Replica set (3 members):** [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- mongodb://user:pass@host1:27017,host2:27017,host3:27017/mydb?replicaSet=rs0 [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- The `defaultauthdb` path component sets the default authentication database only when `authSource` is NOT specified. [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Authentication database resolution order: explicit `authSource` option → `defaultauthdb` path → `admin`. [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Multiple hosts require `replicaSet=<name>` to avoid topology ambiguity. [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- UNIX domain sockets are supported: `mongodb://%2Ftmp%2Fmongodb-27017.sock/mydb`. [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- mongodb+srv://[username:password@]host[/[defaultauthdb][?options]] [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Exactly **one hostname**, no port. [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- The driver queries `_mongodb._tcp.<host>` SRV DNS records to discover all members. [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Optional TXT record at `<host>` can specify `replicaSet=<name>&authSource=<db>`. [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Query string options override TXT record values. [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **TLS is enabled by default** (implicit `tls=true`). [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **How DNS resolution works:** [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- DNS SRV query: _mongodb._tcp.cluster0.example.net [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- → mongodb1.example.net:27017 [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- → mongodb2.example.net:27017 [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- → mongodb3.example.net:27017 [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- DNS TXT query: cluster0.example.net [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- → "authSource=admin&replicaSet=atlas-xyz" [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **Atlas SRV example (copied from Atlas UI):** [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- mongodb+srv://myuser:mypassword@cluster0.abcde.mongodb.net/?retryWrites=true&w=majority&appName=Cluster0 [src: mongodb-connection-string]  <!-- privacy-ok -->
- Atlas **always uses SRV format** except for online archive endpoints. [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- `srvMaxHosts` caps how many hosts are selected from the SRV record (default `0` = unlimited; useful for sharded cluster `mongos` selection). [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- `srvServiceName` overrides the default `mongodb` SRV service name (default: `mongodb`). [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- If DNS is unavailable and no cached records exist, connection fails immediately. [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- -- [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Usernames and passwords must **percent-encode** any of these characters: [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Password `P@ss/w0rd!` → `P%40ss%2Fw0rd!` [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **SCRAM-SHA-256 (default):** [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- mongodb://alice:s3cr3t@host:27017/mydb?authSource=admin [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **MONGODB-X509 (no password):** [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- mongodb://host:27017/?authMechanism=MONGODB-X509&tls=true&tlsCertificateKeyFile=/certs/client.pem&authSource=$external [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **MONGODB-AWS with session token:** [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- mongodb://host:27017/?authMechanism=MONGODB-AWS&authMechanismProperties=AWS_SESSION_TOKEN:sess123&authSource=$external [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **GSSAPI (Kerberos):** [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- mongodb://user%40DOMAIN.COM@host:27017/?authMechanism=GSSAPI&authSource=$external&authMechanismProperties=SERVICE_NAME:mongodb [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- -- [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Atlas requires TLS on all connections. Self-hosted deployments with `tls=true` follow the same option set. [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **Warning:** `tlsInsecure=true` sets both `tlsAllowInvalidCertificates=true` and `tlsAllowInvalidHostnames=true`. Never use in production. [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **Standard TLS (server certificate validated via system CA):** [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- mongodb://host:27017/mydb?tls=true [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **Custom CA (self-signed or private CA):** [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- mongodb://host:27017/mydb?tls=true&tlsCAFile=/etc/ssl/ca.pem [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **Mutual TLS (mTLS) — client presents a certificate:** [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- mongodb://host:27017/mydb?tls=true&tlsCAFile=/certs/ca.pem&tlsCertificateKeyFile=/certs/client.pem&tlsCertificateKeyFilePassword=keypass [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **Atlas (SRV — TLS is implicit):** [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- mongodb+srv://user:pass@cluster0.abcde.mongodb.net/mydb?retryWrites=true&w=majority [src: mongodb-connection-string]  <!-- privacy-ok -->
- **Direct connection to replica set member (bypasses discovery, TLS on):** [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- mongodb://replicaMember1:27017/mydb?directConnection=true&tls=true [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **Development with self-signed cert (never production):** [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- mongodb://host:27017/mydb?tls=true&tlsAllowInvalidCertificates=true [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- MongoDB requires the client certificate and private key to be **concatenated in a single PEM file** for `tlsCertificateKeyFile`. [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- The CA chain in `tlsCAFile` should include the full chain to the root. [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- For X.509 authentication, the username in the URI must match the Subject or CN from the certificate, or can be omitted entirely (driver derives it from the cert). [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- -- [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- The driver maintains a pool of persistent connections per server in the topology. Getting pool settings right is critical for throughput and latency under load. [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- → Is an idle connection available? → YES → use it [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- → NO: is pool size < maxPoolSize? [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- → YES: is current connecting count < maxConnecting? [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- → YES → establish new connection (async) [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- → NO  → wait for a connecting slot to free up (bounded by connectTimeoutMS) [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- → NO → wait up to waitQueueTimeoutMS for an in-use connection to be returned [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **Serverless / Lambda / short-lived processes:** [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- maxPoolSize=5&minPoolSize=0&maxIdleTimeMS=10000 [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **High-throughput API server:** [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- maxPoolSize=200&minPoolSize=10&maxConnecting=4&maxIdleTimeMS=120000 [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **Prevent connection storms on startup:** [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Keep `maxConnecting=2` (default) unless you profile a startup bottleneck [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Set `minPoolSize` > 0 to pre-warm the pool before traffic hits [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **Atlas M0/M2/M5 free tiers:** [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Enforce low connection limits — keep `maxPoolSize=5` or lower [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- -- [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Read preference determines which cluster members the driver routes read operations to. [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- > **Note:** There is no `analytics` read-preference *mode*. Atlas Analytics Nodes are targeted with `readPreference=secondary` plus `readPreferenceTags=nodeType:ANALYTICS` (see §5.3). [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Tags filter which members are eligible. Multiple `readPreferenceTags` parameters are tried in order (fallback chain): [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- mongodb://host/db?readPreference=secondary&readPreferenceTags=nodeType:ANALYTICS&readPreferenceTags= [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- The trailing empty `readPreferenceTags=` acts as a catch-all fallback. [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **Atlas Analytics Node example:** [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- mongodb+srv://user:pass@cluster0.abcde.mongodb.net/?readPreference=secondary&readPreferenceTags=nodeType:ANALYTICS [src: mongodb-connection-string]  <!-- privacy-ok -->
- The driver estimates each secondary's staleness using `lastWriteDate` from `hello` responses and excludes members lagging beyond this threshold. [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **Minimum value: 90 seconds** (smaller values cause an error) [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **Not compatible with `primary` mode** (will error) [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **Formula check:** `maxStalenessSeconds` must be >= `heartbeatFrequencyMS / 1000 + 10` [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- mongodb://host/db?readPreference=secondaryPreferred&maxStalenessSeconds=120 [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- -- [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **Atlas default:** Atlas clusters default to `w=majority`. [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **Write concern levels explained:** [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- mongodb://host/db?w=majority&journal=true [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- mongodb://host/db?w=0 [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- mongodb://host/db?w=1&journal=true [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **Read concern levels:** [src: mongodb-connection-string]

- Wire protocol compression reduces bytes transferred between client and server. Effective for large documents and high-latency networks. [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **Ordering matters:** The client sends its list in preference order. The server selects the first match. [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- mongodb://host/db?compressors=zstd,snappy,zlib [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- mongodb://host/db?compressors=zlib&zlibCompressionLevel=9 [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- High-latency connections (cross-region, WAN) [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Large documents or large result sets [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- CPU has spare capacity [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- **Hurts (avoid) when:** [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Data is already compressed (JPEG, PNG, gzip files, encrypted blobs) [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- CPU-bound workloads — compression adds CPU overhead [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Very small documents — overhead exceeds savings [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Low-latency LAN deployments — bandwidth is rarely the bottleneck [src: mongodb-connection-string]

- With `directConnection=true`, the driver does NOT check if the host is actually the primary [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Writes to a secondary with `directConnection=true` will fail with `NotWritablePrimary` [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Useful for reading from a specific secondary for debugging or analytics [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Incompatible with multiple hosts in the URI (only one host is allowed) [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Can be combined with `tls=true` [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Setting `loadBalanced=true` disables topology monitoring (`hello` commands) [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Exactly one host in the URI; `replicaSet` and `directConnection` must NOT be set [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Required for Atlas Serverless instances (MongoDB sets this automatically in the Atlas-provided string) [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Cursors and transactions must stay on the same connection — the driver handles this [src: mongodb-connection-string]

- **What retryWrites covers:** [src: mongodb-connection-string]
- Single insert, update, delete, `findAndModify` [src: mongodb-connection-string]

- A runbook is not a piece of documentation. It is a procedural script someone must execute correctly while tired, under pressure, with paging alerts firing in the background. Every step must be unambiguous to a person who did not write it and may never have run it before. [src: runbook-craft]
- A runbook is only correct if a person who has never run it before, on a freshly provisioned environment, with no tribal context, can complete it successfully. [src: runbook-craft]
- Schedule a quarterly drill where someone who did not author the runbook runs it end-to-end on a sandbox or staging clone. Every pause is a defect in the runbook, not in the runner. [src: runbook-craft]
- Each step performs exactly one action that produces exactly one verifiable result. The verb comes first. [src: runbook-craft]
- Bad: "Now we need to make sure that the broker is running and you may also want to check the lag, and if the lag is high then restart things." [src: runbook-craft]
- Run `kafka-broker-api status --broker mdb-prod-1`. Expected output: `STATUS: HEALTHY`. [src: runbook-craft]
- Run `kafka-consumer-groups --describe --group mdb-tam-consumer`. Record the `LAG` column. [src: runbook-craft]
- If `LAG > 50000`, go to step 7 (broker restart). Otherwise continue to step 4. [src: runbook-craft]
- **Section banners** at the top of each major phase: `=== PHASE 2 of 5: failover the primary ===`. [src: runbook-craft]
- **State-check steps** at the boundary of each phase. [src: runbook-craft]
- **Numbered top-level steps that never restart**: use 1-25 across the whole runbook. [src: runbook-craft]
- A complete prerequisites block contains: [src: runbook-craft]
- **Access**: which SSO group, which IAM role, which secrets vault entry. [src: runbook-craft]
- **Tools and versions**: `mongosh >= 2.0`, `aws-cli >= 2.13`, `jq`. [src: runbook-craft]
- **Inputs**: cluster ID, account ID, ticket number. [src: runbook-craft]
- **Approvals**: who must sign off in writing before step 1. [src: runbook-craft]
- **Communication**: which Slack channel to post in. [src: runbook-craft]
- A rollback section answers four questions: [src: runbook-craft]
- **What signals trigger a rollback?** Quantitative thresholds. ("Error rate > 2% sustained for 5 minutes." Not "if things look bad.") [src: runbook-craft]
- **What is the rollback command?** Exact, copy-pasteable. [src: runbook-craft]
- **What is the rollback verification?** [src: runbook-craft]
- **What is the data-loss / state-loss implication?** [src: runbook-craft]
- Bad: "If memory looks high, restart the service." [src: runbook-craft]
- Good: "If `mem_used_pct > 85` for 3 consecutive samples, restart the service (step 12)." [src: runbook-craft]
- A post-condition check has three parts: [src: runbook-craft]
- **The command to run** (or signal to observe). [src: runbook-craft]
- **The expected result** (exact string, numeric range). [src: runbook-craft]
- **What to do if the result does not match** (rollback, escalate, retry). [src: runbook-craft]
- **Owner** (a team, not a person). [src: runbook-craft]
- **Last reviewed** (date + name). [src: runbook-craft]
- **Next review due** (a real calendar date). [src: runbook-craft]
- **Linked alert / page / dashboard**. [src: runbook-craft]
- **Estimated duration**. [src: runbook-craft]
- **Risk level** (read-only / mutates non-prod / mutates prod / irreversible). [src: runbook-craft]
- **Code-fenced blocks** for every command, with no surrounding prose inside the block. [src: runbook-craft]
- **A "set variables" step at the top** that declares all substitutions once using environment variables. [src: runbook-craft]
- **The narrative blob**: paragraphs where steps should be. [src: runbook-craft]
- **Hardcoded secrets** in code blocks. [src: runbook-craft]
- **"You should know" gaps**: the runbook assumes the runner has the same context as the author. [src: runbook-craft]
- **Ambiguous phrasing**: "investigate the issue", "check the dashboard." [src: runbook-craft]
- **Outdated commands.** [src: runbook-craft]
- **No rollback.** [src: runbook-craft]
- Access: `tam-prod-readwrite` SSO group, VPN connected. [src: runbook-craft]
- Tools: `kubectl >= 1.28`, `mongosh >= 2.0`, `jq`. [src: runbook-craft]
- export CLUSTER_ID=<from alert> [src: runbook-craft]
- **When to split a runbook**: more than 3 levels of branching, more than ~40 atomic steps, or two different audiences. [src: runbook-craft]
- **When to automate vs. document**: a runbook executed > 1x/month and fully deterministic is automation-eligible. [src: runbook-craft]
- **When to mark a step "stop and escalate"**: any condition the runbook author did not anticipate, any post-condition mismatch. [src: runbook-craft]
- **When to retire a runbook**: the underlying alert hasn't fired in 12 months and the system has changed. [src: runbook-craft]

- See ~/.claude/skills/incident-comms/SKILL.md (full skill body too long to inline here; ~269 lines). Skill is also installed at user level. Covers 10 core concepts: what-we-know/what-we-are-doing/next-update-at triple; heartbeat rule and predictable cadence; voice shifts across incident timeline (hour-zero, mid-incident, resolution); internal vs external surfaces separation; no speculation no causes until confirmed; quantified impact not vague gestures; apology calibration (specific, late, owned); designated voice / single source of truth; subscribe affordance and silent audience; all-clear has a checklist not just a message. - A postmortem is a learning artifact disguised as an incident report. It must satisfy three audiences simultaneously: the engineers who need to understand what failed, the leadership who need to evaluate organizational risk, and the people who lived through the incident. [src: postmortem-writing]
- Three substitutions do most of the work: [src: postmortem-writing]
- **Names → roles.** "Alice deployed the bad change" → "The release engineer deployed change #4821." [src: postmortem-writing]
- **Judgments → actions.** "Bob failed to notice the alert" → "The on-call engineer did not see the alert because it was routed to a paused channel." [src: postmortem-writing]
- **Causal verbs → enabling conditions.** "X caused Y" → "X created conditions under which Y became possible." [src: postmortem-writing]
- **The single most damaging phrase:** "should have." Replace it with "the system did not surface the information that would have enabled X." [src: postmortem-writing]
- **UTC timestamps**, always. [src: postmortem-writing]
- **Source for each event**: which dashboard, which log line, which Slack message. [src: postmortem-writing]
- **Actor + action + observable result**, in that order. [src: postmortem-writing]
- **Decision points called out explicitly**, with the information the decider had at the time. [src: postmortem-writing]
- Real incidents have a root cause plus contributing factors. Structure the analysis as: [src: postmortem-writing]
- **Triggering event** (the proximate change). [src: postmortem-writing]
- **Root cause** (the latent defect the trigger exposed). [src: postmortem-writing]
- **Contributing factors**, categorized: [src: postmortem-writing]
- Technical (missing monitoring, single points of failure) [src: postmortem-writing]
- Process (insufficient testing, communication gaps) [src: postmortem-writing]
- Environmental (time pressure, on-call fatigue) [src: postmortem-writing]
- Apply iteratively: "Why did the API return 503s? Because the database connection pool was exhausted." Continue until you reach an organizational or design-level factor. [src: postmortem-writing]
- Allow branching. A single chain of whys is rare. Multiple parallel chains converging on multiple contributing factors is common. [src: postmortem-writing]
- A defensible action item has: [src: postmortem-writing]
- **Owner**: a single named person (not a team). [src: postmortem-writing]
- **Due date**: a real calendar date. [src: postmortem-writing]
- **Severity / priority**: P0/P1/P2 calibrated to actual risk reduction. [src: postmortem-writing]
- **Traceability**: which contributing factor it addresses. [src: postmortem-writing]
- **Definition of done**: how the writer will know the action is complete. [src: postmortem-writing]
- **What worked**: the alert fired correctly, the rollback procedure was executable. [src: postmortem-writing]
- **What we got lucky on**: things that worked but only by accident. [src: postmortem-writing]
- **What we want to preserve**: practices that should be formalized. [src: postmortem-writing]
- Linguistic markers of hindsight bias to delete in revision: [src: postmortem-writing]
- "Clearly..." (it was not clear at the time). [src: postmortem-writing]
- "Obviously..." (it was not obvious to anyone in the moment). [src: postmortem-writing]
- "Should have noticed..." (replace with "the available signals did not surface X"). [src: postmortem-writing]
- **The top (inverted pyramid summary, 4–6 paragraphs).** The verdict first: what broke, when, who was affected, severity, root cause class. [src: postmortem-writing]
- **The turn (one sentence).** "Here is how the incident unfolded, in chronological order." [src: postmortem-writing]
- **The bottom (chronological narrative).** The timeline. [src: postmortem-writing]
- A change deployed at 14:30 UTC introduced a query pattern that saturated [src: postmortem-writing]
- the API connection pool. From 14:32 to 14:46 UTC, approximately 14% of API [src: postmortem-writing]
- requests in us-east-1 returned 503 errors. Five action items have been opened, two are P0. [src: postmortem-writing]
- **Single-root-cause syndrome**: "the root cause was X" with no contributing factors. [src: postmortem-writing]
- **Wishlist action items**: "we should also rewrite the deployment system." [src: postmortem-writing]
- **Hindsight prose**: "obviously the team should have noticed..." [src: postmortem-writing]
- **The publish-and-forget**: no review date, no owner for action items. [src: postmortem-writing]
- Link: [Google SRE Book — Chapter 15: Postmortem Culture](https://sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/) [src: postmortem-writing]
- Link: [Etsy — Debriefing Facilitation Guide (Allspaw, Evans, Schauenberg)](https://extfiles.etsy.com/DebriefingFacilitationGuide.pdf) [src: postmortem-writing]
- Link: [Atlassian — Postmortems: Enhance Incident Management Processes](https://www.atlassian.com/incident-management/handbook/postmortems) [src: postmortem-writing]
- Error messages are the most-read text most software ever produces. They are also the worst-edited. The goal: tell the user **what** went wrong, **why** it went wrong, and **what to do next**. [src: error-message-craft]
- **What went wrong** — the observable failure, stated in user terms. [src: error-message-craft]
- **Why it went wrong** — only when the cause helps the user decide what to do. [src: error-message-craft]
- **What to do next** — a concrete action. [src: error-message-craft]
- The triple does not have to be three separate sentences. For a short field validation: [src: error-message-craft]
- > "Email must include an @ symbol." [src: error-message-craft]
- > "We couldn't save your changes (database unreachable). Wait 30 seconds and retry; if this persists, contact support with request ID `req_abc123`." [src: error-message-craft]
- Three substitutions do most of the no-blame work: [src: error-message-craft]
- **"You [did wrong thing]" → "[Field] requires [thing]"** [src: error-message-craft]
- **"You failed to..." → "[Action] needs..."** [src: error-message-craft]
- **"Invalid input" → "[Field name] must be [format]"** [src: error-message-craft]
- Test: replace "you" with "the system" in the draft. If the sentence now reads as the system admitting a defect, the original was probably user-friendly. If it reads as nonsense, the original was blame language. [src: error-message-craft]
- > "Couldn't connect to the database. Try again in 30 seconds." [src: error-message-craft]
- > `ERROR svc=auth method=login userId=12345 cause=ECONNREFUSED host=db-primary:5432` [src: error-message-craft]
- **UPPER_SNAKE_CASE** for the identifier (`INVALID_API_KEY`, not `invalid-api-key`). [src: error-message-craft]
- **Stable across versions** — once published, never rename. [src: error-message-craft]
- **Categorized by prefix** — `AUTH_*`, `RATE_*`, `VALIDATION_*`. [src: error-message-craft]
- **Documented** — every code has a docs page explaining what triggers it. [src: error-message-craft]
- A complete next-action clause names one of: [src: error-message-craft]
- **A retry hint with a time bound**: "Try again in 30 seconds." Not "try again later." [src: error-message-craft]
- **A specific input fix**: "Add an @ symbol to your email." [src: error-message-craft]
- **An escalation path with diagnostic info**: "Contact support and include request ID `req_abc123`." [src: error-message-craft]
- The Google Developer Documentation Style Guide is explicit: avoid exclamation points in error messages. They read as shouting, performative panic, or sarcasm. [src: error-message-craft]
- **ALL CAPS for emphasis**: reads as shouting. [src: error-message-craft]
- **Ellipses for trailing-off**: reads as passive-aggressive. [src: error-message-craft]
- **Avoid contractions** where translation may be awkward ("can't" → "cannot"). [src: error-message-craft]
- **Avoid idioms** ("hit a snag", "ran into a wall"). They do not translate. [src: error-message-craft]
- **Avoid concatenation in code** ("Error: " + fieldName + " is invalid"). Breaks grammatical agreement in gendered languages. [src: error-message-craft]
- **Plan for pluralization complexity**. Use ICU MessageFormat or equivalent. [src: error-message-craft]
- **Mockery**: "Oops! Something went terribly wrong! 😱" [src: error-message-craft]
- **Self-deprecation**: "Our bad! We messed up." [src: error-message-craft]
- **Vague hedging**: "An unexpected error occurred." [src: error-message-craft]
- **Exposed internals**: stack traces, internal class names, raw DB errors. [src: error-message-craft]
- **Marketing voice in failure**: "Thanks for your patience as we work to deliver an amazing experience!" [src: error-message-craft]
- **Inline, near the field**, not at the top of the form. [src: error-message-craft]

- Produce REST/HTTP API documentation that meets the gold-standard set by Stripe and Twilio: a Diátaxis-organized structure, endpoint reference pages with request/response examples in multiple languages, an error-code catalog with troubleshooting steps, deprecation signaling via RFC-8594 headers and visible banners, and an OpenAPI/Swagger interactive layer. [src: api-docs-craft]
- **Tutorial:** For a beginner. Guarantees a successful outcome. Concrete, specific, opinionated. [src: api-docs-craft]
- **How-to guide:** For a competent user with a specific task. Goal-oriented. [src: api-docs-craft]
- **Reference:** For a developer looking up the exact shape. Comprehensive, accurate, terse. No narrative. [src: api-docs-craft]
- **Explanation:** For a curious developer who wants the *why*. Discursive, opinionated. [src: api-docs-craft]
