- This skill takes a feature idea and produces backlog items the team can groom, estimate, and ship. Covers Mike Cohn's user-story template, the INVEST quality bar (Bill Wake, 2003), Given/When/Then acceptance criteria in Gherkin form, splitting strategies (vertical-slice principle and SPIDR), and the separation between *acceptance criteria* (per-story, varies) and *definition of done* (team-wide, stable). [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- As a <role>, I want <capability> so that <benefit>. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **`As a <role>`** — the user, not the system. "As a user" is the most common failure mode. Name a specific actor type: "As a job seeker", "As an on-call TAM", "As a paid subscriber on the Pro tier." [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **`I want <capability>`** — the *what*, written goal-first, agnostic to *how*. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **`so that <benefit>`** — the *why*. The benefit clause is the most-skipped and most-valuable. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **I — Independent.** The story can be built, demoed, and shipped without waiting on another story. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **N — Negotiable.** The story is a placeholder for a conversation, not a contract. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **V — Valuable.** The story delivers value to a real user or stakeholder. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **E — Estimable.** The team has enough context to size it. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **S — Small.** Fits comfortably inside an iteration. Heuristic: ≤ 50% of one developer's iteration capacity. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **T — Testable.** A definite test exists for "done." [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Then <some observable outcome> [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **`And` and `But`** chain steps in the same phase. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- 3–5 steps per scenario. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- 1–3 acceptance criteria per story. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Each criterion tests a *distinct* aspect. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Concrete values, not generics: "Given a charge of $20.00" not "Given a valid charge." [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- A user story must be a *thin vertical slice through the architecture* — a sliver that touches every layer and delivers end-to-end value. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **Horizontal (wrong):** [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Story 1: Build the UI for case filtering. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Story 2: Build the API endpoint for case filtering. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Story 3: Add the database index for case filtering. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **Vertical (right):** [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Story 1: Filter cases by severity (S1 only, no UI persistence). [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Story 2: Filter cases by status, with severity already shipped. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **S — Spike.** Time-box a research task to remove uncertainty blocking estimation. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **P — Path.** Split by user path. "Pay with credit card" / "Pay with Apple Pay." [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **I — Interface.** Split by client or platform. "Filter cases on desktop" / "Filter cases in mobile app." [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **D — Data.** Split by data scope. "Filter cases for active accounts only" first; "including archived accounts" later. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **R — Rules.** Relax business rules in the first slice. "Refunds, with no approval workflow" first; "Refunds with manager-approval workflow" later. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **Acceptance Criteria (AC):** [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Specific to *this* story. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Authored by the product owner with the team. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Vary between stories. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Answer: "What must this story do for the user to accept it?" [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **Definition of Done (DoD):** [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- A team-wide standard that applies to *every* story. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Stable across sprints. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Answers: "What must any item meet to be called done?" [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- A story is **done** when *both* its acceptance criteria are met *and* the team's definition of done is satisfied. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **Title:** Filter case list by severity [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- I want to filter the case list by severity (S1 / S2 / S3 / S4), [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- so that during a busy on-call shift I can triage S1s first [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- without scrolling through lower-severity cases. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **Acceptance Criteria:** [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Given the case list shows ≥ 1 case at each of S1–S4, [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- When I select "S1 only" in the severity filter, [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Then only S1 cases are visible [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- And the count badge shows the number of visible S1 cases. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Given I have applied a severity filter, [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- When I reload the page, [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Then the same filter is reapplied [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- And the URL contains the filter as a query parameter. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **Out of scope (not in this story):** [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Filtering by status or owner. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Multi-select severity. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **Estimate:** 5 points [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Original (too big, ~21 points): [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- "As an admin, I want to manage subscription plans." [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Split via Path + Rules: [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Story A (5 pts) — read-only plan list [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Story B (8 pts) — create new plan (USD only; no proration) [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Story C (5 pts) — edit plan name (only) [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Story D (8 pts) — edit plan price with proration [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Story E (3 pts) — deactivate a plan [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Link: [ ] Acceptance criteria met (verified by the PM or designate). [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Link: [ ] Unit tests written for new logic; ≥ 80% coverage on changed files. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Link: [ ] Code reviewed by ≥ 1 other engineer. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Link: [ ] CHANGELOG.md updated (or marked N/A in the PR). [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Link: [ ] User-facing docs updated (if UI or API surface changed). [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Link: [ ] No new lint warnings; no new TypeScript `any`. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Link: [ ] Deployed to staging; smoke test passing. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- Link: [ ] Accessibility audit clean for UI changes. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **"As a user, I want..."** — every story starts the same way, tells you nothing. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **Solution-shaped capability clauses** — "I want a dropdown in the top-right corner." [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **No `so that` clause** — strips out the prioritization signal. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **Horizontal-layer stories** ("Build the backend for X") — each is independently unshippable. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **Acceptance criteria that restate the story.** [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **20-criterion acceptance lists** — the story is too big. Split. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **Conflating Acceptance Criteria with Definition of Done.** [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **Forcing bugs / tech-debt / spikes into user-story syntax.** [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **"As a user" or a specific role?** Always specific. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]
- **Story or epic?** If the story has > 1 sprint of work or > 5 acceptance criteria, it's an epic. Split via SPIDR. [src: user-story-and-acceptance-criteria]

- Three reviewer-tested moves: [src: proposal-and-grant-writing]
- **Open in the funder's frame.** Quote the funding opportunity's priority area in the first two sentences. [src: proposal-and-grant-writing]
- **Quantify the problem at the right scope.** National statistics are weak without local data; local data is weak without national context. [src: proposal-and-grant-writing]
- **End on the gap.** Close with the specific knowledge, service, or capacity gap your project will fill. [src: proposal-and-grant-writing]

- Policies prescribe. They do not propose, persuade, or describe — they bind. A reader of a policy needs three things in the first 60 seconds: who is bound by it, what they must do, and what happens if they don't. [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **RFC 8174 clarification:** The normative meaning attaches only when the keyword is in ALL CAPITALS. Lowercase "must", "should", and "may" carry their normal English meaning and have no normative weight. [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Required incantation:** [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- > The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 [RFC2119] [RFC8174] when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here. [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Policy** — *what* must be true, and *why*. Mandatory. Strategic. Changes rarely. [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Standard** — *which* specific implementation satisfies the policy (TLS 1.3, AES-256). Mandatory. Tactical. [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Procedure** — *how* to perform a specific task. Mandatory for the role performing the task. Operational. [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Guideline** — *suggested* approach when no mandatory standard applies. Advisory. [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **The hierarchy test:** if you can answer "yes" to "would this need to change when we upgrade the firewall?", it is not a policy. It is a standard or procedure. [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Title and identifier** — unique policy ID, version number, effective date [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Purpose** — one-paragraph statement of why the policy exists [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Scope** — who, what, where the policy applies; explicit in-scope and out-of-scope lists [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Definitions** — every term of art, listed alphabetically [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Policy statements** — the normative rules, using BCP 14 keywords in ALL CAPS [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Roles and responsibilities** — named role titles (not individuals) mapped to obligations [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Exceptions** — how to request and approve a documented deviation [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Enforcement** — consequences of violation [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Related documents** — pointers to standards, procedures, and laws [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Review schedule** — review cadence, owner, next review date, change-history table [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- A defensible scope section answers: [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **People** — which employees, contractors, vendors, partners, customers? [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Assets** — which systems, data classifications, networks, locations, devices? [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Activities** — which operations, transactions, or behaviors? [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- State each as an inclusion list AND an exclusion list. [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- A well-built exception clause has four elements: [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Who can grant** — the approval authority (named role, not person) [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **What must be documented** — business justification, compensating controls, scope, duration [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **How long it lasts** — maximum duration before re-review (typically 90 or 180 days) [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **How it is tracked** — where the exception register lives [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- ISO/IEC 27001 clause 7.5.3 requires that documents be reviewed and updated as necessary. [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Review cadence** — at least annual [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Document owner** — the role accountable for triggering review [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Change-history table** — a row per version showing version, date, author, change summary, approver [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **In scope:** [people, assets, activities] [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Out of scope:** [explicit exclusions] [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Term** — definition. [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- 1 [Role] MUST [behavior]. [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- 2 [Role] MUST NOT [prohibition]. [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- 3 [Role] SHOULD [strong default]. Deviation requires documented exception per Section 7. [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **The descriptive policy** — lots of background, no rules. [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Lowercase normatives** — using "should" and "must" in lowercase while believing they bind readers. [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **The grab-bag scope** — "This policy applies to everyone and everything." Unenforceable. [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Personal-name responsibilities** — "Jane Smith MUST approve all exceptions." Jane leaves; policy breaks. [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **No exception path** — forces operators to violate or route around. [src: policy-and-governance-writing]
- **Procedure leakage** — step-by-step instructions inside a policy. [src: policy-and-governance-writing]

- **"Studies show..."** with no citation is pseudo-citation. Three repairs: [src: academic-and-citation-writing]
- **Name the source.** "Studies show" → "Cowan (2010) and Baddeley (2012) showed". [src: academic-and-citation-writing]
- **Drop the unsupportable claim.** If you cannot find a citation, you do not yet have evidence. [src: academic-and-citation-writing]
- **Mark it as your own argument.** "I argue that..." is honest. [src: academic-and-citation-writing]
- **Primary** — original research, raw data, firsthand accounts. [src: academic-and-citation-writing]
- **Secondary** — analysis or interpretation of primary sources. [src: academic-and-citation-writing]

- **Grounds** (data, evidence) — the facts that support the claim. [src: academic-and-citation-writing]
- **Warrant** — the underlying principle that lets the grounds support the claim. [src: academic-and-citation-writing]
- **Backing** — support for the warrant itself. [src: academic-and-citation-writing]

- **Rebuttal** — counterclaims and exceptions acknowledged. [src: academic-and-citation-writing]

- Prose craft for the moment between "the customer hit a problem" and "the ticket is closed." Every word in that window is read by a person who is, by definition, having a worse day than they planned. [src: support-ticket-writing]
- A strong first response always contains four moves, in this order: [src: support-ticket-writing]
- **Acknowledge** — name the problem in the customer's own words. [src: support-ticket-writing]
- **Empathize** — name the impact ("I can see how this would block your release"), not a generic "I understand." [src: support-ticket-writing]
- **Commit** — state what you will do next and *when* you will be back. A timestamp or interval. [src: support-ticket-writing]
- **Ask only what you need** — batch diagnostic questions; never trickle. [src: support-ticket-writing]
- The most reliable de-escalation move: **acknowledgment of feeling, then a concrete next step.** Either half alone is weaker. [src: support-ticket-writing]
- > I can see how frustrating this is — your cluster has been failing over for three hours and you're heading into a maintenance window. I'm pulling the FTDC now and will reply within 30 minutes either with a root cause or with the questions I need to narrow it down. [src: support-ticket-writing]
- The phrase "I understand" is overused to the point of suspicion. "That sounds really frustrating," "I can see why this is urgent" land harder because they're specific. [src: support-ticket-writing]
- Never write "we apologize for any inconvenience this may have caused." It is the most universally-detested phrase in support writing. [src: support-ticket-writing]
- **A holding statement:** [src: support-ticket-writing]
- > "Quick update: I'm still working through the logs you sent. I've ruled out network latency and am now looking at the WiredTiger cache. I'll have a clearer picture by 17:00 UTC. No action needed from you in the meantime." [src: support-ticket-writing]
- **The cardinal rule:** never send a holding statement without a next time-boundary. [src: support-ticket-writing]
- **Outgoing owner writes:** [src: support-ticket-writing]
- > "I'm bringing in [Name], who specializes in [area], to take over the deep-dive on this. They have the full context — the FTDC, the timeline, what we've ruled out so far. [Name] will reply within [time] with next steps." [src: support-ticket-writing]
- **Incoming owner writes within the promised window:** [src: support-ticket-writing]
- > "Hi [customer], [outgoing] looped me in. I've read the case and the FTDC; I see what they're describing with the failover loop. Before I dig further, can you confirm: [one or two crisp questions]." [src: support-ticket-writing]
- **Anti-pattern:** the incoming owner asks the customer to "summarize what's been happening." [src: support-ticket-writing]
- **Call the customer when:** [src: support-ticket-writing]
- The case has crossed a sentiment threshold (all-caps, profanity, threats to escalate). [src: support-ticket-writing]
- More than three back-and-forth cycles have occurred without progress. [src: support-ticket-writing]
- The customer is in an active incident. [src: support-ticket-writing]
- The next step requires real-time troubleshooting. [src: support-ticket-writing]
- You're about to escalate up a tier. [src: support-ticket-writing]
- **Stay on the ticket when:** [src: support-ticket-writing]
- The technical context benefits from being written. [src: support-ticket-writing]
- Multiple stakeholders need to read the same answer. [src: support-ticket-writing]
- **After a phone call, *always* post a summary on the ticket.** [src: support-ticket-writing]
- Confirming the index change resolved the slow queries on the `events` collection. [src: support-ticket-writing]

- **Cause:** missing compound index on `{customer_id: 1, created_at: -1}`. [src: support-ticket-writing]

- **"Please be patient."** Direct command to a person who is out of patience. [src: support-ticket-writing]
- **"We apologize for any inconvenience this may have caused."** Disbelief plus minimization. [src: support-ticket-writing]

- > I'll reply by [exact time] either with a root cause hypothesis or with the specific diagnostic data I need from you. In the meantime, if the situation changes on your side — for example, the secondary takes over and you regain availability — please let me know. [src: support-ticket-writing]
- **Generic "I understand"** — use a specific empathy beat instead. [src: support-ticket-writing]
- **Time-vague commitments** — "soon," "shortly," "ASAP." Use clock time in a named timezone. [src: support-ticket-writing]
- **Trickle diagnostics** — asking for one piece of data, waiting, then asking for another. [src: support-ticket-writing]
- **Closing without recap** — no description of cause or fix. [src: support-ticket-writing]
- **Cold handoff** — "I've assigned this to a colleague" with no name, no warm intro. [src: support-ticket-writing]

- Microcopy is every word in a product that is not body content: the buttons, the field labels, the placeholder hints, the validation messages, the empty states, the toasts, the modal titles, the 404 pages. Collectively, microcopy is the voice of the product. [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- Buttons should describe the action they perform. The canonical shape is **verb + noun**. [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- **Echo the action's verb in destructive confirmations.** If the dialog asks "Delete this project?", the destructive button says "Delete project," not "Yes" or "Confirm." [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- **Name the absence** (one short line). [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- **Tell the user what this surface is for.** [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- **Give them the next action** (with a button when possible). [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- **Weak:** "No items." [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- **Stronger:** "No saved designs yet / This is where your saved email designs will live. / [Create your first design]" [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- Nielsen Norman Group's canonical four-part guideline: [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- **State what went wrong** in plain language. [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- **Explain why**, if useful. [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- **Tell the user how to fix it.** [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- **Don't blame the user.** [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- **Never use exclamation points in failure messages.** [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- **Avoid:** "Are you sure?" as a title. "OK" / "Cancel" as button pair. "Yes" / "No" as button pair. [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- **Anti-pattern: Placeholder as label.** When the user starts typing, the label vanishes. [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- Toast copy is the shortest writing in the product. **Single word or short verb-noun phrase.** Past-tense for completed actions: "Saved" not "Your changes were saved successfully." [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- **The path to the more privacy-protective choice must not be harder than the path to the less privacy-protective choice.** [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- NN/g's four dimensions to calibrate tone: [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- **Funny vs Serious** — billing errors are serious; an empty state for a hobby app can be playful. [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- **Formal vs Casual** — enterprise tools lean formal, consumer apps lean casual. [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- **When to drop humor entirely:** anything involving money, security, or privacy; anything destructive or irreversible; anything during an outage or sign-in failure. [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- **"Submit"** — almost never the right word. [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- **Placeholder-as-label** — field with no visible, persistent label. [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- **Apologetic empty states** — "Oh no, you have no projects yet!" [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- **"Are you sure?" as the only confirmation question** — vague. [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- **Yes/No buttons on confirmation dialogs** — forces the user to re-read the title. [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- **Exclamation points in error messages.** [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]
- **Pre-checked marketing opt-ins.** [src: microcopy-and-ui-writing]

- A tutorial is **a lesson**. Its only job is to take a complete newcomer through a meaningful, hand-held experience and leave them with two things: a tiny working artifact they built themselves, and the confidence that they can use this tool. [src: tutorial-writing]
- **The single most-violated rule:** the artifact does not matter; the learning does. A tutorial reader is not there to ship the thing they build — they are there to encounter the tool, the vocabulary, and the shape of the workflow under your protection. [src: tutorial-writing]
- If you find yourself optimizing for "they could use this output in production" — stop. You are writing a how-to. Switch quadrants. [src: tutorial-writing]
- When a learner runs your step, they must see the result you said they would see. This is non-negotiable. Confidence is built layer by layer, and one broken step shakes the whole stack. [src: tutorial-writing]
- **Re-test every step on a clean environment before you ship.** [src: tutorial-writing]
- Tutorials use the first-person plural: *"we'll create a file called `app.py`"*, *"now we'll run it"*. The instructor is present. The learner is not abandoned. [src: tutorial-writing]
- Contrast with how-to voice ("Create a file named `app.py`") which assumes competence. [src: tutorial-writing]
- There will be a hundred interesting tangents — "by the way, you could also…", "in production you'd usually…". **Cut all of them.** Every sentence either moves the learner toward the artifact or it leaves the document. [src: tutorial-writing]
- The learner must finish with **something visible**: a running web server on `localhost:8000`, a printed "Hello, world", a deployed function that responded to a curl. [src: tutorial-writing]
- Human working memory holds roughly 7 ± 2 items. Each step introduces **one** new thing. Earlier-introduced things are reused, not re-explained. [src: tutorial-writing]
- Start at the end. Write down — in one sentence — what the learner can do after the tutorial that they could not do before. Then work backwards. [src: tutorial-writing]
- Tutorials are built around **specific** actions and **specific** outcomes. Not "create a database" — *"create a database called `tutorial_db`"*. Not "you'll see some output" — *"you'll see exactly this output: `{...}`"*. [src: tutorial-writing]
- The reader is a guest in your kitchen; you don't let them touch the hot pan. If the install command on macOS 14 prompts for a password and the learner does not expect it, that is your error, not theirs. [src: tutorial-writing]
- The goal is *"I can do this"*, not *"I have mastered this"*. [src: tutorial-writing]
- Branching kills tutorials. Pick **one** environment, declare it in step 0, and keep one linear path. [src: tutorial-writing]
- In this tutorial we'll build a <small concrete thing>. By the end, you'll have [src: tutorial-writing]
- <artifact> running on <where>. [src: tutorial-writing]
- This tutorial takes about <N> minutes. We assume you have <one prerequisite> [src: tutorial-writing]
- <one or two sentences and ideally a screenshot or sample output> [src: tutorial-writing]
- <copy-pasteable env setup. Pin versions.> [src: tutorial-writing]
- <exact expected output> [src: tutorial-writing]
- <narrator voice: "Let's create a file called …"> [src: tutorial-writing]
- <exact expected output> [src: tutorial-writing]
- <one sentence on what just happened — no theory, no alternatives> [src: tutorial-writing]
- Congratulations. You've built <artifact>. You can find the finished code at [src: tutorial-writing]
- To do <related task>, see the [How to <verb>](…) guide. [src: tutorial-writing]
- To understand *why* <concept> works this way, see [<concept> explained](…). [src: tutorial-writing]
- > "This tutorial covers the `Client` class, which has the following methods…" [src: tutorial-writing]
- Tutorials walk a learner through *doing one thing*; they do not enumerate surface area. [src: tutorial-writing]
- Twelve features, three languages, two installation paths. Pick one concrete artifact, one environment, one path. [src: tutorial-writing]
- Three paragraphs of background before the first command. Get them to `Hello, world` in the first five minutes. [src: tutorial-writing]
- *"Now set up your database."* How? Which database? On what port? Every imperative must be **copy-pasteable**. [src: tutorial-writing]
- Tutorials decay. **Re-run the entire tutorial on a clean VM before each release.** [src: tutorial-writing]
- Either it's exact or you've broken the learner's promise. Show the exact output. [src: tutorial-writing]
- **Is the reader a complete newcomer?** If they could already articulate a specific goal, they need a how-to. [src: tutorial-writing]
- **Is the artifact small enough that you can guarantee every step?** If not, split it. [src: tutorial-writing]
- **Is there exactly one path through?** If you find "if/depending on/optionally", you are drifting toward how-to. [src: tutorial-writing]
- **Does the reader end with a visible, working thing they built themselves?** [src: tutorial-writing]
- When the answer points elsewhere: [src: tutorial-writing]
- Competent reader with a goal → `howto-writing` [src: tutorial-writing]
- "Why does this exist?" → `explanation-doc-writing` [src: tutorial-writing]
- "What are the parameters of `foo()`" → `reference-doc-writing` [src: tutorial-writing]
- Link: [Tutorials — Diátaxis](https://diataxis.fr/tutorials/) [src: tutorial-writing]
- Link: [Collaborative Lesson Development Training — Lesson Design (The Carpentries)](https://carpentries.github.io/lesson-development-training/lesson-design.html) [src: tutorial-writing]
- A how-to guide is **a recipe**. It serves a competent user who has arrived at the page with a specific goal already formed — *"How do I add OAuth to my app?"* — and who needs an efficient series of steps to get there. [src: howto-writing]
- **The single most-violated rule: how-tos answer a question only a competent user could ask.** If your reader cannot even formulate the goal, they need a tutorial. [src: howto-writing]
- *"How to rotate the signing key"*. *"How to add a custom domain"*. If you cannot fit your doc's purpose into that pattern, you do not have a how-to. [src: howto-writing]
- A how-to with three goals is three how-tos that have not yet been separated. Each goal gets its own URL, its own title, its own search hit. [src: howto-writing]
- The first block under the title says what the reader must already have, know, or have done. If the reader can't tick every box, they bounce — which is correct, because the doc is not for them yet. [src: howto-writing]
- Steps are numbered. Each step begins with an imperative verb. *"Create…"*, *"Run…"*, *"Set…"*, *"Verify…"*. Not *"Now you might want to…"*, not *"Let's…"*. [src: howto-writing]
- A how-to does **not** explain what a Kubernetes namespace is. Link out to an explanation or reference doc if useful; do not inline the lesson. [src: howto-writing]
- How-tos can branch: *"If you use Atlas, run X; if you self-host, run Y."* Keep branches shallow (1–2 levels) and label them clearly. [src: howto-writing]
- Tutorials promise *"you'll see exactly this"*. How-tos verify: *"Confirm that `kubectl get pods` shows the new pod in `Running` state."* [src: howto-writing]
- When a step can plausibly fail, name the failure inline: *"If you see `Permission denied`, your role does not have `clusterAdmin` — see [granting roles](…)."* [src: howto-writing]
- When the reader has done the thing, stop. Optional follow-up belongs in a **See also** block, not in the numbered list. [src: howto-writing]
- <One sentence stating the outcome and when you'd want this.> [src: howto-writing]
- You have <prerequisite 1>. [src: howto-writing]
- You have <prerequisite 2>. [src: howto-writing]
- You have <permission / role / credential>. [src: howto-writing]
- <Imperative verb>… <action>. [src: howto-writing]
- <Imperative verb>… <action>. [src: howto-writing]
- Verify the result: [src: howto-writing]
- <verification command> [src: howto-writing]
- You should see <observable indicator>. [src: howto-writing]
- **<Error 1>** — <cause and fix or link>. [src: howto-writing]
- **<Error 2>** — <cause and fix or link>. [src: howto-writing]
- Link: [Related how-to] [src: howto-writing]
- Link: [Background / explanation doc] [src: howto-writing]
- Link: [API reference for <X>] [src: howto-writing]
- > "Before we deploy, let's understand what a deployment is…" [src: howto-writing]
- The reader knows what a deployment is. If they don't, link an explanation doc. [src: howto-writing]
- > "How to configure, deploy, and monitor your service" [src: howto-writing]
- That is three guides. Split them. [src: howto-writing]
- Narrator voice ("we'll now create…"), promise language ("you'll see exactly…"). Either commit to the tutorial form or trust the reader. [src: howto-writing]
- The reader hits step 3 and discovers they needed `kubectl` configured. The prerequisite block is the contract. [src: howto-writing]
- Twelve steps, no checks. Insert verification at every decision point and at the end. [src: howto-writing]
- **Could the reader phrase their question as "How do I <verb>?" before reading?** If they couldn't even ask, they need a tutorial. [src: howto-writing]
- **Is there exactly one goal?** If not, split. [src: howto-writing]
- **Does the reader already own the vocabulary?** If you need to define basic terms, you are drifting into tutorial or explanation. [src: howto-writing]
- **Is the goal a daily task, or a once-ever production-critical event?** Once-ever production-critical events with rollback procedures are **runbooks**, not how-tos. [src: howto-writing]
- Link: [How-to guides — Diátaxis](https://diataxis.fr/how-to-guides/) [src: howto-writing]
- Link: [Documentation Quadrants — Dunn](https://dunnhq.com/posts/2023/documentation-quadrants/) [src: howto-writing]
- Reference documentation is **a description**. It tells the reader what something **is**, what its parts **are**, and what each part **does**. It does not teach, it does not advocate, and it does not narrate. [src: reference-doc-writing]
- **The single most-violated rule: reference does not interpret.** It states facts. Discussion belongs in explanation docs; storytelling belongs in tutorials; opinions belong nowhere in reference. [src: reference-doc-writing]
- If the product has modules, the reference has modules. If a class has methods, the doc has a section per method. The doc topology is **isomorphic** to the API topology. [src: reference-doc-writing]
- Every parameter is listed. Every return value is documented. Every error code is enumerated. There is no "for brevity we omit…" — reference is the *only* place where the reader can be sure they have not missed an option. Omissions are bugs. [src: reference-doc-writing]
- Every function reference has the same sections in the same order. Every parameter table has the same columns. Consistency lets a reader who has read one page **skim** the next page at 10× speed. [src: reference-doc-writing]
- Reference does not say *"you'll usually want…"*, *"the recommended approach is…"*. Reference states: *"`timeout`: integer, milliseconds, default `30000`, minimum `0`, maximum `600000`"*. [src: reference-doc-writing]
- Reference examples are **specimens**, not lessons. A canonical-call example shows the shape — argument positions, return shape, a representative success and a representative failure. [src: reference-doc-writing]
- Anything that could surprise a working reader must be stated explicitly: default values, units (ms vs seconds), whether a field is nullable, whether the method mutates input, whether order matters. [src: reference-doc-writing]
- Reference is read by **search**, not by table-of-contents traversal. The page title and the first sentence must contain the term the reader will type. Headings must be the names of the things they describe (`POST /v1/users`, `createSession(opts)`, `--max-retries`). [src: reference-doc-writing]
- **Alphabetical** for catalogs (CLI flags, config keys, error codes). [src: reference-doc-writing]
- **Logical / call-order** for function references (constructor, then lifecycle methods, then utility methods). [src: reference-doc-writing]
- **Signature-order** for parameter tables (positional first in their declared order; keyword/optional after). [src: reference-doc-writing]
- <One-sentence factual statement of what the function does.> [src: reference-doc-writing]
- **Stability:** stable [src: reference-doc-writing]
- `Promise<Result>` — resolves with `Result` on success. Rejects with one of the errors below. [src: reference-doc-writing]
- const r = await client.fetchThing(id, { timeout: 5000 }); [src: reference-doc-writing]
- `<relatedFunction>` — for the streaming variant. [src: reference-doc-writing]
- Deploy the current project to the configured target. [src: reference-doc-writing]
- mytool deploy [--target <name>] [--dry-run] [--force] [src: reference-doc-writing]
- > "Imagine you have a user signup form. You'd call `createUser` like this…" [src: reference-doc-writing]
- That's a tutorial example. Strip the narrative. [src: reference-doc-writing]
- These are advice. Move them to a how-to. [src: reference-doc-writing]
- Every parameter without a documented default is a footgun. [src: reference-doc-writing]
- > "Throws on failure." — What failures? Under what conditions? With what code? [src: reference-doc-writing]
- Parameters listed alphabetically on one page, by signature on another. The reader's skim speed collapses. [src: reference-doc-writing]
- **Will the reader arrive via search, looking for a specific name?** If yes → reference. [src: reference-doc-writing]
- **Is the content exhaustive coverage of a surface area?** If you can plausibly omit items "for brevity", you are not writing reference. [src: reference-doc-writing]
- **Is the voice neutral and factual?** If you find *"you'll want…"* — that's a how-to hiding inside. [src: reference-doc-writing]
- When it's not reference, switch quadrants: [src: reference-doc-writing]
- Newcomer onboarding → `tutorial-writing` [src: reference-doc-writing]
- Goal-directed recipe → `howto-writing` [src: reference-doc-writing]
- Background / why / discussion → `explanation-doc-writing` [src: reference-doc-writing]
- REST/SDK endpoint authoring → `api-docs-craft` [src: reference-doc-writing]
- Link: [Reference — Diátaxis](https://diataxis.fr/reference/) [src: reference-doc-writing]
- Link: [Reference guides — Divio Documentation](https://docs.divio.com/documentation-system/reference/) [src: reference-doc-writing]
- An explanation doc is **a discussion**. Its purpose is not to instruct, not to enumerate, and not to walk a reader through a goal. Its job is to leave the reader with a clearer **mental model** — of why the system is shaped this way, what alternatives existed, what trade-offs were made. [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- **The single most-violated rule: explanation is not a proposal.** It describes the world as it is — choices already made, designs already shipped, reasoning already settled. If you are arguing for a change, you are writing an **RFC**, not an explanation. [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- *"Why does the cache invalidate on write rather than on read?"* [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- *"Why is the default replication factor 3?"* [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- *"Why do we use append-only logs here when most systems would update in place?"* [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- If the reader's question is "how do I configure replication factor", they need a how-to. Explanation answers the **shape-of-the-world** questions. [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- Lead with the analogy or the one-sentence essence. *"Think of the write-ahead log as a journal: every change is written there first, and only later applied to the data files."* Then add the next layer: *"This means a crash in the middle of an update never leaves the data file half-written."* [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- A decision without alternatives is not a decision; it's a proclamation. The explanation doc names the roads not taken: *"We considered an LSM-tree here, but the workload is read-heavy and the write-amplification penalty was not worth the write throughput gain."* [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- A short history paragraph — *"v1 used Redis for the queue; we hit head-of-line blocking under load in 2024 and moved to Kafka in v2"* — gives the reader context that no amount of current-state description can replicate. [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- Explanation uses words like *because*, *however*, *the trade-off is*, *one consequence is*. It avoids *do this*, *use this*, *configure this*. [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- *"This doc covers our write-path; for read-path discussion see [the read-path doc]"* [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- **RFC** = proposing a change before it ships. Argumentative voice. Open to debate. [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- **ADR** (Architecture Decision Record) = a small, dated note of a decision made. [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- **Explanation doc** = the broader discussion of how and why the system is the way it is. [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- Explanation docs should age slowly. Captures the durable reasoning: invariants, trade-offs, philosophy. [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- <One-paragraph essence: the analogy or the one-sentence mental model.> [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- <The problem <X> was designed to solve.> [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- <2–4 paragraphs building the model. Diagram if useful.> [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- <Where <X> sits relative to neighboring components.> [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- We chose <X> over <Y> because <reason>. <Y> would have given us <advantage> [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- but cost us <disadvantage>. [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- <Short paragraph: how <X> evolved.> [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- This doc covers <scope>. For: [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- *How to <task> with <X>* — see [the how-to](…). [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- *The full <X> API* — see [reference](…). [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- > "To understand caching, let's build a simple cache..." [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- If the reader is creating files, you are running a tutorial. [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- > "You should always set `replication=3` because…" [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- That's a how-to recommendation. Recast: *"Replication factor 3 trades disk and write-bandwidth for the ability to tolerate single-node failure."* [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- A doc that explains a choice without ever naming what was rejected reads as a sales pitch. [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- Argumentative voice, open questions, "we are considering moving to…" — that's an RFC. [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- Link: [Explanation — Diátaxis](https://diataxis.fr/explanation/) [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- Link: [Explanation — Divio Documentation](https://docs.divio.com/documentation-system/explanation/) [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- Michael Nygard, "Documenting Architecture Decisions" (2011) [src: explanation-doc-writing]
- A press release is a short, journalist-facing news document with a single goal: make it so easy to publish your news that a busy reporter (or a wire-service automated feed) can run it nearly verbatim. [src: press-release-writing]
- The defining traits of a press release: [src: press-release-writing]
- Third person, past or present tense, never "we" [src: press-release-writing]
- Inverted-pyramid structure [src: press-release-writing]
- AP Style dateline at the top of the body [src: press-release-writing]
- Stable boilerplate at the bottom (the "About" paragraph) [src: press-release-writing]
- Quote attribution that is publication-ready [src: press-release-writing]
- End mark: `###` centered on its own line [src: press-release-writing]
- 400–600 words is the sweet spot [src: press-release-writing]
- Under ~100 characters. [src: press-release-writing]
- Active verbs. [src: press-release-writing]
- No marketing puffery: avoid "industry-leading," "revolutionary," "best-in-class." [src: press-release-writing]
- State the news, not the spin. [src: press-release-writing]
- Acme Corp Acquires Beta Analytics for $400 Million [src: press-release-writing]
- Deal Doubles Acme's Enterprise Data Footprint and Adds 1,200 Engineers [src: press-release-writing]
- `FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE` — the default [src: press-release-writing]
- `EMBARGOED UNTIL: [Day, Month Day, Year, HH:MM TIME ZONE]` [src: press-release-writing]
- `MEDIA ADVISORY` — for an upcoming event/availability [src: press-release-writing]
- **Always include the time zone** for embargoes. [src: press-release-writing]
- CITY, State Abbreviation, Month Day, Year — <lede starts here> [src: press-release-writing]
- City name in ALL CAPS [src: press-release-writing]
- AP state abbreviation (not USPS!) [src: press-release-writing]
- Date written out: `Nov. 12, 2026` (AP uses abbreviated months for Jan., Feb., Aug., Sept., Oct., Nov., Dec.) [src: press-release-writing]
- Em dash (`—`) before the lede [src: press-release-writing]
- The first sentence must contain Who, What, When, Where, Why. [src: press-release-writing]
- > Acme Corp, a leading provider of analytics solutions, is excited to announce today an important new milestone in its ongoing growth journey. [src: press-release-writing]
- > Acme Corp today announced it has acquired Beta Analytics, a Boston-based real-time data platform, for $400 million in cash and stock. [src: press-release-writing]
- **Paragraph 2**: amplification — the size, the scope, the differentiator. [src: press-release-writing]
- **Paragraph 3**: the executive quote. [src: press-release-writing]
- **Paragraph 4–5**: supporting detail. [src: press-release-writing]
- **Paragraph 6**: optional second quote. [src: press-release-writing]
- **Paragraph 7**: practical info — availability, pricing, link. [src: press-release-writing]
- **Boilerplate**: stable "About" paragraph(s). [src: press-release-writing]
- **Media contact** block. [src: press-release-writing]
- **End mark**: `###`. [src: press-release-writing]
- **Standard pattern:** [src: press-release-writing]
- > "We chose Beta because their real-time architecture is the strongest in the market," said Jane Doe, CEO of Acme Corp. [src: press-release-writing]
- Attribution after the first sentence of the quote. [src: press-release-writing]
- `said` is the AP-standard verb. Avoid `stated`, `commented`, `noted`, `exclaimed`. [src: press-release-writing]
- Full name + title + company on first reference. [src: press-release-writing]
- Acme Corp is a [category] company that helps [audience] [job-to-be-done]. Founded in [year] and headquartered in [city], Acme serves [customer count]. For more information, visit www.acme.com. [src: press-release-writing]
- 60–120 words. Updated when a hard fact changes. [src: press-release-writing]
- Director of Communications, Acme Corp [src: press-release-writing]
- The release ends with `###` centered on its own line (or the older `-30-`). [src: press-release-writing]
- FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE [src: press-release-writing]

- Crisis PR writing is the discipline of communicating publicly during a **reputation crisis** that is not (or is no longer) a live operational incident. Examples: [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- An executive misconduct allegation surfaces [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- A data breach beyond the operational window — now a public-disclosure problem [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- A product recall or safety advisory [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- A supplier or partner exposure [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- A viral social-media controversy [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- The canonical reference response is Johnson & Johnson's 1982 Tylenol cyanide crisis: rapid acknowledgement, decisive action (a full 31-million-bottle recall), transparent media communication, and a visible product redesign. [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- **A good holding statement:** [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- Acknowledges that something happened [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- Expresses concern for anyone affected [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- States you are investigating [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- Promises a substantive update by a specific time [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- Names a point of contact [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- Never speculate. "We don't know yet" beats "we believe." [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- Never minimize. "An incident has been reported" beats "minor disruption." [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- Never blame externally on day one. [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- Always commit to a specific next update time. [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- **Mismatch is the most expensive crisis-PR error.** Treating a preventable-cluster crisis as a victim-cluster crisis creates the secondary crisis: "first they did it, then they lied about it." [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- **Yes — CEO signs:** preventable-cluster crises, executive-conduct issues, large-scale customer-impacting breaches. [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- **No — Communications/Legal signs:** routine product advisories, ongoing investigations where speculation is dangerous. [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- Every statement gets a version number, a timestamp, and an author. When facts change, supersede the prior statement publicly. [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- **Holding statement (T+0 to T+60 min):** Posted on company press page. [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- **Substantive statement (T+2h to T+12h):** Press release; emailed to affected customers. [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- **Update cadence (T+24h, T+72h, then weekly):** Posted in a single "incident log" page. [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- > **Statement — November 14, 2026, 9:42 a.m. ET** [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- > Acme Corp is aware of reports that customer account information may have been accessed without authorization. Our security team is actively investigating and has engaged independent forensic experts. The protection of customer data is a responsibility we take seriously, and we deeply regret any concern this causes. [src: crisis-pr-writing]
- > We will share a substantive update by 5:00 p.m. ET today, November 14. Customers with immediate questions can contact security@acme.com. Press inquiries: press@acme.com. [src: crisis-pr-writing]

- A whitepaper is a long-form, authoritative B2B document that educates a business reader on a problem and positions a solution. [src: whitepaper-writing]
- **Lighter than academic**: persuasion is allowed; citation density is moderate; the author has a point of view. [src: whitepaper-writing]
- **Heavier than a blog post**: data and methodology are visible; claims are sourced. [src: whitepaper-writing]
- **Length**: 8–20 pages typical; 8–12 is the sweet spot for engagement. [src: whitepaper-writing]
- **Voice**: third-person company-as-narrator. [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Gordon Graham identifies three structural types: [src: whitepaper-writing]
- **Backgrounder**: explains a technology, methodology, or product in depth. [src: whitepaper-writing]
- **Numbered-list**: "5 Reasons to Adopt X," "10 Pitfalls of Y." [src: whitepaper-writing]
- **Problem/solution**: describes an industry-wide problem, evaluates current solutions, presents a new approach. [src: whitepaper-writing]
- The arc is **inverted from a sales pitch**: a pitch starts with the product; a whitepaper ends with the product. [src: whitepaper-writing]
- 1–2 pages, no more. [src: whitepaper-writing]
- States the problem, the proposed solution, the most compelling proof point, and the call to action. [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Stands alone. [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Written **last**, after the full paper is drafted. [src: whitepaper-writing]
- **Vendor-neutral rules:** [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Name the problem before naming the product. [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Discuss competing approaches honestly; their drawbacks should be real, not strawmen. [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Cite third-party sources for problem-scoping statistics. [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Use the sponsor "About" block as the only place where company puffery is acceptable. [src: whitepaper-writing]
- A whitepaper that reads as a thinly disguised sales pitch is rejected by 60% of B2B decision-makers. [src: whitepaper-writing]
- The right citation density is **2–6 cited claims per page**. [src: whitepaper-writing]
- **Source hierarchy (descending credibility):** [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Peer-reviewed academic research and government data [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Major analyst firms (Gartner, Forrester, IDC, McKinsey) [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Standards bodies (NIST, ISO, IEEE, W3C) [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Industry surveys with disclosed methodology and sample size [src: whitepaper-writing]
- The sponsor's own anonymized data (acceptable for proof sections) [src: whitepaper-writing]
- **The "verify the verifiable" rule:** every claim of the form "X% of organizations report Y" must cite a source the reader can access. [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Embed a real (or anonymized) customer story in the proof section: [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Challenge → Approach → Result structure (mini case study) [src: whitepaper-writing]
- One direct customer quote, attributed [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Two-to-three quantified outcomes [src: whitepaper-writing]
- 8–12 pages: standard problem/solution [src: whitepaper-writing]
- 12–16 pages: technical or research-heavy [src: whitepaper-writing]
- 16–20 pages: research-grade with original primary data [src: whitepaper-writing]
- 20+ pages: split into a series [src: whitepaper-writing]
- **Design budget:** Branded title page, table of contents (clickable PDF), 2–4 charts/infographics minimum, pull quotes every 2–3 pages, case-study sidebar boxes. [src: whitepaper-writing]
- **Gate when:** Original research with high differentiation value; mid-or-bottom-funnel audience. [src: whitepaper-writing]
- **Ungate when:** Foundational education; high SEO value; technical and form-allergic audience. [src: whitepaper-writing]
- **Hybrid pattern (modern best practice):** First 2–3 pages ungated, full PDF gated behind a form. [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Title: The State of Real-Time Data in Financial Services, 2026 [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Subtitle: Why 73% of risk teams still operate on stale data — and the architectural shift required to fix it [src: whitepaper-writing]
- **References appendix:** [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Numbered or alphabetized [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Full citation: author, title, publisher, year, URL or DOI [src: whitepaper-writing]
- ~5–25 references typical [src: whitepaper-writing]
- **Methodology appendix (for research-based papers):** [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Sample size, geography, role/seniority breakdown [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Survey instrument or interview-protocol summary [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Time frame of data collection [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Disclosure of who funded the research [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Title + subtitle [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Author name(s) + affiliation [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Sponsor disclosure [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Publication date and version [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Executive summary (1–2 pages) [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Problem, Why current approaches fall short [src: whitepaper-writing]
- New approach, Evidence preview, Call to action [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Section 1: The industry problem (2–3 pages) [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Section 2: Why current approaches fall short (2–3 pages) [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Section 3: A new approach (2–4 pages) [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Section 4: Evidence (2–4 pages) [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Section 5: Implementation considerations (1–2 pages) [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Section 6: Call to action (1 page) [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Appendix A: References [src: whitepaper-writing]
- Appendix B: Methodology [src: whitepaper-writing]

- A case study is a published narrative of one customer's outcome with a vendor's product or approach. It is the highest-conversion content asset in B2B marketing because it does the one thing prospects most need: prove that a buyer like them succeeded with this solution. [src: case-study-writing]
- **The defining traits of a case study:** [src: case-study-writing]
- Specific, named (or carefully anonymized) customer [src: case-study-writing]
- Concrete before/after with quantified outcomes [src: case-study-writing]
- At least one direct quote from a named customer stakeholder [src: case-study-writing]
- A clear narrative arc: Challenge → Solution → Result [src: case-study-writing]
- Customer approval in writing before publication [src: case-study-writing]
- A non-marketing tone — the customer is the protagonist, not the vendor [src: case-study-writing]
- **Front-load the result.** Place the hero metric in the title or subtitle, and again in the first paragraph. [src: case-study-writing]
- **Name the customer when:** Written marketing approval is signed; customer is referenceable; naming helps, not hurts. [src: case-study-writing]
- **Anonymize when:** Regulated industry; sensitive admission; customer in quiet period. [src: case-study-writing]
- **Anonymization patterns:** [src: case-study-writing]
- "A Fortune 500 financial-services firm headquartered in the U.S. Northeast" — High trust [src: case-study-writing]
- "A large healthcare provider" — Low trust [src: case-study-writing]
- **Specific baseline**: "down from 4.2 hours to 12 minutes" beats "much faster" [src: case-study-writing]
- **Specific time window**: "in the first 90 days" beats "over time" [src: case-study-writing]
- **Specific scope**: "across 1,200 trades per day" [src: case-study-writing]
- **Verifiable source**: the customer signed off on this number [src: case-study-writing]
- Attributed to a named individual with a title [src: case-study-writing]
- Sounds like a human said it (not vendor-speak) [src: case-study-writing]
- Specific, not generic ("we cut our deploy time in half" beats "Acme has been a great partner") [src: case-study-writing]
- **Bad quote:** "Acme is a true partner who has helped us leverage our data to drive transformational outcomes." [src: case-study-writing]
- **Good quote:** "We used to spend two full days every month reconciling reports. Now it's a 20-minute job for one person." — Sarah Chen, Director of Engineering [src: case-study-writing]
- Customer success identifies a candidate [src: case-study-writing]
- Verbal pre-approval from a customer executive [src: case-study-writing]
- Discovery interview [src: case-study-writing]
- Draft 1 to the customer [src: case-study-writing]
- Customer Legal and PR review [src: case-study-writing]
- Final draft + approval signature [src: case-study-writing]
- Publication [src: case-study-writing]
- Renewal (annually if case study remains live) [src: case-study-writing]
- **Vendor-as-hero (anti-pattern):** [src: case-study-writing]
- > "Acme's revolutionary platform transformed BigCo's operations, delivering 73% productivity gains." [src: case-study-writing]
- **Customer-as-hero (correct):** [src: case-study-writing]
- > "BigCo's engineering team cut deploy time from 4 hours to 22 minutes by replacing their legacy CI system." [src: case-study-writing]
- The cover letter is a narrative artifact — a focused, one-page argument for why this human should be in this role at this company. Customization per application is non-negotiable. [src: cover-letter-writing]
- **Why this company.** Show evidence you've done your homework: a product they shipped, a value they've published. [src: cover-letter-writing]
- **Why this role.** Connect the specific responsibilities to specific skills or experiences you have. Reuse 2-3 keywords from the JD. [src: cover-letter-writing]
- **Why me.** Demonstrate through evidence and stories. Don't list skills; show outcomes. [src: cover-letter-writing]
- "I am writing to apply for the X position at Y." [src: cover-letter-writing]
- "My name is X and I am a [degree/title]." [src: cover-letter-writing]
- **Stronger openers:** [src: cover-letter-writing]
- "I noticed your team published the design for the X system last month — the tradeoffs you made on Y are the same ones I worked through at Z." [src: cover-letter-writing]
- **Weak:** "I have strong project management skills and am highly organized." [src: cover-letter-writing]
- **Stronger:** "Last year I shipped the X migration on a six-engineer team. The original estimate was four months; we delivered in five because I caught a dependency that wasn't in the original scope." [src: cover-letter-writing]
- **One page maximum**, no exceptions. [src: cover-letter-writing]
- **250-350 words** is the standard target. [src: cover-letter-writing]
- **3-4 short paragraphs**, block-formatted. [src: cover-letter-writing]
- At a minimum, customize: [src: cover-letter-writing]
- Company name and the "why this company" paragraph [src: cover-letter-writing]
- 2-3 keywords from the JD [src: cover-letter-writing]
- The job title in the opener [src: cover-letter-writing]
- **Salutation:** "Dear [Name]," when you know the hiring manager's name. [src: cover-letter-writing]
- **Sign-off:** "Sincerely," is the universal safe choice. [src: cover-letter-writing]
- **Capitalization:** Only the first word of the closing phrase is capitalized. [src: cover-letter-writing]
- Count how many sentences open with "I." If more than half do, the letter reads self-absorbed. Vary openings: lead with the company, the role, the project, the result. [src: cover-letter-writing]
- thesis: who you are, the role you're applying for, and why you fit.] [src: cover-letter-writing]
- the role you played, the measurable outcome.] [src: cover-letter-writing]
- **The cliché opener.** "I am writing to apply..." [src: cover-letter-writing]
- **The reused letter.** Generic flattery, no company name in the first paragraph. [src: cover-letter-writing]
- **The skill list.** "Strong communicator, fast learner, team player." [src: cover-letter-writing]
- **The resume rehash.** Repeating the resume's bullets in paragraph form. [src: cover-letter-writing]
- **The two-page letter.** Always cut to one page. [src: cover-letter-writing]
- **The typo in the company name.** Auto-disqualifying. [src: cover-letter-writing]

- A job description is a marketing document, a legal document, and a filter — at the same time. It must attract candidates the company wants, deter candidates who would be a poor fit, comply with US pay-transparency law in 15+ states, and avoid language that systematically suppresses applications from underrepresented groups. [src: job-description-writing]
- **What you'll do** — Responsibilities. Day-to-day work. Outcomes the role owns. [src: job-description-writing]
- **What we look for** — Requirements split into must-haves (3-5 dealbreakers) and nice-to-haves. [src: job-description-writing]
- **What we offer** — Compensation range, benefits, growth path, working model. [src: job-description-writing]
- **Responsibilities** describe what the person does. Verbs in the present tense: "Design and ship," "Mentor," "Own." [src: job-description-writing]
- **Requirements** describe what the person must already have. Adjectives and nouns: "5 years of," "Experience with," "Familiarity with." [src: job-description-writing]
- **Cap must-haves at 3-5.** A must-have is a dealbreaker — if the candidate doesn't have it, you won't hire them. [src: job-description-writing]
- **The evidence:** Women apply for jobs only when they meet ~56% of listed requirements vs men at ~52%. Long requirement lists deter applications from underrepresented groups more than from majority groups (Bohnet 2016). [src: job-description-writing]
- **Heuristic:** If your must-haves list has more than 5 items, ask which two you'd drop. Then drop them. [src: job-description-writing]
- Textio's research found that gender-coded language measurably skews who applies. [src: job-description-writing]
- **Masculine-coded words to avoid:** aggressive, ambitious, analytical, assertive, challenge, competitive, confident, decisive, determined, dominant, driven, fearless, forceful, independent, ninja, outspoken, principled, rockstar, self-reliant, superior. [src: job-description-writing]
- **Action:** Run the JD through a tool like Textio, Gender Decoder, or Datapeople. Aim for balance or feminine-leaning if the role is historically male-coded. [src: job-description-writing]
- States requiring salary range disclosure (verify before posting): [src: job-description-writing]
- **California** (15+ employees) — required [src: job-description-writing]
- **Colorado** (all employers with 1+ CO employee) — required [src: job-description-writing]
- **Illinois** (15+ employees, effective Jan 2025) — required [src: job-description-writing]
- **Massachusetts** (25+ employees, effective Oct 2025) — required [src: job-description-writing]
- **New York** — required statewide [src: job-description-writing]
- **Washington** (15+ employees) — required + benefits description [src: job-description-writing]
- **Practical rule:** If you post a JD that may be viewed from any of these jurisdictions, include a good-faith salary range. [src: job-description-writing]
- In your first 90 days, you'll: [src: job-description-writing]
- Week 1-2: Onboard with the team, shadow on-call, complete platform tour. [src: job-description-writing]
- Week 3-6: Ship your first small change end-to-end with a mentor. [src: job-description-writing]
- Week 7-12: Own a piece of the [X] subsystem; lead one design review. [src: job-description-writing]
- **Age bias signals:** "digital native," "energetic," "fast-paced young team." [src: job-description-writing]
- **Education bias:** "degree from a top university" — replace with the actual skill. [src: job-description-writing]
- **Cultural-fit signals:** "must love startups," "we're a family." These select for sameness. [src: job-description-writing]

- Link: [3-5 dealbreakers only.] [src: job-description-writing]
- Link: [Open-ended list. Use "familiar with," "exposure to," "bonus if."] [src: job-description-writing]

- **The 20-item must-haves list.** Cap at 3-5. [src: job-description-writing]
- **"Competitive salary."** Non-compliant in 15+ states. [src: job-description-writing]
- **"Digital native" / "energetic" / "fast-paced young team."** Age-coded. [src: job-description-writing]

- Performance reviews are not new information — they are **synthesis**. The cardinal rule is "no surprises": anything that appears in a written review should already have been said in a one-on-one. [src: performance-review-writing]
- If a written performance review contains feedback the employee is hearing for the first time, the manager has failed earlier in the year. [src: performance-review-writing]
- **Situation** — When and where the behavior occurred. [src: performance-review-writing]
- **Behavior** — What the person actually did. Observable, factual, non-interpretive. [src: performance-review-writing]
- **Impact** — What followed from the behavior. [src: performance-review-writing]
- **Example (negative):** [src: performance-review-writing]
- > *Situation:* In the design review for the refund system on March 12. *Behavior:* You interrupted the junior engineer three times. *Impact:* She stopped contributing to the discussion, and we lost her input on the rollback design. [src: performance-review-writing]
- **Example (positive):** [src: performance-review-writing]
- > *Situation:* During the Q2 incident on April 8. *Behavior:* You took on the comms role within five minutes. *Impact:* The CSMs were able to respond to customers without paging engineers. [src: performance-review-writing]
- **Weak:** "Sarah is a great team player and is always willing to help." [src: performance-review-writing]
- **Strong:** "Sarah led the cross-team migration of the billing service in Q2, partnering with three teams and coordinating four deployment windows; the migration shipped two weeks ahead of plan with zero customer-visible incidents. **Next step:** I'd like to see Sarah take on a bigger system design role in Q4." [src: performance-review-writing]
- **Weakness phrasing (avoid):** "Tom is too quiet in meetings." [src: performance-review-writing]
- **Growth-area phrasing (use):** "In larger forums (5+ people), Tom contributes less than I think he could. He has the strongest understanding of the search service on the team, but in the Q3 architecture reviews his ideas often landed in the followup chat rather than in the meeting itself. **Growth focus for next cycle:** Tom and I have agreed he'll lead two of the next four architecture reviews." [src: performance-review-writing]
- Two axes: how much you care personally about the person, and how directly you challenge them. [src: performance-review-writing]
- **Radical Candor:** Care + Challenge. The target. [src: performance-review-writing]
- **Ruinous Empathy:** Care without challenge. Soft, vague, no real feedback. The most common manager failure mode. [src: performance-review-writing]
- **Obnoxious Aggression:** Challenge without care. [src: performance-review-writing]
- The failure mode in writing is almost always Ruinous Empathy — burying real feedback in praise sandwich. [src: performance-review-writing]
- **Lead with strengths, not weaknesses.** [src: performance-review-writing]
- **Use concrete examples or cut the point.** [src: performance-review-writing]
- **Negative feedback goes in private.** [src: performance-review-writing]
- **Most of your time should go to talents and achievements.** [src: performance-review-writing]
- Every assertion should be tied to a specific example. Sweeping claims without examples are the single biggest source of perceived unfairness. [src: performance-review-writing]
- **Weak:** "She has strong communication skills." [src: performance-review-writing]
- **Strong:** "When the platform migration ran into the dependency issue on the search team, she wrote the four-paragraph summary that unblocked the cross-team decision." [src: performance-review-writing]
- **False-modesty traps:** [src: performance-review-writing]
- Hedging with "I tried to" and "I worked on" instead of "I led" and "I shipped." [src: performance-review-writing]
- Crediting the team for outcomes you personally drove. [src: performance-review-writing]
- Listing the work without claiming the result. [src: performance-review-writing]
- **The fix:** "I led the migration; the team of four shipped it" beats both "I migrated the system" (overclaim) and "We migrated the system" (underclaim). [src: performance-review-writing]
- Are claims tied to behaviors and outcomes, or to personality? [src: performance-review-writing]
- Have I used different language for different people on the same team for the same observed behavior? [src: performance-review-writing]
- Have I disproportionately commented on style versus substance? [src: performance-review-writing]
- > "Maria is a wonderful teammate and a hard worker. She sometimes can be a bit late on deliverables but overall she's been a great addition to the team." [src: performance-review-writing]
- The real feedback ("late on deliverables") is buried in vague praise, has no specific example, and gives Maria no idea what to change. [src: performance-review-writing]

- Camille Fournier — *The Manager's Path* (O'Reilly, 2017) [src: performance-review-writing]
- Link: [Center for Creative Leadership — SBI Feedback Model](https://www.ccl.org/articles/leading-effectively-articles/sbi-feedback-model-a-quick-win-to-improve-talent-conversations-development/) [src: performance-review-writing]
- A Product Requirements Document (PRD) is a PM-owned artifact that defines **what** a product team will build and **why**, before engineering proposes **how**. PRDs sit upstream of RFCs, design docs, and implementation specs. [src: prd-writing]
- A PRD captures **validated decisions**. It does not perform validation. Validation happens through customer interviews, prototypes, user testing, and data analysis — the PRD records the conclusions. [src: prd-writing]
- A modern PRD opens with the problem, not the solution. Sections proceed in this order: [src: prd-writing]
- **Problem** — what user/business pain are we solving, with evidence [src: prd-writing]
- **Users** — who is affected, segment size, current workarounds [src: prd-writing]
- **Goals** — desired outcomes and what success looks like [src: prd-writing]
- **Proposed solution** — at a high level (often a prototype link) [src: prd-writing]
- **Success metrics** — measurable definition of done [src: prd-writing]
- **Open questions / risks** — what's unresolved [src: prd-writing]
- **Non-goals** — what we are explicitly NOT doing [src: prd-writing]
- **Rollout / milestones** — MVP → v1 → roadmap [src: prd-writing]
- Marty Cagan's classic PRD structure: **Purpose**, **Features**, **Release Criteria**, **Rough Timing**. [src: prd-writing]
- **MVP** — minimum viable: smallest scope that lets us learn whether the proposed solution works. [src: prd-writing]
- **v1 (GA)** — broadly shippable: meets release criteria, addresses the core user need. [src: prd-writing]
- **Roadmap (vNext)** — follow-on work that the PRD acknowledges but does not commit to. [src: prd-writing]
- **Anti-pattern:** Writing one undifferentiated feature list and labeling it "the PRD." Always tag each feature with its scope. [src: prd-writing]
- Basecamp's Shape Up framework replaces the PRD with a **pitch**: problem, **appetite** (2 or 6 weeks of fixed budget), solution sketch (fat marker, not Figma), **rabbit holes** (risks to bound), and **no-gos** (explicit exclusions). [src: prd-writing]
- **Key inversion:** In Shape Up, **scope is the variable; time is fixed.** [src: prd-writing]
- Engineers and reviewers consistently raise questions like "what about X?" A **Non-Goals** section answers these preemptively: [src: prd-writing]
- > - Mobile app support — desktop only [src: prd-writing]
- > - Bulk import — single-record only [src: prd-writing]
- > - Real-time sync — daily batch acceptable [src: prd-writing]
- **Leading indicators** — observable within 1–4 weeks (adoption %, feature engagement, task completion rate) [src: prd-writing]
- **Lagging indicators** — observable in 1–2 quarters (retention, revenue, NPS, churn) [src: prd-writing]
- Always include at least one leading indicator that the team can act on during the first month post-launch. [src: prd-writing]
- **PRD** (this skill) — PM-owned. WHAT to build, for WHOM, WHY now. [src: prd-writing]
- **RFC / Design doc** — engineering-owned. HOW we propose to build it. [src: prd-writing]
- **Spec** — engineering-owned. The contract. API shapes, behavior rules. [src: prd-writing]
- **Plan / Task list** — engineering-owned. Sequenced units of work. [src: prd-writing]
- If a PRD accumulates feedback from N stakeholders and the author tries to honor every comment, the doc becomes incoherent. The PM is the **author**, not a scribe. [src: prd-writing]
- Healthy pattern: collect feedback, summarize disagreements explicitly, **make a call**, and record the call with one-sentence rationale. [src: prd-writing]

- **Last updated:** YYYY-MM-DD · **Target ship:** Quarter/Year [src: prd-writing]

- Secondary segment: [who, how many] [src: prd-writing]

- Performance: [SLO] [src: prd-writing]
- Accessibility: [WCAG level] [src: prd-writing]
- Security: [review completed] [src: prd-writing]
- Link: [ ] Product (name, date) [src: prd-writing]
- Link: [ ] Engineering (name, date) [src: prd-writing]
- Link: [ ] Design (name, date) [src: prd-writing]
- **Solution-first opening** — leading with "we will build X" before establishing why. [src: prd-writing]
- **Designed-by-committee text** — incorporating every comment without making a call. [src: prd-writing]
- **PRD as discovery substitute** — writing a 12-page PRD to "figure out" what users want. [src: prd-writing]
- **Spec-creep** — PRD drifts into API shapes or schema choices. [src: prd-writing]
- **No non-goals** — every reviewer asks "what about X?" [src: prd-writing]
- **Lagging-metric-only success** — no signal during the launch window. [src: prd-writing]
- **Stale doc** — PRD written once and never updated. [src: prd-writing]
