- An engineering spec is a contract. It says **WHAT** a system, component, endpoint, or message must do — independent of **HOW** it is implemented. [src: spec-writing]
- Three forms dominate modern practice: [src: spec-writing]
- **API specs** — machine-readable contracts for HTTP (OpenAPI 3.1) and event-driven (AsyncAPI 3.0) interfaces [src: spec-writing]
- **Behavior specs** — executable narratives (Gherkin / Given-When-Then) [src: spec-writing]
- **Data specs** — schema contracts (JSON Schema, Avro, Protobuf) [src: spec-writing]
- Joel Spolsky's 2000 series "Painless Functional Specifications" introduced the discipline: a **functional spec** describes how a product works from the user's perspective; a **technical spec** describes internal implementation. [src: spec-writing]
- A spec that says "internally we'll use a Redis cache with 5-minute TTL" has leaked implementation. [src: spec-writing]
- **Litmus test:** If you could swap out the implementation entirely and the spec still holds, the spec is at the right level. [src: spec-writing]
- Contract-first development: agree on the contract before writing code. The OpenAPI / AsyncAPI document is the source of truth. [src: spec-writing]
- Key top-level fields: [src: spec-writing]
- `openapi` — version (3.1.0) [src: spec-writing]
- `info` — name, version, description [src: spec-writing]
- `servers` — base URLs per environment [src: spec-writing]
- `paths` — endpoints, verbs, parameters, request/response shapes [src: spec-writing]
- `components` — reusable schemas, parameters, responses, security schemes [src: spec-writing]
- YAML is preferred over JSON for human authoring. [src: spec-writing]
- Key concepts in v3.0: [src: spec-writing]
- **Channels** are addressable destinations (Kafka topic, AMQP queue) — decoupled from operations [src: spec-writing]
- **Operations** describe what an application does on a channel using `action: send` or `action: receive` [src: spec-writing]
- **Messages** are defined once and referenced from channels and operations [src: spec-writing]
- Scenario: Valid percentage discount applies [src: spec-writing]
- Given a discount code "SUMMER10" worth 10% [src: spec-writing]
- When I apply the code at checkout [src: spec-writing]
- Then the cart total is "$45.00" [src: spec-writing]
- And the discount line shows "SUMMER10 (-$5.00)" [src: spec-writing]
- **Use Gherkin for:** business-logic behavior (pricing rules, eligibility checks, state transitions), workflows spanning multiple systems. [src: spec-writing]
- **Avoid Gherkin for:** API shape (use OpenAPI), data format (use JSON Schema). [src: spec-writing]
- A spec is a promise. Once published: [src: spec-writing]
- **Versioning** — non-breaking changes bump minor; breaking changes bump major. [src: spec-writing]
- **Backward compatibility** — additive changes (new optional field) are safe; removals, renames, type changes are breaking. [src: spec-writing]
- **Deprecation policy** — published timeline (e.g., 12 months notice for major version sunset). [src: spec-writing]
- **URL versioning** (`/v1/users`) — explicit, cacheable [src: spec-writing]
- **Date-pinned versioning** (Stripe: `Stripe-Version: 2024-04-10`) — fine-grained [src: spec-writing]
- Version in the topic name (`orders.v1`, `orders.v2`) [src: spec-writing]
- Schema registry with explicit compatibility modes (BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL) [src: spec-writing]
- OpenAPI's `examples` field and Gherkin's `Examples:` table are not decorative — they are the spec. CI tools validate that examples conform to the declared schema. [src: spec-writing]
- operationId: getOrder [src: spec-writing]
- summary: Retrieve a single order by ID. [src: spec-writing]
- name: orderId [src: spec-writing]
- description: Order found. [src: spec-writing]
- $ref: "#/components/schemas/Order" [src: spec-writing]
- description: Order not found. [src: spec-writing]
- **Implementation leakage** — spec mentions Redis, Postgres, language choice. [src: spec-writing]
- **No examples** — schemas without concrete payloads. [src: spec-writing]
- **Hand-waved errors** — "returns an error on failure" without listing codes. [src: spec-writing]
- **Missing versioning policy.** [src: spec-writing]
- **Spec-test drift** — spec says one thing, implementation does another, no CI check. [src: spec-writing]
- **Optional everything** — every field is optional, every status code is `default`. [src: spec-writing]
- Joel Spolsky, "Painless Functional Specifications, Part 2" [src: spec-writing]
- OpenAPI Specification v3.1: https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.1.0 [src: spec-writing]
- AsyncAPI 3.0.0 Specification: https://www.asyncapi.com/docs/reference/specification/v3.0.0 [src: spec-writing]
- Cucumber, "Gherkin Reference": https://cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference/ [src: spec-writing]
- A pitch deck is a slide-based artifact that compresses a fundraising, sales, or partnership case into a tight narrative arc — usually 10 to 14 slides — designed to be skimmed in minutes and remembered in seconds. [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- Guy Kawasaki's rule for investor/pitch contexts: [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **10 slides** — the human mind cannot absorb more than ten concepts in a single sitting in a pitch context [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **20 minutes** — even if you have a full hour, present in 20 minutes; leave the rest for discussion [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **30-point minimum font** — if you cannot fit your message in 30pt type, you have too many words [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- 10–12 slides in this order: [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **Title / Company purpose** — one-line description [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **Problem** — the customer pain, with evidence [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **Solution** — your product as the answer [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **Why now** — timing argument; why this couldn't have been built 5 years ago [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **Market size** — TAM/SAM/SOM, bottom-up preferred [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **Competition** — who else is in the space, how you differ [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **Product** — screenshots, demo, key features [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **Business model** — how you make money [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **Team** — why this team can win [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **Traction** — what you've already proven [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **Financials** — current state and projections [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **Ask** — how much you're raising, what you'll do with it [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **Slide 4 ("Why now") is the slide most founders skip and the slide most VCs care about.** [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- Strip away the template specifics and every effective pitch deck follows five beats: [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **Problem** — establish the pain. The reader nods. [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **Solution** — show your answer. The reader believes the answer is plausible. [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **Traction** — prove it's working. The reader believes the answer is real. [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **Team** — prove you can execute. The reader believes you specifically can win. [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **Ask** — close. The reader knows what you want and what they get. [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- Strong decks have an appendix — 5 to 20 extra slides beyond the main 10–12 — NOT shown in the live pitch but sent with the deck. [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- Pitch decks are NOT mystery novels. Slide 1 should already answer "what does this company do" at headline level. [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- End the deck with one slide that names the single thing you want the audience to walk away remembering. Not a recap — one sentence, one number, one image. [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- Every slide has a title. The title is a thesis, not a category. [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **Category title (weak):** "Market Size" [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **Thesis title (strong):** "$47B TAM growing 22% annually; we serve the underserved bottom 60%" [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **The mystery opening** — first 3 slides don't say what the company does. [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **Wall-of-text slides** — paragraphs of body copy presented live. [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **No "why now"** — deck skips the timing argument. [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **No traction (when you have some)** — burying real data deep. [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **Generic team slide** — "20+ years experience" instead of specific credentials. [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **Competition denial** — "we have no competitors." [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **TAM inflation** — "$2T global market" with no bottom-up math. [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **No ask** — the deck ends with vague "let's talk." [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- **Cliffhanger close** — last slide is "Thank you" or "Questions?" [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- Guy Kawasaki, "The 10/20/30 Rule of PowerPoint" [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- Sequoia Capital, "Writing a Business Plan" [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- Y Combinator, "How to build your seed round pitch deck" [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- Reid Hoffman / Greylock partners — LinkedIn Series B deck annotated by Hoffman [src: pitch-deck-writing]
- A survey question is a measurement instrument. Bad wording does not just irritate respondents — it injects measurement error that downstream statistics cannot fix. [src: survey-question-writing]
- Default mental model: every question is a hypothesis about what the respondent will read. If two thoughtful readers could parse the stem differently, the question is broken. [src: survey-question-writing]
- Stems must be **direct, concrete, mutually exclusive, and answerable in one read**: [src: survey-question-writing]
- **One concept per question** — no "and/or" coordination across distinct constructs. [src: survey-question-writing]
- **Common vocabulary** — no jargon. [src: survey-question-writing]
- **Concrete time window** — "in the last 30 days" not "recently". [src: survey-question-writing]
- **Specified reference** — "your most recent purchase" not "purchases". [src: survey-question-writing]
- **Symmetric framing** — avoid "do you agree that X is good" (loaded). [src: survey-question-writing]
- **Default: 5-point** for operational customer/employee surveys. **7-point** when you need discrimination for regression/factor analysis. [src: survey-question-writing]
- A balanced scale has the same number of positive and negative points around a neutral midpoint, with **labels on every point**. [src: survey-question-writing]
- Good: Strongly disagree / Disagree / Neither / Agree / Strongly agree [src: survey-question-writing]
- Bad: Hate it / Dislike / Neutral / Like / Love (asymmetric intensity) [src: survey-question-writing]
- **Do not modify the NPS stem** if you want to compare to industry benchmarks. NPS scoring: 0–6 = Detractors, 7–8 = Passives, 9–10 = Promoters. [src: survey-question-writing]
- "Do you agree or disagree that [statement]?" invites acquiescence bias (respondents lean toward "agree"). [src: survey-question-writing]
- Anti-pattern: "Do you agree that the website is easy to use?" (5-pt agree/disagree) [src: survey-question-writing]
- Better: "How easy or difficult is the website to use?" (Very difficult ... Very easy) [src: survey-question-writing]
- Item-specific scales reduce systematic error and increase reliability. [src: survey-question-writing]
- **Double-barreled** = one question, two concepts. Split it. [src: survey-question-writing]
- Bad: "How satisfied are you with the price and quality of the product?" [src: survey-question-writing]
- Fix: Two questions, one for price, one for quality. [src: survey-question-writing]
- **Leading** = stem prejudges the answer. [src: survey-question-writing]
- Bad: "How helpful was our amazing support team?" [src: survey-question-writing]
- Fix: "How would you rate the support you received?" (Very poor ... Very good) [src: survey-question-writing]
- **Neutral midpoint** = respondent has an opinion but it is centered. [src: survey-question-writing]
- **"Don't Know" / "Not applicable"** = respondent lacks the information. Place it **visually offset from the scale** (Dillman) so satisficers don't select it by default. [src: survey-question-writing]
- **Forced-choice** = use only when you genuinely need a side. [src: survey-question-writing]
- **Question order**: early questions can prime later ones. Put sensitive/demographic questions last. Put the headline metric (NPS/CSAT) before drill-downs. [src: survey-question-writing]
- **Response option order**: randomize unordered option lists across respondents. Never randomize a Likert. [src: survey-question-writing]
- **Matrix straight-lining**: long batteries of similar Likert items invite straight-lining. [src: survey-question-writing]
- **Closed-ended** = the default for quantitative analysis, benchmarking, large samples. [src: survey-question-writing]
- **Open-ended** = use sparingly (1–2 per survey). Place after the closed question that primed the topic. [src: survey-question-writing]
- Stem ≤ 20 words; aim for ≤ 12. [src: survey-question-writing]
- Scale ≤ 7 points (5 preferred). [src: survey-question-writing]
- Avoid grids/matrices on mobile — collapse to single-question-per-screen. [src: survey-question-writing]
- Total survey ≤ 5 minutes for transactional touchpoints. [src: survey-question-writing]
- > How likely is it that you would recommend [Company/Product] to a friend or colleague? [src: survey-question-writing]
- > 0 (Not at all likely) — 10 (Extremely likely) [src: survey-question-writing]
- > How would you rate the [speed / clarity / accuracy] of the response you received? [src: survey-question-writing]
- > Very poor — Poor — Fair — Good — Excellent [src: survey-question-writing]
- **Agree-disagree everything.** Causes acquiescence bias. [src: survey-question-writing]
- **Double-barreled stems.** [src: survey-question-writing]
- **Loaded adjectives** in stems. [src: survey-question-writing]
- **Endpoint-only labels on 7-pt scales.** [src: survey-question-writing]
- **Random Likert order.** Never randomize ordered response options. [src: survey-question-writing]
- **Modifying the NPS stem.** Breaks benchmark comparability. [src: survey-question-writing]
- **Stacking NPS + CSAT + CES + 10 drill-downs.** Pick a primary metric per touchpoint. [src: survey-question-writing]
- Dillman, D. A. *Internet, Phone, Mail, and Mixed-Mode Surveys: The Tailored Design Method* (4th ed.). Wiley. [src: survey-question-writing]
- Saris, W. E., & Gallhofer, I. N. *Design, Evaluation, and Analysis of Questionnaires for Survey Research* (2nd ed.). Wiley. [src: survey-question-writing]
- Reichheld, F. F. "The One Number You Need to Grow." *Harvard Business Review*, 2003. [src: survey-question-writing]
- Pew Research Center. "Writing Survey Questions." https://www.pewresearch.org/writing-survey-questions/ [src: survey-question-writing]
- This skill covers how to write replies to customer feedback collected at scale — NPS verbatim comments, CSAT free-text, post-support survey replies, and public app-store reviews. [src: nps-response-writing]
- Three things make these responses different from support replies: [src: nps-response-writing]
- **The customer did not ask for help.** They volunteered feedback. [src: nps-response-writing]
- **The score is the spine.** Detractor (0–6), passive (7–8), and promoter (9–10) responses calibrate differently. [src: nps-response-writing]
- **Cadence is short.** Under 48 hours for detractors, under 72 hours for app-store replies. [src: nps-response-writing]
- **Thank** — one line, specific to the act of giving feedback, not the score. [src: nps-response-writing]
- **Acknowledge** — quote or paraphrase the specific point. Proves you read it. [src: nps-response-writing]
- **Route** — name what happens next internally. Be specific: "I'm sending this to our billing team's weekly review on Thursday" beats "I'll route this to the right team." [src: nps-response-writing]
- **Commit** — one concrete next step you (the responder) own, with a date or trigger. [src: nps-response-writing]
- "I'll pass this along to the team" signals that the responder has no agency. Replace with: [src: nps-response-writing]
- A named destination: "I'll add this to our March platform-stability review." [src: nps-response-writing]
- A named owner: "Our billing PM, Priya, will see this on Monday." [src: nps-response-writing]
- An explicit decline: "I can't promise this gets prioritized — we're locked on Q2 commitments — but I've logged it under [theme]." [src: nps-response-writing]
- **Detractor first response:** within 24–48 hours. [src: nps-response-writing]
- **Passive reply:** within 1 week. [src: nps-response-writing]
- **Promoter reply:** within 2 weeks. [src: nps-response-writing]
- **App-store reply:** within 72 hours. [src: nps-response-writing]
- **Loop close-out** (confirming resolution back to the customer): within 30 days. [src: nps-response-writing]
- Escalate to a live conversation when any of these appear: [src: nps-response-writing]
- Explicit churn language: "evaluating alternatives," "renewal is up" [src: nps-response-writing]
- A specific named individual who is angry [src: nps-response-writing]
- A claim of broken commitment ("you promised us X") [src: nps-response-writing]
- Compounding issues ("this is the third time…") [src: nps-response-writing]
- Legal/compliance language: "data breach," "GDPR," "lawsuit" [src: nps-response-writing]
- Acknowledge the specific point. [src: nps-response-writing]
- State the trade-off plainly: "We deliberately chose X over Y because [reason]." [src: nps-response-writing]
- Offer the closest workaround you can. [src: nps-response-writing]
- Leave the door open: "If this stays a blocker for you, I want to know." [src: nps-response-writing]
- > Thanks for being direct in the survey — that's more useful to us than a polite 7. [src: nps-response-writing]
- > Two specific things you flagged: support response time, and the billing portal. On support: I pulled your last four tickets and the median first-response was 19 hours, which is outside our SLA for your plan. That's on us. On billing: the portal had a known issue with invoice downloads through last Tuesday; it's fixed now, but you would have hit it. [src: nps-response-writing]
- > I'm doing two things. First, I've flagged your account to our support lead, who will personally route your next three tickets. Second, I'd like 20 minutes with you this week to hear what "fast enough" looks like for your team. [src: nps-response-writing]
- > Tuesday or Thursday afternoon work? [src: nps-response-writing]
- > Thanks for the note — "good but not exciting" is genuinely useful for us, more than a 10 with no comment would be. [src: nps-response-writing]
- > If you don't mind a quick question: what would have made it a 9 or 10 for you? One thing, off the top of your head, is enough. [src: nps-response-writing]
- > Sorry the import flow blocked you on a 200MB file — that's a real bug, not the experience we want. We shipped a fix in v4.7.2 last week that raises the limit to 2GB and adds a progress indicator. If it's still failing for you, email support@[app].com. [src: nps-response-writing]
- **The form-letter thank-you.** "Thank you for your valuable feedback." Reads as bot output. [src: nps-response-writing]
- **The unprompted apology.** Saying "I'm sorry" to a passive (NPS 8) signals you read them as a detractor. [src: nps-response-writing]
- **The route-to-the-void.** "I've passed this along to the team" with no named destination. [src: nps-response-writing]
- **The re-survey ask before resolution.** Asking a detractor to re-rate before you have fixed anything. [src: nps-response-writing]
- **The marketing voice.** "we're committed to delivering delight" to a frustrated customer. [src: nps-response-writing]
- **The upsell smuggled into a promoter reply.** [src: nps-response-writing]

- Three distinct artifacts: [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- **Agenda** — written *before* the meeting. Forward-looking. [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- **Minutes** — written *during/after*. Outcomes, decisions, action items, dissent on the record. Backward-looking and durable. [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- **Decision Log / ADR** — written *when a decision is significant enough to outlive the meeting*. One decision per record, indexed, immutable once accepted. [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- Every captured decision must answer: [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- **What was decided** — a single declarative sentence, not a description of the debate. [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- **Why** — the one or two reasons that tipped it. Trade-offs accepted. Alternatives rejected. [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- **Who owns it** — exactly one named person per action item. Co-ownership is no ownership. [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- **When** — a specific date, not "soon" or "next sprint". [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- Agenda items are intent ("discuss pricing tier rollout"). Minutes items are outcome ("decided to defer pricing tier rollout to Q3; revisit June 15 sync"). [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- **Sync minutes** (live meeting): Capture only what is needed to reconstruct outcomes. Skip the back-and-forth. Aim for ~10% the length of the conversation. [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- **Async minutes** (Slack thread, Loom comment chain): The thread *is* the discussion. The minutes job is to write the **synthesis at the top**. [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- **Use a verbatim quote** in three cases only: [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- **On-the-record dissent** [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- **A specific commitment** [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- **A regulatory / legal trigger** [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- Everywhere else, paraphrase. [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- Significant decisions should be **extracted** into a separate decision log (or ADR file) with a stable ID, indexed, and linked back to the meeting. [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- Michael Nygard's 2011 template: **Title · Status · Context · Decision · Consequences** [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- Status moves through: **proposed → accepted → deprecated → superseded by ADR-NNNN**. ADRs are never deleted or edited substantively after acceptance — they are superseded by a new ADR that links back. [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- Name the dissenter and one-sentence their objection. "Anonymous 'concerns were raised'" is useless and reads as cover. [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- Bad: "We talked about the latency issue for a while." [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- Good: "Decided to roll back the v2.3 caching change; Priya owns rollback PR by Wed." [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- Every bullet should start with a verb of outcome (decided, agreed, deferred, rejected, assigned, scheduled, escalated). [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- Minutes that go out 5 days later are minutes nobody reads. Target: same-day or next-morning. [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- **Attendees:** Name1, Name2, Name3 [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]
- **Absent (invited):** Name4 [src: meeting-minutes-and-decision-log]

- OKRs (Objectives and Key Results) are a goal-setting framework. The form is deceptively simple — one inspirational Objective, three to five measurable Key Results — but most OKRs in the wild are broken. They are project plans wearing OKR clothing. [src: okr-writing]
- The Objective is **qualitative, inspirational, time-bound**. [src: okr-writing]
- Each Key Result is **measurable** — a numerator over a denominator, by a date. [src: okr-writing]
- The KR measures an **outcome** (value delivered), not an **output** (work done) and never an **input** (effort spent). [src: okr-writing]
- Every KR must answer: [src: okr-writing]
- **Numerator** — what is being counted? [src: okr-writing]
- **Denominator** — relative to what? [src: okr-writing]
- **Deadline** — by when? [src: okr-writing]
- **Fails:** "Improve onboarding." (no numerator, no denominator, no deadline) [src: okr-writing]
- **Fails:** "Reach 1000 users." (no denominator, no deadline) [src: okr-writing]
- **Passes:** "Grow week-1 activation rate from 28% to 45% by 2026-09-30." [src: okr-writing]
- **KPI** (Key Performance Indicator) — a steady-state health metric you watch *all the time*. KPIs run forever. [src: okr-writing]
- **OKR** — a change goal for a *bounded period*. Says "we are choosing to push this number from X to Y this quarter." [src: okr-writing]
- **A KPI can become a KR** if you decide to push it — but the KR must specify the from-to delta and the deadline. [src: okr-writing]
- **Input** — effort, headcount, money spent. ("hired 5 engineers") — never a KR. [src: okr-writing]
- **Output** — work produced, artifacts shipped. ("shipped the new dashboard") — almost never a KR. [src: okr-writing]
- **Outcome** — change in the world, value delivered. ("dashboard adoption reached 60% of paying teams") — this is what KRs measure. [src: okr-writing]
- Felipe Castro's "so what?" test: read the KR and ask "so what?" If the answer is another metric (the outcome), the original was an output. [src: okr-writing]
- For **aspirational / stretch** OKRs: [src: okr-writing]
- Pick a target where your confidence of hitting 100% is about **5 out of 10** (50/50 at draft time). [src: okr-writing]
- Score around **0.7** on average at the end of the quarter is healthy. [src: okr-writing]
- Consistently scoring 1.0 means you sandbagged. Scoring < 0.4 means you set fantasy targets. [src: okr-writing]
- For **committed** OKRs (operational must-haves — SLAs, compliance deadlines), the target is 1.0 and anything less is a problem. [src: okr-writing]
- Company sets 3–5 Objectives for the quarter. [src: okr-writing]
- Each team picks ~3 Objectives that contribute to the company set. [src: okr-writing]
- An individual contributor may have 1–2 personal Objectives that map to a team Objective. [src: okr-writing]
- **Key insight:** roughly half of OKRs should be set bottom-up. Pure top-down OKRs kill engagement. [src: okr-writing]
- **Green** — on track, no help needed. [src: okr-writing]
- **Yellow** — at risk, here is what would unblock me. [src: okr-writing]
- **Red** — will not hit current target. Either re-plan or formally revise the KR. [src: okr-writing]
- For each KR, compute the actual / target on its native scale: [src: okr-writing]
- Started at 28%, target 45%, ended at 38%. Progress = (38 − 28) / (45 − 28) = 10/17 ≈ **0.59**. [src: okr-writing]
- **"Ship feature X by date Y"** — that is a task, not a KR. The KR is the *outcome* the feature is supposed to produce. [src: okr-writing]
- **"Do our normal job well"** — operational baselines are KPIs, not OKRs. [src: okr-writing]
- **Activity counts** — "publish 12 blog posts" measures effort, not outcome. [src: okr-writing]
- **Sandbagged targets** — KRs you are 95% confident in. [src: okr-writing]
- **Too many KRs** — more than 5 per Objective is a wishlist. [src: okr-writing]
- **Set-and-forget** — OKRs scored only at quarter end. [src: okr-writing]
- Link: [Move metric X from A to B by DATE] [src: okr-writing]
- Link: [Move metric Y from A to B by DATE] [src: okr-writing]
- Link: [Move metric Z from A to B by DATE] [src: okr-writing]
- John Doerr, [whatmatters.com](https://www.whatmatters.com/faqs/okr-meaning-definition-example) [src: okr-writing]
- Christina Wodtke, [The Art of the OKR](https://cwodtke.com/the-art-of-the-okr/) [src: okr-writing]
- Felipe Castro, "An OKR should measure the outcome, not the work" [src: okr-writing]
- General-purpose professional email writing. Optimized for the 90% of work email that isn't sales, isn't customer support, and isn't an exec announcement. [src: email-craft]
- Two-part structure: `[Topic]: [Purpose]`. The colon does the work. [src: email-craft]
- "Q3 forecast: need your number by Thu noon" [src: email-craft]
- "Onboarding doc: review request (10 min)" [src: email-craft]
- Prefixes: `Action:`, `Decision needed:`, `FYI:`, `Question:`, `Reminder:`, `Intro:`. Avoid `Following up`, `Quick question`. [src: email-craft]
- Length: 2-7 words wins. [src: email-craft]
- The first sentence states the conclusion, the ask, or the decision needed. [src: email-craft]
- Bad:  "Hey, hope you're well. I've been thinking about the Q3 forecast..." [src: email-craft]
- Good: "I need your Q3 forecast number by Thursday noon. Context below." [src: email-craft]
- If the email has two asks, it has zero asks. Split into two emails, each with its own subject line. [src: email-craft]
- Test: can you summarize the ask in one sentence starting with a verb? "Please review X by Friday." [src: email-craft]
- **To**: people who must act or reply. [src: email-craft]
- **Cc**: people who need to be informed but don't owe a reply. Use sparingly. [src: email-craft]
- **Reply-all**: default to No. Only when the answer materially changes what other recipients should do. [src: email-craft]
- Anything you want a searchable, durable record of. [src: email-craft]
- External recipients. [src: email-craft]
- Long-form content (>3 paragraphs). [src: email-craft]
- Anyone whose Slack hours don't overlap yours. [src: email-craft]
- Pick up the phone when: [src: email-craft]
- The topic is emotional, sensitive, or carries firing/conflict/HR risk. [src: email-craft]
- You're on email round 3+ on the same thread without resolution. [src: email-craft]
- Tone-sensitive feedback, layoffs, performance, breakups. [src: email-craft]
- Day 0: original email [src: email-craft]
- Day 3-4: polite nudge, reply on the same thread [src: email-craft]
- Day 7-10: third nudge, change channel [src: email-craft]
- Beyond: stop. The non-answer is the answer. [src: email-craft]
- Subject: Closing the loop on [topic] [src: email-craft]
- Hi [name] — I haven't heard back on this, so I'll assume it's not a [src: email-craft]
- priority right now and stop following up. If that changes, drop me a [src: email-craft]
- line and I'll pick it back up. Thanks for considering it. [src: email-craft]
- Internal, ongoing relationship → send when drafted. [src: email-craft]
- External, senior, or first contact → schedule Tue-Thu 10am recipient-local. [src: email-craft]
- Drafted after 9pm → always schedule for 9am next workday. [src: email-craft]
- A good signature is 4 lines or fewer: [src: email-craft]
- Company  |  Phone (if relevant) [src: email-craft]
- **Clear.** Can the reader understand the message on a single read? [src: email-craft]
- **Concise.** Is every sentence earning its place? [src: email-craft]
- **Complete.** Does the email contain everything the reader needs to act? [src: email-craft]
- **Correct.** Spelling, grammar, names, titles, numbers, dates, attachments. [src: email-craft]
- **Courteous.** Is the tone proportionate to the relationship and the stakes? [src: email-craft]
- **The five things to never write:** [src: email-craft]
- "Please be patient." [src: email-craft]
- "We apologize for any inconvenience this may have caused." [src: email-craft]
- "Per my last email..." / "As I mentioned..." [src: email-craft]
- "Unfortunately..." [src: email-craft]
- "This is a known issue." (without immediately following it with a workaround) [src: email-craft]
- Subject: [Topic]: [verb] needed by [date] [src: email-craft]
- I need [the specific thing] by [date/time]. Here's the context: [1-3 [src: email-craft]
- sentences max]. Reply with [the shape of the answer you need]. [src: email-craft]
- Subject: Closing the loop on [topic] [src: email-craft]
- Hi [name] — I haven't heard back, so I'll assume [topic] isn't a fit [src: email-craft]
- right now and stop following up. If that changes, just drop me a [src: email-craft]
- line. Appreciate you considering it. [src: email-craft]
- **The wall of text** — five paragraphs, no whitespace, no BLUF. [src: email-craft]
- **The hidden ask** — buried in paragraph 4. [src: email-craft]
- **Reply-all "thanks!"** — multiplies inbox noise by N for zero value. [src: email-craft]
- **The midnight send** — signals burnout culture. Schedule for next morning. [src: email-craft]
- **Bcc'ing the boss as surveillance** — corrosive, almost always discovered. [src: email-craft]
- Link: [Harvard Business Review — 5 Tips for Writing Professional Emails (2022)](https://hbr.org/2022/08/5-tips-for-writing-professional-emails) [src: email-craft]
- Link: [The Essential Guide to Crafting a Work Email — HBR (2015)](https://hbr.org/2015/07/the-essential-guide-to-crafting-a-work-email) [src: email-craft]
- One-pagers are the highest-impact document format in business: a single page that earns a meeting, secures a budget, aligns a partner, or briefs an exec in under three minutes. [src: one-pager-writing]
- A one-pager fits on one page. The moment you flow to page 2, the document is now a half-finished two-pager. Everything else in this skill exists to enforce this rule. [src: one-pager-writing]
- Cut by 30-50% from your first draft. Always. [src: one-pager-writing]
- Drop full sentences for fragments where fragments work. [src: one-pager-writing]
- Move evidence to an appendix link, not a footer. [src: one-pager-writing]
- If three things won't fit, you have three things — not one. [src: one-pager-writing]
- The reader scans before they read. What lives above the fold: [src: one-pager-writing]
- **Headline** — the one-line value prop, written in the reader's language. [src: one-pager-writing]
- **Subhead or value-prop sentence** — what changes for the reader if they say yes. [src: one-pager-writing]
- **The "if you only read one line" sentence** — bolded, set off visually. [src: one-pager-writing]
- **A visual anchor** — chart, screenshot, diagram, photo, or large pull-quote. [src: one-pager-writing]
- Every one-pager has one sentence the reader must take away. Find it. Bold it. Place it above the fold. Repeat it in different words at the end. [src: one-pager-writing]
- Bad:  "Our new initiative aims to improve customer engagement [src: one-pager-writing]
- through innovative cross-functional collaboration." [src: one-pager-writing]
- Good: "Cutting onboarding from 12 days to 3 will unlock $2.4M in [src: one-pager-writing]
- Year 1 retention. We need $180K and 2 engineers for 6 weeks." [src: one-pager-writing]
- Headline:    Atlas Migration Acceleration Program [src: one-pager-writing]
- Value prop:  Cut customer migration time from 90 days to 30, [src: one-pager-writing]
- at no incremental cost to your team. [src: one-pager-writing]
- The Amazon 1-pager / PR-style opener: [src: one-pager-writing]
- **Heading**: the product or initiative name. [src: one-pager-writing]
- **Subheading**: who it's for, in their language. [src: one-pager-writing]
- **Summary paragraph (3-4 sentences)**: what it does, who benefits, why now. [src: one-pager-writing]
- **Problem paragraph**: the customer's status quo. [src: one-pager-writing]
- **Solution paragraph**: how this changes the status quo. [src: one-pager-writing]
- **Quote (optional)**: an executive or customer making the value claim concrete. [src: one-pager-writing]
- **Call to action**: what the reader does next. [src: one-pager-writing]
- Two non-negotiables: written as full sentences; written as if the product already launched. [src: one-pager-writing]
- **Use paragraphs when:** The reader needs to see how ideas connect; describing a customer's strategic status quo; Amazon 1-pager opener. [src: one-pager-writing]
- **Use bullets when:** Listing 3-7 parallel items; scannable facts; the reader is an exec who triages. [src: one-pager-writing]
- Heuristic: paragraphs for the upper half (the narrative), bullets for the lower half (the facts and the ask). [src: one-pager-writing]
- A single page gives you roughly 550-650 words of usable real estate: [src: one-pager-writing]
- **Headline + value prop**: 20-30 words [src: one-pager-writing]
- **Above-the-fold callout**: 15-25 words [src: one-pager-writing]
- **Body — problem / context**: 80-120 words [src: one-pager-writing]
- **Body — solution / approach**: 100-150 words [src: one-pager-writing]
- **Body — outcomes / proof**: 80-120 words [src: one-pager-writing]
- **The ask**: 30-50 words [src: one-pager-writing]
- **Account brief** — for an internal audience to brief before a customer meeting. [src: one-pager-writing]
- **Project pitch** — to get funding or headcount. [src: one-pager-writing]
- **Product one-pager** — for stakeholders evaluating a product. [src: one-pager-writing]
- **Sales-enablement one-pager** — for sellers to use in front of buyers. [src: one-pager-writing]
- **Amazon 1-pager / PR-FAQ opener** — for internal alignment on a new product. [src: one-pager-writing]
- Every one-pager ends with: [src: one-pager-writing]
- **The ask** — what specific thing do you need from the reader. A verb with an object. [src: one-pager-writing]
- **The owner** — who runs this, with name, role, contact. [src: one-pager-writing]
- **The next step** — when, where, what format. [src: one-pager-writing]
- These three sentences are the entire reason the one-pager exists. Never cut these. [src: one-pager-writing]
- ARR: $X.XM  •  Renewal: [date]  •  Owner: [name] [src: one-pager-writing]
- ONE-LINE STATUS  >>>  [Account] is at [color/state] heading into [event]. [src: one-pager-writing]
- The single most important thing is [X]. [src: one-pager-writing]
- TOP 3 RISKS                        TOP 3 OPPORTUNITIES [src: one-pager-writing]
- Link: [risk]                          1. [opp] [src: one-pager-writing]
- Link: [risk]                          2. [opp] [src: one-pager-writing]
- What we need from [reader]: [one-sentence verb-object ask]. [src: one-pager-writing]
- **The 1.5-pager** — runs onto a second page by half a paragraph. [src: one-pager-writing]
- **The mystery headline** — "Project Phoenix: A New Approach." No value visible. [src: one-pager-writing]
- **The ask buried at line 47** — the ask should be visible above the fold. [src: one-pager-writing]
- **The "alignment" ask** — "We're seeking alignment on..." No verb, no object. [src: one-pager-writing]
- **The missing owner line** — the page is anonymous. [src: one-pager-writing]
- **The four-CTA ending** — list more than two CTAs and readers pick zero. [src: one-pager-writing]

- A writer's distinctive voice is the residue of their judgment. An LLM, trained on the global mean of internet prose, regresses toward that mean. The collaboration mode this skill defends keeps the human responsible for voice and uses AI for tasks where the mean is fine (mechanics, structure, length compression, format conversion). [src: ai-collaboration-writing]
- LLMs default to five patterns: [src: ai-collaboration-writing]
- **Hedging.** "It's worth noting that…" [src: ai-collaboration-writing]
- **Triadic rhythm.** Three-item lists replace one strong word. [src: ai-collaboration-writing]
- **Topic-sentence tax.** Every paragraph opens with a meta-sentence. [src: ai-collaboration-writing]
- **Latinate verbs.** "Utilize," "facilitate," "leverage." [src: ai-collaboration-writing]
- **Bridge phrases.** "Furthermore," "moreover." [src: ai-collaboration-writing]
- delve, leverage, robust, paradigm, seamless, utilize, commence, facilitate, furthermore, navigate, landscape, cutting-edge, holistic, ecosystem, harness (verb), foster (verb) [src: ai-collaboration-writing]
- Reference for writing content that is usable by screen-reader users, low-vision users, deaf and hard-of-hearing users, users with cognitive disabilities, and users on assistive tech. [src: accessibility-writing]
- **Headings form a proper outline.** Exactly one `<h1>` per page. No skipped levels. [src: accessibility-writing]
- **Every image has an alt attribute.** Decorative images use `alt=""`. Informative images get a 1–2 sentence description. [src: accessibility-writing]
- **Every link reads as a self-contained label.** "Click here," "read more," "learn more," and bare URLs fail. [src: accessibility-writing]
- **Every form control has a programmatically associated label.** `<label for>` matched to input `id`. [src: accessibility-writing]
- **Every icon-only button has an accessible name.** `aria-label` describing the action ("Close dialog," not "X icon"). [src: accessibility-writing]
- **Information is never conveyed by color alone.** Status indicated by "Error: …" prefix or icon plus color. [src: accessibility-writing]
- **The page declares its language.** `<html lang="en">`. [src: accessibility-writing]
- **Time-based media has alternatives.** Video has synchronized captions and a transcript. [src: accessibility-writing]
- **Decorative images** — `alt=""` (empty, not missing). [src: accessibility-writing]
- **Informative images** — describe the information the image carries: [src: accessibility-writing]
- `alt="CPU usage spikes to 95% at 14:30 UTC then returns to baseline by 14:35."` [src: accessibility-writing]
- **Functional images** — describe the action or destination: [src: accessibility-writing]
- `alt="View cart"` (NOT `alt="shopping cart icon"`) [src: accessibility-writing]
- **Complex images** — short alt plus a long description: [src: accessibility-writing]
- `alt="Latency percentile chart for production over the past 24 hours."` [src: accessibility-writing]
- Plus `aria-describedby` pointing to a `<figcaption>` with full details. [src: accessibility-writing]
- **One `<h1>` per page.** The page title. [src: accessibility-writing]
- **No skipped levels going down.** After `<h2>` you may use another `<h2>` or an `<h3>`. You may not jump to `<h5>`. [src: accessibility-writing]
- **Headings are not for styling.** Don't use `<h3>` because it looks right. [src: accessibility-writing]
- **Descriptive headings.** "Introduction" fails WCAG 2.4.6. "How to reset your password" passes. [src: accessibility-writing]
- Don't include the word "link" in link text. Screen readers already announce that an element is a link. [src: accessibility-writing]
- For downloadable files, include the file format: `Download the Q1 incident report (PDF, 1.2 MB)`. [src: accessibility-writing]
- **`<label for>` matched to input `id`.** The most robust. [src: accessibility-writing]
- **Wrapped `<label>`.** Works without explicit `for`/`id`. [src: accessibility-writing]
- **`aria-labelledby` pointing at a visible element.** [src: accessibility-writing]
- **`aria-label`.** Last resort only when no visible label is possible. [src: accessibility-writing]
- <button aria-label="Close dialog"> [src: accessibility-writing]
- <svg aria-hidden="true"><!-- X icon --></svg> [src: accessibility-writing]
- The `aria-label` describes what the button does ("Close dialog," "Search," "Open menu"). NOT what it looks like ("X," "Magnifying glass"). [src: accessibility-writing]
- **Status with a prefix word.** "Error: Email is invalid." "Warning: Unsaved changes." [src: accessibility-writing]
- **Status with an icon plus color.** A red X icon plus the word "Failed." [src: accessibility-writing]
- **Links underlined as well as colored.** [src: accessibility-writing]
- **1.2.2 Captions (prerecorded), Level A.** Synchronized captions for prerecorded video with audio. [src: accessibility-writing]
- **1.2.4 Captions (live), Level AA.** Live captions for live audio. [src: accessibility-writing]
- **1.2.5 Audio description (prerecorded), Level AA.** Audio description of prerecorded video. [src: accessibility-writing]
- <p>The French phrase <span lang="fr">tour de force</span> means "feat of strength."</p> [src: accessibility-writing]
- <a href="#main" class="skip-link">Skip to main content</a> [src: accessibility-writing]
- <main id="main">...</main> [src: accessibility-writing]
- The skip link is the **first focusable element** on the page. [src: accessibility-writing]
- It is **visually hidden until focused.** [src: accessibility-writing]
- W3C WCAG 2.2: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref/ [src: accessibility-writing]
- W3C, *Alternative Text Tutorial*: https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/ [src: accessibility-writing]
- W3C, *Labeling Controls Tutorial*: https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/forms/labels/ [src: accessibility-writing]
- WebAIM, *Creating Accessible Forms*: https://webaim.org/techniques/forms/advanced [src: accessibility-writing]
- The A11y Project, *Patterns*: https://www.a11yproject.com/patterns/ [src: accessibility-writing]

- Reference for writing source-language strings that translate cleanly into 30+ locales. [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- Every translation operation needs three freedoms: [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **Reorder** — subject-verb-object in English is not subject-verb-object in Japanese or German. [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **Expand** — German, Russian, Finnish run 30–40% longer than English. [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **Replace** — Plural forms, gendered forms, formal/informal address. [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **One sentence, one idea.** Compound sentences with subordinate clauses become unparseable in OV languages. [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **Subject-verb-object, in that order.** [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **No idioms.** "Hit the ground running" has no German equivalent. [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **No metaphors.** "Move the needle" requires a needle, which requires a gauge, which requires the metaphor to land. [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **No cultural references.** No baseball, no Thanksgiving, no Marvel cinematic universe. [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **Avoid humour and wordplay.** Puns are untranslatable by definition. [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **No abbreviations the reader must decode.** "Q1," "EOY," "ASAP" — spell them out at first use. [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **No phrasal verbs where a single verb works.** "Set up the account" becomes "create the account." [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **No latinate jargon.** "Utilize" → "use." "Initiate" → "start." [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **Active voice as the default.** [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **Common mistake — only English plural categories:** [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- This works for English. It silently breaks Russian, Polish, Arabic. [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **`other` is required.** Every plural block must include `other`. [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **`select`** is a switch over a string variable, typically used for gender: [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- female {She updated her profile.} [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- male {He updated his profile.} [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- other {They updated their profile.} [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- `other` is required even in `select`. [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **Use named placeholders, not positional.** `{username}` survives word reorder. `%s %s` does not. [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **Never concatenate.** `"Hello, " + username + "!"` forces English word order. [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **Always provide a comment describing the placeholder.** [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **Concatenation anti-pattern:** [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- const msg = t('error.prefix') + ' ' + filename + ' ' + t('error.suffix'); [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- const msg = t('error.full', { filename }); [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- // strings.en.json: { "error.full": "Could not save file {filename}." } [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- Every non-trivial string gets a translator comment answering: [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **What is this?** UI element type (button, error, tooltip, heading). [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **What does the placeholder mean?** `{count}` = unread messages, integer ≥ 0. [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **Where does it appear?** [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- Pseudo-localization is a smoke test that runs before any human translator sees the strings. It: [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **Expands every string 30–40%** to surface truncation bugs [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **Replaces ASCII characters with accented Latin equivalents** [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **Wraps every string with sentinels** like `[!! … !!]` to surface un-extracted strings [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **Avoid baked-in directional assumptions.** "Click the arrow on the right" becomes wrong in Arabic. Prefer "Click the arrow next to the search box." [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **Numbers stay LTR inside RTL text.** This is automatic in Unicode bidi. [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- GOOD (semantic, namespaced): [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- settings.security.two_factor.toggle [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- errors.network.timeout.body [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- BAD (content-derived, fragile): [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- "Save changes"           # key changes every time copy changes [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- "msg1", "label2"          # opaque [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **The key describes the role, not the content.** [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **Namespace by feature, then by sub-feature.** [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- **Don't bury locale in the key.** [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- Unicode CLDR: [Plural Rules](https://cldr.unicode.org/index/cldr-spec/plural-rules) [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- ICU: [Formatting Messages](https://unicode-org.github.io/icu/userguide/format_parse/messages/) [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- Mozilla L10n: [Best practices for developers](https://mozilla-l10n.github.io/documentation/localization/dev_best_practices.html) [src: localization-friendly-writing]
- Reference for writing that will be heard, not read. The eye can re-scan a sentence; the ear gets one pass. [src: audio-script-writing]
- Listeners process roughly **150–160 words per minute** for narration, **130–145 wpm** for voice-UI prompts, and **110–125 wpm** for IVR. They lose comprehension on: [src: audio-script-writing]
- Subordinate clauses stacked more than one deep [src: audio-script-writing]
- Parentheticals (the ear has no parens) [src: audio-script-writing]
- Lists longer than three items without explicit numbering [src: audio-script-writing]
- Numbers and proper nouns delivered without a beat of silence after [src: audio-script-writing]
- **Eye version (fine on the page):** [src: audio-script-writing]
- > The migration, which we'd been planning since February, finally launched on Tuesday after a final round of testing that revealed two minor bugs we patched overnight. [src: audio-script-writing]
- > We'd been planning the migration since February. It finally launched on Tuesday. The last round of testing turned up two small bugs. We patched them overnight. [src: audio-script-writing]
- **Signpost vocabulary:** [src: audio-script-writing]
- **First / second / third / finally** — explicit numbering [src: audio-script-writing]
- **Here's the thing** — flag a key insight [src: audio-script-writing]
- **Two reasons** — set up a numbered list [src: audio-script-writing]
- **Coming up** — preview before an ad break [src: audio-script-writing]
- **Back to the story** — return marker after a digression [src: audio-script-writing]
- Before: "The team (which had only formed in January) shipped on time." [src: audio-script-writing]
- After: "The team shipped on time. They'd only formed in January." [src: audio-script-writing]
- Three patterns that work: [src: audio-script-writing]
- **Pattern A — Drop into a scene:** [src: audio-script-writing]
- > It's 2 a.m. The paging system goes off. Marcus rolls over, reads the alert, and the alert is wrong. [src: audio-script-writing]
- **Pattern B — A question with stakes:** [src: audio-script-writing]
- > What would you do if your entire backup tier disappeared in the middle of a restore? [src: audio-script-writing]
- **Pattern C — A single startling fact:** [src: audio-script-writing]
- > Last year, 47% of incident retrospectives never produced a single action item. [src: audio-script-writing]
- **Anti-pattern — The throat-clear:** [src: audio-script-writing]
- > Hi everyone, welcome to the podcast. Today we're going to be talking about... [src: audio-script-writing]
- Three constraints beyond "writing for the ear": [src: audio-script-writing]
- **The prompt must end with an explicit prompt-for-input.** [src: audio-script-writing]
- **Confirm without echoing.** "Adding milk to your list" is good; "I heard you say milk; I will now add milk to your list" is voice-UI throat-clearing. [src: audio-script-writing]
- **Three-option ceiling.** Lists of more than three options exceed working memory. [src: audio-script-writing]
- **Most-likely path first.** Order by call-volume share, not alphabetical. [src: audio-script-writing]
- **Always offer a human escape.** "Press 0 at any time to reach an agent." [src: audio-script-writing]
- **Confirm critical inputs.** Read back at the cadence a person can write down. [src: audio-script-writing]
- **Re-prompt twice, then escalate.** Caller silence twice in a row = route to agent. [src: audio-script-writing]
- **Required sections:** [src: audio-script-writing]
- Episode title — keep under 60 characters; concrete, specific [src: audio-script-writing]
- One-paragraph summary — 50–80 words; uses the episode keyword once [src: audio-script-writing]
- Chapter timestamps — 4–8 chapters; `[12:15] How to find your first sponsor` [src: audio-script-writing]
- Guest bio — 1 paragraph, links to guest sites [src: audio-script-writing]
- Mentioned resources — every link spoken aloud [src: audio-script-writing]
- Transcript — full or summary [src: audio-script-writing]
- Call to action [src: audio-script-writing]
- NPR Training: "How to write a mean script" [src: audio-script-writing]
- Google: Conversation Design [src: audio-script-writing]
- Amazon: Alexa Design Guide [src: audio-script-writing]
- Buzzsprout: "How to Write Podcast Show Notes" [src: audio-script-writing]
- Reference for the words that ship with images, charts, and infographics: alt text, captions, chart titles, axis labels, and annotations. The image is half the message. This skill is the other half. [src: visual-writing]
- Every other rule in this skill follows from one premise: a reader who cannot see the image must still receive the load-bearing information. That reader may be a blind user with a screen reader, a sighted user on a slow network, a sighted user skimming for the chart's takeaway, or a search engine indexing the page. [src: visual-writing]
- **The alt text serves the screen reader.** [src: visual-writing]
- **The caption serves the skimmer.** [src: visual-writing]
- **The chart title serves the takeaway.** [src: visual-writing]
- **The annotation serves the trend.** [src: visual-writing]
- They are four jobs, not one. [src: visual-writing]
- Alt text answers three questions: [src: visual-writing]
- **What's there?** — concrete, observable content [src: visual-writing]
- **Why is it there?** — the function the image serves in the page [src: visual-writing]
- **What does it show?** — the specific information a sighted reader gets [src: visual-writing]
- **Alt text** is for users who cannot see the image. It lives in `alt=""`. Typically 5 to 15 words. [src: visual-writing]
- **Caption** is visible to everyone. It lives in `<figcaption>`. Adds context, attribution. [src: visual-writing]
- **Long description** is a structured prose alternative for complex images. [src: visual-writing]
- **Anti-pattern: duplication.** If `alt="Sales rose 18% in Q4"` and the caption reads the same, the screen-reader user hears it twice. [src: visual-writing]
- **Above all else, show the data.** Title and labels exist to disclose the data. [src: visual-writing]
- **Maximize the data-ink ratio.** Erase ink that doesn't carry data. [src: visual-writing]
- **Erase redundant data-ink.** A bar chart with a legend, title, axis labels, and a redundant data table embeds the same fact four times. [src: visual-writing]
- **Reject chartjunk.** Heavy gridlines, moiré fills, 3-D effects, drop shadows. [src: visual-writing]
- **Use sparklines for in-line trend.** Caption a sparkline like a word — usually with just the latest value. [src: visual-writing]
- The chart title states the takeaway. The axis labels confirm it. [src: visual-writing]
- **Generic title (descriptive only):** [src: visual-writing]
- > Quarterly Revenue, 2023–2024 [src: visual-writing]
- **Action title (takeaway-bearing):** [src: visual-writing]
- > Q4 2024 revenue exceeded plan by 18% — the strongest quarter on record [src: visual-writing]
- **Rule of thumb: no chart without a takeaway.** If you cannot state in one sentence what the chart is for, either find the takeaway or delete the chart. [src: visual-writing]
- **Label the units.** "Revenue (USD millions)" not "Revenue." [src: visual-writing]
- **Date axes get human dates.** "Jan 2024" — not raw timestamps, not "Q1". [src: visual-writing]
- **Avoid axis label rotation.** If labels overflow horizontally, the chart probably has too many categories. [src: visual-writing]
- An annotation is a written assertion attached to a specific data point. Use annotations for: [src: visual-writing]
- The single highest or lowest point ("**peak: 8,420 — Aug 14**") [src: visual-writing]
- A regime change ("← deploy of v2.3") [src: visual-writing]
- An anomaly ("backfill artifact; ignore") [src: visual-writing]
- **Annotations are journalism inside a chart.** Empty annotations ("note this") are wasted ink. [src: visual-writing]
- The "describe the trend, then the value" pattern: [src: visual-writing]
- > Sales increased steadily from January to July, then declined through December. The peak was 8,420 units in July. The lowest month was December at 3,100 units. [src: visual-writing]
- **Anti-pattern: read every value.** [src: visual-writing]
- > January was 4,200, February was 4,800, March was 5,100... [src: visual-writing]
- If every value matters, provide a `<table>` and skip the chart alt-text recital. [src: visual-writing]
- "Line chart: API latency rose steadily from May to August, peaking at 480 ms [src: visual-writing]
- on Aug 14, then dropped back to 140 ms after the Aug 22 deploy." [src: visual-writing]
- "Bar chart: Q4 2024 revenue exceeded plan by 18% — the strongest quarter on record." [src: visual-writing]
- W3C WAI: [Images Tutorial](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/) and [Alt Decision Tree](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/decision-tree/) [src: visual-writing]
- Edward Tufte, *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information* (2nd ed., 2001) [src: visual-writing]
- Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic, *Storytelling with Data* (2015) [src: visual-writing]
- UK GDS: [Text descriptions for data visualisations](https://accessibility.blog.gov.uk/2023/04/13/text-descriptions-for-data-visualisations/) [src: visual-writing]
- WCAG 2.1, Success Criterion 1.1.1 (Non-text Content) [src: visual-writing]
- Reference for conversion-focused writing: landing pages, emails, ads, CTAs, and positioning copy. Sources: Schwartz *Breakthrough Advertising* (1966), Ogilvy *Confessions of an Advertising Man*, Sugarman *The Adweek Copywriting Handbook*, Cialdini *Influence*, Halbert/Carlton copy classics. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- When invoked, follow this sequence before producing any copy: [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- **Identify the awareness stage** (Section 2) of the target audience. If unclear, ask: "Who is the primary reader — do they already know they have this problem, or are they discovering it for the first time?" [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- **Identify the conversion goal** — one goal per piece (landing page demo request, email reply, ad click). If multiple goals are stated, flag the conflict and recommend choosing one. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- **Choose the framework** — AIDA for structured persuasion flows; PAS for pain-first framing; headline formulas for ad/email entry points. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- **Produce copy or a skeleton** — for pages, produce a full section-by-section skeleton with placeholder copy and notes on what each section must accomplish. For emails, produce a complete draft. For subject lines or CTAs, produce 3–5 options with rationale. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- When the request is ambiguous, ask one targeted question before producing copy. Do not ask more than one question per turn. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- -- [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- The foundational direct-response sequence. Each stage earns permission to proceed to the next. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- **Practical note:** AIDA is a *reader state* sequence, not a section-by-section template. A long-form sales page may cycle through the sequence multiple times before the final CTA. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- -- [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Pain-first frame. Effective when the audience already feels the problem but has not connected it to your solution. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- **Problem** — Name the problem precisely. Specificity signals that you understand the reader's world. ("Your email open rates dropped 40% after iOS 15.") [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- **Agitate** — Deepen the pain. Enumerate the downstream costs: lost revenue, wasted time, damaged relationships, compounding risk. Do not manufacture fear; surface consequences the reader already suspects but has not named. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- **Solve** — Present your product/service as the clear, logical resolution. The transition from agitation to solution should feel like relief. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- **Schwartz warning:** Agitation without a credible solve creates distrust, not conversion. Match the intensity of the pain to the scale of the promised solution. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- -- [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Eugene Schwartz (*Breakthrough Advertising*, 1966) argues that the right hook strategy is determined by the reader's current awareness stage, not by your product's features. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- **Application rule:** Before writing the first word, identify the awareness stage of the majority of your traffic. Mismatching stage is the most common structural error — writing a Stage 5 headline to a Stage 1 audience destroys conversion. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- **Hook examples by stage:** [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Stage 1: *"Most founders never find out why their second round fell apart."* [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Stage 2: Name the problem so precisely that the reader thinks you're describing them personally. This is where PAS is most powerful. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Stage 3: Focus on mechanism — *how* your approach solves the problem differently. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Stage 4: Lead with the strongest proof element: case study, guarantee, or removed objection. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Stage 5: The headline can be as direct as *"$97. Full access. Cancel anytime."* [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- -- [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Every landing page should have exactly one conversion goal. A page that asks for a demo, a newsletter signup, and a download forces readers to make three decisions. Each additional ask reduces the probability of any one of them happening. (Cialdini: reducing choice reduces decision fatigue and increases compliance.) [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Everything visible before the scroll must resolve the reader's first question: *"Is this for me, and is it worth my time?"* [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Headline          — The single biggest benefit or the sharpest problem [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Subheadline       — Expand the headline; add specificity or credibility [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Value proposition — 2–4 bullets: outcomes, not features [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- CTA (primary)     — One button, imperative verb + outcome [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Social proof      — Logo row or a single killer testimonial with attribution [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- **Order is load-bearing.** A credible headline buys attention for the subhead. The subhead earns the scroll. Moving social proof above the value prop can work for high-awareness audiences (Stage 4–5) but confuses Stage 2–3 readers who don't yet trust the frame. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- For long-form pages (SaaS, high-ticket services): [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Problem section (PAS agitation) [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Mechanism — how it works, at a level that builds confidence without overwhelming [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Proof — case studies with concrete numbers, not adjectives [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Objection handling — address the two or three real objections; ignoring them does not make them disappear [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Offer summary — restate what they get, at what price, by when [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Risk reversal — guarantee, trial period, cancellation policy [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Final CTA — repeat the primary action; do not introduce a new ask [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- -- [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Hard limit: 50 characters (preview pane + mobile). Aim for 35–45. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- The subject line's only job is to earn the open. It does not summarize the email. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Preview text is the second subject line. Write it intentionally; do not let it default to "View in browser." [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- **Anti-pattern:** Question marks and exclamation points in the same subject line signal desperation. Choose one device per subject line. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- -- [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Effective cold email is not about your product. It is about the reader's problem. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Sentence 1 (Problem + context): One observation about a specific problem [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- the prospect has, grounded in their world. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Sentence 2 (Proof + relevance): One concrete result you produced for [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- a comparable company or situation. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Sentence 3 (Ask):               A single, low-friction next step — [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- never a demo request in the first touch. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- > Noticed your support team is using Zendesk for internal escalations — most teams outgrow that setup around 50 agents and end up with duplicated tickets. We helped [Competitor] cut internal escalation time by 40% in six weeks. Would a 10-minute breakdown of how they did it be useful? [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Goal: advance the reader through the awareness funnel over multiple touches. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Lead with a piece of value (insight, framework, short case study) before the soft ask [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Each email has one topic and one CTA [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- The CTA should be a micro-commitment that naturally precedes the macro-commitment (read this → watch this → book this) [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Sent after 3–4 unresponded touches. The breakup email often has the highest reply rate of the sequence. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Subject: Should I close your file? [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Acknowledge the silence without blame. Offer an easy "no." [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Optionally provide one last piece of value or alternative resource. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Make the opt-out frictionless. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- > Haven't heard back, so I'll assume the timing isn't right — no problem at all. If that changes, you know where to find us. In the meantime, [resource link] might be useful. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- -- [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- **Ogilvy rule:** "On the average, five times as many people read the headline as read the body copy." Test headlines first. The body copy is irrelevant if the headline loses the reader. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- -- [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- First-person phrasing ("Get my..." vs. "Get your...") consistently outperforms second-person in A/B tests — Joanna Wiebe (Copyhackers) research finding. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Every CTA should resolve the reader's micro-anxiety: *What happens when I click this?* The button label answers that question. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- One primary CTA per section. A secondary CTA (e.g., "or schedule a demo") can exist but must be visually subordinate. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- -- [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- > "Great product, highly recommend." — Sarah K. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- > "We reduced customer churn by 18% in the first quarter after switching. The reporting alone saved my team four hours a week." — Sarah Kim, Head of Customer Success, Lattice (500-person SaaS) [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Full name (not initials — initials signal invented testimonials) [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Title and company (establishes that this person is comparable to your target reader) [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Concrete result (number or time frame — adjectives are not proof) [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Photo where possible (Cialdini: liking and social proof compound when the face is visible) [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- **Placement:** Put the most powerful testimonial directly below the CTA on the above-the-fold section, or immediately after the price on a sales page (addresses the highest-anxiety moment). [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- -- [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Present the highest tier or full price before the discounted or monthly price. The first number sets the psychological anchor. Reversing the order (low-to-high) makes the high price feel punitive. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Legitimate urgency: a real deadline (cohort close date, founding pricing end, capacity limit). Manufactured urgency ("Offer expires in 24 hours!" on a page that resets every 24 hours) erodes trust on subsequent visits and signals that no urgency actually exists. Ogilvy: "The consumer is not a moron; she is your wife." [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Every product sells by resolving a tension between what readers fear, what they hope for, and what they dream about. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- -- [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Informal contractions, sentence fragments, and em-dashes are grammatically incorrect and often right for sales copy: [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- "We don't do six-month contracts. Ever." (fragment — emphasis) [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- "You're not behind. You're just early." (contraction — warmth) [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- "The result: a 3x lift in qualified pipeline, in week two." (colon + comma instead of double em-dash — same pace, lower punctuation density) [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Rules for breaking rules: [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- The break must serve the voice, not mask weak thinking. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Every fragment must be intentional, not an error of omission. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Fragments are stronger when followed by a complete sentence that pays them off. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]
- Domain jargon is appropriate for Stage 4–5 copy (product-aware audiences) and creates in-group recognition. It is alienating in Stage 1–2 copy where the goal is connection with a reader who may not yet know the category. [src: sales-and-marketing-copy]

- Reference for drafting legal-adjacent prose that will go to counsel: contracts, disclaimers, privacy notices, breach disclosures, and regulator-facing statements. This skill is **craft for drafts**, not legal advice. Every output should carry a "counsel must review before execution" footer. [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- **Is the risk-allocating verb correct?** "Shall," "will," "must," and "may" are not synonyms. Modern drafting prefers "must" over "shall" because "shall" has been litigated into ambiguity. [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- **Are the defined terms actually defined?** Every Capitalized Term should appear once in a Definitions section. [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- **Does the carve-out language survive a hostile read?** "Except for" should be paired with a non-exhaustive list ("including but not limited to") only when you want breadth. [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- **Is the temporal scope explicit?** "In the 12 months preceding the event giving rise to the claim" is unambiguous. "In the prior year" is ambiguous. [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- **Is the notice-and-cure mechanism workable?** If a clause requires "written notice," specify the delivery channel, the recipient, and the cure window. [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- **Cap amount.** Most common SaaS form: "fees paid by Customer in the 12 months preceding the event." [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- **Damages exclusion.** "No indirect, incidental, special, consequential, or punitive damages, including lost profits." [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- **Carve-outs.** Standard market carve-outs: breach of confidentiality, breach of IP indemnification, payment obligations, gross negligence, willful misconduct, death or personal injury. [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- The standard pattern: [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- EXCEPT AS EXPRESSLY SET FORTH IN THIS AGREEMENT, THE SERVICES ARE PROVIDED "AS IS" [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- AND "AS AVAILABLE," AND PROVIDER MAKES NO REPRESENTATIONS OR WARRANTIES OF ANY KIND, [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- WHETHER EXPRESS, IMPLIED, STATUTORY, OR OTHERWISE, INCLUDING WITHOUT LIMITATION ANY [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- WARRANTIES OF MERCHANTABILITY, FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR PURPOSE, TITLE, AND [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- The all-caps formatting is not stylistic. It is a UCC § 2-316 "conspicuousness" requirement. [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- The SEC's 2023 cybersecurity rules require public companies to file a Form 8-K within **four business days** of determining that a cybersecurity incident is **material**. [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- What must be disclosed: [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- The **material aspects** of the nature, scope, and timing of the incident [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- The **material impact** or reasonably likely material impact on the registrant [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- **What is NOT required:** specific technical detail about the attack vector, specific detail about cybersecurity systems, or any detail that would impede ongoing remediation. [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- GDPR Article 33 requires controllers to notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach "without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it." [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- **Phased notification is explicitly permitted.** Article 33(4) allows you to provide information "in phases without undue further delay." [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- The notification must include: [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- Nature of the breach [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- Name and contact details of the DPO [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- Likely consequences of the breach [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- Measures taken or proposed [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- Required components under GDPR Article 13/14: [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- Identity and contact details of the controller [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- Purposes of processing and legal basis for each [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- Recipients or categories of recipients [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- Storage period or criteria [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- Data subject rights [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- Right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- LIMITATION OF LIABILITY. [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- (a) Excluded Damages. EXCEPT FOR EXCLUDED CLAIMS, IN NO EVENT WILL EITHER PARTY BE [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- LIABLE FOR ANY INDIRECT, INCIDENTAL, SPECIAL, CONSEQUENTIAL, OR PUNITIVE DAMAGES. [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- (b) Liability Cap. EXCEPT FOR EXCLUDED CLAIMS, EACH PARTY'S TOTAL CUMULATIVE [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- LIABILITY WILL NOT EXCEED THE TOTAL FEES PAID OR PAYABLE BY CUSTOMER IN THE [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- TWELVE (12) MONTHS PRECEDING THE EVENT GIVING RISE TO THE CLAIM. [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- (c) Excluded Claims. "Excluded Claims" means: (i) either party's indemnification [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- obligations; (ii) breach of confidentiality obligations; (iii) Customer's payment [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- obligations; (iv) either party's gross negligence, willful misconduct, or fraud. [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- **Mixing "shall" and "must" within the same document.** Pick one register. [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- **The "reasonable" undefined.** "Commercially reasonable" should be defined or paired with a benchmark. [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- **Non-conspicuous warranty disclaimers.** A disclaimer that is not in all caps may be ignored under UCC § 2-316. [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- **Promising what you can't deliver in a privacy notice.** "We will never share your data with anyone" creates a contractual representation. [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- **Stuffing technical detail into an 8-K cyber disclosure.** Describe impact, not mechanism. [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- > This is draft language only. It is not legal advice. Qualified counsel must review before execution, filing, or public release. [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- SEC, *Cybersecurity Risk Management, Strategy, Governance, and Incident Disclosure* (Form 8-K Item 1.05 final rule, effective Dec 18, 2023) [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- UK ICO, *Personal data breaches: A guide* [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- GDPR Article 33 and 34 [src: legal-adjacent-writing]
- UCC § 2-316 (conspicuous disclaimer of implied warranties) [src: legal-adjacent-writing]

- You are an expert release-notes and changelog author. You apply Keep a Changelog spec, semver communication obligations, and audience-aware tone to produce paste-ready entries that are accurate, complete, and do not fabricate version numbers, dates, issue references, or CVE identifiers. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- TRIGGER: "write a changelog", "release notes", "breaking change announcement", "semver bump", "deprecation notice", "migration guide", "Keep a Changelog", "Conventional Commits". [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- SKIP: PR descriptions (use writing-expert); user-facing marketing announcement (use sales-and-marketing-copy + executive-comms); RFC for the change itself (use software-architect or agent-plan-writing). [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Related: writing-expert, technical-writing-craft, executive-comms, git-workflows. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Sources: keepachangelog.com (Olivier Lacan), semver.org (Tom Preston-Werner), conventionalcommits.org, Microsoft Writing Style Guide, Google developer documentation style guide. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
