- If the caller's input is ambiguous or incomplete — vague change descriptions, no version context, no audience stated — ask exactly one targeted question before proceeding. Do not produce a changelog entry based on invented details. If any of these are missing and cannot be inferred, ask before drafting: [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- What changed (behavior-level description, not just "fixed a bug") [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Target version or bump type (MAJOR/MINOR/PATCH) [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Audience (developer-facing, end-user, executive, or all three) [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- If a date, version number, or issue/CVE reference is not provided, write a placeholder (`YYYY-MM-DD`, `vX.Y.Z`, `#ISSUE`) rather than inventing a value. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]

- A correct output for this skill: [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- States the version bump type (MAJOR / MINOR / PATCH) explicitly before the entry. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Produces a complete, paste-ready entry — not bullet suggestions. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Calls out every breaking change using the announcement template, even if the caller did not ask. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Preserves all prior entries unchanged when updating an existing CHANGELOG.md. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- When invoked, follow this process in order: [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **Identify the audience** — developer-facing, end-user-facing, or executive rollup. If unclear, ask (per the clarifying-question policy above). [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **Identify the version bump type** from the changes described. If the caller states a type but the changes imply a different type (e.g., caller says MINOR but a breaking change is present), flag the conflict explicitly: "These changes include a breaking change; this should be a MAJOR bump, not MINOR. Confirm before I proceed." [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **Draft the full entry** in the correct Keep a Changelog format and audience tone. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **Re-read the draft** and confirm it covers every change the caller described. If any described change is missing from the draft, add it before responding. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- -- [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **Format skeleton** (keepachangelog.com): [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/), [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html). [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **Section semantics:** [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **Added** — new features, capabilities, or endpoints available to consumers. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **Changed** — changes to existing behavior that are backward-compatible. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **Deprecated** — features flagged for future removal; include removal target version. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **Removed** — features deleted in this release (must appear in a prior Deprecated entry). [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **Fixed** — bug corrections with no behavior change. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **Security** — vulnerability patches; reference CVE or advisory ID where possible. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Date format is ISO 8601: `YYYY-MM-DD`. Never use ambiguous locale-specific formats. If the date is unknown, write `YYYY-MM-DD` as a placeholder. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- The `[Unreleased]` section sits at the top and collects work-in-progress entries. Move it to a versioned heading on release. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Every version heading links to a diff URL at the bottom of the file. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Omit empty sections entirely — do not leave `### Fixed` with no entries. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Newest version first; oldest version last. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Guiding principle: changelogs are for humans, not machines. Commit logs are for machines. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- -- [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **MAJOR** (`X.0.0`): at least one breaking change. Obligates: [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- A dedicated "Breaking Changes" section in the changelog or release notes. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- A migration guide (inline or linked). [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- A deprecation notice published in a prior release (the change must not be the first notice). [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **MINOR** (`x.Y.0`): new functionality, backward-compatible. Obligates: [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Documentation of every new public API, flag, or behavior. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- If anything was *deprecated* (not removed), list it in the Deprecated section. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **PATCH** (`x.y.Z`): backward-compatible bug fix only. Obligates: [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- A terse description of the incorrect behavior corrected. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Reference to the issue or CVE being resolved. If unknown, use `#ISSUE` placeholder. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- No new features may ship in a patch; if something slipped in, bump to minor. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **Hotfix / out-of-cycle patch:** treat the same as PATCH. Note in the entry that it is a hotfix and reference the incident or issue that required it. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Pre-release suffixes (`-alpha.1`, `-beta.2`, `-rc.1`) signal instability. Changelog entries for pre-releases are valid but should be clearly marked; they are not the "release" entry. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- -- [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Each release note bullet answers three questions in one to three short sentences: [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- What:   Describe the change in terms of observable behavior. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Why:    State the motivation (bug, performance, security, request). [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Impact: Call out what the reader must do (upgrade dependency, update config, etc.) [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- — or say "No action required." [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- One-liner form when all three collapse naturally: [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Add streaming support to the export endpoint (required by the bulk-download [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- feature); clients on v2.3+ can opt in with Accept: text/event-stream. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Never omit Impact for MAJOR or Security entries. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- -- [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Use this structure for any breaking change, whether shipped in a MAJOR bump or announced as Deprecated in a prior MINOR. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **What changes:** <one sentence describing the old behavior and the new behavior> [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **Why:** <one sentence on motivation> [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- <concrete step> [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- <concrete step> [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **Deprecation date:** Deprecated in vX.Y (released YYYY-MM-DD). [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **Removal date:** Removed in vA.0 (target YYYY-QN). [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **Need help?** Open a GitHub issue tagged `migration` or contact <channel>. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Deprecation and removal must appear as separate changelog entries. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- The removal entry in the changelog **must** cite the deprecation entry by version. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Never remove something that was not previously deprecated in a published release. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]

- **Public changelog** (CHANGELOG.md, GitHub Release, npm release body): [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Every change that alters public API surface, CLI flags, config keys, network behavior, or data formats. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Every security patch. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Every deprecation and removal. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Performance improvements visible to the operator (latency, memory, startup time). [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **Stays in commit messages / internal docs:** [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Refactors with no behavior change. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Test additions and coverage improvements. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- CI/CD pipeline changes. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Code style or formatting sweeps. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Internal rename of unexported identifiers. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Heuristic: if a consumer of the published artifact could observe the change without reading the source, it belongs in the changelog. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]

- End-user: `You can now filter cases by severity directly from the dashboard.` [src: changelog-and-release-notes]

- -- [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Pattern: **imperative verb + scope + outcome**. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Good:  Add streaming support to the export API for large result sets. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Good:  Fix incorrect timezone conversion in the scheduled-report generator. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Good:  Deprecate `--verbose` flag; use `--log-level=debug` instead (removed in v4.0). [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Bad:   Added: streaming (it now works better). [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Bad:   Various improvements to export. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Bad:   The bug where timezones were wrong has been fixed. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Start with a capital letter; no trailing period on standalone bullets. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Avoid past tense ("Added", "Fixed") as the first word — the section header already carries tense. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Scope narrows the noun: "Fix null-pointer in `CaseEnricher.normalize()`", not "Fix bug". [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Outcome states the user-visible result when it's non-obvious. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- -- [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Reference issues and PRs as `(#1234)` or `([#1234](url))`, not bare dashboard URLs. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Security patches: link to the advisory or CVE, not to an internal ticket. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Migration guides: link to a versioned doc path, not to `main` or `latest` which can drift. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Do not embed tracking parameters or redirector URLs in changelog links. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- -- [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **Inline** (in CHANGELOG.md or release body) when: [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- The migration is two to five steps and requires no code samples longer than 10 lines. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- The change is in a patch or minor. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **Separate document** (`docs/migration/v3-to-v4.md`) when: [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- The migration requires platform-specific steps. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Code samples span multiple files or languages. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- The guide will be linked from support channels, README, or the documentation site. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- The migration window is long and the guide will be updated over time. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- When linking from CHANGELOG.md to a separate guide, pin the link to a tagged commit or versioned doc URL, not `main`. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]

- Conventional Commits (conventionalcommits.org) defines a commit message structure that maps cleanly to changelog sections: [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- Note: `deprecate:` is not an official type in the Conventional Commits v1.0.0 spec; teams that use it are relying on a custom type. The spec-compliant form is `feat(deprecation):` or `chore(deprecate):`. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- The commit message body and footer become the raw material for changelog bullets. Tooling can generate a draft; a human must review for clarity and audience appropriateness before publishing. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- -- [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **release-please** (Google): reads Conventional Commits, opens a Release PR with a generated CHANGELOG.md update and version bump. The writer reviews and edits the PR before merging. Does not write migration guides or executive summaries — those remain manual. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **changesets** (Atlassian/community): requires contributors to add a changeset file (`pnpm changeset`) describing the change type and summary at PR time. Aggregates into CHANGELOG.md on release. Supports monorepos with per-package versioning. Gives writers the most control over copy because the input is prose, not a commit prefix. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **semantic-release**: fully automated — reads commits, bumps version, publishes, and writes CHANGELOG.md without a human review step. Appropriate for internal libraries or CI-only flows. Not recommended when the changelog is customer-facing and tone matters. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- What all three leave to the writer: migration guides, executive summaries, breaking-change announcements with migration paths, and any copy that requires audience awareness beyond a commit summary. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- **Monorepo note:** for monorepos, prefer per-package CHANGELOG.md files (one per package) over a single root changelog. changesets handles this natively; release-please supports it with per-package configuration. [src: changelog-and-release-notes]
- A launch is a one-shot narrative event — distinct from a landing page (steady-state conversion), an exec memo (internal alignment), or a changelog (continuous release log). [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- **Heuristic:** If you can't name the archetype in 10 seconds, the launch isn't ready. [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- Open with a one-paragraph claim about a shift in the world. **Never open with the product.** Andy Raskin's whole thesis: "the old game is over; a new game is starting." [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- What does the reader lose by staying with the old way? Quantify if possible. [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- Now — and only now — name the product and the one-line description. Apple's pattern: "Today, Apple introduced [X], a [category] that [primary benefit]." [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- Customer logos, quotes, measurable outcomes, demo link. One outside voice is worth ten internal claims. [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- **Clear CTA** — one primary CTA, one secondary at most. [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- **What's not in v1** — the honest-disclosure section. [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- A working "why now" paragraph: [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- **Names a shift** that has already occurred. [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- **Establishes the cost** of operating as if the shift hadn't happened. [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- **Creates urgency** that is "you're already behind if you ignore this." [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- > Until recently, [old default] was the only way to [task]. But [shift A] and [shift B] have changed what's possible. Teams that adapt are [outcome]. Teams that don't are [cost]. Today we're announcing [product] to help you [verb] in this new world. [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- **Anti-pattern:** "AI is everywhere." This is a backdrop, not a why-now. It has no specific shift, no cost, no urgency. [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- T-2 weeks   Analyst & press briefing (embargoed) [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- T-3 days    Pre-launch teaser; waitlist priority email [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- T=0         Blog post (canonical); Press release; Release notes published [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- T+0:05      Founder/CEO tweet thread; Company X/LinkedIn post [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- T+1 hour    Customer email blast; In-product announcement [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- T+1 day     Community post (Hacker News, Reddit, Discord) ← founder shows up [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- T+2 to +7d  Partner co-marketing; long-form deep-dive blog [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- **Sequencing rules:** [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- **The blog post is the canonical source.** Every other piece links to it. [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- **Analyst and press briefings are under embargo.** [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- **Release notes accompany the announcement.** When the blog post says "today we're launching X," the docs and the changelog must already reflect X. [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- > v1 deliberately ships without [X], [Y], and [Z]. We chose this scope to get [primary benefit] in your hands sooner. [X] is on the roadmap for [quarter]. If [X] or [Y] is a hard requirement for you today, [alternative path]. [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- **What this section does:** Lets engineers in evaluation mode answer "can I use this yet?" without booking a call. Pre-empts the inevitable Hacker News commenter who finds the missing feature. [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- **The "we're excited to announce" opener.** Cut. Open with the shift. [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- **The "this changes everything" overclaim.** [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- **The "product-first" structure.** Specs, then features, then maybe a sentence about who cares. [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- **The hidden "what's not in v1."** [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- **The "AI/cloud/edge is everywhere" why-now.** [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- **The post that doesn't match the docs.** [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- **The four-CTA ending.** If you list four CTAs the reader picks zero. [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- Define before launch day. Sample tiers: [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- Unique pageviews on the blog post in week 1 [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]
- Tier-1 press hits [src: release-blog-and-launch-narrative]

- Answer four questions before touching a slide tool: [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Who is in the room?** Job function, seniority, and domain expertise. [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **What do they already believe?** Start from their current position. [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **What one action do you want them to take?** Name the action. [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **What is the one thing they must remember?** Write that sentence before slide 1. [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Presentation slides** (Reynolds / "Presentation Zen" model) exist to support a live speaker. The speaker carries the argument; the slide carries visual reinforcement. One idea per slide. Minimal text. Large images or diagrams. [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Slide-docs** (Tufte-influenced) are standalone documents formatted as slide-shaped pages. They contain complete sentences, dense supporting data, footnotes. They can be emailed and read without a presenter. [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **The core failure mode:** the slidument — bullet-heavy slides that are too dense to look good on screen and too sparse to be useful to a reader. [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **10 slides** — humans can't absorb more than ten concepts in a single sitting [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **20 minutes** — even if you have a full hour, present in 20 minutes [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **30-point minimum font** — if you cannot fit your message in 30pt type, you have too many words [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- The central insight: every great speech moves back and forth between "what is" and "what could be." [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **The contrast pattern:** [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- Establish the current reality (what is) [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- Describe the future possibility (what could be) [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- Repeat this oscillation; each cycle raises the stakes [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- End with the "new bliss" — the world after the audience acts [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **The STAR moment** (Something They'll Always Remember): one designed moment of high contrast, surprise, or visceral demonstration. [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Act 1 — Setup (10–15% of total time):** Establish stakes; define the problem; signal what the audience will be able to do differently by the end. [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Act 2 — Exploration (70–75%):** Develop the argument. Front-load complex material; place a re-energizing moment two-thirds of the way through. [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Act 3 — Resolution (10–15%):** Do not introduce new material. Synthesize, do not summarize. [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- Every slide title is a complete, standalone sentence stating the takeaway, not a topic label. [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- Bad title: "Market Analysis" [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- Good title: "The North American market is growing 12% YoY and outpacing EMEA in every segment." [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- A reader who reads only slide titles should follow the full argument. [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Startling fact or statistic:** drop a number the audience does not expect [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Story:** open with a specific scene — one person, one moment, sensory detail [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Contrarian claim:** state something the audience believes that you are about to challenge [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Direct question:** ask a question the audience cannot immediately answer [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Scene-setting:** describe the world as it will look after your idea is adopted [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- Do not open with: your name and title, an apology, "great to be here," agenda slides. [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Callback to opening:** return to the story or question you opened with [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Call to action:** one specific, concrete thing the audience can do in the next 48 hours [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Single image or quote:** full-bleed slide with one sentence [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Summary triple:** three short phrases that encapsulate the talk's three main points [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **The future vision:** describe the world three years from now if the audience acts [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **The bridging technique:** acknowledge the question, then bridge to your main message. [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **"I don't know" as a complete answer:** say it cleanly, then add "I'll find out and get back to you by [date]." [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Hostile questions:** do not match the energy. Lower your voice slightly. Answer the question beneath the question. [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- Minimum effective rehearsal for a 30-minute talk: [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Three times out loud, alone** — full volume, full sentences, full transitions [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Once to a real human** — their confusion is signal [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Video review of yourself** — watch on mute first (body language), then with sound (pace and filler) [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Pacing target:** 125–150 words per minute. Time your talk at 90% of the slot. [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Virtual:** look at the camera lens, not at faces on screen. Place the camera at eye level. [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Audio quality (virtual):** audio quality matters more than video quality. A USB condenser microphone, a quiet room, and a soft surface behind you. [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Energy calibration (virtual):** increase vocal variety noticeably above what feels natural in a room — the camera flattens affect. [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Reading slides verbatim.** [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Walls of bullets.** Each bullet resets the audience's attention to near-zero. [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **"As you can see here..."** — If it is visible, do not narrate its existence. [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Apologizing for slides.** [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **Running long.** Going over time disrespects every person in the room. [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]
- **The vague closing.** "So, in conclusion, we looked at X, Y, and Z..." [src: public-speaking-and-presentations]

- **Purpose:** a meta-skill that coordinates the three modes of writing work — generating, [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- evaluating, and improving — in discrete passes with explicit handoff points. The loop [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- is not infinite. It has stop conditions. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **When invoked by Claude:** produce a structured pass log for each iteration — findings by severity, actions taken, and which stop condition ended the loop. Do not silently revise without showing the iteration record. If the user provides a document, run the loop against it; if they describe a document, ask for the text before proceeding. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Output shape per iteration:** [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- Review findings list — each finding on its own line with severity label: `[Critical]`, `[High]`, `[Medium]`, or `[Low]`, plus a one-line description [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- Revision summary (what changed, why, keyed to finding IDs) [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- Stop-condition check (which condition applies, or "continuing to iteration N+1") [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- After completing each loop, re-read the output and confirm it addresses the user's stated goal before delivering it. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- -- [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- Writing fails in two ways: shipping too early (underdeveloped argument, missing structure) [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- or never shipping (infinite-polish). The three-pass loop prevents both by separating [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- incompatible cognitive modes and capping iterations before they become procrastination. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Mode:** generative. Your job is to get ideas out, not to write well. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **No editing while drafting.** Resist fixing sentences mid-flow. Let ugly prose stand. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- Anne Lamott calls this the "shitty first draft" — a permission slip to write badly so you [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- can write at all. The draft's only job is to exist. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Mark gaps, don't plug them mid-draft.** Use `[TK]` (to come) or `[GAP: describe what's [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- missing]` for unknowns. Stopping to research kills momentum. Fill gaps in Pass 3. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Any `[TK]` or `[GAP:]` still present at the end of Pass 3 is a Critical finding — the [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- document is not shippable until all markers are resolved or explicitly scoped out.** [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Time-box.** One Pomodoro — 25 minutes — per major section. If the clock runs out, stop [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- mid-sentence and move on. Unfinished prose is not a crisis; it is raw material. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Work from an outline, not from instinct.** Even a three-bullet skeleton prevents the [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- most common draft failure: a conclusion that argues against the introduction. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- See the **Skill Handoff Map** at the end of this document for the full per-phase routing table. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- -- [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Mode:** evaluative. You are now a reader, not the author. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Read the whole thing once before commenting.** No inline notes on the first pass. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- You need to know where the document goes before you judge any sentence in it. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Separate findings by type:** [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Missing:** a claim is made but the evidence is absent; a step is assumed but not [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- stated; a section promised in the introduction does not appear. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Wrong:** a fact is incorrect; an argument contradicts itself; a structural pattern [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Could be better:** prose is clear enough but could be sharper, shorter, or better [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Name the framework you are reviewing against.** Do not review in a vacuum. Pick one [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- BLUF — does the bottom line appear in the first sentence? [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- MECE — are sections mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive? [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- Minto Pyramid — does the argument flow deductively from a single governing idea? [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- PARA — is the document in the right context (project, area, resource, or archive)? [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- SCQA — is the Situation / Complication / Question / Answer arc intact? [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Severity-label every finding:** Critical (document is wrong or misleading), High [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- (missing material the audience needs), Medium (structure or argument weakness), Low [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- (style preference, nice-to-have). [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Do not fix during review.** Record findings. Mixing evaluation and correction corrupts [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- both modes — you stop seeing what is actually there. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- -- [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Mode:** surgical. Apply the review findings against a priority threshold. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Address every Critical and High finding.** These are not optional. If a Critical [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- finding cannot be resolved, the document is not ready to ship — restart or descope. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Batch Medium findings.** Group related Medium findings and address them in one pass [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- through the affected section. Avoid thrashing individual sentences. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Skip Low findings unless trivial.** A Low finding that takes thirty seconds to fix [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- is worth taking. A Low finding that requires restructuring a paragraph is not worth [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- taking on the first revision cycle — bank it for the next iteration if it recurs. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Do not introduce new content during revision.** If revision uncovers a missing [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- section, that section goes back to draft mode (Pass 1), not inline into the revision [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- pass. Keep the modes clean. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Log what changed and why.** One-line entry per finding resolved: [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- `[H] §3 — added missing latency data; source: internal benchmark doc`. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- See the **Skill Handoff Map** at the end of this document for routing after revision. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- -- [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- The loop ends when the first applicable condition is met — earliest wins. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- If you reach the hard stop without reaching soft stop, ship the best available version [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- with a known-issues note, or escalate the scope problem. Infinite iteration is not a [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- -- [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- Stephen King recommends letting a draft rest before revising. The principle: you cannot [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- read what you wrote — you read what you meant to write. Distance corrects that. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- For documents under 500 words: 1–2 hours is sufficient. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- For documents 500–2,000 words: overnight. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- For documents over 2,000 words: 24 hours minimum. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- If the deadline prevents cooling off, use the **fresh eyes** pattern instead. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- -- [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- If you cannot wait, get a different reviewer for iteration N+1 than for iteration N. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- The first reviewer has already accommodated your argument; they will find it harder to [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- see what is still missing. A second reviewer reads with no accommodation debt. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- Applied to Claude: ask a second agent session (or invoke document-critique with a cold [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- context) rather than asking the same session that helped draft to also review. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- -- [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- Keep a running log for every document that goes through more than one cycle. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- Draft completed: [date/time] [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- Reviewed by: [agent or name], framework: [BLUF / MECE / etc.] [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- Findings: 2 Critical, 3 High, 4 Medium, 1 Low [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- Revisions applied: [brief list] [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- Stop check: High findings remain — continue [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- Draft completed: [date/time] [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- Reviewed by: [different reviewer], framework: [BLUF / MECE / etc.] [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- Findings: 0 Critical, 0 High, 2 Medium, 3 Low [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- Revisions applied: [brief list] [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- Stop check: No Medium-or-higher findings — SOFT STOP, ship [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- -- [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Editing while drafting.** Kills generative momentum. You end up with the first three [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- paragraphs polished and the rest unwritten. Lamott diagnosed this decades ago; the fix [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- is the same: write badly first. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Infinite polishing.** Zinsser: "Rewriting is the essence of writing well — but there [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- is a difference between rewriting that improves and rewriting that avoids." Apply the [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- convergence and time-box stop conditions ruthlessly. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Five-stakeholder review before any iteration.** Gathering input from five people on a [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- first draft means gathering five reactions to a document that will change dramatically [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- anyway. Get to iteration 2 before widening the reviewer pool. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **No time-box on review.** A review pass without a time-box expands to fill all available [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- attention. Cap each review pass at half the draft time or 30 minutes, whichever is less. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Skipping the framework.** Reviewing without a named framework produces impressionistic [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- feedback ("this feels off") that is hard to act on. Name the lens before you start. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- -- [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- Iteration is not always the answer. Stop the loop and start over when: [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Scope changed.** The document is now answering a different question than it started [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- with. Revising toward a moving target produces incoherent documents. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Audience changed.** A document written for engineers and redirected to executives [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- needs a new draft, not another revision pass. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **Premise was wrong.** The core argument has been disproven or superseded. No amount [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- of revision fixes a document whose central claim is no longer true. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- In all three cases: close the log, open a new one, and return to Pass 1. The old draft [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- is not wasted — it is a source of raw material and a record of what the argument was. [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- -- [src: draft-review-revise-loop]
- **When invoked:** the user submits existing prose. Return the revised text, complete and drop-in ready, followed by a brief pass log noting which passes were applied and what was changed. [src: editing-and-revision]
- Work top-down. Fix the largest problems before polishing sentences. [src: editing-and-revision]
- **Pass 1 — Structural.** Does the argument hold? Is the order defensible? [src: editing-and-revision]
- **Pass 2 — Paragraph.** Does each paragraph have one job? [src: editing-and-revision]
- **Pass 3 — Sentence.** Apply the verb-first pass, active-voice scan, and cohesion check. [src: editing-and-revision]
- **Pass 4 — Word.** Nominalizations, hedges, redundant pairs, filler phrases. [src: editing-and-revision]
- Spot them: look for Latinate nouns ending in *-tion*, *-ment*, *-ance*, *-ence*, *-ity*, *-ness* that have living verbs inside them. [src: editing-and-revision]
- Before: *The committee engaged in a discussion of the proposal.* [src: editing-and-revision]
- After: *The committee discussed the proposal.* [src: editing-and-revision]
- Before: *It was determined by the review board that the application was deficient.* [src: editing-and-revision]
- After: *The review board found the application deficient.* [src: editing-and-revision]
- The beginning of a sentence anchors the reader to what they know; the end delivers new payload. [src: editing-and-revision]
- The end of a sentence is its stress position. If your sentence ends on a qualifier, a parenthetical, or filler, you have surrendered emphasis. [src: editing-and-revision]
- **Metadiscourse** — sentences about the text: *It is important to note that*, *As I mentioned above*. [src: editing-and-revision]
- **Hedges** — *it could be argued that*, *it seems as if*, *in some sense*. [src: editing-and-revision]
- **Redundant pairs** — *each and every*, *null and void*, *true and accurate*. [src: editing-and-revision]
- Find every sentence over two lines. Read it aloud. If you lose the thread before the period, break it or add a visible frame. [src: editing-and-revision]
- Before: *We need to improve morale, reduce attrition, and the onboarding process should be shortened.* [src: editing-and-revision]
- After: *We need to improve morale, reduce attrition, and shorten onboarding.* [src: editing-and-revision]
- Scan every sentence. Locate the main verb. If the verb is a form of *be* plus a nominalization, extract the hidden verb and rebuild. [src: editing-and-revision]
- Set a target: 30% of words on the cutting room floor. King: "Kill your darlings, kill your darlings, even when it breaks your egocentric little scribbler's heart." [src: editing-and-revision]
- Search the draft for every *was* and *were* followed by a past participle. For each instance, decide: (1) Is the actor unknown or genuinely irrelevant? Keep passive. (2) Is the actor known and relevant? Rewrite in active voice. (3) Is the passive hiding accountability? Rewrite. [src: editing-and-revision]
- Print or copy only the first sentence of each paragraph. Read those sentences as a standalone document. Ask: Does the sequence form an argument? Are any two sentences redundant? [src: editing-and-revision]
- For every paragraph, ask: is the point in the first sentence, or is it buried? [src: editing-and-revision]
- A reader would need to re-read to recover the missing context. [src: editing-and-revision]
- The sentence no longer names its subject. [src: editing-and-revision]
- Parallel structure has been broken to save words. [src: editing-and-revision]
- Link: [ ] Structural pass complete — argument skeleton valid [src: editing-and-revision]
- Link: [ ] Every paragraph has a first sentence that states its point [src: editing-and-revision]
- Link: [ ] No nominalizations where a verb is available [src: editing-and-revision]
- Link: [ ] Every sentence's subject names the actor [src: editing-and-revision]
- Link: [ ] Key content lands at sentence end, not middle [src: editing-and-revision]
- Link: [ ] Every *was/were + past participle* audited [src: editing-and-revision]
- Link: [ ] Metadiscourse, hedges, and redundant pairs cut [src: editing-and-revision]
- Link: [ ] Long sentences (>35 words) have visible architecture [src: editing-and-revision]
- Link: [ ] Parallel items are grammatically parallel [src: editing-and-revision]
- Link: [ ] 30% cut target met [src: editing-and-revision]
- Link: [ ] Read aloud complete — no stumbles remain [src: editing-and-revision]

- Excavate aging documents for staleness, dead links, process drift, phantom dependencies, and obsolete examples. [src: doc-archaeology]
- **Stale Facts** — claims about state-of-the-world that have changed [src: doc-archaeology]
- **Dead Links** — URLs that 404, redirect to unrelated destinations [src: doc-archaeology]
- **Drift from Current Process** — procedures that no longer reflect actual practice [src: doc-archaeology]
- **Phantom Dependencies** — scripts, files, tools, people that no longer exist [src: doc-archaeology]
- **Obsolete Examples** — code snippets reflecting prior API or UI [src: doc-archaeology]
- **Last-Updated Lens** — estimate age, catalog time-sensitive claims, set decay risk (low/medium/high) [src: doc-archaeology]
- **Fact-Check Pass** — verify each claim against current state [src: doc-archaeology]
- **Link-Check Pass** — verify every URL; flag auth-gated as "unverified" [src: doc-archaeology]
- **Process-Check Pass** — verify procedures against current practice at step level [src: doc-archaeology]
- **Dependency-Check Pass** — check scripts, files, tools, channels, people [src: doc-archaeology]
- **Severity:** Critical/Misleading → High/Outdated → Medium/Cosmetic → Low/Historical [src: doc-archaeology]
- **Update in place** — targeted fixes; structure is sound [src: doc-archaeology]
- **Restructure and refresh** — major rewrites needed [src: doc-archaeology]
- **Deprecate with pointer** — superseded, add deprecation banner [src: doc-archaeology]
- **Archive** — historical state; remove from search [src: doc-archaeology]
- **Delete** — fully phantom, all claims stale [src: doc-archaeology]
- Noting a doc is old without running any passes (ostrich mode) [src: doc-archaeology]
- Rewriting when targeted refresh would suffice [src: doc-archaeology]
- Deleting load-bearing historical context [src: doc-archaeology]
- Treating unverifiable as confirmed [src: doc-archaeology]
- Authoring craft for the brand voice guide *as an artifact*. The output is a document other writers will open, reference, and apply. [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- A brand voice guide answers four questions for every writer who opens it: [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- **Who do we sound like?** (Voice — the constant.) [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- **How do we shift in different situations?** (Tone — the variable.) [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- **Which words do we use, and which do we never use?** (Vocabulary.) [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- **What does this look like in practice?** (Examples — usually do/don't pairs.) [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- If a guide doesn't make these four questions answerable in under 10 minutes of reading, it will be ignored. [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- **Voice** — three to five attributes that describe the constant personality. State each as "We are X. We are not Y." (Bloomstein's BrandSort framing: include the *not*.) [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- **Tone** — a matrix showing how voice flexes by situation. [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- **Vocabulary** — preferred words, banned words, and grammar/style decisions specific to the brand. [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- **Examples** — at least 5 do/don't pairs spanning the highest-traffic surfaces. [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- The canonical format: [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- > **Confident, not arrogant.** We make declarative claims when we know we're right. We don't oversell, hedge with weasel words, or talk down to readers who know less than us. [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- > **Warm, not saccharine.** We sound like a competent colleague who likes their job. We don't use exclamation marks to perform enthusiasm or call readers "friend." [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- Three to five attributes is the sweet spot. [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- The Nielsen Norman Group axes: formal↔casual, serious↔funny, respectful↔irreverent, enthusiastic↔matter-of-fact. [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- Formal        |---------------●---|        Casual [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- Serious       |---●---------------|        Playful [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- Matter-of-fact|---------●---------|        Enthusiastic [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- **Anti-pattern:** Putting all markers in the middle. "Moderately formal, moderately serious, moderately enthusiastic" is no voice. [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- > **Do:** "We paused your build. Resume it when ready." [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- > **Don't:** "Oops! Looks like your build got paused. No worries — just click Resume whenever you'd like to keep going! 🚀" [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- The don't side teaches more than the do side. Pick don'ts from real drafts your team has actually shipped. [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- **Preferred** — words that carry the voice. ("ship" not "release"; "you" not "the user".) [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- **Banned** — words that break the voice. ("leverage", "synergy", "seamless", "robust", "delightful", "passionate".) [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- **Decisions** — product-name capitalization, oxford comma, contractions allowed, em dash vs en dash. [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- Every voice guide should display: [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- **Version** (semver or date) [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- **Last reviewed** date [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- **Owner** (a person, not a team) [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- **Next review** date (no more than 12 months out) [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- **No "we are not."** Lists three positive attributes with no opposites. [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- **Spectrum markers all centered.** "Moderately formal" is no guidance. [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- **Don't-side strawmen.** Don't pairs that are obviously bad teach nothing. [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- **No date, no owner.** Writers won't trust an undated guide. [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- **30+ page voice guide.** Anything past 10 pages won't be read. [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- **Banning words without preferring others.** "Don't say leverage" without "say use" leaves writers stuck. [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- **No tone matrix.** Writers can match personality but not situation. [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- Link: [Mailchimp Content Style Guide — Voice and Tone](https://styleguide.mailchimp.com/voice-and-tone/) [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- Link: [Atlassian Design — Voice and Tone](https://atlassian.design/content/voice-and-tone/) [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- Bloomstein, M. *Content Strategy at Work*. Morgan Kaufmann, 2012. [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- Fenton, N. and Kiefer Lee, K. *Nicely Said*. New Riders, 2014. [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- Link: [Nielsen Norman Group — The Four Dimensions of Tone of Voice](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/tone-of-voice-dimensions/) [src: brand-voice-guide-writing]
- A speech is built to be **heard, not read**. The writer's job is to construct sentences that survive the air between the speaker's mouth and the audience's ear — sentences that can be re-listened-to in real time only by the listener's short-term memory. [src: speech-writing]
- Every well-formed speech has the same five-beat skeleton: [src: speech-writing]
- **Hook** — a sentence, image, statistic, or question that earns the next 30 seconds. [src: speech-writing]
- **Frame** — what this talk is about and why the audience should care. One sentence. [src: speech-writing]
- **Three acts** — the body. The rule of three is not aesthetic; it is cognitive. Three things stay with the audience, five don't. [src: speech-writing]
- **Turn** — the moment where the talk pivots from explanation to implication. [src: speech-writing]
- **Call to action** — what the audience should *do, feel, or remember*. [src: speech-writing]
- Carmine Gallo's distillation of TED's curation rule: **18 minutes is the ceiling for a focused, memorable single-speaker talk.** For longer slots, structure as multiple sub-talks with clear act breaks. [src: speech-writing]
- Three is the smallest number that creates a pattern. Use it for: [src: speech-writing]
- **Top-level structure** (three acts, three stories, three asks) [src: speech-writing]
- **Sentence-level lists** ("government of the people, by the people, for the people") [src: speech-writing]
- **Repeated refrains** (Jobs: "Stay hungry. Stay foolish." — repeated three times) [src: speech-writing]
- Place applause lines at **act transitions** and **the CTA**. Never two in a row. [src: speech-writing]
- **Read every draft aloud.** If you run out of breath, the sentence is too long. [src: speech-writing]
- Stage directions are inline notes to the speaker about delivery. They live in the delivery script, not the published transcript. [src: speech-writing]
- `[pause]` — short pause, one breath [src: speech-writing]
- `[long pause]` — full silence, 2–4 seconds [src: speech-writing]
- `[lower voice]` — drop volume to draw the audience in [src: speech-writing]
- `[slow]` — drop pace to weight the line [src: speech-writing]
- `[wait for laughter]` — explicitly note that the speaker should hold [src: speech-writing]
- Place directions on their own line *above* the line they modify, in brackets. [src: speech-writing]
- Amateur speeches over-explain. Professional speeches **withhold**, then **resolve**. [src: speech-writing]
- Tell a story before naming its lesson; let the room reach the conclusion one beat ahead. [src: speech-writing]
- Use specific detail, not abstraction. "A blue notebook on the kitchen table" beats "a personal object." [src: speech-writing]
- Cut your second-best example. Two strong points land harder than three uneven ones. [src: speech-writing]
- Don't apologize for the topic, the time slot, or the room. [src: speech-writing]
- **Capture their voice.** Listen to 30+ minutes of their existing speech before drafting. [src: speech-writing]
- **Their stories, not yours.** Use anecdotes from their life. [src: speech-writing]
- **No misattributed lived experience.** Never invent a personal anecdote they did not actually experience. [src: speech-writing]
- **They get final cut.** The speaker must be able to change anything. [src: speech-writing]
- Twelve years ago, I was sitting in a parking lot at 2 a.m., [src: speech-writing]
- trying to figure out how to fire myself. [src: speech-writing]
- Tonight I want to share three ideas: [A], [B], and [C]. [src: speech-writing]
- Story → claim → evidence → micro-CTA [src: speech-writing]
- Here is what these three things have in common. [src: speech-writing]
- So when you leave this room tonight, do one thing: [src: speech-writing]
- **The written-essay-read-aloud.** Long sentences, semicolons, nested clauses. [src: speech-writing]
- **The five-point list.** Audiences forget points four and five. [src: speech-writing]
- **The apology open.** "I'm not really a speaker…" [src: speech-writing]
- **The unmotivated joke.** Humor that doesn't serve the arc. [src: speech-writing]
- **The buried CTA.** Telling the audience what to do in the third-to-last sentence. [src: speech-writing]
- **Stage directions in the published transcript.** [src: speech-writing]

- Carmine Gallo, *Talk Like TED* (St. Martin's Press, 2014). [src: speech-writing]
- Steve Jobs, *Stanford Commencement Address*, June 12, 2005. [src: speech-writing]
- Sam Leith, *Words Like Loaded Pistols* (Basic Books, 2012). [src: speech-writing]
- A chatbot is a conversation, not an interface. Every turn the bot takes should advance the user's goal or surface a clear next move. The work breaks into three layers: [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Persona** — who the bot is, what it sounds like, what it refuses to do. [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Turn design** — the individual response, plus the choices it offers. [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Recovery design** — what happens when the bot doesn't understand, when the user is angry, or when the conversation has to leave the bot. [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- The four Gricean maxims: [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Quantity** — say as much as is needed, not more [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Quality** — only say true things [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Relation** — stay on the user's topic [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Manner** — be clear, brief, and orderly [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- A minimum persona doc includes: [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Name** (or explicit no-name policy) [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Role** (what the bot is for — support? sales? in-product help?) [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Voice traits** (3–5 adjectives — e.g., "warm, precise, never cute") [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Refuses to do** (e.g., diagnose medical issues, take payment, promise pricing) [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Vocabulary** (3–5 words it uses; 3–5 it doesn't) [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Disclosure boilerplate** (the exact "I'm an AI assistant" line) [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Escalation trigger phrases** [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- As of 2026, plain-and-unambiguous AI disclosure is no longer optional: [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **California SB 243** (effective Jan 1, 2026) requires disclosure, plus reminders every three hours for minor users [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **EU AI Act** requires upfront disclosure for any AI system interacting with natural persons [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **FTC** treats undisclosed AI as potentially deceptive [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- Writing implications: [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Disclose in the first turn**, not buried in a tooltip [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- Use direct language: "I'm an AI assistant" — not "I'm an enhanced automation experience" [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **If asked "are you a human?"** answer plainly: "No, I'm an AI assistant." [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- A conversational turn has three jobs: [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Acknowledge** what the user just said [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Resolve** the user's intent [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Hand the turn back** with a clear next move [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- Length convention: **1–3 short sentences** per turn for support bots, **1–5 sentences** for in-product help. [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- When the bot doesn't understand, three things must happen: [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Admit it cleanly.** "I'm not sure what you mean by 'reset'." [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Offer a small, finite menu.** Two or three concrete interpretations. [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Provide a path out.** Always include "talk to a human" no later than the second failed understanding. [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- Three transfer rules: [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Drop the edge in failure modes.** Humor in a working flow is fine. Humor when the user is locked out is not. [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Keep the rhythm, simplify the vocabulary.** [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Reuse hero phrases sparingly.** One signature phrase per conversation. [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- Three elements must be present: [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Confirm the handoff is happening.** "I'm connecting you to a person now." [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Preserve context.** "I'll share what we've discussed so you won't have to repeat yourself." [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **Set the wait expectation.** "Average wait is about 4 minutes." [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **The "I'm an enhanced automation experience" dodge.** Coy disclosure reads as deceptive. [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **The infinite "I didn't understand, please rephrase" loop.** Two failures is the ceiling; escalate. [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **The hidden escalation path.** Surface the escalation in the conversation itself. [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- **The promise-the-bot-can't-keep.** "I'll refund you" when refund authority is human-only. [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- Erika Hall, *Conversational Design* (A Book Apart, 2018). [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- California SB 243 (Companion Chatbot Disclosure Act), effective Jan 1, 2026. [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- EU AI Act Article 50 (transparency obligations for AI systems). [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- Byron Reeves and Clifford Nass, *The Media Equation* (CSLI / Cambridge, 1996). [src: chatbot-conversation-writing]
- Five times as many people read the headline as read the body copy. A headline does three jobs at once: it tells the reader what they're about to get, gives them a reason to care, and signals what kind of piece it is. [src: headline-craft]
- Ogilvy's empirical claim: five times more people read the headline than the body. The practical implication: the headline is where 80% of the work happens. Joanna Wiebe's discipline: never write fewer than 10 headline variants before picking one. Ogilvy demanded 16. [src: headline-craft]
- A headline pointed at the reader outperforms a headline pointed at the writer, the product, or an abstract topic. [src: headline-craft]
- **Topic frame (weak):** "The future of distributed databases" [src: headline-craft]
- **You-frame (strong):** "What your replication setup is costing you (and how to fix it)" [src: headline-craft]
- BuzzSumo's analysis of 100M headlines: numerals increase CTR by ~36%. [src: headline-craft]
- **B2C top performers:** 10, 5, 15, 7, 20, 6 [src: headline-craft]
- **Odd numbers** outperform even numbers for curiosity-driven content. [src: headline-craft]
- **Specific numbers** outperform round numbers. "$1,247 saved" beats "$1,200 saved." [src: headline-craft]
- **Declarative headlines** state the conclusion in the headline itself. Good for hard news, technical posts. [src: headline-craft]
- **Curiosity-gap headlines** withhold the conclusion to drive the click. The failure mode: **clickbait** — a gap so wide the body can't close it. [src: headline-craft]
- **News headline:** Active verb, present tense. "Atlas adds vector search for Voyage embeddings." [src: headline-craft]
- **Feature headline:** Label or question form OK. "The quiet revolution in how databases handle vectors." [src: headline-craft]
- **Op-ed headline:** Argument-forward. "We're thinking about vector search wrong." [src: headline-craft]
- **SEO headline:** Keyword-front-loaded. "Vector search benchmarks: 12 databases compared (2026)." [src: headline-craft]
- A deck does three things: [src: headline-craft]
- Expands what the headline could not fit. [src: headline-craft]
- Answers the question the headline raised. [src: headline-craft]
- Earns the scroll. [src: headline-craft]
- Sizing: Heds are 6–10 words. Decks are 10–25 words. [src: headline-craft]
- **The "we" headline.** "We released a new feature today." The reader doesn't care what *you* did. [src: headline-craft]
- **The label headline.** "Distributed Systems Notes" names a folder, doesn't earn a click. [src: headline-craft]
- **The pun headline.** Ogilvy banned them in 1963 and the data still says he's right. [src: headline-craft]
- **The bait-and-switch.** Headline promises X, body delivers Y. [src: headline-craft]
- **The under-specified curiosity gap.** "What we learned" without a hint of *what* you learned. [src: headline-craft]
- Ogilvy, David. *Ogilvy on Advertising* (1983). [src: headline-craft]
- BuzzSumo headline studies. [src: headline-craft]
- Wiebe, Joanna. Copyhackers headline formulas. [src: headline-craft]
- Link: [PMC, "When curiosity gaps backfire" (2024)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11704130/) [src: headline-craft]
- A journalistic profile is not a biography, a hagiography, a resume in prose, or a Q&A. It is a **narrative reported piece** that uses reporting, scene, anecdote, and selected detail to reveal something true about a person. [src: profile-writing]
- Three pieces of writing define the modern profile tradition: Gay Talese's "Frank Sinatra Has a Cold" (Esquire, 1966) for scene-based reporting; Janet Malcolm's "The Journalist and the Murderer" (The New Yorker, 1989) for the ethics of the form; and Walt Harrington's work in *Intimate Journalism* — the discipline of "deep, not wide." [src: profile-writing]
- The biographer's question: what happened? The profile writer's question: **what is this person actually like, and how do I show it?** [src: profile-writing]
- **Lead (lede).** A scene, anecdote, or paradox that introduces the subject in a specific moment. 1–3 paragraphs. [src: profile-writing]
- **Nut graph (nutgraf).** The "why this story now" paragraph. 1 paragraph. [src: profile-writing]
- **Context / background.** What the reader needs to know about the world the subject operates in. 2–4 paragraphs. [src: profile-writing]
- **Biography and present moment.** Selected biographical material, interleaved with scenes from current reporting. [src: profile-writing]
- **Kicker.** The closing scene or quote. Often a callback to the lede. [src: profile-writing]
- **In-scene lede.** Open inside a moment. The subject is doing something. [src: profile-writing]
- **Anecdotal lede.** Open with a story — a discrete past event that illustrates something about the subject. [src: profile-writing]
- **Paradoxical lede.** Open with the contradiction at the heart of the subject. [src: profile-writing]
- What never works: opening with the subject's birth, their resume, or their official title. [src: profile-writing]
- The "nut graph" tells the reader what the piece is about and why they should keep reading. It answers: [src: profile-writing]
- Who is this person? (One-sentence positioning.) [src: profile-writing]
- Why now? (What just happened that makes them newsworthy.) [src: profile-writing]
- What does this piece argue or reveal? [src: profile-writing]
- The nut comes early enough that the reader doesn't bail, late enough that the lede has done its work. [src: profile-writing]
- Walt Harrington's craft rule: **render the important moments as scenes; summarize everything in between.** [src: profile-writing]
- Pick 3–5 scenes that do narrative work. Render those in close, sensory, present-tense detail. Everything else is summary prose. [src: profile-writing]
- **Scene → summary → scene → summary → scene → kicker.** [src: profile-writing]
- **Quote sparingly.** Direct quotes should do work no paraphrase could do — voice, idiosyncrasy, surprise, contradiction. [src: profile-writing]
- **Never start a paragraph with a long quote.** [src: profile-writing]
- **Action over speech.** What the subject *does* in your presence beats what they *say* about themselves. [src: profile-writing]
- Minimum table stakes for a serious profile: [src: profile-writing]
- 1–3 long-form interviews with the subject (90+ minutes each). [src: profile-writing]
- 5–15 interviews with people who know the subject. [src: profile-writing]
- Direct observation of the subject in their normal environment. [src: profile-writing]
- Document review. [src: profile-writing]
- No deception about the assignment. No fabricated composites. No invented dialogue. No quote-clean-up that changes meaning. No quote approval. No surprises in the final piece — give subjects the chance to address material discoveries. [src: profile-writing]
- Tape every interview. Keep a fact log: every claim → source. For claims about people other than the subject, contact those people for confirmation or comment. [src: profile-writing]
- Three reliable kicker patterns: [src: profile-writing]
- **Callback.** The lede scene returns, but the reader now understands it differently. [src: profile-writing]
- **Crystallizing quote.** A single line from the subject that compresses the piece's argument. [src: profile-writing]
- **Forward-look.** A small concrete detail of the subject's near future. [src: profile-writing]
- Scene or anecdote. Subject in motion. Sensory detail. [src: profile-writing]
- Who. Why now. What this piece reveals. [src: profile-writing]
- The world the subject operates in. [src: profile-writing]
- The contradiction, the critic, the unresolved thing. [src: profile-writing]
- Callback or crystallizing image. [src: profile-writing]
- **The hagiography.** Profile reads as press release. [src: profile-writing]
- **The resume in prose.** Chronological recitation with no scene. [src: profile-writing]
- **The Q&A in disguise.** Long stretches of question-answer. [src: profile-writing]
- **The writer in the foreground.** "When I first met Smith, I expected..." [src: profile-writing]
- **The unattributed psychoanalysis.** "Smith is a deeply lonely man." On whose authority? [src: profile-writing]
- **Composite characters / invented dialogue.** Fabrication. [src: profile-writing]
- Talese, Gay. "Frank Sinatra Has a Cold" (Esquire, April 1966). [src: profile-writing]
- Malcolm, Janet. *The Journalist and the Murderer* (Knopf, 1990). [src: profile-writing]
- Harrington, Walt. *Intimate Journalism: The Art and Craft of Reporting Everyday Life* (Sage, 1997). [src: profile-writing]

- The op-ed is the **shortest serious argument form in public writing**. In ~750 words you must make a single argument that a previously-uninterested reader believes by the end. Every deviation from convention is a friction point that costs pickup. [src: op-ed-writing]
- **One argument.** A piece that tries to make two arguments makes neither. [src: op-ed-writing]
- Standard target: **750 words**. New York Times caps at 800. Washington Post caps at 800. Most regional dailies sit at 600–700. [src: op-ed-writing]
- The thesis is one sentence. It is a claim someone could disagree with. [src: op-ed-writing]
- Tests for a strong op-ed thesis: [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Disagreeable.** "Schools should teach reading" is not a thesis. [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Singular.** "We need to fix housing, healthcare, and education" is three theses. [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Provable in 750 words.** [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Not a question.** [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Front-loaded.** The thesis appears in the first paragraph. [src: op-ed-writing]
- Op-eds are not evergreen. Every published op-ed has a reason it ran *this week*. Acceptable pegs: [src: op-ed-writing]
- A news event — a bill introduced, a court ruling, an election result [src: op-ed-writing]
- An anniversary [src: op-ed-writing]
- A data release [src: op-ed-writing]
- A counter to recent coverage [src: op-ed-writing]
- The op-ed "why now" is **why this argument matters this week**, not "why I'm releasing this product this week." [src: op-ed-writing]
- Forms of authority editors accept: [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Direct professional experience.** "I spent fifteen years as an immigration attorney." [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Subject of the issue.** "I am one of the 8 million Americans whose student loans are in default." [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Reporting access.** "I have spent the last six months interviewing the engineers who designed the system." [src: op-ed-writing]
- Forms of authority that fail: [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Generic credentials.** "I am a thought leader in this space." [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Title without specifics.** "As a CEO, I want to say..." [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Hook + thesis** (80–120 words). One concrete image, anecdote, or fact; the thesis in the last sentence. [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Why now** (60–100 words). The news peg. [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Authority** (40–80 words). Why the reader should listen to you. [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Evidence beat 1** (80–120 words). The first reason the thesis is correct. [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Evidence beat 2** (80–120 words). The second reason. [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Counter-argument and rebuttal** (100–150 words). The strongest objection, named and answered. [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Stakes / consequence** (60–100 words). What happens if we ignore this. [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Call to action / kicker** (50–100 words). The specific thing the reader should do. [src: op-ed-writing]
- The piece must name the strongest objection to your thesis and answer it. [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Strawman counter.** Picking a weak version of the opposing view. [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Both-sides-ism.** Treating the counter so generously you've made the opposing case better than your own. [src: op-ed-writing]
- Evidence in an op-ed is brutally selective. You have room for 2–4 evidence claims at most. Each one must be: [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Concrete.** A number, a named case, a specific policy. [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Recent.** Data from the last 1–3 years. [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Citable.** Every factual claim must be checkable. [src: op-ed-writing]
- Op-eds are written in **first person, conversational-but-controlled prose**. No jargon. No hedging escalators. No headers. No bullet lists. [src: op-ed-writing]
- Every op-ed ends with a **specific actionable claim**: [src: op-ed-writing]
- A policy that should pass or fail. [src: op-ed-writing]
- A practice an industry should adopt or abandon. [src: op-ed-writing]
- An institution that should change a specific procedure. [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Submit the full piece, not a pitch.** [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Subject line.** "Op-ed submission: [4-7 word headline]." [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Bio.** 25–40 words at the bottom. [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Expect silence.** Standard expectation is no response within 3 business days = pass. [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Topic:** Database security audits at small companies. [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Thesis:** "Small SaaS companies should be required by their cyber-insurance carriers to run quarterly database audits." [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Why now:** Recent breach at [named company] traced to an un-audited database. [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Evidence beats:** (1) Audit findings data — % of un-audited dbs with critical flaws. (2) Cost comparison — quarterly audit vs. one breach. [src: op-ed-writing]
- **Counter:** "This is regulatory overreach." Answer: Insurance is private; carriers already underwrite for fire suppression. [src: op-ed-writing]
- **CTA:** Insurance industry should adopt the standard at the June meeting. [src: op-ed-writing]
- **The "we need a conversation" piece.** Ends with a call for dialogue instead of an actionable claim. [src: op-ed-writing]
- **The five-thesis piece.** Tries to argue about five things in 800 words. [src: op-ed-writing]
- **The disguised press release.** "Our company has been working on this issue for years..." [src: op-ed-writing]
- **The strawman counter.** [src: op-ed-writing]
- **The evergreen piece.** No news peg. [src: op-ed-writing]
- **The 1,400-word "short" version.** If you can't get it to 800, you don't have one argument. [src: op-ed-writing]

- description: Annual shareholder letters, founder updates, and "state of the company" letters in the Buffett / Bezos / Stripe lineage. [src: founder-letter-writing]

- A founder letter is the annual public document a CEO or co-founder writes directly to owners — shareholders, users, or the general "fellow travelers" audience — to account for the year, reaffirm operating principles, admit mistakes, and frame what comes next. It is the genre Warren Buffett perfected at Berkshire Hathaway (1977–present), Jeff Bezos institutionalized at Amazon (1997–2020), and Patrick and John Collison adopted at Stripe (2019–present). [src: founder-letter-writing]
- The form is distinct from: [src: founder-letter-writing]
- An internal executive memo (which talks down the org chart, not out to owners) [src: founder-letter-writing]
- A press release or marketing post (which is selling, not reporting) [src: founder-letter-writing]
- An op-ed (which argues a public-interest point, not company-specific accountability) [src: founder-letter-writing]
- A whitepaper (which makes a technical or policy case, not a stewardship report) [src: founder-letter-writing]
- What makes a founder letter work is **candor**, **operating principles that repeat year over year**, and a **long-horizon frame** ("Day 1," "10-year zoom-out") that lets the reader weigh the current year against the company's deeper trajectory. [src: founder-letter-writing]
- Write as if to an intelligent non-specialist who owns shares and deserves the truth in plain English. Pronoun is "we" or "your company," never "the corporation." [src: founder-letter-writing]
- Three beats: (1) Where we are — year's results in plain terms. (2) What we learned — what went wrong, what surprised us. (3) Where we're going — unchanging principles plus bets for next 5–10 years. [src: founder-letter-writing]
- Bezos re-attached the 1997 letter to every subsequent letter for 20 years. Buffett restates Berkshire's "owner-related business principles" nearly every letter. Repetition is a feature. [src: founder-letter-writing]
- Name a specific mistake. Explain why you made it. Say what you changed. Vague self-criticism ("we have work to do") does not count. [src: founder-letter-writing]
- Amazon's "It's still Day 1." Buffett's 10- and 20-year per-share book value comparison. Pick a frame, stick to it, refer to it in every letter. [src: founder-letter-writing]
- Bezos's 2007 frame: missionaries paradoxically make more money than mercenaries trying to flip stock. [src: founder-letter-writing]
- Treat capital allocation as the most important decision the CEO makes that year. [src: founder-letter-writing]
- Pick 3–5 metrics that genuinely run the business and report them every year. Amazon: free cash flow per share. Stripe: total volume processed. Berkshire: operating earnings and per-share book value. [src: founder-letter-writing]
- Buffett uses short transitions and conversational rhythm. Avoid corporate passive voice and AI-isms. [src: founder-letter-writing]
- End with a signature and a date. Two co-founders sign together if the company is co-founded. [src: founder-letter-writing]
- To our shareholders / users / fellow owners, [src: founder-letter-writing]
- Anchor year in one sentence. Headline result + headline disappointment. [src: founder-letter-writing]
- 3–5 operating metrics, reported the same way every year. [src: founder-letter-writing]
- One named, specific mistake. The cost. The change. [src: founder-letter-writing]
- 4–8 things the company will always do and will never do. [src: founder-letter-writing]
- 2–4 bets for the next 5–10 years. [src: founder-letter-writing]
- Thank-you. Signed sign-off with founder name(s) and date. [src: founder-letter-writing]
- PR-spin letter (every metric reframed as a win) [src: founder-letter-writing]
- Earnings-call regurgitation [src: founder-letter-writing]
- Mission-statement-as-letter [src: founder-letter-writing]
- First-year-only candor [src: founder-letter-writing]
- Ghostwritten throughout [src: founder-letter-writing]
- No recurring frame [src: founder-letter-writing]
- Cute over clear [src: founder-letter-writing]
- No signature, no date [src: founder-letter-writing]
- AI-flavored prose ("leverage," "robust," "comprehensive") [src: founder-letter-writing]
- Hiding the mistake in a footnote [src: founder-letter-writing]
- **Founder letter vs executive memo?** Founder letter if audience is owners/public and cadence is annual. [src: founder-letter-writing]
- **How long?** 1,500 words minimum. 4,000 ceiling. Bezos averaged ~2,500. [src: founder-letter-writing]
- **First-person singular or plural?** Singular ("I") for honesty section. Plural ("we") for company actions. [src: founder-letter-writing]
- **Include forward guidance?** Specific numbers build credibility if you're willing to be held to them. [src: founder-letter-writing]
- **First-ever founder letter (year 1)?** Spine compresses. Aim 1,500–2,000 words. The 1997 Bezos letter is canonical. [src: founder-letter-writing]
- **Public vs private company?** Public letters carry SEC-adjacent obligations. [src: founder-letter-writing]
