- **Jeff Bezos — Amazon Shareholder Letters (1997–2020)** — 1997 founding letter, 2016 "Day 1," 2007 "missionaries vs mercenaries" [src: founder-letter-writing]
- **Patrick and John Collison — Stripe Annual Letters (2019–present)** — <https://stripe.com/newsroom/news/stripe-2023-update> [src: founder-letter-writing]
- **BriefCatch — "Five Ways to Write Like Warren Buffett"** — <https://briefcatch.com/articles/five-ways-to-write-like-warren-buffett/> [src: founder-letter-writing]
- **Toptal — "Pearls of Wisdom: The Best Shareholder Letters Nobody Is Reading"** [src: founder-letter-writing]
- Conceptual grounding for a data analysis effort. This skill answers the [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- *before-you-pick-a-tool* questions: what is data analysis, how does it relate to [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- neighboring fields, what kind of analysis is called for, what can the data [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- support given how it was measured, and what assumptions ride underneath. It does [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- not execute techniques — it scopes and frames them. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- This hub consolidates 37 foundations sub-skills as on-demand references — match [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- the task to the table and **Read the listed `references/<name>.md` before [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- answering deep questions**. The overview below is enough for framing and [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- scoping; load the reference when a question needs depth. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- Data analysis is the systematic process of inspecting, cleaning, transforming, and interpreting data to extract useful information, support conclusions, and aid decision-making. In practice it is bounded and goal-directed. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- Distinguish four neighboring terms — they overlap but are not synonyms: [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- **Data analysis** — the act of evaluating data to answer a defined question. The *process verb*. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- **Data analytics** — the broader practice/field built around analyzing data; typically about the past and present, with more elementary statistics. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- **Data science** — a wider, multidisciplinary field that *includes* analytics but reaches into ML, forecasting, and large-scale data engineering; more oriented toward predictive models. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- **Statistics** — the mathematical discipline of collecting, describing, and drawing inferences from data under uncertainty. Data analysis *uses* statistics as a toolkit. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- Rule of thumb: *data analysis is the activity; analytics is the field around it; data science extends it toward modeling and engineering; statistics supplies the inferential mathematics.* State which definition you are using. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- Analysis breaks a whole into parts; synthesis recombines parts into a new integrated whole or recommendation. Name which mode you are in to avoid presenting raw decomposition as a conclusion. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- **Quantitative analysis** operates on numeric measurements (interval and ratio scales). [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- **Qualitative analysis** operates on categorical/textual data (nominal and ordinal scales). The split is about method too, not just data type. Many efforts are mixed-method. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- The four form a maturity progression but are not strictly sequential per project. "Diagnostic" maps loosely onto **exploratory** work, but don't conflate the marketing taxonomy with Tukey's exploratory/confirmatory split. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- The de facto reference is **CRISP-DM** (six phases you can revisit): [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- **Business Understanding** — define the question and success criteria. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- **Data Understanding** — collect, describe, explore, verify quality. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- **Data Preparation** — select, clean, construct, integrate, format. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- **Modeling** — choose technique, build, assess. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- **Evaluation** — check against business goal; review process. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- **Deployment** — deliver, monitor, report. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- The phases are iterative, not a one-way pipeline. A lighter generic framing — define → collect → clean → analyze → interpret → communicate — works for non-mining work. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- **Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)** — Tukey's approach for summarizing a dataset's main characteristics, often with graphics, to *generate* hypotheses and check assumptions. Techniques: box plots, stem-and-leaf, histograms, scatter plots. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- **Confirmatory Data Analysis (CDA)** — classical hypothesis testing: pick a model *before* examining the data, then assess inference precision. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- Researchers need *both*. **Critical pitfall:** running exploratory and confirmatory analysis on the same data introduces systematic bias (double-dipping). Reserve a holdout or fresh sample for confirmation. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- Stevens' four levels (1946): [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- Nominal and ordinal are categorical/qualitative; interval and ratio are continuous/quantitative. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- **Common pitfalls:** computing a mean of ordinal codes (median is safer); treating an arbitrary numeric label as quantitative; forgetting interval scales lack a true zero (ratios are meaningless). **Know the controversy:** Velleman & Wilkinson (1993) and Luce (1997) contested Stevens' typology. Treat the level of measurement as a useful first filter, not an iron law. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- Data does not interpret itself. Every analysis rides on assumptions: representative sample, measurements meaning what labels claim, model preconditions holding. Two practices: [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- **State assumptions explicitly** and tie each to the analysis family and measurement level. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- **Match method to question and to data.** Misalignment — a prescriptive recommendation on descriptive data, or a mean on ordinal categories — is the most common foundational error. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- **Term check** — analysis, analytics, data science, or statistics? State the definition. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- **Family** — descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, or prescriptive? [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- **Mode** — exploratory or confirmatory? Don't mix on the same data. [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- **Lifecycle** — which CRISP-DM phase; what's next? [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- **Measurement** — what level is each variable; which statistics are licensed? [src: da-1-foundations-theory]
- **Assumptions** — what must be true; have I checked? [src: da-1-foundations-theory]

- **Taxonomy context:** Data Analysis > Data Analysis Lifecycle (Process) [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- The Data Analysis Lifecycle is the structured, iterative process that carries a project from an [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- initial business question through data acquisition, preparation, analysis, and interpretation, to [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- communicated and operationalized insight. No single canonical standard exists; instead several [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- well-adopted frameworks describe roughly the same phases with different emphasis and vocabulary. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Understanding the lifecycle helps analysts know which phase they are in, what must be true before [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- advancing, and when to loop back. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- -- [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- This hub consolidates 13 lifecycle sub-skills as on-demand reference files. When a task matches a [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- row, **Read the listed `references/<name>.md` before answering** — do not rely on this table alone [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- -- [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Raw data does not automatically answer questions. Each phase in the lifecycle performs a distinct [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Reduces ambiguity** — turning vague questions into measurable objectives. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Ensures fitness of data** — catching quality problems before they corrupt findings. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Separates concerns** — keeping exploratory work from confirmatory work, and analysis from [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Creates checkpoints** — natural gates where the team can confirm alignment with stakeholders [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- before investing further. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Without an explicit lifecycle, projects commonly suffer from scope creep, premature modeling on [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- dirty data, and findings that cannot be reproduced or deployed [Source 1, Source 2]. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- -- [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Developed in the late 1990s by Daimler-Chrysler, SPSS, and NCR. Still the most widely cited open [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- standard for data mining and analytics projects [Source 3]. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Six phases arranged in a cycle (the outer ring can restart after deployment): [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Arrows in the CRISP-DM diagram flow in both directions: unsatisfactory evaluation sends the team [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- back to modeling or data preparation; business understanding may be revised when data understanding [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- reveals the original question is unmeasurable [Source 3]. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Popularized by EMC's *Data Science and Big Data Analytics* book and Wiley's companion edition. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Six phases with a heavier emphasis on analytic sandboxes and operationalization [Source 4]: [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Discovery [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Data Preparation (ELT/ETL into sandbox) [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Model Planning [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Model Building [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Communicate Results [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Operationalize [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Distinct from CRISP-DM in that it explicitly names the sandbox as a prerequisite for phase 2, and [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- distinguishes "Model Planning" (choosing techniques) from "Model Building" (executing them). [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- A minimalist five-step mnemonic popular in academic data science courses: [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **O**btain [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **S**crub [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **E**xplore [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **M**odel [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- i**N**terpret [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Strengths: simple and memorable. Weaknesses: omits business framing (starts at "Obtain"), ignores [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- deployment, and treats the process as linear [Source 5]. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Published by Microsoft in 2017. Closest to CRISP-DM but adds explicit team roles, deliverable [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- templates, and agile sprint cadence. Five stages: Business Understanding → Data Acquisition and [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Understanding → Modeling → Deployment → Customer Acceptance [Source 5]. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- -- [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- The following synthesizes the phases common across frameworks into a single reference. The [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- `references/` files listed in the Sub-skill routing table cover each phase and framework in detail. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Input:** stakeholder intent, existing domain knowledge, prior analyses. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Output:** a written problem statement, success criteria (KPIs or evaluation metrics), and an [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- initial set of hypotheses. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- The team works with business owners to translate a vague goal ("improve customer retention") into [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- a concrete, measurable objective ("predict 30-day churn with precision ≥ 0.75 at recall ≥ 0.60"). [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Resources, timeline, and risks are assessed here. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Why it matters:** an ill-defined question cannot be answered with data. Changing the question [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- halfway through wastes preparation and modeling effort. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Pitfall:** treating this phase as a formality. Teams that skip or rush it often discover midway [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- through modeling that the available data cannot actually answer the question they care about [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Input:** problem statement, knowledge of available data sources. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Output:** a data inventory, quality assessment report, initial summary statistics, and a [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- decision on whether the data is sufficient to proceed. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- The team collects initial data, examines its structure and provenance, documents quality issues [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- (nulls, duplicates, encoding errors, date range gaps), and explores distributions and [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- inter-variable relationships. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Pitfall:** trusting that data labeled "clean" actually is clean. Source systems commonly have [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- undocumented conventions (e.g., sentinel values like -9999 for missing) that only domain knowledge [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- or careful profiling reveals [Source 1, Source 2]. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Input:** raw or semi-structured data, quality assessment. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Output:** an analysis-ready dataset (feature matrix + target variable, or cleaned tabular data [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- for descriptive work). [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- This phase typically consumes 60–80% of total project time. It includes: [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Cleaning:** removing or imputing nulls; correcting format inconsistencies; deduplication. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Transformation:** normalization, encoding categorical variables, date parsing, log transforms. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Integration:** joining tables across systems, resolving entity mismatches. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Feature engineering:** constructing derived columns that encode domain knowledge. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- An **analytic sandbox** — a compute environment with sufficient CPU, RAM, and storage to hold [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- working copies of the data — is often set up at the start of this phase [Source 4]. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Pitfall — data leakage:** features that encode information from the future (relative to the [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- prediction point) will inflate model performance metrics while producing a model that fails in [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- production. Any transformation that aggregates across the full dataset (e.g., computing a [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- z-score mean on both training and test rows) must be fit on training data only and applied to [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- test data [Source 6]. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Pitfall — aggressive outlier removal:** deleting extreme values simplifies modeling but can [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- remove the most informative signals, especially in anomaly detection or fraud contexts [Source 6]. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Input:** analysis-ready dataset, modeling plan (technique selection, validation strategy). [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Output:** trained model(s) or analytical findings with performance metrics. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- For **descriptive** and **exploratory** analysis, this phase produces summary statistics, [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- visualizations, and identified patterns. For **predictive** analysis, it produces one or more [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- fitted models with cross-validated performance estimates. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Model planning (choosing the technique family and validation design) is logically distinct from [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- model building (running training and tuning loops). Conflating them leads to technique choices [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- driven by familiarity rather than problem fit [Source 4]. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Pitfall — overfitting through hyperparameter tuning:** testing many parameter combinations [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- without a held-out test set causes the model to fit noise in the validation set, producing [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- strong validation scores that do not transfer to new data [Source 6]. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Input:** model or analysis output, success criteria from Phase 1. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Output:** judgment of whether findings meet the original objective; recommendation to proceed [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- The team compares model performance against the thresholds established in Phase 1, assesses [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- whether the findings have practical as well as statistical significance, and checks that the [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- model's behavior makes sense to domain experts (a sanity check that catches leakage and [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- labeling errors not surfaced by metrics alone). [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- If evaluation fails, the team loops back — usually to Phase 3 (more features, different [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- cleaning) or Phase 2 (additional data sources). [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Pitfall — confusing statistical and practical significance:** a result can be statistically [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- significant yet too small to matter operationally. A 0.1% improvement in click-through rate may [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- not justify the cost of implementation [Source 6]. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Input:** evaluated findings, audience knowledge of domain. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Output:** narrative report, dashboard, or presentation that conveys key findings and [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- recommended actions to decision-makers. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Effective communication requires translating technical outputs into business terms. The team [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- quantifies business value (revenue impact, cost savings, risk reduction), documents key [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- assumptions, acknowledges limitations, and prepares supporting materials (code, data [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- dictionaries, reproducibility documentation). [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Pitfall — model explainability missteps:** presenting SHAP plots or feature importances [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- without business context confuses rather than informs stakeholders. Explanation tools are most [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- useful when tied to a specific decision the audience must make [Source 6]. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Input:** approved findings or model, deployment environment specifications. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Output:** running system (scheduled report, API endpoint, embedded model), monitoring plan. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- The team deploys the model or analysis process so that stakeholders can regularly access results. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Pilot deployments in a controlled environment precede full rollout. Monitoring tracks whether [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- model performance degrades as data distributions shift over time. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Pitfall — ignoring concept drift:** a model trained on historical data may fail silently as [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- real-world behavior changes. Without a monitoring plan and retraining schedule, model staleness [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- goes undetected [Source 6]. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- -- [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- All frameworks represent the lifecycle as cyclic or iterative, not strictly linear. Common [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Evaluation → Data Preparation:** model fails to meet threshold; team engineers additional [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- features or acquires more data. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Modeling → Business Understanding:** the most predictive variables are ones the business [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- cannot act on; problem definition must be revised. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Communication → Problem Definition:** stakeholders raise a follow-up question not covered [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- by the original scope; a new project iteration begins. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- **Operationalization → Data Understanding:** production data differs from training data in [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- distribution; team must re-examine source systems. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Treating the lifecycle as strictly sequential is a recognized anti-pattern. Teams that refuse to [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- revisit earlier phases when evidence demands it produce analyses that are technically complete but [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- practically useless [Source 1, Source 5]. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- -- [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- These concerns apply across all phases rather than belonging to a single one: [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Every transformation applied to data should be recorded so that findings can be reproduced and [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- audited. Missing metadata about data origins is one of the top causes of unreproducible analyses [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Checkpoints between phases — presenting phase outputs to stakeholders before proceeding — catch [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- misalignment early. The cost of rework grows with each phase completed before a mismatch is [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- In TDSP, roles are explicitly assigned: project lead, data scientist, data engineer, solution [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- architect, and business analyst each own specific deliverables. In smaller teams one person [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- covers multiple roles, but the responsibilities remain distinct [Source 5]. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- Data collection and use must comply with applicable regulations (GDPR, HIPAA, etc.) and internal [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- data governance policies. These checks are easiest to apply at phase transitions, not after [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]

- **Scenario:** a retail company wants to reduce stockouts. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- At evaluation, the team discovers that weather features add noise rather than signal; they loop [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]
- back to Phase 3, drop those columns, and re-evaluate — a normal iteration, not a failure. [src: da-2-data-analysis-lifecycle]

- name: da-7-machine-learning [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- description: Curriculum reference for Machine Learning — section 7 of the data analysis curriculum. Covers the ML taxonomy (supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, self-supervised), bias-variance tradeoff and regularization, deep learning architectures (CNNs, RNNs, Transformers), foundation models and the 2026 LLM landscape (Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Llama 4, DeepSeek V3.2), hyperparameter tuning (Optuna, Ray Tune, BOHB, Bayesian optimization), evaluation methodology for both classical ML (precision/recall/F1, ROC-AUC, regression metrics) and LLMs (HELM, MMLU, MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena, SWE-bench), and MLOps (drift detection, train-serve skew, MLflow, W&B, feature stores). TRIGGER: ML taxonomy and learning paradigms; bias-variance, overfitting, regularization; CNN/RNN/Transformer selection; foundation model selection 2026; hyperparameter search strategy or tool choice; classification/regression/ranking/LLM eval metrics; drift monitors, train-serve skew, experiment tracking; curriculum review covering section 7. SKIP: pure statistical inference (use da-1-4); data cleaning/EDA (use da-4); post-train viz/reporting (use da-8/da-9); production prompt engineering (use prompt-engineering); RAG system architecture (use rag-architecture); MongoDB-specific ML/AI features (use mongodb-atlas-vector-search or mongodb-atlas-search). [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- when_to_use: Reviewing or teaching ML fundamentals; selecting a learning paradigm or architecture; choosing hyperparameter-tuning tooling; designing an evaluation harness for either a classical or LLM workload; standing up production monitoring (drift, skew, retraining triggers); comparing 2026 frontier models for a build-vs-buy decision. - -- [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Machine learning is the curriculum step where the analyst stops merely describing a sample and starts building a function that generalizes from data to unseen inputs. Section 6 (`da-6-statistical-modeling`) covered parametric statistical models grounded in explicit probabilistic assumptions. This section widens the lens to algorithms that learn flexible, often non-parametric mappings from data — and to the engineering scaffolding (tuning, evaluation, deployment, monitoring) that turns a trained model into a system that keeps working. [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- This skill is the curriculum reference for the seventh section of the data analysis path. It is intentionally broad: it sketches the territory and points to the deeper skills you should pull in for any specific build. [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- **Supervised learning.** Input–output pairs `(x, y)`. Sub-shapes: classification (discrete `y`) and regression (continuous `y`). [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- **Unsupervised learning.** No labels. Discovers clusters (k-means, DBSCAN, HDBSCAN), topics (LDA, NMF), manifolds (PCA, t-SNE, UMAP, autoencoders), density (KDE, GMM), or anomalies (isolation forest, one-class SVM). [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- **Reinforcement learning.** Agent → environment → reward; optimizes policy `pi(a | s)`. Modern flavors: PPO, GRPO, DQN. RLHF/RLAIF align LLMs. [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- **Self-supervised learning.** Labels constructed from the data: next-token prediction (GPT/Claude/Gemini), masked LM (BERT), masked patch (DINO/MAE), contrastive (CLIP). The engine behind every foundation model. [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Edge shapes: semi-supervised (small labeled + large unlabeled), active learning (model picks next labels). [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- `E[(y - f_hat(x))^2] = Bias[f_hat(x)]^2 + Var[f_hat(x)] + sigma^2` [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Bias (underfitting) drops with capacity; variance (overfitting) rises. Regularization, more data, and ensembling trade variance for some bias. The classical U-curve is an idealization — in over-parameterized regimes (most modern DL) test error follows "double descent": rises near the interpolation threshold, then falls again as capacity grows. [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- L1 (Lasso, feature selection), L2 (Ridge / weight decay, default in DL), ElasticNet, Dropout (ensemble averaging), early stopping, data augmentation (often the strongest), label smoothing, normalization layers. [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Linear/logistic regression, decision trees, random forests, gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost still win most tabular competitions in 2026), SVM, kNN, Naive Bayes. On tabular: start with a GBT. [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Grid-structured data. Convolution (weight sharing, translation equivariance), pooling, hierarchical feature learning. LeNet → AlexNet → VGG → ResNet (residual connections) → EfficientNet → ConvNeXt. Still competitive on edge devices, limited-data medical imaging, and as hybrid backbones. [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Sequential state `h_t = f(x_t, h_{t-1})`. Vanilla RNNs (vanishing gradients), LSTM (gated cell, workhorse 2014–2018), GRU (simpler, comparable), bidirectional. Mostly displaced by Transformers; still useful for streaming inference, tiny edge time-series, and as the conceptual ancestor of state-space models (Mamba, S4, S6) that scale linearly in sequence length. [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Transformer is the 2026 default, but consider inductive bias (CNNs encode locality), sequence length (attention is quadratic — sliding window/sparse/linear/SSMs win on long contexts), and latency budget (a 7B Transformer is overkill for keyword-spotting on a watch). [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- *Attention Is All You Need* (Vaswani et al., 2017). Per token: query `Q`, key `K`, value `V`. Attention = `softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V`. Multi-head runs several attention ops in parallel. Parallelizable training, one-hop long-range dependencies, modality-agnostic (text, images via ViT, audio via Whisper, proteins via AlphaFold). [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Pretrain large on broad data with self-supervision, adapt via: zero-shot prompting, few-shot in-context learning, fine-tuning (full, LoRA/QLoRA, DPO/KTO, RLHF/RLAIF), RAG, tool use / function calling. 2024–2026 era is agent-shaped systems built around pretrained foundations. [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Selection heuristics: agentic coding → Claude Opus 4.7; general reasoning → GPT-5.5; multimodal → Gemini 3.1 Pro; self-hosted → Llama 4; budget/high-volume → DeepSeek V3.2 or smaller specialists. Use LiteLLM/OpenRouter for per-request routing. Treat the LLM as replaceable, not a vendor commitment. [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Manual, grid (only ≤3 hyperparams), random (dominates grid when few hyperparams matter), Bayesian optimization (GP or TPE + EI/UCB acquisition, default for 10–100 trials), HyperBand (successive halving), BOHB (BO + HyperBand, production default for DL), PBT (population-based, learns schedules). [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Optuna (Python-native, TPE + pruning, individual default), Ray Tune (distributed, all algorithms above), Weights & Biases Sweeps (if W&B is your tracker), KerasTuner/AutoGluon/FLAML (AutoML), Vizier/SigOpt (hosted). [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Tune on validation, never on test. Nested CV when small. Log-uniform LR/weight decay. Tune learning rate first. Cap wall-clock per trial. Re-tune on dataset/architecture/optimizer change. Save trial history for `get_param_importances`. [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Train/val/test (test touched once). k-fold CV, stratified k-fold (imbalanced), group k-fold (leakage by group ID), time-series splits (never shuffle), nested CV (small data + many hyperparams). [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Accuracy (misleading on imbalance). Precision `TP/(TP+FP)` — optimize when false positives expensive. Recall `TP/(TP+FN)` — optimize when false negatives expensive. F1 harmonic mean. F-beta. ROC-AUC (insensitive to class balance). PR-AUC (preferred when positive class rare). Log-loss / cross-entropy (proper scoring rule). Calibration plots + Brier score. Macro/weighted/micro F1 for multi-class. [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- MAE (robust), RMSE (penalizes outliers), MAPE / sMAPE, R^2, quantile / pinball loss. [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- MAP@k, NDCG@k, MRR, Hit-rate@k. [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- MMLU (saturated — frontier >90%), MT-Bench (multi-turn, LLM-as-judge), HELM (Stanford CRFM; accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, efficiency), Chatbot Arena (Elo from pairwise preference), SWE-bench / SWE-bench Verified / SWE-bench Pro (real GitHub issues; Claude Opus 4.7 leads Verified at 87.6%), HumanEval / MBPP / LiveCodeBench, GPQA / ARC-AGI / FrontierMath (not yet saturated), domain-specific (MedQA, LegalBench, FinanceBench, MMMU). [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Pros: fast, scalable. Cons: position bias, self-preference, verbosity bias, rubric drift. Mitigations: randomize position; use different judge family than model under test; calibrate against small human-labeled gold set; prefer pairwise to absolute scoring. Tools: G-Eval, DeepEval, Patronus, Braintrust. [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- MLflow (OSS default), Weights & Biases (commercial), Neptune.ai / Comet, DVC + Git (small teams). Log: code hash, dataset hash, hyperparams, environment, train/val metrics, artifact, evaluation report. [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Covariate shift `P(x)` changes, concept drift `P(y|x)` changes, label drift `P(y)` changes. Detection: PSI, JS divergence, KL divergence, KS test, chi-squared, Wasserstein. When labels arrive late, monitor proxies (prediction distribution, confidence). Tools: Evidently AI (best OSS), WhyLabs, Arize, Fiddler. W&B 2023 data: 62% of orgs see meaningful degradation within 12 months without monitoring. [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Distinct from drift (drift = world changes; skew = code inconsistency). Feature parity (use a feature store: Feast, Tecton, Hopsworks). Schema parity (TFX SchemaGen, Great Expectations, Pandera). Lookup parity. Time-leakage (use as-of timestamps). [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Shadow, canary, A/B (tied to business metric), multi-armed bandit, champion/challenger. [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Scheduled, drift-triggered, performance-triggered, continuous. [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Pinned deps (uv.lock/poetry.lock/conda-lock), hashed datasets (DVC, LakeFS, Delta), fixed seeds (not bit-identical on GPU), containerized training, MLflow run recording. [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Tuning on the test set [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Mean accuracy on imbalanced data [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Different splits across compared models [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Shuffling a time series [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Ignoring calibration [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Validating the model in isolation rather than the pipeline [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Vibes-only LLM eval [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Treating the LLM as a fixed dependency [src: da-7-machine-learning]
- Skipping monitoring because "it works in dev" [src: da-7-machine-learning]

- This skill covers the **third stage** of the data analysis curriculum: getting data into a form the [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- analysis can operate on, and constructing a sample that supports valid inference about the target [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- population. The two activities are intertwined: the choice of source constrains what sampling design [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- is possible, and the sampling plan determines which sources are acceptable. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- A common mistake is to treat acquisition as a logistics problem — "just pull the data" — and discover [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- only at the analysis stage that the population was wrong, the sample frame had coverage gaps, the [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- schema drifted mid-pull, or the file format made the planned query infeasible. This stage owns the [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- responsibility for catching these failures *before* they contaminate downstream work. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]

- -- [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- Three orthogonal axes characterize any source. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Primary data** is collected directly to answer the current question (surveys you designed, interviews, sensor data, A/B exposure logs). **Secondary data** was collected by someone else for a different purpose and is reused (Census/BLS, commercial panels, academic archives, third-party API exports). Strong analyses combine both. The trade-off is purpose-fit (primary) versus speed/scale/cost (secondary). [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Structured**: row/column tabular with fixed schema (relational DBs, warehouses, CSV/Parquet). [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Semi-structured**: hierarchical/self-describing (JSON, XML, logs, NoSQL docs, Avro/Protobuf). [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Unstructured**: free-form text, images, audio, video; requires feature extraction (OCR, ASR, embeddings) or a model interface. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- Vector embeddings and LLMs reduced the cost of operating on unstructured data, but the closer a source is to structured form, the cheaper and more deterministic the analysis. Schema-on-read (data lakes) defers structure to query time; schema-on-write (warehouses) enforces it at load time. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- Internal sources (production DBs, event logs, CRM, telemetry) are more reliable and granular but may not generalize. External sources (APIs, public datasets, scraped pages, panels) broaden the population but add coverage uncertainty, licensing risk, and schema drift. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- -- [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **REST** (HTTP+JSON): broadest compatibility, HTTP caching, OpenAPI contracts. Downside: over/under-fetching. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **GraphQL**: client asks for exactly the fields it needs; eliminates over/under-fetch. Downside: HTTP caching is harder, rate limiting via query-cost budgets, per-field authorization. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **gRPC** (HTTP/2 + Protobuf): code-generated clients, multiplexed streaming, 3-10x smaller payloads. Best for internal service-to-service traffic. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- Common 2026 pattern: REST public, GraphQL BFF/frontend, gRPC internal. For acquisition you mostly meet REST and GraphQL. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **API key**: shared secret in a header; identifies the app, not a user; TLS only; rotate. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **OAuth 2.0**: access + refresh tokens. Authorization Code with PKCE for user apps; Client Credentials for service-to-service. Validate scopes server-side. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **JWT**: signed bearer token; stateless verification; keep short-lived; verify the `alg` header (avoid `alg: none`). [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **mTLS / certificate auth**: high-trust internal/financial/healthcare APIs. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- Treat refresh tokens as the most sensitive secret: encrypt at rest, rotate on suspicion, log every refresh. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Offset/limit** and **page number**: simple but break under concurrent writes. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Cursor-based** (opaque token): stable under writes; preferred for high-volume APIs. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Keyset/seek** (sort key + tiebreaker): cheap on indexed columns. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- Persist the cursor after every page so a partial failure can resume. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- Fixed window, sliding window, token bucket, cost-based (GraphQL). Build clients with exponential backoff on `429`/`503`, respecting `Retry-After`. Cap retries. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- Inverse of polling. Always verify the signature header (HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body) before trusting the payload; treat unsigned webhooks as untrusted input. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- -- [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- Acquisition without a contract. Use only when there is no API and the legal/ethical posture is sound. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **`requests` + BeautifulSoup**: static HTML, no JS. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Scrapy**: full crawling framework (concurrency, throttling, retries, pipelines). [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Playwright / Selenium**: headless browsers for JS-rendered or auth-gated pages; slower. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **TLS-impersonation tooling** (`curl_cffi`): a signal the site does not want to be scraped. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- As of 2026 the hiQ v. LinkedIn line: scraping publicly accessible data generally does not violate the CFAA. But the full risk surface includes CFAA (bypassing auth/access controls), Terms of Service (civil claims), copyright (bulk reproduction), GDPR/CCPA (personal data, stricter in the EU), and EU database rights. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- Respect `robots.txt`; set a descriptive `User-Agent` with contact info; throttle (≤1 req/sec for small sites); cache aggressively; avoid PII without a lawful basis; never bypass authentication, paywalls, or rate-limiting controls. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- -- [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- `SELECT *` into CSV/Parquet/Avro. Simple for cold historical data; anti-pattern for large operational tables. Use native utilities (`mongoexport`, `pg_dump`, `mysqldump --single-transaction`, `bq extract`, Redshift UNLOAD). [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- Connectors (Kafka Connect JDBC, Airbyte, Fivetran, Meltano) poll on a schedule, identifying changes by `updated_at` or auto-increment `id`. Gaps: hard deletes invisible, backdated updates missed, high-frequency polling stresses the source, schema changes break connectors. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- Read the transaction log (MySQL binlog, PostgreSQL WAL, MongoDB oplog/change streams, SQL Server CDC). Debezium is the dominant open-source platform. Advantages: captures inserts/updates/**deletes**, every intermediate state, minimal source load, sub-second latency, stable per-row ordering. Typical pipeline: initial snapshot, then stream the log from the snapshot's LSN/position; persist resume tokens/offsets for recovery. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- -- [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Kafka** (MSK, Confluent, Redpanda): de facto standard, open protocol, strongest ecosystem, highest throughput. Best for multi-cloud and complex stream processing. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Kinesis Data Streams**: AWS-native, shard-based; 2026 trend favors MSK for new AWS deployments unless small/serverless. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Pub/Sub**: GCP-native, serverless, regional exactly-once (2024). [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- At-most-once / at-least-once / exactly-once. Kafka: idempotent producers + transactions API. Kinesis: KCL checkpoints + idempotent downstream. Pub/Sub: regional exactly-once API. Practical guidance: make consumers idempotent, default to at-least-once, invoke exactly-once only when duplicates are costlier than the coordination. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- Partition key sets parallelism and ordering (same key → same partition → in-order). Hot partitions are the primary failure mode. Handle back-pressure at the consumer: buffer (memory), drop (loss), or pause the source (propagation). [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- -- [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **ETL**: transform before load (Informatica, Talend, SSIS, Glue). [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **ELT**: load raw, transform in-warehouse (Snowflake/BigQuery/Redshift/Databricks). Default 2026 pattern; keeps raw history, decouples ingest from transformation. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Ingest/EL**: Fivetran, Airbyte, Meltano (Singer), Stitch. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Transform/T**: dbt (needs an orchestrator; doesn't extract/load). [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Orchestration**: Airflow, Dagster, Prefect, Mage. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Warehouse**: Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Redshift, ClickHouse, MotherDuck. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Reverse ETL**: Hightouch, Census. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Catalog/governance**: DataHub, OpenMetadata, Atlan, Collibra. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Observability**: Monte Carlo, Bigeye, Lightup, Soda. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- Small all-SaaS team: Fivetran + dbt Cloud + Snowflake + Hightouch (watch Fivetran per-MAR pricing). [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- Mid-size open-source: Airbyte + dbt Core + Snowflake/BigQuery + Airflow. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- Code-first team: Meltano + dbt Core + Airflow + Snowflake/BigQuery. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- -- [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- The operational list of population members that can actually be reached — rarely identical to the target population. This gap creates **coverage bias**. Document the frame explicitly at design time; if it doesn't match the population, no sample size or design can fix the resulting bias. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- Bias is systematic distortion; it does **not** shrink with sample size. Forms: nonresponse, acquiescence (yea-saying), social desirability, recall, order effects, mode effects, selection bias. Mitigations: track response rate, reverse-coded items, anonymous administration, randomize order, demographic benchmarking. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- Pilot with 10-20 respondents; use vertical scales for mobile; cap length (completion falls past 5-7 min); use attention checks sparingly; pre-register the analysis plan for high-stakes work. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- -- [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- Every unit has a known, non-zero selection probability — the only basis for valid frequentist inference. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **SRS**: equal probability `1/N`; the reference design. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Stratified**: sample within mutually exclusive strata. Proportional allocation (size-proportional) vs Neyman optimal allocation (size × stdev; minimizes variance for fixed `n`). [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Cluster**: randomly select clusters, then sample within. Loses precision vs SRS (design effect; effective sample size `n / DEFF`). [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Systematic**: every `k`th element after a random start; biased if the frame has periodicity matching `k`. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- Selection probability unknown or zero; treat as exploratory unless you can model selection. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Convenience**: whoever is at hand. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Quota**: hit target subgroup counts; biased on non-quota dimensions. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Snowball**: respondents refer others; good for hidden populations. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- **Purposive/judgment**: researcher selects informative units; fine for case studies, never for population estimates. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]
- Modern hybrid: **online panel + post-stratification weighting** — weight non-probability panel responses to population marginals. Reduces but does not eliminate selection bias on outcome-correlated dimensions not in the weighting variables. [src: da-3-data-acquisition-sampling]

- **Taxonomy context:** Data Analysis > Data Visualization [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- Data visualization is the principled translation of data into visual form so that the human visual system — which is fast, parallel, and pattern-seeking — can extract structure that the verbal system alone cannot. Done well, a chart compresses a table of numbers into a single glance and surfaces the comparison the audience needs to make a decision. Done poorly, it distorts, distracts, or actively deceives. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- Two modes recur: **exploratory visualization** (analyst draws many quick charts to find something; iteration speed > polish; matplotlib, seaborn, ggplot2, altair) and **explanatory visualization** (analyst has found the point and needs the audience to see it; polish, narrative, accessibility > iteration speed; Tableau / Power BI dashboards, D3 / Plotly for web, publication matplotlib / ggplot2). [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- Encodings ranked by accuracy of magnitude estimation (most to least accurate): position along common scale > position along non-aligned scales > length / direction / angle > area > volume / curvature > shading / color saturation / hue. Implication: encode the focal comparison along position. Reach for area, angle, or color only when position is taken or the chart's job is pattern recognition rather than precise estimation. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Data-ink ratio.** Maximize ratio of data-ink to total ink. Erase non-data-ink and redundant data-ink within reason. Heuristic, not commandment — accessibility and clarity can override. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Chartjunk.** Unnecessary elements (3D bevels, animated gradients, decorative iconography, moiré). [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Small multiples.** Grid of the same chart type repeated for each level of a categorical variable, with shared scales. Replaces stacked bars and multi-series spaghetti. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Sparklines.** Word-sized, axis-free trend lines inline with prose or next to a value. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Graphical integrity / Lie Factor.** (Visual change shown) / (actual change in data). Should be ~1. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Preattentive attributes.** Color, size, position, orientation are processed by visual system in ~200ms, before conscious attention. Use to direct attention to the one thing the chart is about; grey out the rest. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Decluttering.** Remove border, gridlines, redundant tick marks. Soften axis labels. Push legend onto the line. Apply preattentive emphasis last. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Action titles.** Title states the finding ("Revenue declined 12% in Q3, driven by APAC"), not a description ("Quarterly Revenue"). [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Few's dashboard rules.** Single screen, no scroll. Inverted pyramid of detail. Encode by importance. Consistent encoding across panels. Context always (target, prior period, sparkline). No gratuitous decoration. Refresh timestamp on screen. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **BAN tiles (Big-Ass Numbers).** Large headline KPI value with small trend indicator or sparkline. Dashboard analog of an action title. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- Proximity, similarity, enclosure, closure, continuity, connection — describe how the visual system groups elements. Turn data-ink abstractions into concrete layout decisions: removing a border works (closure), small multiples scan quickly (similarity + proximity), stray red dot pops (similarity-violation). [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Sequential palettes** — single-hue ramp for continuous ordered data with no meaningful midpoint. Viridis (perceptually uniform, colorblind-safe), Cividis (optimized for protanopia / deuteranopia), Magma, Inferno, Plasma, ColorBrewer Blues / Greens. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Diverging palettes** — two contrasting hues meeting at a neutral midpoint, for continuous data with a meaningful reference. ColorBrewer RdBu, BrBG, PiYG, PuOr. Midpoint must match the reference value, not dataset median. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Categorical palettes** — distinct unordered hues for nominal categories. Hard limit ~6-8 hues. Okabe-Ito (Wong palette, colorblind-safe), ColorBrewer Set2 / Dark2, Tableau 10. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Never color alone.** Pair with shape, pattern, direct label, or position (WCAG 1.4.1). [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Grayscale test.** Viridis and Cividis pass; jet / rainbow does not. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Avoid rainbow / jet.** Not perceptually uniform; distorts magnitude reads. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- Alt-text template: `[chart type] of [what is measured] by [grouping]. [Headline finding].` [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- Chart = data + aesthetic mapping (x, y, color, size, shape) + geom + stat (identity, bin, count, smooth, boxplot, density) + position adjustment (identity, dodge, stack, fill, jitter) + scales + coordinate system + faceting. The named-chart taxonomy (bar / pie / line) is a cache of common grammar configurations. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Python notebook / static:** matplotlib (imperative foundation, max control), seaborn (statistical convenience), altair (Vega-Lite declarative), plotly express, plotnine (ggplot2 in Python), bokeh. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **R:** ggplot2 (the layered grammar reference), lattice. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **JS interactive:** D3 (low-level, max control), Observable Plot (high-level by D3 team), Vega-Lite (declarative JSON), Plotly.js (WebGL), Chart.js (simple), ECharts (enterprise dashboards). [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **BI / dashboard platforms:** Tableau (long-time category leader), Power BI (Microsoft ecosystem default), Looker Studio (free, Google ecosystem), Looker enterprise (semantic-modeling-first, LookML), Metabase (open source, easy for non-technical), Apache Superset (open source, enterprise, 40+ connectors), MongoDB Atlas Charts (native to Atlas, document-aware). [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Selection heuristic:** notebook / paper → matplotlib / seaborn / ggplot2; public web → plotly / observable plot / vega-lite / D3; dashboard → BI tool; product surface → plotly / ECharts / React-charting library bound to design system. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- Single screen, no scroll. Inverted pyramid of detail (BANs top, trends middle, detail bottom). Encode by importance. Consistent encoding across panels. Context always. No gratuitous decoration. Color carries meaning, not personality. Drill-down paths, not detail-everywhere. Refresh cadence visible on screen. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Truncated y-axis on a bar chart** — bars encode magnitude; truncating lies. (Line charts exempt when range is small relative to absolute value; state baseline.) [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **3D charts** — distort perception, add chartjunk. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Pie charts with > 3 slices** — angle and area are low-accuracy encodings. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Dual y-axis charts** — independent scales fabricate apparent relationships. Use small multiples, connected scatter, or index normalization instead. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Rainbow / jet colormap** — not perceptually uniform. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Color as only encoding** — fails for colorblind viewers. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Spaghetti line charts** — small multiples or grey-out non-focal instead. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Choropleth of raw counts** — dominated by population. Use rates or cartogram. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Cumulative-only line hiding rate** — show daily/weekly delta alongside cumulative. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Mixing absolute and relative scales without labeling.** [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Stacked bars when audience must compare segments** — use grouped bar or small multiples. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Bubble charts encoding diameter instead of area.** [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Mercator for global statistical maps** — use equal-area (Robinson, Equal Earth, Mollweide). [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- **Animated bar-chart races** — fun to watch, terrible for comparing specific values. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- Write the headline finding as a one-sentence claim before touching the chart tool. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- Identify audience and medium. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- Pick the intent (comparison / composition / distribution / relationship / temporal / spatial). [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- Pick chart type (apply Cleveland & McGill; avoid pie / 3D / dual-axis unless required). [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- Draft and declutter (remove border, soften gridlines, push legend onto line). [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- Apply preattentive emphasis (grey for non-focal, color for focal, direct labels). [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- Write the action title (the headline claim, not a description). [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- Verify graphical integrity (zero baseline on bars, 100% pie sum, no 3D, no dual axis). [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- Accessibility pass (contrast, alt text, color-alone check, grayscale test, screen-reader description). [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- Show to someone who has not seen the data; if the headline does not land within 5 seconds, iterate. [src: da-8-data-visualization]
- Tufte 1983 *Visual Display of Quantitative Information*; Tufte 1990 *Envisioning Information*; Few 2013 *Information Dashboard Design*; Few 2009 *Now You See It*; Knaflic 2015 *Storytelling with Data*; Cairo 2016 *The Truthful Art*; Cairo 2019 *How Charts Lie*; Wilkinson 2005 *Grammar of Graphics*; Wickham 2016 *ggplot2*; Munzner 2014 *Visualization Analysis and Design*; Cleveland & McGill 1984 *Graphical Perception* (JASA 79); Wickham 2010 *A Layered Grammar of Graphics* (JCGS 19); Heer & Bostock 2010 *Crowdsourcing Graphical Perception* (CHI); ColorBrewer 2.0 (colorbrewer2.org); Viridis (matplotlib documentation); Cividis (Nuñez Anderton Renslow 2018 PLoS One); Wong 2011 *Color blindness* (Nature Methods, Okabe-Ito); W3C WCAG 2.2; Lundgard & Satyanarayan 2022 *Accessible Visualization via Natural Language Descriptions* (IEEE VIS). - **Taxonomy context:** Data Analysis > Reporting and Communication [src: da-9-reporting-communication]
- Reporting and Communication is the phase that converts analytical work into decisions. Every upstream phase — problem framing, data preparation, modeling, evaluation — is wasted if the audience cannot understand the finding, cannot trust its rigor, and cannot act on the recommendation. Reporting is not a write-up of what the analyst did; it is an argument constructed for a specific decision-maker. [src: da-9-reporting-communication]

- The discipline of separating "normal" from "not normal" when you mostly only have examples of normal. This skill covers the working methods, when each fits, and the gotchas that bite teams in production. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- Activate when the user: [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- is looking for unusual rows / events / time points [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- is setting up monitoring with alerting on a metric stream [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- is building fraud / fault / intrusion detection [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- needs to compare methods (Isolation Forest vs LOF vs autoencoder) [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- needs streaming anomaly detection [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- needs to distinguish data drift from anomalies [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- Forecasting → `da-analytical-methods` (references/da-15-forecasting.md) [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- Supervised classification on labeled fraud → `da-analytical-methods` (references/da-7-machine-learning.md) [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- Outlier spot-check during cleaning → `da-analytical-methods` (references/da-4-data-cleaning-preparation.md or references/da-5-exploratory-data-analysis.md) [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- Causal investigation → `da-analytical-methods` (references/da-12-ab-testing-causal-inference.md) [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- -- [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- Before picking a method, name the problem type. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- Methods don't transfer cleanly between types. A z-score finds point anomalies but misses contextual and collective ones. STL-residual analysis handles contextual time-series anomalies. Sequence models or windowed statistics handle collective. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- -- [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- `z = (x - μ) / σ`. Flag if `|z| > 3`. Assumes approximately normal; sensitive to the very outliers you're trying to find (μ and σ get pulled). [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- `z_mod = 0.6745 × (x - median) / MAD`. Flag if `|z_mod| > 3.5` (Iglewicz & Hoaglin 1993). Robust to outliers because median and MAD don't move much. **Use this instead of plain z-score.** [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- Tests whether the single most extreme point is an outlier under a normality assumption. Tests one at a time; for multiple outliers use ESD. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- Iteratively tests up to k suspected outliers in a normal sample. Computes test statistic for the most extreme point, removes it, repeats. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- `lower = Q1 - 1.5·IQR`, `upper = Q3 + 1.5·IQR`. Used by boxplots. Robust to outliers, no distribution assumption, but not statistically calibrated. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- **When to reach for each:** modified z-score for clean tabular numerical data, IQR for a quick exploratory boxplot, ESD for the formal "are there k outliers in this sample" answer, Grubbs only for the single-outlier case. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- -- [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- **CUSUM** (Cumulative Sum) — accumulates deviations from the target. Triggers when the cumulative sum exceeds a threshold. Best for small persistent shifts. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- **EWMA** (Exponentially Weighted Moving Average) — exponentially-weighted average crosses control limits. Smoother than CUSUM; good for medium drifts. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- **Shewhart 3σ** — the classic; sensitive to single large jumps but slow on small persistent shifts. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- These come from manufacturing SPC (statistical process control) but transfer to any monitored stream. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- When the *distribution* changes, not just one point. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- Use change-point detection when "anomaly" really means "this segment is from a different distribution than the previous segment." [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- Decompose the series via STL (`statsmodels.tsa.seasonal.STL`) into trend + seasonality + residual. Apply a point-anomaly method to the residual. This automatically handles seasonality, so you don't false-alarm on every December spike. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- -- [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- Distance to the k-th nearest neighbor. Big distance = anomaly. Simple, works in low dimensions, scales badly past ~50 features. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- A point's anomaly score is the ratio of its local density to the local density of its neighbors. Catches anomalies in non-uniform-density data where global thresholds fail. Implemented in scikit-learn. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- Density-based clustering — anything not in a dense region is a "noise" point. Outlier detection is a free side-effect. Sensitive to `eps` and `min_samples`. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- -- [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- Build random trees by randomly picking a feature and a random split until each point is isolated. Anomalies have shorter average path lengths because random splits separate them quickly. Linear time, constant memory, **the default for tabular numerical data above a few features**. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- Hyperparameters: `n_estimators=100` (default fine), `max_samples=256` (canonical), `contamination` (your guess at anomaly rate; affects threshold). [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- Fixes a known IF flaw: standard IF only splits on axes, biasing it on rotated data. EIF allows arbitrary hyperplane splits. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- -- [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- Fits a boundary that encloses most of the training data. Anomalies fall outside the boundary. Sensitive to the `nu` parameter and kernel choice. Slow on > ~10k samples. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- Assumes Gaussian distribution; fits a covariance matrix; distance from the center weighted by the inverse covariance. Works on roughly elliptical data. `EllipticEnvelope` in scikit-learn uses robust covariance estimation (MCD — Minimum Covariance Determinant) so it isn't pulled by the very outliers you're trying to find. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- -- [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- Train an autoencoder on normal data. At inference, reconstruction error = anomaly score. Works because the model never learned to reconstruct rare patterns. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- Same idea but with a probabilistic latent space. The likelihood of the data under the model is the anomaly score. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- Train a GAN on normal data. Anomaly score from the difference between the input and the closest sample the generator can produce. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- 2024-2026 frontier. Models like Anomaly-Transformer, TranAD, and time-series foundation models (Chronos, Moirai, TimesFM) can be adapted for anomaly detection by computing prediction error or likelihood under the model. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- **When deep learning is overkill:** if your data is < 10 features and < 100k rows, Isolation Forest or LOF will outperform a neural net while running in seconds. Reach for deep methods when you have images, audio, dense time series with structure, or millions of features. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- -- [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- In production you rarely batch-score; you score one event at a time. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- Production constraints: [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- **Memory** — streaming detectors must bound state (e.g., reservoir sampling) [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- **Latency** — score in microseconds for fraud, milliseconds for monitoring [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- **Concept drift** — distribution shifts over time; the detector must adapt [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- -- [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- These look similar but require different responses. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- Production ML systems need **both**. Most monitoring failures come from confusing them. For full drift tooling (PSI, KS, NannyML, Evidently), see `da-analytical-methods` (references/da-42-ml-model-monitoring.md). [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- -- [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- -- [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- The hard part: by definition, anomalies are rare, so you usually don't have labeled validation data. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- When you do have labels (post-hoc): use precision-recall, F1, PR-AUC. Accuracy is meaningless because the class is imbalanced. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- When you don't have labels: use known synthetic anomalies, or use the time-shifted holdout where you assume the holdout had a similar anomaly rate. Or measure proxy metrics like "% of incidents the system caught." [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- **The threshold choice** is usually the hardest decision. The model emits a score; you choose where to cut. Tune for the cost-benefit ratio: if a false positive costs 1 minute of investigation and a false negative costs $10k, the threshold should be aggressive. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- -- [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- **Z-score on data full of outliers** — μ and σ are dragged; use modified z (MAD). [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- **Single threshold on a seasonal series** — false-alarms on every Monday or every December. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- **Confusing drift with anomaly** — retraining on the anomaly, or investigating drift as if it were an event. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- **Autoencoder for 5-feature tabular** — overkill; IF will outperform with seconds of compute. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- **No baseline period** — declaring everything new "anomalous" when you simply lack history. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- **Treating anomaly score as a probability** — most methods produce uncalibrated scores; pick a threshold from PR data, not "p > 0.05". [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- **Alert fatigue** — a noisy detector trains the on-call to ignore it. Tune precision before deploying. [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
- **Forgetting concept drift** — the model that worked last quarter no longer represents "normal." [src: da-16-anomaly-detection]
