- **Data observability** is the discipline of measuring and maintaining the health and reliability of data across its lifecycle — the ability to fully understand the state of the data in your systems, so you can detect, triage, resolve, and prevent **data incidents** before they reach downstream consumers. The term was popularized by Monte Carlo (Barr Moses, 2019) as an explicit analog to software **observability** (the logs/metrics/traces discipline for services): instead of asking "is my service up?", data observability asks "is my data trustworthy, and if not, why?" [src: da-19-data-observability]
- It is a distinct discipline, not a synonym for any of its neighbors: [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Data quality** is the *target state* (accurate, complete, trustworthy data) and the broad discipline of achieving it. Observability is one modern *tactic* for sustaining quality at scale. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Data testing** (e.g. dbt tests, Great Expectations) is *assertion-based*: you declare expected conditions up front and check them. It catches the failures you anticipated. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Monitoring** watches individual pipeline/job metrics. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Observability** is broader than all three: it continuously watches the *behavior* of data and systems, surfaces *unexpected* anomalies (not just the ones you wrote tests for), and ties them to **lineage and context** so you can answer "what broke, where, who is affected, and why." Testing tells you about known-unknowns; observability surfaces unknown-unknowns. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- Why it matters now: as data stacks fragment (ingestion, warehouse, transform, BI, reverse-ETL, ML/AI features), the surface area for silent failure explodes, and bad data quietly poisons dashboards, ML features, and AI products. Gartner projects ~50% of enterprises with distributed data architectures will adopt data observability tooling by 2026 (up from ~20% in 2024). [src: da-19-data-observability]
- Monte Carlo's canonical framework decomposes data health into five measurable pillars. The first four are *table-/field-level signals*; the fifth is the connective tissue. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Freshness** — Is the data up to date? How recently was a table updated, and does the update cadence match expectations? Stale tables (e.g. a daily table that didn't load by 9 AM) are the most common, most user-visible incident. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Volume** — Is the amount of data as expected? Row-count completeness over time. Sudden drops (a partial load) or spikes (a duplicate load / fan-out bug) signal problems. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Schema** — Has the structure changed? Added/removed/retyped columns, dropped or renamed tables. Schema drift from upstream producers is a leading root cause of breakage ("who changed this column type?"). [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Distribution / Quality** — Is the data within expected ranges at the field level? Null rates, uniqueness, value ranges, category cardinality, percent-zero, format conformance. This pillar is where field-level *data-quality* signals live. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Lineage** — The map of upstream sources and downstream consumers for every asset, ideally to **column level**. Lineage is the holistic pillar: it turns a freshness/volume/schema/distribution anomaly into an *impact assessment* ("which 14 dashboards and 2 ML features depend on this broken table, and what upstream job caused it"). Lineage powers both root-cause (upstream) and blast-radius (downstream) analysis. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Data downtime** is the period when data is partial, erroneous, missing, or otherwise wrong. It is the headline reliability metric and is modeled as: [src: da-19-data-observability]
- > Data downtime ≈ **N × (TTD + TTR)** [src: da-19-data-observability]
- where **N** = number of incidents, **TTD** = time-to-detection, **TTR** = time-to-resolution. Observability programs drive downtime down by reducing all three: fewer incidents (shift-left/contracts), faster detection (automated monitors vs. "an exec noticed the dashboard was wrong"), faster resolution (lineage-accelerated root cause). [src: da-19-data-observability]
- Borrowed from SRE and applied to **data products**: [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **SLI** (indicator) — the actual measurement: e.g. % of days the table landed by 9 AM; null rate of `customer_email`; row-count vs. 7-day baseline. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **SLO** (objective) — the internal target on an SLI: e.g. "freshness ≤ 6h for 99.5% of loads"; "null rate of key columns < 0.1%". [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **SLA** (agreement) — the *external, formal* commitment to stakeholders/consumers, often with consequences/escalation if breached. A data SLA bundles measurable targets for **freshness, availability, volume, and quality** of a data product. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- Common starting target: **99.9%** ("three nines") ≈ 43.8 min downtime/month; pick SLOs per data product's criticality, not one blanket number. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- Treating data issues with the rigor of software incidents. The lifecycle: **detection → triage/severity → ownership → resolution → retrospective**. Key practices: explicitly *declared* incidents (a human or system declares it, giving a clean basis for uptime/SLA math), severity levels tied to blast radius (use lineage), an on-call/owner model for data assets, blameless postmortems, and tracking **MTTD/MTTR** trends. Incident data is the empirical basis for SLAs — you can't promise reliability you don't measure. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- Observability detection ranges from simple to ML-driven: [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Rule/threshold monitors** — fixed bounds ("row count must be > 1M"). Cheap, explicit, but brittle on seasonal data: they false-alarm at peaks and miss off-peak drops. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Statistical / time-series monitors** — learn a baseline from history and flag deviations (z-score/IQR on a metric's history, moving averages, STL/Prophet-style seasonal decomposition). Handle daily/weekly seasonality, trend, and growth. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **ML/automated monitors** — platform-trained models that auto-tune per table, adapt to growth/seasonality, and self-onboard new assets without one-by-one config. Teams report ~40–60% fewer false positives vs. static thresholds. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- Practical guidance: each metric/anomaly type may warrant a different method; reserve ML for high-cardinality, seasonal, or numerous assets and keep cheap thresholds for hard invariants (e.g. PK uniqueness). Watch timezone/DST shifts — they silently break seasonal models. (See **da-16-anomaly-detection** for the underlying algorithms; this skill covers their *application to pipeline/table health*.) [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **OpenLineage** is the open standard (LF AI & Data) for collecting lineage metadata, modeling **Run / Job / Dataset** entities with consistent naming; it instruments jobs *as they run* and supports **column-level** lineage (notably via the Spark integration, with facets for inputs/outputs). [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Marquez** is the reference implementation/metadata server that collects, aggregates, and visualizes the lineage graph; it added column-level lineage and job-to-job lineage. Integrations exist for Airflow, dbt, Spark, etc. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- Column-level lineage enables fine-grained root cause and **sensitive-data tracking** (where does PII flow?), valuable for governance/compliance. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- The 2024–2026 evolution of the discipline: stop catching issues only *after* the warehouse load ("shift right") and move checks *earlier* — into dbt runs, CI/CD, and at the producer boundary. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Data contracts** formalize the producer↔consumer interface: schema, freshness SLA, volume expectations, semantic/quality thresholds, and versioning. They prevent incidents at the source rather than detecting them downstream, and bridge testing (pre-merge assertions) with observability (runtime monitoring). [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Shift-left** emphasizes prevention and "design for trust from the start," pairing producer-side contracts with leadership-visible quality dashboards. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- Selection heuristics: **dbt-centric stack →** Elementary (then Soda/GX for extra checks). **Need vendor-neutral lineage →** OpenLineage + Marquez. **Enterprise, many sources, want automated full-coverage ML monitoring + incident mgmt →** Monte Carlo / Bigeye / Anomalo. **Lightweight, CI-embedded checks in code →** Soda Core or Great Expectations. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Inventory & prioritize assets.** You can't (and shouldn't) monitor everything equally. Rank tables/data products by downstream blast radius (use lineage) and business criticality. Define **tiers**. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Establish lineage.** Stand up column/table lineage (OpenLineage+Marquez or a platform) so every later step has impact context. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Baseline the five pillars.** Turn on freshness, volume, schema monitors broadly (cheap, high ROI); add distribution/quality monitors on key fields of high-tier assets. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Set SLIs → SLOs → SLAs per tier.** Define indicators, internal objectives, and (for the top tier) external agreements with consumers. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Choose detection per metric.** Thresholds for hard invariants; statistical/ML monitors for seasonal/high-cardinality metrics. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Wire incident management.** Route alerts to owners, set severities by blast radius, declare incidents, track TTD/TTR. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Shift left.** Add data contracts and CI/dbt checks at producer boundaries to cut incident count (N) at the source. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Measure & iterate.** Track data downtime (N×(TTD+TTR)), false-positive rate, SLO attainment; retune monitors and prune noise. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Lineage-first triage.** When a metric breaks, walk lineage *up* for root cause and *down* for blast radius before touching code. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Tier your coverage.** Broad cheap metadata monitors (freshness/volume/schema) everywhere; expensive value-level + ML monitors only on tier-1 assets. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Freshness SLO as the first win.** It's the most common, most visible incident and the cheapest to monitor — start here to build trust in the program. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Contract the producer boundary.** A schema/freshness contract on the most unstable upstream source prevents the largest class of incidents. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Declare incidents explicitly.** Gives clean SLA/uptime math and a paper trail for postmortems. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Co-locate observability with transformation.** dbt-native (Elementary) keeps monitors versioned alongside the models that produce the data. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Track the false-positive rate as a first-class metric.** Alert fatigue kills observability programs faster than missed incidents. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Treating observability as "more dbt tests."** Tests cover known-unknowns; observability must also surface unknown-unknowns via anomaly detection + lineage. Don't conflate the two. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Static thresholds on seasonal data.** Guarantees false alarms at peaks and misses during troughs; use seasonal/ML monitors for cyclical metrics. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Monitoring everything equally.** Untiered, full-coverage value-level monitors produce overwhelming noise and cost; nobody acts on the alerts. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **No lineage.** Without lineage, every incident is a manual archaeology dig; triage time (and TTR) balloons. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Detection without resolution ownership.** Alerts with no owner, severity, or incident process just become a noisy dead-letter channel. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **SLAs you don't measure.** Promising freshness/quality with no SLIs/incident tracking is theater. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Shift-right only.** Catching everything post-load means consumers see bad data first; push contracts/CI checks upstream. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Ignoring timezone/DST in seasonal models.** Silent drift in seasonal baselines → spurious anomalies. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Flood of false-positive alerts** → metrics are seasonal/trending under static thresholds, or monitors lack enough history to baseline. Switch to seasonal/ML monitors, widen training windows, and add DST/timezone handling. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Incidents found by consumers, not monitors** → coverage gap. Add freshness/volume monitors on the affected lineage path; this is a TTD problem. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Long TTR** → missing/incomplete lineage. Stand up column-level lineage so root cause and blast radius are immediate. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Schema-drift breakage recurs from one source** → reactive monitoring only; add a producer-side **data contract** + CI check (shift-left). [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **"Is this a quality or an observability problem?"** → If you can write the assertion up front, it's a test (GX/dbt/Soda check). If you need to detect a deviation you didn't anticipate and trace its impact, it's observability. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **OpenLineage events missing column lineage** → confirm the integration emitting them supports column facets (Spark integration is the most complete); not all integrations emit column-level yet. [src: da-19-data-observability]
- **Tool sprawl** → consolidate: dbt shops standardize on Elementary + one platform; vendor-neutral lineage standardizes on OpenLineage to avoid lock-in. [src: da-19-data-observability]

- Network (graph) analytics models data as **nodes (vertices)** connected by **edges (links)** and measures the resulting structure to answer questions that row/column tables cannot: who is influential, what clusters exist, what is the shortest path, what links are likely to form. It is the analytics counterpart to graph theory — the goal is **insight from relationships**, not just storing them. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- Use a graph framing when the *connections* carry the signal: social networks, fraud rings, supply chains, citation/co-authorship, recommendation, knowledge graphs, dependency graphs, transaction flows. If the question is answerable with a `GROUP BY`, you probably do not need a graph. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- This skill is the network/graph node of the data-analytics curriculum (da-1 onward). [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Directed vs undirected**: edges with vs without a direction (following vs friendship). **Weighted vs unweighted**: edges carry a cost/strength. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Adjacency matrix**: V×V matrix, O(V²) space, O(1) edge lookup — good for dense graphs and linear-algebra ops (PageRank, spectral methods). [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Adjacency list**: per-node neighbor lists, O(V+E) space — the default for sparse real-world graphs; faster traversal. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Bipartite graph**: two disjoint node sets with edges only across sets (users↔products, authors↔papers). [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Ego network**: the subgraph of one focal node ("ego"), its direct neighbors ("alters"), and edges among them — the unit of local social-structure analysis. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Multigraph / multi-relational**: parallel edges or typed edges (knowledge graphs). [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Connected components**: maximal sets of mutually reachable nodes. In directed graphs distinguish **weakly** (ignore direction) vs **strongly** connected components. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Shortest paths**: **BFS** for unweighted; **Dijkstra** for non-negative weights (O(E log V) with a heap on an adjacency list); **Bellman-Ford** when negative-weight edges exist (Dijkstra fails on negatives). All-pairs via repeated Dijkstra or Floyd-Warshall. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Diameter / eccentricity / average path length**: global reachability measures (expensive on large graphs — sample). [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Degree centrality**: number of edges (in/out for directed) — local popularity, cheap. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Betweenness centrality**: fraction of shortest paths passing through a node — bridges/brokers/bottlenecks. Expensive (Brandes ≈ O(VE)); approximate via sampling on big graphs. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Closeness centrality**: inverse of mean shortest-path distance to all others. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Eigenvector centrality**: recursive importance — you matter if connected to nodes that matter. Can fail to converge on some directed graphs. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **PageRank**: eigenvector centrality with a damping factor (~0.85) modeling a teleporting random surfer. Handles directed graphs reliably; the production default for influence ranking. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Modularity (Q)**: edges-inside-communities vs expected at random, range roughly −1..1; higher = stronger structure. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Louvain** (Blondel et al., 2008): fast greedy modularity maximization. Ubiquitous but suffers the **resolution limit** (merges small real communities) and can produce badly/disconnected communities. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Leiden** (Traag, Van Eck & Waltman, 2019): adds a refinement phase; guarantees communities are connected and well-separated, faster and higher-quality — the recommended default. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Label propagation**: near-linear, no objective — fast but unstable/non-deterministic. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- CPM (constant Potts model) and resolution parameters address the resolution limit. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- Local proximity scores for non-adjacent pairs x,y (Γ = neighbor set): [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Common Neighbors**: |Γ(x) ∩ Γ(y)|. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Jaccard Coefficient**: |Γ(x) ∩ Γ(y)| / |Γ(x) ∪ Γ(y)|. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Adamic-Adar**: sum of 1/log(degree) over shared neighbors — rare shared neighbors count more. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Preferential Attachment**: deg(x)·deg(y) — "rich get richer." [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- Embedding/GNN methods are the supervised upgrade. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Motifs**: statistically over-represented subgraphs (feed-forward loops, triangles). Compare against a degree-preserving null model. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Bipartite (one-mode) projection**: collapse a two-set graph onto one set (two authors linked if they co-wrote a paper). Loses information — weight edges by shared-neighbor count / Newman weighting to avoid hub-dominated dense graphs. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **DeepWalk** (Perozzi et al., 2014): uniform random walks → skip-gram (Word2Vec) node vectors. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **node2vec** (Grover & Leskovec, 2016): biased walks with return parameter p and in-out parameter q interpolating BFS-like (structural roles) vs DFS-like (community) exploration. Outperforms DeepWalk/LINE on classification and link prediction. Vectors feed downstream ML. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **GCN** (Kipf & Welling, 2017): neighborhood aggregation via normalized adjacency; transductive — needs the whole graph, retrain on new nodes. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **GraphSAGE** (Hamilton, Ying & Leskovec, NeurIPS 2017): learns aggregator functions over a sampled neighborhood → inductive, generalizes to unseen nodes, scales to large/dynamic graphs. Use GNNs when you have rich node features + a supervised target; use node2vec when you only have structure. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- Rule of thumb: prototype in NetworkX, move to igraph/graph-tool when slow, cuGraph when huge, Neo4j GDS when the graph already lives in Neo4j. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Frame the question as a graph** — define node, edge, direction, weight. Wrong definition dooms everything downstream. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Build & sanity-check** — node/edge counts, degree distribution (expect heavy tails), components, density. Restrict to the giant component when appropriate. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Match analytic to question**: influence → centrality (PageRank default); clusters → community detection (Leiden default); reachability → components/shortest paths; missing links → link prediction or embeddings. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Scale-match the tool** before running O(VE) measures. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Validate** — compare against a null model; check modularity *and* stability across seeds; for link prediction use a temporal train/test split and AUC/precision@k. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Communicate** — layouts for small graphs only (<~1k nodes); for large graphs report metrics, ranked tables, community summaries — not hairball plots. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **PageRank as the default influence score** on directed graphs: degree is cheap but naive; betweenness is informative but slow; PageRank is the reliable middle ground. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Leiden over Louvain** unless you have a hard dependency on Louvain output. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **node2vec for structure-only data, GraphSAGE for feature-rich + supervised** targets needing inductive generalization. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Work on the giant connected component** — isolates distort global metrics. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Approximate expensive centralities** (sampled betweenness/closeness) over ~10⁵ nodes. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Weight bipartite projections** rather than using raw co-occurrence. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Tune node2vec p/q deliberately**: low q → community-flavored; high q (low p) → structural-role embeddings. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Treating any join table as a graph.** If a `GROUP BY` answers it, a graph adds cost, not insight. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Trusting Louvain communities as connected.** Up to ~25% badly connected in the original study. Use Leiden or verify. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Ignoring the modularity resolution limit** — don't over-interpret community count without a resolution sweep. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Exact betweenness on million-node graphs in NetworkX** — won't finish; sample or use graph-tool/cuGraph. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Adjacency matrix for sparse graphs** — O(V²) memory blows up; use adjacency lists. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Dijkstra with negative weights** — silently wrong; use Bellman-Ford. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Plotting a 100k-node hairball** — summarize with metrics and community-level rollups. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Comparing motif/community counts without a null model.** [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Using transductive GCN on a growing graph** — use GraphSAGE. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Eigenvector centrality won't converge** → directed graph with sinks; use PageRank or `eigenvector_centrality_numpy`. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Everything is one giant community** → resolution limit; lower the resolution parameter, switch to Leiden/CPM. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Community results change every run** → expected for Louvain/label propagation; fix the seed, take consensus, or use Leiden. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Centrality job never finishes** → O(VE)-class; sample, restrict to giant component, or move to C/GPU backend. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Link prediction AUC ≈ 0.5** → no temporal split (leakage) or too sparse; try embedding features. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **node2vec embeddings look random** → walks too short/few, or p/q untuned. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- **Out of memory building the graph** → dense matrix; switch to edge list / sparse (CSR) or igraph/cuGraph. [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- NetworkX docs — centrality, components, shortest paths, link prediction. https://networkx.org/documentation/stable/ (2024) [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- Brandes. "A Faster Algorithm for Betweenness Centrality." J. Math. Sociology (2001). [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- Page, Brin et al. "The PageRank Citation Ranking." Stanford (1999). [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- Blondel et al. "Fast unfolding of communities in large networks" (Louvain). (2008). https://arxiv.org/abs/0803.0476 [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- Fortunato & Barthélemy. "Resolution limit in community detection." PNAS (2007). https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0607100 [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- Traag, Van Eck & Waltman. "From Louvain to Leiden." Scientific Reports (2019). https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.08473 [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- Liben-Nowell & Kleinberg. "The Link Prediction Problem for Social Networks." (2007). https://www.cs.cornell.edu/home/kleinber/link-pred.pdf [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- Arthur. "Modularity and Projection of Bipartite Networks" (2019). https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.02520 [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]

- Neo4j Graph Data Science docs. https://neo4j.com/docs/graph-data-science/current/ (2024) [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- igraph documentation. https://igraph.org/ (2024) [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]

- Benchmark of popular graph/network packages. https://www.timlrx.com/blog/benchmark-of-popular-graph-network-packages-v2/ (2020) [src: da-27-network-graph-analytics]
- Applied Bayesian modeling: specify a generative model, fit the posterior with a probabilistic programming language (PPL), interrogate it with predictive checks and diagnostics, and compare alternatives. This skill is the *workflow and tooling* layer — it assumes Bayes' theorem and the frequentist/Bayesian contrast are already understood (see da-1-3-5, da-1-4-3). [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- A Bayesian model combines a **prior** `p(θ)` and a **likelihood** `p(y|θ)` into a **posterior** `p(θ|y) ∝ p(y|θ) p(θ)`. For all but trivial models the posterior is intractable analytically, so we approximate it by sampling (MCMC) or optimization (variational inference). The discipline is an iterative loop — model, fit, check, expand — formalized as the **Bayesian workflow** ([Gelman, Vehtari, Simpson et al. 2020, arXiv:2011.01808](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.01808)). [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- Use Bayesian methods when you want: full uncertainty quantification (posteriors, not just point estimates), principled regularization via priors, partial pooling across groups (hierarchical models), the ability to incorporate domain knowledge, and propagation of uncertainty into predictions/decisions. [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **The Bayesian workflow (iterative).** Build → simulate from priors → fit → diagnose computation → check against data → compare models → expand/simplify → repeat. Treats *computational failure* (divergences, bad R-hat) and *model misfit* (failed PPCs) as distinct problems ([Gelman et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.01808); [Betancourt "Principled Bayesian Workflow" 2020](https://betanalpha.github.io/assets/case_studies/principled_bayesian_workflow.html); [Gabry et al. JRSS-A 2019](https://academic.oup.com/jrsssa/article/182/2/389/7070184)). [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Priors & prior predictive checks.** Favor **weakly-informative priors** (`Normal(0,1)` on standardized predictors, `HalfNormal`/`Exponential` on scales, `LKJ` on correlations) over flat/diffuse priors. Validate via **prior predictive check**: draw θ from prior, simulate y, confirm plausibility ([Stan Prior Choice wiki 2024](https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations); [PyMC v5 docs 2024](https://www.pymc.io/projects/docs/en/stable/learn/core_notebooks/posterior_predictive.html)). [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **MCMC: HMC & NUTS.** HMC uses gradients for distant, high-acceptance moves; **NUTS** auto-tunes trajectory length + step size and is the default in every modern PPL. Continuous params only — marginalize discrete ones ([Hoffman & Gelman JMLR 2014](https://jmlr.org/papers/v15/hoffman14a.html); [Betancourt arXiv:1701.02434 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.02434); [Stan Reference Manual 2024](https://mc-stan.org/docs/reference-manual/mcmc.html)). [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Variational inference (VI/ADVI).** Approximates the posterior by maximizing the ELBO — fast, scalable, but *underestimates* variance and can miss multimodality. **ADVI** automates it; normalizing flows enrich it. Validate against MCMC ([Kucukelbir et al. JMLR 2017](https://jmlr.org/papers/v18/16-107.html); [PyMC VI docs 2024](https://www.pymc.io/projects/docs/en/stable/api/vi.html); [NumPyro SVI docs 2024](https://num.pyro.ai/en/stable/svi.html)). [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Hierarchical/multilevel models.** Group-level params drawn from a shared population distribution → **partial pooling** (data-determined shrinkage toward the global mean). The biggest practical reason to go Bayesian ([Gelman & Hill 2006](http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/arm/); [McElreath *Statistical Rethinking* 2020](https://xcelab.net/rm/); [PyMC multilevel primer 2024](https://www.pymc.io/projects/docs/en/stable/learn/core_notebooks/GLM_hierarchical.html)). [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Posterior predictive checks (PPC).** Simulate `y_rep` from the posterior predictive, compare to observed `y` — overlaid densities, test statistics, **LOO-PIT** calibration. A model that can't reproduce key data features is misspecified ([Gabry et al. JRSS-A 2019](https://academic.oup.com/jrsssa/article/182/2/389/7070184); [ArviZ API 2024](https://python.arviz.org/en/stable/api/index.html)). [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Model comparison: LOO-CV (PSIS), WAIC.** Compare predictive accuracy with **PSIS-LOO** (`elpd_loo`); the **Pareto-k** diagnostic flags unreliable points (`k > 0.7` problematic). LOO preferred over WAIC for its self-diagnostics; prefer LOO over Bayes factors ([Vehtari et al. Stat&Computing 2017, arXiv:1507.04544](https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.04544); [Vehtari et al. PSIS, JMLR 2024, arXiv:1507.02646](https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.02646)). [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Convergence diagnostics.** Use **rank-normalized split-R-hat** (target `< 1.01`) and **bulk-ESS/tail-ESS**. HMC adds **divergent transitions** (curvature the sampler can't resolve — reparameterize/prior fix), **max-treedepth** (efficiency), and **E-BFMI < 0.3** (poor energy exploration) ([Vehtari et al. Bayesian Analysis 2021, arXiv:1903.08008](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.08008); [Stan Warnings 2024](https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html)). [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **PPLs.** **PyMC** (Python v5+, PyTensor backend, pluggable NUTS: default/nutpie/numpyro/blackjax); **Stan** (reference HMC, via **CmdStanPy**/cmdstanr); **NumPyro** (JAX, fastest NUTS, GPU); **Bambi**/**brms** (formula GLMM interface `y ~ x + (1|g)`); **ArviZ** (backend-agnostic diagnostics on `InferenceData`) ([PyMC](https://www.pymc.io/); [CmdStanPy](https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanpy/); [NumPyro](https://num.pyro.ai/); [Bambi](https://bambinos.github.io/bambi/); [ArviZ](https://python.arviz.org/), all 2024). [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Bayesian regression & GLMs.** GLM link families carry over: Gaussian/Bernoulli/Poisson/Negative-Binomial; coefficient priors regularize (Normal≈ridge, Laplace≈LASSO, horseshoe for sparsity). Student-t likelihood for robust regression. Standardize predictors ([McElreath 2020](https://xcelab.net/rm/); [Bambi examples 2024](https://bambinos.github.io/bambi/notebooks/)). [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **ArviZ — diagnostics & plotting hub.** `az.summary` (R-hat/ESS/HDI), `plot_trace`, `plot_ppc`, `loo`/`compare`/`plot_compare`, `plot_forest`, `plot_energy` (BFMI), `plot_pair` (divergences) ([ArviZ API 2024](https://python.arviz.org/en/stable/api/index.html)). [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Scope & generative story.** Write the model as a data-generating process; pick the likelihood family from the outcome type first. [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Priors + prior predictive check.** Weakly-informative priors on standardized variables; `sample_prior_predictive`; reject absurd priors. [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Fit.** NUTS, ≥4 chains. `target_accept=0.8` default; raise to 0.9–0.99 on divergences. Try NumPyro/nutpie for large continuous models. [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Diagnose computation.** R-hat < 1.01, bulk/tail-ESS, **zero divergences**, E-BFMI > 0.3, no treedepth saturation. Fix *here* before interpreting. [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Posterior predictive check.** `sample_posterior_predictive` → `az.plot_ppc`, test statistics, LOO-PIT. [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Compare.** `az.loo` per model, `az.compare`; inspect Pareto-k. [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Iterate.** Expand (hierarchy/interactions/robust likelihood) or simplify; re-run. [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Standardize continuous predictors** (mean 0, sd 1) so default priors behave; back-transform for interpretation. [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Non-centered parameterization for hierarchical models.** Replace `θ_g ~ Normal(μ, σ)` with `θ_g = μ + σ·z_g, z_g ~ Normal(0,1)` (the "Matt trick") — removes the funnel that causes divergences with sparse groups ([Stan User's Guide 2024](https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/efficiency-tuning.html#reparameterization); [Betancourt & Girolami 2015, arXiv:1312.0906](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0906)). [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **≥4 chains, multiple seeds**, inspect trace plots — R-hat alone misses problems. [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Marginalize discrete parameters** so NUTS can run. [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Use Bambi/brms for standard GLMMs**; drop to raw PyMC/Stan only for custom structure. [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Save full `InferenceData`** (posterior + predictive + log-likelihood + sample stats) so LOO/PPCs are reproducible. [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Ignoring divergences** — they bias the posterior. Reparameterize, raise `target_accept`, or tighten priors. [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Flat/diffuse "uninformative" priors as default** — rarely uninformative on quantities of interest; prefer weakly-informative. [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Trusting VI/ADVI without MCMC comparison** — VI understates variance. [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Old R-hat < 1.1 as the bar** — use rank-normalized R-hat < 1.01 and check ESS. [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Comparing on in-sample fit / DIC / raw likelihood** — use LOO/WAIC; read Pareto-k first. [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Centered hierarchical parameterization with sparse groups** — the classic funnel generator; go non-centered. [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]
- **Reading the posterior mean only** — report HDIs, propagate the full posterior. [src: da-25-bayesian-data-analysis]

- Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) is the present value of the future cash flows attributed to a customer relationship. This skill covers the **probabilistic "buy-till-you-die" (BTYD) family** — statistical models that decompose CLV into (1) *how often* a customer transacts while active, (2) *whether/when* they silently churn, and (3) *how much* they spend per transaction — then discount the expected future stream to present value. [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- Two orthogonal axes define the model landscape (Fader/Hardie taxonomy): [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- Choosing the wrong quadrant is the #1 modeling error. Subscriptions/SaaS are **contractual** (you see the cancellation) → sBG / survival. Retail, e-commerce, donations are **non-contractual** (you infer churn) → Pareto/NBD family. [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- Authoritative source corpus: Bruce Hardie's notes (brucehardie.com), the Fader/Hardie/Lee Marketing Science papers, and the three reference implementations — `lifetimes` (Python, archived), `CLVTools` (R), and `PyMC-Marketing` (Python, Bayesian, the active successor). [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- A customer is "alive" until an unobserved dropout, transacting stochastically while alive. Models pair a **counting process** (transactions while alive) with a **timing process** (lifetime/dropout), each with cross-customer heterogeneity. First introduced by Schmittlein, Morrison & Colombo, "Counting Your Customers: Who Are They and What Will They Do Next?", *Management Science* 33(1):1–24 (1987) (https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/10.1287/mnsc.33.1.1). Lineage: Retina.ai "History of BTYD" (2023). [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- The original non-contractual continuous-time model. **NBD** (Poisson–gamma mixture) for transaction counts while alive; **Pareto** (exponential–gamma mixture) for the unobserved lifetime. Four parameters (r, α, s, β). Powerful but numerically awkward (Gaussian hypergeometric functions), which motivated BG/NBD. (Schmittlein et al. 1987; CLVTools `pnbd`; PyMC-Marketing Pareto/NBD notebook.) [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- The workhorse. Replaces Pareto's continuous dropout with a **beta-geometric** story: a customer flips a coin to churn *immediately after each transaction* (prob. p, beta-distributed across customers); active counts are NBD. Far easier to fit (estimable in Excel), nearly identical predictive accuracy. Fader, Hardie & Lee, *Marketing Science* 24(2):275–284 (2005) (http://brucehardie.com/papers/018/fader_et_al_mksc_05.pdf). **Quirk:** in BG/NBD a customer cannot churn until *after* their first repeat purchase, so it understates one-and-done customers — which MBG/NBD fixes. [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- Adds a dropout opportunity at time zero (right after the first purchase), so customers who never repeat can be "dead". Expected-repeat estimates nearly match BG/NBD, but alive/dead classification of zero-repeat customers is more realistic. Batislam, Denizel & Filiztekin, *IJRM* 24(3) (2007); implemented as `ModifiedBetaGeoModel`. [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- Separately models **spend per transaction** (frequency models only predict counts). Assumptions: (a) value varies randomly around the customer's mean; (b) mean spend varies across customers but not over time; (c) spend is independent of the transaction process — **verify frequency and monetary value are roughly uncorrelated before trusting it.** Fit only on repeat purchasers. Fader, Hardie & Lee, "RFM and CLV: Using Iso-Value Curves", *JMR* 42(4):415–430 (2005) (https://www.brucehardie.com/papers/rfm_clv_2005-02-16.pdf). [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- BTYD models need only per-customer **Recency, Frequency, and "T"** — R and F are *sufficient statistics* for the likelihood. Conventions (easy to get wrong): [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **frequency** = number of *repeat* purchases (total − 1). [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **recency** = time between **first and last** purchase (NOT time since last purchase, the marketing-RFM convention). [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **T** = customer "age" = first purchase to end of observation. [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **monetary_value** = average value of repeat transactions. [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- CLV (non-contractual) = **(expected spend from Gamma-Gamma) × DERT**, where DERT is the present value of all expected future transactions discounted to the end of the calibration period (integral from T to ∞). Use a **continuously-compounded** discount rate (e.g. 15%/yr ≈ 0.0027/week). Fader/Hardie originally called this DET. (RFM-CLV 2005; CLVTools `pnbd_DERT`; Fader/Hardie note 033.) [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **Subscriptions/contractual** settings: each period a customer renews with prob. θ or cancels with 1−θ; θ is fixed per customer, beta-distributed across the base. Projects observed retention into a full survival curve and explains the **observed rise in aggregate retention over time** as a heterogeneity sorting effect, not behavior change. Fader & Hardie, "How to Project Customer Retention", *J. Interactive Marketing* 21(1):76–90 (2007); extended in "Customer-Base Valuation in a Contractual Setting", *Marketing Science* 29(1):85–93 (2010). [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- Discrete-time analog of Pareto/NBD: transactions per period are Bernoulli (buy/no-buy) instead of Poisson, paired with a beta-geometric dropout — for "transaction opportunities" data (annual donations, periodic catalog buyers). Closed-form. Fader, Hardie & Shang, *Marketing Science* 29(6):1086–1108 (2010); lifetimes `BetaGeoBetaBinomFitter`. [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **Historical CLV** sums realized past margin (backward-looking). **Predictive CLV** forecasts future value via models (BTYD, ML, or naive ARPU/churn). The naive `ARPU ÷ churn` shortcut assumes a single constant retention rate — biased low when retention is heterogeneous (Fader/Hardie 2010). Prefer model-based predictive CLV with uncertainty intervals. [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- Group customers by acquisition period and track value per cohort. Reveals retention dynamics and acquisition-quality drift a base-wide average masks; pairs with sBG on multicohort data. (Keep retention-curve fitting itself in **da-34**; here it is a CLV input/segmentation lens.) [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- LTV:CAC measures payback on acquisition spend. Rules of thumb: **~3:1 healthy target** (B2C SaaS ≈ 2.5:1, B2B SaaS ≈ 4:1); below 2:1 = unsustainable; above ~5:1 = likely under-investing. CAC payback: healthy 6–12 months, elite < 3 months. Use a **margin-based, discounted** predictive LTV — gross-revenue LTV inflates the ratio. [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **Confirm the quadrant.** Non-contractual + continuous → proceed. Contractual → sBG/survival. Discrete opportunities → BG/BB. [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **Build RFM summary** (`rfm_summary()` / lifetimes `summary_data_from_transaction_data`). Watch the recency definition. [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **Fit a frequency/dropout model** (BG/NBD default; MBG/NBD if many one-and-done; Pareto/NBD as benchmark). [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **Check the model**: holdout calibration, tracking plot, `P(alive)` distribution. [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **Fit Gamma-Gamma on repeat purchasers**; first verify low corr(frequency, monetary). [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **Compute discounted CLV** = E[spend] × DERT over a finite horizon, continuously-compounded discount rate. [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **Validate** on a holdout window by RFM decile. [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **Segment / act**: rank by predicted CLV and `P(alive)`; feed CAC:LTV. [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **Wrong quadrant** (Pareto/NBD on a subscription business, or sBG on e-commerce). [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **Marketing-RFM recency** ("days since last purchase" instead of "first-to-last span") — silent severe bias. [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **Gamma-Gamma without the independence check.** [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **Naive ARPU ÷ churn as ground truth** — biased low under heterogeneity. [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **Un-discounted / infinite-horizon CLV** — inflates value and LTV:CAC. [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **Fitting Gamma-Gamma on all customers** instead of repeat purchasers only. [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **Trusting `lifetimes` for new long-lived projects** — it's archived. [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **`P(alive)` implausibly high for everyone** → BG/NBD with many one-and-done customers; switch to MBG/NBD. [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **Optimizer fails / NaN log-likelihood (Pareto/NBD)** → numerical instability in hypergeometric terms; use log-sum-exp-patched BTYD or BG/NBD. [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **Gamma-Gamma returns absurd spend** → filter to frequency > 0; use *average repeat* value, not total. [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **Holdout over-predicted** → calibration window caught a promo spike; re-split or model seasonality outside BTYD. [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]
- **CLV explodes** → infinite horizon or zero discount rate; cap horizon, set continuously-compounded rate. [src: da-23-customer-lifetime-value]

- Modeling the *time until an event happens* when some observations are **incomplete** (censored or truncated). This is its own discipline because ordinary regression cannot use a row that says "this customer had not churned yet when we stopped looking" — survival methods extract information from exactly those incomplete rows. Canonical textbooks: Klein & Moeschberger *Survival Analysis: Techniques for Censored and Truncated Data* (2nd ed, 2003); Therneau & Grambsch *Modeling Survival Data* (2000). Primary Python tooling: **lifelines** and **scikit-survival**; R: **survival** + **survminer**. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- The outcome is a *duration* until an event: death, machine failure, churn, loan default, conversion, hospital readmission. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- Some subjects have **not** experienced the event by end of observation (censoring), or only entered observation partway through (truncation). [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- You need a survival curve, hazard ratio, median time-to-event, or cumulative incidence. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- Forecasting a numeric series over calendar time → `da-15-forecasting` [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- Regression/classification with fully observed outcomes → `da-6` / `da-7` [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- Causal/experiment analysis with no time component → `da-12` [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- A descriptive cohort retention table (no estimator, no model) → `da-21-product-analytics` [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- Computing a CLV dollar figure with BG/NBD, Pareto/NBD, or Gamma-Gamma spend models → `da-23-customer-lifetime-value` (this skill covers only the time-to-churn / survival-curve half) [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- -- [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- The reason survival analysis exists. Get this wrong and every downstream estimate is biased. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- Key distinction: **censoring keeps the subject but loses event-time detail; truncation removes the subject from the sample entirely** (Stats Ox lecture notes, 2020; NJIT Math 659 Ch.3, 2011; GeeksforGeeks, 2024). The standard estimators assume censoring is **non-informative** (independent of the event process). [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- Three interchangeable views of the same distribution; pick whichever the audience reads best. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Survival function** `S(t) = P(T > t)` — probability of surviving past `t`. Monotone non-increasing from 1. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Hazard function** `h(t) = lim Δ→0 P(t ≤ T < t+Δ | T ≥ t)/Δ` — instantaneous event rate *given survival so far*. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Cumulative hazard** `H(t) = ∫₀ᵗ h(u)du`, with the bridge identity `S(t) = exp(−H(t))`. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- The hazard is the modeling target for most methods (lifelines Quickstart v0.30, 2025; Klein & Moeschberger Ch. 2, 2003). [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- The first thing to compute on any survival dataset — assumption-free descriptive curves. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Kaplan-Meier (product-limit) estimator** of `S(t)`: at each event time multiply by `(1 − dᵢ/nᵢ)`. Step function; censored subjects drop out of the risk set without a step. Report **median survival** and confidence bands. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Nelson-Aalen estimator** of `H(t)`: sum of `dᵢ/nᵢ`. Estimates cumulative hazard under independent right-censoring and left-truncation (lifelines NelsonAalenFitter docs, 2025). [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- from lifelines import KaplanMeierFitter [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- kmf = KaplanMeierFitter() [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- kmf.fit(durations=df["tenure"], event_observed=df["churned"], entry=df.get("entry")) [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- kmf.median_survival_time_; kmf.plot_survival_function() [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- Sources: lifelines Quickstart (2025); Klein & Moeschberger Ch. 4 (2003); CPSC 330 Survival lecture (2023). [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- Compares two-or-more KM curves; null = **equal survival across groups**. Chi-square test accumulating observed-minus-expected events at each event time; weights all time points equally (Wilcoxon/Tarone-Ware variants weight early times more). Gives a p-value, not an effect size — for an effect size use Cox. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- from lifelines.statistics import logrank_test, multivariate_logrank_test [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- logrank_test(durA, durB, eventA, eventB).p_value [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- Sources: lifelines.statistics (2025); STHDA (2018); Klein & Moeschberger Ch. 7 (2003). [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- Semi-parametric: `h(t|x) = h₀(t) · exp(βᵀx)`. Baseline hazard `h₀(t)` is unspecified; `β` estimated via **partial likelihood** (Cox 1972). `exp(βⱼ)` is the **hazard ratio** — multiplicative, time-constant. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- from lifelines import CoxPHFitter [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- cph = CoxPHFitter(penalizer=0.1) [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- cph.fit(df, duration_col="tenure", event_col="churned") [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- cph.print_summary()          # coef, exp(coef)=HR, p, CI [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- Tie handling: Efron (default) or Breslow. Report HRs with CIs. Sources: lifelines CoxPHFitter (2025); Therneau & Grambsch (2000); Researchers' Guide (2021). [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- Cox is only valid if hazard ratios are **constant over time**. Always check. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Scaled Schoenfeld residuals**: zero slope against (a function of) time under PH. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Grambsch-Therneau test** (`cox.zph` in R, `cph.check_assumptions()` / `proportional_hazard_test` in lifelines): null = PH holds; small p-value flags a violation. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Graphical**: `ggcoxzph()` (survminer) — LOESS smooth should be flat. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Fixes when violated**: stratify (`strata=`), add a covariate×time interaction, split follow-up into intervals, or switch to AFT. Sources: UCLA OARC (2021); Stata stcox (2015); STHDA (2018). [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- For a smooth curve, extrapolation, or a generative model. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Exponential**: constant hazard `h(t)=λ`. Memoryless baseline. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Weibull**: monotone increasing (`ρ>1`) or decreasing (`ρ<1`) hazard. The default parametric choice. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **AFT**: `log(T) = βᵀx + error`; covariates accelerate/decelerate time-to-event (`exp(β)` = time ratio). More interpretable for "this doubles the expected lifetime." [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Weibull is the only distribution expressible as both PH and AFT.** Log-logistic / log-normal AFT allow non-monotone hazards. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- from lifelines import WeibullAFTFitter [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- aft = WeibullAFTFitter().fit(df, duration_col="tenure", event_col="churned") [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- Sources: AFT model — Wikipedia (2025); CRAN eha (2024); AFT vs Cox PMC4645729 (2015). [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- When a subject can fail from **mutually exclusive** causes, naïve KM/Cox on one cause **over-estimates its incidence** by treating competing events as censored. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Cause-specific hazard** (Cox per cause): rate of cause `k` among those still at risk. Best for **etiology**. Censor competing events. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard**: links covariates to the **cumulative incidence function (CIF)** — the actual probability of cause `k`, accounting for competing events. Best for **prediction / risk communication** (`sHR`). Competing-event subjects stay in the risk set with decaying weights. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- Caveats: separate Fine-Gray per cause → CIFs can sum > 1; **avoid multiple Fine-Gray models** — prefer cause-specific for multi-event questions. For causal effects, Fine-Gray is discouraged. Sources: Austin & Fine, Stat Med (2017); Austin et al. (2021); Statistical Horizons (2023). [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- When a predictor changes during follow-up, a single baseline value is wrong. Use **long (counting-process) format**: one row per subject per interval `(id, start, stop, event, covariates)`. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- from lifelines import CoxTimeVaryingFitter [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- ctv = CoxTimeVaryingFitter() [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- ctv.fit(long_df, id_col="id", start_col="start", stop_col="stop", event_col="event") [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- Also the standard fix for a time-varying *coefficient* (a PH violation) — though that needs a covariate×time interaction. Sources: lifelines Time-varying regression (2025); CoxTimeVaryingFitter docs (2025); Therneau & Grambsch Ch. 3 (2000). [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- When time is naturally **binned** and many events tie at the same bin, discrete-time survival beats continuous Cox. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Method**: expand to **person-period** rows, fit ordinary **logistic regression** with the period (or a flexible function of it) as predictor. Fitted per-period probabilities are the **discrete hazards**; chain into a survival/retention curve. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Churn / retention**: tenure = duration, churn = event, active customers = right-censored. KM gives the retention curve; Cox/AFT give "what drives churn timing"; integrating `S(t)` gives expected lifetime, the backbone of **CLV** (`CLV ≈ Σ margin·S(t)·discount`). [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- Survival beats a static churn classifier: it answers *when*, uses censored customers correctly, and yields retention curves and CLV directly. Sources: SAS Survival Data Mining (2012); SAS CLV (2003); Springer churn prediction (2025). [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- When effects are nonlinear/interacting/high-dimensional and accuracy beats interpretability. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Random Survival Forests (RSF)**: survival trees split on the **log-rank statistic**; ensemble cumulative-hazard estimate; handles nonlinearities, right-censoring, variable importance. Ishwaran et al. (2008). [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Gradient-boosted survival**: boosts weak learners against a survival loss; often the strongest tabular baseline. scikit-survival `GradientBoostingSurvivalAnalysis` ~0.75 C-index on the standard example. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **DeepSurv** (Katzman et al., 2018): deep net optimizing the **Cox partial-likelihood** loss; nonlinear Cox for personalized risk. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Evaluation**: **Harrell's concordance index (C-index)** (0.5 random, 1.0 perfect); time-dependent AUC; integrated Brier score. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- from sksurv.ensemble import RandomSurvivalForest [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- from sksurv.metrics import concordance_index_censored [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- rsf = RandomSurvivalForest(n_estimators=200).fit(X, y_structured)  # y = (event_bool, time) [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- Sources: Ishwaran et al., Ann. Appl. Stat. 2(3):841-860 (2008); scikit-survival RSF & boosting guides (2025); Katzman et al., DeepSurv, BMC Med Res Methodol / arXiv 1606.00931 (2018). [src: da-24-survival-analysis]

- **Define the timeline**: `t=0` origin, the event, the censoring rule; check for left truncation / delayed entry. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Describe**: KM curve + median survival; Nelson-Aalen for cumulative hazard; stratify by key groups. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Compare groups**: log-rank (effect size deferred to Cox). [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Model effects**: Cox PH first; parametric/AFT for extrapolation or a smooth curve. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Check assumptions**: Schoenfeld residuals / `cox.zph`; repair PH violations. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Handle structure**: competing risks → cause-specific or Fine-Gray; changing covariates → time-varying; binned time → discrete-time logistic. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Predict at scale**: RSF / gradient boosting / DeepSurv. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Validate**: C-index, time-dependent AUC, integrated Brier, calibration; never plain accuracy. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Always plot KM first** — reveals crossing curves (PH violation), plateaus (cured fraction), data problems. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Encode the outcome as a pair** `(event_indicator, time)` — scikit-survival needs a structured array; lifelines takes two columns. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Report hazard ratios with CIs** and translate: "HR 1.4 → 40% higher instantaneous churn rate." [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Use the right time origin** (calendar / age / time-since-enrollment); left-truncate on delayed entry. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **For churn/CLV**, integrate the survival curve for expected lifetime instead of averaging completed tenures (which ignores censored = still-active customers). [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Dropping censored rows** — the cardinal sin; discards most information and badly biases estimates. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Treating time-to-event as an OLS regression target** — censoring makes the target undefined for survivors. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Treating competing events as plain censoring** when estimating one cause's incidence — over-states it; use CIF / Fine-Gray. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Fitting Cox without checking PH** — silently corrupts every hazard ratio. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Reporting only a log-rank p-value** with no effect size or curve. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **Evaluating an ML survival model with accuracy/AUC on a binarized label** instead of C-index / Brier. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]
- **One Fine-Gray model per cause read together** — CIFs can sum past 1; prefer cause-specific for multi-event questions. [src: da-24-survival-analysis]

- **Causal discovery** (a.k.a. structure learning) learns the *causal graph itself* [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- from observational and/or interventional data — the edges and their directions — [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- rather than assuming the graph and estimating an effect. This is the upstream [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- problem to causal **inference**. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **This skill (discovery):** "What is the causal structure? Which variables [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- cause which?" → output is a graph (DAG, CPDAG, or PAG). [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **da-12 (inference):** "Given this DAG, what is the effect of X on Y?" → DiD, [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- RDD, IV, propensity scores, synthetic control, backdoor/frontdoor adjustment. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- If the user already has/assumes a DAG and wants an effect estimate, defer to [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **da-12-ab-testing-causal-inference**. Use this skill only when the *structure* [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- The hard truth of discovery: from purely observational data you usually cannot [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- recover a single DAG — only an **equivalence class** of DAGs (a CPDAG or PAG). [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- Pinning down direction requires extra assumptions (non-Gaussianity, nonlinearity), [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- interventions, or time order. Always communicate which edges are oriented vs. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- Two DAGs are **Markov equivalent** if they entail the same conditional [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- independences — they have the same skeleton (undirected edges) and the same [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **v-structures / colliders** (A → C ← B with A, B not adjacent). Equivalent DAGs [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- cannot be distinguished by observational independence tests alone (Verma & Pearl, [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- 1990; Andersson, Madigan & Perlman, 1997). [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- A **CPDAG** (Completed Partially Directed Acyclic Graph, a.k.a. essential [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- graph) represents the whole Markov equivalence class: directed edges are [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- oriented in *every* member, undirected edges flip across members. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- Constraint- and score-based methods return a **CPDAG**, not a DAG. Reporting a [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- single oriented DAG from such output is a common, serious error. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Causal Markov condition:** each variable is independent of its [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- non-descendants given its parents. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Faithfulness:** every conditional independence in the distribution is [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- implied by the graph structure (no exact cancellations). Near-violations cause [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- unstable orientation in finite samples (Spirtes, Glymour & Scheines, 2000). [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Causal sufficiency:** no unmeasured common causes (latent confounders). PC [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- and GES assume this; **FCI does not**. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Acyclicity:** most methods assume a DAG (no feedback loops). [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- Identifiability hinges on these. Be explicit which the chosen method needs. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **PC algorithm** (Peter–Clark; Spirtes, Glymour & Scheines, 2000): start from a [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- complete undirected graph, remove edges via conditional-independence (CI) tests, [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- then orient colliders and propagate (Meek rules). Output: **CPDAG**. Assumes [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- causal sufficiency + faithfulness. Order-dependence fixed by **PC-stable** [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- (Colombo & Maathuis, 2014). CI tests: Fisher-Z (linear-Gaussian), G²/χ² [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- (discrete), KCI (kernel, nonlinear). [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **FCI** (Fast Causal Inference) and **RFCI**: drop causal sufficiency — handle [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **latent confounders and selection bias**. Output: a **PAG** (Partial Ancestral [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- Graph) over a **MAG**, with edge marks ○ (unknown), → (ancestor), ↔ (latent [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- common cause) (Spirtes et al., 2000; Zhang, 2008). [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **GES** (Greedy Equivalence Search; Chickering, 2002): searches over CPDAG space [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- with a two-phase forward (edge-add) / backward (edge-delete) greedy search, [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- scoring with a **decomposable, consistent** score — **BIC** (continuous) or [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **BDeu** (discrete). Asymptotically returns the true equivalence class. **fGES** [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- is the fast/parallel variant (TETRAD). [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **GIES** (Hauser & Bühlmann, 2012): GES extended to **interventional data** — [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- searches over interventional Markov equivalence classes, exploiting experiments [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- to orient more edges. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **GRaSP** and **BOSS** (Lam, Andrews & Ramsey, 2022): search over variable [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- *orderings*; more accurate and scalable than GES on many benchmarks, available [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- in causal-learn and TETRAD. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- By assuming a functional form, these identify a **unique DAG**, not just a CPDAG. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **LiNGAM** — Linear, Non-Gaussian, Acyclic Model (Shimizu, Hoyer, Hyvärinen & [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- Kerminen, 2006, JMLR 7:2003–2030): linear SEM with non-Gaussian noise → full [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- causal order is **identifiable**. **ICA-LiNGAM** uses ICA; **DirectLiNGAM** [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- (Shimizu et al., 2011) is regression-based and avoids ICA local optima. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **ANM** — Additive Noise Models (Hoyer, Janzing, Mooij, Peters & Schölkopf, [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- 2008/2009): Y = f(X) + N with N ⟂ X. Nonlinear f breaks the X↔Y symmetry → [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- cause/effect direction identifiable. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Post-Nonlinear (PNL)** model (Zhang & Hyvärinen, 2009): Y = g(f(X) + N) — most [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- general identifiable FCM. In causal-learn. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- Reframe combinatorial DAG search as smooth optimization with a differentiable [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- acyclicity constraint — scales and integrates with deep learning. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **NOTEARS** (Zheng, Aragam, Ravikumar & Xing, NeurIPS 2018): the acyclicity [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- breakthrough — `h(W) = tr(e^{W∘W}) − d = 0` is a smooth, exact characterization [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- of acyclicity, solved via augmented Lagrangian. Originally linear; NOTEARS-MLP [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- extends to nonlinear. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **GOLEM** (Ng, Ghassami & Zhang, NeurIPS 2020): likelihood-based score with soft [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- acyclicity — faster and more accurate than NOTEARS in the linear-Gaussian/EV [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **DAG-GNN** (Yu et al., ICML 2019): VAE/GNN variant for nonlinear and discrete [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Caveat:** Reisach, Seiler & Weichwein (NeurIPS 2021, "Beware of the Simulated [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- DAG") showed continuous-optimization methods can exploit **varsortability** — [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- marginal-variance artifacts of synthetic data scaling. **Standardize data** and [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- don't trust synthetic-benchmark wins blindly. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Granger causality**: X Granger-causes Y if past X improves prediction of Y [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- beyond Y's own past. Predictive, not structural; fails with latent confounders / [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- instantaneous effects / nonlinearity. Use only as a baseline. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **PCMCI / PCMCI+** (Runge et al., *Science Advances* 2019; PCMCI+ in UAI 2020): [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- two-stage — a PC-style condition-selection step, then **Momentary Conditional [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- Independence (MCI)** tests controlling for autocorrelation and indirect links. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- PCMCI+ adds contemporaneous links. Implemented in **Tigramite**; pairs with any [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- CI test (ParCorr, GPDC, CMI). **LPCMCI** handles latent confounders. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **VAR-LiNGAM** (Hyvärinen et al., 2010): combines a VAR model with LiNGAM to [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- recover both lagged and instantaneous causal effects. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **causal-learn** (py-why, Python; Zheng et al., 2024; docs [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- https://causal-learn.readthedocs.io/): the reference Python toolkit — PC, FCI, [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- GES, GRaSP, BOSS, LiNGAM family, ANM, PNL, CD-NOD, plus CI tests and graph [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- utilities. Default first choice for general discovery. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **gCastle** (Huawei Noah's Ark Lab; Zhang et al., 2021): gradient-based focus [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- (NOTEARS, GOLEM, DAG-GNN, GraN-DAG, ...), PyTorch + GPU, data simulators, and a [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- built-in metrics module (SHD, FDR, TPR, F1, NNZ). [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Tigramite** (Runge; https://github.com/jakobrunge/tigramite): the standard for [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- time-series discovery (PCMCI, PCMCI+, LPCMCI, RPCMCI). [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **pcalg** (R; Kalisch et al., *JSS* 2012): mature PC/FCI/RFCI/GES with IDA effect [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **DoWhy** (py-why; https://www.pywhy.org/dowhy/): primarily inference, but its [src: da-32-causal-discovery]

- **CausalNex** (QuantumBlack): NOTEARS-based structure learning + Bayesian-network [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- reasoning, with expert-knowledge constraints (tabu edges, required edges). [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **TETRAD / py-tetrad**: large library of search algorithms and the [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- knowledge/background-constraint framework. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Always inject background knowledge.** Forbidden edges, required edges, and [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- tiered time order (a cause can't follow its effect) dramatically reduce the [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- equivalence class. Every major tool supports knowledge/tabu constraints — use [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Match method to assumptions and data type:** [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- Possible latent confounders → **FCI / RFCI** (get a PAG), not PC/GES. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- Linear + non-Gaussian noise → **DirectLiNGAM** (gets a full DAG). [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- Nonlinear, continuous → **ANM / PNL**, or NOTEARS-MLP / DAG-GNN. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- Discrete/categorical → score-based with **BDeu**, or G²-test PC. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- High-dim time series → **PCMCI+**. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- Have interventions/experiments → **GIES** or interventional NOTEARS. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Standardize/scale continuous variables** before continuous-optimization [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- methods to avoid varsortability artifacts. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Bootstrap for edge stability.** Resample, re-run discovery, and report [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- edge-presence and orientation frequencies rather than one point graph. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Discover → refute → estimate.** Use discovery to *propose* a graph, validate [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- with domain experts and refutation/sensitivity checks, then hand the validated [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- DAG to **da-12** for effect estimation. Discovery output is a hypothesis, not [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Evaluate with the right metric:** [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **SHD** (Structural Hamming Distance): count of edge insert/delete/reverse [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- ops to match the truth — lower is better; compare against the CPDAG, not a [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- DAG, when methods return equivalence classes. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **SID** (Structural Intervention Distance; Peters & Bühlmann, 2015): counts [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- intervention-distribution errors — closer to what matters for downstream [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- effect estimation than SHD. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- Also F1 / precision / recall on the skeleton, FDR, TPR. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Reporting a single DAG when the method returns a CPDAG/PAG.** Undirected / [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- circle-marked edges are genuinely undetermined; orienting them implies [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- assumptions you didn't make. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Treating Granger causality as structural causality.** It's lagged prediction; [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- silent on confounders and contemporaneous effects. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Trusting synthetic-benchmark performance of NOTEARS-family methods** without [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- standardizing data (varsortability — Reisach et al., 2021). [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Ignoring latent confounders.** Running PC/GES when unmeasured common causes are [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- plausible yields confident but wrong edges. Use FCI or sensitivity analysis. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Skipping faithfulness/sufficiency disclosure.** Stakeholders must know the [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- result is conditional on assumptions that can't be verified from data alone. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Using discovery output directly for policy.** Discovery proposes; it does not [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- prove. Validate before acting. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Doing effect estimation here.** Backdoor adjustment, IV, DiD, propensity [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- scores, synthetic control → **da-12-ab-testing-causal-inference**. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Too many undirected edges in the CPDAG:** expected with observational-only [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- data. Add background knowledge, use an FCM method (LiNGAM/ANM) if assumptions [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- hold, or collect interventional data. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Unstable edges across runs/bootstraps:** likely faithfulness near-violations, [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- small n, or wrong CI test. Increase data, switch CI test (e.g., KCI for [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- nonlinearity), use PC-stable. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **PC gives different graphs depending on variable order:** use **PC-stable** [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- (Colombo & Maathuis, 2014). [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Dense, implausible graph from NOTEARS:** increase the L1 sparsity penalty, [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- standardize data, threshold small weights; consider GOLEM. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Nonlinear relationships missed:** linear methods (Fisher-Z PC, linear NOTEARS, [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- LiNGAM) can't see them — use KCI tests, ANM/PNL, NOTEARS-MLP, or DAG-GNN. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **Time-series links look confounded by autocorrelation:** that's exactly what [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
- **PCMCI** (MCI step) controls for; plain Granger does not. [src: da-32-causal-discovery]
