- Prescriptive analytics is the fourth and highest rung of Gartner's analytics maturity ladder (descriptive → diagnostic → predictive → prescriptive). It answers **"what should be done?"** rather than "what happened?" or "what will happen?" by recommending (or automating) a specific action. Gartner defines it as advanced analytics that examines data to answer "what should be done?" using techniques such as **optimization, simulation, complex event processing, graph analysis, heuristics, recommendation engines, and machine learning** ([Gartner, Data & Analytics](https://www.gartner.com/en/topics/data-and-analytics)). [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- The mental model: **predictive feeds prescriptive.** A demand forecast (da-15) or a propensity model (da-7) produces *parameters*; prescriptive analytics wraps those parameters in a **decision model** — an objective to optimize, decision variables you control, and constraints you must respect — and returns the action that best trades off the objective against the constraints. This skill is the **optimization + decision-science** layer of the curriculum; da-6/da-7 supply the predictions it consumes. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- A useful framing is the **decision = objective + decision variables + constraints + uncertainty** quadruple. Choosing a method is mostly about which of those four is hard: linear and continuous → LP; discrete choices → MILP/CP; nonlinear-but-convex → convex/QP; uncertainty dominates → stochastic/robust; many competing objectives → multi-objective; analytical model intractable → simulation. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- Descriptive/diagnostic give hindsight; predictive/prescriptive give foresight, and **human involvement decreases** as you move toward prescriptive (which can drive automated action). Prescriptive consumes a prediction and adds a *decision rule or optimization* on top ([EAG, 4 types of analytics](https://eaginc.com/understanding-data-analytics/); [Qlik](https://www.qlik.com/blog/embrace-the-future-moving-from-descriptive-to-prescriptive-analytics); [Gartner glossary](https://www.gartner.com/en/topics/data-and-analytics)). [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- Continuous variables, linear objective and constraints. Solved at a polytope vertex by simplex or interior-point. Canonical teaching cases: **blending** (min-cost mix meeting specs) and **product-mix** (max profit s.t. resource limits). LP is the substrate everything else extends ([SciPy linprog](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.optimize.linprog.html); [PuLP](https://coin-or.github.io/pulp/); [Real Python LP](https://realpython.com/linear-programming-python/)). [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- Some/all variables integer or **binary** (yes/no: open a facility, assign a job, select an item). NP-hard; solved by **branch-and-bound / branch-and-cut** with LP relaxations. Binary variables unlock assignment, knapsack, facility location, scheduling, routing. For pure integer problems OR-Tools recommends **CP-SAT**; for mixed continuous+integer it recommends SCIP or a commercial solver ([OR-Tools MIP](https://developers.google.com/optimization/mip); [Gurobi](https://www.gurobi.com/resources/); [SciPy milp](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.optimize.milp.html)). [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- Nonlinear but **convex** → any local optimum is global; solvers reliable and fast. Includes least-squares, quadratic programming (e.g., **Markowitz portfolio**), second-order cone, semidefinite programs. **Disciplined Convex Programming (DCP)** is the rule system CVXPY uses to *verify* convexity before solving — build expressions from functions with known curvature ([CVXPY DCP](https://www.cvxpy.org/tutorial/dcp/index.html); [CVXPY intro](https://www.cvxpy.org/tutorial/intro/index.html); [Boyd & Vandenberghe](https://web.stanford.edu/~boyd/cvxbook/)). [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- Declarative: state variables, domains, and combinatorial **constraints** (`AllDifferent`, no-overlap, cumulative); solver searches via propagation + SAT/backtracking. Excels at feasibility-heavy combinatorial problems — **scheduling, rostering, timetabling**. OR-Tools **CP-SAT** is the flagship and has repeatedly won the MiniZinc Challenge ([OR-Tools CP](https://developers.google.com/optimization/cp); [CP-SAT solver](https://developers.google.com/optimization/cp/cp_solver); [OR-Tools, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OR-Tools)). [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Stochastic programming with recourse**: first-stage (here-and-now) and second-stage **recourse** (wait-and-see corrective) decisions; optimize *expected* cost over scenarios. Classic: newsvendor / two-stage capacity-then-adjust. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Robust optimization**: optimize the **worst case** over an uncertainty set (no distribution needed) — more conservative. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Distributionally robust (DRO)**: hedge over a *set of distributions*; between stochastic and robust. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Chance constraints**: hold a constraint with probability ≥ 1−α ([NEOS Guide](https://neos-guide.org/guide/types/stochastic/); [SIAM J. Optimization, DR Two-Stage SP](https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/20M1370227); [Birge & Louveaux](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-1-4614-0237-4)). [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- Competing objectives (cost vs. service, risk vs. return) yield a **Pareto front** of non-dominated tradeoffs. Scalarization: **weighted-sum** (simple, misses non-convex regions) and **epsilon-constraint** (optimize one, bound others — recovers non-convex fronts). Population methods like **NSGA-II** (non-dominated sorting + crowding distance) approximate the whole front in one run; `pymoo` implements both ([pymoo](https://pymoo.org/); [NSGA-II](https://pymoo.org/algorithms/moo/nsga2.html); [Blank & Deb](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2002.04504)). [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- For discrete decisions under uncertainty with few alternatives: [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Decision trees** alternate decision and chance nodes; fold back by **expected monetary value (EMV)**. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **EVPI** = (expected value *with* perfect information) − (best EMV *without*) — max you'd pay for perfect info; **EVSI** is the sample-info analogue (Bayesian update). [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Utility theory**: replace dollars with a **utility function** to encode risk attitude (concave = risk-averse); maximize *expected utility*, not EMV ([Wikipedia, EVPI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expected_value_of_perfect_information); [Analytica](https://docs.analytica.com/index.php/Expected_value_of_information_--_EVI,_EVPI,_and_ESVI); [TreeAge](https://www.treeage.com/help/Content/31-Analyzing-Decision-Trees/9-Expected-value-perfect-information-EVPI.htm)). [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- When the system is too complex for a closed-form model: [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Discrete-event simulation (DES)**: entities flowing through resources/queues over event-driven time (`SimPy`; Arena/AnyLogic commercially) — staffing, throughput, capacity. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Monte Carlo**: propagate input distributions to an output *distribution* and risk metrics (P10/P50/P90). [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Simulation-optimization**: wrap a simulation as the objective for an optimizer when no analytic form exists. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Queueing theory** (M/M/1, M/M/c, Little's Law `L = λW`) gives analytic baselines for waiting-line/staffing decisions ([DES with SimPy, TDS](https://towardsdatascience.com/object-oriented-discrete-event-simulation-with-simpy-53ad82f5f6e2/); [OR and simulation, ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1569190X08000439); [SimLLM, arXiv 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06543v1)). [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- Gartner's operationalizing umbrella: a discipline that **explicitly models decisions as reusable assets**, linking data → analytics → action and closing the loop with outcome feedback. **Decision Intelligence Platforms (DIPs)** compose data, analytics, decision modeling, and AI to support/augment/automate decisions. Per the 2024 Gartner Market Guide, ~33% of surveyed organizations had already deployed DI ([Gartner DI glossary](https://www.gartner.com/en/information-technology/glossary/decision-intelligence); [Market Guide for DI Platforms](https://www.gartner.com/en/documents/5599159); [FICO](https://www.fico.com/blogs/what-decision-intelligence-software-and-should-you-invest-it)). [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Selection heuristic:** convex/continuous nonlinear → CVXPY; combinatorial / scheduling / routing → OR-Tools CP-SAT; plain LP/MILP prototyping → PuLP; large or nonlinear/stochastic algebraic models → Pyomo; performance at scale → Gurobi; many objectives → pymoo; no analytic model → SimPy + an outer optimizer. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Frame the decision, not the prediction.** Name the *objective* (one unit), *decision variables* (what you control), *constraints* (what limits you), *uncertainty* (what you don't know). If you can't write these four, it isn't yet an optimization problem. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Classify the problem** → pick the method family (LP / MILP / convex / CP / stochastic / robust / multi-objective / simulation). [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Source parameters** from predictive/statistical models (da-6/da-7/da-15); keep the parameter pipeline separate from the decision model. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Build small, validate, scale.** Prototype on a tiny instance; check feasibility and shadow prices before scaling to a production solver. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Quantify the value of certainty** before buying data: compute **EVPI/EVSI**; run **sensitivity / shadow-price** analysis on LP/MILP. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Stress-test under uncertainty.** Re-solve across scenarios (stochastic) or over an uncertainty set (robust); report the *distribution* of outcomes via Monte Carlo. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Close the loop (DI).** Deploy, capture realized outcomes, feed back to refit parameters and re-tune. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Blending / diet**: LP, min cost s.t. composition specs → PuLP or SciPy. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Product mix / capacity**: LP, max margin s.t. resource limits; read shadow prices for the bottleneck. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Assignment / matching**: binary MILP (Hungarian for the pure case) → OR-Tools. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Knapsack / selection**: binary MILP, max value s.t. budget → CP-SAT. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Scheduling / rostering**: CP-SAT with `NoOverlap` / cumulative + interval vars. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Vehicle routing (VRP/CVRP/VRPTW)**: OR-Tools routing library with capacity/time-window dimensions. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Inventory / newsvendor**: stochastic — balance overage vs. underage; critical-ratio quantile of demand is the optimal order. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Portfolio**: convex QP (Markowitz) in CVXPY; multi-objective (return vs. risk) → efficient frontier. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Staffing / call center**: queueing baseline (Erlang-C) → DES (SimPy) → simulation-optimization for shift design. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Optimizing a forecast instead of a decision.** A prediction with no objective/constraints/action is still predictive analytics (→ da-15/da-7). [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Forcing nonlinearity into LP** or ignoring non-convexity. Linearize deliberately (piecewise, big-M) or move to convex/MINLP. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Big-M too large.** Loose big-M wrecks MILP relaxations and numerics; pick the tightest valid bound. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Weighted-sum for non-convex Pareto fronts.** Silently misses regions; use epsilon-constraint or NSGA-II. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Single-scenario "optimal" plans.** Deterministic optimization on a point forecast is brittle; use stochastic/robust or Monte Carlo stress. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Trusting a local optimum as global** on non-convex/MINLP without saying so. Report the optimality gap. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Decision tree with made-up probabilities** and no EVPI. If the recommendation flips under plausible probabilities, you need more info. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Ignoring solver status.** Optimal vs. feasible/time-limit vs. infeasible vs. unbounded are different answers — check the status code. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Infeasible.** Relax/soften constraints (slack with penalty); use IIS/conflict refiner (Gurobi, CP-SAT); usual culprit is over-tight equalities or unit mismatches. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Unbounded.** Missing upper bound or sign error in objective; add realistic bounds. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **MILP too slow.** Tighten big-M, add cuts/symmetry-breaking, warm-start, set a MIP gap, or switch MILP → CP-SAT. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **CVXPY "not DCP".** Expression has unknown/wrong curvature; rewrite with DCP atoms (`cp.quad_form`, `cp.norm`, `cp.log_sum_exp`). [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Numerical issues.** Rescale variables/coefficients to similar magnitudes; avoid mixing 1e-6 and 1e9. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Simulation too noisy.** More replications, common random numbers, report confidence intervals. [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- **Stochastic model explodes.** Reduce scenarios via scenario reduction / sample average approximation (SAA). [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]

- Qlik / EAG — descriptive→prescriptive maturity, 2024. https://www.qlik.com/blog/embrace-the-future-moving-from-descriptive-to-prescriptive-analytics [src: da-33-prescriptive-analytics]
- Applied NLP for turning **unstructured text into measurable signal**. The audience is an analyst, not an ML engineer: the goal is defensible insight from reviews, support tickets, survey open-ends, call transcripts, social posts, and documents — not training novel models. Prefer the simplest method that answers the question; escalate to embeddings/transformers/LLMs only when classical methods fall short. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Rule of thumb:** establish a cheap, interpretable baseline (TF-IDF + linear model, or VADER) before any transformer or LLM. Report the baseline number even when you ship the fancier model — it is your sanity check and your cost/latency benchmark. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- The decisions here silently determine every downstream result. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Tokenization**: splitting into tokens (words, subwords, sentences). spaCy and NLTK do linguistic word/sentence tokenization; transformers use subword tokenizers (WordPiece/BPE/SentencePiece) — never lowercase or strip punctuation before a transformer tokenizer, it expects raw text. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Normalization**: lowercasing, Unicode normalization (NFC/NFKC), accent folding, contraction expansion, whitespace cleanup. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Stopword removal & stemming/lemmatization**: helps bag-of-words / topic models; *harmful* for embeddings and transformers, which need full context. Lemmatization (spaCy) is preferred over crude stemming (Porter/Snowball) when you keep tokens human-readable. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **What to keep**: for sentiment, keep negations, emojis, intensifiers, ALL-CAPS — VADER and good models use them as signal. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Pitfall**: applying the bag-of-words preprocessing recipe (lowercase, de-punct, stem, strip stopwords) before embedding/transformer steps destroys signal. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **BoW / Count**: document = vector of token counts. Simple, sparse, ignores order. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **TF-IDF**: down-weights terms common across the corpus, up-weights distinctive terms. `TfidfVectorizer` in scikit-learn is the analyst's workhorse for distinctive-term and baseline-classifier work. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **n-grams**: capture short phrases ("not good", "customer service") that unigrams miss. Set `ngram_range=(1,2)` (sometimes `(1,3)`); watch dimensionality blow-up — use `min_df`/`max_df` and `max_features`. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Still relevant in 2026**: cheap, transparent, fast, and a strong classification baseline. Use it before anything heavier. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **LDA** (Latent Dirichlet Allocation, Gensim/scikit-learn): probabilistic, each doc = mixture of topics; needs `num_topics` chosen up front; works best on longer, cleaned text; tune with coherence (c_v / u_mass). [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **NMF** (scikit-learn, on TF-IDF): deterministic-ish matrix factorization; often crisper topics than LDA on short text; also needs k. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **BERTopic** (MaartenGr): modular pipeline — **embeddings (sentence-transformers) → UMAP (dim reduction) → HDBSCAN (density clustering, auto-detects topic count + outliers) → c-TF-IDF (per-cluster distinctive terms) → optional representation tuning (KeyBERT/MMR/LLM labels)**. Each stage is swappable. Default choice for modern, especially short/noisy, text because it does not force a topic count and handles outliers. Use `reduce_outliers`, `nr_topics` to merge, and pass a fixed `random_state` to UMAP for reproducibility. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Choosing**: short/messy/lots of docs → BERTopic; small clean corpus or need probabilistic doc-topic mixtures → LDA/NMF; need speed/transparency → NMF on TF-IDF. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **VADER** (Hutto & Gilbert, 2014): lexicon + rule-based, tuned for social media; handles negation, intensifiers, punctuation, emoji, caps. Returns `compound` in [-1, 1] (thresholds ≈ ±0.05). No training, instant, fully transparent, free — ideal first pass on tweets/reviews/short informal text. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Transformer** (e.g. fine-tuned BERT/RoBERTa via Hugging Face `pipeline("sentiment-analysis")`): context-aware, handles sarcasm/domain nuance better, but heavier, slower, and can carry positivity/domain bias. Studies consistently rank transformer/Flair > BERT > VADER on correlation with human ratings, with VADER competitive on short informal text and far cheaper. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Aspect-based sentiment (ABSA)**: sentiment *per aspect* ("battery good, screen bad") — use when one polarity per doc is too coarse. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Analyst guidance**: VADER for fast directional reads and big volumes; transformer when domain/sarcasm matters and you can validate on a labeled sample. Always sanity-check both against a hand-labeled set — domain mismatch (finance, clinical) breaks generic models. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **spaCy**: statistical transition-based NER labeling non-overlapping spans (PERSON, ORG, GPE, DATE, PRODUCT, MONEY, …). `en_core_web_sm/md/lg` for speed, `en_core_web_trf` for accuracy. Add an `EntityRuler` for deterministic patterns (SKUs, ticket IDs) before/after the statistical NER. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **LLM / spacy-llm**: zero/few-shot extraction of custom entity types without training data; good for niche schemas, but validate and watch for hallucinated spans. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Analyst uses**: aggregate mentions of competitors/products/locations, redact PII, link entities for rollups. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Baseline**: TF-IDF + linear model (LogisticRegression / LinearSVC) or Naive Bayes. Fast, interpretable, hard to beat on small/medium labeled data. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **spaCy textcat** (`textcat` mutually-exclusive, `textcat_multilabel` for overlapping labels) for an integrated trainable pipeline. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Transformers** (Hugging Face): fine-tune or use zero-shot (`facebook/bart-large-mnli`) when labels are scarce or semantics are subtle. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **LLM zero/few-shot**: fastest path to a working classifier with no training data; pin the label set, give examples, and measure against a gold sample. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- Mind **class imbalance** (use class weights, stratified splits, macro-F1) and **label leakage**. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **RAKE**: fast, unsupervised, co-occurrence based; great for speed, weak on stopword handling and precision. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **YAKE**: statistical, single-document, language-agnostic, no corpus needed; can emit near-duplicates. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **KeyBERT** (MaartenGr): embeds doc and candidate phrases (sentence-transformers) and ranks by cosine similarity; most accurate/contextual; use **MMR / `diversity`** to reduce redundancy. Slower (needs a model). [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Choose**: RAKE/YAKE for speed and no dependencies; KeyBERT for quality and contextual relevance. Combine with c-TF-IDF for per-cluster keywords inside BERTopic. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **word2vec / GloVe / fastText** (Gensim): static word vectors; useful for analogy, vocabulary exploration, lightweight similarity; no context sensitivity. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **sentence-transformers (SBERT)**: contextual *sentence/paragraph* embeddings — `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` (fast, 384-d, default) vs `all-mpnet-base-v2` (best quality, slower); 2024+ multilingual & matryoshka/`gte`/`bge` options. Compute with `model.encode()`; compare with `model.similarity()` (cosine). [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Semantic clustering**: embed → reduce (UMAP/PCA) → cluster (HDBSCAN for variable density + outliers, KMeans when you want fixed k). This is the engine under BERTopic and the analyst's go-to for "group these open-ends by meaning." [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Document similarity / dedup / near-search**: cosine over embeddings; paraphrase mining for dedup; add a **cross-encoder reranker** when top-k precision matters. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Deductive coding** (codebook exists): prompt the LLM with the codebook + definitions + few-shot examples; LLMs give a systematic, reliable platform for code identification at scale — but **human validation is mandatory**; measure agreement (Cohen's/Krippendorff's) against human coders on a sample. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Inductive/exploratory**: embed + cluster first, then have the LLM label/summarize clusters (reflexive thematic analysis); multi-agent (coder/aggregator/reviewer) roles can improve rigor. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Structured extraction**: constrain output to JSON schema; extract fields, entities, ratings from free text reliably. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Risks**: hallucination, prompt-injection from the text itself (treat corpus content as untrusted data, not instructions), drift across runs (pin model + temperature=0), cost/latency at corpus scale. Performance varies by construct — validate per code. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Classification/sentiment**: accuracy, precision/recall, **macro-F1** (for imbalance), confusion matrix; always hold out a labeled test set. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Topic models**: coherence (c_v, NPMI), topic diversity, and **human inspection of top terms/exemplars** — coherence alone is not enough. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Clustering**: silhouette, but mostly qualitative inspection of exemplars; report % outliers (HDBSCAN -1). [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Retrieval/similarity**: precision@k, recall@k, MRR, nDCG. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Coding/extraction**: inter-rater agreement vs human gold (Cohen's κ, Krippendorff's α). [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Always**: a labeled sample (even 100–300 items) is the cheapest insurance against shipping a wrong conclusion. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **spaCy** — production NLP: tokenization, lemmatization, POS, NER, `textcat`, `EntityRuler`, transformer pipelines, spacy-llm. Analyst default for linguistic preprocessing + entities. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **NLTK** — teaching/classic toolkit: tokenizers, stopwords, stemmers, and **VADER** (`nltk.sentiment.vader`). [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **scikit-learn** — `TfidfVectorizer`/`CountVectorizer`, LDA, NMF, LogisticRegression/SVM, metrics, pipelines. The classical-NLP backbone. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Gensim** — LDA, word2vec/fastText, phrase detection, similarity indexes; good for large streaming corpora. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Hugging Face Transformers / Hub** — fine-tuned/zero-shot sentiment, classification, NER, embeddings; `pipeline()` API. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **sentence-transformers (SBERT)** — embeddings for similarity, clustering, semantic search, paraphrase mining; cross-encoder rerankers. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **BERTopic** — modular transformer topic modeling (embeddings → UMAP → HDBSCAN → c-TF-IDF → representation). [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **KeyBERT / YAKE / RAKE** — keyphrase extraction across the speed↔accuracy spectrum. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Frame the question** in measurable terms ("what share of tickets mention billing AND are negative?"). [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Profile the corpus**: length distribution, language(s), duplicates, source noise (HTML, emoji, boilerplate). [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Preprocess deliberately** — match the recipe to the method (heavy for BoW/LDA, light for embeddings/transformers). [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Baseline first**: TF-IDF distinctive terms, VADER, or TF-IDF + linear classifier. Record the number. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Escalate only if needed**: embeddings/BERTopic/transformer/LLM, justified by a baseline gap. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Validate on a labeled sample** before trusting aggregates. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Aggregate and visualize** with uncertainty (counts, %, CIs); never report a single sentiment number without volume + a sample of exemplars. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Document** preprocessing, model versions, thresholds, and seeds for reproducibility. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Distinctive-terms report**: TF-IDF with `ngram_range=(1,2)`, top terms per segment — cheap, persuasive, interpretable. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Open-end theming**: SBERT `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` → BERTopic with fixed UMAP `random_state` → label topics with KeyBERT/LLM → reduce outliers. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Directional sentiment at scale**: VADER pass for volume; transformer on a sampled/uncertain subset; reconcile. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **PII scrub / entity rollup**: spaCy NER + EntityRuler; aggregate ORG/PRODUCT mentions. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Codebook coding**: LLM deductive pass with few-shot codebook → human reviews a random 10–20% → report κ. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Dedup near-identical feedback**: SBERT embeddings + cosine threshold or paraphrase mining. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- Reporting one global sentiment score with no volume, no time trend, no exemplars. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- Stemming/stopword-stripping before embeddings or transformer tokenizers (destroys signal). [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- Picking LDA `num_topics` by gut and never checking coherence or exemplars. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- Trusting LLM/transformer output on a new domain without a labeled validation sample. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- Treating corpus text as trusted instructions to the LLM (prompt-injection exposure). [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- Using accuracy on imbalanced labels instead of macro-F1. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- Jumping to transformers/LLMs before a TF-IDF/VADER baseline (cost, latency, and no benchmark). [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- Non-reproducible runs: unpinned model versions, no seeds, non-zero temperature for extraction. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Topics are garbage / one giant topic** → too few/noisy docs, bad preprocessing, or HDBSCAN merging; tune `min_topic_size`, embeddings, or use NMF; check % outliers. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Everything looks "neutral" in VADER** → wrong domain (formal/clinical/financial), translation needed, or compound thresholds wrong; try a domain transformer. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Embeddings cluster by length/language not meaning** → mixed languages or huge length variance; segment by language, chunk long docs. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **KeyBERT returns near-duplicates** → enable MMR / raise `diversity`. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Classifier great in CV, bad live** → leakage, distribution shift, or imbalance; re-check splits and macro-F1. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **LLM coding disagrees with humans** → tighten codebook definitions, add few-shot exemplars, lower temperature, measure κ per code. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- **Slow at corpus scale** → batch `encode()`, use MiniLM not mpnet, cache embeddings, sample for exploration. [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- BERTopic docs & algorithm — modular embeddings/UMAP/HDBSCAN/c-TF-IDF pipeline (MaartenGr, 2022–2025): https://maartengr.github.io/BERTopic/ , https://maartengr.github.io/BERTopic/algorithm/algorithm.html , https://github.com/MaartenGr/BERTopic [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- Sentence-Transformers (SBERT) docs — semantic similarity, pretrained models, computing embeddings (2024–2025): https://www.sbert.net/docs/quickstart.html , https://www.sbert.net/docs/sentence_transformer/pretrained_models.html , https://www.sbert.net/docs/sentence_transformer/usage/semantic_textual_similarity.html [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- VADER: Hutto & Gilbert, "A Parsimonious Rule-Based Model for Sentiment Analysis of Social Media Text," ICWSM 2014: https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/ICWSM/article/view/14550 ; repo: https://github.com/cjhutto/vaderSentiment ; docs: https://vadersentiment.readthedocs.io/ [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- Transformer vs lexicon sentiment comparisons (2024–2025): https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10115-024-02214-3 ; healthcare VADER/BERT/Flair: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12382424/ [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- spaCy docs — NER, textcat, training pipelines, LLM integration (v3, 2024–2025): https://spacy.io/usage/spacy-101 , https://spacy.io/api/entityrecognizer , https://spacy.io/usage/training , https://spacy.io/usage/large-language-models , https://github.com/explosion/spacy-llm [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- KeyBERT (MaartenGr) + keyword-extraction benchmarks (RAKE/YAKE/KeyBERT, 2024): https://github.com/MaartenGr/KeyBERT , https://arxiv.org/pdf/2409.10640 , https://towardsdatascience.com/keyword-extraction-a-benchmark-of-7-algorithms-in-python-8a905326d93f/ [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- scikit-learn text feature extraction (TF-IDF, n-grams) & decomposition (LDA/NMF): https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/feature_extraction.html#text-feature-extraction , https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/decomposition.html [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- Gensim — LDA, word2vec, similarity: https://radimrehurek.com/gensim/ [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]
- Hugging Face Transformers — pipelines (sentiment, zero-shot classification, NER): https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main_classes/pipelines [src: da-36-text-analytics-nlp]

- Data FinOps applies the FinOps Foundation's operating model — **Inform → Optimize → Operate** — to consumption-based data and analytics platforms. The defining difference from infrastructure FinOps: traditional cloud bills for *provisioned* resources over time, while data cloud platforms bill for *activity* — queries executed, bytes scanned, and consumption of virtual units (Snowflake **credits**, BigQuery **slots**, Databricks **DBUs**). Cost therefore lives in *workload telemetry* (queries, jobs, pipelines, platform metadata), not in a server inventory. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- The 2025 FinOps Framework formalized **Scopes** and a dedicated **"FinOps for Data Cloud Platforms"** technology category covering Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery, Redshift, and Microsoft Fabric ([finops.org/framework/scope](https://www.finops.org/framework/scope/finops-for-data-cloud-platforms/), 2025; [2025 Framework](https://www.finops.org/insights/2025-finops-framework/)). The discipline pairs data engineers, data scientists, product, and finance to connect spend to value. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- Scope note: this skill covers analytics/warehouse FinOps. For **MongoDB / Atlas** cost and sizing, defer to `mongodb-cost-optimization`. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Inform** — ingest billing exports + query history + metadata; allocate shared/transient compute; report, forecast, and build unit economics. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Optimize** — query tuning, storage lifecycle, workload placement, rate optimization (commitments), right-sizing. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Operate** — make cost-awareness a daily habit: tagging policy, governance, budgets, anomaly alerts, chargeback. ([FinOps phases](https://www.finops.org/framework/phases/), 2025; [State of FinOps 2025](https://data.finops.org/2025-report/)) [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Snowflake — credits / virtual warehouses.** Compute bills per-second of active warehouse runtime with a **60-second minimum on every start**. Each warehouse size step (XS→S→M→L…) **doubles credits/hour**. On-demand credits run ~$2–4 each; commitments ~$1.50–2.50. Storage and serverless features (clustering, MVs) bill separately. ([Snowflake cost controls](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/cost-controlling-controls), 2025; [SELECT pricing](https://select.dev/posts/snowflake-pricing), 2025; [Revefi 2026 guide](https://www.revefi.com/blog/snowflake-cost-optimization)) [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **BigQuery — on-demand vs Editions/slots.** [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- *On-demand:* **$6.25/TB scanned** (first 1 TB/mo free per project). Billed on *columns selected*, not rows returned — `LIMIT` does **not** cut cost; fewer columns + partition/cluster pruning do. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- *Editions (capacity):* pay-as-you-go slot-hours — Standard ~$0.04, Enterprise ~$0.06, Enterprise Plus ~$0.10. 1-yr commit ~25–30% lower, 3-yr ~40% lower. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- *Crossover:* sustained >~100 slots usually favors capacity over on-demand. Autoscaling bills **slots allocated, not used**, scales in steps of 100 with a 1-minute floor — a 10s query still costs a full minute. ([BigQuery pricing](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/pricing), 2025; [Editions intro](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/editions-intro), 2025; [Revefi slot guide](https://www.revefi.com/blog/bigquery-slot-cost-explained), 2025) [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Databricks — DBUs.** Bill = **DBU rate × node count × runtime hours × cloud VM list price** (the VM is separate, except serverless which bundles it). DBU rate is fixed per **SKU**; the SKU choice dominates cost: [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- *All-Purpose Compute* — highest rate (~$0.55/DBU Premium). [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- *Jobs Compute* — 40–60% cheaper than All-Purpose; **migrating scheduled work here is the single highest-return change.** [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- *SQL Warehouses* — SQL Classic (~$0.22/DBU) cheapest, SQL Pro (~$0.55), Serverless SQL (~$0.70–0.91, infra bundled). [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- *Photon* — vectorized C++ engine; faster but **raises the DBU rate** — a 3× faster query may cost ~1.5× DBUs/hr, so validate net savings. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- Standard tier sunset on AWS/GCP Oct 2025, Azure by Oct 2026. ([CloudZero](https://www.cloudzero.com/blog/databricks-pricing/), 2026; [Flexera guide](https://www.flexera.com/blog/finops/databricks-pricing-guide/), 2026; [Revefi guide](https://www.revefi.com/blog/databricks-pricing-guide), 2026) [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Showback** = show teams their consumption without billing them (central budget absorbs cost). **Chargeback** = bill teams directly via internal transfer. Showback first builds trust; chargeback drives accountability. ([Revefi showback vs chargeback](https://www.revefi.com/blog/chargeback-vs-showback-for-snowflake-databricks-and-bigquery), 2025) [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Snowflake:** `QUERY_ATTRIBUTION_HISTORY` gives per-query compute cost; `WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY` gives warehouse credit usage; **query tags** associate queries to teams/projects. ([Snowflake attributing cost](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/cost-attributing), 2025) [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Databricks:** `system.billing.usage` (Unity Catalog) + the `custom_tags` field on each record; tag clusters/jobs via Terraform. ([Databricks attribution queries](https://community.databricks.com/t5/technical-blog/queries-for-cost-attribution-using-system-tables/ba-p/76558), 2025) [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **FOCUS 1.3** (ratified Dec 2025) added shared-cost allocation, commitment datasets, and recency signals — the first spec making **cross-provider** warehouse FinOps tractable. ([DataLakehouseHub FinOps](https://datalakehousehub.com/blog/2026-05-finops-warehouse-cost/), 2026) [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- Move past raw warehouse cost to value-linked metrics: **cost per query, per pipeline, per dashboard, per model run, per TB processed/stored**; plus **storage decay / dark-data ratio** and **commitment-utilization score**. These connect billing exports to unit consumption (credits/DBUs/slots) so leaders can decide what to scale, tune, or retire. ([FinOps value insight](https://www.finops.org/insights/finops-for-data-cloud-platforms/), 2025; [Revefi KPIs](https://www.revefi.com/blog/kpis-finops-leaders-must-know), 2025; [Vantage unit economics](https://www.vantage.sh/blog/automate-unit-economics), 2025) [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Identify the billing unit** for each platform (credits / slots / DBUs) and where it accrues. You cannot optimize what you cannot price. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Inform — establish visibility.** Ingest billing exports + query history (`QUERY_ATTRIBUTION_HISTORY`, `system.billing.usage`, BQ `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS`). Build a cost dashboard and a baseline. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Allocate & attribute.** Enforce tags at the *framework* level — in dbt profiles, Airflow operators, and query runners — not by asking analysts to remember. Decide showback vs chargeback. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Define unit economics.** Pick 2–3 metrics (cost/query, cost/dashboard, cost/pipeline) that map to business value; track them over time. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Optimize — usage.** Right-size warehouses; tune auto-suspend; add partition/cluster pruning + MVs; convert heavy dbt models to incremental; tier/lifecycle storage; move scheduled Databricks jobs to Jobs Compute. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Optimize — rate.** Move sustained workloads to commitments/Editions; validate Photon net savings; consolidate idle warehouses. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Operate — sustain.** Resource monitors / budgets with hard caps; cost-anomaly alerts to Slack; cost in PR review (`state:modified+`); periodic heavy-model and dark-data review. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Right-size by parallelism test.** If doubling Snowflake warehouse size halves query time, the workload is parallelizable and the bigger size is *cost-neutral but faster*. If it doesn't, you're overpaying. ([Yuki guide](https://yukidata.com/blog/snowflake-warehouse-optimization-guide/), 2025) [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Auto-suspend tiers.** ~60s for BI/interactive warehouses, ~30s for programmatic ETL (dbt/Airflow/Tasks). Most workloads tolerate the resume delay. ([Anavsan](https://www.anavsan.com/blog/snowflake-warehouse-optimization-beyond-auto-suspend), 2025) [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Prune before you scan.** Partition on date; cluster large tables on predictable filter columns; use materialized views for repeated aggregations. Partition pruning is the single biggest cost+perf lever in both Snowflake and BigQuery. ([e6data](https://www.e6data.com/query-and-cost-optimization-hub/snowflake-query-optimization), 2025; [Flexera tuning](https://www.flexera.com/blog/finops/snowflake-query-tuning-part1/), 2026) [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Incremental dbt models with predicates.** Process only new/changed rows; add `incremental_predicates` to bound the merge scan window. Bilt Rewards cut ~$20K/mo BigQuery; some models dropped 3h→40m. ([dbt reduce BigQuery costs](https://www.getdbt.com/blog/reduce-bigquery-costs), 2025; [TDS incremental](https://towardsdatascience.com/reduce-computing-costs-with-dbt-incremental-models-a2025d42e633/), 2025) [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **dbt + Snowflake cost formula:** `Total Cost = Warehouse Size × Runtime × Run Frequency`. Every optimization reduces one of the three. ([dbt 4 decisions](https://medium.com/@blakelassiter/4-decisions-that-control-90-of-your-dbt-snowflake-costs-299113dc408c), 2025) [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Storage lifecycle tiering.** Move dormant data to COOL/COLD tiers (Snowflake Storage Lifecycle Policies cut 55–90% for dormant data); use periodic clones instead of long Time Travel windows. ([Snowflake storage lifecycle](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/storage-management/storage-lifecycle-policies), 2025; [analytics.today](https://articles.analytics.today/snowflake-best-practices-time-travel-fail-safe-and-data-retention), 2025) [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Anomaly alerts to humans.** Snowflake Cost Anomalies (GA Dec 2025) decomposes 28 days into trend + weekly seasonality and flags deviations; route to Slack/email and pair with Resource Monitor hard caps. ([Snowflake cost anomalies GA](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/release-notes/2025/other/2025-12-02-cost-anomalies-ga), 2025; [Anomaly Insights](https://www.snowflake.com/en/engineering-blog/anomaly-insights-spending-patterns/), 2025) [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Optimizing performance without pricing the unit.** A "faster" Photon or larger-warehouse query can cost *more*. Always check net DBUs/credits, not just wall-clock. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **`LIMIT` to save BigQuery cost.** On-demand bills bytes scanned across selected columns — `LIMIT` changes nothing. Select fewer columns and prune partitions instead. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **`SELECT *` in models/dashboards.** Forces full-column scans on columnar engines; explodes cost at scale. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Auto-suspend too long (or off).** Idle warehouses burn credits; a 10-minute auto-suspend on a bursty BI warehouse wastes most of every hour. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Tag-when-you-remember.** Manual per-analyst tagging yields unallocatable spend. Enforce tags in dbt/Airflow/runners. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **90-day Time Travel everywhere.** Long CDP retention silently multiplies storage cost; clone instead. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Editions/commitments before measuring.** Buying slots/commitments for spiky, low-volume workloads locks in waste — short, spiky queries usually stay cheaper on-demand. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **Photon-by-default.** It raises the DBU rate; only worth it when the speedup outpaces the rate increase. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **"Bill spiked overnight."** Check cost-anomaly view; query `QUERY_ATTRIBUTION_HISTORY` / `system.billing.usage` / BQ `JOBS` for the top consumers by tag in the window; look for a runaway scheduled job, a removed `LIMIT`-less full scan, or auto-suspend regression. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **"BigQuery cost high but queries look small."** It's bytes *scanned*, not returned — inspect `total_bytes_processed`; add partition/cluster filters; cache or materialize repeated aggregations. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **"Snowflake warehouse always-on."** Verify `AUTO_SUSPEND` and that no keep-alive query/dashboard polls it; consolidate near-idle warehouses; set a Resource Monitor. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **"Can't attribute spend to teams."** Tags missing at source — instrument dbt `query-comment`/tags, Airflow operator tags, Databricks Terraform `custom_tags`; backfill via query-text parsing only as a stopgap. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **"Databricks bill dominated by one SKU."** Audit `system.billing.usage` by SKU; migrate scheduled work off All-Purpose to Jobs Compute (40–60% cheaper). [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]
- **"Storage cost creeping up."** Check Time Travel/Fail-safe retention and dark-data ratio; apply lifecycle tiering; drop or archive stale tables. [src: da-37-data-finops-cost-optimization]

- Retention answers the single most important growth question: do users who join [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- keep coming back? Acquisition without retention is a leaky bucket — you pour [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- users in the top and they fall out the bottom, so growth stalls no matter how [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- much you spend. This skill covers the math and methods for measuring retention [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- across **cohorts** (groups of users grouped by a shared start or behavior), [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]

- **Acquisition (time) cohort** — users grouped by *when* they first signed up [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- or activated (same day/week/month). Answers *when* users churn and lets you [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- compare cohort quality over time. It does not tell you *why* [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- ([Amplitude, Cohort Retention Analysis, 2024](https://amplitude.com/blog/cohorts-to-improve-your-retention)). [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Behavioral cohort** — users grouped by *what they did* (completed [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- onboarding, used a key feature, invited a teammate), independent of join [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- date. Answers *which behaviors correlate with retention* — the input to [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- finding your activation/aha moment [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- ([Amplitude, Guide to Behavioral Cohorting, 2024](https://amplitude.com/blog/guide-to-behavioral-cohorting); [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- Workflow: use acquisition cohorts to *detect* a retention problem, behavioral [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- cohorts to *diagnose and fix* it (find the behavior that separates retained [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- ([Chameleon, Cohort Analysis 101, 2024](https://www.chameleon.io/blog/cohort-analysis)). [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- A retention curve plots % of a cohort still active against periods-since-start. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- Canonical shapes ([Amplitude, Retention Curve](https://amplitude.com/explore/analytics/retention-curve); [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Declining** — slopes to zero; no group finds lasting value → no PMF. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Flattening** — steep early drop, then levels off at a **retention floor** [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- (the long-term stable %). A flattening curve is the classic *signal of [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- product/market fit*: a stable set of users is hooked. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Smile** — drops, flattens, then rises as churned users resurrect (often [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- via network effects or re-engagement). The aspirational shape (Slack, Airbnb). [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Dead-on-arrival** — near-vertical drop to ~0 by period 2; users tried it [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- once and never returned. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- The **retention floor** (where the curve flattens) is your real long-term [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- retention. Improving the *floor* (curve flattens higher) compounds far more [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- than improving early-period retention that still decays to the same floor. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- Choosing the definition changes the numbers dramatically — always state which [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- you use ([Amplitude, 3 Ways to Measure Retention, 2024](https://medium.com/@amplitudeHQ/3-ways-to-measure-user-retention-2af5e4e82a45); [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **N-day (classic / bounded)** — % of cohort active on *exactly* day N. Strict; [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- best for daily-use products. Day-2 retention = 50% means 50% came back [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- specifically on day 2. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Unbounded ("rolling" in Mixpanel's loose sense)** — % active on day N *or [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- any day after*. Always ≥ N-day. Good for infrequent-use products. Note: this [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- is **not** a true moving average despite the "rolling" label. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Bracket / range** — % active within a custom window (Day 0; Days 1–7; Days [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- 8–14). A flexible generalization of N-day; matches a product's natural cadence. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Rolling retention (classic survival sense)** — % active on day N or later, [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- used to estimate a survival/lifetime curve; conceptually same as unbounded. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Bounded vs unbounded asymmetry:** bounded undercounts weekly/monthly-cadence [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- products; unbounded inflates if you never re-baseline. Match the metric to the [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- product's expected frequency. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- Retention is **binary** (active or not in a period) and is the *output*; [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **engagement depth** (frequency × breadth of actions) is the leading indicator. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- Deeper engagement → habit → retention → sustainable growth — Reforge frames [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- retention/engagement as "the power plant of the growth model" [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- ([Reforge, Retention is the Silent Killer](https://www.reforge.com/blog/retention-engagement-growth-silent-killer); [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- Practical move: don't just track the retained/churned flag — track *how deeply* [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- retained users engage, because depth predicts long-term value and is the lever [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- you pull to raise the retention floor. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- Decompose period-over-period active users into additive components. The [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **fundamental identity** ([Social Capital / Jonathan Hsu, Diligence Part 1, 2017](https://medium.com/swlh/diligence-at-social-capital-part-1-accounting-for-user-growth-4a8a449fddfc); [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- MAU(t) = MAU(t-1) + new(t) + resurrected(t) - churned(t) [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **new** — first-ever active this period. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **retained** — active last period AND this period (carried over). [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **resurrected** — active in some past period, inactive last period, active now. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **churned** — active last period, inactive now (enters as a negative). [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **User Quick Ratio (QR)** = (new + resurrected) / churned. Users gained per user [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- lost. QR > 1 means growing; rule of thumb QR ≥ ~1.5 is healthy [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- ([Hsu, Diligence Part 1, 2017](https://medium.com/swlh/diligence-at-social-capital-part-1-accounting-for-user-growth-4a8a449fddfc); [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- Same identity applied to dollars ([Social Capital / Hsu, Diligence Part 2, 2017](https://medium.com/swlh/diligence-at-social-capital-part-2-accounting-for-revenue-growth-551fa07dd972); [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- MRR(t)   = new(t) + retained(t) + resurrected(t) + expansion(t) [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- MRR(t-1) = retained(t) + churned(t) + contraction(t) [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **expansion** — existing customers paying more (upsell/seats). [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **contraction** — existing customers paying less (downgrade) but not zero. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **churned** — dropped to zero. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **SaaS Quick Ratio** = (new MRR + expansion MRR) / (churned MRR + contraction [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- MRR). Mamoon Hamid (Social Capital) popularized a target of **QR ≥ 4** for [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- early-stage SaaS — $4 of growth for every $1 lost [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- ([The SaaS CFO, 2024](https://www.thesaascfo.com/saas-quick-ratio/); [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **DAU / WAU / MAU** — unique active users in a 1-day / 7-day / 30-day window [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- ([Mixpanel, MAU Benchmarks, 2026](https://mixpanel.com/blog/mau/); [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Stickiness ratio = DAU/MAU** (× 100) ≈ how many days/month an average [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- monthly user shows up; DAU/MAU = 20% ≈ 6 days/month. Use **WAU/MAU** for [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- products not meant for daily use [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- ([Statsig, Understanding DAU/MAU](https://www.statsig.com/perspectives/understanding-daumau-key-metrics-for-product-success)). [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- Benchmarks: daily-habit/social aim for DAU/MAU > 50%; B2B SaaS averages ~30%; [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- <20% can be fine for infrequent products [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- ([CleverTap, DAU vs MAU, 2024](https://clevertap.com/blog/dau-vs-mau-app-stickiness-metrics/)). [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- Single-period complements: **Retention = 1 − Churn** [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- ([Churnkey, Churn vs Retention](https://churnkey.co/blog/churn-rate-vs-retention-rate/); [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **The compounding asymmetry:** churn compounds multiplicatively — 5%/mo churn [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- ≈ 0.95¹² ≈ 54% retained after a year, NOT 1 − (5%×12). Always state the period [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- and never linearly annualize. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- Customer (logo) churn ≠ revenue churn — a small customer and a whale count the [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- same in logo churn but very differently in revenue churn. Track both. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- Cohort the *revenue* of a customer group and measure it a year later [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- ([Drivetrain, GRR](https://www.drivetrain.ai/strategic-finance-glossary/what-is-gross-revenue-retention-formula-benchmarks); [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- GRR = (Starting ARR − churn − contraction) / Starting ARR              # ≤ 100%, no expansion [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- NRR = (Starting ARR − churn − contraction + expansion) / Starting ARR  # can exceed 100% [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **GRR** measures pure leak prevention (best-in-class 90–100%). [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **NRR** measures retention *plus* expansion — NRR > 100% means a cohort grows [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- in revenue with zero new logos (the "negative net churn" holy grail). [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- Benchmarks (private B2B SaaS, ~2024): median NRR ~100–106%; enterprise (>$100K [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- ACV) ~118%; SMB (<$25K ACV) ~97%; best-in-class NRR > 120–130%; median GRR [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- ~88–90% ([Optifai, B2B NRR Benchmarks](https://optif.ai/learn/questions/b2b-saas-net-revenue-retention-benchmark/); [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Sean Ellis (40%) test** — survey: *"How would you feel if you could no [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- longer use [product]?"* If ≥ 40% say **"very disappointed,"** you likely have [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- ([FitSignal, Sean Ellis 40% Test](https://www.fitsignal.com/blog/sean-ellis-40-percent-test); [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Power-user curve (L28 / L30)** — histogram of users by active days in the [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- month (1 of 30 … 30 of 30), coined by the Facebook growth team ("Ln" = active [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- n of last 30). A right-skewed "smile" with a heavy right tail signals strong [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- engagement a single DAU/MAU average hides [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- ([a16z / Andrew Chen, Power User Curve, 2018](https://a16z.com/the-power-user-curve-the-best-way-to-understand-your-most-engaged-users/); [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- Use together: Sean Ellis = attitudinal PMF; flattening curve + heavy-tailed [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- power-user curve + healthy stickiness = behavioral PMF. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- Canonical three-step pattern ([Holistics, Cohort Retention with SQL](https://www.holistics.io/blog/calculate-cohort-retention-analysis-with-sql/); [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Assign each user a cohort** (their first-activity period). [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Compute period offset** for every activity (`period − cohort_period`). [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Pivot/aggregate** counts per (cohort, offset) and divide by cohort size. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- WITH first_activity AS (          -- 1. cohort assignment [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(event_date)) AS cohort_month [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- FROM events GROUP BY user_id [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- activity AS (                     -- 2. period offset per active month [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- SELECT e.user_id, fa.cohort_month, [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- DATE_TRUNC('month', e.event_date) AS active_month, [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- (DATE_PART('year',  e.event_date) - DATE_PART('year',  fa.cohort_month)) * 12 [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- + (DATE_PART('month', e.event_date) - DATE_PART('month', fa.cohort_month)) AS month_number [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- JOIN first_activity fa USING (user_id) [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- SELECT cohort_month, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS cohort_size [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- FROM first_activity GROUP BY cohort_month [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- SELECT a.cohort_month, a.month_number,           -- 3. retention table [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) AS active_users, [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) / s.cohort_size, 1) AS retention_pct [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- FROM activity a JOIN sizes s USING (cohort_month) [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- GROUP BY a.cohort_month, a.month_number, s.cohort_size [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- ORDER BY a.cohort_month, a.month_number; [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- For **zero-activity periods** (gaps), build a date spine with [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- `generate_series`/recursive CTE, `LEFT JOIN` activity, and `COALESCE(...,0)` [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- so missing months render as 0 rather than vanishing [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- ([Holistics, 2024](https://www.holistics.io/blog/calculate-cohort-retention-analysis-with-sql/)). [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- Self-joins read more clearly for **N-day** retention; window functions are [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- terser but harder to review. Pick legibility for shared analytics code. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Amplitude / Mixpanel** — built-in N-day/unbounded/bracket retention, [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- behavioral cohorts, stickiness, power-user curves. Read the docs for the [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- *exact* retention definition each uses before comparing dashboards. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **SQL warehouse (BigQuery / Snowflake / Postgres)** — `DATE_TRUNC`, [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- `DATE_DIFF`/`DATE_PART`, `generate_series`, window functions; the portable [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- ground truth behind any BI tool. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Reforge / Lenny's Newsletter / a16z (Andrew Chen)** — growth loops, [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- retention/engagement engine, power-user curve. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Social Capital "8-ball" growth accounting** — the canonical [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- new/resurrected/churned decomposition and quick ratio. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **BI layer (Looker/Cube/Metabase)** — cohort retention as a reusable model; [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- Cube ships a retention recipe. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Define the active event** explicitly (login? key action? value moment?). [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- Everything downstream depends on this. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Pick the retention definition** (N-day vs unbounded vs bracket) to match [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- product usage frequency. State it on every chart. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Build acquisition cohorts**, plot curves, find the **retention floor**. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Segment by behavioral cohort** to find the activation behavior that lifts [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]

- Lead every retention chart with the **definition + active-event + cohort [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- granularity**; otherwise numbers are uncomparable. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- Optimize the **retention floor (curve shape)**, not just Day-1 — a higher [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- Report **NRR and GRR together**: NRR can mask churn that expansion papers [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- over; GRR exposes the underlying leak. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- Use **WAU/MAU** (not DAU/MAU) for weekly-cadence products so stickiness isn't [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]

- **Linearly annualizing churn** (5%/mo ≠ 60%/yr). Compound it. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Comparing N-day to unbounded** numbers as if equivalent — unbounded is [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Reporting only NRR** and hiding gross churn behind expansion. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **A single DAU/MAU average** masking a bimodal power-user split — show the [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Day-1-retention obsession** while the curve still decays to the same floor. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Ignoring the survivorship of recent cohorts** — the newest cohort has no [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- long-tail data yet; don't compare its Day-30 to an old cohort's before 30 days [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- **Retention "improved" suspiciously** → check whether the active-event [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]

- **Recent cohorts look worse** → likely **right-censoring**, not real decline; [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]
- only compare offsets that have fully matured for all cohorts shown. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]

- expansion from a few whales can hide broad SMB churn. [src: da-34-cohort-retention-analytics]

- Synthetic data is artificial data produced by a model fit to real data, designed to reproduce the real data's statistical properties (marginals, correlations, joint structure) without being a copy of any real record. The goal is to make synthetic records *useful* for a downstream task while breaking the one-to-one link to real individuals. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- This skill treats synthetic data generation as a discipline: when to use it, which generator to reach for, how to make it private, and most importantly how to prove it is good enough on the three axes that always compete: fidelity, utility, privacy. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- Use it when the task is to *create* data rather than analyze existing data: share data you cannot share in raw form, augment a too-small or imbalanced training set, populate a test/dev/CI environment without production PII, or release a public benchmark from a sensitive source. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- Do **not** use it for plain class-rebalancing with off-the-shelf SMOTE (data-prep step, see da-4), abstract differential-privacy/k-anonymity theory (da-11), or feature encoding (da-17). Those skills are adjacent; this one owns the generation pipeline and its evaluation. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Privacy / data sharing.** Replace a protected dataset with a synthetic surrogate. Gartner projected synthetic data would let organizations avoid 70% of privacy-violation sanctions by 2025, and estimated ~60% of AI/analytics data in 2024 would be synthetic (Gartner 2024; MIT Sloan 2023). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Augmentation.** Fill gaps, enlarge small datasets, balance rare classes, simulate scarce scenarios (fraud, failure). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Testing / dev / CI.** Populate non-prod at scale with realistic-but-fake records (Gartner 2024 Data Masking Market Guide). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Class rebalancing.** Generate minority-class examples to de-skew a classifier. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- Inference, not fact: "synthetic surpasses real by 2030" is a vendor/analyst projection. Treat market-size and adoption numbers as directional. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- Tabular is the hard case: mixed types, non-Gaussian/multimodal continuous columns, imbalanced categoricals. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Gaussian copula.** Transform each column to standard-normal via its CDF, fit a multivariate Gaussian for correlation structure, sample, invert to original margins. Fast, transparent, stable on small data; weak on highly non-linear dependencies (SDV docs). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **CTGAN (Conditional Tabular GAN).** Mode-specific normalization for multimodal continuous columns + conditional generator + training-by-sampling for imbalanced categoricals. Beat Bayesian-network and prior GAN baselines on >=87% of test datasets (Xu et al., NeurIPS 2019). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **TVAE (Tabular VAE).** VAE from the same NeurIPS 2019 paper; strong on smaller datasets, trains more stably than a GAN. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **CopulaGAN.** Hybrid applying the copula transform before GAN modeling (experimental in SDV). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **CART / sequential synthesis.** Non-deep classical approach (R synthpop): synthesize one column at a time conditioned on already-synthesized columns via CART trees. Interpretable, fast, official-statistics default. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **GANs.** Adversarial generator vs discriminator; high fidelity but training instability and mode collapse. CTGAN is the tabular workhorse. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **VAEs.** Encoder/decoder with latent prior; smoother, more stable, good diversity. TVAE is the tabular instance. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Diffusion.** Iterative denoising from a Gaussian prior. TabDDPM (ICML 2023) handles numerical + categorical features and beat prior SOTA on several benchmarks; concurrent STaSy, CoDi; later TabSyn, TabDiff (Kotelnikov et al., ICML 2023). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **SMOTE** interpolates minority points along segments to k nearest minority neighbors (local info only). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **ADASYN** adapts the number of synthetic points per minority sample by density, generating more in harder-to-learn regions. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Generative (GAN/VAE/diffusion)** captures complex non-linear joint structure SMOTE/ADASYN miss; hybrids like SMOTE->GAN refine unrealistic SMOTE points (MDPI Mathematics 2023; SMOTified-GAN 2021). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Rule of thumb.** Low-dim numeric, small budget -> SMOTE/ADASYN. High-cardinality categoricals, non-linear interactions, or privacy need -> generative. SMOTE before the train/test split leaks information; resample inside the CV fold only. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- Plain synthetic data is **not** automatically private; formal guarantees require DP built into training. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **DP-GAN / DP-SGD GANs.** Calibrated noise + gradient clipping on the discriminator; post-processing theorem makes the generator DP. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **PATE-GAN.** PATE ensemble of teacher discriminators trains a student via noisy aggregated votes; DP by post-processing, often better utility than DP-GAN at equal epsilon (Jordon, Yoon, van der Schaar, ICLR 2019). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Marginal-based (PrivBayes, MST).** Privately measure low-order marginals (Laplace/Gaussian mechanism), then reconstruct a distribution: a Bayesian network (PrivBayes, Zhang et al. 2017) or a graphical model over a maximum-spanning-tree of marginals (MST). MST won the 2018 NIST DP Synthetic Data Challenge; both strong against membership inference with high utility (McKenna, Miklau, Sheldon 2021; NIST). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **SmartNoise (OpenDP).** Microsoft + Harvard toolkit; smartnoise-synth exposes DP synthesizers (MST, PrivBayes, AIM) with a uniform fit()/sample() API (Microsoft 2021). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- Caveat: high epsilon hollows out the guarantee. MST/PrivBayes at high epsilon still leak (arXiv 2402.06699, 2024). DP is only as strong as the epsilon you actually set. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **SDV (Synthetic Data Vault)** Python one-stop: single-table (GaussianCopula, CTGAN, TVAE, CopulaGAN), multi-table (HMA), sequential (PAR); metadata-driven fit()/sample(). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **SDMetrics** SDV evaluation: Quality Report (column shapes, column-pair trends), Diagnostic Report (validity/structure), privacy metrics. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **CTGAN (sdv-dev/ctgan)** standalone CTGAN + TVAE. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **synthcity** van der Schaar lab; tabular/time-series/survival + privacy benchmarks. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **SmartNoise-synth (OpenDP)** DP synthesizers with formal guarantees. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **imbalanced-learn** SMOTE/ADASYN variants. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **synthpop (R)** CART/sequential synthesis. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- The three axes trade off (especially privacy vs fidelity/utility under DP). Measure all three. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Fidelity** (looks like real): per-column shape (KS continuous, total-variation/chi-sq categorical), pairwise correlation/contingency similarity, validity/structure (SDMetrics). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Utility** (works like real): TSTR (Train on Synthetic, Test on Real) vs TRTR (train-real-test-real); TSTR ~= TRTR means high utility (AWS ML blog 2023). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Privacy** (attacker recovery): Distance to Closest Record (DCR) flags near-copies; Membership Inference Attack (MIA) tests whether an adversary can tell a record was in training (Frontiers Digital Health 2025). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Text.** Instruction-tuned LLMs generate synthetic text/labels (DataGen, MagPie); quality/diversity and label noise are limits; DP-via-API (Aug-PE/Private Evolution) exists (2023-24). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Images.** GANs gave limited augmentation benefit; diffusion era (Stable Diffusion, DALL-E, Imagen) sharply improved fidelity and dropped per-image cost (2024-25 reviews). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- Synthetic data is **not automatically anonymous** or out of GDPR scope. Fully synthetic data meeting the anonymisation bar escapes GDPR; partially synthetic data usually remains personal data. ICO's March 2025 anonymisation guidance: effective anonymisation is a high bar requiring a documented re-identification-risk assessment (GDPR Local; RPC 2025; NIST). Treat a privacy claim as something you must *measure* (DCR + MIA, ideally under a DP budget), not something the word "synthetic" grants. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Define the goal first** (privacy share / augmentation / test data / rebalancing) — sets which axis you optimize and which gates you must pass. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Profile and build metadata** (types, keys, datetime formats, constraints). Bad metadata is the #1 cause of bad output. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Split before you fit** — hold out a real test set before training so TSTR and MIA are honest. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Pick a generator by data + constraint** — copula baseline; escalate to CTGAN/TVAE; diffusion (TabDDPM) for highest fidelity; switch to a DP synthesizer (PATE-GAN, MST/PrivBayes via SmartNoise) the moment a formal privacy guarantee is required. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Fit, then enforce constraints** — apply business rules / valid ranges; reject or post-process invalid rows. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Evaluate on all three axes** — fidelity, utility (TSTR vs TRTR), privacy (DCR + MIA). For DP, report epsilon. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Iterate against the binding constraint** — privacy fails: lower epsilon/regularize; utility fails: more capacity/epochs or change family. Expect to trade. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Document** generator, hyperparameters, epsilon, seed, metrics, and the re-identification-risk assessment (required for any GDPR/anonymisation claim). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- Copula-first ladder; don't start with a GAN. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- Resample inside the fold (never before the split). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- DP by construction, not post-hoc filtering. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- Conditional sampling (CTGAN/SDV) for rare classes. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- Report TSTR next to TRTR; the gap is the signal. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- Keep metadata in version control; regenerate from it. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- Calling synthetic data "anonymous" with no DCR + MIA test. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- Evaluating fidelity only (a perfect KS can still memorize records or be useless downstream). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- SMOTE before the split / on test data (leakage). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- Treating high epsilon as "private" (MST/PrivBayes leak at high epsilon). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- GAN by default on small/simple data (mode collapse; copula or TVAE is faster/better). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- Ignoring constraints/keys (synthesizers emit out-of-range values and broken keys unless constrained). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- One synthetic draw as ground truth (sample multiple; metrics vary, especially for GANs). [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Mode collapse / low diversity (GAN):** switch to TVAE/diffusion; add conditional generator; tune batch size / PacGAN packing. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Categorical cardinality blows up training:** group rare categories or use copula/CART. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **DP output useless (utility floor):** epsilon too small or marginals too high-order; raise epsilon within policy, lower marginal order (MST), or swap PATE-GAN <-> marginal-based. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **TSTR far worse than TRTR:** fidelity gap in relied-on columns; inspect per-column shape + correlation reports. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Synthetic rows duplicate real rows (DCR ~0):** overfitting; reduce epochs/capacity, add DP, or add training data. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
- **Invalid rows (out of range, broken keys):** add SDV constraints/metadata; post-process and re-validate. [src: da-35-synthetic-data-generation]
