- A **knowledge graph (KG)** represents entities (nodes) and the typed, meaning-bearing relationships between them (edges), with attributes (properties) on both, plus a **schema/ontology** that says what the types *mean*. The point is not just to store connections (that is da-27's graph-algorithms angle) but to encode **semantics** — shared, machine-interpretable meaning — so that data from many sources can be integrated, queried by meaning, validated against a model, and reasoned over to infer new facts. [src: da-41-knowledge-graphs-and-semantic-analytics]
- Reach for a KG when the **connections and their meaning carry the signal and must be queried, integrated, or reasoned about**: multi-hop questions, heterogeneous data integration under one vocabulary, provenance/lineage, regulatory traceability, and grounding LLMs. A KG beats relational/dimensional modeling when traversal depth is variable and deep. If the question is answerable with a `GROUP BY` or a couple of JOINs over a stable schema, you do **not** need a KG — use a warehouse/dimensional model (da-29). [src: da-41-knowledge-graphs-and-semantic-analytics]
- This is the semantic/ontology node of the data-analytics curriculum (da-1 onward). [src: da-41-knowledge-graphs-and-semantic-analytics]
- **da-27-network-graph-analytics** owns graph *algorithms* (centrality, community detection, link prediction, GNNs). This skill owns *meaning*: ontologies, RDF/OWL/SHACL, semantic queries, reasoning, KG construction, GraphRAG. [src: da-41-knowledge-graphs-and-semantic-analytics]
- **ai-datastores ("Knowledge Graphs for AI")** owns the vector-DB / agent-memory / KG-as-storage angle. This skill owns the analytics/semantic-integration angle. [src: da-41-knowledge-graphs-and-semantic-analytics]
- **da-18-semantic-layer-headless-bi** owns the *metrics* layer (dbt SL, Cube, MetricFlow). A KG semantic layer is about *entities and their meaning*. [src: da-41-knowledge-graphs-and-semantic-analytics]
- **da-30-data-governance-catalogs** owns governance/catalog policy generally; this skill covers modeling the catalog itself as a knowledge graph. [src: da-41-knowledge-graphs-and-semantic-analytics]
- **Two graph data models**: Labeled Property Graph (LPG; Neo4j/TigerGraph/Memgraph; Cypher/GQL) vs RDF triple store (subject-predicate-object with global IRIs; GraphDB/Jena/Stardog/Virtuoso; SPARQL). Plain RDF can't attach properties to one relationship instance — **RDF-star** fixes this. Choose RDF for interoperability/reasoning/standards, LPG for speed/traversal/AI; hybrid (RDF of record + LPG projection) is common. [src: da-41-knowledge-graphs-and-semantic-analytics]
- **Semantic web stack (W3C)**: RDF (Turtle/N-Triples/JSON-LD), RDFS (lightweight schema), OWL 2 (Description-Logic ontologies; EL/QL/RL profiles), SPARQL (graph patterns, property paths, federation, CONSTRUCT), SHACL (shapes validation), named graphs (quads for provenance/trust/versioning). [src: da-41-knowledge-graphs-and-semantic-analytics]
- **OWL vs SHACL**: OWL = inference (open-world; derives new facts). SHACL = validation (closed-world; checks constraints, reports violations). Modern practice: OWL for modeling + SHACL for validation together. [src: da-41-knowledge-graphs-and-semantic-analytics]
- **Ontology & taxonomy engineering**: taxonomy (hierarchy) vs ontology (taxonomy + typed relations + axioms). SKOS for controlled vocabularies; upper ontologies (BFO/DOLCE/SUMO/gist) for alignment; Ontology Design Patterns; schema.org as pragmatic web vocab. [src: da-41-knowledge-graphs-and-semantic-analytics]
- **KG construction**: schema-first vs data-first; NER + relation extraction; entity resolution/dedup; entity linking to canonical IDs (Wikidata Q-numbers); R2RML/RML schema mapping; Ontology-Based Data Access (OBDA)/virtual KGs (Ontop rewrites SPARQL→SQL); LLM-assisted construction (2024-2026) validated via OWL/SHACL. [src: da-41-knowledge-graphs-and-semantic-analytics]
- **Querying, reasoning & analytics**: SPARQL vs Cypher vs **GQL** (ISO/IEC 39075:2024, first new ISO query standard since SQL); reasoning/materialisation (sound entailment, unlike approximate embedding-based completion); semantic analytics (entity-centric aggregation, multi-hop joins, lineage traversal). [src: da-41-knowledge-graphs-and-semantic-analytics]
- **Enterprise KGs**: data fabric (plumbing) + KG (semantic intelligence); metadata knowledge graph as unified queryable catalog; data catalog as a graph (discovery via traversal/semantic search). [src: da-41-knowledge-graphs-and-semantic-analytics]
- **GraphRAG & semantic retrieval**: RAG over a KG (hybrid vector+graph); handles multi-hop/global questions with explainable, grounded, entity-centric answers; 2025-2026 pattern is hybrid routing (vector/KG-traversal/SQL by query type); agentic GraphRAG plans multi-hop traversals. [src: da-41-knowledge-graphs-and-semantic-analytics]
- Neo4j + neosemantics (n10s), RDFLib, Apache Jena/Fuseki, Ontotext GraphDB, Stardog, Amazon Neptune (RDF+LPG), TigerGraph, Virtuoso, Ontop (virtual RDF/OBDA), Wikidata, schema.org. [src: da-41-knowledge-graphs-and-semantic-analytics]
- Decide if you need a KG (variable-depth traversal/integration/reasoning/provenance/LLM grounding — else use da-29). [src: da-41-knowledge-graphs-and-semantic-analytics]
- Pick the model (RDF vs LPG vs hybrid/RDF-star). [src: da-41-knowledge-graphs-and-semantic-analytics]
- Design the ontology/taxonomy (reuse SKOS/schema.org/upper ontologies/ODPs; keep OWL and SHACL distinct). [src: da-41-knowledge-graphs-and-semantic-analytics]
- Construct (extract, resolve, link, map via R2RML/RML or OBDA; validate LLM extraction with SHACL). [src: da-41-knowledge-graphs-and-semantic-analytics]
- Validate & reason (SHACL for quality; materialise or query-time reason). [src: da-41-knowledge-graphs-and-semantic-analytics]
- Query & serve analytics (SPARQL/Cypher/GQL; layer GraphRAG; route hybrid by query type). [src: da-41-knowledge-graphs-and-semantic-analytics]
- Using a KG as a slow relational DB; confusing OWL (infers, open-world) and SHACL (validates, closed-world); plain RDF for edge attributes instead of RDF-star/LPG; skipping entity resolution; ontology over-engineering; trusting unvalidated LLM extractions. [src: da-41-knowledge-graphs-and-semantic-analytics]

- Five evidence-based models of motivation and behavior change, combined into one [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- applied toolkit for technical account managers, customer success, and enablement [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- teams. The job-to-be-done: **a customer bought the product, but people aren't [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- changing what they actually do.** These models explain why, and what to do about it. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- The throughline: adoption is a *behavior-change* problem, not a *feature-awareness* [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- problem. Telling users about value rarely changes behavior. Engineering motivation, [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- ability, prompts, habits, and goals does. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- -- [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- Most real accounts need **two or three models layered**. A typical adoption play: [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- set a clear goal (goal-setting) → make the first action trivially easy and prompted [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- (Fogg) → repeat it against a reliable cue until automatic (habit) → support [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- autonomy/competence so motivation internalizes (SDT) → stage-match the asks across [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- the buying group (TTM). See *Combined adoption playbook* below. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- -- [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Core claim.** Durable, high-quality motivation comes from satisfying three innate [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- psychological needs. Frustrate them and you get compliance at best, resistance at [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- worst. [Ryan & Deci 2000](https://selfdeterminationtheory.org/SDT/documents/2000_RyanDeci_SDT.pdf) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- The three basic psychological needs: [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Autonomy** — feeling the behavior is self-chosen, not coerced. (Not independence; it's volition.) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Competence** — feeling effective, making visible progress, experiencing mastery. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Relatedness** — feeling connected to and valued by others who matter. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **The motivation continuum (Organismic Integration Theory).** Extrinsic motivation [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- is not one thing. It runs along a continuum of *internalization*: [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- `amotivation → external regulation → introjected → identified → integrated → intrinsic` [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **External regulation** — "I use it because my manager checks." (rewards/punishments) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Introjected** — "I'd feel guilty if I didn't." (internalized pressure, ego) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Identified** — "This genuinely helps me hit my goals." (personally valued) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Integrated** — "This is how my team works now." (aligned with identity) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Intrinsic** — "I find this genuinely satisfying to use." [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- The TAM goal is to move stakeholders *rightward* — from external to identified/integrated. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- You rarely get true intrinsic motivation for enterprise software, and you don't need [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- it; **identified/integrated regulation is the durable target.** [Ryan & Deci 2020 (CEP)](https://selfdeterminationtheory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/2020_RyanDeci_CEP_PrePrint.pdf), [Organismic Integration Theory overview](https://psychologyfanatic.com/organismic-integration-theory/) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **The overjustification effect.** Giving an *expected, tangible, controlling* reward [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- for an activity someone already finds interesting can *reduce* their intrinsic [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- motivation — the perceived reason for acting shifts from internal interest to the [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- external reward. In Deci's classic 1971 study, paid puzzle-solvers played less in [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- free time than unpaid ones. The mechanism: a shift in *perceived locus of causality* [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- from internal to external. Crucially, **informational** rewards (that signal [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- competence) are far less corrosive than **controlling** ones. [Overjustification effect (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overjustification_effect), [The Decision Lab](https://thedecisionlab.com/biases/overjustification-effect), [Deci, Koestner & Ryan 2001 meta-analysis](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.3102/00346543071001001) [src: behavior-change-psychology]  <!-- privacy-ok -->
- **Autonomy:** Offer paths, not mandates. "Here are three ways teams like yours [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- roll this out — which fits you?" Co-design the adoption plan with the champion [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- rather than handing them one. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Competence:** Sequence enablement from quick wins to mastery. Celebrate visible [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- progress (dashboards, certifications, "you're now in the top 10% of power users"). [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Relatedness:** Connect users to a community/peer cohort; make the CSM a trusted [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- partner, not an auditor. User groups and customer advisory boards satisfy relatedness. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Avoid the overjustification trap:** Don't bolt cash/swag bounties onto a feature [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- users already like — when the bounty ends, usage can fall *below* baseline. Prefer [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- *informational* recognition ("your team's query latency dropped 40%") over [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- *controlling* incentives ("log in 5× this week for a gift card"). [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- > SDT is *the* lens for the "exec mandated it and the team resents it" problem and [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- > for diagnosing when an incentive program will backfire. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- -- [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Core formula.** `B = MAP`: a **B**ehavior happens only when **M**otivation, [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **A**bility, and a **P**rompt converge *at the same moment*. Remove any one and the [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- behavior doesn't occur. Developed by BJ Fogg (Stanford Behavior Design Lab), expanded [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- in *Tiny Habits* (2019). [BJ Fogg — behaviormodel.org](https://www.behaviormodel.org/), [Behavioral Scientist](https://www.thebehavioralscientist.com/articles/fogg-behavior-model) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **The action line (compensatory relationship).** Motivation and Ability trade off [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- along a curved threshold. If a behavior is *easy enough*, even low motivation crosses [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- the line. If motivation is *sky-high*, people will tolerate a hard behavior. Because [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **motivation fluctuates (the "motivation wave") and is unreliable, the durable lever [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- is almost always Ability — make the behavior easier.** [The Decision Lab — Fogg](https://thedecisionlab.com/reference-guide/psychology/fogg-behavior-model) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Six ability factors** (what "simplicity" means — the scarcest one is your bottleneck): [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- time, money, physical effort, mental effort (cognitive load), social deviance, and [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- non-routine (unfamiliarity). [Triple Whale guide](https://www.triplewhale.com/blog/fogg-behavior-model) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Three prompt types** (match the prompt to where the user is): [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Spark** — raises motivation when motivation is low (highlight a benefit/risk). [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Facilitator** — raises ability when motivation is high but the task feels hard (templates, defaults, "do it for me"). [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Signal** — a simple reminder when motivation *and* ability are already sufficient. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Tiny Habits recipe.** `After I [ANCHOR MOMENT], I will [TINY BEHAVIOR]. Then I [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- celebrate.` The tiny behavior must take <30 seconds and need almost no motivation; [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- the celebration wires in positive emotion to accelerate habit formation. [EasyHabits — Tiny Habits](https://www.easyhabits.io/blog/tiny-habits-bj-fogg), [BeWay — B=MAP & Tiny Habits](https://blog.beway.com/en/bmap-big-changes-with-tiny-habits/) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- Diagnose stalled adoption with three questions: *Is there a prompt? Is the first [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- action easy enough? Is there enough motivation for how hard it is?* Fix the missing [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- element — usually start with prompt and ability before trying to pump motivation. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Shrink the first action.** Don't ask a user to "migrate their workflow." Ask them [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- to "run one saved query." Time-to-first-value should be minutes, not weeks. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Engineer prompts into existing systems:** in-app nudges, Slack/email triggers tied [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- to a real moment, calendar holds — not a generic "please use the product" email. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Pre-load ability:** ship templates, sample dashboards, sensible defaults, and [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- "white-glove" first-config so the user's effort approaches zero. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- > Fogg is the first tool to reach for on *any* "they're not using it" symptom because [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- > it's the fastest diagnostic: prompt? ability? motivation? [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- -- [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Core claim.** Behavior change is a *process through stages*, not a single event. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- People at different stages need different interventions. Developed by Prochaska & [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- DiClemente (1980s). [Transtheoretical model (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transtheoretical_model), [Simply Psychology](https://www.simplypsychology.org/transtheoretical-model.html) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Precontemplation** — not even considering change; unaware of the problem/value. (No intent within ~6 months.) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Contemplation** — aware of the upside, but ambivalent; weighing pros vs cons. (Intends to act within ~6 months.) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Preparation** — committed and planning; has an action plan, often a small first step taken. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Action** — actively doing the new behavior (recent, <6 months). [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Maintenance** — sustaining the behavior, guarding against relapse (6+ months). [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- (A sixth stage, **termination**, where relapse risk is gone, is often omitted in practice.) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Three supporting constructs:** [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Decisional balance** — the perceived pros vs cons of changing. Progress happens [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- as pros come to outweigh cons. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Self-efficacy** — confidence the user can sustain the behavior under temptation. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Processes of change** — the *how*: ten techniques (consciousness-raising, etc.) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- that move people between stages. The key practice is **stage-matching** — using the [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- right technique for the stage. Stage-matched interventions roughly *double* the odds [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- of progressing to action. [Stages of Change Theory — StatPearls/NIH](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK556005/), [ScienceDirect — TTM overview](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/nursing-and-health-professions/transtheoretical-model) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **TAM application — stage-matched plays across the buying group:** [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Precontemplation:** Don't pitch features. Raise awareness of the cost of the [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- status quo. Share peer benchmarks and a relevant "what others are losing by not [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- doing this" narrative. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Contemplation:** Resolve ambivalence. Build a decisional-balance sheet *with* them; [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- address the cons explicitly (migration cost, retraining fear). This is where [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- motivational-interviewing change-talk helps (→ `writing-expert` (references/interview-and-conversational.md)). [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Preparation:** Co-build a concrete 30-60-90 adoption plan and a tiny first step. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Action:** Remove friction, provide hands-on enablement, celebrate early wins. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Maintenance:** Guard against relapse to the old tool — QBRs, health monitoring, [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- expansion to new use cases, reinforce habits. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- Map each stakeholder (champion, end users, economic buyer) to a stage; they're [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- rarely all in the same one. The most common mistake is pitching Action-stage tactics [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- to a Precontemplation-stage audience. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Known limitation (state it honestly).** TTM is widely critiqued: the stage time- [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- boundaries (6 months, 30 days) are arbitrary, people skip/regress through stages [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- non-sequentially, and systematic reviews question whether stage-based interventions [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- beat non-staged ones. Use it as a *diagnostic vocabulary for readiness*, not a rigid [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- ladder. For a factors-based alternative, see **COM-B / Behavior Change Wheel** (Michie [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- et al.) in *Adjacent models*. [Wikipedia — TTM criticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transtheoretical_model), [The Behavioral Scientist — TTM](https://www.thebehavioralscientist.com/glossary/transtheoretical-model) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- -- [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Core claim.** Durable adoption = behavior that runs automatically, with low [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- conscious effort, triggered by a context cue. The brain shifts control from the [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- prefrontal cortex (effortful) to the basal ganglia (automatic) through repeated [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- cue→behavior→reward cycles. [Simply Psychology — science of habit formation](https://www.simplypsychology.com/articles/science-of-habit-formation) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **The habit loop (Duhigg):** **Cue → Routine → Reward.** A cue triggers a routine; [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- the routine yields a reward the brain wants to repeat. James Clear's *Atomic Habits* [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- inserts a fourth element, **craving**, between cue and routine — useful when designing [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- a habit deliberately (cue → craving → response → reward). [Habi — habit loop](https://habi.app/insights/habit-loop/), [James Clear — habit triggers](https://jamesclear.com/habit-triggers) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **How long it takes.** Lally et al. (UCL, 96 participants) found automaticity forms [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- in **18-254 days, median ~66** — *not* the mythical 21. Simple behaviors form faster [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- than complex ones. Plan adoption support over months, not weeks. [Mentalzon — 66 days / Lally](https://mentalzon.com/en/post/7770/66-days-to-build-a-new-habit-why-it%E2%80%99s-not-a-myth-but-real-habit-psychology) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Two high-impact techniques:** [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Implementation intentions (Gollwitzer):** `I will [behavior] at [time] in [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- medium-to-large effect (d ≈ 0.65) on goal attainment. Pre-deciding the *when/where* [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- bridges the intention-action gap. [Habit-formation guide (Gollwitzer d=0.65)](https://goalsandprogress.com/habit-formation-complete-guide/) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Habit stacking:** `After I [existing habit], I will [new habit].` Anchors the new [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- behavior to an existing, well-cued routine so you borrow its trigger and neural [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- pathway. (This is the Tiny Habits anchor in habit-loop language.) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Anchor product usage to an existing work ritual:** "After the daily standup, the [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- on-call engineer checks the cluster health dashboard." The standup is the cue; you [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- don't have to manufacture a new one. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Design the reward to be immediate and visible.** The basal-ganglia loop needs a [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- reward *now*: a fast result, a satisfying confirmation, a saved-time indicator. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- Delayed ROI doesn't reinforce a habit; instant feedback does. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Use implementation intentions in enablement:** have champions commit, in writing, [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- to *when and where* the team will use the feature ("every Monday at 9am, in the [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- release-planning meeting, we open the X report"), not just *that* they will. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Target a "usage threshold."** Identify the repetition count that predicts [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- stickiness (e.g., Slack's ~2,000-messages signal) and drive the account to it [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- before declaring onboarding done. [Slack PAI threshold — SaaS onboarding science](https://www.saasfactor.co/blogs/the-science-of-saas-onboarding-a-comprehensive-framework-for-reducing-friction-improving-activation-and-preventing-churn) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- -- [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Core claim (Locke & Latham).** Specific, challenging goals produce higher [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- performance than vague ("do your best") or easy goals — *provided* certain conditions [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- hold. The most-validated theory in organizational psychology. [Positive Psychology — goal-setting theory](https://positivepsychology.com/goal-setting-theory/), [Mindtools — Locke's theory](https://www.mindtools.com/azazlu3/lockes-goal-setting-theory/) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Clarity** — specific, measurable goals beat vague ones. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Challenge** — harder (but attainable) goals drive more effort than easy ones. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Commitment** — the person must own the goal; self-efficacy fuels commitment. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Feedback** — progress feedback is required to adjust effort/strategy. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Task complexity** — for complex tasks, break into sub-goals and provide support/time. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **SMART** (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic, Time-bound) operationalizes [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- clarity + challenge + a deadline. Useful as a *checklist*, but it's a packaging of the [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- principles, not a replacement for them — SMART alone omits commitment and feedback. [Notion — goal-setting theory](https://www.notion.com/blog/goal-setting-theory) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **The goal-gradient effect (Hull; revived by Kivetz, Urminsky & Zheng 2006).** Effort [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- *accelerates* as people get closer to a goal. In the famous coffee-card study, [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- customers bought faster the nearer they were to a free drink; raters rated more songs [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- near the reward. Critically, the **endowed progress effect** shows that giving people [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- *artificial* initial progress (a punch card pre-stamped 2 of 12 vs a blank 10-stamp [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- card — same 10 to go) speeds completion, because the finish line feels closer. [Kivetz et al. 2006 — Goal-Gradient Hypothesis Resurrected (PDF)](https://home.uchicago.edu/ourminsky/Goal-Gradient_Illusionary_Goal_Progress.pdf), [Learning Loop — goal gradient](https://learningloop.io/plays/psychology/goal-gradient-effect) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Set adoption goals as SMART + committed:** not "drive adoption" but "the data team [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- runs ≥20 production queries/week on the new cluster by end of Q3," co-owned with the [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- champion (commitment), with a weekly usage dashboard (feedback). [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Decompose big rollouts into sub-goals** (task complexity): per-team, per-use-case, [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- per-milestone — each a visible finish line. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Exploit goal-gradient in onboarding UX and success plans:** progress bars, [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- completion checklists, "3 of 5 onboarding steps done," tiered milestones. Show the [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- near finish line. [Lampstellar — goal gradient for customer success](https://www.lampstellar.com/blog/customer-success/power-goal-gradient-effect-elevate-customer-success) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Use endowed progress:** start the customer's onboarding checklist *already partly [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- complete* ("Account created ✓, SSO configured ✓ — 2 of 6 done") to pull them toward [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **The dark side (use challenging goals responsibly).** "Goals Gone Wild" (Ordóñez, [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- Schweitzer, Galinsky, Bazerman 2009) documents that over-aggressive goals can narrow [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- focus, crowd out unstated priorities, increase risk-taking, and motivate *unethical [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- shortcuts* — especially when someone is just short of the goal, and when ability is [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- lacking. Latham & Itzchakov (2024) frame these as boundary-condition failures: the [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- side effects appear when moderators (notably **ability** and **commitment**) are [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- ignored. For customers: don't set adoption targets so aggressive they drive vanity [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- metrics or gaming (e.g., logins with no real work). Pair stretch goals with capability [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- and genuine commitment. [HBS — Goals Gone Wild (PDF)](https://www.hbs.edu/ris/Publication%20Files/09-083.pdf), [Goal setting (Wikipedia) — dark side & moderators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goal_setting) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- -- [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- A durable adoption motion layers all five. Run roughly in this order: [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Frame the goal** (Goal-Setting): co-set a specific, challenging, committed [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- adoption goal with feedback. Decompose into sub-goals with visible finish lines. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Locate readiness** (TTM): map each stakeholder to a stage; stage-match the ask. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- Don't sell Action tactics to a Precontemplation audience. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Engineer the first behavior** (Fogg B=MAP): add a prompt, crush ability barriers, [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- shrink the first action to <30 seconds of effort. Reach time-to-first-value fast. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Repeat into a habit** (Habit loop): anchor usage to an existing ritual (habit [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- stacking), use written implementation intentions, ensure an immediate reward, and [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- drive to the usage threshold over ~weeks-to-months. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Internalize the motivation** (SDT): support autonomy (choices not mandates), [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- competence (quick wins → mastery, informational feedback), and relatedness (peer [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- community). Move stakeholders from external → identified/integrated regulation. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Reward without backfiring** (overjustification guardrail): prefer informational [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- recognition over expected, controlling incentives — especially for behaviors users [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- already value. Watch for usage cliffs when an incentive ends. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Worked example — stalled feature rollout:** [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- A bank's platform team bought a feature; six weeks in, usage is near zero. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- *Fogg diagnosis:* no in-app prompt, and first use requires a 9-step config (ability [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- too low). → TAM ships a pre-built config and a Slack trigger tied to deploys. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- *TTM diagnosis:* champion is in Action, end-users in Precontemplation. → TAM runs a [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- status-quo-cost session for end-users, not a feature demo. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- *Goal-setting:* co-set "≥15 deploys/week use the feature by end of next month," [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- weekly dashboard. Onboarding checklist starts 2/6 complete (endowed progress). [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- *Habit:* "after each deploy, check the X panel" — anchored to the existing deploy ritual. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- *SDT:* offer three rollout paths (autonomy); spotlight the team's latency win [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- (informational competence feedback), *not* a gift-card-per-login scheme. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- -- [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Treating adoption as an awareness problem.** More demos and feature emails rarely [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- change behavior. Engineer prompts, ability, habits, and goals instead. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Pumping motivation while ignoring ability.** Motivation is a wave; it recedes. The [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- cheaper, more durable lever is making the behavior easier (Fogg). [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Bolting controlling incentives onto valued behaviors.** Expected, tangible rewards [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- can crowd out intrinsic interest (overjustification); usage often falls *below* [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- baseline when they stop. Prefer informational feedback. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **One message for the whole buying group.** Stakeholders sit in different stages [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- (TTM); a single pitch mis-serves most of them. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Vague goals ("drive adoption").** No clarity, no challenge, no feedback → no effect. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- Make goals SMART *and* committed. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Over-aggressive targets without capability.** Stretch goals minus ability/commitment [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- → vanity metrics, gaming, narrowed focus (Goals Gone Wild). [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Declaring "onboarded" before a habit forms.** Adoption that hasn't crossed a usage [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- threshold and become a cued routine relapses to the old tool. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Expecting habits in 21 days.** Real automaticity is ~66 days median (18-254); plan [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- the success motion accordingly. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Treating TTM stages as a rigid, linear ladder.** People skip and regress; stages [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- are a readiness vocabulary, not a fixed sequence. [src: behavior-change-psychology]

- **COM-B / Behavior Change Wheel** (Michie, van Stralen & West 2011) — behavior needs [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **C**apability, **O**pportunity, **M**otivation. A factors-based ("why") complement to [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- TTM's process ("how") view; the most-cited modern alternative. [COM-B model](https://www.habitweekly.com/models-frameworks/the-com-b-model) [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Motivational interviewing (OARS)** — the conversational technique for resolving [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- ambivalence in Contemplation. → `writing-expert` (references/interview-and-conversational.md). [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Hook Model** (Eyal) — trigger/action/variable-reward/investment; a consumer-product [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- habit-engineering variant of the loop above. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Nudge / choice architecture** (Thaler & Sunstein) — defaults and friction design; [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- overlaps Fogg's ability lever. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **Adoption/activation metrics** (aha moment, time-to-value, feature velocity, cohort [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- retention) — the *measurement* layer. → `da-applied-and-communication` (references/da-21-product-analytics.md), `da-34-cohort-retention-analytics`. [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- **The learning SCIENCE of making the training itself stick** — cognitive load, retrieval [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- practice, spacing, interleaving, deliberate practice, the illusion of fluency. This skill [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- gets a customer *motivated* to learn and keep practicing; designing the enablement so the [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- knowledge actually *retains* is → `learning-and-expertise-psychology`. [src: behavior-change-psychology]

- **Learning science of retention** (cognitive load, retrieval practice, spacing, interleaving, deliberate practice, illusion of fluency) → `learning-and-expertise-psychology` [src: behavior-change-psychology]
- The **descriptive** account of judgment and decision-making: how people *actually* decide, not how they *should*. Use it to read why a customer, buyer, or stakeholder made a seemingly irrational choice, to ethically shape the decision environment, and to catch bias in your own forecasts and recommendations. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- > Installed as a Claude Code skill with four on-demand reference files (not duplicated here): `references/biases-catalog.md` (full heuristics-and-biases catalog with canonical experiments + TAM application notes), `references/choice-architecture.md` (defaults, EAST, MINDSPACE, sludge vs nudge vs boost, choice overload, ethics of influence), `references/debiasing-and-application.md` (debiasing procedures + worked operator scenarios), and `references/replication-status.md` (what survived vs what is contested/failed, with citable sources — read before citing any effect externally). [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- **Descriptive vs normative: keep them separate.** This skill is descriptive (the psychology of real decisions). For the *normative* side, computing the optimal action under constraints (linear programming, decision trees, EVPI, expected-utility maximization), use `da-33-prescriptive-analytics`. The gap between the two *is* the subject matter here: people deviate from the normative optimum in systematic, predictable ways. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- **The honesty rule (read first).** Decision/social psychology went through a replication crisis. Several once-famous effects did **not** survive (power posing, social priming, and ego depletion are contested/failed). The core judgment-and-decision-making findings (anchoring, framing, the disposition effect, present bias, default effects) replicate well; several adjacent social-psych effects do not. **Never present a debunked effect as established fact.** See `references/replication-status.md` before citing any effect to a customer or in a written recommendation. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- A customer/buyer made a choice that looks irrational -> name the bias, then address the real driver. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- You're setting a price, an opening offer, or a contract renewal -> anchoring and framing. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- A renewal/expansion stalls on "we already invested in X" -> sunk-cost; on "let's keep things as they are" -> status-quo/default bias. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- You're designing a signup, plan-selection, or opt-in/opt-out flow -> choice architecture (and the sludge you should *remove*). [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- You're writing a forecast, capacity plan, or project timeline -> debias your *own* judgment (overconfidence, planning fallacy). [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- Someone cites "power posing" / "priming" / "ego depletion" as fact -> check replication status first. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- If the task is changing a customer's *behavior over time* (adoption, habit, enablement), that's `behavior-change-psychology`, not this skill. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- Two modes of cognition. **System 1** is fast, automatic, associative, affect-laden, and effortless; it produces most snap judgments and most biases. **System 2** is slow, deliberate, effortful, and lazy (it endorses System 1 unless prompted). Labels coined by **Stanovich & West**, popularized by **Kahneman** (*Thinking, Fast and Slow*, 2011). Biases are System 1 outputs that System 2 fails to catch. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- *Caveat:* treat "two systems" as a **useful metaphor, not literal brain architecture**. The strict two-box model is contested (better read as a continuum of automaticity). Don't oversell it. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- *Operator use:* high-stakes decisions (renewals, escalations, architecture calls) deserve a deliberate System-2 step (a checklist or premortem) precisely because the default is a System-1 gut call. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- Mental shortcuts that are "highly economical and usually effective" but produce "systematic and predictable errors." The working set every operator should recognize: **anchoring-and-adjustment** (the first number dominates; the single most useful effect in negotiation), **availability** (judging probability by ease of recall; the loud outage feels likelier than the silent risk), **representativeness** (stereotype/similarity over base rates; the conjunction fallacy), **confirmation bias** (the engine behind most bad root-cause calls), **hindsight bias** ("knew it all along"; corrupts postmortems), **overconfidence** (90%-confident estimates are right far less than 90% of the time; the planning fallacy), **status-quo / default bias**, and **sunk-cost fallacy** (honoring unrecoverable past spend instead of deciding on the margin). Detail and operator scripts: `references/biases-catalog.md`. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- How people choose under risk, the descriptive replacement for expected-utility theory: **reference dependence** (outcomes judged as gains/losses from a reference point; whoever sets the reference frames the decision), **loss aversion** (losses loom larger than equivalent gains; classic estimate ~2x, but CONTESTED, do not state "2x" as universal law), **diminishing sensitivity** (concave for gains, convex for losses), **probability weighting** (small probabilities overweighted, hence lottery tickets AND insurance; the certainty effect), **the fourfold pattern** (risk-averse for likely gains and unlikely losses; risk-seeking for unlikely gains and likely losses), and **framing effects** ("90% uptime" vs "10% downtime" flip the choice). [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- > **Loss aversion is contested, not debunked.** Gal & Rucker (2018), "The Loss of Loss Aversion," argue it is far more context-dependent than the "universal 2x law" implies; gains can loom larger at small magnitudes (Harinck et al., 2007) and predicted pain of loss overstates the actual (Kermer et al., 2006). Real in many settings (especially higher-stakes, endowed goods) but **not** a context-free constant. Use it as a *hypothesis to test for this customer*, not a guaranteed lever. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- **Bounded rationality (Herbert Simon)** — limited information/time/compute, so people **satisfice**: pick the first option clearing an aspiration threshold rather than optimizing. Buyers rarely run an exhaustive comparison; they stop at "good enough." [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- **Ecological rationality / fast-and-frugal heuristics (Gerd Gigerenzer)** — the *counterpoint* to heuristics-and-biases. Simple heuristics (take-the-best, recognition, 1/N) are **adaptive** and often *more* accurate than complex models under scarce/uncertain information (less-is-more). A heuristic is "rational" relative to its environment. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- *Why both matter:* one says shortcuts cause errors, the other says shortcuts are often the smart move. The truth is conditional: **match the diagnosis to the environment** before "fixing" a heuristic. These two programs are the respective foundations of nudging and boosting. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- **Mental accounting (Thaler)** — money sorted into non-fungible mental "buckets" (budget categories, "house money," renewal-vs-new-purchase), violating fungibility. A spend framed against the "innovation budget" lands differently than against "BAU/maintenance." [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- **Present bias / hyperbolic discounting** — near-term costs/rewards discounted far more steeply than distant ones (quasi-hyperbolic beta-delta; Laibson 1997). Produces **time-inconsistency**: "we'll migrate next quarter" gets reversed when next quarter arrives. Upfront-cost / delayed-benefit work (migrations, upgrades, tech-debt paydown) is chronically under-chosen. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- **Choice architecture** — every presentation of options (order, defaults, count, framing) influences choice; there is no neutral presentation, so design it deliberately. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- **Nudge** — alters behavior predictably without forbidding options or changing incentives (libertarian paternalism). The most powerful nudge is the **default** (opt-out organ donation, 401(k) auto-enrollment, pre-checked tiers). [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- **EAST** (UK Behavioural Insights Team) — make the desired action **Easy, Attractive, Social, Timely**. The most practical operator checklist. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- **MINDSPACE** — Messenger, Incentives, Norms, Defaults, Salience, Priming, Affect, Commitments, Ego. (The "Priming" element rests on social-priming research that largely failed to replicate; treat it as the weakest element.) [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- **Sludge** — friction added *against* the person's own interest (cancellation mazes, hidden opt-outs). **Find and remove sludge in your own onboarding/renewal flows**; don't deploy it. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- **Boosts (Hertwig & Grüne-Yanoff, 2017)** — the *contrast* to nudges. Instead of steering the chooser, **build their competence** (teach a decision rule, give a fast-and-frugal tree, present risks as natural frequencies). Boosts preserve agency and persist after the intervention; prefer them for long-term, trust-based relationships, which is most TAM work. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- *Ethics:* nudge toward the chooser's *own* interest, keep it transparent, never sludge. Full applied detail (incl. choice overload): `references/choice-architecture.md`. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- You cannot will a bias away, but structured procedures help: **consider-the-opposite** (best-evidenced general debiaser, strong against anchoring/overconfidence), **premortem (Gary Klein)** (imagine the project has failed and explain why; prospective hindsight, cheap and high-yield), **reference-class forecasting (Flyvbjerg / Kahneman's "outside view")** (estimate from the distribution of comparable past cases; the fix for the planning fallacy), and **checklists** (force System 2 through a disciplined pass; only work with consistent adherence). Procedures and worked scenarios: `references/debiasing-and-application.md`. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- **This table is a hypothesis generator, not a verdict.** Treat the observed "tell" (what the customer said or did) as *data*, not a confirmed diagnosis. A tell suggests a *candidate* effect; confirm it against this specific person/context before acting (several effects are context-dependent). If the tell is ambiguous, gather one more observation or ask a clarifying question first. Never state the bias label *to* the customer or imply they are irrational; the label is your internal hypothesis, the "move" is what you do. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- **Calling a customer "irrational."** They're predictably *boundedly* rational. Name the mechanism and design around it. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- **Citing a debunked effect.** Power posing, social priming, ego depletion are contested/failed; the "2x loss-aversion constant" is over-stated. Check `references/replication-status.md` first. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- **Weaponizing nudges (sludge / dark patterns).** Steering a customer against their own interest is self-defeating in a TAM relationship. Prefer boosts. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- **Treating System 1/2 as literal neuroanatomy.** It's a model. Don't overclaim. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- **One-shot debiasing.** Awareness alone barely moves biases; only structured procedures reliably help, and only with disciplined use. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- **Over-applying loss aversion / "fixing" a heuristic that's actually ecologically rational.** Diagnose the environment first (Gigerenzer's caution). [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- `behavior-change-psychology` — adjacent and complementary. *This* skill = the descriptive psychology of a **decision** (biases, framing, choice architecture). *That* skill = changing **behavior over time** (motivation, Fogg B=MAP, stages-of-change, habit loops, adoption). "Design an onboarding nudge to drive adoption" -> that skill; "what default/framing shapes this purchase decision" -> this skill. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- `da-33-prescriptive-analytics` — the **normative** counterpart (optimal action under constraints: LP/MILP, decision trees, EVPI, utility theory). Compute the optimum there; understand why humans deviate from it here. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- `executive-comms` — persuasion and decision-driving *communication* (board memos, negotiation prep, influence). For the rhetoric/persuasion craft go there; for the underlying decision psychology stay here. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- `postmortem-writing` — applies hindsight-bias control in incident reviews. [src: behavioral-decision-making]
- `deep-research-methods` — covers confirmation bias / echo chambers as research anti-patterns. [src: behavioral-decision-making]

- How humans decide whether to follow, override, or ignore an AI system, and how [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- to design and coach for the *right* amount of reliance. This is human-factors [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- and decision psychology applied to **trust in machines**, not interpersonal [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- trust. The central problem is not "more trust" or "less trust" but **calibrated [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- trust**: reliance that tracks the system's *actual* reliability in the specific [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- A TAM, customer, or team is **over-relying** (rubber-stamping AI output) or [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- **under-relying** (ignoring a tool that outperforms them). [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- An AI feature hits **adoption resistance** rooted in distrust, or **dangerous [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- over-adoption** where users stop checking. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- You are **designing an AI-assisted workflow** (copilot, recommender, triage [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- assistant, autoremediation gate) and must decide what to surface (confidence, [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- explanations, friction) to get appropriate reliance. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- A **confidently wrong** AI answer was believed and you need the vocabulary to [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- You are coaching a customer on a **human-in-the-loop** override policy. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- **Trust is an attitude; reliance is a behavior; appropriate reliance is the [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- goal.** They are routinely conflated and must be kept separate. Optimizing for [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- "trust" (a survey number) is the wrong target — optimize for **reliance that [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- matches reliability**: follow the AI when it is right, override it when it is [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- wrong. Most failures in AI-assisted decisions are *miscalibration*, not a global [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- **Trust** = "the attitude that an agent will help achieve an individual's goals [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- in a situation characterized by uncertainty and vulnerability." **Reliance** = [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- the observable behavior that follows. **Calibration** = correspondence between [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- trust and the system's true capability. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- **Over-trust → over-reliance / misuse.** Defers when it shouldn't. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- **Under-trust → under-reliance / disuse.** Rejects help that would have worked. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- The **trust-calibration curve** plots trust against true reliability; the [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- diagonal is perfect calibration. **Resolution** = fine-grained trust that [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- discriminates which cases the system handles well from those it doesn't (good [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- calibration on average can still have poor resolution). Calibration is a closed [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- loop, updated by performance feedback, disposition, and organizational norms. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- > Operator translation: don't ask "do you trust the tool?" Ask "for *which* [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- > decisions does it earn the follow?" Coach for resolution, not blanket trust. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- With an imperfect aid: **commission errors** (following a wrong automated [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- directive without cross-checking) and **omission errors** (missing what the [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- automation failed to flag because you weren't monitoring). **Automation [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- complacency** is the attentional root — under load, monitoring drops. Appears in [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- experts and novices; **not reliably removed by training**; occurs in teams [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- (redundancy can backfire via diffused responsibility); worsens with very high [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- automation reliability. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- > Operator translation: "a human reviews it" is a control only if it forces [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- > engagement; under load it decays to rubber-stamping. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- People **abandon algorithms faster than humans after seeing them err**, even [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- when the algorithm outperforms them. **Error visibility** is the trigger (seeing [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- it fail, not the failure rate). The 2018 follow-up: letting people **adjust the [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- algorithm's output even slightly** restores willingness to use it (control lever). [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- > Operator translation: a single visible miss can sink a net-better tool — [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- > counter with adjustability, expectation-setting before the first error, and [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- > framing errors as bounded. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- In six experiments people **weighted advice MORE heavily when told it came from [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- an algorithm** (Weight-On-Advice). Appreciation waned with **domain expertise** [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- and when choosing algorithm-vs-**their own** judgment. The two literatures are [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- reconciled by moderators: [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- **Plausible-but-wrong explanations increase over-reliance** (Bansal et al., [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- 2021, "Does the Whole Exceed Its Parts?"): explanations raised acceptance [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- whether the AI was right or wrong — agreement up, accuracy not. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- **Confidence helps only if calibrated**; miscalibrated confidence degrades [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- decision quality, and displayed AI confidence shifts the human's own [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- self-confidence (anchoring uncertainty without improving ability). [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- **Mechanism (dual-process):** explanations feed the accept-heuristic rather [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- than interrupting it. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- > Operator translation: "we added explanations/confidence" is not evidence of [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- > appropriate reliance — verify behaviorally (does override-rate track [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- > error-rate?). Ship confidence numbers only if validated as calibrated. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- Friction that compels analytical engagement at decision time: **commit-first** [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- (judge before the AI is revealed), **on-demand reveal / wait**, **show reasoning [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- on request** + surface disagreement/uncertainty. These reduced over-reliance on [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- incorrect AI more than explanation-only designs. Costs: effort, often disliked, [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- benefit interacts with the user (Need for Cognition) — reserve for high-stakes / [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- likely-wrong cases. Adjacent levers: onboarding on error boundaries, selective [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- explanations, adjustable outputs. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- **Complementary Team Performance** = human+AI beat both alone, achieved only [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- when their errors differ and each defers where the other is better. **CTP is [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- rare by default** — teams often do worse than the AI alone. Put the human where [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- they have an information edge the model lacks (context, unobservables), not as a [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- Anthropomorphic cues (persona, warmth, avatar) can raise initial trust but are [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- mediated by perceived empathy/interaction quality. **Uncanny valley** (Mori, [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- 1970): near-human-but-not affinity drops sharply; an "uncanny valley of trust" [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- raises competence expectations the bot can't meet. A warm, fluent, confident [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- persona **manufactures over-trust** regardless of correctness (fluency reads as [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- competence) — match persona confidence to validated capability. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- Target appropriate reliance, measured behaviorally (override tracks error) — [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- not a trust survey number or raw agreement. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- Set honest expectations before the first error. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- Show confidence only if calibrated; communicate uncertainty honestly. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- Don't expect explanations to create skepticism (they raise acceptance); pair [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- with friction; prefer selective explanations on likely-error cases. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- Engineer friction where stakes are high (commit-first, on-demand reveal) — [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- and reserve it; it has a cost. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- Give users control/adjustability over outputs (restores reliance after errors). [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- Place the human where they have an information edge, not as a generic reviewer. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- Match persona confidence to validated capability. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- Treat "a human reviews it" as a design problem, not a safeguard. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- Optimizing for "trust" as a survey number instead of calibrated reliance. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- Shipping explanations/confidence and declaring over-reliance solved (they [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- Treating a human-in-the-loop step as a guaranteed control. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- Letting one visible AI error kill adoption of a net-better tool. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]
- Maxing out a confident anthropomorphic persona on a high-stakes tool. [src: human-ai-interaction-psychology]

- Three distinct but interlocking literatures govern professional relationships. **Trust** is dyadic willingness to be vulnerable. **Rapport** is the moment-to-moment relational tone. **Psychological safety** is a group-level climate belief. They are not the same thing — build all three deliberately. [src: trust-and-psychological-safety]
- This skill is about trust **between people**. For trust in *machines/automation* (over-reliance, algorithm aversion, calibration), use `human-ai-interaction-psychology`. [src: trust-and-psychological-safety]
- **Meta-finding across all three:** trust and safety are slow to build and fast to destroy (Slovic). Match every move to that asymmetry. [src: trust-and-psychological-safety]
- Deep detail, the repair decision aid, the full 7-item scale, and source citations live in `references/trust-rapport-safety-detail.md`. Load it when you need specifics. [src: trust-and-psychological-safety]
- -- [src: trust-and-psychological-safety]
- See the 6-step repair decision aid in the reference file. [src: trust-and-psychological-safety]
- **Safety is NOT niceness.** Pair high safety with high accountability/standards (Edmondson's learning zone). Never sell it as "be nice." And trust is NOT blindness — mature trust is calibrated by evidence. [src: trust-and-psychological-safety]
