- Every modern LLM (Llama 3, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen 3, Mistral, Gemma 2) is a stack of near-identical decoder blocks. This reference is the **anatomy of one block** and the menu of **variants** the frontier labs swap in. It answers: *what is actually inside the box, why is it shaped that way, and which knob did DeepSeek/Llama/Mistral turn?* [src: transformer-architecture]
- **The one mental model that unlocks everything here: the residual stream.** A decoder-only transformer is a *residual stream* of width `d_model` that every layer reads from and writes back to additively: `x = x + Attention(Norm(x))` then `x = x + FFN(Norm(x))`. Attention *moves information between token positions*; the FFN *processes each position independently*. Normalization keeps the stream numerically sane; positional encoding tells attention where tokens sit. Almost every "variant" below is a cheaper/longer/sparser way to compute one of those two sublayers (attention or FFN) without changing the residual-stream contract. Hold that and the whole zoo becomes legible. [src: transformer-architecture]
- > Scope guard: this file is the **architecture**. For *serving* it (vLLM, paged KV cache, continuous batching, speculative decoding) see `llm-inference-serving.md`, which explicitly defers attention math here. For *shrinking* it (GPTQ/AWQ/GGUF/FP8 algorithms) see `llm-compression.md`. For *training/aligning* it see `llm-alignment-post-training.md`. For *which* model to pick see `llm-models.md`. [src: transformer-architecture]
- The canonical block, modern (pre-norm, decoder-only) form: [src: transformer-architecture]
- ┌─────────────────────── residual stream (width d_model) ───────────────────────┐ [src: transformer-architecture]
- tokens → embed │→(+)→[ Norm → Self-Attention (+ pos. enc.) ]→(+)→[ Norm → FFN (gated) ]→ … ×L │→ Norm → unembed → logits [src: transformer-architecture]
- └──────↑──────────────────────────────────────↑─────────────────────────────────┘ [src: transformer-architecture]
- residual add                          residual add [src: transformer-architecture]
- -- [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Core idea.** Attention lets each token build a query, compare it against every token's key, and pull a weighted blend of every token's value. It is the only sublayer that mixes information *across positions*. "Self"-attention means Q, K, V are all projections of the same sequence. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **The mechanism — scaled dot-product attention** (Vaswani et al. 2017, "Attention Is All You Need", arXiv:1706.03762): [src: transformer-architecture]
- Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( Q Kᵀ / √d_k ) V [src: transformer-architecture]
- `Q = XW_Q`, `K = XW_K`, `V = XW_V` are linear projections of the input `X` (shape `[seq, d_model]`). [src: transformer-architecture]
- `√d_k` scaling stops the dot products from growing with dimension and saturating the softmax into near-one-hot (vanishing gradients). [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Causal masking**: for autoregressive LMs, set the upper-triangular entries of `QKᵀ` to `-∞` before softmax so position *t* can only attend to positions `≤ t`. This is what makes the model a left-to-right next-token predictor. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Multi-head attention (MHA).** Run `h` attention computations in parallel on `d_model/h`-sized slices, concatenate, project back: `MHA = Concat(head₁…head_h) W_O`. Each head can specialize (one tracks syntax, another tracks a referent). Cost: `O(seq² · d_model)` compute and an `O(seq²)` attention matrix, the quadratic wall that drives every efficiency variant below. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **The KV cache (why inference memory explodes).** During autoregressive *decode*, the K and V for past tokens never change, so they are cached and reused, turning per-step attention from quadratic into linear *compute*. But the cache itself grows as `2 · n_layers · n_kv_heads · d_head · seq · batch · dtype_bytes`, and at long context / large batch it becomes the dominant memory consumer and the thing that caps throughput. **Shrinking the KV cache is the single biggest motivation for MQA/GQA/MLA (§3).** (The *serving-side* management of this cache, via PagedAttention and offload, is `llm-inference-serving.md`'s job; here it explains *why the variants exist*.) [src: transformer-architecture]
- -- [src: transformer-architecture]
- Attention is permutation-invariant: `softmax(QKᵀ)V` doesn't know token order. Positional encoding injects order. This is one of the most consequential architecture choices because it governs **how far the model can extrapolate beyond its training context**. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **RoPE — the one to understand.** It applies a rotation matrix to each 2-D pair of Q/K dimensions: [src: transformer-architecture]
- R(m,θ_i) = [ cos(m·θ_i)  −sin(m·θ_i) ;  sin(m·θ_i)  cos(m·θ_i) ] [src: transformer-architecture]
- ⟨R(m)·q,  R(n)·k⟩  ∝  ⟨q,k⟩ · cos((m−n)·θ) [src: transformer-architecture]
- Because the inner product collapses to a function of `(m−n)`, **RoPE encodes relative position while only ever rotating absolute-position-indexed vectors**: cheap, no extra parameters, and it composes with the KV cache. It also has a **long-term decay** property (distant tokens attend less). The base/`θ` value is the knob long-context extension turns (§7). *Adoption: essentially every open-weight frontier model in 2025-2026.* [src: transformer-architecture]
- -- [src: transformer-architecture]
- These keep the *same* attention math but reduce how many distinct K/V projections exist, directly shrinking the KV cache and the memory-bandwidth bottleneck during decode. This is a spectrum: [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Multi-Head Attention (MHA)** — `h` query heads, `h` KV heads. Best quality, biggest cache. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Multi-Query Attention (MQA)** (Shazeer 2019, arXiv:1911.02150) — `h` query heads share a **single** K/V head. Cache shrinks ~`h×`, decode gets dramatically faster, but quality can degrade and training can destabilize. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)** (Ainslie et al. 2023, arXiv:2305.13245, EMNLP 2023) — the **interpolation**: split query heads into `G` groups, each group shares one K/V head. **GQA-1 = MQA; GQA-h = MHA.** A typical setting (e.g. 8 KV heads for 64 query heads) recovers near-MHA quality at near-MQA speed. The paper also gives an **uptraining** recipe to convert an existing MHA checkpoint to GQA with **~5% of original pretraining compute**. *Adoption: Llama 2 70B, Llama 3 (all sizes), Mistral, Qwen, Gemma — the mainstream default for dense models.* [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA)** (DeepSeek-V2, carried into DeepSeek-V3, arXiv:2412.19437) — the 2024-2026 frontier move. Instead of sharing K/V heads, MLA **compresses K and V jointly into a low-rank latent vector** `c_KV` (compression dim `d_c ≪ d_head·n_head`, LoRA-style down-then-up projection) and **caches only the latent** `c_KV`, decompressing to full K/V on the fly. Result: KV cache as low as **~4-14% of MHA** while *beating* MHA quality. The catch and its fix — **decoupled RoPE**: low-rank compression doesn't commute with RoPE's rotation, so MLA carries position on a small set of **extra, dedicated RoPE dimensions** (a separate shared key `k_R` and per-head query component) outside the compressed path. *Adoption: DeepSeek-V2/V3/R1; the headline efficiency mechanism behind their long-context economics.* [src: transformer-architecture]
- > Why this lives here, not in serving: GQA/MLA change the *model's parameter structure and what gets cached*. The serving engine's `PagedAttention` then *manages* that cache in GPU memory. Architecture decides the cache *shape*; serving decides its *placement*. See `llm-inference-serving.md` §KV-cache. [src: transformer-architecture]
- -- [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Core idea.** FlashAttention is not an approximation and not a new attention formula; it is the *same* `softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V`, computed in an order that never writes the giant `seq × seq` attention matrix to slow memory. It is the reason long-context training/inference is affordable. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Why "IO-aware" is the whole point.** A GPU has a memory hierarchy: huge-but-slow **HBM** (high-bandwidth memory) and tiny-but-fast on-chip **SRAM**. Naive attention is **memory-bound, not compute-bound**: it materializes the `N×N` scores in HBM, reads them back for softmax, reads again for the `×V`; the bottleneck is HBM traffic, not FLOPs. FlashAttention (Dao et al. 2022, arXiv:2205.14135, NeurIPS 2022): [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Tiling** — loads blocks of Q, K, V into SRAM, computes attention block-by-block, and updates the output incrementally so the full score matrix never touches HBM. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Online softmax** — keeps a running max and running sum, rescaling partial results as new blocks arrive, so softmax is exact without seeing all scores at once. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Recomputation** in the backward pass — instead of storing the `N×N` matrix for gradients, recompute it from the cached softmax statistics. Trades a little extra compute for a large memory saving. [src: transformer-architecture]
- Net effect: memory drops from `O(N²)` to `O(N)`, with a ~7.6× attention speedup reported originally. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **The version progression (architecture-relevant differences):** [src: transformer-architecture]
- **FlashAttention-2** (Dao 2023, arXiv:2307.08691) — better **work partitioning** and **parallelism over the sequence dimension**, fewer non-matmul FLOPs; reaches 50-73% of A100 peak (~2× over v1). [src: transformer-architecture]
- **FlashAttention-3** (Shah, Dao et al. 2024, arXiv:2407.08608) — **Hopper-specific**: exploits **asynchrony** (overlap GEMM and softmax via **warp specialization**, async **TMA**/**WGMMA**) and **FP8 low precision** with incoherent (Hadamard) processing to cut quantization error ~2.6×. Hits **~740 TFLOPs/s (75% H100 utilization) in FP16** and **~1.2 PFLOPs/s in FP8**. [src: transformer-architecture]
- > Boundary: the *kernel implementation* and how a serving engine integrates it is `llm-inference-serving.md`. Here the takeaway is conceptual: **FlashAttention is exact attention reordered to respect the GPU memory hierarchy**, which is why context windows grew without the quadratic memory wall. [src: transformer-architecture]
- -- [src: transformer-architecture]
- **What normalization does.** It rescales activations to keep the residual stream numerically stable as it passes through dozens of layers; without it, deep transformers diverge. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **LayerNorm** (Ba et al. 2016) — subtract the mean, divide by std, then learned scale `γ` and shift `β`. Two stats, two parameter vectors. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **RMSNorm** (Zhang & Sennrich 2019, arXiv:1910.07467) — **drop the mean-centering**; just divide by the root-mean-square and apply a learned scale `γ`. `RMSNorm(x) = x / √(mean(x²) + ε) · γ`. Cheaper (no mean, no shift), and empirically **no quality loss**. *Adoption: essentially every LLM since 2023 — Llama, Mistral, DeepSeek, Qwen, Gemma, Phi.* (A Pre-LN transformer is arithmetically convertible to Pre-RMSNorm; arXiv:2305.14858.) [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Placement — pre-norm vs post-norm** (Xiong et al. 2020, "On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture"): [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Post-norm** (original Transformer): `x = Norm(x + Sublayer(x))`. Norm sits *on the residual path* — strong regularization but **fragile to train deep** (needs learning-rate warmup, gradients can explode). [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Pre-norm**: `x = x + Sublayer(Norm(x))`. Norm sits *inside the branch*, leaving the residual path a clean identity highway. **Gradients flow cleanly, scales to 100+ layers, little warmup sensitivity.** This is **why pre-norm is the universal modern choice.** [src: transformer-architecture]
- **DeepNorm** (Wang et al. 2022) — a post-norm variant with up-scaled residuals that trains to 1000 layers; a niche alternative when post-norm's properties are wanted at depth. [src: transformer-architecture]
- *Modern default: pre-RMSNorm. DeepSeek-V3 adds an extra norm after the compressed-attention/MoE paths for stability.* [src: transformer-architecture]
- -- [src: transformer-architecture]
- **What the FFN does.** After attention mixes positions, the FFN (a.k.a. MLP) processes **each position independently** through an expand-then-contract MLP. It holds the bulk of a dense model's parameters (~2/3) and is where most "knowledge" is stored. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Classic FFN**: `FFN(x) = W₂ · σ(W₁x + b₁) + b₂`, with `σ = ReLU` or `GELU`, expanding `d_model → 4·d_model → d_model`. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Gated Linear Units (GLU variants)** (Shazeer 2020, "GLU Variants Improve Transformer", arXiv:2002.05202) — split the up-projection into a **value path and a gate path** and multiply them elementwise: `GLU(x) = (xW) ⊙ σ(xV)`. **SwiGLU** uses Swish/SiLU as the gate (`Swish(x)=x·sigmoid(x)`); **GeGLU** uses GELU. Gating lets the network learn *which* features to pass — consistently lower loss for free. Because GLU adds a third weight matrix, the hidden dim is scaled to ~**2/3·(4·d_model)** to keep parameter count constant. [src: transformer-architecture]
- SwiGLU-FFN(x) = ( Swish(x W_gate) ⊙ (x W_up) ) W_down [src: transformer-architecture]
- *Adoption: SwiGLU is the modern default — PaLM, Llama 1/2/3, Mistral, DeepSeek, Qwen, Gemma.* [src: transformer-architecture]
- -- [src: transformer-architecture]
- Models are pretrained at a fixed context (e.g. 4K-8K) but deployed at 128K-1M+. Because RoPE (§2) is a *function of position*, you can **rescale its frequencies** to cover positions never seen in training, usually with a short fine-tune, sometimes zero-shot. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Position Interpolation (PI)** (Chen et al. 2023) — linearly **downscale** position indices so length `L'` maps into the trained `[0, L]` range. Simple; needs fine-tuning; loses high-frequency (local) resolution. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **NTK-aware / "NTK-by-parts" scaling** — scale the RoPE *base* rather than the positions, so high-frequency (local) dimensions are preserved while low-frequency (long-range) ones are stretched. Better than naive PI, often zero-shot. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **YaRN** (Peng et al. 2023, arXiv:2309.00071, ICLR 2024) — the **NTK-by-parts** scheme plus an **attention-logit temperature** (scale logits before softmax, zero runtime cost). **~10× less data and ~2.5× fewer training steps** than PI to reach a target context, with better long-sequence perplexity. **Dynamic YaRN** extends >2× *without any fine-tuning*. *Adoption: the standard RoPE-extension recipe — Qwen, many Llama/Mistral long-context derivatives.* [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Context-parallel / Ring Attention** — an orthogonal axis: instead of changing positions, **shard the sequence across GPUs** and pass KV blocks ring-style so no single device holds the full `seq`. This is what makes million-token *training/inference* physically fit. (The serving-side mechanics are `llm-inference-serving.md`.) [src: transformer-architecture]
- -- [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Core idea.** Replace the single dense FFN (§6) with **many expert FFNs** and a **router** that sends each token to only a few. Total parameters (capacity) grow huge while **compute per token stays fixed**: you "activate" only a sparse slice. MoE is applied to the FFN sublayer; attention stays dense. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Top-k routing** — a lightweight gating network scores each token against each expert; the token goes to its top-`k` experts (often `k=1` or `2`), and their outputs are combined weighted by gate scores. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Load-balancing loss** — naive routing collapses (a few experts hog all tokens). The classic fix (Switch Transformer, Fedus et al. 2021) adds an **auxiliary load-balancing loss** encouraging uniform expert usage — but that loss can *hurt* model quality. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **DeepSeek-V3-style MoE — the 2024-2026 frontier design** (arXiv:2412.19437): [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Fine-grained experts** — slice experts smaller (grow count `N→mN`, shrink each to `1/m`, activate `m×` more) for sharper specialization at equal FLOPs. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Shared experts** — `1` (or few) expert that **every** token always uses, to absorb common/general knowledge so routed experts can specialize. DeepSeek-V3: **1 shared + 256 routed experts, top-8 routed activated per token.** [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Auxiliary-loss-free load balancing** (Wang et al. 2024, arXiv:2408.15664) — instead of an auxiliary loss, add a **per-expert bias** to the routing scores and **nudge the bias up/down by γ** when an expert is under/over-loaded. Balances load **without the quality tax** of an auxiliary loss. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Scale realized**: DeepSeek-V3 = **671B total parameters, only 37B activated per token.** That ratio is the entire point of MoE. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Expert parallelism** — experts are sharded across GPUs; tokens are dispatched/combined with all-to-all communication (a serving/training-systems concern — see `llm-inference-serving.md` for expert-parallel serving). [src: transformer-architecture]
- *Adoption: DeepSeek-V3/R1, Mixtral, Qwen-MoE, Llama 4, GPT-class frontier models — MoE is the dominant way to scale frontier capacity in 2025-2026.* [src: transformer-architecture]
- -- [src: transformer-architecture]
- Attention is `O(seq²)`. A parallel research line replaces or dilutes it with **sub-quadratic sequence mixers** that keep a fixed-size recurrent state. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **State-Space Models (SSMs) / Mamba** (Gu & Dao 2023) — model the sequence as a linear **state-space recurrence** with **input-dependent ("selective")** parameters, computed via a hardware-aware parallel scan. **Linear time, constant memory per step** (no growing KV cache), strong on very long sequences. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Mamba-2** (Dao & Gu 2024) — the **State-Space Duality (SSD)** framework shows SSMs and attention are two views of the same structured-matrix operation, letting Mamba-2 use matmul-friendly kernels (much faster) and larger states. The key bridge result connecting the two model families. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Linear attention** — drop the softmax so attention factorizes into a recurrent form (`O(seq)` instead of `O(seq²)`); the conceptual root of the SSM/RWKV family, historically weaker than softmax attention on recall. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **RWKV** (RWKV-7, 2025) — an **attention-free RNN** trainable in parallel like a transformer but with recurrent constant-memory inference; RWKV-7 reaches ~Llama-3.1-8B-class quality on several tasks at comparable scale. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Hybrids (the pragmatic winner)** — interleave a *few* full-attention layers among many SSM/linear layers to get linear-ish cost *and* attention's precise recall. **Jamba** (AI21, 2024) mixes Mamba + attention + MoE (52B total / 12B active, 256K context, higher throughput than equal-size transformers). NVIDIA's hybrid studies report ~8× faster inference at competitive quality. *Frontier reality 2026: pure transformers still lead general benchmarks, but hybrids dominate long-context efficiency and are shipping in production.* [src: transformer-architecture]
- -- [src: transformer-architecture]
- Before any of the above runs, text is split into tokens. The choice affects vocabulary size, sequence length, and multilingual/code coverage, but it's *upstream* of the architecture. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE)** — start from a base alphabet, greedily **merge the most frequent adjacent pair** repeatedly until the vocab hits a target size. Balances vocabulary size against sequence length; the dominant family. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Byte-level BPE** — run BPE over **raw UTF-8 bytes** (256-symbol base), so *any* string is encodable with **no out-of-vocabulary** — emoji, code, any language. Used by GPT-2/3/4 and Llama 3. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **SentencePiece** — a tokenizer *framework* (implements BPE and Unigram) that operates on raw text/codepoints language-agnostically (treats whitespace as a symbol `▁`), with **byte-fallback** for rare codepoints. Used by Llama 1/2, Gemma, many multilingual models. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **tiktoken** — OpenAI's fast byte-level-BPE library/tokenizers (e.g. `cl100k_base`, `o200k_base`) for GPT-3.5/4/4o. [src: transformer-architecture]
- *Rule of thumb: GPT family → byte-level BPE via tiktoken; Llama/Gemma → SentencePiece (Llama 3 moved to a tiktoken-style 128K byte-level BPE). Tokenizer choice is a data/efficiency decision, not part of the transformer block.* [src: transformer-architecture]
- -- [src: transformer-architecture]
- **The throughline:** every modern choice (RMSNorm, pre-norm, RoPE, GQA/MLA, SwiGLU, FlashAttention, MoE) is the *cheaper or longer-context* substitute for an original-Transformer component, chosen to push more capability through the same FLOP and memory budget. [src: transformer-architecture]
- -- [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Confusing FlashAttention with an approximation.** It is *exact* — same outputs, reordered IO. If results change, it's a bug, not the algorithm. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Treating GQA/MQA as free quality.** MQA can degrade quality and destabilize training; GQA is the safe interpolation. Picking KV-head count is a real quality/throughput tradeoff. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Forgetting RoPE doesn't extrapolate for free.** Past the trained context, raw RoPE degrades sharply — you need PI/NTK/YaRN scaling (usually + a short fine-tune). [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Extending context by only changing the tokenizer or max_position config.** Without RoPE rescaling (and ideally fine-tuning), the model produces garbage beyond its trained length. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **MoE without load balancing.** Routing collapses to a few experts; you pay for capacity you never use. Use aux-loss-free bias balancing or an auxiliary loss. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Assuming hybrids/SSMs beat transformers everywhere.** As of 2026 they win on long-context *efficiency*, not uniformly on benchmark quality — they shine in hybrids, not as wholesale replacements. [src: transformer-architecture]
- **Mixing up architecture vs serving.** "Why is my KV cache huge?" is architecture (use GQA/MLA). "How is my KV cache laid out in GPU memory?" is serving (PagedAttention). Don't solve one in the other's layer. [src: transformer-architecture]
- -- [src: transformer-architecture]

- The evidence-based psychology of **sustaining performance over the long haul** — [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- your own and your team's — without burning out. Ten constructs, organized into [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **What drives effort** — mindset, grit, achievement goals, regulatory focus. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **What sustains it in the moment** — flow, self-efficacy, self-regulation. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **What protects against collapse** — stress appraisal & coping, burnout, recovery & resilience. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- The throughline: **high performance is not a trait you have or lack; it is a [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- state you engineer** — through how you frame ability, structure goals, manage [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- attention and arousal, appraise stress, and recover. Each section gives a [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **self-management note** (sustaining your own performance) and a [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **team / coaching note** (leading and developing others). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- This field has a serious **replication problem**, and this skill is honest about [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- it: two of its most famous constructs (growth-mindset interventions, ego [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- depletion) have weak or failed-to-replicate evidence, and a third (grit) is [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- largely redundant with an older trait. Use the strong constructs confidently; [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- treat the contested ones as heuristics, not laws. Where the science is thin, the [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Core idea.** People hold an implicit "lay theory" about whether ability is [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **fixed** (an *entity* theory — you have a fixed amount of intelligence/talent) [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- or **malleable** (an *incremental* theory — ability grows with effort and [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- strategy). A fixed mindset makes effort feel like evidence of low ability and [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- makes failure identity-threatening, so people avoid challenge and disengage. A [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- growth mindset reframes effort and failure as the mechanism of getting better, so [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- people seek challenge and persist ([Dweck — Mindset Works](https://www.mindsetworks.com/science/)). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Be honest about the effect size.** This is the single most over-sold construct [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- in popular performance psychology. The Sisk et al. (2018) two meta-analyses are [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- Across 273 studies / ~365,000 people, mindset accounted for only **~1% of the [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- variance** in academic achievement (a weak correlation). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- Across 43 intervention studies / ~57,000 people, growth-mindset interventions [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- produced a **standardized mean difference of d ≈ 0.08** — very small ([Sisk et al. 2018, Psychological Science](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0956797617739704); [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29505339/)). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- Moderator finding: **low-SES and academically at-risk** people benefited more, [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- which is the strongest remaining case for targeted intervention. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- The debate is live: Yeager & Dweck (2020) argue that for a cheap, scalable [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- intervention even a small average effect concentrated in the right subgroup is [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- meaningful; Macnamara & Burgoyne (2022) re-analyzed and still found weak, [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- inconsistent effects ([Macnamara & Burgoyne 2022, PDF](https://englelab.gatech.edu/articles/2022/Macnamara%20and%20Burgoyne%20(2022)%20-%20Do%20Growth%20Mindset%20Interventions%20Impact%20Students%E2%80%99%20Academic%20Achievement.pdf)). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Takeaway:** mindset is a real and useful *frame*, but it is **not** a high-impact [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- intervention you can sprinkle on a team and expect performance to jump. Treat [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- "praise effort/strategy, not innate talent" as a sound default, not a silver bullet. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Self-management note.** Catch fixed-mindset self-talk ("I'm just not a numbers [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- person") and convert it to a strategy question ("what approach haven't I tried [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- yet?"). The value is in keeping yourself *in* hard problems rather than fleeing [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- them — not in expecting a mindset shift to manufacture skill you haven't built. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Team / coaching note.** Praise **process** (strategy, effort, choices), not the [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- person ("you're so smart"). Person-praise installs a fixed mindset and makes the [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- next failure threatening. Critically, do **not** weaponize "growth mindset" as a [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- way to blame people for outcomes ("you just need a better mindset") — that is a [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- "false growth mindset" and it is demotivating. Pair the frame with actual [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- resources, feedback, and time to improve. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Core idea.** Grit is **perseverance and passion for long-term goals** — the [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- tendency to sustain effort and interest over years despite failure and plateaus, [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- measured by the Grit Scale across two facets: *perseverance of effort* and [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- *consistency of interest* ([Duckworth et al. 2007, summary](https://positivepsychology.com/grit-scale/)). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Be honest about the critique.** The Credé, Tynan & Harms (2017) meta-analysis [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- (584 effect sizes, 88 samples, ~66,800 people) is the essential corrective and is [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- often called the "jangle fallacy" paper (two different names for the same thing): [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- Grit correlates with conscientiousness at **ρ ≈ .84** — so strong that grit is [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- arguably **redundant** with a personality trait psychology has measured for [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- Grit explains **almost no incremental variance** in performance once you control [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- for conscientiousness. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- The higher-order "grit" structure (combining the two facets) was **not confirmed**; [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- the two facets behave differently. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Perseverance of effort** carries essentially all the predictive value; [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **consistency of interest** predicts little. So "keep working hard" matters; [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- "never change your passion" does not ([Credé et al. 2017, JPSP, PDF](https://gwern.net/doc/psychology/personality/conscientiousness/2016-crede.pdf); [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27845531/)). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- Implication: grit *interventions* likely have only weak effects on performance. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Takeaway:** the useful, evidence-backed half of grit is **perseverance of effort**, [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- which is just the actionable edge of conscientiousness. The "stick with the same [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- passion for a decade" half is not well supported and can be actively bad advice [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- (it discourages adaptive pivoting). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Self-management note.** Optimize for **sustained effort on the current important [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- goal**, not for never changing direction. Re-evaluating and pivoting is not a grit [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- failure — consistency-of-interest is the facet that doesn't predict success. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Team / coaching note.** Don't screen or label people by "grit." It mostly [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- re-measures conscientiousness, and using it as a virtue can shade into blaming [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- people for structural problems (bad systems, unrealistic load). Reward visible [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- perseverance through difficulty; never use "lacks grit" as a performance verdict. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Core idea.** Flow is the state of **complete absorption** in an activity, where [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- action and awareness merge, self-consciousness drops, time distorts, and the [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- activity becomes **autotelic** (rewarding in itself) ([Positive Psychology — Csikszentmihalyi](https://positivepsychology.com/mihaly-csikszentmihalyi-father-of-flow/)). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **The challenge-skill balance (the flow channel).** Flow occurs when the [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **challenge of the task and your skill level are both high and roughly balanced**. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- Plot challenge (y) against skill (x): the diagonal band where they match is the [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **flow channel**. Off-diagonal you get the failure modes: [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- High challenge + low skill → **anxiety**. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- Low challenge + high skill → **boredom**. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- Low + low → **apathy**. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- As skill grows, the task must get harder to stay in the channel — flow is a moving [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- target ([Yu-kai Chou — Flow Theory & the 9 components](https://yukaichou.com/gamification-analysis/flow-theory-complete-guide-csikszentmihalyi-optimal-experience/)). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Antecedents (the conditions you can engineer).** The reliable preconditions are [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **(1) clear, proximal goals** and **(2) immediate, unambiguous feedback**, on top [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- of the challenge-skill match. Characteristics during flow include intense [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- concentration, a sense of control, merging of action and awareness, and loss of [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- self-consciousness ([Investigating the Flow Experience, PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7033418/)). An **autotelic [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- personality** disposes some people to enter flow more readily. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Self-management note.** Manufacture the antecedents: protect an uninterrupted [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- block, define a single concrete sub-goal for the session, and create a fast [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- feedback loop (tests, a checklist, a draft you can see growing). Tune difficulty — [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- if anxious, shrink the task; if bored, raise the bar. Notifications are the [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- single biggest flow-killer because they reset concentration and break the feedback loop. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Team / coaching note.** Design work to keep people in the channel: **match [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- assignment difficulty to growing skill** (stretch, don't drown or bore), make [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- goals concrete, and shorten feedback latency (frequent, specific feedback beats an [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- annual review). Meeting-fragmented calendars make team flow nearly impossible — [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- defend maker-time blocks as a performance lever, not a perk. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Core idea.** Self-efficacy is the **task-specific belief that you can execute the [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- actions required to produce a given outcome** ("I can do *this*"). It predicts [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- which goals people set, how much effort they invest, and how they persist under [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- setback — often more strongly than actual ability does ([Simply Psychology — self-efficacy](https://www.simplypsychology.org/self-efficacy.html)). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Distinguish it from two neighbors (this matters):** [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Self-esteem** = global self-worth ("I am a good/worthy person"). Self-efficacy [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- is *domain-specific competence belief*, not worth. You can have high efficacy at [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- coding and low at public speaking; self-esteem doesn't move that way. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Outcome expectancy** = belief that an action *leads to* an outcome. Efficacy is [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- belief that *you can perform the action*. You can believe studying produces good [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- grades (outcome expectancy) yet doubt you can make yourself study (low efficacy). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **The four sources (in order of power):** [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Mastery experiences** — *actually succeeding* at the task. By far the [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- strongest source; nothing builds efficacy like a track record of overcoming [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- difficulty. Easy wins build fragile efficacy; wins through effort build durable efficacy. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Vicarious experience** — *watching a similar other succeed* ("if someone like [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- me can, I can"). Model similarity is what makes it work. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Verbal/social persuasion** — *credible encouragement*. Weaker, and bounded by [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- the persuader's credibility; empty cheerleading backfires. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Physiological & affective states** — *how you interpret your own arousal*. A [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- pounding heart read as "I'm choking" lowers efficacy; read as "I'm fired up" [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- raises it. Weakest source but a useful lever via reappraisal ([Bandura's 4 sources — Yu-kai Chou](https://yukaichou.com/behavioral-analysis/self-efficacy-theory-bandura-belief-ability/); [PsychologyNotesHQ](https://www.psychologynoteshq.com/selfefficacy/)). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- > Cross-reference: `behavior-change-psychology` touches self-efficacy as one input [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- > into a customer's *decisional balance* for adoption. This skill owns the construct [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- > itself — the four sources and how to build efficacy in yourself and your team. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Self-management note.** Build efficacy bottom-up: **sequence tasks so you bank [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- genuine mastery experiences** on an upward difficulty curve, rather than starting [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- with the scariest thing and failing. Before a high-stakes moment, reframe arousal [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- ("this is energy/readiness," not "this is panic"). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Team / coaching note.** Use all four sources deliberately: (1) **engineer early [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- wins** through real challenge (mastery is strongest); (2) **show peer models** — a [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- similar teammate who did it beats an expert who makes it look effortless; [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- (3) make encouragement **specific and credible**, tied to evidence; (4) **normalize [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- nerves** before stretch assignments so people don't read arousal as proof they [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- can't. Stretch assignments are the single most effective development tool *because* a [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- mastery experience under genuine difficulty is what builds durable confidence. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Core idea.** *Why* you pursue achievement shapes outcomes. The classic split: [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Mastery goals** — aim to *develop competence / learn the task* (self-referenced [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Performance goals** — aim to *demonstrate competence relative to others* [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- (normative standard) ([Grading for Growth — achievement goal orientations](https://gradingforgrowth.com/p/achievement-goal-orientations-and)). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **The 2x2 framework (Elliot & McGregor, 2001).** Crossing the mastery/performance [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- *definition* with an **approach vs avoidance** *valence* gives four goals: [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Mastery-approach** — strive to learn and improve. Most consistently linked to [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- positive outcomes (deep learning, intrinsic interest, persistence). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Performance-approach** — strive to outperform others. Mixed: can boost grades [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- and effort but is fragile and tied to extrinsic, contingent motivation. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Mastery-avoidance** — strive *not to fail to learn / not to lose skill* [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- (e.g., a declining expert). Generally maladaptive. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Performance-avoidance** — strive *not to look incompetent*. The most [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- maladaptive — drives anxiety, self-handicapping, and withdrawal ([Elliot & McGregor 2001 — Semantic Scholar](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/A-2-X-2-achievement-goal-framework.-Elliot-Mcgregor/54fcbb82c0eb8b3c50c1dbf48781af7111ca0b12)). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **The 3x2 framework (Elliot, Murayama & Pekrun, 2011).** Splits "mastery" into [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **task-based** (did I do the task well?) and **self-based** (did I do better than [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- my past self?), each crossed with approach/avoidance, yielding six goals [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- (task-approach, task-avoidance, self-approach, self-avoidance, other-approach, [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- other-avoidance) ([3x2 model — Frontiers](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.628004/full); [3x2 systematic review/meta-analysis, PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10416154/)). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Self-management note.** Frame your own hard goals as **mastery-approach** ("get [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- better at X," "beat my last attempt") rather than performance-avoidance ("don't [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- look bad in the review"). The avoidance frame predicts anxiety and self-handicapping; [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- the mastery frame predicts persistence and learning from failure. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Team / coaching note.** The *climate* you set pushes people toward a goal type. A [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- purely **normative, ranked, comparative** environment (stack-ranking, leaderboards, [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- "top performer of the month") nudges people into performance goals — and, for those [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- who doubt they'll win, into **performance-avoidance** (the most toxic quadrant: [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- fear, self-handicapping, hiding mistakes). Build a **mastery climate**: reward [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- improvement and learning, frame goals against the person's own prior level, and [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- make it safe to attempt hard things and fail. Use comparison sparingly and only [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- where it genuinely motivates the specific person. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Core idea.** People pursue goals through one of two motivational systems [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- ([Regulatory focus theory — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulatory_focus_theory); [Higgins 1998, PDF](https://business.columbia.edu/sites/default/files-efs/pubfiles/529/HIGGINSADVANCES_1998REG_FOC_.pdf)): [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Promotion focus** — oriented to **gains, ideals, growth, aspirations**. Driven [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- by *eagerness*; sensitive to the presence/absence of positive outcomes; pursues [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- "ideal self" goals (hopes, what you *want* to be). Favors speed, risk, and [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Prevention focus** — oriented to **security, duties, oughts, avoiding losses**. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- Driven by *vigilance*; sensitive to the presence/absence of negative outcomes; [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- pursues "ought self" goals (responsibilities, what you *should* do). Favors [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- accuracy, caution, and thoroughness. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- Focus is both a **chronic disposition** and a **situationally inducible state** — [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- you can frame a task to evoke either. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Regulatory fit.** Motivation intensifies and the activity "feels right" when the [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **means of pursuit match the focus**: promotion-focused people are energized by [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- eager, gain-framed strategies; prevention-focused people by vigilant, loss-framed [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- ones. Fit increases engagement, persistence, and even perceived value — in one [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- study, fit raised willingness-to-pay for the same mug by ~40–70% ([Yu-kai Chou — regulatory focus](https://yukaichou.com/behavioral-analysis/regulatory-focus-theory-higgins-promotion-prevention/); [BehavioralEconomics.com](https://www.behavioraleconomics.com/resources/mini-encyclopedia-of-be/regulatory-focus-theory/)). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Self-management note.** Match the **frame to the work**. For creative/exploratory [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- or growth work, adopt a promotion frame ("what could we gain / what's the upside"). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- For quality-critical, security, or compliance work — where errors are costly — [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- adopt a prevention frame ("what must not go wrong"). Mis-fit (a prevention person [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- forced to "move fast and break things," or a promotion person buried in checklists) [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Team / coaching note.** **Frame goals and feedback to fit the person and the task.** [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- A promotion-focused report responds to opportunity and aspiration ("here's how this [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- moves you up"); a prevention-focused report responds to responsibility and risk [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- ("here's what we'd lose if this slips"). Same message, different framing, very [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- different motivational pull. Also staff to fit: put prevention-focused people on [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- accuracy-critical work and promotion-focused people on exploration — and frame the [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Core idea.** Self-regulation is steering your own behavior toward goals against [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- competing impulses and distractions — the engine behind every other construct here. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **The ego-depletion claim — and why to be skeptical.** The dominant model for two [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- decades (Baumeister) held that **willpower is a limited resource** that depletes [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- with use, like a muscle that fatigues, so exerting self-control on Task A leaves [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- you worse at Task B. This is the famous "ego depletion" effect — and it is **one of [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- the headline casualties of the replication crisis**: [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- Carter et al. (2015) re-analyzed the literature correcting for publication bias [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- and concluded the likely true effect was **near zero**. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- Hagger et al. (2016) ran a **preregistered multilab replication** across 23 labs [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- (N ≈ 2,141) and **failed to find the effect** — no medium or even small [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- ego-depletion effect ([Hagger et al. 2016, Perspectives on Psychological Science](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1745691616652873); [PDF](https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/wp-content/uploads/2017/11/Hagger_0-407863.pdf)). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- Caveat in both directions: some argue the specific depleting task used was weak, [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- and the construct isn't *disproven* so much as **not robustly demonstrated**. But [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- the strong "willpower is a finite fuel tank" story should **not** be treated as [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- > Cross-reference: `behavioral-decision-making` covers ego depletion as a *decision- [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- > effect* and carries the broader replication-crisis methodology (preregistration, [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- > publication bias, p-hacking). Go there for the meta-science; this section covers [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- > the performance implication. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **What replaces it.** Two more durable ideas: [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Motivation/attention model** (Inzlicht): apparent "depletion" is better [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- explained as **shifts in motivation and attention** over time, not a drained [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- resource — you disengage from effortful control when something feels less worth it. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Implicit theories of willpower** (Job, Dweck, Walton): people who *believe* [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- willpower is limited show depletion-like patterns; those who believe it's not [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- limited often don't. The belief partly creates the effect. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Self-management note.** Stop budgeting a mythical "willpower tank." Instead, [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **reduce the need for self-control** through environment design (remove the [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- distraction, pre-commit, use implementation intentions — see [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- `behavior-change-psychology`), and **protect motivation/attention** (rest, meaning, [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- single-tasking). Fatigue is real; a depleting "willpower fuel gauge" is not well [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Team / coaching note.** Don't design work on the assumption that people have a [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- fixed daily ration of self-control to spend. Performance dips usually signal [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **eroded motivation, unclear priorities, or genuine fatigue/overload**, not a [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- depleted willpower battery. Fix the environment and the meaning, not the person's [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Core idea — the transactional model.** Stress is **not in the event**; it's in the [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **transaction between person and situation**, mediated by *appraisal*. The same [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- deadline is energizing to one person and crushing to another because they appraise [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- it differently ([Transactional model — EBSCO](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/psychology/transactional-model-stress-and-coping); [Mindtools](https://www.mindtools.com/aari1kl/lazarus-and-folkmans-transactional-model-of-stress-and-coping/)). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Primary appraisal** — *"Is this at stake for me, and is it harm/loss, threat, or [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- challenge?"* Crucially, a stressor can be appraised as a **threat** (potential for [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- loss/harm, → fear, defensiveness, narrowed thinking) or as a **challenge** [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- (potential for growth/gain that's demanding but masterable, → energized, [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- approach-oriented). Same demand, opposite physiology and performance. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Secondary appraisal** — *"Can I cope? What are my resources and options?"* Your [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- appraised coping capacity is what flips threat into challenge. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Two coping families:** [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Problem-focused coping** — act on the stressor itself (plan, gather info, [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- remove the obstacle, renegotiate the deadline). Most adaptive **when the situation [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Emotion-focused coping** — regulate the distress (reframe, seek support, [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- acceptance, distraction). Most adaptive **when the situation is uncontrollable** [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- and you must endure it. Maladaptive emotion-focused coping (denial, rumination, [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- avoidance, substances) is where this family goes wrong. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- The art is **matching coping to controllability** — problem-focus what you can [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- change, emotion-focus what you can't, and accurately telling the two apart. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- > Cross-reference: the *mechanics* of emotion-focused coping — reappraisal vs [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- > suppression, Gross's process model of emotion regulation — live in [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- > `emotion-and-affect-psychology`. This section owns the appraisal-and-coping frame; [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- > that skill owns the regulation toolkit. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Self-management note.** Run the two appraisals explicitly under pressure: [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- (1) **reappraise threat as challenge** where honest — focus on what's masterable [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- and what you stand to gain, not only what you could lose (this is the single most [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- useful move; it changes your physiology toward approach); (2) **match coping to [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- control** — make a concrete plan for the controllable parts, and use acceptance/ [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- support/reframing for the parts you can't change. Pure emotion-focus on a [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- controllable problem (venting instead of acting) prolongs the stress. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Team / coaching note.** You shape your team's *primary appraisal*. Framing a hard [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- quarter as a **threat** ("if we miss this we're in trouble") triggers defensive, [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- narrowed, risk-averse behavior; framing it as a **challenge** ("this is a hard, [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- winnable problem and here's what we'll gain") triggers approach and creativity — [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- *provided* you also bolster **secondary appraisal** by visibly supplying resources [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- and support so the challenge is actually copable. Challenge framing without resources [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- is just a threat with a smile. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Core idea — the three dimensions.** Burnout is a **prolonged response to chronic [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- job stressors**, defined by three dimensions ([Maslach — Job Burnout, Annual Reviews](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev.psych.52.1.397); [Maslach Burnout Inventory — Mind Garden](https://www.mindgarden.com/117-maslach-burnout-inventory-mbi)): [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Exhaustion** — depleted emotional and physical energy (the stress dimension). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Cynicism / depersonalization** — negative, detached, callous attitude toward [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- the work and the people in it (the disengagement dimension). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Reduced professional efficacy / inefficacy** — a sense of incompetence and [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- unproductiveness; feeling you're no longer making a difference. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- Maslach's key insight: burnout is **not just exhaustion**. Someone tired but still [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- engaged isn't burned out; the cynicism and inefficacy are what make it burnout. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Work engagement — the positive pole.** Engagement is the **opposite profile**: [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- high **energy** (vs exhaustion), high **involvement** (vs cynicism), high [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **efficacy** (vs inefficacy). "Energy turns into exhaustion, involvement turns into [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- cynicism, efficacy turns into ineffectiveness." So burnout is an *erosion of [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- engagement*, and the goal isn't merely "less burnout" but **building engagement** [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- ([Burnout and work engagement: the JD-R approach](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/263851330_Burnout_and_Work_Engagement_The_JD-R_Approach)). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **The Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model — the causal engine.** Every job has two [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Job demands** — workload, time pressure, emotional load, role conflict, etc. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- Chronic high demands drive the **health-impairment path → exhaustion → burnout**. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Job resources** — autonomy, feedback, social support, growth opportunities, [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- meaningful work, etc. Resources drive the **motivational path → engagement**, and [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- they also **buffer** the impact of demands. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- Burnout, in JD-R terms, is what happens when **demands chronically exceed resources**. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- The lever is not just "reduce demands" (often impossible) but **increase resources** [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- ([Schaufeli & Bakker — JD-R, PDF](https://www.wilmarschaufeli.nl/publications/Schaufeli/209.pdf)). The six classic [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **areas of work-life** mismatch (Maslach & Leiter) name where demands/resources go [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- wrong: **workload, control, reward, community, fairness, and values**. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Self-management note.** Watch for the *cynicism* signal, not just tiredness — [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- growing detachment and "why bother" is the early-warning light that distinguishes [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- burnout from ordinary fatigue. Audit your own job along the six mismatches [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- (workload, control, reward, community, fairness, values) to locate *which* resource [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- is depleted, and protect/grow it (claim autonomy, seek feedback and meaning, rebuild [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- support) rather than just trying to rest your way out of a structural deficit. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Team / coaching note.** Burnout is primarily an **organizational/job-design [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- problem, not an individual resilience failure** — Maslach is emphatic that putting [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- the fix entirely on the worker ("be more resilient") is both wrong and unjust. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- Manage the **JD-R balance**: where you can't cut demands, deliberately **add [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- resources** — autonomy, recognition, social support, clear priorities, fairness, [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- and connection to purpose. Diagnose along the six mismatch areas to find the real [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- driver. And treat **rising cynicism** on the team as a leading indicator of burnout [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- risk, not an attitude problem to discipline. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Core idea.** Resilience is the capacity to **maintain or regain functioning in the [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- face of adversity** — to bend without breaking and bounce back. It is *not* a rare [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- trait; it's an ordinary, trainable set of **protective factors**: social support, [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- adaptive coping, optimism/realistic self-awareness, and hardiness ([Resilience factors — Grand Rising](https://www.grandrisingbehavioralhealth.com/blog/resilience-factors-in-trauma-recovery)). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Recovery (Sonnentag) — the daily/weekly mechanism.** Resilience over time depends [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- on **recovery from work stress**. Sonnentag & Fritz (2007) identify **four recovery [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- experiences** that restore the resources work depletes: [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Psychological detachment** — *mentally* switching off from work (not just being [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- physically away). The **most consistently powerful** recovery experience; it's [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- not enough to leave the office if your mind is still in the meeting. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Relaxation** — low-activation, low-effort states (a walk, music, rest). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Mastery experiences** — off-work challenges that build competence (a hobby, [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- learning something) — restores via accomplishment, not idleness. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Control** — deciding how you spend your own off time. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- Detachment most reliably predicts vitality and well-being; chronic failure to detach [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- (always-on, ruminating) is a direct path toward exhaustion ([Sonnentag & Fritz 2007, REQ — PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17638488/); [Stressor-detachment model, Sonnentag 2015](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/job.1924)). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Post-traumatic growth (Tedeschi & Calhoun) — beyond bouncing back.** Some people, [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- after struggling with major adversity, report **positive transformation** along five [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- domains: personal strength, relating to others, appreciation of life, new [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- possibilities, and spiritual/existential change. Critically, PTG is **distinct from [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- resilience**: resilience is *resistance to / recovery from* harm (returning to [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- baseline), whereas PTG is **growth beyond the prior baseline** — it comes *through* [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- the struggle and cognitive processing, not from avoiding distress. (Counterintuitively, [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- very high resilience can mean *less* PTG, because the highly resilient person isn't [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- shaken enough to reconstruct their assumptions) ([Tedeschi & Calhoun — PTG overview](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/302504970_Posttraumatic_Growth_Positive_Changes_Following_Adversity_-An_Overview); [Resilience vs PTG, PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6846631/)). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Self-management note.** Build recovery into the cadence, don't wait for collapse. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- The most effective move is **psychological detachment** — a real mental off-switch [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- between work and rest (kill notifications, a shutdown ritual, no email rumination at [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- dinner). Physical time off without mental detachment doesn't recover you. Add [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- relaxation, off-work mastery (a hobby that grows competence), and control over your [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- own time. After a genuinely hard period, leave room for sense-making — growth often [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- comes *through* the difficulty, not from skipping past it. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Team / coaching note.** Recovery is a **performance input, not slack to be cut**. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- Protect your team's detachment: model and enforce real off-hours (no "quick" [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- after-hours pings that re-engage the mind), discourage always-on availability, and [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- treat sustainable pace as a productivity strategy. Resilience-building belongs [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- *alongside* — never *instead of* — fixing the job demands that cause the strain [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- (see §9). After a crunch or incident, build in genuine recovery and a reflective [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- debrief; that's where both recovery and post-traumatic growth happen. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- These ten constructs interlock. A practical sequence for **sustaining your own and [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- your team's performance**: [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Frame ability and goals well** (mindset §1, achievement goals §5) — process [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- over person, mastery-approach over performance-avoidance. (But don't expect a [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- "mindset intervention" to do heavy lifting — §1 effect sizes are small.) [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Frame the work to fit motivation** (regulatory focus §6) — promotion frame for [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- exploration/growth, prevention frame for accuracy-critical work; create regulatory fit. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Build confidence through real wins** (self-efficacy §4) — sequence mastery [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- experiences, use peer models, reappraise arousal. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Engineer deep work** (flow §3) — challenge-skill match, clear goals, fast [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- feedback, protected focus blocks. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Manage pressure by appraisal, not grit** (stress §8, self-regulation §7) — [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- reframe threat as challenge, match coping to controllability, design the [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- environment to reduce the need for willpower (don't budget a mythical fuel tank). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Protect the system from burnout** (burnout/JD-R §9) — balance demands with [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- resources; watch cynicism as the early signal; fix job design, don't just tell [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **Recover deliberately** (recovery/resilience §10) — psychological detachment [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- first; build recovery and reflection into the cadence as a performance input. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- The meta-lesson and the honesty check: **the strongest interventions are the structural [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- ones** — job design (JD-R), recovery, challenge-skill matching, and engineering [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- genuine mastery experiences. The popular "just be grittier / fix your mindset / use [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- more willpower" advice is exactly where the evidence is **weakest** (§1, §2, §7). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- When in doubt, change the system before you exhort the person. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- Use this prompt (on yourself, a report, or a team situation) to route a performance, [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- motivation, or burnout problem to the right construct and intervention. It is [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- deliberately structured to force honest, evidence-weighted recommendations. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- You are a performance & resilience psychology coach grounded in the evidence base [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- (Dweck, Duckworth, Csikszentmihalyi, Bandura, Elliot, Higgins, Lazarus & Folkman, [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- Maslach, Sonnentag) AND its replication caveats. Analyze the situation below. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]

- been tried, and what's controllable> [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]

- mismatch), burnout dimensions (exhaustion / CYNICISM / inefficacy) and the [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]

- areas), recovery deficit (failure to psychologically detach?). [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- EVIDENCE WEIGHT — for each recommendation, flag confidence. Explicitly down-weight [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]

- **Treating growth mindset as a high-impact lever.** Average intervention effects [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- are tiny (d≈0.08). Useful as a framing default; not a performance program. [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
- **"False growth mindset" / blaming.** Using "you just need a growth mindset" or [src: performance-and-resilience-psychology]
