- > Hub reference under `ai-agent-engineering` (hub-and-spoke). Owns the LLM **training-infrastructure** layer: how you split a model + optimizer + activations across many GPUs to TRAIN it. Loaded on demand when the hub routing row matches. Local copy: `~/.claude/skills/ai-agent-engineering/references/distributed-training.md`. [src: distributed-training]
- Training a modern LLM does not fit on one GPU. A 70B model in BF16 is 140 GB of weights alone; add Adam optimizer states (≈12 bytes/param → 840 GB), gradients (another 140 GB), and activations, and you are far past any single accelerator's 80–192 GB. **Distributed training is the discipline of splitting the four things that consume GPU memory — parameters, gradients, optimizer states, and activations — across tens to tens of thousands of GPUs, while keeping the math identical to single-device training and keeping the expensive accelerators busy.** [src: distributed-training]
- **The one mental model that unlocks everything:** every parallelism strategy is a different answer to "what do we split, and what must we therefore communicate?" [src: distributed-training]
- **Data parallel** — split the *batch*; replicate the model; communicate *gradients* (all-reduce). [src: distributed-training]
- **Sharded data parallel (FSDP / ZeRO)** — split the *model states* too; communicate *parameters* (all-gather) on demand + *gradients* (reduce-scatter). [src: distributed-training]
- **Tensor parallel** — split *layers / matmuls*; communicate *activations* every layer (high bandwidth → keep inside one NVLink node). [src: distributed-training]
- **Pipeline parallel** — split *layers into stages*; communicate *activations* at stage boundaries (point-to-point); introduces the *bubble*. [src: distributed-training]
- **Sequence / context parallel** — split the *sequence dimension*; communicate *attention* partials (unlocks long context). [src: distributed-training]
- **Expert parallel** — split *MoE experts*; communicate *tokens* (all-to-all). [src: distributed-training]
- **Data parallelism & DDP** — replicate model, all-reduce gradients; PyTorch DDP gradient bucketing (~25 MB) + backward/comm overlap; scales throughput not model size (the reason FSDP/ZeRO exist); ring all-reduce moves `2·(N-1)/N·|params|`. [src: distributed-training]
- **ZeRO** — partition training states across the DP group: Stage 1 (optimizer states, ~4×), Stage 2 (+gradients, ~8×), Stage 3 (+parameters, linear in DP degree, ~1.5× comm). ZeRO-Offload (CPU RAM), ZeRO-Infinity (CPU+NVMe) for capacity. ZeRO-3 ≈ FSDP. [src: distributed-training]
- **FSDP & FSDP2** — PyTorch-native ZeRO-3. FSDP1 FlatParameter (deprecated) → FSDP2 per-parameter DTensor (`fully_shard`): communication-free sharded state dicts, mixed dtypes (FP8) in one model, partial freezing → LoRA composes. HSDP (`HYBRID_SHARD`) shards within node, replicates across nodes. [src: distributed-training]
- **Tensor parallelism** — Megatron column/row matmul split; two all-reduces of full activation per block per direction → kept inside one NVLink node (TP ≤ 8). **Sequence parallelism** shards the inter-matmul norm/dropout regions along the sequence dim (paired with TP). [src: distributed-training]
- **Pipeline parallelism** — contiguous layer stages, P2P at boundaries; the **bubble** (idle fill/drain). GPipe bubble ≈ `(P-1)/m`; 1F1B caps in-flight activations; interleaved 1F1B (virtual stages) shrinks bubble by `v`; Seq1F1B / zero-bubble / DualPipe (DeepSeek-V3) push further. [src: distributed-training]
- **Context / sequence parallelism** — shard the sequence across GPUs for 100K–1M+ tokens. Ring Attention (rotate K/V, overlap P2P) and DeepSpeed-Ulysses (all-to-all, head-subset attention); USP combines both (2D). Cuts attention memory up to ~87.5%. [src: distributed-training]
- **3D / ND parallelism** — compose TP × PP × CP × EP × DP. Placement heuristic: **TP innermost (NVLink), then CP, then PP across nodes, then DP/FSDP outermost.** `micro_batch × grad_accum × DP = global batch`; `TP×PP×CP×EP×DP = total GPUs`. Llama 8B = FSDP2; 405B = TP×PP×CP×DP; DeepSeek-V3 = EP×PP×DP. [src: distributed-training]
- **Mixed precision** — FP16 (narrow range → needs dynamic loss scaling); **BF16** (FP32-range, no loss scaling, the pretraining default); **FP8** (Hopper/Blackwell + Transformer Engine, ~42% memory / ~64% faster vs BF16, needs per-tensor `DelayedScaling`). Keep master weights + moments in FP32. [src: distributed-training]
- **Gradient checkpointing & accumulation** — recompute activations in backward (trade compute for memory, ~`O(√L)`); **selective** recompute (Megatron) checkpoints only memory-heavy/cheap-to-recompute ops. Gradient accumulation decouples global batch from memory; wrap non-final micro-steps in `no_sync()` under DDP/FSDP. [src: distributed-training]
- **Collective communication** — NCCL AllReduce (=reduce-scatter+all-gather), ReduceScatter (FSDP grad), AllGather (FSDP param / TP+SP), All-to-All (MoE / Ulysses), P2P (pipeline). Ring (bandwidth-optimal, large msgs) vs Tree (`O(log N)` latency, small msgs). **Compute-comm overlap** (prefetch, async-TP) is the main scaling lever. [src: distributed-training]
- **Training stability** — loss spikes/NaN; LR **warmup** (ramp from ~0); **z-loss** (push softmax normalizer → 0, curb logit growth) + QK-LayerNorm; scaled init (`1/√(2·n_layers)`); global-norm grad clip + ZClip; checkpoint-often + roll-back-and-curate recovery. [src: distributed-training]
- **Distributed checkpointing, frameworks & MFU** — PyTorch DCP saves per-rank shards (DTensor), async writes (5–15× less overhead), resharding on load. Frameworks: torchtitan, Megatron-Core, DeepSpeed, NeMo, MosaicML Composer. **MFU** = observed ÷ peak FLOPs (`6N` per token); 35–55% healthy (PaLM 46%, MegaScale 55.2% @ 12,288 GPUs); HFU counts recompute, so HFU > MFU when checkpointing. [src: distributed-training]
- **Inference / serving parallelism** (vLLM/SGLang TP+PP, paged KV, continuous batching) → `llm-inference-serving`. Serving has no backward pass, no optimizer state, no gradient sync. [src: distributed-training]
- **GPU kernels / CUDA / Triton / roofline / occupancy** → GPU-kernels reference (pointer only). Kernels are a black box here. [src: distributed-training]
- **LoRA / QLoRA single-GPU fine-tuning depth** → `llm-fine-tuning-peft`. FSDP2+LoRA composition is noted here; LoRA mechanics live there. [src: distributed-training]
- **Attention / MoE-routing / norm architecture** → `transformer-architecture`. EP *placement* is a parallelism axis here; MoE routing math is there. [src: distributed-training]
- **Pretraining objectives, data mixtures, scaling laws (Chinchilla)** → pretraining reference (pointer only). This reference covers the *systems* of training. [src: distributed-training]
- 35+ primary docs and papers (2024–2026): PyTorch FSDP2 `fully_shard` docs + FSDP VLDB'23 paper + FSDP blog; DeepSpeed ZeRO tutorial/docs + ZeRO-Infinity; Megatron-LM SC'21 + Megatron-Core parallelism guide + pipeline schedules; torchtitan repo + ICLR 2025 paper; NVIDIA NeMo DeepSeek-V3 recipe + activation-recomputation docs; NCCL collectives docs + deep-dive blog; PyTorch Distributed Checkpoint blog + async recipe; arXiv 2205.05198 (activation recompute), 2405.07719 (unified SP), 2406.03488 (Seq1F1B), 2310.18313 (FP8-LM), 2411.08719 (FP8 vs BF16), 2410.19313 (COAT), 2410.16682 (stability), 2504.02507 (ZClip), 2402.15627 (MegaScale), NeurIPS 2024 (LR warmup). Full citation list in the local reference file. [src: distributed-training]

- person reliably *is* across time and situations, applied to one practical job: [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- tailoring how you communicate with and manage different stakeholders, **grounded [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- in evidence and avoiding the MBTI trap**. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- The single most important thing this skill enforces: **use the dimensional [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- trait model (Big Five / HEXACO), not type systems (MBTI, DISC, Enneagram, True [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- Colors).** The Big Five is the consensus, replicated, predictive model of [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- personality structure in academic psychology. Type systems are popular, fun, and [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- psychometrically weak. This distinction is the whole game. Get it wrong and [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- every downstream inference is built on sand. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]

- > deterministic; *descriptive*, not diagnostic. You **observe behavior**, you do [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > not "diagnose" or label a person. Never use trait inferences for hiring, [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > promotion, or selection decisions about a real individual — that is both [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > scientifically unjustified and, in many jurisdictions, illegal. The legitimate [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > use here is adapting *your own* communication to *observed* behavior, holding [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > every inference loosely. See **Ethics & Limits** at the end — it is not optional. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- -- [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- Five broad, continuous dimensions describe the bulk of stable personality [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- variance. The acronym is **OCEAN** ([Wikipedia: Big Five](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Five_personality_traits)): [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Each dimension is a continuum, normally distributed.** Most people are in the [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- middle on any given trait; extreme scorers are rare. There are **no "types"**, [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- which matters enormously for the MBTI critique below. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Facets matter.** Each of the five domains splits into six narrower **facets** [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- (30 total in the NEO-PI-R; Costa & McCrae 1992, 240 items) ([Big Five history](https://yukaichou.com/behavioral-analysis/big-five-personality-ocean-traits-costa-mccrae/)). [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- Two people can share an Extraversion score but differ sharply on facets: one [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- high on Assertiveness/low on Warmth (a driving, task-focused executive), another [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- high on Warmth/low on Assertiveness (a relational, non-pushy collaborator). When [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- a domain score doesn't fit what you observe, **drop to the facet level.** [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- The Big Five was *discovered*, not invented, via the **lexical hypothesis**: the [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- idea that the most important individual differences become encoded as single [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- words in natural language ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Five_personality_traits)). [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Allport & Odbert (1936)** extracted ~4,504 personality-descriptive adjectives from the dictionary. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Raymond Cattell (1940s)** reduced the list and built the 16PF. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Tupes & Christal (1961)** analyzing Air Force ratings, repeatedly recovered **five** factors (Surgency, Agreeableness, Dependability, Emotional Stability, Culture). [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Norman (1963)** replicated it, relabeling Surgency → Extraversion and Dependability → Conscientiousness. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Lewis Goldberg (1981)** coined the term **"Big Five"** and built the marker adjective scales. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Costa & McCrae** operationalized the questionnaire tradition (NEO-PI → **NEO-PI-R, 1992**), giving the **Five-Factor Model (FFM)** and the OCEAN naming. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > **"Big Five" vs "Five-Factor Model" — a real but minor distinction.** "Big Five" [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > comes from the *lexical/adjective* tradition (Goldberg); "FFM" from the [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > *questionnaire* tradition (Costa & McCrae). They converge on the same five [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > dimensions; use them interchangeably in practice, but know they have slightly [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > different historical roots and factor-recovery methods. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- Personality predicts real outcomes — modestly but reliably. **Conscientiousness** [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- is the standout: it predicts job performance across virtually every occupation [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- (Barrick & Mount 1991 meta-analysis; corrected ρ ≈ .19–.22) and academic [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- performance even more strongly (≈ .28) ([job-performance meta-analysis](https://jobcannon.io/blog/big-five-ocean-job-performance)). [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- Low Conscientiousness shows strong links to common mental disorders across a [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- meta-analysis of n > 75,000. Other traits predict job-specifically: Extraversion [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- for sales, Agreeableness for customer service. **Calibrate expectations** — these [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- are correlations in the .1–.3 range, not destiny. Personality nudges the odds; it [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- does not dictate the outcome of any single interaction. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Cross-cultural replication is good but imperfect.** The five replicate across [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- dozens of cultures, with documented exceptions: Openness is weakly supported in [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- some Asian samples, and some languages don't yield a clean single Agreeableness [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- factor ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Five_personality_traits)). [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- -- [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Ashton & Lee** (early 2000s) re-ran lexical studies across many languages and [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- recovered **six** factors, not five. HEXACO = **H**onesty-Humility, [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **E**motionality, e**X**traversion, **A**greeableness, **C**onscientiousness, [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **O**penness ([SAPA Project](https://www.sapa-project.org/blogs/HEXACOmodel.html); [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- The new factor, **Honesty-Humility (H)**, captures sincerity, fairness, [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- greed-avoidance, and modesty. Broadly, it is *the degree to which someone refrains [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- from exploiting others when they could get away with it.* [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > **HEXACO is not "Big Five + 1."** It is a *re-partitioning*. Big Five [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > Agreeableness and Neuroticism are carved up differently: the [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > "even-tempered / not-angry" content that sits inside Big Five Agreeableness [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > moves into HEXACO **Agreeableness**, the anxiety/sentimentality content moves [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > into HEXACO **Emotionality**, and a distinct honesty/fairness/non-exploitation [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > dimension separates out as **H** ([HEXACO vs Big Five](https://high5test.com/big-five-vs-hexaco/)). [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > HEXACO Extraversion, Conscientiousness, and Openness map closely to their Big [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > Five counterparts; the other three differ substantially. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Why H matters for stakeholder work:** Honesty-Humility is the best [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- single-factor predictor of exploitative, manipulative, and unethical behavior, [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- better than anything in the Big Five, because the Big Five *lacks* a dedicated [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- factor for it. Low H is the trait core of the **Dark Triad** (§6). When a [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- counterpart's behavior is making your antennae twitch — over-claiming, subtle [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- manipulation, win-at-any-cost framing — you are usually detecting **low H**, and [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- the Big Five alone would have under-weighted it. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- -- [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- Traits are stable, **but not frozen**, and stability has two distinct meanings [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- people constantly conflate: [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Rank-order stability** — does a person keep their *position relative to [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- peers*? (If you're more conscientious than 80% of your cohort at 25, are you [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- still at ~25?) Roberts & DelVecchio's (2000) meta-analysis of 152 studies [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- (3,217 correlations) found rank-order consistency rising with age: **.31 in [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- childhood → .54 in college → .64 at age 30 → a plateau around .74 at ages [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- 50–70** ([Roberts & DelVecchio 2000, PDF](http://jenni.uchicago.edu/Spencer_Conference/Representative%20Papers/Roberts%20&%20DelVecchio,%202000.pdf)). [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- This is the **cumulative-continuity principle**: personality gets more stable [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- as we age, but is never perfectly fixed. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Mean-level change** — does the *average level* of a trait shift across the [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- population with age? Roberts, Walton & Viechtbauer's (2006) meta-analysis of [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- 92 samples found it does, in a systematic direction now called the **maturity [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- principle**: people rise in **Conscientiousness, Emotional Stability, and [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- social dominance (a facet of Extraversion)** through young adulthood (20–40); [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- Openness and social vitality rise in adolescence then decline in old age [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- ([Roberts, Walton & Viechtbauer 2006, PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16435954/)). [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- People, on average, become more dependable and even-keeled as they age. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **State vs trait.** A *trait* is your characteristic average; a *state* is how you [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- are *right now*. A low-Extraversion person can be lively at their own product's [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- launch; a stable person can be visibly anxious during an outage. **Fleeson's [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- Whole Trait Theory** resolves this elegantly: a trait is a **density distribution [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- of states** — each person varies enormously moment-to-moment, but the *shape* of [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- their distribution (their average and spread) is highly stable over time [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- ([Whole Trait Theory, PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4472377/)). [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- Practically: **judge a stakeholder on their distribution (the pattern over many [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- interactions), never on one data point.** A single tense meeting tells you about a [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Heritability.** Twin studies put Big Five heritability at **~40–60%** (Jang et [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- al. 1996: N 41%, E 53%, O 61%, A 41%, C 44%) ([heritability twin study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5068715/)). [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- The non-genetic variance is almost entirely the **non-shared environment** (unique [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- individual experiences), *not* shared family upbringing. Siblings raised together [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- are barely more alike in personality than strangers, once genes are accounted for. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- -- [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- In 1968, **Walter Mischel's** *Personality and Assessment* nearly ended trait [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- psychology. He pointed out that correlations between a trait measure and behavior [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- in any *single* situation rarely exceed **r ≈ .30** — the so-called **"personality [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- coefficient"** — and argued broad cross-situational traits were therefore [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- "untenable" ([Wikipedia: person-situation debate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Person%E2%80%93situation_debate)). [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- This is the **consistency paradox**: we *intuit* that people are consistent, yet [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- single-situation correlations look weak. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- The resolution — now the settled consensus — is **interactionism**: [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Epstein's aggregation principle (1979):** the .30 ceiling is an artifact of [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- measuring *one* behavior on *one* occasion. **Aggregate** across many [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- occasions and trait–behavior correlations climb to .60–.80. Traits predict [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- *patterns over time*, not isolated acts. (This is the §3 "judge the [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- distribution" point in another guise.) [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Situational strength:** **strong situations** (a funeral, a tightly scripted [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- compliance review, a hard contractual deadline) suppress trait expression — [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- everyone behaves similarly. **Weak situations** (an open-ended discovery call, [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- an unstructured workshop) let traits show. *Personality is most visible, and [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- most useful to read, in weak, ambiguous situations.* [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Mischel & Shoda's CAPS (1995):** the **Cognitive-Affective Personality [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- System** reframes consistency as stable **if…then behavioral signatures** — "if [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- challenged in front of peers, *then* this person digs in; if challenged [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- privately, *then* they concede." The signature itself is the stable trait, even [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- though raw behavior varies by situation. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > **The operator takeaway:** "behavior = trait × situation." Don't over-attribute [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > a stakeholder's behavior to their personality when the *situation* (a tense [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > escalation, an exec in the room, a renewal deadline) is doing the work. This is [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > the **Fundamental Attribution Error** applied to reading people — see [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > behavioral-decision-making and persuasion-and-influence-psychology for the [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > attribution machinery; this skill owns the trait side of the equation. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- -- [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- The **Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI)** sorts people into 16 types across four [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- binary dichotomies (E/I, S/N, T/F, J/P), loosely derived from Jung. It is the [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- world's most popular personality instrument and **the textbook example of what [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- not to trust.** Four fatal flaws: [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Low test-retest reliability.** Studies find **39–76% of people get a [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- *different* four-letter type** on retaking the instrument within weeks [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- ([MBTI validity, Truity](https://www.truity.com/blog/myers-briggs/mbti-validity-challenges)). [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- A measure that reclassifies up to half its takers in five weeks cannot be [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- measuring something stable. (The publisher reports higher scale-level [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- coefficients; the *type-flipping* problem is the damning one, and it follows [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- directly from flaw 2.) [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **False dichotomies — the bimodality failure.** MBTI forces a binary [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- (you're "an Extravert" or "an Introvert"), but every trait is **continuous and [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- normally distributed**, with most people clustered in the middle. Someone at [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- 49/100 is labeled the *opposite type* from someone at 51/100, despite being [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- functionally identical. Cutting a normal distribution at the mean manufactures [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- two "types" that don't exist in nature ([Truity](https://www.truity.com/blog/myers-briggs/mbti-validity-challenges)). [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Weak predictive validity.** MBTI type does not reliably predict job [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- performance or life outcomes. Even the Myers-Briggs Company states it is [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **inappropriate and potentially illegal to use for hiring or selection.** [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **The Forer / Barnum effect.** Type descriptions feel uncannily accurate [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- because they are **vague enough to fit almost anyone.** In Forer's 1949 [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- classic, students rated a "personalized" profile 4.3/5 for accuracy — it was [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- 13 generic statements (many lifted from an astrology book) handed identically [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- to everyone ([Barnum effect, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnum_effect)). [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- "That's *so* me!" is **not** evidence of validity — it is the failure mode to [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **DISC, the Enneagram, True Colors, Insights Discovery** share flaws 1, 2, and 4: [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- they impose discrete types/colors on continuous dimensions and lean on [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- Barnum-style feedback. They can be fine as low-stakes team-bonding [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- *vocabulary*, but never treat their categories as real, stable, or predictive. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **What to do instead:** when someone asks "what's my type / their type," redirect [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- to **dimensional thinking.** Don't ask "are they an introvert?"; ask "where do [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- they sit on Extraversion, and on which facets?" The honest, useful, evidence-based [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- model is the Big Five (or HEXACO). When in doubt, use the validated, free [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **IPIP-NEO** items rather than a branded type test. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- -- [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Paulhus & Williams (2002)** grouped three *subclinical*, socially aversive but [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- non-pathological traits that share a callous-manipulative core: the **Dark Triad** [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- ([Paulhus & Williams 2002, PDF](http://www.sakkyndig.com/psykologi/artvit/paulhus2002.pdf)). [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Narcissism** — grandiosity, entitlement, need for admiration, thin skin to criticism. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Machiavellianism** — strategic manipulation, cynicism, ends-justify-means, low warmth. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Psychopathy** (subclinical) — callousness, impulsivity, low empathy, low anxiety, thrill-seeking. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- A fourth, **sadism** (taking pleasure in others' distress), extends it to the [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Dark Tetrad**. Measured with the **Dirty Dozen** and the **Short Dark Triad [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- (SD3)** (Jones & Paulhus 2014). Research debates whether the three are distinct or [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- share a single **"dark core" / D-factor** (Moshagen et al. 2018) — an underlying [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- tendency to maximize one's own utility at others' expense, with whatever [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- justifying beliefs ([Dark Triad, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_triad)). [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **In trait terms,** the Dark Triad maps cleanly onto **very low Honesty-Humility** [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- (§2) and **low Agreeableness** — which is exactly why HEXACO detects this profile [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- that the Big Five tends to under-weight. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > **Use this defensively, not diagnostically.** You are **not** qualified to [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > diagnose anyone, and you must not call a stakeholder a "narcissist" or [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > "psychopath" — that's defamatory and clinically meaningless from the outside. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > The *only* legitimate use: notice a **pattern** of manipulative, exploitative, [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > or callous behavior over time, then **adjust your own posture** — get [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > agreements in writing, reduce reliance on goodwill, document, set firm [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > boundaries, and avoid being manipulated by flattery or false urgency. For the [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > influence/manipulation tactics themselves and how to counter them, defer to [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > persuasion-and-influence-psychology and trust-and-psychological-safety. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- -- [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- The legitimate workflow: **observe behavior → infer a trait *tendency* (held [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- loosely) → adapt your own communication → update on new evidence.** You are [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- tuning *your* style, not boxing *them* in. Below, each trait is paired with what [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- to do when a stakeholder's *observed behavior* sits high or low. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **High C** (organized, deadline-driven, detail-oriented): lead with structure — [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- agendas, clear next steps with owners and dates, thorough written follow-ups. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- Be punctual and reliable; sloppiness erodes trust fast. They reward precision. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Low C** (flexible, big-picture, spontaneous): don't bury them in process. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- Lead with the headline and the "why," keep documents short, offer to own the [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- logistics so they don't have to track details. Over-structuring reads as friction. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **High E** (talkative, energetic, thinks out loud): give space for live [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- discussion, calls over email, brainstorming, social warmth. They process [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- externally — silence can read as disengagement. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Low E** (reserved, reflective, drained by big meetings): send materials in [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- advance so they can process alone; favor written or small-group channels; don't [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- mistake quiet for disagreement or low engagement. Give them time to respond. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **High O** (curious, idea-driven, likes novelty): engage the vision, the [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- roadmap, the novel approach; analogies and possibilities land well. Rigid [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- "this is the only way" framing bores them. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Low O** (practical, prefers the proven, concrete): lead with track record, [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- references, standards, and the conventional path. Frame change as low-risk and [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- incremental; "new and experimental" reads to them as *risk*, not appeal. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **High A** (cooperative, harmony-seeking, conflict-averse): they may agree [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- outwardly while privately hesitant — **explicitly invite dissent and surface [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- concerns**, or you'll miss real objections. Don't mistake politeness for buy-in. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Low A** (skeptical, blunt, hard-bargaining, competitive): expect challenge; [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- don't take pushback personally. Bring evidence, expect negotiation, be direct. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- They often *respect* a counterpart who holds their ground over one who folds. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **High N / reactive** (anxious, stress-sensitive, especially in escalations): [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- over-communicate, reduce uncertainty, give frequent reassuring status, avoid [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- surprises, name and validate the concern. Calm, predictable cadence lowers the [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Low N / stable** (calm under pressure): you can be more direct and [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- matter-of-fact about risks and bad news without extensive cushioning. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > Most stakeholders are mid-range on most traits. The high-payoff moves are at the [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > *clear extremes* you can actually observe — a visibly detail-obsessed buyer, a [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > visibly skeptical security lead, an anxious champion during an outage. **Match [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- > their distribution, don't manufacture a type.** [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- This skill owns *who the stakeholder is* (trait structure). For *what you say and [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- how to move them*, defer: [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Persuasion / influence mechanism and tactics** → persuasion-and-influence-psychology [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Building trust, rapport, psychological safety** → trust-and-psychological-safety [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Framing decisions, anchoring, debiasing, attribution errors** → behavioral-decision-making [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Driving product adoption via motivation/habit** → behavior-change-psychology [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Reading emotion/mood and emotional intelligence in the moment** → emotion-and-affect-psychology [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Motivation/grit/mindset/resilience as performance traits** → performance-and-resilience-psychology [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- -- [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Probabilistic, not deterministic.** A trait shifts the odds of a behavior; it [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- never guarantees one. Treat every inference as a hypothesis to update, not a verdict. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Observe behavior; do not diagnose.** You read *what people do*, over many [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- interactions. You never assign clinical labels ("narcissist," "neurotic case") [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- — you are not a clinician, and from the outside such labels are meaningless and harmful. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **No selection misuse.** Never use trait inferences to make hiring, promotion, [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- firing, or selection decisions about a real person. It is scientifically [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- unsupported (effect sizes too small for individual decisions) and frequently illegal. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **It's about adapting *you*, not boxing *them*.** The whole legitimate purpose is [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- tuning your own communication to be more effective and respectful — not building [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- a dossier or a manipulation map. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Beware your own biases.** Confirmation bias makes you "see" the trait you [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- expect; the Barnum effect makes vague reads feel precise; the Fundamental [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- Attribution Error makes you blame personality when the *situation* is the cause [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- (§4). Hold every read loosely and seek disconfirming evidence. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Privacy and consent.** Don't administer personality tests to customers, don't [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- record speculative "personality profiles" of individuals in CRM/notes, and don't [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- share trait speculation about a named person as if it were fact. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- **Clinical scope is off-limits.** Personality disorders, mental-health diagnosis, [src: personality-and-individual-differences]
- and therapy are out of scope — refer to a licensed professional. [src: personality-and-individual-differences]

- -> [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- Pretraining is the expensive part: take a randomly-initialized transformer and run **next-token prediction over trillions of tokens** until it becomes a *base model* — a raw next-token predictor with broad world knowledge but no instruction-following. Everything in `llm-alignment-post-training.md`, `llm-fine-tuning-peft.md`, and `reasoning-models.md` *starts from this checkpoint*. This reference answers the four questions that define a pretraining run: **what objective**, **what data**, **how big / how long** (scaling laws + the compute budget), and **how do I know it worked** (base-model eval). [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **The one identity that anchors everything here — `C ≈ 6ND`.** A dense transformer with `N` parameters trained on `D` tokens costs about `6ND` floating-point operations. That single equation is the budget line: every scaling-law result (Kaplan, Chinchilla, data-constrained, inference-aware) is an answer to *"given a fixed `C`, how do I split it between `N` and `D` to minimize loss?"* Hold `C = 6ND` and the whole field becomes a constrained-optimization story. The 2022 → 2026 arc is the field realizing that the loss-optimal split (`N : D`) and the *deployment*-optimal split are different things — and that data, not parameters, is now the binding constraint. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **This reference** = pretraining a base model: objectives (causal LM, MLM, prefix-LM, FIM, UL2), the data pipeline (curation, dedup, filtering, mixtures, tokenizer *training*, decontamination), scaling laws (Kaplan, Chinchilla, data-constrained, inference-aware), the `6ND` compute budget, emergent abilities + the mirage debate, LR schedules at scale (cosine, WSD), data curriculum/annealing, continual/domain-adaptive pretraining, and base-model evaluation. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **The transformer architecture** — attention, MoE, RoPE, RMSNorm, and the tokenizer *algorithms* (BPE/byte-level-BPE/SentencePiece/tiktoken) → `transformer-architecture.md`. The line: **what to train and on how much data is here; how the block is wired is there.** Tokenizer *training* (picking vocab size, the training corpus, measuring fertility) is here because it is a *data* decision; the tokenization *algorithm* is architecture. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Distributed-training infrastructure** — FSDP, DeepSpeed ZeRO, tensor/pipeline/expert parallelism, gradient checkpointing, MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) — is the *engineering* of spending `6ND` FLOPs across a cluster → `distributed-training.md`. We own the *budget arithmetic* (`6ND`, token/param ratios) and *what to train*; that sibling owns *how the GPUs cooperate*. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Post-training** (SFT, RLHF/PPO, DPO family, Constitutional AI, RLAIF) → `llm-alignment-post-training.md`. **Pretraining produces the base model; alignment turns it into an assistant.** The handoff is the base checkpoint. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Fine-tuning / PEFT** (LoRA/QLoRA, domain SFT, instruction tuning) → `llm-fine-tuning-peft.md`. *Continual pretraining* (more self-supervised next-token prediction on a new corpus, §10) lives here; *supervised* adaptation lives there. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]

Note: "inference-time scaling laws" *there* (spend more compute at answer time) are a different axis from the *pretraining* scaling laws *here* (spend more compute at train time) — §6 distinguishes them. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Benchmark-harness mechanics** (how MMLU/HELM/LLM-as-Judge are scored) → `da-7-machine-learning`. Base-eval *strategy* and *decontamination* are here. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- -- [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- The objective decides what the base model is good at before any post-training. Five matter (2024–2026). [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Causal / autoregressive LM (CLM, next-token prediction).** Predict token `t` from tokens `<t` with a causal mask; cross-entropy loss on every position. **This is the dominant objective** for every modern generative LLM (GPT, Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, Gemma). It is *self-supervised* (the label is the next token), trivially parallel over positions during training (teacher forcing), and produces a model that can generate. Loss is reported as **cross-entropy in nats**; `perplexity = exp(loss)`. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Masked LM (MLM).** Corrupt ~15% of tokens with `[MASK]` and predict them from *bidirectional* context (BERT). Produces strong *encoders* for understanding/embedding tasks but **cannot generate** left-to-right. Largely displaced for *generative* pretraining; still relevant for embedding models and retrievers. Boundary: embedding-model use lives in `rag-architecture.md` / `ai-datastores.md`. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Prefix-LM.** A hybrid: bidirectional attention over a *prefix*, causal attention over the *continuation* (one sequence, a "non-causal prefix"). Used by the UL2 S-denoiser and by some encoder-decoder setups; lets the model fully attend to the conditioning context while still generating. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Fill-in-the-Middle (FIM).** *(Bavarian et al. 2022, arXiv:2207.14255.)* Teach a **causal** model to infill by a pure **data transformation** — no architecture change. Split a document into (prefix, middle, suffix) and reorder into `Prefix–Suffix–Middle` (PSM) or `Suffix–Prefix–Middle` (SPM) with sentinel tokens (`<PRE>`, `<SUF>`, `<MID>`), then train next-token as usual. The model learns to generate the middle given both ends. Key results: it is **"free"** — the **FIM rate** (fraction of docs transformed, 50–90% is fine) buys infilling with *no loss* on left-to-right ability (the "FIM-for-free property"); **context-level** FIM (transform after chunking to context length) beats **document-level**; **joint PSM+SPM** training transfers positively. This is why code models (StarCoder, Codestral, DeepSeek-Coder) and modern general models support `<FIM>` infilling and IDE tab-completion. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **UL2 — Mixture-of-Denoisers (MoD).** *(Tay et al. 2022, arXiv:2205.05131.)* Unify objectives by training on a **mixture of span-corruption "denoisers"**: **R-denoiser** (regular T5-style short spans, ~15% / span≈3), **S-denoiser** (sequential = prefix-LM, corrupt a contiguous tail → forces generation), **X-denoiser** ("extreme": long spans and/or high corruption rate, the hardest). A **paradigm token** (`[R]`/`[S]`/`[X]`) prepended at train time lets you **mode-switch** the model toward the most suitable behavior downstream. UL2 showed one objective family can be competitive across both understanding and generation; the *conceptual* legacy (mix easy + hard self-supervised tasks; the prefix-LM-as-S-denoiser framing) outlived the specific recipe. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Decision in practice (2026):** generative LLMs use **CLM**, often **+ FIM** (especially for code), trained on **packed** sequences (multiple documents concatenated to a fixed context length with separators — packing keeps GPUs full; whether to mask cross-document attention is a live choice). MLM is for encoders. UL2/prefix-LM matter mostly historically and for encoder-decoder niches. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- -- [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- Data quality, not architecture, is the dominant lever on a fixed compute budget. The canonical open reference is **FineWeb** *(Penedo et al. 2024, arXiv:2406.17557)*: 15T GPT-2 tokens from **96 Common Crawl snapshots (2013–early 2024)**, with every design choice **ablated** (each stage shown to monotonically improve downstream benchmarks). The pipeline stages: [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Text extraction.** Pull main content from raw HTML/WARC (FineWeb uses `trafilatura`); good extraction beats Common Crawl's own WET text. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Language ID + filtering.** Classifier-based language detection; keep target languages above a confidence threshold. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Quality / heuristic filtering.** Rule-based filters (line-length, symbol-to-word ratio, fraction of duplicate lines, bad-words, repetition) à la MassiveText/Gopher and C4. Removes boilerplate, SEO spam, gibberish. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Deduplication (the single highest-impact stage).** **Near-dedup** with **MinHash + LSH** on n-gram shingles (FineWeb: per-snapshot MinHash dedup). Removes the long tail of near-identical pages. Counter-intuitive finding from FineWeb: **global cross-snapshot dedup can hurt** — it disproportionately removes *recently* re-crawled, often higher-quality content and over-upweights ancient low-quality pages; **per-snapshot** dedup worked better. Dedup also matters because *repeated* data interacts with epoch-counting (§5). [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Model-based quality classification.** Train a lightweight classifier to score "is this high-quality / educational?" **FineWeb-Edu** is a **1.3T-token** subset filtered by an **educational-quality classifier** (a linear/small head trained on **Llama-3-70B annotations** of educational value). Models pretrained on FineWeb-Edu show **large gains on knowledge/reasoning benchmarks (MMLU, ARC)** versus unfiltered FineWeb — strong evidence that *aggressive* quality filtering pays off, even at the cost of raw token count. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Synthetic data** is now a standard ingredient (rephrased web, textbook-style generation à la Phi, distilled chains). Risk: **model collapse** (degenerate distributions when training on too much un-curated model output across generations) — mitigate by anchoring to real data and limiting synthetic share. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- > Cross-ref: the *tokenization algorithm* (how text becomes IDs) is in `transformer-architecture.md` §10. *Tokenizer training* (choosing the vocab, the corpus to train it on) is §4 here because it is a data decision. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- -- [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- Once you have cleaned sources (web, code, books, arXiv, Wikipedia, math, multilingual), you must choose **mixture proportions** (domain weights). This is a first-class hyperparameter — getting it wrong wastes compute. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **The Pile / fixed heuristic weights** — early models hand-set weights (upweight Wikipedia/books, cap web). Simple, manual, suboptimal. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **DoReMi (Domain Reweighting with Minimax Optimization)** *(Xie et al. 2023, arXiv:2305.10429, NeurIPS 2023).* Train a **small proxy model** (e.g. 280M) with **Group DRO** to find domain weights that minimize *worst-case* excess loss versus a reference model — *without* knowing downstream tasks. Reuse those weights to train a model **30× larger** (8B). Result: **+6.5% average few-shot accuracy** over The-Pile default weights and the baseline accuracy reached in **2.6× fewer steps**; perplexity improved across *all* domains even ones it downweighted. The principle — **use a cheap proxy run to set mixture weights for the expensive run** — generalizes (online/learned mixtures, RegMix, data-mixing laws). [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Mixture scaling laws.** A live 2024–2026 thread: the *optimal* mixture **shifts with scale and with token budget** (and with repetition — §5). Web fraction that is optimal at 1T tokens is not optimal at 15T; code/math get upweighted as you train longer. Treat the mixture as scale-dependent, not fixed. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Practical pattern:** set a base mixture (heuristic or DoReMi-derived), then **upsample high-value domains (code, math, curated/synthetic) during the annealing phase** (§9) rather than uniformly — the decay phase is where domain emphasis is cheapest and most effective (the MiniCPM/Yi-Lightning recipe). [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- -- [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Tokenizer training (a data decision; algorithm → `transformer-architecture.md`).** Before pretraining you *train* the tokenizer on a sample of the corpus and freeze it; vocab choice then constrains everything. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Vocabulary size.** A bigger vocab → fewer tokens per document (lower *fertility*, cheaper sequences, more text per context) but a larger embedding/unembedding matrix and rarer-token undertraining. **~128K is the modern sweet spot** for multilingual models (Llama 3 moved to 128K byte-level BPE; many 2024–2026 models sit at 128K–256K). There are even *scaling laws for vocabulary* — larger models warrant larger vocabularies. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Training corpus & multilinguality.** Train the tokenizer on a mixture *representative of the pretraining mix* — an English-heavy tokenizer gives terrible fertility on other languages (more tokens per word → more expensive, worse). Returns on tokenizer *training data* diminish (1GB → 900GB studied; gains saturate early). [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Fertility & parity** (tokens-per-word; cross-language token-count ratio) are the standard intrinsic metrics — but **caveat: they are not always predictive of downstream quality**, so validate the tokenizer on a small pretraining proxy, not on fertility alone. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Eval-set decontamination (do not skip — it is how you avoid lying to yourself).** Web-scale corpora contain copies of benchmark test sets; if MMLU/GSM8K leak into pretraining, your eval is inflated. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **n-gram overlap** is the standard filter: scan the corpus and remove (or flag) documents overlapping a test item. **GPT-3 used 13-gram overlap; GPT-4 used a 50-character span.** Maximum-matching-subsequence (MMS) is a variant. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **n-gram matching is fragile.** *(Yang et al. 2023, "Rethinking Benchmark and Contamination… with Rephrased Samples", arXiv:2311.04850.)* **Paraphrased or translated test items slip past string matching** and still contaminate — a model can memorize a rephrased benchmark and ace it while passing decontamination. Mitigations: embedding/semantic-similarity decontamination, **contamination-resistant / freshly-collected benchmarks** (post-cutoff data, e.g. LiveCodeBench, private held-out sets), and **canary strings**. Always **decontaminate, then prefer time-gated evals** for the headline number. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- -- [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- Scaling laws predict loss as a smooth power law in model size `N`, data `D`, and compute `C`, and tell you how to *split* a fixed `C` between `N` and `D`. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Kaplan et al. 2020 (arXiv:2001.08361).** First clean power laws: test loss falls predictably as a power of `N`, `D`, and `C`. Their compute-optimal prescription **favored very large models** — given more compute, grow `N` fast and `D` slowly (`N_opt ∝ C^0.73`). This drove the GPT-3 / Gopher / MT-NLG "scale parameters" era. *(It turned out to be skewed — see the reconciliation below.)* [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Chinchilla — Hoffmann et al. 2022 (arXiv:2203.15556).** Refit the laws carefully and found Kaplan-era models were **massively under-trained on data**. Compute-optimal scaling is **balanced**: `N_opt ∝ C^0.50` and `D_opt ∝ C^0.50` — i.e. **scale `N` and `D` equally** (every doubling of params should double tokens). The famous heuristic: **≈ 20 tokens per parameter** is compute-optimal. They trained **Chinchilla (70B on 1.4T tokens)** and it **beat Gopher (280B)** using the *same* compute — a smaller, longer-trained model won. Loss is fit as `L(N, D) = E + A/N^α + B/D^β`. **This reset the field**: GPT-3 (175B/300B tokens) was ~10× too few tokens. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Reconciling the two** *(Porian et al. 2024, "Resolving Discrepancies…", arXiv:2406.12907, NeurIPS 2024; also Besiroglu et al. replication arXiv:2404.10102).* Kaplan's `0.73` vs Chinchilla's `0.50` is **mostly an artifact**, explained by three things: (1) **Kaplan counted only non-embedding parameters** (Chinchilla counts *all* params); (2) Kaplan **under-counted FLOPs** by ignoring the last-layer/embedding cost at the small scales they used; (3) **warmup duration and optimizer tuning** were not adapted per model size. Fix all three and the curves **collapse onto Chinchilla's 0.50**. **Lesson: count *total* params and *all* FLOPs, tune warmup/LR per scale — then scaling fits agree.** Epoch AI's replication broadly **confirmed** Chinchilla's estimates while noting its confidence intervals were too tight. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- -- [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- Chinchilla is **training-compute-optimal**, not **deployment-optimal**, and assumes **unlimited unique data**. Both assumptions break in practice. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Inference-aware / "over-training"** *(Sardana & Frankle 2023, "Beyond Chinchilla-Optimal", arXiv:2401.00448).* If you will *serve* the model to many users, total cost = training **+** inference, and inference cost scales with `N`. So you should deliberately train a **smaller model on far more tokens than Chinchilla** (`>20` tok/param) — paying more at train time to get a cheaper, faster model forever. **"Over-training" is a misnomer**: it is only "over" relative to the *training*-optimal point. **Llama 3 8B is the canonical example: ~15T tokens ≈ 1,875 tokens/param** (vs Chinchilla's ~200B / 20× for an 8B), and loss kept improving log-linearly far past the Chinchilla point. **Mid-2026 reality: almost every shipped model is deliberately over-trained.** (Related 2026 thread: *test-time scaling can make over-training even more attractive* — a small over-trained model + inference-time compute beats a compute-optimal bigger one at equal serving cost; reasoning-time scaling itself → `reasoning-models.md`.) [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Data-constrained scaling** *(Muennighoff et al. 2023, arXiv:2305.16264, JMLR 2025).* When unique tokens run out (we are approaching the limit of high-quality web text), you **repeat data (multiple epochs)**. Findings, now load-bearing: **repeating up to ~4 epochs is almost as good as fresh data** (negligible loss penalty); gains continue but **decay out to ~16 epochs** (a repeated token retains ~63% of a fresh token's value around there) and approach **zero by ~40 epochs**. Their scaling law adds a **decay term for repeated tokens and excess parameters**, and prescribes **smaller models trained for more epochs** when data-bound (the opposite of naively applying Chinchilla to repeated data). **Allocating excess compute to more *params* also decays** once data is fixed. Practical rule: **≤4 epochs is safe; 4–16 is diminishing; >16 wastes compute** — and budget extra FLOPs into *quality filtering / synthetic data* rather than blind repetition. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Synthesis of the three regimes:** Chinchilla (balanced) is the textbook answer when **data and inference are free**. **Inference-aware** (over-train a small model) is the answer when you will **serve at scale**. **Data-constrained** (repeat ≤4 epochs, prefer smaller models) is the answer when you are **out of unique tokens**. Mid-2026 frontier runs live at the **intersection**: small-ish models, heavily over-trained, on **heavily-filtered + synthetic** data, a few epochs at most. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- -- [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- The arithmetic that turns all of the above into a project plan. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **`C ≈ 6ND` FLOPs** to train a dense model of `N` non-embedding params on `D` tokens. The **6** decomposes as **2 (forward) + 4 (backward)** FLOPs per parameter per token: a matmul is one multiply + one add = **2 FLOPs** per weight (so `2N` forward per token), and the backward pass does **~2× the forward matmuls** (gradient w.r.t. inputs *and* weights) = `4N`. Multiply by `D` tokens → `6ND`. **Inference is `≈ 2ND`** (forward only). *(Standard derivation; see the Chinchilla appendix and "Transformer FLOPs", Casson 2023.)* [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **What it is good for.** Back-of-envelope budgeting: pick any two of `{C, N, D}` and solve the third. *E.g.* an 8B model on 15T tokens ≈ `6 × 8e9 × 15e12 ≈ 7.2e23` FLOPs. Combine with hardware throughput and **MFU** (Model FLOPs Utilization, the fraction of peak FLOP/s actually used — typically 30–55%) to get wall-clock and GPU-hours: `time ≈ C / (peak_FLOP/s × MFU × num_GPUs)`. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Caveats.** `6ND` **ignores attention FLOPs** (the `O(seq²·d)` term), which is fine while `seq` ≪ `d_model · layers / seq` but bites at long context. For **MoE**, use **active** params, not total, in `N` (only the routed experts fire per token). The *engineering* of hitting high MFU across a cluster — FSDP/ZeRO sharding, parallelism, gradient checkpointing — is the **distributed-training sibling's** job; `6ND` is the *budget*, MFU-engineering is *spending it efficiently*. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- -- [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **The claim (Wei et al. 2022, arXiv:2206.07682).** Some abilities are **emergent**: absent in small models, present in large ones, appearing **sharply and unpredictably** at a scale threshold (e.g. multi-step arithmetic, word unscrambling, certain BIG-Bench tasks) — not extrapolable from smaller models' performance. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **The rebuttal — "Are Emergent Abilities a Mirage?" (Schaeffer et al. 2023, arXiv:2304.15004, NeurIPS 2023 Outstanding Paper).** The sharp jumps are often an **artifact of the metric**, not the model. **Discontinuous/nonlinear metrics** (exact-match, multiple-choice accuracy — all-or-nothing) manufacture apparent step-changes; switch to **continuous/smooth metrics** (token edit distance, Brier score, log-likelihood per token) on the *same* models and the curve becomes **smooth and predictable**. They reproduce "emergence" by choosing metrics and erase it by changing them, and predict where it will/won't appear on the GPT-3 family + BIG-Bench. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **The 2024–2026 synthesis (what to actually believe).** Both are partly right and the distinction is practical: **per-token loss scales smoothly and predictably** (this is what scaling laws fit and what you should plan against); **downstream task *scores* under harsh metrics can still jump**, because crossing a usefulness threshold (the model finally gets the *whole* multi-step answer right) is real for the user even if the underlying capability grew smoothly. **Operationally: forecast with smooth metrics (loss, log-prob), but don't be surprised when a hard pass/fail benchmark lurches.** This is also why a base model can look unimpressive on accuracy yet be a fine pretraining checkpoint (§11). [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- -- [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- The LR schedule is a pretraining-specific lever with a surprising amount of pull on the final loss. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Warmup.** Linearly ramp LR from 0 over a few hundred–few thousand steps (and tune warmup *per scale* — it was one of the Kaplan/Chinchilla reconciliation factors, §5). Skipping warmup destabilizes early training. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Cosine decay (the long-time default).** After warmup, decay LR following a cosine curve to a small floor **over the whole planned token budget**. Works well but has a **coupling problem**: the schedule is **tied to a pre-committed total step count**, so you cannot cleanly extend a run or take a good intermediate checkpoint (any checkpoint before the end is at a high, un-decayed LR and underperforms). [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD)** *(Hu et al. 2024, MiniCPM, arXiv:2404.06395).* Three phases: **(1) warmup → (2) a long *stable* phase at a constant high LR → (3) a short, sharp *decay/cooldown*** (often the last ~10–20%). Properties that made it a 2024–2026 favorite: **(a)** during the stable phase loss sits *higher* than cosine, but the **decay phase drops loss sharply**, often *below* cosine's final loss; **(b)** it is **compute-agnostic** — the stable phase can run indefinitely and you decay *whenever* you decide to stop, so you can **reuse the stable checkpoint** for runs of different lengths; **(c)** the decay phase is the natural place to **anneal in high-quality / domain / synthetic data** (see below). MiniCPM used WSD to run efficient **data-model scaling studies** and reported a much higher **compute-optimal data/model ratio of ~192×** (vs Chinchilla's 20×) — reinforcing the over-training story (§6). A "river-valley loss landscape" account (arXiv:2410.05192) explains *why* the sharp decay helps. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **The annealing/decay phase = where the data curriculum lives (§3, §10).** The dominant 2024–2026 pattern is **two-phase pretraining**: phase 1 trains on broad web data at high/stable LR; the **annealing phase** (the WSD decay, or the cosine tail) **upsamples high-quality, instruct-like, synthetic, math/code, and rare-language data** while LR drops. Yi-Lightning's three-stage recipe (diversity → upsample-high-quality-during-anneal → fast-decay-on-best-data) is representative. Caveat (arXiv:2511.18903): **aggressive LR decay can *waste* your best data** (the model is barely learning by the time you feed it) — a *moderate* decay, or **decoupling the curriculum from LR via model averaging / a constant LR + checkpoint-averaging**, can do better. Continual-pretraining "infinite LR" schedules (arXiv:2503.02844) push the WSD idea further for never-ending training. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- -- [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- You rarely retrain from scratch to add a domain, a language, or fresher data. **Continual pretraining (CPT)** = keep doing **next-token prediction** on a new corpus starting from an existing base checkpoint. (Distinct from fine-tuning/PEFT, which uses *supervised* data → `llm-fine-tuning-peft.md`.) [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **The naive failure.** Resuming on new data at the *decayed* end-of-run LR barely adapts; resuming at the *original high* LR causes a **loss spike** and **catastrophic forgetting** of the old distribution. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **The recipe that works** *(Gupta et al. 2023, arXiv:2308.04014; Ibrahim et al. 2024, "Simple and Scalable Strategies to Continually Pre-train LLMs", arXiv:2403.08763).* Three ingredients: **(1) LR re-warming** (ramp the LR back up at the start of the new phase) **+ (2) LR re-decaying** (cosine/WSD decay over the new phase) **+ (3) replay** (mix in a **modest fraction of the *old* data**, e.g. 1–5%, to prevent forgetting). This combination **matches the performance of fully retraining from scratch on the union of old+new data, at a fraction of the compute** — the headline result that made CPT standard practice for domain/language/freshness updates. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Domain-adaptive pretraining (DAPT).** The same machinery aimed at a *domain* (code, biomed, legal, finance): continue pretraining on in-domain text before any task fine-tuning. Strong when the domain is far from the base distribution; combine with replay to avoid losing general ability. Related: GQA "uptraining" (converting MHA→GQA with ~5% of pretraining compute) is a continual-pretraining-style cheap conversion — see `transformer-architecture.md`. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- > Where CPT meets the schedule: re-warm/re-decay is literally a fresh WSD/cosine cycle (§9); the new domain data is often introduced in the **decay/annealing phase** for the same reason §9 gives. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- -- [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- A base model is a **raw next-token predictor** — it does **not follow instructions** or chat. Evaluating it requires different methods than an aligned model, and confusing the two is a common error. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Intrinsic: perplexity / loss on held-out text.** The most reliable signal *during* pretraining — smooth, comparable across checkpoints, no prompt-format confound. Compare on a **fixed, decontaminated** held-out set (and remember §8: per-token loss is the smooth metric to forecast against). Caveat: perplexity is tokenizer-dependent, so only compare same-tokenizer models. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Few-shot / in-context, log-likelihood scored.** Base models are evaluated **few-shot** (provide k exemplars in the prompt) because they have no zero-shot instruction-following. The standard tool is **EleutherAI's `lm-evaluation-harness`** (`lm-eval`), which scores any causal LM on the *same* inputs via **log-likelihood of answer choices** (multiple-choice: pick the highest-likelihood option — MMLU, ARC, HellaSwag) and **constrained generation** (GSM8K, etc.). Using the harness is how results stay comparable across papers. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Base vs instruct is not "instruct is always better."** A 2025–2026 finding (arXiv:2601.13244, arXiv:2501.08716): **base models often *beat* their instruction-tuned versions in pure few-shot/zero-shot settings** (drops of ~30%+ reported for some instruct models zero-shot) — instruct tuning trades raw few-shot capability for prompt-following and safety. So **evaluate the base model on its own terms (few-shot, log-likelihood)**; do not judge it by chat behavior or zero-shot instruction tasks. This also informs the pretraining→alignment handoff: a strong base on few-shot benchmarks is the right thing to hand to `llm-alignment-post-training.md`. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Always decontaminate first (§4).** A headline benchmark number is meaningless without decontamination, and even then prefer **time-gated / contamination-resistant** benchmarks for the number you trust. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- -- [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Applying Chinchilla 20× literally when you will serve the model.** You will ship a too-big, too-expensive model. Over-train a smaller one (§6). [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Applying Chinchilla to *repeated* data.** Chinchilla assumes unique tokens; with repetition use the data-constrained law and **train a smaller model for more epochs** (§6). And don't blow past ~4–16 epochs expecting fresh-token value. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Skipping decontamination, or trusting n-gram decontamination alone.** Inflated evals; paraphrased leakage passes string matching (§4). Decontaminate *and* time-gate. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Counting non-embedding params / under-counting FLOPs in scaling fits.** This is *exactly* the Kaplan artifact (§5) — count total params and all FLOPs, tune warmup per scale. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Committing a cosine schedule to a fixed length, then wanting to extend or branch.** Use WSD so you can decay whenever and reuse the stable checkpoint (§9). [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Decaying LR too aggressively over your best (annealing-phase) data.** The model is barely learning by then — use moderate decay or decouple curriculum from LR (§9). [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Continual pretraining without re-warming or without replay.** Either fails to adapt (no re-warm) or catastrophically forgets (no replay) (§10). [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Judging a base model by chat / zero-shot instruction behavior.** Base models predict tokens; evaluate few-shot with log-likelihood (§11). [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Uniform data mixture / hand-set weights at scale.** Use a proxy-model-derived mixture (DoReMi) and upsample high-value domains in the anneal (§3, §9). [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Treating `6ND` as exact at long context or for MoE.** Add attention FLOPs at long seq; use *active* params for MoE (§7). [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Loss plateaus / model under-performs at a given compute.** Check the `N:D` split against the regime (§5–6): likely under-trained on tokens (raise `D`, the Chinchilla lesson) or wrong mixture (§3). Verify warmup and LR floor (§9). [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Eval scores look too good.** Suspect contamination (§4) — re-run decontamination (semantic, not just n-gram) and re-test on a post-cutoff benchmark. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **A capability "suddenly appears" (or fails to).** Likely a metric artifact (§8) — re-measure with a smooth metric (log-prob, edit distance) to see the true trend before concluding. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Adding a domain wrecked general ability.** Forgetting from CPT without replay (§10) — add 1–5% old-data replay and re-warm/re-decay. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Multilingual / code tokenization is wasteful (high fertility).** Tokenizer trained on too-English a corpus or too-small a vocab (§4) — retrain on a representative mix, consider 128K+ vocab. [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
- **Intermediate checkpoint is much worse than final under cosine.** Expected — the LR has not decayed yet; this is the WSD motivation (§9). [src: llm-pretraining-scaling-laws]
