- <!-- Provenance: reference under the `ai-agent-engineering` hub. Created 2026-05-31 by authoring directly from the saved deep-research report `research-rlhf-rl-training-infrastructure-2026-05-31.md` (22 primary sources, High confidence) — HybridFlow/veRL (arXiv:2409.19256) + verl docs, OpenRLHF (arXiv:2405.11143), the vLLM "Accelerating RLHF" blog, NeMo-Aligner (arXiv:2405.01481) + NeMo-RL docs, AReaL (arXiv:2505.24298) + AReaL-Hex (arXiv:2511.00796), TRL vLLM-integration / async-GRPO docs, vLLM weight-transfer / NCCL / sleep-mode RFC docs, ROLL (arXiv:2506.06122), slime (LMSYS blog + DeepWiki), the HuggingFace "Keep the Tokens Flowing" 16-library survey, OPPO (arXiv:2509.25762), APRIL (arXiv:2509.18521), ServiceNow-AI "Correctness Before Corrections", the LLM-Data-Co / Swift train-inference-mismatch writeups, TRL issues #4159/#5312, CodeScaler/RLVR sources, and SkyPilot "RL Doesn't Work on Slurm". Scope: the RL *SYSTEMS / INFRASTRUCTURE* layer — the actor–rollout–learner loop and the engineering that makes post-training RL run. NOT the RL ALGORITHMS — PPO/GRPO/DPO math (→ `llm-alignment-post-training`, `reasoning-models`, `agentic-rl`); NOT generic supervised distributed training — FSDP/ZeRO/parallelism internals (→ `distributed-training`); NOT production serving of one model (→ `llm-inference-serving`; the rollout-engine-IN-THE-LOOP is here). --> [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- The **systems stack** that post-training reinforcement learning runs on — RLHF, RLVR, reasoning-RL, and agentic-RL all share it. This is deliberately *not* the RL **algorithm** (PPO/GRPO/DPO — those live in the alignment, reasoning, and agentic-RL references) and *not* generic supervised distributed training (FSDP/ZeRO for pretraining — that lives in `distributed-training`). It is the third thing those two references keep pointing at: **how do you actually run an RL post-training job — generate samples, score them, update weights, and not leave half your GPUs idle.** [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- The one-sentence framing: **a supervised step is one engine doing forward+backward; an RL step is three engines — a generator, a scorer, and a trainer — passed through an experience buffer, and the whole discipline exists because the generator dominates wall-clock (60–90%+ of step time) and the naive synchronous schedule leaves the trainer's GPUs idle while the generator works.** Every design decision below — colocate vs disaggregated placement, the per-step weight resync, async/off-policy systems, the train/inference logprob mismatch — follows from attacking that bottleneck. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **This reference** = the RL *systems* layer: the actor–rollout–learner architecture and experience buffer; GPU **placement** (colocate/hybrid vs disaggregated); the rollout/generation **bottleneck** and the inference-engine-in-the-loop; the train→infer **weight resync** (NCCL/IPC/resharding); **async/off-policy** systems and staleness; the **framework landscape** (veRL, OpenRLHF, NeMo-RL/-Aligner, TRL, slime, AReaL, ROLL, SkyRL, TorchForge); **reward-model serving** + verifier/code-sandbox infra; **scaling** the trainer (FSDP/Megatron) alongside the rollout engine (TP); the RL **utilization "bubble"** and overlap fixes; and RL-systems **failure modes** (logprob mismatch, weight-sync desync, reward over-optimization). [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **The RL *algorithm* itself** — what PPO's clipped objective is, how GRPO drops the value model, what a KL penalty does, the DPO loss — is **out of scope**. RLHF/PPO and the DPO family live in `llm-alignment-post-training`; GRPO/RLVR and the DeepSeek-R1 recipe live in `reasoning-models`; multi-turn/agentic RL (POMDP, trajectory credit assignment, observation masking, the Echo Trap) lives in `agentic-rl`. **The line: those references answer "what loss am I optimizing and why"; this one answers "what does the cluster look like that runs it."** GRPO here is just "a critic-free algorithm that drops the value engine," not a derivation. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Generic supervised distributed training** — FSDP/FSDP2, ZeRO stages, tensor/pipeline/expert parallelism, NCCL collective *mechanics*, distributed checkpointing — lives in `distributed-training`. This reference *uses* those (the trainer is FSDP or Megatron) but only owns the **RL-specific** twist: the train-vs-infer **layout mismatch** and the **resharding** it forces (§8). Supervised training has no rollout engine, no weight resync, no logprob mismatch — those are the RL-only surfaces here. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Serving one model in production** — vLLM/SGLang config, PagedAttention, continuous batching, speculative decoding, autoscaling — lives in `llm-inference-serving`. RL post-training **embeds** that exact inference engine *inside the training loop* as the rollout generator (§3). **The line: serving an endpoint for users = there; running vLLM/SGLang as the in-loop trajectory generator with per-step weight sync = here.** [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- -- [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- An RL post-training step decomposes into **three logically distinct engines** that exchange data through an **experience buffer**: [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Generation / rollout engine** — autoregressively samples responses (for agents, multi-turn trajectories) from the *current* policy. Implemented with an **inference** engine (vLLM/SGLang), *not* the training framework, because sampling is the throughput-critical step (§3). [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Reward / verifier module** — scores responses: a learned reward model (RM), a rule-based verifier, or a code-execution sandbox (RLVR). A served system component in its own right (§7). [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Policy training engine (learner)** — runs forward + backward + optimizer to update the policy weights (FSDP or Megatron). [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Model count by algorithm.** Classic **PPO-RLHF runs four models**: actor (policy, trained), critic/value (trained), reward model (frozen), and reference model (frozen, for the per-token KL penalty). **Critic-free algorithms (GRPO and kin) drop the value model**, collapsing the systems problem to actor + reward/verifier + reference — one fewer trained network to place, shard, and resync. *(Why GRPO can drop the critic is an algorithm question → `reasoning-models`; that it removes an engine from the topology is the systems consequence that matters here.)* [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **The per-step dataflow:** prompts → **(rollout)** responses → **(reward)** scores + (recomputed) logprobs → advantages → **(learner)** gradients → updated weights → **resync to the rollout engine** (§4). That last arrow — pushing fresh weights back into the generator every step — is the loop-closing step that supervised training does not have, and it is the source of much of the difficulty. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **The design space (HF survey).** The "Keep the Tokens Flowing" survey frames the whole field as **seven orthogonal axes**; the three that matter most are: (1) the **orchestration / concurrency primitive** (Ray actors, asyncio, pub/sub, HTTP); (2) the **rollout buffer design** (how rollouts flow from inference into training); (3) the **weight-synchronisation protocol**. The remaining axes are sync/async degree, GPU placement, batching, and reward integration. **A framework is essentially a point in that 7-axis space** — knowing the axes lets you read any framework's design in minutes. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- -- [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- The central placement decision: do the trainer and the rollout engine **share one GPU pool** (colocate / hybrid) or run on **separate pools** (disaggregated)? This single choice cascades into the weight-resync mechanism (§4), the utilization profile (§9), and how easy async is (§5). [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Colocate / hybrid engine** — training and generation **time-share the same GPUs**. The trainer offloads/sleeps while the rollout engine generates; then weights are **resharded in place** and the trainer wakes. veRL's **3D-HybridEngine** is the canonical implementation: it reshards the actor between a **training layout** (e.g. FSDP DP=2 / TP=8) and an **inference layout** (e.g. vLLM DP=16 / TP=4) **on the same GPUs with zero memory redundancy** and reduced communication, by *transforming the single model in place* rather than holding a second copy. **Pro:** highest GPU utilization, no idle pool. **Con:** memory contention on the shared GPUs (trainer optimizer state + inference KV-cache fighting for HBM). [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Disaggregated / separated** — inference runs continuously on one pool, the optimizer on another. **OpenRLHF pioneered this with Ray Placement Groups**, scheduling vLLM engines, actor, critic, reference, and reward each on their own GPUs (with the Adam optimizer optionally on CPU). **Pro:** isolation, independent scaling of the two pools, easier async. **Con:** in a *synchronous* schedule a pool sits idle waiting on the other, and weights must cross the **network** every step. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **The programming model underneath (HybridFlow's core contribution).** RL dataflow is awkward because it is *nested and multi-model*. HybridFlow combines a **single-controller** paradigm (one process expresses the whole dataflow graph — flexible, easy to express PPO/GRPO/DAPO) with a **multi-controller** paradigm (each device runs its own SPMD program — efficient, low dispatch overhead). Pure single-controller has high control-dispatch overhead at scale; pure multi-controller is too rigid for nested RL dataflow. The hybrid reports **1.53×–20.57× throughput** over baselines like DeepSpeed-Chat and NeMo-Aligner. **ROLL and slime** use the same single-controller + parallel-worker abstraction. **Practical read:** colocate when GPUs are scarce and you want max utilization; disaggregate when you want isolation, independent scaling, or fully-async (§5). [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- -- [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- The dominant systems fact: **RL post-training is rollout-dominated** — generation accounts for **60–90%+ (up to >90% worst case) of total RL step time**. The reason is structural: **autoregressive per-token decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound** and runs at **<40% GPU utilization** in the actor, whereas the scoring and training stages are compute-intensive. *(The prefill-compute-bound vs decode-memory-bound mechanics are a kernel-layer fact → `llm-gpu-kernels`; the consequence — generation is the expensive stage — is what drives every choice here.)* [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- This is **why frameworks plug a dedicated inference engine — vLLM or SGLang — into the loop as the rollout generator** (with PagedAttention, continuous batching, often FP8/INT8 inference for extra speed), rather than generating with the training framework's slow eval path. veRL supports both vLLM and SGLang as interchangeable rollout backends; slime is SGLang-native; OpenRLHF/TRL default to vLLM. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **The long-tail straggler problem compounds it.** Response lengths are **long-tailed**, so a few very long generations stall an *entire synchronous batch* — most GPUs sit idle waiting on the slowest few sequences. This one fact — "rollout is the bottleneck *and* the tail makes it worse" — is the direct motivation for async (§5), overlap (§9), and partial-rollout recycling (APRIL). If you remember one thing about RL systems: **optimize the rollout, or nothing else matters.** [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- -- [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- After **every** policy update, the learner's new weights must be pushed into the rollout engine *before* the next generation — otherwise the generator samples from a **stale** policy. This per-step **weight resync** is a notable systems cost and a frequent source of subtle bugs. It is the step supervised training simply does not have. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Transfer mechanisms:** [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **NCCL broadcast (default)** — trainer rank 0 broadcasts weights to all inference workers in a process group. vLLM's `update_weights` API supports `packed=True` (pack many tensors into large contiguous buffers to cut the number of NCCL ops), with **double/triple buffering and dedicated CUDA streams** to overlap packing, broadcast, and unpacking. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **CUDA IPC** (`backend="ipc"`) — for **colocated** transfers on the same node, hand off via shared GPU memory instead of a network collective. Faster, but only works when trainer and inference share a node/GPU. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Checkpoint reload / Hub bucket** — the slow fallback. TRL's **"delta weight sync"** ships only the *changed* weights through a Hub bucket for trillion-parameter models where a full broadcast is impractical. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **The hard part — resharding across mismatched layouts.** The trainer is sharded one way (FSDP, or Megatron TP×PP×…), the inference engine another (vLLM/SGLang TP). veRL handles this with **sharding managers** — `FSDPVllmShardingManager` and `MegatronVLLMShardingManager` — that reshard actor→rollout weights on the fly; the **in-place zero-copy reshard is only possible in colocated engine mode** (disaggregated must send weights over the network). slime exposes the same split as two APIs: **`UpdateWeightFromTensor`** (colocated) vs **`UpdateWeightFromDistributed`** (multi-node). Dedicated tools now target this step specifically — Ant's **AWEX** advertises "second-level parameter updates from training to inference." vLLM has added native weight-syncing APIs plus **sleep/wake** support so a colocated engine can free KV-cache memory during training and reload weights on wake. **Practical read:** weight resync is where colocate (cheap IPC/in-place) and disaggregate (network broadcast) diverge most sharply, and it is a top source of "the reward curve is stuck" bugs (§10b). [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- -- [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- Synchronous RL forces the trainer to **wait for the slowest rollout** (the §3 tail). **Asynchronous RL decouples generation from training**: rollout workers generate *continuously* while training workers update whenever a batch is ready. The price is **off-policy staleness** — rollouts were produced by an *older* policy than the one being updated, which biases the gradient and must be corrected (and is the systemic root of the logprob mismatch in §10a). [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **AReaL (Ant Research) — the canonical fully-async system.** Four pieces: **streaming generation** (each rollout worker generates without waiting), **interruptible rollout workers**, **dynamic batching** for variable-length outputs, and a **parallel reward service**. It uses a **staleness-controlled, modified PPO** that tolerates samples up to **8 steps old with no performance drop**, plus a data-filtering step to cap staleness — achieving **~2× speedup** at equal final accuracy. **AReaL-Hex** extends this to **heterogeneous GPUs** (mixed device types in one async job). [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **The sync↔async spectrum** (not a binary): [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Fully synchronous** — trainer waits for the whole batch; on-policy, simplest, slowest (the tail kills it). [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **One-step-off / periodic asynchrony** — overlap generation of step *k+1* with training of step *k* (at most one step stale); near on-policy accuracy with async throughput. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Partial rollouts (APRIL)** — over-provision requests, **stop when the target count is reached, and recycle the unfinished long generations into the next step** — taming the tail *without* full async decoupling: **+22.5% avg (up to 44%) rollout throughput**. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Fully async (AReaL-style)** — continuous decoupling; max throughput, most staleness to manage. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- NeMo-RL and OpenRLHF both ship async rollouts + replay buffers for off-policy training; TRL ships an async GRPO trainer. **Practical read:** more async = more throughput *and* more staleness you must correct (TIS, §10a). Most teams start one-step-off or partial-rollout (APRIL) before reaching for fully-async. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- -- [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **The survey's meta-finding:** **16 libraries built independently converged on the same fix** — *get off the synchronous pipeline*, because idle training GPUs are the throughput killer. They differ mainly along the seven axes (§1). **Choosing:** **veRL** if you want the most-used, hybrid, in-place-reshard default; **OpenRLHF** for Ray-disaggregated; **NeMo-RL/-Aligner** at the largest (Megatron + TRT-LLM) scale; **TRL** for accessibility and a gentle on-ramp; **slime** for SGLang-native; **AReaL** for fully-async SOTA throughput; **ROLL** for an agentic-friendly rollout scheduler. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- -- [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- The **reward source is itself a served system component**, not a passive function — and at scale it can become the bottleneck. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Learned RM serving** — a frozen reward model served as a **separate inference service** (its own GPUs in disaggregated setups, or colocated). AReaL runs a **parallel reward service** so scoring overlaps generation rather than blocking it. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Rule-based verifiers** — math-answer checking, regex/format checks (the RLVR case); cheap, deterministic, no GPU. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Code-execution sandboxes** — for code RL, generated programs are **executed against unit tests inside a sandbox** to produce a binary verifiable reward. **Execution-based RLVR outperforms learned reward models** on code, which suffer instability and reward hacking. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Systems concerns specific to the reward stage:** the **verifier/reward can become the bottleneck** (unit-test test-time-scaling shows a clear performance–latency trade-off); at scale teams serve **hundreds of environments as autoscaled managed sandbox endpoints** (e.g. serving 330+ RL environments backed by 4.5M+ tasks on autoscaled sandbox compute). Sandbox **isolation and throughput** — parallel execution, timeouts for non-terminating generated code, side-effect containment — are first-order infra problems. The standing warning: **verifier quality is the real bottleneck** — weak auto-generated reward functions teach the wrong behavior at scale (the systems face of reward over-optimization, §10c). *(The agentic-RL flavor of environments — Gymnasium `step`/`reset`, OpenEnv, SkyRL-Gym — is detailed in `agentic-rl` §3; here the focus is serving the reward/verifier as throughput-critical infra alongside the rollout engine.)* [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- -- [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- Training and inference **want different parallelism layouts** — and that mismatch is the *root reason* the weight resync (§4) is non-trivial. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Trainer** must shard parameters + gradients + **optimizer states** + activations → FSDP (ZeRO-3-style) or Megatron 3D/5D (TP×PP×DP, +CP/EP). Optimized for **backward-pass memory** (the optimizer state is ~2× the params for Adam). [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Rollout engine** has **no backward, no optimizer, no gradient state** → it wants a layout that minimizes *inference* latency: typically a **smaller tensor-parallel degree with high data-parallel replication** for batch throughput (e.g. train TP=8 vs infer TP=4). [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **When colocated**, the two layouts **contend for the same GPU memory**, so frameworks **offload the trainer (params/optimizer to CPU or freed) while generating**, then reload — exactly what vLLM **sleep/wake** and the **3D-HybridEngine reshard** enable. **When disaggregated**, the two pools size independently but pay the **network resync**. veRL exposes both FSDP and Megatron trainer backends behind a common worker API and maps them to vLLM/SGLang rollout workers. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Boundary:** the *supervised* parallelism mechanics — ZeRO stages, FSDP2 internals, TP/PP/CP/EP composition, NCCL collective tuning — belong to **`distributed-training`**. This reference owns only the **RL-specific train-vs-infer layout mismatch** and the resharding it forces. If the question is "how do I shard a 405B model to train it," that is `distributed-training`; if it is "why do my trainer and generator disagree on layout and how do I bridge them every step," it is here. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- -- [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- In a naive synchronous PPO/GRPO loop the stages run **sequentially with hard dependencies**: the reward model cannot score until the actor finishes generating; the learner cannot step until rewards are in. This creates an **idle "bubble"** — generation GPUs busy while training GPUs idle, then vice-versa — *amplified* by the long-tailed response lengths (§3). Measured actor-generation utilization is **<40%**. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- Mitigations (distinct from full async, §5 — these keep an on-policy-ish schedule): [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Intra-step overlap** — stream upstream outputs in chunks so the downstream model begins **prefill while the upstream is still decoding** (OPPO). [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Inter-step overlap** — overcommit prompts and **defer long generations to the next step** to cut tail latency (OPPO). [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Partial-rollout recycling** — APRIL's over-provision-and-recycle. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Reported gains:** OPPO **1.8×–2.8×** end-to-end with **1.4×–2.1×** higher GPU utilization, no convergence loss; APRIL **+20–44%** rollout throughput. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Orchestration corollary:** classic Slurm **gang-scheduling** fits supervised training but *not* the heterogeneous, long-lived, multi-role RL job (a generator pool + a trainer pool + a reward service, each a different shape, all long-running). This is why these systems lean on **Ray** rather than Slurm — "RL doesn't work on Slurm" is a recurring lesson, because RL is not one homogeneous gang of identical workers. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- -- [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- The rollout engine (vLLM/SGLang) and the trainer (FSDP/Megatron) produce **different log-probabilities for the same sequence under the same weights**, because they use **different kernels, precision, and batching paths**. This silently turns nominally **"on-policy" RL into off-policy RL** with nontrivial bias — the behavior policy (inference) differs from the proxy policy (training) even before any async staleness is added. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Corrections:** **token-level Truncated Importance Sampling (TIS)** downweights tokens with severe mismatch and is stable, outperforming no correction despite its bias; alternatives mask out off-policy tokens or use sequence-level IS. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **The famous gotcha:** with **temperature ≠ 1, vLLM does not apply temperature scaling to returned logprobs by default**, producing a huge *spurious* mismatch that breaks TIS. If TIS suddenly destabilizes training, check this first. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Correctness-before-corrections:** the vLLM V0→V1 work argues for **fixing correctness at the source** (batch-invariance, kernel alignment) so the mismatch *shrinks* before you reach for IS corrections — corrections paper over a gap that better kernels can close. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **MoE is worse:** for Mixture-of-Experts models the mismatch is larger (routing can differ between engines), and **no current open-source async library implements the "Keep Routing" fix** (replaying expert routing) — a correctness gap for DeepSeek-V3 / Mixtral-class RL. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- Stale or partially-synced weights leave the rollout engine generating from an **old policy**. Real-world example: vLLM weights silently **not synchronized when `vllm_enable_sleep_mode=True`** (the sleep/wake path skipped the update). **Symptoms look like a "stuck" or diverging reward curve** — easy to misdiagnose as an algorithm problem when it is a resync (§4) bug. When the reward curve is flat or wrong, **verify the generator actually received the latest weights** before touching hyperparameters. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- As RL scales, the policy **exploits flaws in the reward source** — reward keeps rising while true quality stalls or drops (Goodhart). **Execution-based code rewards are more robust** than learned RMs, which suffer instability and hacking. The **algorithmic** mitigations (KL penalty, RM ensembles, ODIN) live in the **alignment-algorithm** domain (`llm-alignment-post-training`); the **systems** responsibility here is **verifier quality, sandbox correctness, and reward-service monitoring** — i.e. making sure the thing the policy is gaming is actually correct and observable. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- -- [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Profile the rollout first.** Generation is 60–90%+ of the step; if you optimize anything else first you are tuning noise. Plug in vLLM/SGLang as the in-loop generator and measure its share before touching the trainer. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Pick placement by GPU scarcity vs isolation.** Scarce GPUs / want max utilization → **colocate** (veRL 3D-HybridEngine, vLLM sleep/wake, CUDA-IPC resync). Want isolation, independent scaling, or fully-async → **disaggregate** (OpenRLHF Ray placement groups, NCCL/network resync). [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Treat weight resync as a first-class step.** Decide the mechanism up front: **CUDA-IPC / in-place reshard** (colocated) vs **packed NCCL broadcast or delta-sync** (disaggregated/huge models). Use sharding managers to bridge the train↔infer layout mismatch. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Climb the async ladder, don't leap.** Start synchronous → **one-step-off** or **APRIL partial-rollout** (tames the tail cheaply) → **fully-async (AReaL)** only when you need the throughput and can manage ≤8-step staleness. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Run the reward as a parallel service.** Overlap scoring with generation (AReaL parallel reward service); sandbox code execution with isolation + timeouts; size it so the verifier doesn't become the new bottleneck. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Match trainer and rollout parallelism deliberately.** Trainer FSDP/Megatron for backward-memory; rollout smaller-TP + high-DP for inference throughput; offload/sleep the trainer during generation when colocated. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Instrument the logprob gap.** Log the per-token train-vs-infer logprob difference; apply **TIS** if it is nonzero; verify vLLM temperature-logprob handling before trusting TIS. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Generating rollouts with the training framework's eval path** instead of a real inference engine — you eat the full <40%-utilization decode cost with none of vLLM/SGLang's PagedAttention/continuous-batching wins. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Running a naive fully-synchronous loop at scale** and wondering why GPUs are half-idle — the §9 bubble + the §3 tail. Add overlap or async. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Ignoring the weight resync** — forgetting it, or letting sleep-mode skip it, leaves the generator on a stale policy and produces a "stuck reward" that looks like an algorithm bug (§10b). [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Assuming on-policy because the code says on-policy** — the train/infer logprob mismatch (§10a) makes it off-policy by construction; without TIS or correctness fixes the gradient is biased. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Trusting TIS with vLLM temperature ≠ 1 and default logprob settings** — the un-scaled logprobs create a spurious mismatch that breaks the correction. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Colocating without offload/sleep** — trainer optimizer state and inference KV-cache fight for HBM and you OOM; use 3D-HybridEngine reshard or vLLM sleep/wake. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Treating the reward model as a cheap function** — a learned RM is a served GPU workload that can bottleneck the loop and be reward-hacked; serve it in parallel and monitor it. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Confusing this with the RL algorithm or with serving** — if the question is "what is PPO/GRPO/DPO," that is the alignment/reasoning/agentic-RL references; if it is "how do I serve one model to users," that is `llm-inference-serving`. This is the *training-loop systems* layer. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **GPUs ~half-idle, throughput dominated by generation** → the synchronous bubble + long-tail stragglers. Add intra/inter-step overlap (OPPO), APRIL partial-rollout recycling, or move to async (§5/§9). [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Reward curve stuck / diverging despite a sane algorithm** → suspect a **weight-sync bug** (§10b): is the generator actually getting the latest weights? Check sleep-mode resync, sharding-manager reshard, the broadcast group. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Training unstable, "on-policy" RL behaving off-policy** → the **train/inference logprob mismatch** (§10a). Log the per-token gap; apply TIS; check vLLM temperature-logprob scaling; consider correctness fixes (kernel/batch-invariance) for MoE. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **OOM only when colocated** → trainer + inference KV-cache contending for HBM. Enable trainer offload / vLLM sleep-wake / 3D-HybridEngine in-place reshard, or disaggregate. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Reward rises but quality stalls/drops** → reward over-optimization (§10c). For code, prefer execution-based verifiers over learned RMs; audit verifier/sandbox correctness; monitor the reward service. (Algorithmic KL/ensemble mitigations → `llm-alignment-post-training`.) [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Weight resync is slow and dominates the step** → switch to packed/double-buffered NCCL broadcast, CUDA-IPC (colocated), or delta-weight sync (huge models); a dedicated tool like AWEX targets "second-level" updates. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **MoE RL is unstable where dense was fine** → the logprob mismatch is worse for MoE and the "Keep Routing" fix is not in OSS async libraries yet; expect a correctness gap. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **HybridFlow: A Flexible and Efficient RLHF Framework** (arXiv:2409.19256) + verl docs (HybridFlow programming guide, FSDP/Megatron/SGLang worker backends, FSDPVllmShardingManager issue #3232) — single+multi-controller hybrid, 3D-HybridEngine in-place reshard, sharding managers, 1.53–20.57×. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **OpenRLHF: Easy-to-use, Scalable, High-performance RLHF** (arXiv:2405.11143) + GitHub — Ray Placement Groups, disaggregated/separated placement, four-model PPO, Adam-on-CPU. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Accelerating RLHF with vLLM (OpenRLHF best practice)** — vLLM blog (blog.vllm.ai 2025-04-23) — vLLM as in-loop generator, the generation bottleneck. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **NeMo-Aligner: Scalable Toolkit for Efficient Model Alignment** (arXiv:2405.01481) + **NVIDIA-NeMo/RL** docs — Megatron 3D parallel + TensorRT-LLM generation, 1000-GPU scale, re-architected NeMo-RL async GRPO. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **AReaL: Large-Scale Asynchronous RL System** (arXiv:2505.24298) + **AReaL-Hex** (arXiv:2511.00796) — fully-async, streaming/interruptible rollout, ≤8-step staleness, parallel reward service, ~2×, heterogeneous GPUs. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **TRL** vLLM-integration + async-GRPO docs — colocate vs server mode, NCCL weight sync every `weight_sync_steps`, GRPOTrainer/PPOTrainer. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **vLLM weight-transfer / NCCL-engine docs** + native-weight-syncing RFC #31848 + sleep-mode RFC #15254 — `update_weights` packed/double-buffered, NCCL vs IPC, sleep/wake; **TRL delta-weight-sync** blog. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **ROLL: RL Optimization for Large-Scale Learning** (arXiv:2506.06122) + GitHub — single-controller + parallel worker, rollout scheduler with per-sample lifecycle, env/reward workers, 200B MoE. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **slime (THUDM/Z.ai)** GitHub + LMSYS blog + DeepWiki — SGLang-native, UpdateWeightFromTensor vs UpdateWeightFromDistributed, colocate/decoupled, SlimeRouter/StringRadixTrie. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Keep the Tokens Flowing: Lessons from 16 Open-Source RL Libraries** (HuggingFace blog) — the seven design axes, the universal idle-GPU finding, the MoE "Keep Routing" gap. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **OPPO: Accelerating PPO-based RLHF via Pipeline Overlap** (arXiv:2509.25762) — <40% generation GPU util, intra/inter-step overlap, 1.8–2.8×. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **APRIL: Active Partial Rollouts to Tame Long-tail Generation** (arXiv:2509.18521) — ~90% rollout time, over-provision+recycle, +20–44%. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **ServiceNow-AI: vLLM V0→V1, Correctness Before Corrections** (HF blog) + **Mismatch Praxis** (LLM Data Co.) + Swift train-inference-mismatch docs + **TRL issues #4159 (vLLM temp logprobs) / #5312 (sleep-mode weight sync)** — the logprob mismatch source, TIS token-vs-sequence, the temperature gotcha, concrete weight-sync bug. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Promptfoo RLVR**, **CodeScaler** (arXiv:2602.17684), **RL Environments Taxonomy** (leehanchung.github.io) — verifier/sandbox-as-bottleneck, execution rewards vs learned RM, verifier quality, autoscaled sandbox endpoints. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **SkyPilot "RL Doesn't Work on Slurm"** + **Anyscale OSS RL libraries / SkyRL** — Ray-vs-Slurm orchestration, SkyRL disaggregated/VLM RL. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- **Boundaries** — RL algorithm math → `llm-alignment-post-training` (PPO/DPO), `reasoning-models` (GRPO/RLVR), `agentic-rl` (multi-turn/POMDP); supervised distributed-training internals → `distributed-training`; production serving of one model → `llm-inference-serving`. [src: rlhf-infrastructure]
- Reference under the `ai-agent-engineering` hub. The **multi-model serving-decision** layer — choosing/orchestrating WHICH model(s) answer each request to ride the cost/quality/latency Pareto frontier — distinct from serving ONE model well (that is `llm-inference-serving`). Full reference: `references/llm-routing-cascades.md`. [src: llm-routing-cascades]
- **Three families, by when the decision happens:** route = pick a model *before* generation (1 call); cascade = run cheap, *observe*, escalate on low confidence (1–N sequential); ensemble/mixture = run several and *fuse* (N parallel). Plus the zeroth route: cache = serve a remembered answer (0 calls). [src: llm-routing-cascades]
- **Predictive routing (RouteLLM, arXiv:2406.18665)** — pick a model before generation. Four router types: similarity-weighted ranking, matrix factorization (best on MT-Bench), BERT classifier, causal-LLM classifier. Trained on Chatbot-Arena preference data + LLM-judge/golden-label augmentation. Strong-vs-weak binary with a cost-quality threshold; metrics PGR (Performance Gap Recovered) and CPT (Call-Performance Threshold); ~85% cost cut on MT-Bench at 95% GPT-4. [src: llm-routing-cascades]
- **Route-by-difficulty** — Route-to-Reason (2505.19435, model+strategy under budget, −60% tokens), RADAR (multi-objective Pareto), adaptive think/non-think (reasoning models overthink easy queries). [src: llm-routing-cascades]
- **Cascades + deferral/abstention (FrugalGPT, arXiv:2305.05176)** — cheap-first, score, escalate; learned scorer + thresholds; up to 98% cost cut matching GPT-4. Calibration is the whole game (over/under-defer). Router (upfront, no feedback) vs cascade (observes cheap answer, pays latency). [src: llm-routing-cascades]
- **Speculative cascades (arXiv:2405.19261, ICLR 2025)** — token-level flexible deferral across two models. NOT speculative decoding: decoding is loss-less within one model (output identical); speculative cascade routes across models with a controlled quality change. [src: llm-routing-cascades]
- **Mixture-of-Agents (MoA, arXiv:2406.04692)** — layered proposers + aggregator; collaborativeness (better with others' outputs, even weaker ones); 65.1% AlpacaEval 2.0 LC (OSS) vs GPT-4o 57.5%. Cost: many calls + high TTFT; Self-MoA critique (one strong model resampled can win). [src: llm-routing-cascades]
- **Output ensembling (LLM-Blender, arXiv:2306.02561)** — PairRanker (rank candidates) + GenFuser (fuse top-K). Input-level (routing/MoA) vs output-level (run N, fuse once). [src: llm-routing-cascades]
- **Semantic / prompt caching as routing (GPTCache)** — embedding-similarity cache (paraphrases hit), ~68.8% call reduction; exact-match/prefix vs semantic; the cheapest "route" (0 calls). [src: llm-routing-cascades]
- **Cost/quality/latency Pareto modeling** — maintain a frontier across models; per-request constrained optimization (max quality s.t. cost/latency budget); routers push the frontier outward vs any single point. [src: llm-routing-cascades]
- **Router evaluation (RouterBench, arXiv:2403.12031)** — 405k pre-computed outcomes; evaluate on cost-quality curves / AIQ, not a single operating point; RouterArena (2510.00202). [src: llm-routing-cascades]
- **Tooling** — gateway (LiteLLM, OpenRouter transport: load-balance/fallback) vs quality-predictive (RouteLLM OSS, NotDiamond [powers OpenRouter Auto], Martian, vLLM Semantic Router 'Iris' v0.1 Jan-2026). [src: llm-routing-cascades]
- **Failure modes** — routing collapse (defaults to the expensive model as budget rises), tail miscalibration (rare high-stakes queries), added latency (cascade escalation, MoA TTFT), maintenance (re-fit on fleet/price change). [src: llm-routing-cascades]
- **Boundaries:** serving ONE model (vLLM/batching/KV/autoscaling) → `llm-inference-serving`; speculative DECODING within one model → `llm-inference-serving`; reasoning route-by-difficulty cost bullet → `reasoning-models`; agent orchestration / tool loops → `agent-ecosystem`/`autonomous-loops` (this is model SELECTION). [src: llm-routing-cascades]
- **Primary sources:** RouteLLM 2406.18665; FrugalGPT 2305.05176; Speculative cascades 2405.19261; MoA 2406.04692; LLM-Blender 2306.02561; RouterBench 2403.12031; Route-to-Reason 2505.19435; GPTCache; vLLM Semantic Router; "When Routing Collapses" 2602.03478. [src: llm-routing-cascades]

- How Node.js does concurrency on a single main thread: the **libuv event loop** that [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- orchestrates everything, the **thread pool** that absorbs blocking work, **stream [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- backpressure** that keeps memory bounded, and the **three parallelism models** [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- (`worker_threads`, `cluster`, `child_process`) for escaping the single thread. Treat the [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- as the source of truth for version-sensitive behavior. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- This is the deep-internals companion to `references/javascript-nodejs.md` (broad language / [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- runtime-API reference). When a question is about *ordering, blocking, throughput, or [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]

- -- [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- Node runs JavaScript on a **single main thread**. libuv drives an **event loop** that, on [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- each iteration ("tick" of the loop), passes through six phases **in this fixed order**, each [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- with its own FIFO callback queue ([Node.js Event Loop](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/asynchronous-work/event-loop-timers-and-nexttick), [libuv design](https://docs.libuv.org/en/v1.x/design.html)): [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- After phase 6 the loop wraps back to phase 1. The loop's notion of **`now`** is sampled once [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- at the start of an iteration and is *not* updated again mid-iteration — a timer that becomes [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- due while earlier timers are still running waits until the next iteration. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- The poll phase is the heart of the loop ([Node.js Event Loop](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/asynchronous-work/event-loop-timers-and-nexttick)): [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **Poll queue not empty** → run its callbacks synchronously until the queue drains or a system limit is hit. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **Poll queue empty:** [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- If `setImmediate()` callbacks are scheduled → end poll, go to **check**. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- Else → **block here waiting for I/O**, with a computed timeout equal to the nearest pending timer (so timers fire roughly on time). If no timers and no handles keep the loop alive, the process exits. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- A process stays alive only while there are **active handles or requests** (open sockets, [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- listening servers, pending timers, active worker threads). When none remain, the loop ends [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- For **network I/O**, libuv uses the OS's native async primitives (epoll on Linux, kqueue on [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- BSD/macOS, IOCP on Windows) — no extra threads. For work the OS **cannot** do [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- asynchronously (notably file-system I/O, and DNS via `getaddrinfo`), libuv falls back to the [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **thread pool** (Section 3) ([libuv design](https://docs.libuv.org/en/v1.x/design.html)). [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- -- [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `process.nextTick()` and the **Promise microtask queue** are **not** event-loop phases. They [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- are two separate queues that drain **between every callback and between every phase [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- transition** — they run before the loop is allowed to advance ([Node.js Event Loop](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/asynchronous-work/event-loop-timers-and-nexttick)). [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **Drain order at each checkpoint:** [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- The entire **`process.nextTick` queue** (highest priority), then [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- The entire **Promise microtask queue** (`.then` / `await` continuations, `queueMicrotask`). [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- Both are fully drained before the next phase callback runs. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- setImmediate(() => console.log('immediate'));   // check phase [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('promise')); // microtask [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- process.nextTick(() => console.log('nextTick'));      // nextTick queue [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- // Output: sync, nextTick, promise, immediate [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- Because these queues drain *completely* before the loop advances, **recursively scheduling [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `process.nextTick()` (or microtasks) starves the loop** — I/O, timers, and `setImmediate` [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- function starve() { process.nextTick(starve); } // poll phase never reached again [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- Prefer `setImmediate()` when you want to yield back to the loop. Legitimate `nextTick` uses: [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- defer a callback so the caller's synchronous code finishes first, emit an event after a [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- constructor returns (so listeners can attach), or normalize an API to "always async." [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **In the main module / top level:** order is **non-deterministic** — it depends on how [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- fast the process reaches the timers phase vs whether the 0-ms timer's threshold has elapsed. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **Inside an I/O callback (poll phase):** `setImmediate` **always** fires before [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `setTimeout(…, 0)`, because the loop goes poll → check next, and only reaches timers on the [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- const fs = require('node:fs'); [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- fs.readFile(__filename, () => { [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- setTimeout(() => console.log('timeout'), 0); [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- setImmediate(() => console.log('immediate')); [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- // Always: immediate, then timeout [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- -- [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- A **global thread pool**, shared across all event loops in the process, runs work that has no [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- async OS primitive ([libuv threadpool](https://docs.libuv.org/en/v1.x/threadpool.html)): [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **Default size: 4 threads.** Configurable via the **`UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`** environment [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- variable, **max 1024** (raised from 128 in libuv 1.30.0). Must be set **before** the pool is [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- first used (effectively at process start); libuv preallocates the threads on first use. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **What uses it:** `fs.*` file operations, `dns.lookup()` (`getaddrinfo`/`getnameinfo`), [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `crypto` (`pbkdf2`, `randomBytes`, `scrypt`), and `zlib` compression. **Network sockets do [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- NOT** — they use the OS event mechanism, not the pool. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **Saturation symptom:** with the default 4 threads, 5+ concurrent `fs`/`crypto`/`zlib`/DNS [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- operations queue; the 5th waits for a free thread even though the CPU is idle. Latency climbs [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- with no obvious CPU cause. Raise `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` (a common starting point is the number [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- of logical cores, or higher for I/O-heavy workloads) and measure. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- > Pitfall: `dns.lookup()` uses the pool; the lower-level `dns.resolve*()` family uses the [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- > network and does **not**. A burst of `dns.lookup()` (which most connection code calls [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- > implicitly) can starve the pool. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- -- [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- Node serves many clients with few threads, so **any synchronous CPU work on the main thread [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- stalls every other client** — a throughput problem and a DoS vector ([Don't Block the Event Loop](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/asynchronous-work/dont-block-the-event-loop)). [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **Things that block the main thread:** [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- Synchronous APIs in request paths: `fs.readFileSync`, `crypto.pbkdf2Sync`, `zlib.*Sync`, `child_process.execSync`, `JSON.parse`/`JSON.stringify` on large payloads. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **ReDoS** — catastrophic backtracking from nested quantifiers (`/(\/.+)+$/`), overlapping alternation (`/(a|a)*/`), or backreferences; an attacker triggers exponential time. Mitigate with `indexOf`, `safe-regex`, or `node-re2` (linear-time engine), and bound input size. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- Long synchronous loops / O(n²) work per request. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **Partitioning** (keep work on the loop but yield): break the loop into chunks and [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- reschedule each chunk with `setImmediate()` so other callbacks interleave. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **Offloading** (move work off the loop): `worker_threads` for CPU-bound JS, [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `child_process` for separate programs. Use a **pool** of workers — never spawn one per [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- request (fork-bomb / unbounded memory). [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **Measure event-loop lag** with `perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay()` (histogram) or [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `performance.eventLoopUtilization()` (ELU). Don't block the **pool** either: one slow [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- thread-pool task (e.g. reading `/dev/random`) ties up 1 of 4 threads; partition large reads [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- or use streams (auto-partitioned). [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- -- [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- A stream moves data in chunks instead of buffering it all in memory. **Backpressure** is the [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- flow-control signal that stops a fast producer from outrunning a slow consumer; ignoring it [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- lets internal buffers grow without bound ([Backpressuring in Streams](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/modules/backpressuring-in-streams), [Node.js Stream API](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html)). [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **Four stream types:** `Readable` (source), `Writable` (sink), `Duplex` (both, independent [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- sides, e.g. a TCP socket), `Transform` (Duplex where output is a function of input, e.g. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `zlib.createGzip()`). [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- Each stream has a **`highWaterMark`** buffer threshold — default **16384 bytes (16 KB)** for [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- byte streams, **16 objects** in `objectMode`. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `writable.write(chunk)` returns **`true`** → keep writing. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- It returns **`false`** → the internal buffer is at/over `highWaterMark`. **Stop writing and [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- wait for the `'drain'` event** before resuming. (`write()` still accepts the chunk; the [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- return value is purely the backpressure signal.) [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- // Manual writing MUST honor backpressure: [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- readable.on('data', (chunk) => { [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- if (!writable.write(chunk)) readable.pause(); [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- writable.on('drain', () => readable.resume()); [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- Real impact: compressing a ~9 GB file with backpressure held memory at ~88 MB; ignoring it [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- ballooned to ~1.5 GB (≈17× more) with far worse GC pauses. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `pipe()` and `pipeline()` **handle backpressure automatically** (you don't manage [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `drain`/`pause`/`resume`). Always prefer **`stream.pipeline()`** over manual `.pipe()` chains: [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- on any stream's failure it destroys *all* streams and propagates the error, where `.pipe()` [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- leaks file descriptors and sockets on error. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- const { pipeline } = require('node:stream/promises'); [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- fs.createReadStream('in.mkv'), [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- fs.createWriteStream('out.mkv.gz'), [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- ); // throws on any stage failure, cleans up everything [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **`Readable._read`:** respect `push()`'s return value — when `this.push(chunk)` returns [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `false`, stop pushing (the consumer's buffer is full). `push(null)` signals end-of-stream. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **`Writable._write(chunk, enc, cb):`** call `cb` **exactly once** (use `return cb()` on [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- every branch so it can't be called twice). [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **Batching:** `cork()` buffers writes; `uncork()` flushes them in one go. Schedule the [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `uncork()` with `process.nextTick()` so multiple synchronous `write()`s batch into a single [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- flush rather than flushing per call. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- Modern alternative: build pipelines from **async iterators / async generators** as [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- Transform stages — `pipeline()` accepts them and applies backpressure automatically. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- -- [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- Alongside classic `node:stream` (Section 5), Node implements the **WHATWG Web Streams** [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- standard — the same `ReadableStream`/`WritableStream`/`TransformStream` you get in browsers, [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `fetch`/`undici` response bodies, and edge runtimes (Workers, Deno). Use them for [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **cross-runtime / edge-portable** code and when consuming `fetch` bodies; reach for classic [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `node:stream` for Node-centric server I/O and the richer ecosystem. The three stream classes [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- plus `TextEncoderStream`/`TextDecoderStream`/`CompressionStream`/`DecompressionStream`/the [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- queuing-strategy classes are **globals** in modern Node — no import. Only `node:stream/consumers`, [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `node:stream/promises`, and the `toWeb`/`fromWeb` bridge methods need importing [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- ([Web Streams API](https://nodejs.org/api/webstreams.html), [MDN Streams concepts](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Streams_API/Concepts)). [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- Web Streams take a plain object describing the source/sink, optionally followed by a queuing [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- strategy. The hook names differ from classic `_read`/`_write` (Section 5): [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- // ReadableStream: { start, pull, cancel }, type:'bytes' for a byte stream [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- const rs = new ReadableStream({ [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- start(controller) {}, [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- pull(controller) { controller.enqueue(chunk); /* controller.close() to end */ }, [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- }, new CountQueuingStrategy({ highWaterMark: 16 })); [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- // WritableStream: { start, write, close, abort } [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- const ws = new WritableStream({ [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- write(chunk, controller) { /* return a Promise to apply backpressure */ }, [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- close() {}, abort(reason) {}, [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- }, new ByteLengthQueuingStrategy({ highWaterMark: 64 * 1024 })); [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- // TransformStream: { start, transform, flush } + separate writable/readable strategies [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- const ts = new TransformStream({ transform(chunk, controller) { controller.enqueue(chunk); } }); [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- Same goal as Section 5 (bound memory, throttle a fast producer) but a different surface — so [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **don't re-derive the classic `write()===false` + `'drain'` contract; note the delta:** [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- A **queuing strategy is an object** (`new ByteLengthQueuingStrategy({highWaterMark})` for byte [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- streams, `new CountQueuingStrategy({highWaterMark})` for object streams), not a numeric [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `highWaterMark` option as in classic streams. There is **no fixed default `highWaterMark`** — [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- the *model*, not a magic number, is the contract (classic streams keep the 16 KB / 16-object [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- defaults from Section 5). [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- Backpressure is read via **`controller.desiredSize`** (= `highWaterMark` − queued size). When [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- it drops to **≤ 0**, the producer is outrunning the consumer; stop enqueuing. It can go [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- The runtime calls **`pull(controller)`** only while the queue is below the high-water mark, and [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- — if `pull` returns a Promise — won't call it again until that Promise settles. This is a [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **demand-driven pull** loop, whereas classic streams are push-with-a-`drain`-backstop. Apply [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- backpressure on the write side by returning a Promise from the sink's `write()` (or awaiting [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `writer.ready` / reading `writer.desiredSize`). [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **`stream.pipeTo()` / `stream.pipeThrough()`** propagate backpressure end-to-end automatically [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- (the Web-Streams analogue of `pipeline()`), and `tee()` forks one readable into two independent [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- readables — a fan-out classic streams have no direct equivalent for. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `getReader()` yields a `ReadableStreamDefaultReader` (opaque chunks). For a `type: 'bytes'` [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- stream, `getReader({ mode: 'byob' })` yields a **`ReadableStreamBYOBReader`** whose [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `read(view)` fills a caller-supplied `TypedArray`/`DataView` — a **zero-copy** read straight [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- into your buffer. (Never hand it a pooled Node `Buffer`: BYOB detaches the backing [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `ArrayBuffer`.) Async iteration works too: `for await (const chunk of readable)`. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- Static methods on the classic stream classes convert both directions — bridge a Node [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- file/socket stream into a Web pipeline, or wrap a `fetch` body as a classic `Readable`: [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]

- const nodeWritable = Writable.fromWeb(webWritableStream); [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- // Duplex.toWeb(d) → { readable, writable }; Duplex.fromWeb(pair) → Duplex (e.g. for a socket) [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- These bridges were historically flagged experimental — check the **stability index** for your [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- Node version and pin Node versions for production use. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `node:stream/consumers` collects **either** a Web `ReadableStream`, a classic `stream.Readable`, [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **or** any `AsyncIterable` into one value — no manual chunk loop: [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- import { text, json, arrayBuffer, blob, buffer, bytes } from 'node:stream/consumers'; [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- const obj = await json(response.body);          // Web ReadableStream → parsed JSON [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- const str = await text(fs.createReadStream('x')); // classic Readable → UTF-8 string [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- // also: arrayBuffer → ArrayBuffer, blob → Blob, buffer → Buffer, bytes → Uint8Array [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `node:stream/promises` spans both worlds too: **`pipeline()`** accepts Web streams, classic [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- streams, and async iterables/generators in one chain, and **`finished()`** accepts a [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `ReadableStream`/`WritableStream` as well as a classic stream. Prefer these over hand-rolled [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `getReader()`/`read()` loops when you just need the collected result or a completion signal. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- -- [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- Rule of thumb: **CPU-bound JS → worker_threads; scaling an HTTP/TCP server → cluster; shelling [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- out to another program → child_process.** None of these help **I/O-bound** work — plain async [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- I/O on one thread is already optimal and cheaper. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- -- [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- Each `Worker` is a **separate V8 isolate with its own event loop and heap**, inside the same [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- OS process — far cheaper than a process, and able to share memory ([worker_threads](https://nodejs.org/api/worker_threads.html)). [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- import { Worker } from 'node:worker_threads'; [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- const worker = new Worker(new URL('./worker.js', import.meta.url), { [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- workerData: { rows: 1_000_000 }, [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- worker.on('message', (result) => console.log(result)); [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- worker.on('error', (err) => { /* uncaught worker error */ }); [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- worker.on('exit', (code) => { /* code !== 0 → abnormal */ }); [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- import { parentPort, workerData } from 'node:worker_threads'; [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- const result = heavyCompute(workerData.rows); [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- parentPort.postMessage(result); [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `postMessage()` copies data using the **HTML structured clone algorithm** (not JSON): it [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- handles `Map`/`Set`/`Date`/`RegExp`/`BigInt`/typed arrays and circular refs, but **drops [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- class prototypes** (a class instance arrives as a plain object) and cannot clone functions. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **`transferList`:** move (don't copy) ownership of an `ArrayBuffer` / `MessagePort`: [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `port.postMessage(view, [view.buffer])`. The buffer becomes **detached** (length 0) on the [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- sender side, and *all* views over it become unusable — zero-copy handoff. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **`MessageChannel` / `MessagePort`:** dedicated bidirectional channels (transfer one port to [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- the worker). **`BroadcastChannel`:** one-to-many by channel name. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **`SharedArrayBuffer` + `Atomics`:** true shared memory for high-frequency coordination. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- Use `Atomics.add/compareExchange/...` for race-free updates and `Atomics.wait` / [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `Atomics.notify` to block/wake threads. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **Caveats:** workers don't share `process.stdin/stdout/stderr` unless piped; can't [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `process.chdir()` or handle process signals; `worker.unref()` lets the process exit without [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- waiting on the worker; `worker.terminate()` force-stops it (returns a Promise). For many small [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- tasks, **reuse a worker pool** (e.g. `Piscina`) rather than creating a worker per task. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- -- [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `cluster` forks multiple **Node worker processes that all listen on the same server port**, [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- letting a server use every core. It is built on **`child_process.fork()`** with an IPC channel [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- and server-handle passing ([cluster](https://nodejs.org/api/cluster.html)). [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- import cluster from 'node:cluster'; [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- import http from 'node:http'; [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- import { availableParallelism } from 'node:os'; [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- if (cluster.isPrimary) { [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- for (let i = 0; i < availableParallelism(); i++) cluster.fork(); [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- cluster.on('exit', (worker) => cluster.fork()); // respawn on death [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- http.createServer((req, res) => res.end('ok')).listen(8000); // shared port [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **Scheduling policy** (`cluster.schedulingPolicy` / `NODE_CLUSTER_SCHED_POLICY`): [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **`SCHED_RR`** (round-robin) — **default everywhere except Windows.** The primary accepts [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- connections and hands them out evenly. Usually the right choice. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **`SCHED_NONE`** — the OS distributes connections; can be badly unbalanced (e.g. most [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- connections landing on a couple of workers). [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **Lifecycle events** (primary): `fork`, `online`, `listening`, `message`, `disconnect`, [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `exit`. Communicate via `worker.send()` / `process.on('message')`. Graceful shutdown: [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `worker.disconnect()` (stop accepting, drain) then a kill-timeout fallback. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **Caveats:** workers have **separate memory** — never keep session/login state in process [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- memory; use a shared store (Redis) or a load balancer with **sticky sessions** for stateful [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- connections. `cluster.isMaster`/`setupMaster()` are deprecated → use [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `isPrimary`/`setupPrimary()`. Many deployments instead run N single-process instances behind [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- an external balancer (or a process manager like PM2). [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- -- [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- Run other programs (or other Node scripts) as separate OS processes ([child_process](https://nodejs.org/api/child_process.html)). [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- Each has a `*Sync` variant (`spawnSync`, `execSync`, `execFileSync`) that **blocks the event [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- loop** — startup/CLI use only, never in a server. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **Command injection:** `exec`/`shell: true` interpolate strings through a shell, so untrusted [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- input enables injection (`exec(\`echo ${userInput}\`)` with `userInput = "; rm -rf /"`). Prefer [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **`spawn`/`execFile` with an args array** — arguments bypass shell parsing, so metacharacters [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- are inert. Reach for a shell only when you genuinely need shell features, and sanitize input. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **Other essentials:** [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **`maxBuffer`** (exec/execFile): exceeding it kills the child with [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER_EXCEEDED`; raise it or switch to `spawn` for big output. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **`stdio`** option: `'pipe'` (default; streams on the child object), `'inherit'` (share the [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- parent's stdio), `'ignore'`, or `'ipc'` (message channel — what `fork` adds). [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **IPC:** `fork` (or `spawn` with an `'ipc'` stdio slot) gives `child.send(msg)` ↔ [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `process.on('message')`, using structured clone. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **`detached: true` + `subprocess.unref()`** lets a child outlive the parent (with [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `stdio: 'ignore'`). `ref()`/`unref()` toggle whether the child keeps the parent's loop alive. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- **Events:** `'spawn'` (started) → `'exit'` (process ended, stdio may still be open) → [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]
- `'close'` (stdio fully closed; always after `'exit'`); `'error'` on spawn failure. [src: nodejs-concurrency-internals]

- A `programming-languages` hub reference covering the **non-Node JS/TS runtime landscape** and the [src: javascript-runtimes-deno-bun-edge]
- **cross-runtime interop standard** that ties them together. For Node.js language/runtime APIs and [src: javascript-runtimes-deno-bun-edge]
