- <!-- Provenance: reference under the `programming-languages` hub. Mirrored from ~/.claude/skills/programming-languages/references/v8-engine-internals.md by scripts/persist-spoke.mjs. --> [src: v8-engine-internals]
- V8 is Google's open-source JavaScript/WebAssembly engine (C++) powering Chrome, Node.js, Deno, Electron, [src: v8-engine-internals]
- and Edge. Performance comes from three coupled subsystems: a **hidden-class object model** that gives [src: v8-engine-internals]
- dynamically-typed objects predictable, comparable shapes; an **inline-cache + multi-tier JIT** that [src: v8-engine-internals]
- speculatively specializes hot code on observed shapes; and **Orinoco**, a mostly-concurrent generational [src: v8-engine-internals]
- garbage collector that keeps pause times low. The three are inseparable — the JIT speculates on hidden [src: v8-engine-internals]
- classes via inline-cache feedback, and bad shapes (megamorphism) defeat both the IC and the optimizer. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- -- [src: v8-engine-internals]
- JavaScript has no static classes, so V8 synthesizes them. Every object holds, as its first word, a pointer [src: v8-engine-internals]
- to a **Map** (V8's internal name for a *hidden class*; also called a "shape"). The Map describes the [src: v8-engine-internals]
- object's structure — which properties exist, their order, their storage location, and attributes. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **DescriptorArray** — lists a Map's properties with metadata and storage offset. Multiple Maps can [src: v8-engine-internals]
- *share* one DescriptorArray by tracking how many leading descriptors each Map "owns," because property [src: v8-engine-internals]
- insertion order is preserved. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **TransitionArray** — the edges between Maps: "from Map A, adding property `x` → Map B." Adding a [src: v8-engine-internals]
- property doesn't mutate the Map; it *transitions* to (or creates) a new Map. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Transition tree** — objects that receive the same properties **in the same order** walk the same [src: v8-engine-internals]
- chain of Maps and end up sharing the terminal Map. This is what makes them "the same shape" and lets the [src: v8-engine-internals]
- IC/JIT treat them identically. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Property storage:** [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **In-object properties** — stored inline in the object's own memory slots; fastest access. V8 pre-reserves [src: v8-engine-internals]
- a number of in-object slots based on the constructor. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Property backing store ("fast properties")** — once in-object slots are exhausted, extra named [src: v8-engine-internals]
- properties spill to a separate `properties` array, still described by the Map (offset lookup). [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Dictionary mode ("slow properties")** — if an object is mutated pathologically (many deletes, huge [src: v8-engine-internals]
- sparse key sets), V8 abandons the hidden class and falls back to a hash-table dictionary. This kills IC [src: v8-engine-internals]
- optimization for that object. Deleting a property with `delete` is a common trigger. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Elements** — integer-indexed properties are tracked separately as *elements kinds* (e.g. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- `PACKED_SMI_ELEMENTS`, `PACKED_DOUBLE_ELEMENTS`, `PACKED_ELEMENTS`, and `HOLEY_*` variants). Creating [src: v8-engine-internals]
- "holes" (sparse arrays, `arr[100]=x` on a short array, `delete arr[i]`) transitions to a slower HOLEY [src: v8-engine-internals]
- kind that never transitions back. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Why initialization order matters:** initialize all of an object's properties in the **same order**, ideally [src: v8-engine-internals]
- in the constructor, so every instance shares one transition chain. Adding properties out of order (e.g. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- inserting `rating` between `name` and `height` on some instances but not others) *bifurcates* the [src: v8-engine-internals]
- transition tree, producing distinct Maps for structurally identical objects — which turns a monomorphic [src: v8-engine-internals]
- call site polymorphic or megamorphic downstream. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- -- [src: v8-engine-internals]
- A property access (`obj.x`), method call, or operator is compiled with an **inline cache**: a per-site [src: v8-engine-internals]
- cache of "for Map M, property `x` lives at offset N." On the next hit with the same Map, V8 skips the [src: v8-engine-internals]
- full lookup and loads directly. ICs are the primary *type-feedback* source the optimizing tiers consume. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- IC states for a site, in order of degradation: [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Practical implications** [src: v8-engine-internals]
- Keep call sites **monomorphic**: feed a given function objects of one shape. A function that handles [src: v8-engine-internals]
- many shapes (e.g. a generic serializer over heterogeneous objects) tends toward megamorphic and stays [src: v8-engine-internals]
- Polymorphism of 2–4 shapes is acceptable; the cliff is at megamorphic. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- The optimizing compilers (Maglev/TurboFan) read IC feedback: monomorphic → emit a single map-check fast [src: v8-engine-internals]
- path with inlined load and (for `const` fields) inlined values; polymorphic → a check chain; megamorphic [src: v8-engine-internals]
- → generic, unoptimized access. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- `Function.prototype` shape stability matters: monkey-patching prototypes after instances exist invalidates [src: v8-engine-internals]
- ICs and forces re-learning. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- -- [src: v8-engine-internals]
- V8 is no longer "interpreter + one optimizer." Since 2021–2023 it runs **four tiers**, escalating a [src: v8-engine-internals]
- function as it gets hotter and gathering feedback at every step. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Ignition (interpreter, since 2016)** — all JS is first compiled to compact **bytecode** and [src: v8-engine-internals]
- interpreted. Ignition's register machine collects type feedback (in *feedback vectors*) and tracks [src: v8-engine-internals]
- shapes/IC states. Bytecode also keeps memory low (it replaced caching full baseline machine code). [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Sparkplug (baseline JIT, 2021)** — a *non-optimizing* compiler that translates bytecode to machine [src: v8-engine-internals]
- code in a single linear pass with **no IR and no optimization**, so compilation is extremely fast. It [src: v8-engine-internals]
- removes interpreter dispatch overhead. Roughly **~2× faster** than Ignition for warm code; the machine [src: v8-engine-internals]
- code stays compatible with the interpreter's stack frame so on-stack replacement is cheap. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Maglev (mid-tier optimizing JIT, GA 2023–2024)** — an **SSA-based compiler over a CFG (control-flow [src: v8-engine-internals]
- graph)**, *not* sea-of-nodes. A minimal set of passes and a simple IR make it **~10× slower than [src: v8-engine-internals]
- Sparkplug but ~10× faster than TurboFan**, producing solidly optimized code without TurboFan's compile [src: v8-engine-internals]
- cost. It uses IC feedback to emit specialized SSA nodes, inserts map/shape checks, inlines de-facto [src: v8-engine-internals]
- constant globals, and exploits "stable" feedback (shape transitions never observed) and "unstable" [src: v8-engine-internals]
- feedback (just-allocated objects that can skip write barriers). Targets warm-to-hot code and hot loops [src: v8-engine-internals]
- that don't yet justify TurboFan. ~5× over baseline on hot code. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **TurboFan (top-tier optimizing JIT)** — the heavyweight, using a **"sea of nodes"** IR. It performs [src: v8-engine-internals]
- aggressive speculative optimizations: type specialization, inlining, escape analysis, redundancy [src: v8-engine-internals]
- elimination, constant folding of `const` fields, range analysis. Slowest to compile, best code [src: v8-engine-internals]
- (**~10×+** over baseline). Reserved for the very hottest functions; speculation is guarded by deopt [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Tiering / profile-guided escalation:** functions accumulate an *invocation/loop budget* (interrupt [src: v8-engine-internals]
- budget). Crossing thresholds promotes a function to the next tier; **on-stack replacement (OSR)** can swap [src: v8-engine-internals]
- a long-running loop into optimized code mid-execution. Recent V8 adds **profile-guided tiering** that uses [src: v8-engine-internals]
- profiling to decide *which* tier to jump to (e.g. skip Maglev straight to TurboFan, or stay at Sparkplug) [src: v8-engine-internals]
- rather than always climbing one rung at a time. Tiers cache compiled code; very hot code can even persist [src: v8-engine-internals]
- across runs in some embedders. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Where V8 is going (Turboshaft / Turbolev):** **Turboshaft** is V8's newer backend/IR framework [src: v8-engine-internals]
- (block-and-edge CFG, cache-friendlier than sea-of-nodes) that TurboFan's later phases have migrated onto. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- The **Turbolev** project (in progress, 2025) feeds Maglev's CFG-based IR into the Turboshaft backend, [src: v8-engine-internals]
- aiming to eventually replace the classic TurboFan front end. Treat these as direction, not stable API. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- -- [src: v8-engine-internals]
- Optimized code is **speculative**: it assumes the shapes/types observed so far keep holding. When an [src: v8-engine-internals]
- assumption breaks, V8 must **deoptimize** — discard the optimized code for that function and resume in [src: v8-engine-internals]
- Ignition bytecode at the equivalent point. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Eager deopt** — the currently-executing optimized code hits a failed assumption (e.g. an object [src: v8-engine-internals]
- arrives with the wrong Map) and bails out immediately. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Lazy deopt** — code is invalidated for a *not-currently-running* function (e.g. a global it inlined [src: v8-engine-internals]
- changed); it's unlinked and recompiled on next call. ("Lazy unlinking" defers the cleanup.) [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Soft deopt** — an optimization was attempted with **insufficient type feedback**; the function bails [src: v8-engine-internals]
- back to gather more feedback, then re-optimizes. Often seen right after forcing [src: v8-engine-internals]
- `%OptimizeFunctionOnNextCall`. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- V8 has **~70 deopt reasons** — e.g. `WrongMap`, `NotASmi`, `InsufficientTypeFeedbackForBinaryOperation`, [src: v8-engine-internals]
- `OutOfBounds`. Repeated deopt/reopt cycling ("deopt loop") on a hot function is a serious perf bug: [src: v8-engine-internals]
- the function never stays optimized. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Diagnostic flags** (pass via `node --v8-options` names, or use `d8`): [src: v8-engine-internals]
- `--trace-opt` — log which functions get optimized and to which tier. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- `--trace-deopt` — log every deopt with its reason and the function/bytecode offset. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- `--print-opt-code`, `--code-comments` — dump generated machine code with annotations. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- `--trace-ic` — log inline-cache state transitions per site (monomorphic→…→megamorphic). [src: v8-engine-internals]
- `--allow-natives-syntax` enables intrinsics like `%OptimizeFunctionOnNextCall(fn)`, [src: v8-engine-internals]
- `%GetOptimizationStatus(fn)`, `%HasFastProperties(obj)`, `%DebugPrint(obj)` (shows the Map) for [src: v8-engine-internals]
- micro-investigations. Run under `d8` or Node with the flag; never ship with it. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- -- [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Orinoco** is the umbrella name for V8's modern GC: a **generational, parallel, concurrent, incremental** [src: v8-engine-internals]
- collector designed to minimize main-thread pause time. It rests on the **generational hypothesis** — most [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Young generation (new space)** — small; split into two equal **semi-spaces** (From / To). New objects [src: v8-engine-internals]
- allocate here. Also has a "nursery" + "intermediate" sub-generation: surviving one Scavenge promotes an [src: v8-engine-internals]
- object to intermediate, surviving again promotes it to old space. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Old generation (old space)** — long-lived objects; collected by the major GC. Plus specialized spaces: [src: v8-engine-internals]
- large-object space, code space, map space, read-only space. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Minor GC — the Scavenger (Cheney's semi-space copying)** [src: v8-engine-internals]
- Collects only the young generation, frequently and cheaply. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- Live objects in From-space are **evacuated** (copied) to To-space (or promoted to old space); the rest of [src: v8-engine-internals]
- From-space is reclaimed wholesale by flipping spaces. Half the young space is always empty to allow the copy. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- Since V8 6.2 the Scavenger is **parallel** (dynamic work-stealing across helper threads), cutting [src: v8-engine-internals]
- young-gen pause time **~20–50%**. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Write barriers** record old→young pointers in remembered sets, so a minor GC never has to scan the [src: v8-engine-internals]
- whole old generation to find roots into the nursery. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Major GC — Mark-Sweep-Compact (Orinoco's concurrent machinery)** [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Mark** — trace the object graph from roots to mark all reachable objects. Done largely with [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **concurrent marking** on background threads while JS runs; **incremental marking** interleaves small [src: v8-engine-internals]
- marking steps with execution; write barriers track references mutated during marking. **Black [src: v8-engine-internals]
- allocation** allocates new objects pre-marked-black during marking so they aren't prematurely collected. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Sweep** — reclaim dead-object gaps into free-lists (can be concurrent/lazy). [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Compact** — selectively evacuate/defragment the most fragmented pages (**parallel compaction**); pages [src: v8-engine-internals]
- with many long-lived objects are swept-in-place instead of copied to avoid expensive moves. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Idle-time GC** — embedders (e.g. Chrome) can hand V8 idle slices (the ~16.6 ms gaps at 60 fps) to do GC [src: v8-engine-internals]
- proactively. Concurrent marking can cut heavy-workload pauses **up to ~50%**. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- Net effect: most GC work happens off the main thread or in tiny incremental slices, so user-visible [src: v8-engine-internals]
- stop-the-world pauses are short. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- -- [src: v8-engine-internals]
- V8 sizes its heap conservatively; long-running servers and memory-constrained containers usually need [src: v8-engine-internals]
- explicit flags. Pass V8 flags directly to `node` (or via `NODE_OPTIONS`). [src: v8-engine-internals]
- `--max-old-space-size=<MB>` — cap the **old generation**. The classic OOM lever; raise it (e.g. `4096`) [src: v8-engine-internals]
- when you hit `FATAL ERROR: ... JavaScript heap out of memory`. The historical default is ~1.5–2 GB on [src: v8-engine-internals]
- 64-bit, but newer Node derives a default from available system memory. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- `--max-semi-space-size=<MB>` — max size of **each** young-generation semi-space (so young space ≈ 2× this). [src: v8-engine-internals]
- Default is small (a few MB). **Raising it (e.g. 16–128 MB) is often the single biggest GC win**: a larger [src: v8-engine-internals]
- nursery means fewer, less-frequent Scavenges and fewer premature promotions to old space — trading a bit [src: v8-engine-internals]
- of RAM for materially less GC CPU. Sweet spots are typically 16–256 MB depending on allocation rate. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- `--min-semi-space-size=<MB>` — initial/floor young size. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- `--expose-gc` — exposes `global.gc()` to force a collection (diagnostics, or reclaiming after a big batch). [src: v8-engine-internals]
- Don't rely on manual GC in production logic; it's mainly for testing/measurement. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- `--trace-gc` / `--trace-gc-verbose` — log every GC with type (Scavenge vs Mark-Compact), durations, and [src: v8-engine-internals]
- heap sizes; the first thing to enable when diagnosing GC pressure. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Programmatic observation** — use `perf_hooks` `PerformanceObserver` with `entryTypes: ['gc']` to record GC [src: v8-engine-internals]
- events (kind: minor/major/incremental/weakcb, duration) in-process; pair with `process.memoryUsage()` [src: v8-engine-internals]
- (`rss`, `heapTotal`, `heapUsed`, `external`, `arrayBuffers`) and `v8.getHeapStatistics()` / [src: v8-engine-internals]
- `v8.getHeapSpaceStatistics()`. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Containers / serverless** — V8 doesn't read cgroup limits by default, so it can size the heap for the host, [src: v8-engine-internals]
- not the container, and get OOM-killed. Set `--max-old-space-size` to ~75–85% of the container memory limit, [src: v8-engine-internals]
- and bump `--max-semi-space-size` for high-allocation services. (Recent Node has better cgroup awareness, but [src: v8-engine-internals]
- explicit flags remain the safe play.) [src: v8-engine-internals]
- -- [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Initialize every property in the constructor, in a fixed order.** One transition chain → one shared Map [src: v8-engine-internals]
- → monomorphic ICs. Avoid adding properties after construction. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Keep object shapes stable.** Don't `delete` properties (use `obj.x = undefined` or restructure); don't [src: v8-engine-internals]
- add properties conditionally so some instances differ in shape. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Keep arrays packed and same-kind.** Don't create holes; don't mix Smis, doubles, and objects in one [src: v8-engine-internals]
- hot array (forces the more general `PACKED_ELEMENTS`/`HOLEY_*` kind). Prefer `push` over sparse index [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Keep hot call sites monomorphic** (≤4 shapes). For genuinely heterogeneous data, consider per-shape [src: v8-engine-internals]
- specialized functions over one generic megamorphic function. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Avoid `arguments` / `with` / `eval` / non-strict sloppy patterns** that historically blocked [src: v8-engine-internals]
- optimization; use rest params instead of `arguments`. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Let functions warm up before benchmarking.** Measure steady-state (post-TurboFan), not cold first calls. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Pre-size known collections** to reduce backing-store reallocation; reuse objects/arrays to cut young-gen [src: v8-engine-internals]
- allocation churn (fewer Scavenges). [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Right-size the nursery** (`--max-semi-space-size`) for allocation-heavy services before reaching for [src: v8-engine-internals]
- -- [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Shape thrash** — mutating object structure in a loop, conditional property addition, or `delete` on hot [src: v8-engine-internals]
- objects → polymorphic/megamorphic ICs and dictionary-mode fallback. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Megamorphic dispatch** — one generic function consuming many object shapes; it never specializes even [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Deopt loops** — an optimized function repeatedly bails out (`WrongMap`, `NotASmi`, type instability) and [src: v8-engine-internals]
- re-optimizes; net slower than staying interpreted. Catch with `--trace-deopt`. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Polymorphic/holey arrays** — mixing element kinds or punching holes forces slow element access that [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Manual `global.gc()` in production** — usually pauses the main thread and hurts more than it helps; [src: v8-engine-internals]
- tune heap sizes instead. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Ignoring container limits** — default V8 heap > cgroup limit → silent OOM kill. Always set [src: v8-engine-internals]
- `--max-old-space-size` in containers. [src: v8-engine-internals]
- **Treating Maglev/TurboFan/Turbolev internals as stable API** — flag names, thresholds, and IR details [src: v8-engine-internals]
- change between V8 versions; pin behavior to the V8 version shipped in your Node release. [src: v8-engine-internals]

- <!-- Provenance: reference under the `programming-languages` hub. Mirrored from ~/.claude/skills/programming-languages/references/uv-python-toolchain.md by scripts/persist-spoke.mjs. --> [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- `uv` is an extremely fast Python package and project manager written in Rust by [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- Astral (the Ruff team). It is a single static binary that consolidates the jobs [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- previously spread across `pip`, `pip-tools`, `virtualenv`/`venv`, `pyenv`, [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- `pipx`, `poetry`, `twine`, and `build` — typically **10-100x faster** than the [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- `pip`/`pip-tools` baseline. This reference covers the five pillars named in the [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- brief: **project/workspace management**, the **universal lockfile**, [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- **Python-version install/pinning**, the **tool/pipx replacement**, and the [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- **pip-compatible interface** — plus the build backend, PEP 723 scripts, and [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- configuration/caching. [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- > For everyday Python idioms, async, typing, and a uv quick-start cheat sheet, [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- > see `references/python-patterns.md`. For static type checkers (mypy/Pyright/ [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- > ty/Pyrefly) see `references/python-static-type-checking.md`; for pytest/ [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- > Hypothesis see `references/python-testing.md`. This file is the deep, [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- > tool-specific reference for uv itself. Defer to the official docs [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- > (https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) as the source of truth for exact flags/versions. [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- `uv <command>` top-level commands (uv 0.11.x): [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- Two front-doors that confuse newcomers: the **project interface** (`uv add`, [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- `uv sync`, `uv run` — operates on `pyproject.toml` + `uv.lock`, the recommended [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- path) and the **pip interface** (`uv pip ...` — a drop-in low-level imperative [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- layer with no lockfile). Don't mix them on the same environment expecting [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- managed state; the project interface owns `uv.lock`, the pip interface does not. [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- -- [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- uv init myproject          # app layout: pyproject.toml, main.py, .python-version, .gitignore [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- uv init --lib mylib        # library layout: src/mylib/__init__.py + [build-system] [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- uv init --package myapp    # packaged app (installable, has [build-system]) [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- uv add requests 'httpx>=0.27' [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- uv add --dev pytest ruff   # dev dependency group (PEP 735 [dependency-groups]) [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- uv add --group docs mkdocs # named dependency group [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- uv run pytest              # run a command inside the project env (auto-syncs first) [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- uv run python script.py [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- uv tree                    # show the resolved dependency tree [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- uv version --bump minor    # read/update [project].version [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- `uv run` and `uv sync` **auto-create** the `.venv`, **auto-install** the pinned [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- Python if missing, **auto-lock**, and **auto-sync** before running — so the venv [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- is an implementation detail you rarely activate manually. Key files: [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- `pyproject.toml` — standard PEP 621 metadata + `[tool.uv]` config, `[dependency-groups]`, `[tool.uv.sources]`. [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- `uv.lock` — the universal lockfile (commit to git; never hand-edit). [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- `.python-version` — the pinned interpreter (written by `uv python pin`). [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- `.venv/` — the project virtualenv (gitignored). [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- **Dependency groups** (PEP 735, the modern replacement for `[project.optional-dependencies]` [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- "extras" used as dev deps): `dev` is the implicit default group. Control install [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- scope on `sync`/`run`: `--group <g>`, `--only-group <g>`, `--no-dev`, `--no-default-groups`, [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- `--all-groups`. Extras (consumer-facing optional features) are separate: [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- `--extra <e>`, `--all-extras`. [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- **Dependency sources** — `[tool.uv.sources]` redirects a dependency away from PyPI: [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- mylib       = { workspace = true }                        # local workspace member [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- httpx       = { git = "https://github.com/encode/httpx", tag = "0.27.0" } [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- foo         = { path = "../foo", editable = true }         # local editable path [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- bar         = { url = "https://example.com/bar-1.0-py3-none-any.whl" } [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- torch       = { index = "pytorch" }                        # pin to a named [[tool.uv.index]] [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- `[tool.uv.sources]` is **non-standard metadata** that uv strips when building a [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- distribution — it affects your dev resolution, not what downstream consumers get. [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- A workspace is multiple packages in one repo sharing **one `uv.lock`** and one [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- `.venv`, each with its own `pyproject.toml`. Inspired by Cargo workspaces. [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- dependencies = ["bird-feeder", "tqdm>=4,<5"] [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- members = ["packages/*"] [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- exclude = ["packages/seeds"] [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- bird-feeder = { workspace = true }   # resolve from the workspace, editable [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- Members are addressed with `uv run --package <member>` / `uv add --package <member> <dep>`. [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- `workspace = true` sources are treated as **editable** — cross-package edits are live. [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- Root `[tool.uv.sources]` apply to all members unless a member overrides them. [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- Use a workspace when packages are **co-released and tightly coupled**; use [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- separate projects (path/git sources) when versions must diverge or a member [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- needs a conflicting dependency (a single shared lock forbids conflicts). [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- -- [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- `uv.lock` is a **universal (cross-platform) resolution**: one lockfile valid for [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- every OS, architecture, and Python version inside the project's `requires-python` [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- range. A package can appear multiple times with different versions/URLs gated by [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- **environment markers** (`sys_platform`, `python_full_version`, etc.); the marker [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- chooses which entry installs on a given machine. [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- uv lock                 # create/update uv.lock [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- uv lock --check         # CI gate: fail if lockfile is stale (was --locked/--frozen era) [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- uv lock --upgrade       # re-resolve everything to newest allowed [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- uv lock --upgrade-package requests   # bump just one package [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- uv sync                 # install exactly what the lock says into .venv [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- uv sync --frozen        # install from lock without re-resolving (fail if missing/stale) [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- uv sync --locked        # assert lock is up-to-date, then install (CI) [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- uv sync --no-install-project   # deps only, skip the project itself (Docker layer caching) [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- **Resolution knobs** (also valid in the pip interface): [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- `--resolution {highest|lowest|lowest-direct}` (env `UV_RESOLUTION`). `lowest` [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- is for testing your declared lower bounds; `lowest-direct` lowers your direct [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- deps but keeps transitive at highest. [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- `--prerelease {disallow|allow|if-necessary|explicit|if-necessary-or-explicit}`. [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- `--fork-strategy {requires-python|fewest}` — `requires-python` (default) picks [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- the latest version compatible with each supported Python minor; `fewest` [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- minimizes the number of distinct versions. [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- `requires-python` semantics: uv considers **only lower bounds** of dependency [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- `requires-python` and ignores upper bounds (`>=3.8,<4` is treated as `>=3.8`), [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- because honoring upper bounds causes pathological backtracking. Your project's [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- `requires-python` must be a **subset** of every dependency's range. [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- **Export / interop** — `uv.lock` is uv-native; export to standard formats for [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- uv export --format requirements.txt -o requirements.txt [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- uv export --format pylock.toml      -o pylock.toml      # PEP 751 standard lock [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- uv export --format cyclonedx1.5     -o sbom.json        # SBOM [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- uv **reads** `pylock.toml` (PEP 751) for install but keeps `uv.lock` as its [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- native format because PEP 751 doesn't yet capture everything uv needs (e.g. full [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- fork/marker model). Treat `uv.lock` as the source of truth and `pylock.toml`/ [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- `requirements.txt` as generated artifacts. [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- `uv.lock` is **deterministic and committed**. The cross-platform guarantee is [src: uv-python-toolchain]
- the headline benefit over a platform-specific `pip-compile` `requirements.txt`. [src: uv-python-toolchain]

- <!-- Provenance: reference under the `programming-languages` hub. Mirrored from ~/.claude/skills/programming-languages/references/python-supply-chain-security.md by scripts/persist-spoke.mjs. --> [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- Python application security splits into two layers that share one toolchain: [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Application security (SAST)** — find vulnerabilities in *your own code* (bandit). [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Supply-chain security** — defend the dependencies and the path your artifacts travel: know what you ship (SBOM), know if it is vulnerable (pip-audit), prove where it came from (sigstore/PEP 740 attestations), and guarantee you install exactly what you locked (hash pinning). [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- The canonical layered ("defense in depth") posture for a 2026 Python project: **pin + hash** dependencies → **audit** them in CI (`pip-audit`) → **SAST-scan** your code (`bandit`) → **generate an SBOM** → **publish with Trusted Publishing + attestations**. Each layer closes a gap the others cannot; none is sufficient alone (hash pinning, for example, will faithfully pin a package that was *already* malicious on day one). [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- The four foundational PyPA/PyCQA tools — `pip-audit`, `bandit`, `pip` hash mode, and the PEP 740 attestation chain — are free, open source, and require no account or API key for the scanning paths. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **What it is:** the official PyPA tool that audits Python environments, `requirements` files, and dependency trees for packages with **known** vulnerabilities (SCA — software composition analysis). Maintained by the Python Packaging Authority. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Vulnerability sources:** queries the **PyPA Advisory Database** and the **OSV** database. Select via `--vulnerability-service {osv,pypi}` (osv is default); `--osv-url` points at a custom OSV mirror. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Input modes:** audit the live environment (`pip-audit`), a requirements file (`pip-audit -r requirements.txt`), or a **PEP 751 lockfile** (`pylock.toml`, supported in recent releases). For fully pinned input, skip resolution with `--no-deps` (pinned, no hashes) or `--require-hashes` (pinned + hashed). [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Auto-fix:** `--fix` upgrades vulnerable pins in place to the first non-vulnerable version; `--dry-run` previews. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Output / SBOM:** `-f {columns,json,cyclonedx-json,cyclonedx-xml,markdown}` — it can itself emit a CycloneDX SBOM with vulnerabilities linked to affected components via the `affects` field. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Why:** a machine-readable inventory of every component (incl. transitive) so downstream consumers and scanners can answer "am I affected by CVE-X?" Increasingly required by regulation (US EO 14028, EU Cyber Resilience Act). [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Two formats:** [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **CycloneDX** — security-first; built for vulnerability identification and outdated-dependency analysis. Dominant in the Python ecosystem (of the ~1.6% of PyPI packages shipping an SBOM, effectively all are CycloneDX). [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **SPDX** — license-compliance-first; richer license fields. ISO/IEC 5962 standard. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Tools:** [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- `cyclonedx-py` (the `cyclonedx-bom` distribution) — the most accurate Python-native generator; reads environments, `requirements.txt`, `poetry.lock`, `Pipfile.lock`, and pip lockfiles with proper hash support. Subcommands: `cyclonedx-py environment`, `... requirements`, `... poetry`. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- `uv export --format cyclonedx` — straight from `uv.lock` (see `references/uv-python-toolchain.md`). [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Syft** (Anchore) — ecosystem-agnostic; SBOMs from filesystems/container images; emits both CycloneDX and SPDX. Use for the *container* layer. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- `lib4sbom` — parse/convert SBOMs between SPDX and CycloneDX. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **PEP 770 (SBOMs inside wheels):** standardizes shipping SBOMs in a wheel's `.dist-info/sboms/` directory, so consumers get the SBOM automatically on `pip install`. Solves the "phantom dependency" problem (bundled non-Python libs invisible to Python-level tools). [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **What it is:** the PyCQA SAST linter for Python. Builds an **AST** per file and runs security plugins against it. Catches insecure patterns *before* runtime. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **B-codes (rule families):** B1xx general (B101 `assert`, B102 `exec`, B105/B106/B107 hardcoded passwords, B108 temp-file); B3xx blacklisted calls/imports (B301 `pickle`, B303/B304 weak MD5/SHA1 / insecure ciphers, B307 `eval`, B311 non-crypto `random`); B5xx crypto/cert (B501 `verify=False`); B6xx injection (B602 `subprocess` with `shell=True`, B608 SQL string-build); plus newer AI/ML checks (B614 unsafe `torch.load`, B615 insecure Hugging Face download). [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Severity × confidence:** every finding has a **severity** (LOW/MEDIUM/HIGH) and a **confidence** (how sure bandit is it is real). Filter both: `--severity-level medium --confidence-level medium` is the standard noise cut. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Config:** `[tool.bandit]` in `pyproject.toml` or a `.bandit` INI / `bandit.yaml` — set `exclude_dirs`, `skips` (e.g. `B101`), `tests` (allowlist), per-plugin options. Inline suppression: `# nosec B602` on the offending line (scope the code — bare `# nosec` is an anti-pattern). [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Baseline workflow:** `bandit -r src/ -f json -o baseline.json`, then `bandit -r src/ -b baseline.json` so CI only flags **newly introduced** issues — the practical way to adopt bandit on a legacy codebase without a wall of red. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **The problem PGP couldn't solve:** PyPI deprecated/removed PGP signatures — almost nobody verified them and key management was broken. PEP 740 replaces them with **identity-based** signing. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Trusted Publishing (OIDC):** instead of a long-lived API token, a CI workflow (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, etc.) presents a short-lived **OIDC identity** to PyPI and receives a short-lived upload token. No secret to leak/rotate. This is the prerequisite layer. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **PEP 740 digital attestations:** cryptographically signed, publicly verifiable statements about a package (notably **build provenance**). Built on **Sigstore** with **short-lived signing keys bound to the OIDC identity** (keyless signing → Rekor transparency log), and the payload follows the **in-toto Attestation Framework**. Because there is no private key sitting around, key loss/theft is largely designed out. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **How to get it:** if you already publish via Trusted Publishing with `pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish` **v1.11.0+**, build provenance attestations are generated and uploaded **automatically** — usually zero code change. PyPI exposes attestations + Trusted-Publishing metadata as **provenance objects** through the HTML and JSON Simple APIs. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Verification:** the `pypi-attestations` CLI / library verifies a downloaded file's attestation against the expected identity. Track ecosystem adoption at the "Are we PEP 740 yet?" dashboard. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **What it does:** records a cryptographic digest (`--hash=sha256:…`) for every artifact. On install, pip recomputes and compares; a mismatch **aborts the install**. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **What it protects against:** tampering in transit, in a cache, or on a compromised mirror; a PyPI or TLS-chain compromise; a package whose *content* changes without a version bump. It is the integrity backstop. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **What it does NOT protect against:** a package that is malicious from the first install (you just pin the malicious hash), and it says nothing about *whether* a dependency is vulnerable (that's `pip-audit`'s job). [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Generating hashes:** [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- `pip-tools`: `pip-compile --generate-hashes requirements.in` → fully pinned `requirements.txt` with `--hash` lines. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- `uv`: `uv lock` (hashes in `uv.lock`) or `uv pip compile --generate-hashes` / `uv export --format requirements-txt` (see `references/uv-python-toolchain.md`). [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- Pipenv records hashes in `Pipfile.lock` natively. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Enforcing:** `pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt`. `--require-hashes` is auto-enabled if any line has a hash; it then demands **every** requirement be pinned (`==`) and hashed, including transitive deps — which is why a hash-generating compiler is mandatory. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Lock + hash** every dependency (`uv lock` or `pip-compile --generate-hashes`); install with `--require-hashes` (`uv sync` enforces the lock). [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Audit in CI** — `pip-audit -r requirements.txt` (or against the lockfile); fail the build on findings; use `--fix --dry-run` to triage upgrades. Do **not** auto-update to latest blindly. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **SAST in CI** — `bandit -r src/ -c pyproject.toml`; run **HIGH-severity only** as a blocking gate, full set as non-blocking/local; adopt via a baseline. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Generate an SBOM** as a build artifact (`cyclonedx-py` for the app, `syft` for the image); attach to the release; PEP 770 to embed in wheels you publish. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Publish with provenance** — Trusted Publishing (OIDC, no token) + automatic PEP 740 attestations via `gh-action-pypi-publish`. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Harden the pipeline itself** — pin third-party Actions to a full commit SHA, run **zizmor** on workflows, track posture with **OpenSSF Scorecard**. The supply chain includes your *CI*, not just your deps. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- pip-audit -r requirements.txt --strict --desc [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- pip-audit -r pylock.toml -f cyclonedx-json -o sbom.json [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- bandit -r src/ -c pyproject.toml --severity-level high --confidence-level medium [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- bandit -r src/ -f json -o .bandit-baseline.json   # once, on a clean-enough commit [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- bandit -r src/ -b .bandit-baseline.json            # every PR: only NEW issues fail [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- pip-compile --generate-hashes -o requirements.txt requirements.in [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- cyclonedx-py environment -o sbom.cdx.json [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- exclude_dirs = ["tests", ".venv", "build"] [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- skips = ["B101"]            # asserts are fine in tests; scope properly instead of blanket-skipping in src [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- id-token: write            # REQUIRED for OIDC Trusted Publishing + attestations [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- runs-on: ubuntu-latest [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- uses: actions/checkout@<full-commit-sha>   # pin 3rd-party actions to a SHA [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- uses: pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish@release/v1   # ≥1.11.0 → provenance by default [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Trusting hash pinning to vet packages.** Hashes guarantee *integrity*, not *safety*. Pair with `pip-audit` (known CVEs) and review for first-time deps. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Blanket `# nosec`** with no rule code — silently suppresses *all* future findings on that line. Always `# nosec Bxxx`. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Running bandit at default severity in CI** — B101 assert noise drowns real findings; teams disable the whole tool. Filter to medium/high and use a baseline. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Long-lived PyPI API tokens in CI secrets.** Migrate to Trusted Publishing; a leaked token (cf. the 2025 GhostAction theft of 3,300+ secrets) is a full publish compromise. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Unpinned third-party GitHub Actions (`@v4`/`@main`).** A tag can be force-moved to malicious code. Pin to a full commit SHA; verify with zizmor. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Partial hashing.** `--require-hashes` requires *every* (incl. transitive) requirement pinned + hashed; a half-hashed file fails. Always regenerate via a compiler. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Generating an SBOM once and never again.** An SBOM is only useful if regenerated on every release and stored as an artifact you can query when a new CVE drops. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Auditing only direct dependencies.** Most CVEs and most supply-chain attacks ride in *transitive* deps; audit the full resolved tree/lockfile. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **`pip-audit` exits non-zero but you must ship now:** triage with `--fix --dry-run`; if a finding is a known false positive / unfixable, `--ignore-vuln <GHSA/PYSEC id>` (document why). [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **`pip install --require-hashes` fails "hashes are required for all packages":** a transitive dep is unpinned/unhashed — regenerate with `pip-compile --generate-hashes` or `uv export`. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Hash mismatch on install:** the artifact differs from the locked hash — could be a mirror/cache problem **or** tampering. Do not bypass; re-resolve from PyPI and compare. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **bandit flags `B608` SQL or `B602` subprocess you know is safe:** restructure to remove the pattern (parameterized query, `shell=False` + list args) rather than suppress — the rule is usually right. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Attestations not appearing on PyPI:** confirm `permissions: id-token: write`, `gh-action-pypi-publish` ≥ 1.11.0, and that the repo is registered as a Trusted Publisher (not token auth). [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **SBOM missing bundled native libs ("phantom dependencies"):** Python-level generators can't see vendored C libs; use Syft on the built artifact/image, and adopt PEP 770 for wheels you publish. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Typosquatting & dependency confusion** remain the top vectors: malicious packages named like `requests`/`tensorflow` (500+ typosquats in waves), and internal-name confusion pulling a public package over a private one. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **2025 PyPI phishing** — `noreply@pypj.org` (note the `j`) proxy credential harvester targeting maintainers. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **GhostAction (Sept 2025)** — injected workflows across 570+ repos, exfiltrating 3,300+ secrets incl. PyPI/npm/AWS tokens — the canonical case for Trusted Publishing over tokens and for pinning/auditing CI. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- **Shai-Hulud worm (Nov 2025)** — cross-ecosystem (npm-origin) worm that also hit PyPI via monorepos sharing credentials. [src: python-supply-chain-security]
- PyPI processed **2,000+ malware reports in 2025**, 66% within 4 hours — fast, but reactive; your pinning + audit + provenance layers are the proactive defense. [src: python-supply-chain-security]

- > Hub reference under `programming-languages`. Created via `/dr` (2026-06-01). Sources: official Python docs (profile/pstats), project docs/GitHub (py-spy, Scalene, memray, pytest-memray, Cython), the Scalene arXiv paper, pyperf docs. [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- Performance work in Python is two phases, in this order: **measure** (profile and benchmark to find the real bottleneck) then **accelerate** (fix it, native last). The most-violated rule is to optimize before profiling; the second is to trust measurements that the profiler's own overhead has distorted. Pick the tool by the *question* you are asking. [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- Monitors **every** call/return/exception with precise timing. Use the C-extension `cProfile` (low overhead); `profile` is the pure-Python, hookable, much slower twin (used for calibration). [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- python -m cProfile -o out.prof -s cumtime script.py [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- import cProfile, pstats [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- from pstats import SortKey [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- with cProfile.Profile() as pr:        # context manager (3.8+) [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- pstats.Stats(pr).strip_dirs().sort_stats(SortKey.CUMULATIVE).print_stats(15) [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- Columns: **ncalls** (call count); **tottime** (in-function, excludes subcalls — sort to find hot loops); **cumtime** (cumulative incl. subcalls — find expensive chains); two **percall**. SortKey enum (3.7+): CALLS, CUMULATIVE, FILENAME, LINE, NAME, NFL, PCALLS, STDNAME, TIME. Stats: `add()` (merge), `print_callers/callees()`, `get_stats_profile()` (3.9+). Calibration: `bias = profile.Profile().calibrate(10000)`. Visualize with **snakeviz** / **gprof2dot** / tuna. Tradeoff: per-call overhead distorts many-tiny-call workloads — use sampling for production. [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- **py-spy** (Rust, benfred; rbspy lineage) profiles a process you can't/won't instrument, including production. Separate process reading target memory (process_vm_readv / vm_read / ReadProcessMemory) — zero code changes, very low overhead. [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- py-spy record -o profile.svg --pid 12345 [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- py-spy record -o p.json --format speedscope -- python prog.py [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- py-spy top --pid 12345 [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- py-spy dump --pid 12345        # all thread stacks (find a hang) [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- Flags: `--rate`, `--duration`, **`--native`** (C/C++/Cython frames), **`--gil`** (only GIL-holding threads), `--subprocesses`, `--idle`, `--nonblocking`. Output: flamegraph SVG (default), speedscope, raw. Permissions: spawning is unprivileged; **attaching** needs sudo/ptrace on Linux (ptrace_scope), root on macOS, SYS_PTRACE in Docker/K8s. **Austin** is a sibling C frame-stack sampler for the same flamegraph/speedscope pipeline. [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- plasma-umass profiler that **separates Python vs native (C/C++) vs system (I/O) time** plus GPU + memory at per-line granularity — instantly answers "is this even optimizable in Python?" (mostly *system* time = I/O-bound; mostly *native* = inside a C library). [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- scalene run prog.py            # → scalene-profile.json [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- scalene view --html            # or --cli/--standalone/--json [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- Flags: `--cpu-only`/`--gpu`/`--memory`, `--reduced-profile`, `--profile-only/-exclude`, thresholds. Target with `@profile` or `scalene_profiler.start()/stop()`. **Copy volume (MB/s)** flags costly silent C↔Python / CPU↔GPU copies. Low overhead via sampling + signal handlers + native stack stitching (~10–20%). AI suggestions (⚡/💥) via Bedrock/Azure/OpenAI/Ollama; experimental `--memory-leak-detector`. [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- Tracks allocations in **Python, native extensions, and the interpreter** by intercepting allocators. **Linux/macOS only (no Windows).** [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- memray run [--native] [--follow-fork] [--trace-python-allocators] script.py   # → capture.bin [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- memray run --live script.py [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- memray flamegraph capture.bin     # default reporter (also: table, tree, summary, stats) [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- memray flamegraph --leaks capture.bin      # allocations never freed [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- memray flamegraph --temporal capture.bin   # over-time [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- `--native` adds C/C++ frames (essential for numpy/pandas). **pytest-memray:** `--memray` + `@pytest.mark.limit_memory("100 MB")`. Default = high-watermark (peak); `--leaks`/`--temporal` switch modes. [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- kernprof -l -v script.py        # @profile-decorated functions; → script.py.lprof [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- Reports Hits / Time / Per Hit / % Time per source line. **py-heat** = heatmap. Real overhead — scope to the one function under investigation. [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- **timeit** — micro-snippets (`python -m timeit "..."`); weak isolation. [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- **pyperf** (PSF) — rigorous: multi-process, warmup (skips first value), mean±stdev, keeps GC, `pyperf system tune` to suppress outliers. Use for any "A vs B" claim that matters. [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- **pytest-benchmark** — benchmarks in the test suite, regression tracking; pair with CI perf budgets. [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- **Width = cost** (time, or bytes for memray). X-axis is **not** time order in a classic flame graph — it's grouped/sorted stacks. [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- **Self time** (frame's own bar minus children) vs **cumulative** (whole stack width). Wide frame + narrow children = work is here; wide children = cost is below. [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- **speedscope** views: Time Order, Left Heavy (best for biggest contributors), Sandwich. py-spy `--gil` shows real on-CPU Python. [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- **Algorithm / data structure** — biggest wins (O(n²)→O(n log n), set/dict membership, generators). [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- **Builtins / vectorization** — push loops into C (comprehensions, str.join, itertools, **NumPy** vectorized ops). [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- **Concurrency** — asyncio/threads for I/O; processes (or free-threaded 3.13t+) for CPU-bound. [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- **Native compilation** of the proven hotspot: [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- Cython: use **typed memoryviews** (`double[:, ::1]`) for fast array access (unlocks nogil); `prange(..., nogil=True)` for OpenMP; run **`cython -a`** and drive yellow (Python-object) lines white. Pure-Python mode keeps source runnable as plain `.py`. [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- **Optimizing before profiling** — intuition about Python hotspots is usually wrong. [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- **Trusting overhead-distorted numbers** — cProfile inflates many-small-call code; line_profiler inflates the line under test. Cross-check with py-spy/Scalene before a rewrite. [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- **Optimizing the wrong layer** — system-time (I/O) or native-time (C library) lines won't get faster from Python changes; Scalene's split catches this. [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- **Micro-benchmarking without warmup/isolation** — use pyperf for decisions. [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- **Reaching for native too early** — exhaust algorithm/vectorization/concurrency first. [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- **Wall-clock vs CPU time** — a sleep/network-bound function isn't a JIT candidate. [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- **Forgetting `--native`** — hides the C-extension frames where cost often lives (numpy/pandas/torch). [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- **memray on Windows** — unsupported; use py-spy or tracemalloc there. [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- Python docs — Profilers: https://docs.python.org/3/library/profile.html • pstats: https://docs.python.org/3/library/pstats.html [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- py-spy: https://github.com/benfred/py-spy [src: cpython-performance-profiling]
- Scalene: https://github.com/plasma-umass/scalene • arXiv: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.07597 [src: cpython-performance-profiling]

- Cython parallelism: https://cython.readthedocs.io/en/latest/src/userguide/parallelism.html • memoryviews: https://docs.cython.org/en/latest/src/userguide/memoryviews.html [src: cpython-performance-profiling]

- <!-- Provenance: reference under the `devops-infra` hub. Mirrored from ~/.claude/skills/devops-infra/references/linux-boot-init.md by scripts/persist-spoke.mjs. --> [src: linux-boot-init]
- On a modern machine the boot is a **chain of trust and handoffs**, each stage finding, optionally [src: linux-boot-init]
- verifying, and launching the next: [src: linux-boot-init]
- └─ UEFI firmware (PEI/DXE)  → reads BootOrder/Boot#### EFI vars, runs a boot entry from the ESP [src: linux-boot-init]
- └─ shim (MS-signed)    → [Secure Boot] verifies next stage against db + MOK; loads GRUB or sd-boot [src: linux-boot-init]
- └─ boot loader    → GRUB 2 / systemd-boot: picks a menu entry, loads kernel + initrd [src: linux-boot-init]
- └─ kernel    → decompresses, mounts the initramfs as a tmpfs root, runs its /init [src: linux-boot-init]
- └─ initramfs (early userspace, dracut) → finds/assembles/unlocks the REAL root [src: linux-boot-init]
- └─ switch_root → exec /sbin/init (= systemd) as PID 1 on the real root [src: linux-boot-init]
- └─ systemd → reaches default.target (multi-user / graphical) [src: linux-boot-init]
- This reference covers everything up to and including `switch_root`. What systemd does **after** it [src: linux-boot-init]
- becomes PID 1 (units, targets, ordering) is `references/systemd.md`. Kernel internals after [src: linux-boot-init]
- decompression (scheduler, syscall ABI, module loading, `init=`) are `references/linux-kernel-architecture.md`. [src: linux-boot-init]
- Legacy BIOS/MBR boot still exists (boot.img in the MBR → core.img from the post-MBR gap or BIOS Boot [src: linux-boot-init]
- Partition), but UEFI is the default on essentially all hardware since ~2012 and is assumed throughout; [src: linux-boot-init]
- BIOS differences are called out where they matter. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **EFI System Partition (ESP):** a FAT32 partition (GPT type `c12a7328-...`), conventionally mounted at [src: linux-boot-init]
- `/boot/efi` (older) or `/efi` (newer, when `/boot` is a separate XBOOTLDR). Holds `.efi` PE executables [src: linux-boot-init]
- under `\EFI\<vendor>\`. Firmware can read FAT directly — no filesystem driver needed in the OS yet. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Boot manager + NVRAM variables:** firmware stores `Boot0000`…`BootFFFF` entries (each a device path + [src: linux-boot-init]
- loader path + optional args) and an ordered `BootOrder`, plus `BootNext`/`BootCurrent`. Manage from [src: linux-boot-init]
- Linux with `efibootmgr` (e.g. `efibootmgr -c -d /dev/sda -p 1 -L "Linux" -l '\EFI\fedora\shimx64.efi'`). [src: linux-boot-init]
- These live in `efivarfs` at `/sys/firmware/efi/efivars/`. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Fallback/removable path:** `\EFI\BOOT\BOOTX64.EFI` (BOOTAA64.EFI on ARM) is the default the firmware [src: linux-boot-init]
- runs when no valid NVRAM entry matches — important for removable media and recovery. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **DXE/BDS phases:** firmware initializes silicon (PEI), loads drivers (DXE), then the Boot Device [src: linux-boot-init]
- Selection (BDS) phase walks BootOrder. Secure Boot enforcement begins here. [src: linux-boot-init]
- Secure Boot makes the firmware refuse to run any boot binary whose signature is not chained to a trusted key. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Key hierarchy:** **PK** (Platform Key, owns the machine) → **KEK** (Key Exchange Keys) → [src: linux-boot-init]
- **db** (allowed signatures/hashes) and **dbx** (forbidden/revoked — *blacklist wins*). OEMs ship [src: linux-boot-init]
- Microsoft's certs in db by default. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **shim:** because distros can't get every kernel signed by Microsoft, they ship **shim** — a small [src: linux-boot-init]
- first-stage loader signed by **Microsoft's UEFI CA**. Firmware verifies shim against db; shim then [src: linux-boot-init]
- carries the **distro's** embedded certificate (e.g. Canonical/Red Hat) and verifies GRUB and the kernel [src: linux-boot-init]
- against it, plus a local **MOK** list. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **MOK (Machine Owner Key):** a user-enrolled key shim also trusts. Enroll with `mokutil --import key.der` [src: linux-boot-init]
- (sets a one-shot password; on next boot **MokManager** prompts to confirm — this UI cannot be scripted, [src: linux-boot-init]
- by design). Used to sign your own kernels, out-of-tree modules (NVIDIA/VirtualBox/DKMS), or custom GRUB. [src: linux-boot-init]
- The kernel honors a MOK with the module-signing KeyUsage OID `1.3.6.1.4.1.2312.16.1.2`. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **SBAT (UEFI Secure Boot Advanced Targeting):** generation-based revocation embedded in shim/GRUB so a [src: linux-boot-init]
- vulnerable bootloader can be revoked via a metadata bump (a `.sbat` section + `SbatLevel` var) instead of [src: linux-boot-init]
- blacklisting thousands of individual hashes in dbx. This is how the 2020 BootHole and later GRUB CVEs [src: linux-boot-init]
- were rolled out; a `dbx`/SBAT update that outpaces your installed shim is a classic "stopped booting [src: linux-boot-init]
- after a firmware/Windows update" cause. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Lockdown:** when Secure Boot is on, the kernel enters **lockdown (integrity) mode**, blocking [src: linux-boot-init]
- `/dev/mem`, kexec of unsigned images, unsigned module load, certain BPF, hibernation, etc. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **GRUB 2** (the default on most general-purpose distros): [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Stages:** `boot.img` (BIOS: 446-byte MBR stub) → `core.img` (built by `grub-mkimage`/`grub-install`, [src: linux-boot-init]
- contains just enough modules — a filesystem driver, etc. — to read `/boot/grub`). On UEFI the equivalent [src: linux-boot-init]
- is `grubx64.efi` (loaded by shim). Stage modules (`*.mod`) live under `/boot/grub/`. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Config:** `/boot/grub2/grub.cfg` (RHEL) or `/boot/grub/grub.cfg` (Debian) is **generated, not [src: linux-boot-init]
- hand-edited**: `grub-mkconfig -o …` (Debian: `update-grub`) stitches together `/etc/default/grub` [src: linux-boot-init]
- (e.g. `GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX`) and the `/etc/grub.d/` scripts (`10_linux`, `30_os-prober`, `40_custom`). [src: linux-boot-init]
- **`menuentry`:** each entry runs `linux /vmlinuz-… root=… <cmdline>` then `initrd /initramfs-….img`. [src: linux-boot-init]
- The kernel version in the `linux` line **must** match the `initrd` line. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **BLS (Boot Loader Spec) Type 1 entries:** Fedora/RHEL ≥8 no longer regenerate full menus — `grub.cfg` [src: linux-boot-init]
- becomes a thin loader that reads drop-in `*.conf` files from `/boot/loader/entries/` [src: linux-boot-init]
- (`<machine-id>-<kernel-version>.conf` with `title`/`linux`/`initrd`/`options` keys). Managed by [src: linux-boot-init]
- `kernel-install` / `grubby`. Edit `options` with `grubby --update-kernel`. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **systemd-boot (`sd-boot`)** — a much simpler UEFI-only manager: [src: linux-boot-init]
- Drops `systemd-bootx64.efi` on the ESP; **auto-discovers** kernels from BLS Type 1 entries in [src: linux-boot-init]
- `$BOOT/loader/entries/` **and** Type 2 UKIs in `$BOOT/EFI/Linux/` — no generated config, no scripting. [src: linux-boot-init]
- Installed/updated with `bootctl install|update`. Global settings in `loader/loader.conf`. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Unified Kernel Image (UKI)** — the modern direction: [src: linux-boot-init]
- A single signed UEFI PE binary bundling **stub + kernel + initrd + cmdline + (optional) splash/devicetree** [src: linux-boot-init]
- in named PE sections (`.linux`, `.initrd`, `.cmdline`, `.osrel`, …). The reference stub is [src: linux-boot-init]
- **systemd-stub** (`linuxx64.efi.stub`); build with `ukify` or `dracut --uefi`. [src: linux-boot-init]
- Because the cmdline and initrd are *inside the signed image*, Secure Boot now covers them too (a plain [src: linux-boot-init]
- GRUB+initrd setup leaves the initrd and cmdline unsigned). Place in `$BOOT/EFI/Linux/*.efi`; bootable [src: linux-boot-init]
- directly by firmware or auto-listed by sd-boot. Standardized by the UAPI Group (UAPI.5). [src: linux-boot-init]
- Passed by the loader (or baked into a UKI). Selected high-value parameters: [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Root:** `root=UUID=…` / `root=/dev/mapper/…`, `rootflags=`, `ro`, `rootfstype=`. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **initramfs control (dracut):** `rd.break[=pre-mount|mount|pre-pivot]`, `rd.shell`, `rd.debug`, [src: linux-boot-init]
- `rd.luks.uuid=`, `rd.lvm.lv=vg/lv`, `rd.md.uuid=`, `rootdelay=`. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Init/handoff:** `init=/bin/sh` (override PID 1 — recovery), `systemd.unit=rescue.target`, [src: linux-boot-init]
- `systemd.unit=emergency.target`, `single`/`1`. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Diagnostics:** `quiet`/`splash` (remove to see messages), `loglevel=`, `nomodeset`, `systemd.log_level=debug`. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Why it exists:** the kernel needs drivers and userspace logic to *find* the real root — but those may [src: linux-boot-init]
- live *on* the root (chicken-and-egg) or require assembly (LVM, LUKS decryption, mdraid, multipath, [src: linux-boot-init]
- iSCSI/NFS, ZFS). The **initramfs** is a CPIO archive the kernel unpacks into a tmpfs and runs as a [src: linux-boot-init]
- temporary root; it loads modules, assembles/unlocks the real root, mounts it, and pivots. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **initrd vs initramfs:** old `initrd` = a block-device image mounted as root; modern **initramfs** = a [src: linux-boot-init]
- CPIO archive extracted into rootfs (tmpfs). Both are commonly called "the initrd"; the file is gzip/zstd [src: linux-boot-init]
- CPIO (sometimes a concatenation, e.g. an early-cpio microcode blob + the main archive). [src: linux-boot-init]
- **dracut** (RHEL/Fedora/SUSE/Arch; Debian/Ubuntu historically use `initramfs-tools`/`mkinitcpio` on Arch): [src: linux-boot-init]
- builds the image **event-driven and host-specific by default** (`hostonly`, only the modules this machine [src: linux-boot-init]
- needs) vs `--no-hostonly` (generic, portable to other hardware — what distro installers ship). [src: linux-boot-init]
- Build: `dracut [--force] /boot/initramfs-$(uname -r).img $(uname -r)`; inspect with `lsinitrd`. [src: linux-boot-init]
- Config: `/etc/dracut.conf` + `/etc/dracut.conf.d/*.conf` (`add_dracutmodules`, `omit_dracutmodules`, [src: linux-boot-init]
- `add_drivers`, `install_items`). [src: linux-boot-init]
- **dracut modules** (under `/usr/lib/dracut/modules.d/`, e.g. `90lvm`, `90crypt`, `90mdraid`, `95nfs`, [src: linux-boot-init]
- `01systemd`) declare dependencies and inject scripts. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Two execution models inside the initramfs:** [src: linux-boot-init]
- **systemd-in-initrd** (now the default on systemd distros): systemd itself is PID 1 in the initrd and [src: linux-boot-init]
- drives it via `initrd.target` → `initrd-root-device.target` → mount real root at `/sysroot` → [src: linux-boot-init]
- `initrd-root-fs.target` → `initrd-switch-root.target`. The contract is in `systemd.io/INITRD_INTERFACE` [src: linux-boot-init]
- (real root must end up at `/sysroot`). [src: linux-boot-init]
- **legacy dracut `/init` script** with **hook directories** run in order: [src: linux-boot-init]
- `cmdline → pre-udev → pre-trigger → initqueue (main loop, settles devices) → pre-mount → mount → [src: linux-boot-init]
- pre-pivot → cleanup`. Custom logic drops scripts into the matching `hooks/<name>/` dir. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **The handoff — `switch_root`:** once `/sysroot` (the real root) is mounted, early userspace kills udev, [src: linux-boot-init]
- cleans up, and calls **`switch_root`** — which *deletes* the initramfs tmpfs contents, `chroot`s into the [src: linux-boot-init]
- real root, and `exec`s the real `/sbin/init` (systemd) as PID 1. (`pivot_root` is the older mechanism; [src: linux-boot-init]
- `switch_root` is purpose-built for an initramfs-on-rootfs and frees the RAM.) On shutdown, systemd can [src: linux-boot-init]
- jump *back* into `/run/initramfs/shutdown` to tear down complex storage it is itself running from. [src: linux-boot-init]
- Distinct from Secure Boot (which *gates*), **measured boot** *records*: each stage hashes the next into [src: linux-boot-init]
- TPM2 **PCRs** before running it (PCR 4 = boot loader/EFI apps, PCR 7 = Secure Boot policy/keys, [src: linux-boot-init]
- **PCR 11** = UKI sections via systemd-stub, PCR 12 = cmdline/credentials, PCR 13 = sysext). [src: linux-boot-init]
- **systemd-cryptenroll --tpm2-device=auto** seals a LUKS key to a PCR policy so the root disk [src: linux-boot-init]
- auto-unlocks **only if the boot chain is unmodified**. `systemd-measure` pre-computes/signs expected [src: linux-boot-init]
- PCR 11 values for a UKI so unlock survives kernel updates (signature-based PCR policy). [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Where did it stop?** Firmware screen → no entry/Secure Boot reject. GRUB prompt → loader OK, config/kernel [src: linux-boot-init]
- issue. Kernel panic "VFS: unable to mount root" or dracut emergency shell → initramfs couldn't find/assemble [src: linux-boot-init]
- root. Login/systemd errors → you're past `switch_root`; this is now a `systemd.md` problem. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Is Secure Boot involved?** `mokutil --sb-state`. If it broke right after a firmware/Windows/`dbx` update, [src: linux-boot-init]
- suspect SBAT/dbx revocation outpacing your shim/GRUB. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Inspect the chain:** `bootctl status` (loader + ESP + entries), `efibootmgr -v` (NVRAM order), [src: linux-boot-init]
- `lsinitrd /boot/initramfs-….img` (is the needed storage module/key present?). [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Reproduce/interrupt:** at GRUB press `e`, remove `quiet`, add `rd.break` (or `rd.break=pre-mount`) to land [src: linux-boot-init]
- in the dracut shell at the chosen stage. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Fix forward:** correct the cause, then **always rebuild** (`dracut --force`) and **regenerate loader [src: linux-boot-init]
- config** so the fix is persistent and survives the next kernel update. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Sign your own boot chain (Secure Boot, your keys):** `sbctl` is the easy path — `sbctl create-keys`, [src: linux-boot-init]
- `sbctl enroll-keys` (optionally `-m` to keep Microsoft certs for firmware/Option ROMs), then [src: linux-boot-init]
- `sbctl sign -s /boot/vmlinuz-… ` / sign your UKI. Verify with `sbctl verify`. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Move to a UKI + systemd-boot:** generate a UKI (`ukify`/`dracut --uefi`) into `/efi/EFI/Linux/`, [src: linux-boot-init]
- `bootctl install`. Gains signed cmdline+initrd and clean TPM PCR 11 measurement; drop GRUB entirely. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Recover a borked root password / fstab:** boot to `emergency.target` or `init=/bin/sh`; for SELinux [src: linux-boot-init]
- systems use `rd.break`, `mount -o remount,rw /sysroot`, `chroot /sysroot`, fix, and `touch /.autorelabel`. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Persist a kernel arg the right way:** edit `GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX` + `grub-mkconfig` (classic GRUB), or [src: linux-boot-init]
- `grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args="…"` (BLS), or the UKI's `.cmdline`/`kernel-install` (UKI) — not the [src: linux-boot-init]
- generated `grub.cfg`. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Hand-editing `grub.cfg`.** It is regenerated on the next kernel update and your change vanishes. Edit the [src: linux-boot-init]
- source (`/etc/default/grub`, `/etc/grub.d/`, or the BLS `options`). [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Mismatched `linux`/`initrd` versions** in a menuentry → kernel boots but can't load matching modules. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **`hostonly` initramfs cloned to different hardware** → missing storage/NIC driver → unbootable. Use [src: linux-boot-init]
- `--no-hostonly` for portable/golden images and rescue initramfs. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Forgetting to rebuild the initramfs** after adding LUKS/LVM/RAID, changing the root device, or installing [src: linux-boot-init]
- a storage driver → "unable to mount root" on next boot. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Plain GRUB+initrd and assuming Secure Boot protects you end-to-end** — the cmdline and initrd are [src: linux-boot-init]
- *unsigned* there; only a UKI (or signed initrd scheme) closes that gap. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Enrolling a MOK and walking away** — MokManager needs the physical/interactive confirmation on reboot; [src: linux-boot-init]
- unattended enrollment silently does nothing. [src: linux-boot-init]
- **Sealing LUKS to PCRs without a signed/`pcrlock` policy** → every kernel/firmware update changes the PCRs [src: linux-boot-init]
- and locks you out. Use PCR 11 signature policy (systemd-measure) or `systemd-pcrlock`. [src: linux-boot-init]
