- <!-- Provenance: reference under the `programming-languages` hub. Mirrored from ~/.claude/skills/programming-languages/references/python-in-browser-wasm.md by scripts/persist-spoke.mjs. --> [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- "Python in the browser" means compiling a Python interpreter to **WebAssembly (WASM)** so it runs inside the browser's WASM VM (or a server-side WASM runtime) instead of a native OS process. There is no native Python in a browser; everything routes through one of two WASM targets of CPython: [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- **`wasm32-emscripten`** — CPython compiled with **Emscripten**, which emulates a POSIX-ish environment (a virtual filesystem, a JS-backed libc) on top of the browser/JS host. This is the target **Pyodide** ships, and is the one that runs *in a browser tab* or in Node.js. CPython tier-3 since 3.14 (restored Oct 2024). [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- **`wasm32-wasi`** — CPython compiled against the **WASI** (WebAssembly System Interface) ABI, a capability-based syscall layer. Runs in standalone WASM runtimes (**wasmtime**, Wasmer, WasmEdge) for server-side/edge/sandboxed/plugin use, *not* the browser DOM. CPython **tier 2** since 3.13.0 (the first final release to ship it). [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- A third lever is the **interpreter choice**: full **Pyodide (CPython)** — large but complete, with NumPy/SciPy/pandas — versus **MicroPython** — tiny (~300 KB) and near-instant but a reduced language/stdlib. PyScript lets you pick per-page. [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- The defining reality of all WASM Python: **single-threaded, sandboxed, no OS.** No real threads, no raw sockets, no blocking stdin, and a multi-megabyte cold-start download for full CPython. Design around these from the start. [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- Browser tab ── Pyodide (wasm32-emscripten) ──► JS host (DOM, fetch, Web APIs) via FFI [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- Web Worker ── Pyodide/MicroPython ───────────► off-main-thread, keeps UI responsive [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- Server/edge ── CPython (wasm32-wasi) ────────► wasmtime/Wasmer, capability-gated FS/net [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- PyScript ──── polyscript core ───────────────► orchestrates either runtime + DOM components [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- Both targets cross-compile CPython. Emscripten produces a `.wasm` + a JS loader (`pyodide.js`) plus a packaged stdlib; WASI produces a `python.wasm` you feed to a runtime. WASM is **single-threaded by default**; pthreads need SharedArrayBuffer + cross-origin isolation (COOP/COEP headers) and are still not generally usable for CPython's threading model. The **PEP 11 platform tiers** govern support: WASI is **tier 2** (3.13+, PEP 816 pins WASI + WASI-SDK versions per release), Emscripten is **tier 3** (3.14+, PEP 776 defines it). Everything else (Pyodide FFI, packaging) layers on top of this. [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- Pyodide is **a port of CPython to Emscripten/WASM** providing three things: (a) the CPython interpreter compiled with Emscripten + a few patches; (b) a **JS⟺Python foreign function interface (FFI)**; (c) a catalog of third-party packages (NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, etc.) precompiled to WASM. Loaded with the async `loadPyodide()`; run code with `pyodide.runPython(code)` (sync) or `pyodide.runPythonAsync(code)` (supports top-level `await` via `eval_code_async`). Hit ~1B+ JsDelivr requests in 2025; usage doubling year-over-year. Also powers **Cloudflare Python Workers** and Node.js Python embedding. [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- The FFI is the heart of in-browser Python. Two translation strategies: **convert** (copy a value into a native object of the other language) or **proxy** (wrap the original). Crossing the boundary yields proxies: a Python object handed to JS becomes a **`PyProxy`**; a JS object handed to Python becomes a **`JsProxy`**. `PyProxy.toJs()` (JS) / `to_js()` (Python) does an explicit deep conversion; `create_proxy()` wraps a Python callable as a persistent JS function (e.g. for `addEventListener`). **PEP 818** is upstreaming the *core* of this FFI into CPython itself (the `js` module + proxy machinery) so it's standard, not Pyodide-private. [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- PyScript is **not a runtime**; it's a framework built on a small core called **polyscript** that orchestrates a runtime (Pyodide *or* MicroPython) plus DOM integration. You write `<script type="py">…</script>` (Pyodide) or `<script type="mpy">…</script>` (MicroPython), configure via `<py-config>`/`<mpy-config>` or an external `pyscript.toml`/`.json`, and get components like `<py-editor>`/`<mpy-editor>` (REPL widgets) and the `pyscript` Python module (`display()`, `when`, `PyWorker`, DOM access). Pyodide is the default runtime "for the foreseeable future"; MicroPython is the lightweight option. [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- **Pyodide (CPython):** ~11 MB+ runtime download (full distribution effectively ~15 MB; big packages like pandas/SciPy add more), slow cold start, but real CPython with the C-extension scientific stack and `micropip`/PyPI. [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- **MicroPython:** ~300 KB total, **loads instantly and runs in <100 ms**, ideal for mobile/constrained/educational/visualization use. No `micropip`/PyPI; uses `mip` + `micropython-lib`. A reduced language and stdlib. [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- Choose MicroPython when startup latency and footprint dominate; choose Pyodide when you need the real CPython ecosystem. [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- Historically you could not put WASM wheels on PyPI; you used anaconda.org or jsdelivr. **PEP 783 (accepted)** defines a `pyodide_${YEAR}_${PATCH}_wasm32` platform tag (the **PyEmscripten** ABI) so binary wheels can ship on PyPI. Key rule: **one ABI per Python version** — wheels built for one Pyodide build work across all Pyodide versions sharing that Python version. Build with `pyodide build`/`pyodide-build` or `cibuildwheel`; no Docker needed (just Linux + matching Python/Node/Emscripten). Pure-Python wheels install via **`micropip.install()`**; Pyodide-built C-extension packages also load via `pyodide.loadPackage()` (lower overhead, more limited). [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- WASI CPython runs *outside* the browser in a WASM runtime (**wasmtime** is the officially recommended one). Use cases: sandboxed plugin execution, edge functions, embedding Python as a guest with host-provided functions, and capability-secure execution (the runtime grants explicit FS/socket capabilities; nothing is ambient). Cross-compile via `Tools/wasm/` / `Platforms/WASI` in the CPython tree (configure for the build Python, then the host WASI Python with the WASI-SDK). You can even drive a WASI CPython from a host and extend it with host functions. **PEP 816** governs which WASI/WASI-SDK versions a CPython release targets. [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- **Where does it run?** Browser DOM → Emscripten (Pyodide/PyScript). Server/edge/plugin/sandbox → WASI + wasmtime. [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- **How much Python do you need?** Scientific stack / real CPython → Pyodide. Tiny + instant → MicroPython. [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- **Hand-rolled or framework?** Direct JS control / embedding → Pyodide JS API. Declarative HTML app → PyScript. [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- **Keep the UI alive:** run the interpreter in a **Web Worker** so heavy compute / package loads don't block the main thread. [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- **Plan the FFI boundary:** decide convert-vs-proxy per value, and own PyProxy/JsProxy lifetimes (destroy explicitly). [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- **Package strategy:** prefer PyPI wheels via `micropip`; for C extensions ensure a PEP 783 `pyodide_*` wheel or a Pyodide-built package exists. [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- **Bootstrap Pyodide and run code (browser/Node):** [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- const pyodide = await loadPyodide();              // async; loads the WASM + stdlib [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- await pyodide.loadPackage("numpy");                // load a Pyodide-built package [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- await pyodide.runPythonAsync(` [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- `);                                                 // top-level await supported [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- **Install a pure-Python PyPI wheel at runtime:** [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- await pyodide.loadPackage("micropip"); [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- const micropip = pyodide.pyimport("micropip"); [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- await micropip.install("snowballstemmer");          // from PyPI / JsDelivr / URL [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- **FFI: persistent callback + explicit cleanup:** [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- const proxy = pyodide.runPython("lambda evt: print('clicked', evt.type)"); [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- const handler = proxy.create_proxy ? proxy : pyodide.ffi.create_proxy(proxy); [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- document.body.addEventListener("click", handler); [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- // later, when removed: handler.destroy(); proxy.destroy();  // avoid the leak [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- **PyScript app with external config + worker:** [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- <script type="py" src="./main.py" config="./pyscript.toml" worker></script> [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- packages = ["pandas"]              # micropip names (Pyodide only) [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- "./data.csv" = "data.csv"          # mount a file into the virtual FS [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- **Run CPython under WASI with wasmtime (server-side):** [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- wasmtime run --dir=. python.wasm -- script.py     # --dir grants FS capability explicitly [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- **Assuming threads/multiprocessing work.** Pyodide has **no threading or multiprocessing**; packages using them need patching to disable it. Don't port a thread-pool design unchanged. [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- **Expecting raw sockets / blocking network.** No raw socket access; only HTTP(S), subject to CORS; no synchronous networking on the main thread. The `socket` module is present but always non-blocking and needs a server-side WebSocket-to-TCP proxy. [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- **Leaking PyProxy/JsProxy.** A return-value `PyProxy` must be `destroy()`-ed or it leaks; a JS→Python→JS reference loop never gets GC'd. Don't rely solely on `FinalizationRegistry`. [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- **Blocking the main thread.** Loading Pyodide + big packages on the UI thread freezes the page. Use a Web Worker. [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- **Shipping full Pyodide for trivial logic.** Don't download 15 MB to run 10 lines — use MicroPython, or lazy-load Pyodide only when needed. [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- **Treating files as persistent.** The Emscripten virtual FS is in-memory; files vanish on refresh/close unless you persist them out (IndexedDB/server). [src: python-in-browser-wasm]
- **Putting raw WASM wheels on PyPI pre-PEP-783, or mixing ABIs.** Use the `pyodide_*` tag and respect one-ABI-per-Python-version. [src: python-in-browser-wasm]

- <!-- Provenance: reference under the `devops-infra` hub. Mirrored from ~/.claude/skills/devops-infra/references/linux-package-management.md by scripts/persist-spoke.mjs. --> [src: linux-package-management]
- A Linux *package* is an archive of files plus metadata (name, version, dependencies, scripts, [src: linux-package-management]
- signature). A *package manager* resolves dependencies, fetches packages from *repositories*, [src: linux-package-management]
- verifies their signatures, and applies the change as a *transaction* recorded in a local database. [src: linux-package-management]
- There are two layers in every native stack: [src: linux-package-management]
- **Low-level tool** — operates on a single local package file and the package DB. No dependency [src: linux-package-management]
- resolution, no network: `dpkg` (.deb), `rpm` (.rpm), `pacman -U` (.pkg.tar.zst). [src: linux-package-management]
- **High-level tool** — resolves dependencies and talks to repositories: `apt`, `dnf`, `pacman -S`. [src: linux-package-management]
- Use the high-level tool for normal work; drop to the low-level tool only to install a downloaded [src: linux-package-management]
- file or to inspect/repair the database. The three native ecosystems map cleanly onto each other, [src: linux-package-management]
- so once you know the model you mostly translate verbs. Above the native layer sit the [src: linux-package-management]
- **universal formats** (Flatpak, Snap, Nix) which bundle dependencies and are cross-distro. [src: linux-package-management]
- These ideas are identical across apt, dnf, and pacman — learn them once. [src: linux-package-management]
- **Package + metadata.** Files + a manifest declaring `Depends`/`Requires`/`depends`, [src: linux-package-management]
- `Conflicts`, `Provides` (virtual packages, e.g. `mail-transport-agent`), version constraints, [src: linux-package-management]
- and pre/post install scripts. [src: linux-package-management]
- **Dependency resolution.** Given a request, the solver computes a consistent set of installs, [src: linux-package-management]
- upgrades, and removals. Modern solvers are SAT/backtracking-based (APT's *solver3*, dnf's [src: linux-package-management]
- *libsolv*, pacman's internal resolver). When no consistent set exists you get a conflict the [src: linux-package-management]
- **Repositories.** Signed collections of packages + an index (Debian `Release`/`Packages`, [src: linux-package-management]
- RPM `repodata/repomd.xml`, Arch `*.db`). The client downloads the index, then packages. [src: linux-package-management]
- **Metadata cache vs installed DB.** Two distinct things: the *downloaded repo index* (refreshed by [src: linux-package-management]
- `apt update`, `dnf makecache`, `pacman -Sy`) and the *local installed-package DB* [src: linux-package-management]
- (`/var/lib/dpkg`, the rpmdb in `/var/lib/rpm` or `/usr/lib/sysimage/rpm`, `/var/lib/pacman/local`). [src: linux-package-management]
- **Transaction.** An all-or-nothing batch. dnf records every transaction with full undo/rollback; [src: linux-package-management]
- dpkg/apt and pacman keep logs (`/var/log/dpkg.log`, `/var/log/pacman.log`) but weaker rollback. [src: linux-package-management]
- **Trust/signing.** Repos sign their index; clients verify against a trusted keyring before [src: linux-package-management]
- trusting any package hash. This is the security boundary — never disable it casually. [src: linux-package-management]
- **Explicit vs dependency (orphan tracking).** Managers mark whether you asked for a package or it [src: linux-package-management]
- came in as a dependency, so orphans can be auto-removed (`apt autoremove`, `dnf autoremove`, [src: linux-package-management]
- **APT 3.0+ (Debian 13 "trixie", Ubuntu 25.04+)** ships a colorized UI and **solver3**, a [src: linux-package-management]
- backtracking, SAT-solver-inspired resolver with unit propagation — faster, more predictable, [src: linux-package-management]
- better at preserving the order of alternatives and explaining conflicts than the classic solver. [src: linux-package-management]
- 1 added per-repo package excludes; 3.3.1 continued solver tuning. Signature verification moved [src: linux-package-management]
- to **Sequoia-PGP** (`sqv`) instead of GnuPG. [src: linux-package-management]
- **Repository config**: `/etc/apt/sources.list` (legacy one-line) or `*.list` / [src: linux-package-management]
- modern **deb822** `*.sources` files in `/etc/apt/sources.list.d/`. Each repo's signing key goes in [src: linux-package-management]
- `/usr/share/keyrings/*.gpg` (or `.pgp`) and is bound with `Signed-By:` (deb822) or [src: linux-package-management]
- `[signed-by=…]` (one-line). `apt-key` is **deprecated** — never add keys to the global keyring. [src: linux-package-management]
- `apt` is the human-facing CLI; `apt-get`/`apt-cache` are the stable scripting interfaces. [src: linux-package-management]
- **dnf5** (default in Fedora 41+; the C++ rewrite) is faster and replaces `dnf`/`microdnf`. Note [src: linux-package-management]
- **partial parity gaps**: some users hit `Unknown argument 'undo'` and rollback edge cases on dnf5 [src: linux-package-management]
- — verify history subcommands on your version. dnf 5.4 improved transaction history precision. [src: linux-package-management]
- **RHEL caveat**: `dnf history undo`/`rollback` is **not supported** for downgrading core packages [src: linux-package-management]
- (`kernel`, `glibc`, `selinux-policy-*`); downgrading to a prior minor version can leave the system [src: linux-package-management]
- **Verification**: repos set `gpgcheck=1` and `gpgkey=` in their `.repo`. Verify with [src: linux-package-management]
- `rpm --checksig pkg.rpm`; `rpm -V` audits an installed package against the DB (size, mode, digest, [src: linux-package-management]
- ownership drift). rpmdb may live at `/usr/lib/sysimage/rpm` on newer systems. [src: linux-package-management]
- **Flag grammar**: operations are `-S` sync, `-R` remove, `-Q` query, `-U` upgrade(local); modifiers [src: linux-package-management]
- stack (`y` refresh DB, `u` upgrade, `s` search, `i` info, `c` clean). So `-Syu` = refresh + upgrade. [src: linux-package-management]
- **AUR (Arch User Repository)**: user-submitted **PKGBUILD** recipes, not binaries. Workflow: [src: linux-package-management]
- `git clone` the AUR repo → review the PKGBUILD → `makepkg -si` (build + install with deps). AUR [src: linux-package-management]
- helpers (`paru`, `yay`) automate this but you own the security review. Popular PKGBUILDs graduate [src: linux-package-management]
- to the `extra` repo as binaries. [src: linux-package-management]
- **Signing**: pacman verifies via the **archlinux-keyring** (`pacman-key`). A stale keyring causes [src: linux-package-management]
- "invalid or corrupted package (PGP signature)" — fix with `sudo pacman -Sy archlinux-keyring` [src: linux-package-management]
- then retry the upgrade, or `sudo pacman-key --refresh-keys`. [src: linux-package-management]
- **Flatpak** — sandboxed desktop apps, community-governed via **Flathub**, shared *runtimes* to cut [src: linux-package-management]
- duplication, fine-grained portal permissions. `flatpak install flathub <app-id>`, [src: linux-package-management]
- `flatpak update`, `flatpak run <app-id>`. Best security/disk profile of the three. [src: linux-package-management]
- **Snap** — Canonical's compressed read-only **SquashFS** images mounted by `snapd`; auto-updating; [src: linux-package-management]
- centralized **Snap Store**. `snap install <name>`, `snap refresh`. Slower cold start (mount cost), [src: linux-package-management]
- **Nix** — declarative, immutable, content-addressed `/nix/store`; reproducible and rollback-able; [src: linux-package-management]
- 122k+ packages (largest, most current repo as of 2025). Not a distro-native verb — it's a different [src: linux-package-management]
- model (see the `immutable-atomic-linux` reference for NixOS-as-OS). `nix profile install`, flakes. [src: linux-package-management]
- When no package exists, the version is too old, or you need custom build flags. [src: linux-package-management]
- **Autotools** (`./configure && make && sudo make install`): `configure` probes the host for [src: linux-package-management]
- toolchain/libraries and generates the Makefile; `make` compiles; `make install` copies into the [src: linux-package-management]
- **CMake**: `cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=/usr/local && cmake --build build -j$(nproc) [src: linux-package-management]
- && sudo cmake --install build`. [src: linux-package-management]
- **Meson + Ninja**: `meson setup build --prefix=/usr/local && meson compile -C build && [src: linux-package-management]
- sudo meson install -C build`. [src: linux-package-management]
- **Get the deps first.** `sudo apt build-dep <pkg>` / `sudo dnf builddep <spec>` / [src: linux-package-management]
- pull `makedepends` via the PKGBUILD. Read the project `README`/`INSTALL` — honor its [src: linux-package-management]
- recommendation over generic advice. [src: linux-package-management]
- **Verify the tarball.** Download from a trusted origin; check the **GPG signature or checksum** [src: linux-package-management]
- before extracting. Supply-chain risk lives here. [src: linux-package-management]
- **Never build or run `make` as root.** Build as your user; only `make install` (the copy step) [src: linux-package-management]
- **Isolate the prefix for easy removal.** Default `/usr/local` collides nothing with the package [src: linux-package-management]
- manager (which owns `/usr`), but an explicit versioned prefix like `/opt/foo-1.2.3` or [src: linux-package-management]
- `--prefix=$HOME/.local` is cleaner and trivially removable. There is usually **no `make [src: linux-package-management]
- uninstall`**, so isolation matters. [src: linux-package-management]
- **Make it removable / trackable.** Prefer one of: [src: linux-package-management]
- **`checkinstall`** — wraps `make install` to produce a real `.deb`/`.rpm`/`.tgz` so the package [src: linux-package-management]
- manager tracks and can cleanly remove it. [src: linux-package-management]
- **GNU Stow** — `make install` into `/usr/local/stow/foo-1.2.3`, then `stow` symlinks it into [src: linux-package-management]
- `/usr/local`; `stow -D` removes it atomically. [src: linux-package-management]
- Building a proper native package (`.deb` via `debuild`, `.rpm` via `rpmbuild`/`.spec`, [src: linux-package-management]
- `.pkg.tar.zst` via PKGBUILD) for anything you'll ship. [src: linux-package-management]
- **Run ldconfig** after installing shared libraries to a new path; add the dir to [src: linux-package-management]
- `/etc/ld.so.conf.d/` if outside the default search path. [src: linux-package-management]
- Compiling a custom kernel from `kernel.org` source (or your distro's source) — for new hardware, [src: linux-package-management]
- debugging, custom config, or learning. [src: linux-package-management]
- **Get source + deps.** Extract the tarball; install build deps (`build-essential`/`gcc make`, [src: linux-package-management]
- `bison flex libssl-dev libelf-dev bc`, ncurses for menuconfig). [src: linux-package-management]
- **Configure** — produce a `.config`: [src: linux-package-management]
- `make menuconfig` — ncurses menu editor (also `nconfig`, `xconfig`, `gconfig`). [src: linux-package-management]
- **`make localmodconfig`** — the practical shortcut: reads `lsmod` and disables every module not [src: linux-package-management]
- currently loaded, producing a lean, fast-building config tailored to *this* machine. (Pass a [src: linux-package-management]
- captured `lsmod` via `LSMOD=file` to target another machine.) [src: linux-package-management]
- `make olddefconfig` — carry an existing `.config` forward, defaulting new symbols. [src: linux-package-management]
- Common base: `cp /boot/config-$(uname -r) .config` then `make olddefconfig`. [src: linux-package-management]
- **Build.** `make -j$(nproc)` — uses all cores; still typically 1–2+ hours for a full config, [src: linux-package-management]
- minutes for a `localmodconfig`-trimmed one. Produces `arch/x86/boot/bzImage` (the compressed [src: linux-package-management]
- kernel image) and the built modules. [src: linux-package-management]
- **Install modules.** `sudo make modules_install` → copies into `/lib/modules/<version>/`. [src: linux-package-management]
- **Install kernel.** `sudo make install` (distro-friendly: copies bzImage to `/boot`, generates the [src: linux-package-management]
- initramfs, and updates the bootloader on most distros) — or manually copy `bzImage` to [src: linux-package-management]
- `/boot/vmlinuz-<ver>`, build the initramfs (`dracut`/`update-initramfs`), and regenerate GRUB [src: linux-package-management]
- (`grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg` or `grub2-mkconfig`). See `linux-boot-init` for the [src: linux-package-management]
- initramfs + bootloader chain and `linux-kernel-architecture` for module/ABI internals. [src: linux-package-management]
- **Reboot** and pick the entry; verify with `uname -r`. Keep the old kernel as a fallback boot [src: linux-package-management]
- entry — never delete the working kernel until the new one boots clean. [src: linux-package-management]
- **`pacman -Sy <pkg>` (partial upgrade).** The single most dangerous Arch mistake. It refreshes the [src: linux-package-management]
- DB and installs/upgrades *one* package (pulling new library deps) without upgrading the rest of the [src: linux-package-management]
- system. Because Arch is rolling and keeps no old library versions, this breaks other packages [src: linux-package-management]
- linked against the now-removed library. **Always `pacman -Syu`** — and refusing the upgrade prompt [src: linux-package-management]
- after `-Sy` is just as bad. Never `-Sy` then `-S`. [src: linux-package-management]
- **`apt-key add` / dropping keys in the global keyring.** Deprecated and insecure (one bad repo can [src: linux-package-management]
- sign *anything*). Use a per-repo keyring + `Signed-By:`. [src: linux-package-management]
- **`sudo make install` of an untracked source build into `/usr` or `/`.** Collides with the package [src: linux-package-management]
- manager and is near-impossible to remove. Use `/usr/local`, an isolated prefix, `checkinstall`, or [src: linux-package-management]
- **Mixing repos / "Frankendebian".** Pinning packages from a newer release (e.g. Debian [src: linux-package-management]
- testing/unstable on stable, or random third-party repos) without proper apt pinning causes [src: linux-package-management]
- dependency hell. Use `apt-pinning` deliberately or not at all. [src: linux-package-management]
- **Disabling GPG checks** (`--allow-unauthenticated`, `gpgcheck=0`, `--nosignature`) to "fix" a key [src: linux-package-management]
- error. Fix the key, don't disable the trust boundary. [src: linux-package-management]
- **`rm`-ing files instead of removing the package.** Leaves the DB believing the package is present. [src: linux-package-management]
- Always go through the manager. [src: linux-package-management]
- **`dnf history rollback` on RHEL core packages** (kernel/glibc/selinux) — unsupported; can brick [src: linux-package-management]
- **Running a full `menuconfig` from scratch.** Thousands of symbols; you'll misconfigure something. [src: linux-package-management]
- Start from the running config or `localmodconfig`. [src: linux-package-management]
- APT 3.0 / solver3 — LWN, "What's new in APT 3.0": https://lwn.net/Articles/1017315/ [src: linux-package-management]
- Ubuntu Community Hub, "Evaluating the new APT solver in 25.04": https://discourse.ubuntu.com/t/evaluating-the-new-apt-solver-in-25-04/55618 [src: linux-package-management]

- <!-- Provenance: reference under the `tam-operations` hub. Mirrored from ~/.claude/skills/tam-operations/references/tam-commercial-metrics.md by scripts/persist-spoke.mjs. --> [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- This reference is the **numbers-and-definitions** layer for a TAM. It answers three recurring questions: [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- what a retention metric *is* and how to compute it, what MEDDPICC means and how to apply it to an [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- installed-base account, and what the *current* SaaS benchmark figures are. It carries formulas, a scoring [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- rubric, and dated tables — not document structure or framework selection (that lives in [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- `tam-operations (references/tam-expertise.md)`), and not prose drafting (that lives in `executive-comms`). [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- Every benchmark figure below is **dated and attributed**. Benchmarks move year to year and differ by data [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- set. **Verify before customer-facing use** — pull the current figure from the named source rather than [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- quoting this file in a deliverable. [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- All retention metrics measure one cohort's recurring revenue over a fixed window (usually 12 months), [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- comparing the **starting ARR** of customers who existed at the start of the period to what that same cohort [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- is worth at the end. New-logo ARR landed *during* the window is excluded — these metrics describe the [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- Four movements act on a cohort's starting ARR over the window: [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- **GRR** counts only the losses. **NRR** also credits expansion. GRR is always ≤ 100%; NRR can exceed 100% [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- when expansion outweighs losses. [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- Also called Net Dollar Retention (NDR) or Net ARR Retention — same metric. [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- NRR = (Starting ARR + Expansion − Contraction − Churn) / Starting ARR [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- A cohort starts the year at **$1,000,000** ARR. Over 12 months: **+$180,000** expansion, **−$40,000** [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- contraction, **−$70,000** churn. [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- NRR = (1,000,000 + 180,000 − 40,000 − 70,000) / 1,000,000 [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- = 1,070,000 / 1,000,000 [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- The same cohort's **GRR** (losses only, no expansion credit): [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- GRR = (1,000,000 − 40,000 − 70,000) / 1,000,000 = 890,000 / 1,000,000 = 89% [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- Read together: this book is **growing the existing base 7%** net, but is **losing 11%** to contraction and [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- churn before any expansion. A wide NRR–GRR gap means expansion is masking a leaky base — a churn problem the [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- expansion motion is papering over. [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- The Optifai segmentation above is cross-referenced with ChartMogul (2024) and widely re-reported by [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- aggregators citing SaaS Capital. SaaS Capital's own Sep 2025 read is by ACV tier rather than named segment: [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- median NRR **102%** for the $25K–$50K tier (top quartile 111%, bottom quartile 97%), with the explicit finding [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- that higher ACV correlates with higher retention. Whole-population medians span a range across data sets: [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- ~106% (Optifai, 2025-2026) down to ~101% in compressed-market reads (Vena / industry, 2025). The single [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- number means little without segment, ARR stage, and pricing model — always pair NRR with its ACV tier. [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- Reading rule: **97% NRR is at-median for SMB but a red flag for enterprise.** SMB books churn more and expand [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- less on self-serve motions; holding 100%+ at SMB scale is genuinely strong. The same 97% in an enterprise [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- book signals a structural retention problem. [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- NRR rises by lifting expansion or cutting losses. A TAM's influence is mostly on the loss side and on [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- **Expansion** — drive adoption depth and new use cases so the account *qualifies* for upsell; surface [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- expansion signals (usage near tier limits, new teams onboarding) to the AE early; time the play to a [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- realized-value moment. [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- **Churn reduction** — protect against the renewal risks below: catch health decline early, close adoption [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- gaps, keep a live executive relationship, and document realized value before the renewal window opens. [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- **Contraction reduction** — defend seat/usage counts by tying them to outcomes the buyer tracks; renegotiate [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- rather than let a silent downgrade ride. [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- GRR has a hard ceiling of 100% — a TAM cannot grow GRR, only stop it leaking. NRR is the metric where TAM [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- adoption work shows up as upside. [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- MEDDPICC is a B2B deal-qualification framework: eight elements that test whether a deal is real, winnable, and [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- worth forecasting. Lineage: **MEDDIC** (6 elements) was created at PTC in 1996; **MEDDICC** added Competition [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- as categories crowded; **MEDDPICC** added **Paper Process** for modern procurement, legal, and security [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- review. A TAM uses it less for net-new qualification and more to **de-risk renewals and qualify expansion** [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- inside the installed base. [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- > The **TAM application** column is a customer-success adaptation, not sourced sales doctrine. Published [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- > MEDDPICC sources address net-new deal qualification; the renewal/expansion recast is this reference's own [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- Two common rubrics — use whichever your team standardizes on: [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- **0–4 evidence scale:** 0 = unknown, 1 = assumed, 2 = stated by the buyer, 3 = tested with the buyer, [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- 4 = documented and confirmed. [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- **Red / Yellow / Green:** Green = fully validated from the buyer; Yellow = partial, gaps remain; [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- Red = unknown or guessed. [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- Forecast discipline: a renewal or expansion carrying **any Red** (or a 0–1) on Economic Buyer, Champion, or [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- Paper Process should not sit in the commit forecast until the gap is closed. Weight the elements to your [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- motion — e.g., for a renewal, weight Champion and Paper Process higher because a departed champion or a [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- surprise security re-review is what actually stalls the signature. [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- All figures dated and attributed. **Verify before customer-facing use.** [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- A TAM reading: at scale, **expansion drives the majority of new ARR** — which is exactly the revenue a TAM's [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- adoption and renewal work influences. Growth gets easier as retention rises because you are not refilling a [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- leaking bucket before you can grow. [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- **Quoting one NRR median without the segment.** 97% is healthy for SMB and a crisis for enterprise; a bare [src: tam-commercial-metrics]
- "good NRR is 110%" is wrong for most segments. [src: tam-commercial-metrics]

- mean NRR — GRR above 100% is a definitional error. [src: tam-commercial-metrics]

- the two together; the gap is the churn signal. [src: tam-commercial-metrics]

- an unscoped paper process — qualify those before forecasting the renewal. [src: tam-commercial-metrics]

- > **Reference skill — part of the `tam-operations` family** (the "Semantic Monitoring → Reporting → Dashboards → TAM Methodology" value-chain synthesis). This file owns the *practice* of defining, driving, measuring, and **proving** customer outcomes. Defer the neighbors it touches: [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- > - CLV / retention **math** (BTYD, NRR/GRR computation, DERT) → `da-23-customer-lifetime-value` [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- > - health-score **composite algorithm** → `account-health-scorer` [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- > - EBR/QBR meeting **structure** & success-framework selection → `tam-expertise` [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- > - adoption / motivation / habit **psychology** → `applied-psychology ▸ behavior-change-psychology` [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- Defining, driving, or **proving** the business outcomes a customer bought your product to achieve. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- Building a mutual success plan, success criteria, or value scorecard. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- Setting up time-to-value or outcome metrics; designing a value-realization review cadence. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- Turning "the customer uses our product" into "the customer achieved outcome X worth $Y, baselined." [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- Choosing or comparing a customer-success platform. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- Computing CLV, NRR, or retention curves as **quantities** → `da-23-customer-lifetime-value`. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- Designing the **weighted health-score algorithm** → `account-health-scorer`. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- Structuring the EBR/QBR **meeting** or picking BLUF/Pyramid/SCQA → `tam-expertise`. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- Driving adoption via motivation/habit models (SDT, Fogg B=MAP, stages-of-change) → `applied-psychology`. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- **Value realization** is the practice of closing the gap between **promised** value (the pre-sale business case), **perceived** value (what the customer subjectively feels), and **realized** value (the quantified, baselined outcome you can defend). Outcomes — not activity — are the unit of account. For a TAM it is the discipline that converts "the customer uses our product" into "the customer achieved outcome X worth $Y, here is the baseline-to-current proof, and here is why they should renew and expand." The 2024–2026 industry shift frames value realization (not health scores) as the true driver of NRR, with AI agents increasingly delivering and measuring it at scale. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- **Time-to-Value (TTV)** = how fast a customer begins realizing benefit after purchase; **Time-to-First-Value / "aha"** = the first meaningful result. The load-bearing distinction is **promised vs. perceived vs. realized** value. TTV is a churn lever, not a vanity stat (Gainsight reports a large share of churned customers say they never saw value early enough). [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- Activity-based CS counts tasks (calls held, onboarding sessions); outcome-based CS measures results (the customer's own business KPIs, retention, expansion). The signature failure is "90% adoption with zero ROI" — high usage producing no measurable value. Outcome-based CS starts from a business outcome tied to financial performance and works backward to the activities that should produce it. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- **Desired Outcome = Required Outcome + Appropriate Experience.** Required Outcome (RO) is what the customer needs to achieve — *not* the functional use of the product ("more event attendees," not "send emails"). Appropriate Experience (AX) is the segment-appropriate *way* they achieve it. Deliver RO without AX and the customer doesn't *feel* successful — they won't advocate or expand. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- The **mutual success plan / mutual action plan (MAP)** is a shared, living, co-owned document recording desired outcomes, **success criteria**, KPIs, action steps, owners, and timelines — anchored in *buyer-defined* criteria with mutual accountability. A **value scorecard** tracks proof-of-value as **baseline → current → target** per metric. Together they form a "definition of done" for value. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- A **value hypothesis** posits a causal chain: an adopted workflow → a downstream business result (cost saved, cycle-time cut). Operationalizing it requires a **baseline captured before/at onboarding**, ongoing value tracking, and periodic **value-realization reviews** (baseline→current vs. target). Pair an adoption metric to a business outcome and keep the correlation **defensible**. The **EBR/QBR is the value-narrative vehicle** — lead in the customer's language ("$2.4M saved") with a before→action→after arc (meeting mechanics live in `tam-expertise`). [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- Post-sale lifecycle: **onboarding → adoption → value realization → growth/expansion → advocacy** (Practical CSM inserts an explicit value-realization phase before renewal). Journey maps plot value milestones against stages; vendor-side **maturity models** (e.g., TSIA Forming→Storming→Norming→Performing) track CS-org sophistication. 2025–2026: journeys reframed as AI-orchestrated, predictive next-best-action flows. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- Activity (calls) → output (features adopted) → **outcome** (business result) is the meaningfulness ladder. **Leading indicators** (TTV, adoption, health, conversation completion) *predict*; **lagging indicators** (renewal, churn, NPS) *confirm*. **NRR/GRR are lagging evidence of realized value, not value itself** — drive them via upstream leading indicators. Realized value should be a **health-score input** (a green score with no realized value is a false positive — composite mechanics → `account-health-scorer`). [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- Digital CS delivers value one-to-many for the long tail (often ~70% of ARR in PLG). The 2026 reframe: old one-way "tech-touch" (batch emails, in-app banners "nobody opened") *caused* churn because problems surfaced only at renewal; modern digital-led CS is **conversational, asynchronous, AI-mediated "scaled qualitative listening"** with a closed loop (route every signal to a response within ~7 days). Watch **conversation completion rate (35–55%)**. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- (1) **Onboarding** — co-author a mutual success plan capturing the Required Outcome, success criteria, and a **baseline**. (2) **Adoption** — instrument leading value indicators; tie adoption to the outcome via a value hypothesis. (3) **Mid-lifecycle** — run value-realization reviews on a cadence; update the scorecard baseline→current→target. (4) **Pre-renewal** — assemble the value narrative ("achieved X worth $Y") as renewal/expansion evidence. Cadence is the antidote to surfacing value only at renewal. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- **Capture a baseline before/at onboarding** — realized value is meaningless without a "before"; it is the single most-skipped, most-load-bearing artifact. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- **Anchor on the customer's Required Outcome, in their language and units** ("$2.4M saved," "cycle time −26%"), and pair RO with an Appropriate Experience (Murphy). [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- **Make the success plan genuinely mutual** — co-owned, named customer owners, agreed success criteria and dates. A vendor-only plan is a project plan, not a success plan. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- **State an explicit value hypothesis; keep the adoption→outcome link defensible** — a modest defensible claim beats an impressive unfalsifiable one. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- **Run value realization on a cadence, not at renewal** — quarterly value reviews + executive reviews that lead with value milestones. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- **Drive NRR via leading indicators; treat NRR/GRR as confirmation** — act months ahead of the scoreboard. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- **Use the one-slide value scorecard (baseline / current / target)** framed before→action→after so it ports into any EBR, renewal deck, or champion's internal pitch. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- **Deliver long-tail value digitally and conversationally, with a closed loop** — replace one-way nudges with AI-mediated conversations; measure completion and risk-flag precision. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- **Make realized value a health-score input** (don't double-count usage as value) — defer composite mechanics to `account-health-scorer`. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- **Pick the platform to the operating model, not the logo** (see tooling table). [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- **Vanity/usage metrics mistaken for value** — logins/seats/"90% adoption" presented as outcomes. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- **No baseline** — improvement claimed with no "before"; collapses under executive scrutiny. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- **Vendor-defined (not customer-defined) outcomes** — metrics flatter the vendor's deck, not the customer's Required Outcome. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- **Value surfaced only at renewal** — first value conversation is a defensive scramble 60 days out. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- **Success plans that aren't mutual** — unilateral, no customer owners, no shared accountability. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- **Activity theater** — calls held / QBRs delivered reported as if effort equals outcome. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- **Tech-touch as cost-cutting, not listening** — one-way batch comms for the long tail; produces churn, not savings. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- **Health score with no value dimension** — green driven by engagement that masks an unrealized business case. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- **"NRR is built on value realization, not health scores"** (TSIA 2025) is a deliberate *repositioning* of value realization above health scoring as the renewal driver — a directional industry stance, not settled fact. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- **Tech-touch reframe** is genuinely contested: the 2026 claim that 2018–2023 cost-cutting tech-touch *caused* churn is stronger than the consensus "tech-touch is fine for low-ARR." [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]
- **AI agents in CS platforms** (Gainsight Atlas/Staircase, Totango-Catalyst AI scores, Vitally Copilot) are the dominant 2024→2026 tooling shift; verify vendor claims against your own scaled-CS needs. [src: value-realization-outcome-cs]

- > **Reference skill — part of the `da-applied-and-communication` / `tam-operations` value-chain family** ("Semantic Monitoring → Reporting → Dashboards → TAM Methodology"). This file owns the *design discipline* of analytics shown to a company's **own customers/end-users**. Defer the neighbors it touches: [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- > - chart selection, encodings, dashboard-design *rules* → `da-8-data-visualization` [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- > - analysis-to-narrative / reporting craft → `da-9-reporting-communication` [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- > - the governed **metric/semantic layer** itself → `da-18-semantic-layer-headless-bi` [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- > - OLAP **serving engines** (ClickHouse/Druid/Pinot) → `da-28-realtime-olap-databases` [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- > - MongoDB-specific embedded charts → `mongodb-atlas-charts` [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- > - internal/admin component & dashboard UX → `ui-ux-pro-max` [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- > - streaming/chat AI UI → `ai-native-ux-generative-ui` [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- > - the *value/outcome content* of a customer health dashboard → `value-realization-outcome-cs`; health-score algorithm → `account-health-scorer` [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- Designing analytics surfaces shown to **your customers / end-users** (embedded, customer-facing, white-label, in-product). [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- Securing a multi-tenant dashboard; choosing an embedded-analytics platform or running build-vs-buy. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- Deciding what to expose vs. suppress for an external audience; adding freshness/export/alerts; making customer-facing charts accessible. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- Picking a chart type or fixing encodings → `da-8-data-visualization`. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- Shaping an analysis into a narrative/report → `da-9-reporting-communication`. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- Defining/governing the metric layer → `da-18-semantic-layer-headless-bi`. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- Tuning the OLAP engine underneath → `da-28-realtime-olap-databases`. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- Customer-facing analytics is the design discipline of building analytics surfaces a company shows to its **own customers/end-users** — dashboards, reports, and metrics embedded inside a product so users see the value, activity, or outcomes that pertain to *them*. It sits on top of OLAP engines and is governed by the host product's identity and permissions. Defining constraints: external-audience **trust** (every number is seen by a paying customer), strict **tenant isolation**, **sub-second performance at concurrency**, and **visual nativeness**. The 2024→2026 shift is generative/conversational "GenBI" and tenant-scoped LLM grounding inside the embedded surface. *This field is heavily vendor-marketed — positioning claims and headline stats below are attributed to their (often self-interested) source, not treated as fact.* [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- Embedded analytics / customer-facing analytics / in-product analytics / embedded BI are one idea: analytics surfaced inside a non-analytics app, controlled by the host's identity model, styled to feel native. **White-label** is the mature variant (all vendor branding removed; custom domain + theming). Maturity progression: *iframe with visible branding → themed/white-labeled embed → headless/SDK-driven native UI → self-service authoring + GenBI*. Parallel framing: "analytics as a product" / data products — analytics shipped as premium tiers, usage-based add-ons, white-label OEM (a revenue lever). [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- Three structural categories: **off-the-shelf embedded** (Luzmo, Explo — fast multi-tenant, limited customization); **repurposed embedded BI** (Tableau, Power BI, Looker, Metabase, Sisense — strong governance, iframe-dependent, enterprise pricing); **headless/hybrid** (Cube + your frontend, Embeddable — full UI control + sub-second, more engineering). Looker/Tableau/Power BI carry six-figure pricing and weren't built for customer-facing use; ThoughtSpot Everywhere leads on NL/AI search but is weaker on UI control; GoodData repositioned to API-first web-component embedding; Superset/Preset is the open-source route (Embedded SDK + guest tokens + RLS). 2026 newcomers (Upsolve AI, Knowi, Toucan) lead with GenBI + semantic-layer automation. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- Governing principle: **decision-first curation** — identify the 3–5 critical decisions a customer makes per week, map the data those need, design a minimal surface, then validate before scaling. Suppress internal jargon, raw operational metrics, admin controls; expose decision-tied metrics plus **value framing** (the ROI/value they're getting) and **contextual comparisons** (vs. history, vs. target, vs. anonymized peers). **Progressive disclosure** is near-universal (headline KPIs first, drill-down on demand). Sane default filters, query rate-limiting, and column/row masking keep self-service from becoming a foot-gun. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- Tenant isolation = **token-based auth (signed JWT/SAML/OIDC) + row-level filters applied server-side at query time** — never hide rows in the frontend. The host authenticates the user, mints a short-lived signed token encoding identity + tenant/org ID + optional filters; tampering invalidates the signature (Cube "security context" → `queryRewrite`/RLS; Superset "guest tokens"). **Canonical failure mode** (Tinybird, Jan 2026): passing `customer_id` as a *client-side query parameter* is insecure — tenant scope must live in the signed token's RLS definition. Cross-tenant leakage is the single most trust-destroying failure here. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- Sub-second expectations **under high concurrency** (Tinybird cites p99 ~139 ms at 9,500 req/s as the target class); >2–5 s loads erode trust. Levers: pre-aggregation/rollups, result caching with auto-invalidation, concurrency-tuned OLAP. **Freshness ≠ latency**: a 50 ms query can serve hours-stale data. Use age-based freshness ("time since most recent record") + a visible **"last updated" timestamp / color-coded freshness indicator** + per-asset freshness SLOs. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- Customer-facing numbers must agree with the vendor's other surfaces (sales reports, the invoice, in-app counters). Ground every surface in a **governed semantic/metric layer** — one definition reused across BI, embedded analytics, reverse-ETL, and AI rather than re-implemented per surface (dbt Semantic Layer metrics-as-code; **Cube** headless, one definition via SQL/REST/GraphQL/MDX). In 2026 the semantic layer is the shared control point and the grounding source for NL/AI queries (stops the LLM inventing metric logic). *Depth → `da-18-semantic-layer-headless-bi`.* [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- Customers immediately want **filters, drill-down, export, scheduled email/report delivery, configurable threshold alerts** — access is where the journey begins, not ends. Embed in-workflow (external link-switching causes anxiety + infosec issues); support role-based variants and responsive/mobile. **WCAG 2.1/2.2 AA for charts**: high-contrast palettes, never color as the sole channel (labels/patterns too), full keyboard operability, screen-reader support, and **accessible exports** (CSV/structured-table PDF) that double as a Section 508 path. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- The value/ROI dashboard a vendor exposes *to the account itself* — usage, adoption depth, support posture, and **value realized** (time-to-value, outcomes, $/hours saved). Trusted (not ignored) when: definitions are consistent across systems, thresholds are actionable, views are role-relevant, and visuals are clear (RYG traffic-lights). Persistent gap (2025 CS commentary): many surfaces track *adoption activity* but few track *outcomes/value*, so customers discount them — and health scores "flag conditions rather than draw conclusions," so a customer-facing value view earns trust only paired with human context. *Outcome/value content → `value-realization-outcome-cs`.* [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- Headline failure: **dashboards no one opens** (vendor commentary cites ~70% of dashboard metrics never influencing a decision — directional, not firmly sourced). Specific traps: **vanity metrics** (flattering totals/pageviews that crowd out real metrics), **starting from available data** instead of user decisions, **internal jargon/operational noise**, **no freshness label**, **metric drift** vs. other reports, **standalone silos** disconnected from workflow, **over-interactivity/widget overload** for non-technical users. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- **Curate decision-first** — anchor each dashboard to 3–5 concrete customer decisions; validate with real users before adding widgets. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- **Lead with value, not activity** — ROI/outcomes + contextual comparisons (vs. target/period/peers). [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- **Enforce tenant isolation server-side via signed tokens + RLS** — encode tenant scope in the token; never trust a client-side tenant param. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- **Engineer for sub-second at concurrency** — pre-aggregate, cache with auto-invalidation, concurrency-tuned OLAP; treat >2–5 s as a trust bug. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- **Always show data age** — "last updated" / freshness indicator + per-metric freshness SLOs; latency ≠ freshness. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- **Ground every number in a governed semantic/metric layer** so embed, invoice, and AI answers agree. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- **Use progressive disclosure** — headline KPIs first; filters/drill-down on demand. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- **Ship the after-access features** — accessible export (CSV/PDF), scheduled delivery, customer-configurable alerts. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- **Meet WCAG AA for charts** — contrast, non-color encodings, keyboard nav, screen-reader, accessible data-table exports. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- **Run build-vs-buy on TCO, not sticker price** — buy/hybrid when analytics is a feature (not the product), 20+ tenants, and you need white-label/multi-tenant/SSO + AI readiness in 3–6 months; build only when analytics is your core differentiator. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- **Dashboards nobody opens** — built for reporting, not action; retire any metric not referenced in ~90 days. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- **Vanity metrics** prominently displayed; they starve attention from real metrics. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- **Starting from "what data we have"** instead of the customer's decisions. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- **Exposing internal jargon / operational metrics** meant for the vendor's engineers. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- **No freshness label** — customers act on silently stale data. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- **Metric drift** — embedded number disagrees with the invoice / other reports (no shared semantic layer). [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- **Client-side tenant filtering** (`customer_id` as a query param) — the classic cross-tenant data-leak vector. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- **Widget/filter overload & over-interactivity**; external-link-out instead of in-workflow embedding. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- **GenBI** (NL-to-chart + tenant-scoped LLM grounding) is the biggest 2024→2026 shift and now argues for "buy" (AI readiness). [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- **iframe → web-component/headless SDK** is the architectural trend (performance + native feel). [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]
- **Semantic-layer consolidation** (dbt SL / Cube) as the shared metric + AI-grounding control point. [src: customer-facing-embedded-analytics]

- programming-languages hub reference for the JavaScript/TypeScript **build toolchain**: bundlers, parsers/transpilers, minifiers, linters, and formatters — and the 2025-2026 **Rust/Go rewrite wave** reshaping all of them. Sibling to `javascript-nodejs` (language/runtime), `javascript-runtimes-deno-bun-edge` (non-Node runtimes), and `typescript-expert` (type system). [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- **TRIGGER:** choosing or migrating a bundler/build tool; Vite/Rolldown/VoidZero questions; Rspack↔webpack or Turbopack↔Next.js decisions; Oxc/oxlint/Biome vs ESLint/Prettier; "why is my build slow"; configuring tree-shaking, code-splitting, HMR, or source maps. [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- **SKIP:** Node/Deno/Bun *runtime* semantics → `javascript-runtimes-deno-bun-edge` / `javascript-nodejs`; TypeScript *type-system* → `typescript-expert`; package install / workspaces / monorepo task-orchestration → package-management (concept-tree gap, not yet built). [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- The fastest tool in every toolchain category is now written in **Rust or Go**. The pivotal driver is **VoidZero** (Evan You's company, founded late 2024) building a unified Rust toolchain under one parser. [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- **Rolldown** — Rust bundler, drop-in replacement for *both* esbuild (dev) and Rollup (prod) inside Vite. Hit **1.0 Release Candidate in Jan 2026**; API stable, production-ready for early adopters. [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- **Oxc** (Oxidation Compiler) — the Rust parser/transformer/resolver *underneath* Rolldown. **oxlint** is ~50-100× ESLint; Oxc formatting ~30× Prettier. [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- **Vite 8** — runs on Rolldown by default, replacing the historical esbuild+Rollup two-engine split (which caused dev/prod output divergence bugs). [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- > Single-parser convergence (Oxc) under one bundler (Rolldown) inside one dev tool (Vite) is the structural story: it removes the class of bugs where dev (esbuild) and prod (Rollup) disagreed. [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- **Migration rule of thumb:** Rspack for webpack migrations (compat) · Turbopack for Next.js · **Vite for everything else**. [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- **Oxc** — Rust parser/transformer/minifier/resolver; the new substrate. [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- **SWC** — Rust; powers Next.js compilation and many transforms; Parcel's transformer. [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- **esbuild** — Go; transpile + minify, extremely fast, the prior speed king. [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- **Babel** — JS; still the most plugin-extensible transpiler (custom syntax, legacy targets), but slow — being displaced for plain transpilation. [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- **tsc** — TypeScript's own compiler; use for **type-checking** (`--noEmit`), not bundling. The transpile-vs-typecheck split matters: bundlers strip types fast but don't type-check (see `javascript-nodejs` native-TS notes). [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- **Terser** — JS minifier; legacy default, now outpaced by esbuild/Oxc minify. [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- Common 2026 pattern: **oxlint or Biome for the fast 90%** in CI/pre-commit, **ESLint + typescript-eslint** retained for type-aware rules the Rust linters don't yet implement. [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- **Dev** optimizes for *startup + HMR latency*: native ESM, on-demand transform, no full bundle (Vite's historical esbuild role; now Rolldown). [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- **Prod** optimizes for *output*: tree-shaking, code-splitting, chunking, minification, source maps, asset hashing (historically Rollup; now Rolldown). [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- Keeping **one engine for both** (Rolldown) is why Vite 8 matters — it ends dev/prod output drift. [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- **Framework lock-in?** Next.js → Turbopack. Otherwise → Vite. [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- **Migrating webpack?** → Rspack (compat) before considering a rewrite to Vite. [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- **Library, not app?** → Rollup/Rolldown (clean ESM) or `tsup`/esbuild for speed. [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- **Lint/format speed pain?** → add oxlint/Biome to CI; keep ESLint for type-aware rules. [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- **"Build is slow"** → identify the stage (transpile vs bundle vs typecheck vs lint); move transpile to esbuild/SWC/Oxc, move typecheck to a separate `tsc --noEmit` job, parallelize. [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- Running Babel for plain TS/JS transpile when esbuild/SWC/Oxc do it 20-100× faster. [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- Treating the bundler as a type-checker — bundlers strip types, they don't verify them. [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- Adopting a bleeding-edge RC (e.g. Rolldown 1.0 RC) for a critical legacy app without a fallback path. [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]
- Mixing ESLint legacy `.eslintrc` and flat `eslint.config.js` — pick flat config. [src: javascript-build-tooling-bundlers]

- programming-languages hub reference for the **browser-side JavaScript platform** — the APIs that ship in the *browser*, not in the ECMAScript language (`javascript-nodejs`) or in Node. This is the half of "JavaScript" that lives between the language and the framework. Sibling to `javascript-nodejs`, `javascript-runtimes-deno-bun-edge`, and `frontend-design`. [src: web-platform-browser-apis]
- **TRIGGER:** which browser API to use; DOM/events; the observer family; Fetch/Streams/abort; Web Components & Shadow DOM; Service Workers / offline / PWA; client-storage choice; real-time transports (WebSocket/WebRTC/WebTransport/SSE); View Transitions, Navigation API, WebGPU. [src: web-platform-browser-apis]
- **SKIP:** JS language/runtime semantics → `javascript-nodejs`; non-Node runtimes → `javascript-runtimes-deno-bun-edge`; framework rendering (React/Vue/Svelte) → `frontend-design` / frontend-frameworks (concept-tree gap); CSS & visual design → `frontend-design`; Chrome-extension MV3 surfaces → `chrome-dev`. [src: web-platform-browser-apis]
- **Navigation API → Baseline Newly Available (Jan 2026)** — Chrome, Edge, Firefox 147, Safari 26.2. The modern replacement for the History API: single `navigate` event, intercept + transition, proper SPA routing. Prefer it over `history.pushState` for new SPAs. [src: web-platform-browser-apis]
- **View Transitions API** — same-document *and* cross-document; **element-scoped** transitions now enable targeted animations without animating the whole page. [src: web-platform-browser-apis]
- **WebGPU** — in production browsers; 2026 is the consistency/predictability year. Compute + 3D; the successor to WebGL. [src: web-platform-browser-apis]
- **HTML-in-Canvas** — render real DOM elements into a canvas (WebGL/WebGPU) while staying accessible, searchable, translatable. [src: web-platform-browser-apis]
- **Document Picture-in-Picture** — always-on-top window with arbitrary HTML (Firefox 151 desktop + Chromium). [src: web-platform-browser-apis]
- **Soft Navigations API** — brings Core Web Vitals measurement to SPA route changes. [src: web-platform-browser-apis]
- **`Temporal`** (language, via `javascript-nodejs`) lands alongside as the modern date/time layer these APIs increasingly assume. [src: web-platform-browser-apis]
- **One-way server push?** SSE (`EventSource`) — simplest, auto-reconnect. **Bidirectional low-latency?** WebSocket. **Media or P2P?** WebRTC. **HTTP/3 streams / unreliable datagrams?** WebTransport. [src: web-platform-browser-apis]
- **Client storage:** key/value tiny + sync → `localStorage`; structured/queryable/large → IndexedDB (via Dexie); HTTP responses → Cache API; real files / SQLite-in-browser → OPFS. [src: web-platform-browser-apis]
- **Watching layout/visibility?** Use the matching observer, never a `scroll`/`resize` polling loop. [src: web-platform-browser-apis]
- **Encapsulated, framework-free widget?** Custom Element + Shadow DOM. [src: web-platform-browser-apis]
- **CPU-heavy work?** Web Worker (+ `Atomics`/`SharedArrayBuffer` for shared state); push to WASM if numeric. [src: web-platform-browser-apis]
- **SPA routing (new)?** Navigation API + View Transitions, not `history.pushState` + manual diffing. [src: web-platform-browser-apis]
- Polling `scroll`/`resize`/`setInterval` where an observer exists. [src: web-platform-browser-apis]
- Assuming a Service Worker keeps in-memory state across events — it gets terminated. [src: web-platform-browser-apis]
- Hand-rolling crypto instead of `crypto.subtle`; using `Math.random()` for tokens instead of `crypto.getRandomValues`/`randomUUID`. [src: web-platform-browser-apis]
- Blocking the main thread with heavy compute instead of a Worker. [src: web-platform-browser-apis]
- New SPA routing on the History API when the Navigation API is now Baseline. [src: web-platform-browser-apis]
- Unbounded `fetch` with no `AbortSignal.timeout()` — leaks pending requests. [src: web-platform-browser-apis]

- <!-- Provenance: reference under the `lang-js-ts` hub. Mirrored from ~/.claude/skills/lang-js-ts/references/nodejs-diagnostics-profiling.md by scripts/persist-spoke.mjs. --> [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- This reference is about **measuring a real Node.js process** — locating where CPU [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- time is spent, where memory is retained, and how to instrument code paths with [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- near-zero overhead in production. It is the "find the bottleneck" companion to two [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- sibling references that own the *explanatory* and *tuning* layers: [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- **`v8-engine-internals`** — owns GC mechanics and heap **tuning** (`--max-old-space-size`, [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- semi-space sizing, deopt reasons). This file uses heap *snapshots* to find leaks; [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- it does **not** re-explain generational GC. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- **`nodejs-concurrency-internals`** — owns the libuv event-loop **phase model**, [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- microtask ordering, and stream backpressure. This file *measures* event-loop lag [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- (`monitorEventLoopDelay`, `eventLoopUtilization`); it does not re-derive the phases. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- **`javascript-node-html-css-debugging-expert`** — owns interactive breakpoint/step [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- debugging and browser HTML/CSS DevTools. This file is about **profiling**, not stepping. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- The mental model: **Doctor → Flame/CPU profile → Heap snapshot.** First classify the [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- symptom (CPU-bound, I/O-bound, GC-bound, event-loop-blocked), then reach for the tool [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- that resolves that class. Guessing without a profile is the cardinal anti-pattern. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- Node embeds the **V8 Inspector**, which speaks the **Chrome DevTools Protocol over a [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- WebSocket**. Every richer tool (Chrome DevTools, VS Code, clinic, programmatic [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- profiling) is a CDP client underneath. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- `--inspect[=[host:]port]` activates the inspector (default `127.0.0.1:9229`; port `0` [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- = random). `--inspect-brk` breaks at the first line of the user script; `--inspect-wait` [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- (v22.2+) blocks until a client attaches. `--inspect-port` + `SIGUSR1` lets you attach [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- to an already-running process. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- **Security**: the inspector is a full code-execution channel. Never bind it to a public [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- interface (`0.0.0.0`) without a firewall — `--inspect` on a public IP is remote code [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- execution. Default to localhost and tunnel over SSH. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- The WebSocket URL is discoverable at `http://host:port/json/list` or via [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- `inspector.url()`. `--inspect-publish-uid` controls where it's published. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- Open `chrome://inspect` (or `edge://inspect`) → the target appears under "Remote Target" [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- → "inspect" gives a full DevTools UI (Performance + Memory tabs) wired to the Node process. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- You don't need an external client — drive the protocol in-process for self-profiling [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- (e.g., profile only a hot window, or on a signal). The promises API is cleanest: [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- import { Session } from 'node:inspector/promises'; [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- import fs from 'node:fs'; [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- const session = new Session(); [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- await session.post('Profiler.enable'); [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- await session.post('Profiler.start'); [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- // ... run the workload you want to profile ... [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- const { profile } = await session.post('Profiler.stop'); [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- fs.writeFileSync('./hotpath.cpuprofile', JSON.stringify(profile)); // open in DevTools [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- **`Profiler.*`** domain → CPU profiles (`.cpuprofile`). **`HeapProfiler.*`** domain → [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- heap snapshots (`.heapsnapshot`) and allocation sampling; snapshot chunks arrive via the [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- `HeapProfiler.addHeapSnapshotChunk` event. Do **not** pass `reportProgress: true` to [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- `HeapProfiler.takeHeapSnapshot`. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- `inspector.open(port, host, wait)` activates the inspector at runtime and (v20.6+) [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- returns a `Disposable` so `using` auto-closes it. `inspector.waitForDebugger()` blocks [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- until a client sends `Runtime.runIfWaitingForDebugger`. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- In worker threads use `session.connectToMainThread()`; setting breakpoints on a [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- same-thread session is unsupported. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- For batch jobs, CI, or servers you can't attach to, the flags write artifacts to disk: [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- `--diagnostic-dir` sets the base directory for all of the above. `NODE_OPTIONS` can carry [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- the flags (`NODE_OPTIONS='--cpu-prof' node app.js`) when you can't edit the launch command. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- A heap snapshot is a full graph of live objects and their retainers. Capture one: [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- **On signal** (production): `--heapsnapshot-signal=SIGUSR2`, then `kill -USR2 <pid>`. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- **Near OOM** (catch the growth): `--heapsnapshot-near-heap-limit=<count>` (stable v25.4) [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- writes a snapshot as the heap approaches the limit — pair with `--max-old-space-size`. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- **Programmatically**: `v8.writeHeapSnapshot()` or the `HeapProfiler` domain above. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- **The three-snapshot technique** (the standard leak workflow in DevTools' Memory tab): [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- Snapshot at steady state (baseline). [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- Drive the suspected-leaking operation N times; force a GC; snapshot again. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- Repeat; snapshot a third time. Use **"Comparison"** view between snapshots and the [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- **"Objects allocated between snapshot 1 and 2"** filter: anything still retained after [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- step 3 that grows linearly with N is the leak. Inspect the **Retainers** pane to find [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- what holds it — the usual culprits are module-scope `Map`/array caches without [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- eviction, event listeners never removed (`emitter.on` in a hot path), closures [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- capturing large scope, and timers holding references. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- Where profilers sample stacks, `perf_hooks` gives precise, programmatic numbers: [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- **`PerformanceObserver`** with `entryTypes` (`mark`, `measure`, `function`, `gc`, `http`, [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- `dns`, `net`, …) and `buffered: true` to catch entries created before `observe()`. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- **`performance.mark()` / `measure()` / `timerify(fn)`** — `timerify` wraps a function so [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- each call emits a `function` timeline entry (works with async, reports on settlement). [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- **`monitorEventLoopDelay({ resolution })`** → an `IntervalHistogram` sampling event-loop [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- delay in ns: `enable()/disable()`, `percentile(p)`, `mean`, `max`, `stddev`, `reset()`. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- This is the right signal for "is the event loop lagging?" — a p99 in the tens of ms [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- means something is blocking. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- **`performance.eventLoopUtilization()`** → `{ idle, active, utilization }`. Take two [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- snapshots and diff (`eventLoopUtilization(prev)`); utilization near 1.0 means the loop is [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- saturated (CPU-bound), near 0 means it's mostly waiting (I/O-bound). It is the canonical [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- signal for **worker-pool / thread-pool sizing** decisions. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- **`createHistogram()`** → a `RecordableHistogram` (`record`, `recordDelta`, `percentile`) [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- for your own latency distributions. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- The publish/subscribe channel built into Node for **library + production instrumentation**. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- Its defining property: **`channel.hasSubscribers` is false until something subscribes**, so [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- guarded publishing costs almost nothing when no APM is attached. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- import dc from 'node:diagnostics_channel'; [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- const ch = dc.channel('app:db:query');           // create at module top level [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- if (ch.hasSubscribers) ch.publish({ sql, ms });  // guard the expensive prep [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- dc.subscribe('app:db:query', (msg, name) => metrics.record(name, msg.ms)); [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- **`TracingChannel`** (`dc.tracingChannel(name)`) emits a coordinated set of sub-channels [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]

- **The canonical combo** — profile *under load*: `0x` sets a `$PORT` to the first port the [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]

- **Reproduce under load.** A profile of an idle process is noise. Drive realistic traffic [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- with `autocannon` (or your load tool). [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- **Classify with `monitorEventLoopDelay` + `eventLoopUtilization`** (or clinic doctor): [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- high ELU + high event-loop delay → **CPU-bound / blocking**; low ELU + high latency → [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- **I/O-bound / async**; sawtooth memory + GC pauses → **GC/leak**. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- **CPU-bound** → `--cpu-prof` or a flame graph (0x / clinic flame). Read top-down for the [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]

- **I/O-bound** → clinic bubbleprof or `diagnostics_channel` HTTP/net channels; look for [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]

- **Memory growth** → heap snapshot three-snapshot diff; find the retainer. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- **Instrument the winner** with `diagnostics_channel` / `perf_hooks` so the metric is [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]

- **Profile a window, not the whole run** — use the programmatic `Profiler.start/stop` [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]

- **Guard every `publish`** with `hasSubscribers` so instrumentation is free when no [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]

- **Alert on `eventLoopUtilization` and event-loop delay p99**, not just CPU% — they catch [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]

- **Optimizing without a profile.** "I think this loop is slow" → measure first; the hot [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- path is almost never where intuition points. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- **Profiling an idle / unrealistic process** — no load, or synthetic data that doesn't [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
- exercise the real path. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]

- unknown bottleneck; it can't see native frames or aggregate. [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]

- (which pauses before your code). [src: nodejs-diagnostics-profiling]
