- This reference is the **networking + HTTP core of Node** plus the **modern HTTP client**: [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- the layered stack from raw TCP/UDP sockets up through HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, TLS, and the [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `fetch`/undici client. It is the "talk to the network correctly and keep the sockets [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- healthy" companion to three siblings that own neighbouring layers: [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`nodejs-backend-frameworks`** owns the *framework* layer (Express/Fastify/NestJS/Hono, [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- routing, middleware, framework selection). This file is the primitives those frameworks [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- are built on — `http.Server`, the Agent, timeouts, TLS. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`nodejs-concurrency-internals`** owns the libuv **event-loop phase model** and **stream [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- backpressure** (`highWaterMark`, `pipe` vs `pipeline` flow control). This file *uses* [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- streams (request/response bodies are streams) but defers the backpressure mechanics there. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`http-security-headers`** owns CSP/HSTS/CORS and mTLS *hardening posture*. This file [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- covers the TLS *plumbing* (SNI, ALPN, session resumption); the security headers go there. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- The mental model has four layers: **net/dgram** (TCP/UDP sockets) → **tls** (encryption, [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- SNI, ALPN) → **http / http2 / https** (framing) → **fetch/undici** (the high-level pooled, [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- retrying client). Most production incidents here are **timeout** and **socket-pool** problems, [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- not protocol problems — so the timeout knobs and Agent/Pool sizing get the most attention below. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `http.createServer([options][, requestListener])` returns an `http.Server`. The lifecycle is [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- event-driven, and the events you actually wire up are: [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`'request'`** `(req, res)` — the normal path; `req` is an **`IncomingMessage`** (a readable [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- stream: `req.method`, `req.url`, `req.headers`, `req.on('data'|'end')`), `res` is a [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`ServerResponse`** (a writable stream: `res.writeHead(status, headers)`, `res.setHeader`, [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `res.getHeader`, `res.flushHeaders()`, `res.write`, `res.end`). [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`'connection'`** `(socket)` — a new TCP socket (pre-parse); **`'clientError'`** `(err, socket)` [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- — malformed request or header overflow. The default `clientError` handler replies `400 Bad [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- Request`, or **`431`** on `HPE_HEADER_OVERFLOW`; override it but always check `socket.writable` [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- and ignore `ECONNRESET`. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`'upgrade'`** `(req, socket, head)` — protocol upgrade (WebSocket handshake lives here). [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **Client side:** `http.request(options|url[, callback])` returns a writable [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `ClientRequest`; `http.get` is the same but auto-`end()`s and is GET-only. Key options: [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `hostname`/`host`, `port` (default 80), `method` (default `GET`), `path`, `headers`, `agent`, [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `timeout`. Header size is capped by **`--max-http-header-size`** (default **16 KiB**), readable as [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `http.maxHeaderSize`. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **The `http.Agent`** manages the socket pool for outbound requests (the default is [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `http.globalAgent`, which historically has **`keepAlive: false`**). Construct your own to reuse [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- connections. Options and defaults: [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- These four properties are the most operationally important thing in the module. Misconfigured, [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- they cause hung requests, leaked sockets, and the infamous **502 behind a load balancer**: [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`server.headersTimeout`** (default **60000 ms**) — max time to receive the *complete* request [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- headers. Defeats slowloris header-dribbling. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`server.requestTimeout`** (default **300000 ms** / 5 min) — max time from socket connect to the [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- full request being received. Defeats slow-body attacks. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`server.keepAliveTimeout`** (default **5000 ms**) — how long an idle keep-alive socket stays [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- open between requests. **Must be larger than the upstream load-balancer / proxy idle timeout**, [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- or the LB reuses a socket Node just closed → `ECONNRESET` surfaces as a 502. (AWS ALB idle is 60s; [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- set Node's `keepAliveTimeout` above that.) [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`server.maxRequestsPerSocket`** (default unlimited) — close a keep-alive socket after N requests. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `server.timeout` (legacy socket inactivity timeout) and `server.setTimeout()` still exist but the [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- three above are the modern, attack-aware controls. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`http2.createServer()`** = cleartext **h2c** (rarely used by browsers); **`http2.createSecureServer({ key, cert })`** = **h2 over TLS** and the one browsers speak — it advertises **ALPN `'h2'`** automatically. `allowHTTP1: true` lets a secure server fall back to HTTP/1.1 for non-h2 clients. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **Streams, not connections.** A single TCP connection (`Http2Session`) multiplexes many [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`Http2Stream`**s. Server side: `server.on('stream', (stream, headers) => { stream.respond({ ':status': 200 }); stream.end(body); })`. Client: **`http2.connect(authority)`** returns a `ClientHttp2Session`; `session.request(headers)` returns a `ClientHttp2Stream` that emits `'response'`. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- Pseudo-headers (`:method`, `:path`, `:scheme`, `:authority`, `:status`) replace the request line. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `session.settings()` tunes **`initialWindowSize`** (default 65535), **`maxConcurrentStreams`**, [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `enablePush`. Sessions emit `'goaway'` (graceful shutdown) and `'frameError'`. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **Server push (`stream.pushStream`) is deprecated** — RFC 9113 removed it and Chrome/modern [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- browsers no longer support it. Prefer **`103 Early Hints`** (`res.writeEarlyHints`) for preloading. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- Stream **priority** signaling is likewise deprecated. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **Compatibility API:** `Http2ServerRequest`/`Http2ServerResponse` mimic `http`'s [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `IncomingMessage`/`ServerResponse` so Express-style `(req, res)` handlers run on h2 with minimal [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- change. `respondWithFile`/`respondWithFD` stream a file/FD directly. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`node:https`** is HTTP semantics carried over `node:tls`: `https.createServer(options, listener)` [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- and `https.request` take the same shape as their `http` counterparts **plus** TLS options. There is a [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- dedicated **`https.Agent`**, which additionally keeps a **client-side TLS session cache** (keyed by [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- host) so reconnections can resume the TLS session and skip a round trip — a meaningful win for a [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- keep-alive-light, many-origins client (`maxCachedSessions` bounds it). [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- The real depth is **`node:tls`**: [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`tls.createSecureContext({ key, cert, ca, pfx, passphrase, minVersion, maxVersion, ciphers })`** — [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- the reusable cert/key bundle. `ca` overrides the default trust store; `minVersion: 'TLSv1.2'` is the [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **SNI (one server, many certs):** server option **`SNICallback(servername, cb)`** or [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`server.addContext('*.example.com', ctx)`** picks the cert by requested hostname. Client: [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`servername`** sets the SNI hostname. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **ALPN:** **`ALPNProtocols: ['h2', 'http/1.1']`** on server and client negotiates the protocol; read [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- the result from **`socket.alpnProtocol`** (`false` if none). This is exactly how h2-vs-h1.1 is chosen. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **Session resumption** (skip the full handshake on reconnect), two mechanisms: [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **session IDs** (server caches state; `'newSession'`/`'resumeSession'` events) and **TLS tickets** [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- (server encrypts state into a ticket the client returns; no server cache, and **`ticketKeys`** / [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `getTicketKeys`/`setTicketKeys` let a fleet share keys behind a load balancer). Client saves the [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `'session'` event buffer and passes it back as `session:` to `tls.connect`. `sessionTimeout` bounds it. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `node:net` is the TCP/IPC layer everything above sits on. `net.createServer([opts][, listener])` [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- emits **`'connection'`** `(socket)`; `net.connect`/`net.createConnection` open a client [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`net.Socket`** (a `Duplex` stream emitting `'data'`, `'end'`, `'close'`, `'error'`, `'timeout'`, [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `'ready'`). The socket controls you reach for: [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`socket.setNoDelay(true)`** disables **Nagle's algorithm** (send small writes immediately instead [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- of coalescing) — important for low-latency request/response and chatty protocols. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`socket.setKeepAlive(true, delay)`** enables TCP-level keep-alive probes (detect dead peers). [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`socket.setTimeout(ms)`** fires `'timeout'` on inactivity (it does **not** auto-close — you must [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `socket.destroy()` in the handler). [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`allowHalfOpen`** (default `false`): when the remote sends FIN (readable `'end'`), Node by default [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- also ends the writable side; set `true` to keep writing after the peer is done reading. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `pauseOnConnect` lets you hand a socket to another process before data flows. `net.BlockList` [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- (`addAddress`/`addRange`/`addSubnet`) does IP allow/deny lists. *(Backpressure mechanics of the [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- socket stream live in `nodejs-concurrency-internals`.)* [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- Connectionless UDP. **`dgram.createSocket('udp4'|'udp6')`** → a socket you **`bind([port])`** and read [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- via the **`'message'`** `(msg, rinfo)` event; **`socket.send(msg, port, address)`** to transmit (no [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- connection, no delivery guarantee). **`socket.connect(port, address)`** pins a default remote so you [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- can `send(msg)` without re-specifying it. Multicast: **`addMembership`/`dropMembership`**, [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `setMulticastTTL`, `setMulticastLoopback`; broadcast: `setBroadcast(true)`. Used for DNS, mDNS/SSDP [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- discovery, metrics (StatsD), and as the substrate under QUIC/HTTP-3. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- Node's global **`fetch`/`Request`/`Response`/`Headers`** (stable since v21) is implemented by [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **undici**, Node's from-scratch HTTP/1.1 client. Understanding undici *is* understanding `fetch`'s [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`Dispatcher`** is the base abstraction; everything is a dispatcher with a `.dispatch()` (and the [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- higher-level **`request`/`stream`/`pipeline`/`connect`/`upgrade`** methods). The concrete types: [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`Client`** — a single keep-alive connection to one origin. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`Pool`** — a pool of `Client`s to one origin (option **`connections`**); this is what gives you [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- parallelism to a single host. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`BalancedPool`** — spreads load across **multiple** upstream origins. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`Agent`** — the default dispatcher: opens a `Pool` per origin on demand (this backs `fetch`). [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`undici.request(url, opts)`** returns `{ statusCode, headers, body }` where `body` is a stream with [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- convenience readers (`body.json()`, `body.text()`); it's lower-overhead than `fetch` when you don't [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- need the WHATWG semantics. `undici.stream`/`pipeline` are for zero-copy piping. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`setGlobalDispatcher(dispatcher)`** / `getGlobalDispatcher()` swap the dispatcher that **global [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `fetch` uses** — the supported way to set client-wide pool size, timeouts, TLS (`connect` options), [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- or a proxy for all `fetch` calls in a process. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **Interceptors** compose behaviour onto a dispatcher: **`dispatcher.compose(interceptor, ...)`** with [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- built-ins for **redirect**, **retry**, **dns**, and **cache** (the modern replacement for the older [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `maxRedirections` option style). **`RetryAgent`** wraps a dispatcher with a `RetryHandler` (backoff, [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- idempotent-method retries). **`ProxyAgent`** / **`EnvHttpProxyAgent`** route through an HTTP(S) proxy [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- (the latter reads `HTTP_PROXY`/`HTTPS_PROXY`/`NO_PROXY`). **`MockAgent`** + `setGlobalDispatcher` [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- intercepts requests in tests without a real network. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `Client`/`Pool` constructor options and their **current** defaults (verify against your undici [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- version — these changed historically): [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`pipelining`** — default **off** (effectively 1 in-flight per connection); HTTP/1.1 pipelining is [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- off because of head-of-line blocking. Set higher only against servers you control. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`keepAliveTimeout`** — default **4 s**; **`keepAliveMaxTimeout`** — default **10 min** (caps how far [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- a server `keep-alive` hint can extend it); `keepAliveTimeoutThreshold` trims a safety margin. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`headersTimeout`** — default **30 s** (wait for response headers); **`bodyTimeout`** — default [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **30 s** (max gap between body chunks). A connection-establishment timeout (~10 s) is configured as a [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **Connector** option (`connect: { timeout }`), not a top-level Client default. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `connect: { ... }` carries TLS options (`ca`, `rejectUnauthorized`, `servername`, ALPN) for HTTPS [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- origins; `maxRequestsPerClient` recycles a connection after N requests. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **Always set client keep-alive.** A bare `http.request` with the default `globalAgent` [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- (`keepAlive: false`) opens and tears down a TCP+TLS connection per request. Use a shared [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `new http.Agent({ keepAlive: true, maxSockets: <bounded> })`, or for `fetch` call [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `setGlobalDispatcher(new Agent({ connections: N }))` once at startup. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **Order the timeout sandwich correctly:** Node `server.keepAliveTimeout` **>** upstream LB idle [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- timeout, and give `headersTimeout`/`requestTimeout` finite values so a stuck client can't pin a [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- socket forever. Mirror it on the client with undici `headersTimeout`/`bodyTimeout`. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **Bound `maxSockets`/`connections`.** `Infinity` (the default) means a downstream slowdown lets [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- pending requests open unbounded sockets → fd exhaustion. Size the pool to the downstream's capacity. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **Pick the protocol deliberately:** HTTP/2 (`createSecureServer` + ALPN `'h2'`) for many concurrent [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- streams to one origin; HTTP/1.1 + a `Pool` of `connections` when the server isn't h2. Don't enable [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- HTTP/1.1 `pipelining` on the open internet. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **Reuse a `SecureContext`** across connections instead of re-reading PEM per request; enable session [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- resumption (tickets + shared `ticketKeys` behind an LB) to cut handshake round-trips. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **Test with `MockAgent`**, not a live network: `const mock = new MockAgent(); setGlobalDispatcher(mock); mock.get(origin).intercept({ path }).reply(200, body)`. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **No timeouts anywhere.** A `fetch`/`http.request` with no `bodyTimeout`/`headersTimeout` to a slow [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- peer hangs forever and holds a socket; a server with the defaults removed is a slowloris target. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`keepAliveTimeout` below the LB idle timeout** → the LB reuses a socket Node already closed → [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `ECONNRESET` → intermittent **502s** that look random. The #1 Node-behind-ALB bug. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`maxSockets: Infinity` / unbounded `connections`** → socket & file-descriptor exhaustion under load [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- (`EMFILE`), often mistaken for a memory leak. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **A fresh `Agent`/`Pool`/`Client` per request** → you've thrown away pooling entirely; create it once [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **Enabling HTTP/1.1 pipelining to arbitrary servers** → head-of-line blocking and corruption with [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- non-compliant intermediaries; that's why undici ships it off. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **Relying on HTTP/2 server push** → removed from browsers and deprecated in RFC 9113; use `103 Early [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **Disabling `rejectUnauthorized` to "fix" a TLS error** → silently disables cert validation (MITM). [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- Fix the trust chain via `ca:` instead. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **Intermittent 502 / `ECONNRESET` behind a proxy** → raise `server.keepAliveTimeout` above the [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- upstream idle timeout; confirm with `curl -v` keep-alive reuse. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`fetch` is slow / opens too many connections** → you're on the default per-origin pool; install a [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- tuned `Agent` via `setGlobalDispatcher` and check `keepAlive` is in effect. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`socket hang up` / `UND_ERR_HEADERS_TIMEOUT` / `UND_ERR_BODY_TIMEOUT`** → the server didn't respond [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- within undici's 30 s header/body timeout; raise the relevant option or fix the upstream. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`EMFILE: too many open files`** → unbounded `maxSockets`/`connections` (or leaked sockets that never [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- `end`); bound the pool and `ulimit -n`. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **`HPE_HEADER_OVERFLOW` / `431`** → headers exceed `--max-http-header-size` (16 KiB); raise the flag or [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- shrink cookies/headers. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **HTTP/2 client gets HTTP/1.1** → ALPN didn't negotiate `'h2'`; check `ALPNProtocols` on both ends and [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- read `socket.alpnProtocol` to confirm. [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- **TLS handshake slow under load** → no session resumption; wire up tickets/`ticketKeys` and reuse a [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- single `SecureContext`. (Event-loop lag while throughput is fine is a different problem — profile the [src: nodejs-http-networking]
- loop; see `nodejs-concurrency-internals`.) [src: nodejs-http-networking]

- <!-- Provenance: reference under the `lang-js-ts` hub. Mirrored from ~/.claude/skills/lang-js-ts/references/nodejs-module-resolution.md by scripts/persist-spoke.mjs. --> [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- This reference is about **HOW Node.js turns a specifier into a loaded module** — the two [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- resolution algorithms (CommonJS `require` and ESM) and the interop seam between them. It [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- assumes you already know *what* a module is and *how to write one*; that intro is owned by [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- the **`javascript-nodejs`** reference. Two other siblings own adjacent layers and are [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- explicitly out of scope here: [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **`nodejs-typescript-and-runtime-features`** — TypeScript native type-stripping, the [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `--experimental-strip-types` / `--experimental-transform-types` flags, and the [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `.ts`/`.mts` import-extension rules. This file covers JS/JSON/Wasm resolution only. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **Bundlers/transpilers** (esbuild, webpack, Vite, `tsc`'s `moduleResolution`) — they [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- reimplement resolution with their own rules. This file is the **Node runtime** resolver. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- The two mental models you must hold separately: **CommonJS resolution is synchronous, [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- filesystem-probing, and extension-tolerant** (`require('./util')` tries `util`, `util.js`, [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `util.json`, `util.node`, then `util/index.js`…). **ESM resolution is URL-based, mostly [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- specifier-exact, and requires file extensions** (`import './util.js'` — no extension [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- guessing, no directory index). The `"exports"`/`"imports"` package.json fields, the [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- condition system, and the dual-package hazard are the shared machinery that both algorithms [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- now route through, and `require(esm)` (stable since the v20.19/v22.12 LTS lines) is the [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- bridge that finally lets CommonJS load ES modules synchronously. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `require(X)` from a module at path `Y` runs a fixed, synchronous sequence (the [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- spec-pseudocode names are load-bearing — they appear in errors and docs): [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **Core / `node:` builtin** → return it and STOP. The `node:` prefix always hits the [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- builtin and bypasses `require.cache`. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **`/`, `./`, `../`** (relative/absolute) → `LOAD_AS_FILE(Y+X)` then `LOAD_AS_DIRECTORY(Y+X)`. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **`#`-prefixed** → `LOAD_PACKAGE_IMPORTS` (private internal specifiers, concept 4). [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `LOAD_PACKAGE_SELF` (self-reference by package name), then [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `LOAD_NODE_MODULES(X, dirname(Y))` — the `node_modules` walk. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- Else THROW `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **`LOAD_AS_FILE(X)`** probes extensions in order: `X` (verbatim) → `X.js` → `X.json` → [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `X.node` (native addon). The `.js` case consults the **closest `package.json` `"type"`** [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- to decide ESM vs CJS (and otherwise detects module syntax). [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **`LOAD_INDEX(X)`** probes `X/index.js` → `X/index.json` → `X/index.node`. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **`LOAD_AS_DIRECTORY(X)`** reads `X/package.json`'s `"main"`, runs `LOAD_AS_FILE` then [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `LOAD_INDEX` on it, and falls back to `LOAD_INDEX(X)`. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **`LOAD_NODE_MODULES(X, START)`** iterates `NODE_MODULES_PATHS(START)`, trying [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `LOAD_PACKAGE_EXPORTS` then `LOAD_AS_FILE` then `LOAD_AS_DIRECTORY` in each dir. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **`NODE_MODULES_PATHS(START)`** generates the walk: append `node_modules` at every [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- ancestor directory up to the filesystem root, then `GLOBAL_FOLDERS`. So [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `/home/ry/projects/foo.js` requiring `bar` searches [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `/home/ry/projects/node_modules/bar` → `/home/ry/node_modules/bar` → [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `/home/node_modules/bar` → `/node_modules/bar`. This array is exposed as `module.paths`. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `require.cache` keys loaded modules by resolved filename (delete a key to force reload). [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `require.resolve(req[, {paths}])` runs the machinery without loading; `require.resolve.paths(req)` [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- returns the search list (or `null` for a core module). `require.main` is the entry module — [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `require.main === module` is the CJS "am I the entry point?" idiom. `NODE_PATH` (colon-/ [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- semicolon-delimited absolute paths) is a legacy prepend to the walk; prefer `"exports"` over it. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- ESM resolution is URL-based and specified as **`ESM_RESOLVE(specifier, parentURL)` → `{ format, resolved }`**: [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- Valid URL → parse and reserialize. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `/`, `./`, `../` → resolve relative to `parentURL` (a `file:` URL). [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `#…` → `PACKAGE_IMPORTS_RESOLVE`. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- Bare specifier → **`PACKAGE_RESOLVE`**: if it's a builtin, return `node:` + name; else walk [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `node_modules`, read `package.json`, and if `"exports"` exists call [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **`PACKAGE_EXPORTS_RESOLVE`**, else resolve `"main"`/subpath directly. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- For `file:` URLs: reject percent-encoded `/` or `\`; **throw `ERR_UNSUPPORTED_DIR_IMPORT` [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- for a directory** (no index lookup); **throw `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` if absent**; then set [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- format via `ESM_FILE_FORMAT`. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **`PACKAGE_EXPORTS_RESOLVE`** and **`PACKAGE_TARGET_RESOLVE`** evaluate the `"exports"` map: [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- target objects are walked **in insertion order**, returning the first key that is `"default"` [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- or present in the active condition set; arrays try each entry; `null` blocks. **`ESM_FILE_FORMAT`** [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- maps extension → format: `.mjs`→`module`, `.cjs`→`commonjs`, `.json`→`json`, `.wasm`→`wasm`, [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `.js`→`"type"`-driven (or syntax-detected), no-extension→`"type"` or detection. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- The consequences that bite developers: **file extensions are mandatory** (`import './x'` [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- fails — use `'./x.js'`), **directory indexes don't work** (`import './lib'` fails — use [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `'./lib/index.js'`), and a package with `"exports"` is **encapsulated** (concept 3). [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `"exports"` is the modern public-API surface for a package. Three powers: [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **Conditional exports** — map the same specifier to different files by environment. The [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- condition keys, in the documented **most-specific-to-least order**: `"types"` (MUST be [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- first, for type systems), `"node-addons"` (Node with native addons; off under [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `--no-addons`), `"node"` (any Node), `"import"` (loaded via `import`/`import()`), [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `"require"` (loaded via `require()`), `"module-sync"` (via `import`/`import()`/`require()` — [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- a synchronous ESM with no top-level await), `"default"` (MUST be last). **Key order is [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- significant** — the resolver returns the first match, so an `"import"` listed after [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `"default"` is dead. `"import"` and `"require"` are mutually exclusive at resolve time. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- Custom community conditions are matched via `node --conditions=<name>` (`-C`). [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- { "exports": { "types": "./index.d.ts", "import": "./index.mjs", "require": "./index.cjs" } } [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **Subpath exports** — expose specific deep entry points: `{ ".": "./index.js", [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- "./feature": "./src/feature.js" }`. **Subpath patterns** use `*` as a **flexible string [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- substitution (NOT a glob)**: `"./features/*.js": "./src/features/*.js"` maps [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `pkg/features/x.js` → `./src/features/x.js`, and `*` spans `/`. Map a target to `null` to [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- block a private subtree (`"./features/internal/*": null`). [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **Encapsulation** — once `"exports"` exists, **only listed subpaths are importable**; [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- everything else throws **`ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED`**. Add `"./package.json": [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- "./package.json"` if consumers need it. (Encapsulation is not "strong" — an absolute path [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `require('/abs/node_modules/pkg/secret.js')` still works.) **Exports sugar**: when only [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `"."` exists, `"exports": "./index.js"` is shorthand for `{ ".": "./index.js" }`. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `"imports"` defines specifiers **only resolvable from inside the same package**. Keys MUST [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- start with `#` (to disambiguate from bare external specifiers). Targets can be **internal [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- files OR external packages**, and support the **same conditions and `*` patterns** as [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- { "imports": { "#dep": { "node": "dep-node-native", "default": "./dep-polyfill.js" }, [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- "#internal/*.js": "./src/internal/*.js" } } [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- Then `import dep from '#dep'` / `import x from '#internal/util.js'` resolve per condition. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- Unlisted `#` specifiers throw **`ERR_PACKAGE_IMPORT_NOT_DEFINED`**. This is the standard [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- replacement for fragile `../../..` relative paths and for swapping implementations by env. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- When one package ships **both** a CJS and an ESM build (via `import`/`require` conditions), an [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- app can end up loading **both copies** — once through each entry. The hazard: [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **Two instances** of the module exist simultaneously; **module-level state diverges** [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- (caches, registries, singletons are not shared). [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **`instanceof` breaks** — a class from the ESM copy is not the same identity as the class [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- from the CJS copy, so `x instanceof Pkg.Thing` fails across the seam. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- Two documented cures: **(a) ESM-first with a thin CJS wrapper** — author in ESM and make the [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `"require"` target a `.cjs` that does `module.exports = require('./index.js')` (now viable [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- because `require(esm)` works, concept 6); or **(b) isolate all stateful logic into a single [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- CJS file** that *both* the ESM and CJS entry points load (the ESM entry uses `createRequire`), [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- so there is exactly one state object. With `require(esm)` unflagged, shipping a **single ESM [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- build** consumable by both `import` and `require` is increasingly the simplest answer. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **`require(esm)` — synchronous require of ES modules.** Timeline: added behind [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `--experimental-require-module` in **v22.0.0** (backported to v20.17), **unflagged/default [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- in v23** and across the LTS lines (**v20.19.0+, v22.12.0+**), now marked stable. With it, [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `require()` of an ES module no longer throws `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM`. **Constraint:** the target [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- must be unambiguously ESM (`.mjs` or `"type":"module"`) and **fully synchronous** — a [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- top-level `await` anywhere in its graph throws **`ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE`**. Disable with [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `--no-experimental-require-module`. The returned object is the module namespace: the ESM [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- default is on `.default`, and (v23+) a `'module.exports'` key mirrors the CJS-interop view. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **Importing CommonJS from ESM.** `module.exports` is exposed as the **default export**; [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- Node additionally runs **`cjs-module-lexer`** to statically detect named exports so [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `import { name } from './cjs.cjs'` works. Detection is a **heuristic** — dynamically [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- assigned or computed exports are not seen; fall back to the default import and destructure. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **`module.createRequire(filename)`** builds a `require` scoped to an ESM file: [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `const require = createRequire(import.meta.url)` — the standard way to pull a CJS-only [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- package (or JSON) into ESM. (Requires created this way are not affected by async hooks.) [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **`import.meta`** (ESM only): `import.meta.url` (the module's `file:` URL); [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `import.meta.resolve(specifier)` — **synchronous since v20** (returns a URL **string**, not [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- a Promise; honors `"exports"`); `import.meta.dirname` and `import.meta.filename` (stable [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- v22/v24; the ESM equivalents of `__dirname`/`__filename`, `file:` modules only); [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `import.meta.main` (newer) ≈ `require.main === module`. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- Node lets you intercept resolution and loading with **hooks**, registered before app code via [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `--import ./register-hooks.js`: [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **`module.registerHooks({ resolve, load })`** (v23.5+, release candidate) — **synchronous, [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- in-thread** hooks. The recommended default: simpler, no inter-thread overhead, and works [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- cleanly for CommonJS in the graph. Returns `{ deregister() }`. Registration is **LIFO** — [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- the last-registered hook runs first, then chains toward Node's default. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **`module.register(specifier[, parentURL][, options])`** (v20.6+) — registers a hooks [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- module that runs **asynchronously on a separate loader thread**. Use it when a hook must do [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- async work and you want Node to own the worker/atomics plumbing; `options.data` + [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `options.transferList` (e.g. a `MessagePort`) pass data to `initialize`. (It carries [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- documentation-only deprecation **DEP0205** steering most users to `registerHooks`, but it is [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **not** runtime-deprecated and remains the off-thread API.) [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **The hooks.** `initialize(data)` runs once at registration. **`resolve(specifier, context, [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- nextResolve)`** receives `context.{conditions, importAttributes, parentURL}` and returns [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `{ url, format?, importAttributes?, shortCircuit? }`. **`load(url, context, nextLoad)`** [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- returns `{ format, source, shortCircuit? }` where `format` ∈ `'builtin' | 'commonjs' | [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- 'json' | 'module' | 'wasm'` (+ addon/typescript variants). Each hook must either call [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `next…()` (to chain) or set `shortCircuit: true`. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **History.** The old `--experimental-loader ./loader.mjs` flag (v8.8) was the original API; [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- its `getFormat`/`getSource`/`transformSource`/`globalPreload` hooks were removed in v16.12 [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- and the whole flag superseded by `register`/`registerHooks`. `module.builtinModules`, [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `module.isBuiltin(name)`, and `module.syncBuiltinESMExports()` round out the introspection. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **Import attributes** — `import data from './x.json' with { type: 'json' }` (and the dynamic [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `import('./x.json', { with: { type: 'json' } })`). No longer experimental (v20.18/v22.12+). [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- They **replaced** the older `assert { type: ... }` "import assertions" syntax (deprecated). [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **JSON modules** require `with { type: 'json' }`, expose **only a default export** (no named [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- exports), and share a cache entry with the CJS JSON cache. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **`data:` and `node:` imports** — `data:text/javascript,…` / `data:application/json,…` (no [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- relative resolution) and `node:fs` builtins. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **Import maps** are a **browser/HTML** standard (`<script type="importmap">`) for remapping [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- bare specifiers in the browser; Node has **no built-in import-map support** — the Node [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- equivalent of "remap a bare specifier" is `"imports"` (concept 4) or a `resolve` hook. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **Authoring a package's public API: lead with `"exports"`.** List every supported entry [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- point; rely on encapsulation to keep deep imports private; put `"types"` first and [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `"default"` last in every condition object. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **Ship dual packages only when forced.** Prefer a single ESM build now that `require(esm)` [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- is unflagged. If you must ship both, use the ESM-source + `.cjs`-wrapper pattern, or [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- isolate state into one shared CJS file — never let both builds carry independent state. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **Pull CJS-only deps / JSON into ESM with `createRequire`** rather than fighting named-export [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- detection; pull pure data with `with { type: 'json' }`. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **Use `"imports"` (`#…`) for internal aliases and env-swapped implementations** instead of [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `../../..` chains or build-time aliasing. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **Prefer `module.registerHooks` (in-thread)** for transforms/instrumentation; reach for [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `module.register` (off-thread) only when a hook genuinely needs async I/O. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **Register hooks via `--import`**, not inside app code, so they affect the entry module and [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **Relying on extensionless / directory imports in ESM.** `import './util'` and [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `import './lib'` fail — ESM needs `'./util.js'` and `'./lib/index.js'`. Only CJS guesses. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **Mis-ordering conditions.** Putting `"default"` (or `"require"`) before `"import"` makes [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- the later, more specific branch unreachable — the first match wins. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **Forgetting that `"exports"` blocks deep imports.** Adding `"exports"` silently breaks [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `pkg/lib/internal.js` consumers with `ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED`; list (or deliberately [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- withhold) every subpath, and re-add `"./package.json"` if needed. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **A dual package with shared mutable state in both builds** → divergent singletons and [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `instanceof` failures (the dual-package hazard). [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **`require()`-ing an ESM with top-level await** → `ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE`; use dynamic [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `import()`, or remove the top-level `await`. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **Treating `*` in `"exports"` as a glob.** It is a plain string substitution; `./*` exposes [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- *everything*, including dotfiles, unless narrowed or blocked with `null`. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **`assert { type: 'json' }`** — the deprecated assertion syntax; use `with { type: 'json' }`. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **`ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`** → ESM couldn't find the `file:` URL: missing extension, wrong [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- relative base, or a bare specifier not exported. Check the exact specifier string; [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- `import.meta.resolve` shows what Node computes. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **`ERR_REQUIRE_ESM`** → you're on an old Node (or `--no-experimental-require-module`), or the [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- target isn't unambiguously ESM. Upgrade to a current LTS, or use dynamic `import()`. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **`ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE`** → the required ESM (or a transitive dep) uses top-level await. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **`ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED`** → the subpath isn't in the dependency's `"exports"`; use [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- a listed entry point, or (last resort) an absolute path past `node_modules`. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **`ERR_UNSUPPORTED_DIR_IMPORT`** → ESM import of a directory; point at the index file. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **`ERR_PACKAGE_IMPORT_NOT_DEFINED`** → a `#…` specifier with no `"imports"` entry (or no [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **Named import from a CJS module is `undefined`** → `cjs-module-lexer` couldn't statically [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- see it (dynamic/computed `exports`); import the default and destructure at runtime. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- **A loader hook isn't applied to the entry file** → register it with `--import` (preload), [src: nodejs-module-resolution]
- not from within application code, which runs too late. [src: nodejs-module-resolution]

- Between Node.js v20 and v26 (2024-2026) the runtime absorbed a wave of capabilities that [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- historically required an npm dependency. A SQLite driver, a WebSocket *client*, `.env` [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- parsing, a task runner, file watching, glob matching, terminal colors, deep cloning, and a [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- V8 startup cache now all ship in core. The practical upshot: many small projects can drop [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- `better-sqlite3`, `ws`, `dotenv`, `nodemon`, `chalk`, `glob`, and `lodash.cloneDeep` [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- The catch — and the reason this reference exists — is **stability is per-feature and [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- recent**. Some of these are fully Stable (2), several are Release Candidate (1.2), and a [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- few are still Experimental (1) or "Active development" (1.1). Shipping an Experimental API [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- to production without pinning the Node version is the cardinal sin here. Every concept [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- below states its **added-in version and current stability index explicitly**; treat those [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- as the load-bearing facts, because an API that is RC today may change a method signature in [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- Scope boundaries (owned by sibling references in this family): Single-Executable [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- Applications, the `--permission` model, and native TypeScript stripping live in [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- `nodejs-typescript-and-runtime-features`; the **deep** `node:test` runner (mocking, [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- coverage, reporters, snapshots) lives in `nodejs-test-runner` — `node:test` is mentioned [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- here only as "it exists, it replaces Jest/Mocha for many projects, see the sibling"; [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- Bun/Deno/edge equivalents live in `javascript-runtimes-deno-bun-edge`. [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- A note on reading stability: index **2** = Stable; **1.2** = Release Candidate (API frozen, [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- shipping unflagged, final polish); **1.1** = Active development (unflagged but may change); [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- **1** = Experimental; **1.0** = Early development. Anything below 2 deserves a pinned [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- `engines.node` and a changelog read on upgrade. [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]

- The in-core replacement for **`dotenv`**. Three surfaces: [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- **`--env-file=.env`** (CLI) — added **v20.6.0**, **Stable** since **v24.10.0 / v22.21.0**. [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- Loads the file into `process.env` before the app runs; Node-config vars like [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]

- **`node --run <script>`** (added **v22.0.0**, **Stability 1.1 - Active development**) runs a [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]

- migrating from npm — chained build steps silently stop running. It also doesn't read npm [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- config or run arbitrary shell features npm provides. [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- **Watch mode** restarts the process on file changes — the in-core **`nodemon`**: [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]

- **`--watch-path=<dir>`** — watch explicit paths instead of the dependency graph (repeatable). [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- **`--watch-preserve-output`** — don't clear the terminal on restart (keep prior logs). [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]

- Node ships a full test runner (`node --test`, `node:test`, `node:assert`) that replaces [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]

- **`util.parseArgs([config])`** — added **v18.3.0 / v16.17.0**, **Stability 2 - Stable** [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]

- arg parsing). `config.options` keys are long names; each value is `{ type: 'string' | [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- 'boolean' (required), short, multiple, default }`. Parser flags: `args` (defaults to [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]
- `process.argv` minus execPath+filename), `strict` (default `true` — throws on unknown [src: nodejs-builtin-modules-modern]

- This reference is the layer **above** basic promises. Once you can `await`, three problems [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- remain: how do you **cancel** an in-flight operation, how do you carry **structured error [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- information** (not just a string), and how do you keep **per-request context** (a request [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- id, a trace span, a tenant) alive as control hops across `await` points, timers, and [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- callbacks. Cancellation, structured errors, and async context are what this file covers. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- It defers three adjacent topics: the *intro* layer (what a promise is, `async`/`await`, [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- `.then`/`.catch`) → **`javascript-nodejs`**; the libuv **event-loop phase model**, [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- microtask-vs-macrotask ordering, and `process.nextTick` starvation → **`nodejs-concurrency-internals`**; [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- and `diagnostics_channel` / `channel.bindStore()` / `TracingChannel` for APM-style [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- instrumentation → **`nodejs-diagnostics-profiling`** (this file uses `AsyncLocalStorage` [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- for *your own* request context). [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- The mental model: a unit of async work should be **cancellable** (carries an `AbortSignal`), [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- should **fail with a typed, chainable error** (carries `code` + `cause`), and should run [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **inside a context** (`AsyncLocalStorage`) any nested async call can read without threading [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- an argument through every function. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- `AbortController` is the standard cancellation primitive (Web-platform, available globally [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- in Node — no import). A controller owns one `signal`; calling `controller.abort(reason)` [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- flips `signal.aborted` to `true`, records `signal.reason`, and fires the `'abort'` event. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- const ac = new AbortController(); [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- ac.signal.addEventListener('abort', () => console.log('cancelled:', ac.signal.reason), [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- { once: true });            // { once: true } avoids a leak [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- setTimeout(() => ac.abort(new Error('user navigated away')), 5_000); [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- await fetch(url, { signal: ac.signal });               // rejects with the reason on abort [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **The signal is the cancellation token.** Pass `signal` into the options of any [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- abort-aware API: `fetch(url, { signal })`, `node:timers/promises` [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- (`setTimeout(ms, value, { signal })`), `fs.readFile(path, { signal })`, [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- `events.once(emitter, name, { signal })`, and stream/pipeline operations. The API [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- rejects (or rejects the awaited promise) with an `AbortError` (`err.code === 'ABORT_ERR'`) [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- — or with your custom `reason` if you passed one to `abort()`. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **`signal.reason`** is whatever you passed to `abort(reason)`; if you passed nothing it [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- defaults to a `DOMException` named `AbortError`. **`signal.throwIfAborted()`** throws that [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- reason immediately — call it at the top of and between steps in a long async function so a [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- late-arriving cancellation short-circuits. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **`'abort'` event**: register a listener (with `{ once: true }`) to run teardown that the [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- awaited API can't do for you (close a file you opened, roll back). [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- The two static factories are what make cancellation composable: [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **`AbortSignal.timeout(ms)`** returns a signal that auto-aborts after `ms` (with a [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- `TimeoutError` reason). It does **not** keep the event loop alive — it won't, by itself, [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- prevent the process from exiting. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **`AbortSignal.any([...signals])`** returns a signal that aborts as soon as **any** input [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- aborts, adopting that signal's `reason`. This is how you OR together a request-deadline [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- import { setTimeout as delay } from 'node:timers/promises'; [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- const userCancel = new AbortController(); [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- const signal = AbortSignal.any([userCancel.signal, AbortSignal.timeout(10_000)]); [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- await fetch(url, { signal });   // aborts on whichever fires first; reason tells you which [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- `AbortSignal.abort(reason)` returns an already-aborted signal — handy for tests or for [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- passing "already cancelled" into a function uniformly. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- A thrown string loses information. Node + modern JS give you three structuring tools: [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **`Error.cause`** — the second-argument options bag: `new Error('msg', { cause })`. It [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **chains** a low-level failure to a higher-level one without flattening the message, and [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- `util.inspect`/stack printing walks the chain. Re-throw with context, keep the original: [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- try { await db.query(sql); } [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- catch (cause) { throw new Error('failed to load user profile', { cause }); } [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **`AggregateError`** — holds *multiple* errors in `err.errors` (an array). This is exactly [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- what **`Promise.any`** rejects with when every input rejects, and the right type to throw [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- when you've collected several failures (see `Promise.allSettled` below). [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **Custom error classes** — subclass `Error`, set a stable `code`, and (optionally) carry [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- `cause`. Always set `name` and `code`: [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- class ConfigError extends Error { [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- constructor(message, opts) { super(message, opts); this.name = 'ConfigError'; this.code = 'E_CONFIG'; } [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- Node attaches a stable **string `code`** to its errors (`ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE`, [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- `ABORT_ERR`, `ENOENT`, `ECONNREFUSED`, …). The docs are explicit: `error.code` changes [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- only across **major** Node versions, while `error.message` may change in **any** version. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **Branch on `code`, not on the message** — message matching is a latent bug that breaks on [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- upgrade and across locales. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- try { await fs.readFile(p); } [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- if (err.code === 'ENOENT') return null;   // stable [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- if (err.code === 'ABORT_ERR') return;     // cancelled, not an error [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- throw err;                                // unknown — re-throw, don't swallow [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- Two `process` events are the safety net of last resort: [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **`'unhandledRejection'`** `(reason, promise)` — a `Promise` rejected with no handler [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- attached within a turn of the loop. **`'rejectionHandled'`** `(promise)` fires if a [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- handler is attached *later* — track a `Map` keyed by the promise to reconcile the two [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- (add on `unhandledRejection`, delete on `rejectionHandled`) and report only the survivors. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **`'uncaughtException'`** `(err, origin)` — an exception bubbled to the loop with no [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- `try/catch`. **`'uncaughtExceptionMonitor'`** observes it *without* changing the [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- crash-or-not behavior (use it to log to an APM, then let the normal handling run). [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **Why `uncaughtException` must generally be fatal.** The docs state it plainly: an uncaught [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- exception means the app is in an **undefined state**; `'uncaughtException'` is *not* an [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- `On Error Resume Next`. The correct use is **synchronous cleanup of resources** (flush a [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- log, release file descriptors) and then **exit** — let an external supervisor restart the [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- process. Resuming after it is unsafe. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **Exit semantics.** Prefer setting **`process.exitCode = n`** and letting the loop drain [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- naturally over **`process.exit(n)`**, which terminates synchronously and can **truncate** [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- buffered `stdout`/`stderr`. The **`'exit'`** event handler may run **synchronous code only** [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- — queued async work is abandoned the instant it returns. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **`--unhandled-rejections=<mode>`** controls rejection handling: `throw` (the default since [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- Node 15 — emit the event, else raise as an uncaught exception), `strict` (always raise as [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- uncaught), `warn` (always warn, never throw), `warn-with-error-code` (warn and set a nonzero [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- exit code), and `none` (silence entirely). [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- The four combinators differ on **fail-fast vs collect-all** and on **fulfillment vs first-settled**: [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- The teaching point: **`all` is fail-fast** (one rejection abandons the others' results), [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **`allSettled` is collect-all** (you get every outcome, success and failure, and inspect [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- `status`). Use `all` when any failure should abort the batch; use `allSettled` for "do all [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- of these, then tell me what worked." `race` settles on the *first* outcome of either kind; [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- `any` ignores rejections until a fulfilment (or gives you an `AggregateError`). [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **Concurrency limiting.** `Promise.all(items.map(fn))` fires *all* tasks at once — fine for [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- 10, a thundering herd for 10,000 (socket exhaustion, rate-limit bans). Cap in-flight work [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- with a pool (a small worker-count loop pulling from a shared iterator, or a library like [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- `p-limit`). This is the practical complement to the combinators. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **`AsyncLocalStorage`** (from `node:async_hooks`) carries a value through an async call [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- chain **without** threading it as a parameter — the canonical use being a per-request id or [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- trace context that any nested function can read: [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- import { AsyncLocalStorage } from 'node:async_hooks'; [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- const als = new AsyncLocalStorage(); [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- http.createServer((req, res) => { [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- als.run({ reqId: crypto.randomUUID() }, () => handle(req, res)); // store survives awaits [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- function log(msg) { console.log(als.getStore()?.reqId, msg); }     // reads it anywhere downstream [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **`run(store, cb, ...args)`** is the API you want 95% of the time: it scopes `store` to [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- `cb` and every async operation spawned inside it, then restores the previous store. Nested [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- `run` calls shadow cleanly. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **`getStore()`** returns the current store (or `undefined` outside any `run`). [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **`enterWith(store)`** sets the store for the **rest of the current synchronous execution** [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- and onward — with **no automatic exit**. The docs warn this leaks easily (e.g. a second [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- event-handler on the same emitter inherits it). **Prefer `run()`; reach for `enterWith()` [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- only with a strong reason.** `exit(cb)` runs `cb` *outside* the store; `disable()` tears [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **`AsyncLocalStorage.snapshot()`** captures the current context and returns a function [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- that re-enters it later — useful for re-binding a callback to the context it was created [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- in without a full `AsyncResource`. `AsyncLocalStorage.bind(fn)` wraps a function so it [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- always runs in the captured context. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **Performance / when to use.** It is the *recommended, stable, optimized* mechanism — far [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- better than rolling your own with `async_hooks`. It is not free (context tracking has a [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- measured cost), so use it for genuinely cross-cutting state (request id, trace, tenant), [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- not as a general-purpose variable bag. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **When the context is lost,** the propagation broke at a boundary `AsyncLocalStorage` can't [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- see — a callback queued by native/3rd-party code, an object-pool worker, or a long-lived [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- emitter. That is the job of **`async_hooks`** and **`AsyncResource`**, the low-level layer: [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **`async_hooks.createHook({ init, before, after, destroy })`** registers lifecycle [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- callbacks for *every* async resource; `executionAsyncId()` / `triggerAsyncId()` expose the [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- current resource and the one that scheduled it. This is the machinery `AsyncLocalStorage` [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **`AsyncResource`** is the piece you actually use directly: wrap a callback that will be [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- invoked later (from a connection pool, a cache, a custom emitter) so it runs in the [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- correct context. Construct `new AsyncResource('MyThing')` and call [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- `resource.runInAsyncScope(cb, thisArg, ...args)`, or wrap once with the static [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **`AsyncResource.bind(fn)`**. This is how you re-attach context across a pool boundary. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **Caveat:** `async_hooks` is **Stability 1 (experimental)** and low-level; the docs [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- *explicitly discourage* using the hook API directly and steer you to `AsyncLocalStorage` [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- for context tracking. Use `AsyncResource.bind` for the pool-callback case; avoid building [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- context systems on raw `createHook`. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **`util.promisify(fn)`** converts an **error-first callback** function `(…, (err, value) => …)` [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- into a promise-returning one; **`util.callbackify(fn)`** does the reverse for an async [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- function. If a function ships a better promise form, it advertises it on the [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **`util.promisify.custom`** symbol and `promisify` returns that instead of wrapping the [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- callback. (Most core modules already expose `node:fs/promises` etc. — promisify is for [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- third-party or legacy callback APIs.) [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **Thread one signal through a whole operation.** Accept `{ signal }` in your own async [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- functions, call `signal.throwIfAborted()` between steps, and forward the same signal to [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- every downstream call (`fetch`, timers, fs) so one `abort()` unwinds the entire tree. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **Time-box with `AbortSignal.any([userSignal, AbortSignal.timeout(ms)])`** instead of [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- racing a manual `setTimeout` reject — composition is cleaner and you keep the abort reason. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **Reconcile rejections** with the `Map` pattern: add on `'unhandledRejection'`, delete on [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- `'rejectionHandled'`, report the residue on shutdown. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **Re-bind pool callbacks** with `AsyncResource.bind(cb)` (or `AsyncLocalStorage.bind`) at [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- enqueue time so the dequeued callback runs in the right request context. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **Serialized awaits in a loop** — `for (const x of xs) await f(x)` when the calls are [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- independent. That's sequential latency; use `await Promise.all(xs.map(f))` (with a [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- concurrency cap for large `xs`). [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **Unbounded `Promise.all` over a huge array** — fires every task at once and exhausts [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- sockets / trips rate limits. Cap in-flight work. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **Treating `'uncaughtException'` as resume-and-continue** — the process is in an undefined [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- state; do sync cleanup, then exit and let a supervisor restart. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **`process.exit()` to "finish"** — truncates buffered output and abandons pending work; [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- set `process.exitCode` and let the loop drain. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **Matching on `err.message`** — breaks across versions and locales; match on `err.code`. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **Swallowing errors** (`catch {}`), or catching without re-throwing the unknown ones — you [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- lose the failure and the `cause` chain. Narrow on `code`, re-throw the rest. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **`AsyncLocalStorage.enterWith()` in shared/event-handler code** — leaks the store into [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- unrelated later callbacks; use `run()`. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **Building a context system on raw `async_hooks.createHook`** — it's experimental and [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- error-prone (a throw in a hook is fatal); use `AsyncLocalStorage` / `AsyncResource`. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **`fetch`/op doesn't actually stop on abort** → you logged `'abort'` but didn't pass [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- `signal` into the call's options, or you created a *new* controller per retry; pass the [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- *same* `signal` down and check `signal.aborted`. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **Caught error but `instanceof MyError` is false** → you compared types across a module [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- boundary or the error was re-wrapped; branch on `err.code` (and inspect `err.cause`) instead. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **`Promise.any` "fails" unexpectedly** → it rejects with an `AggregateError` only when [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **all** inputs reject; read `err.errors`. If you wanted first-*settled*, use `race`. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **Process crashes despite an `uncaughtExceptionMonitor` listener** → monitor does not [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- suppress the crash; install an `'uncaughtException'` handler (that then exits) if you must [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- intercept, but don't resume. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **`als.getStore()` is `undefined` downstream** → context was lost at a native/pool/emitter [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- boundary; wrap the callback with `AsyncResource.bind` / `AsyncLocalStorage.bind`, or [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- promisify a callback API so the store propagates. Don't paper over it with `enterWith()`. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- **Unhandled rejection silently ignored** → check `--unhandled-rejections`; if set to [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]
- `warn`/`none` it won't crash. Default (`throw`) surfaces it. [src: nodejs-async-patterns-error-context]

- The mental model: `node:test` is **TAP-emitting and isolation-by-default**. The [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `test()` function and the `TestContext`/`MockTracker` objects are the API; the `--test*` [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- CLI flags are the *runner* that discovers files, isolates them in child processes, [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- filters by name, and aggregates reporters — both halves matter. Two `import` surfaces: [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- functions come from `node:test` (`test`, `describe`, `it`, `before`, `mock`, …); reporter [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- classes from `node:test/reporters` (`spec`, `tap`, `lcov`, …). The runner is **stable [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- since Node.js 20** (coverage thresholds and snapshots stabilized later — noted per feature). [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `test(name, options?, fn)` registers a test; `fn` receives a `TestContext` named `t` [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- (and may be `async`, or use the second `done` callback for callback-style). `describe()` [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- (alias `suite()`) groups tests and `it()` (alias of `test`) reads naturally inside it — [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `describe`/`it` is the BDD style, bare `test()` the flat style. Both compose. [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- **Subtests**: call **`t.test(name, fn)`** to nest a test *inside* a parent test. The [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- parent **must `await`** its subtests (or `await Promise.all([...])`) — an un-awaited [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- subtest is cancelled when the parent finishes and reported as failing. This is the [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- single most common node:test mistake. [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- **The `TestContext` `t`** exposes: [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `t.diagnostic(message)` — emit a TAP diagnostic line (not an assertion). [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `t.plan(count, options?)` — assert that exactly `count` assertions/subtests run; [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `{ wait }` can wait for asynchronous assertions. The test fails if the count is off. [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `t.skip(message?)` / `t.todo(message?)` — mark the running test skipped/todo at [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- runtime; `t.runOnly(bool)` enables only-mode for *this context's* subtests. [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `t.signal` — an `AbortSignal` aborted on timeout/cancellation; pass it into [src: nodejs-test-runner]

- `t.waitFor(fn, options?)` — poll `fn` until it stops throwing (for eventually-true [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- conditions), with `interval`/`timeout`. [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `t.assert` — per-test assertion methods (see §7); `t.mock` — a per-test [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `MockTracker` (see §2) that auto-restores after the test. [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `describe`/`suite` callbacks get a `SuiteContext` (`signal`, `name`) rather than a [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- Four hooks, importable as top-level functions or callable as `t.before*`: [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `before(fn, options?)` / `after(fn, options?)` — run **once** per suite (file or [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `describe` block), around all its tests. `after` runs even if tests fail. [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `beforeEach(fn, options?)` / `afterEach(fn, options?)` — run around **each** test in [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- the current suite; `afterEach` runs even when the test fails (use it for teardown). [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- **`HookOptions`**: `{ signal, timeout }` — abort/limit a slow hook independently of [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- the tests. Hooks receive the test/suite context as their argument. [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- Hooks **nest**: an outer `describe`'s `beforeEach` runs before each test in nested [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `describe`s too. Scope hooks to a block by declaring them inside that `describe`, or [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- per-test via `t.beforeEach()`. [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- The `MockTracker` (`import { mock } from 'node:test'`, or per-test `t.mock`) creates [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- spies/stubs and tracks calls. Top-level `mock` persists across tests — call [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `mock.reset()`/`mock.restoreAll()` (or prefer `t.mock`, which auto-restores). [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- **`mock.fn(original?, implementation?, options?)`** — a mock function; without args [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- it's a no-op spy. `options.times` lets `implementation` apply for the first N calls [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- then fall back to `original`. [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- **`mock.method(object, methodName, implementation?, options?)`** — replace a method [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- in place while spying; restored on `restore()`. `mock.getter()` / `mock.setter()` [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- mock an accessor; **`mock.property(object, propertyName, value?)`** (Node 24+) mocks a [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- plain data property's reads/writes. [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- **Introspection — the `MockFunctionContext` at `someMock.mock`**: [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `mock.calls` — array of call records (`{ arguments, result, error, this, stack }`). [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `mock.callCount()` — number of invocations. [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `mock.mockImplementation(fn)` / `mock.mockImplementationOnce(fn, onCall?)` — swap the [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- implementation, permanently or for one (specific) call. [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `mock.resetCalls()` — clear recorded calls; `mock.restore()` — undo this one mock. [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `mock.timers` fakes timers and `Date` so time-dependent code is deterministic and fast. [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- **`mock.timers.enable({ apis, now })`** — turn on faking for the chosen `apis`: [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `setImmediate`, `Date`, and `scheduler.wait`. Faked APIs [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- cover the globals **and** `node:timers` + `node:timers/promises`. `now` seeds the [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- starting time (number or `Date`). [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- **`mock.timers.tick(ms)`** — advance fake time by `ms`, synchronously firing every [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- timer that would have elapsed (and moving the faked `Date`). `runAll()` fires all [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- pending timers and jumps to the last one's time. **`setTime(ms)`** sets the current [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- faked `Date` without running timers. [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- **`mock.timers.reset()`** — clear scheduled timers and restore real ones (also done by [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `mock.reset()` / disable). Faking `Date` makes `Date.now()` / `new Date()` follow the [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- **`mock.module(specifier, options?)`** replaces a module's exports for code imported [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- *after* the mock is installed — covering ESM, CommonJS, JSON, and builtin modules. [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- **Requires the `--experimental-test-module-mocks` flag** (and the API is experimental). [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `options`: `namedExports` (object of named exports), `defaultExport` (the default), [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- and `cache` (default `false` — by default the module is freshly evaluated and the [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- real cache is untouched; references obtained *before* mocking are not affected). [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- Because mocks apply to subsequent loads, the module under test must be brought in via [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- **dynamic `import()` after** the `mock.module()` call (static top-level imports are [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- already resolved). The mock is reverted by `restore()` / `restoreAll()`. [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- **Coverage.** Start with **`--experimental-test-coverage`** to collect and print line/ [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- branch/function coverage after the run. **Thresholds are stable (Node 22.8+)**: [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `--test-coverage-lines=<pct>`, `--test-coverage-branches=<pct>`, [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- `--test-coverage-functions=<pct>` make the process **exit non-zero** when coverage is [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- below target. `--test-coverage-exclude=<glob>` / `--test-coverage-include=<glob>` tune [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- scope; `node_modules/`, core modules, and the matched **test files themselves are [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- excluded by default**. Emit a real report with the **lcov** reporter (below) for CI. [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- **Reporters** (`node:test/reporters`): **`spec`** (human-readable, the CLI default on a [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- TTY), **`tap`** (TAP, the default when piped), **`dot`** (compact `.`/`X`), **`junit`** [src: nodejs-test-runner]
- (JUnit XML for CI), and **`lcov`** (an `lcov.info` file, only meaningful with [src: nodejs-test-runner]
