- **Workflow-as-code + a journal.** You write ordinary-looking async code; the [src: durable-agent-execution]
- runtime records every step's input/output into an append-only event log (a [src: durable-agent-execution]
- "journal" or "checkpoint"), keyed per execution/thread. On crash, the runtime [src: durable-agent-execution]
- restores the pre-failure state so the function continues "effectively once and to [src: durable-agent-execution]
- completion — whether it runs for seconds or years." [src: durable-agent-execution]
- Three architectural camps solve this. **This axis drives every selection [src: durable-agent-execution]
- *(Temporal, Restate, DBOS, Hatchet, Resonate, Vercel Workflow, Inngest)* [src: durable-agent-execution]
- On recovery the workflow function is **re-executed from the start**, but completed [src: durable-agent-execution]
- steps return their **recorded results** instead of re-running. This demands the [src: durable-agent-execution]
- workflow body be **deterministic**: same inputs -> same command sequence. Hence [src: durable-agent-execution]
- **all non-determinism — LLM calls, tool I/O, time, randomness, UUIDs — must live [src: durable-agent-execution]
- in journaled steps/activities, outside the replay path.** This is THE friction [src: durable-agent-execution]
- when applying classic durable execution to agents. [src: durable-agent-execution]
- Temporal: `NondeterminismError` if re-generated commands don't match the Event [src: durable-agent-execution]
- History. Use SDK-provided replay-safe time/random; **move all I/O to Activities**; [src: durable-agent-execution]
- write replay tests before changing workflow code. [src: durable-agent-execution]
- The "function looks normal but is secretly re-run many times" mental model is [src: durable-agent-execution]
- shared by Restate, DBOS, Resonate, and Vercel WDK ("must be deterministic to [src: durable-agent-execution]
- allow resuming after failures"). [src: durable-agent-execution]
- *(LangGraph / LangSmith Deployment)* [src: durable-agent-execution]
- Instead of replay-from-start, the runtime saves a **snapshot of graph state at [src: durable-agent-execution]
- every super-step** — a *checkpoint* — keyed by **thread**. Resume = load the [src: durable-agent-execution]
- latest checkpoint and continue. No determinism constraint on node bodies. [src: durable-agent-execution]
- Caveat: replay/time-travel re-executes nodes *after* the chosen checkpoint, so [src: durable-agent-execution]
- LLM/API/interrupt calls there fire again and may differ. [src: durable-agent-execution]
- *(Cloudflare Agents SDK on Durable Objects)* [src: durable-agent-execution]
- Each agent is an addressable stateful micro-server with an **embedded SQLite DB**. [src: durable-agent-execution]
- It consumes **zero compute when hibernated**, wakes on an event (HTTP / WebSocket [src: durable-agent-execution]
- / alarm / email), reads its state, works, then sleeps. State lives *with* the [src: durable-agent-execution]
- actor, not in a central journal. [src: durable-agent-execution]

- Total memory ≈ **model weights + KV cache + ~0.5-1 GB runtime overhead**. [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- **Weights = params(B) × bytes-per-weight**, set by the **quant level**: [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- **Quick formula:** `memory_GB ≈ params_B × bytes_per_weight × 1.2`. [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- Selection rule (in priority order): **(1) fit your RAM/VRAM ceiling, (2) quality, [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- (3) speed.** Q4_K_M is the community default; bump to Q5/Q6 for code & reasoning [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- (they punish aggressive quant); Q8_0 when fidelity matters and it fits. Avoid Q2. [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- *(How k-quants pack bits / imatrix calibration -> `llm-compression`.)* [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- **KV cache — the silent long-context killer.** It grows **linearly with context**. [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- A 70B at 4K ctx ≈ ~2 GB KV; at 128K ctx ≈ ~64 GB **for the cache alone** before [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- weights. Mitigate with **KV-cache quantization** (`--cache-type-k q8_0`) and [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- **GQA** (Llama 3.1 8B: 8 KV heads vs 32 query heads -> ~4x smaller cache). [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- **VRAM-tier cheat sheet (Q4_K_M, ~4K ctx):** [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- When weights exceed VRAM, use **partial offload**: llama.cpp `--n-gpu-layers N` [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- (GPU layers, rest on CPU) — graceful but slower. [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- **Apple Silicon vs consumer NVIDIA (the durable frame).** Two philosophies: [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- **Apple unified memory** — one large pool (up to 128-512 GB on Max/Ultra), but [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- **bandwidth-bound** (~546 GB/s on M4 Max). *Lets large models load that a 24 GB [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- card can't hold at all.* [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- **NVIDIA discrete VRAM** — faster (~1008 GB/s on RTX 4090), **~2x+ faster per [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- token when the model fits**, but **24 GB is a hard wall** — spill to system RAM [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- and throughput collapses. [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- **Takeaway: NVIDIA for speed at sizes that fit; Apple to *run* models that don't [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- fit a consumer GPU.** Indicative single-stream decode: dense **70B-Q4 ~8-15 tok/s [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- on an M4 Max** (faster at short context). Treat headline "2,000+ tok/s" figures [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- with care — those are MoE (few active params) and/or prefill/batched, not dense [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- decode. For multi-user throughput on one box you eventually outgrow these [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]
- single-stream runtimes -> **`llm-inference-serving`**. [src: on-device-local-llm-runtimes]

- The trust / permission / value layer for autonomous AI agents acting with [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- **delegated authority**. When an agent can browse, call tools, move data, and [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- spend money on a user's behalf, three questions must be answered before it acts: [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- **Who is this agent?** (identity), **What is it allowed to do, for whom, and for [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- how long?** (authorization), and **How does it pay, within what bounds, with what [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- audit trail?** (payments). This skill is the agent-specific answer to all three. [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- It is current to mid-2026 and is explicit about what is a ratified standard, a [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- draft, a vendor GA, or an announcement — this area is moving fast and much of it [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]

- the user's; wiring OAuth 2.1 on-behalf-of / token-exchange delegation; issuing [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- scoped least-privilege short-lived tokens; figuring out how an agent gets [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- *authorized to call* MCP servers; evaluating non-human / agentic identity [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- vendors; standing up a token vault / credential broker; adding human-in-the-loop [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- approval; or letting an agent transact with spend caps, mandates, and an audit [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]

- federated SSO/SAML, posture) -> **`okta-expert`**. This skill assumes an IdP [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]

- An agent is neither a human nor a classic service: it is an **intermediary** that [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- acts on a human's behalf yet is not that human. Today's identity systems offer [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- two bad defaults, both of which *misidentify* the agent: [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- **Impersonation (agent borrows the user's token/session).** Trivial to ship — [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- just pass the user's token — but the agent inherits *every* permission the [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- user holds, the audit trail collapses into a single human identity across all [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- downstream hops, and a **prompt injection becomes a confused-deputy attack**: [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- an attacker who controls part of the agent's context (an email, ticket, PDF, [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- webpage) can redirect the agent's standing authority to exfiltrate data. The [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- token authenticates correctly the entire way. [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- **Shared / static service account (long-lived API key).** Individual agent [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- behavior becomes **unattributable** — logs show which *account* acted, not [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- which agent or which user delegated — and revoking one misbehaving agent [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- revokes access for *every* agent on that account. [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- Both are the same root failure: **overscoped, long-lived, shared credentials.** [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- The consensus fix (CyberArk, Red Hat, Descope, Microsoft, AWS, multiple 2025-26 [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- arXiv papers) is **dedicated agentic identity**: each agent gets short-lived, [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- *scoped* credentials bound to a specific **user + agent + task**, so blast radius [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- is bounded and an agent can be revoked without touching the human. A separate [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- identity does not stop prompt injection, but **narrow agent-specific scopes [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- sharply reduce what a confused deputy can do.** [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- The community term is **non-human identity (NHI)** / **agentic identity** — [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- treated as a first-class identity type alongside humans and services. [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- Cryptographic foundations being adopted: workload identity (SPIFFE/SPIRE X.509 / [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- JWT-SVIDs, optionally bound to a measured workload via remote attestation on [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- TDX / SEV-SNP / Nitro Enclaves), and DIDs + Verifiable Credentials for cross-org [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- **RFC 8693 — OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RATIFIED, 2020).** The backbone. The [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- agent presents a `subject_token` (the user) and an `actor_token` (itself) and [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- receives a **composite token** whose `act` claim names the actor acting on the [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- subject's behalf. Supports **nested `act` claims** (agent A -> agent B -> API) [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- and a **`may_act`** claim to pre-authorize the next hop. **Critical caveat:** [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- token exchange does *not* automatically enforce least privilege or narrow [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- scope — narrowing + enforcement is the implementer's responsibility. [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- **OAuth 2.1 (IETF DRAFT, draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1).** Mandatory PKCE, exact [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- redirect-URI matching, short-lived access tokens, refresh-token rotation for [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- public clients. The baseline every agent auth flow should follow. [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- **draft-oauth-ai-agents-on-behalf-of-user-02 (IETF INTERNET-DRAFT, 2026).** [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- The key *new* agent-specific piece. Adds a **front-channel consent** flow that [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- RFC 8693 lacks: `requested_actor` on the authorization request (names the agent [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- on the consent screen) and `actor_token` on the token request (agent proves who [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- it is). The issued token names **user + client + agent** and documents the [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- **Microsoft "On-Behalf-Of" (OBO)** is a well-known RFC 8693 implementation; [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- agent platforms adapt it (grant types: `client_credential`, `jwt-bearer`, [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- One **OAuth client ID per agent**, with scopes limited to exactly what the task needs. [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- **Short-lived** access tokens (minutes), refresh-token rotation, and a clear [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- **per-agent revocation** path that does not disable the human. [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- **Narrow at each hop**: an orchestrator that calls sub-agents/tools should [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- *exchange* its delegated token for a new token scoped + audience-addressed to [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- each immediate destination — never forward the original credential. [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- **Just-in-time / Just-enough-access (JIT/JEA):** mint a least-privilege token [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- at action time rather than holding standing access. [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- This is the **MCP client / agent side** of MCP auth. (Authoring the server -> [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- `mcp-builder`.) The MCP authorization spec selects a subset of OAuth 2.1 + four [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- The MCP server is an **OAuth 2.1 resource server**; the agent is the **OAuth [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- 1 client**. (Applies to HTTP transports; stdio servers read creds from the [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- environment instead.) [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- **Discovery:** server returns **401 with a `WWW-Authenticate`** header -> client [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- fetches **`/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`** (**RFC 9728 Protected [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]

- **RFC 7591 Dynamic Client Registration** is SHOULD-level for zero-friction onboarding. [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- **Audience binding (RFC 8707 Resource Indicators — RATIFIED, mandatory):** the [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- client MUST send a `resource` parameter (the canonical MCP server URI) in *both* [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- authorization and token requests; the server MUST validate the token's [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- **audience is itself** and reject foreign-audience tokens. [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- **No token passthrough (security-critical):** if the MCP server calls upstream [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- APIs it acts as an OAuth client to *them* with a **separate** token — it MUST [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- NOT forward the agent's token. This is the documented fix for the confused- [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- deputy / token-replay class. Tokens go in `Authorization: Bearer` on *every* [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]
- request, never in the query string. [src: agent-identity-authz-payments]

- A mapped type `{ [P in keyof T]: ... }` is **homomorphic** -- it preserves the property modifiers (readonly, optional) of the source type `T`. This is what makes `Readonly<T>` and `Partial<T>` work correctly. [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- Key fact (a common myth, corrected): the compiler keys homomorphism on the **`in keyof T` constraint**, *not* on the presence of an `as` clause. Adding `as` does **not** by itself break homomorphism -- modifiers are still copied for every key that *survives* the remap. Only keys whose **identity changes** (e.g. remapped to a template-literal string) lose 1:1 modifier provenance, because the output key differs from the source key. So `{ [K in keyof T as F<K>]: ... }` remains modifier-homomorphic over its surviving keys. [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- // Homomorphic: preserves readonly/optional modifiers [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- type Copy<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] }; [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- // Still homomorphic over surviving keys: `as` does NOT disable modifier copying. [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- // Only keys whose identity CHANGES (here, renamed to template-literal strings) lose [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- // their 1:1 modifier mapping, because the output key differs from the source key. [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- type Renamed<T> = { [K in keyof T as `prefix_${string & K}`]: T[K] }; [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- -- [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- TypeScript uses structural typing. Branded types simulate nominal typing by adding a phantom property that makes structurally identical types incompatible. [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- type Brand<T, B extends string> = T & { readonly __brand: B }; [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- type UserId = Brand<string, "UserId">; [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- type OrderId = Brand<string, "OrderId">; [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- function getUser(id: UserId) { /* ... */ } [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- const userId = "abc" as UserId; [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- const orderId = "xyz" as OrderId; [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- getUser(userId);   // OK [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- getUser(orderId);  // Error: OrderId not assignable to UserId [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- getUser("raw");    // Error: string not assignable to UserId [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- Unique symbols guarantee the brand key is truly unique, even across modules: [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- declare const UserIdBrand: unique symbol; [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- declare const OrderIdBrand: unique symbol; [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- type UserId = string & { readonly [UserIdBrand]: true }; [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- type OrderId = string & { readonly [OrderIdBrand]: true }; [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- Flavored types accept unbranded values but reject differently-flavored ones: [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- type Flavor<T, F extends string> = T & { readonly __flavor?: F }; [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- type Meters = Flavor<number, "Meters">; [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- type Seconds = Flavor<number, "Seconds">; [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- function travel(distance: Meters, time: Seconds) { /* ... */ } [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- travel(100 as Meters, 10 as Seconds);  // OK [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- travel(100, 10);                        // OK -- unbranded accepted [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- travel(100 as Seconds, 10 as Meters);   // Error -- cross-flavor rejected [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- **Brand vs Flavor decision:** Use Brand when all values MUST go through a factory/validator. Use Flavor when you want softer guardrails that still catch cross-domain mistakes. [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- type Email = Brand<string, "Email">; [src: typescript-advanced-types]

- `satisfies` validates a value against a type WITHOUT widening the inferred type: [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- type ColorMap = Record<string, [number, number, number] | string>; [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- // With `: ColorMap` annotation -- widens, loses literal info [src: typescript-advanced-types]

- colorsAnnotated.red.map(x => x);  // Error: string | number[] has no .map [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- // With `satisfies` -- validates but keeps narrow inference [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- } satisfies ColorMap; [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- colors.red.map(x => x);      // OK: inferred as [number, number, number] [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- colors.green.toUpperCase();   // OK: inferred as string [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- **When to use `satisfies`:** [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- Config objects where you want validation + precise autocomplete [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- Discriminated union values where the discriminant literal must be preserved [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- `as const` objects that must conform to a schema [src: typescript-advanced-types]

- Deeply nested generics are the primary cause of slow type checking. The compiler has hard limits: [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- **Type instantiation depth:** 50 levels (error: "Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite") [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- **Type instantiation count:** 5,000,000 total instantiations [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- **Union constituent limit:** 100,000 members [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- TypeScript recognizes tail-position recursive type aliases and can handle deeper recursion: [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- // NON-TAIL -- accumulator is wrapped, hits depth limit quickly [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- type Reverse_Bad<T extends unknown[], Acc extends unknown[] = []> = [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- T extends [infer H, ...infer Rest] [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- ? Reverse_Bad<Rest, [H, ...Acc]>  // recursive call is in tail position here [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- // TAIL -- the recursive call IS the result (good pattern) [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- type TupleToUnion<T extends readonly unknown[]> = [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- T extends [infer H, ...infer Rest] [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- ? H | TupleToUnion<Rest>     // each branch resolves directly [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- // BAD: creates deep instantiation chain [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- type DeepPartial<T> = { [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- // BETTER: add a depth limiter [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- type DeepPartial<T, Depth extends unknown[] = []> = [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- Depth["length"] extends 5 [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- ? T  // bail out at depth 5 [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- ? DeepPartial<T[K], [...Depth, unknown]> [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- **Flatten unions early.** Large intermediate unions compound in later type operations. [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- **Avoid `Extract`/`Exclude` on large unions** in hot paths -- each distributes over every member. [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- **Prefer `interface` over `type` for object shapes.** Interfaces are cached by name; type aliases are structurally re-evaluated. [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- **Use `skipLibCheck: true`** to avoid type-checking `node_modules` .d.ts files in development. [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- **Profile with `--generateTrace`.** Run `tsc --generateTrace traceDir` and open the trace in `chrome://tracing` to find expensive types. [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- **Keep template literal interpolations small.** Two 10-member unions produce 100 variants; three produce 1,000. [src: typescript-advanced-types]
- **Use `interface extends` over intersection `&`** for combining object types -- intersections create anonymous types that are harder for the compiler to cache. [src: typescript-advanced-types]

- <!-- Provenance: reference under the `lang-js-ts` hub. Mirrored from ~/.claude/skills/lang-js-ts/references/typescript-compiler-config.md by scripts/persist-spoke.mjs. --> [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- A `lang-js-ts` reference for the **`tsconfig.json` file and the full `compilerOptions` surface**. The [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- goal: pick a correct, version-appropriate config the first time, know what each strictness flag costs, [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- and copy a sane baseline for a Node app, a bundler/web app, or a published library. Defer module [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- *resolution algorithm* internals, project references / `tsc -b`, and external bundler config to the [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- siblings listed in the provenance block. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- `tsconfig.json` marks a directory as the **root of a TypeScript project** and tells `tsc` (and every [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- editor, bundler plugin, and `ts-node`/`tsx`) what files to compile and under what rules. Running `tsc` [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- with no input files makes it search up from the CWD for the nearest `tsconfig.json`; `tsc -p ./path` [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- points at a specific one. The shape is two halves: a small set of **top-level fields** (which files, [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- what to extend) and the large **`compilerOptions`** object (how to type-check, resolve, and emit). [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **Version anchor (memorize — these drive "is this flag available / on" questions):** [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- > **Defaults vs `tsc --init`.** Through TS 5.x the *compiler* defaults are permissive (`strict: false`, [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- > `target: ES5`, `module` keyed off `target`), even though `tsc --init` *scaffolds* a strict-on file — [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- > "default" in this doc means the compiler default for the stated version line, not what a generated [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- > file shows. **TS 6.0 changes the compiler defaults themselves** (see the TS 6.0 delta). The robust [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- > habit either way: set `strict`, `target`, `module`, and `lib` explicitly so behavior doesn't shift [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- > under you across versions. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`extends`** — inherit another config: a relative path or a package, e.g. `"@tsconfig/node20/tsconfig.json"`. Accepts an **array** (TS 5.0+) merged left→right. The child wins on conflicts; `files`/`include`/`exclude` from the parent are overwritten (not merged) if redefined. Relative `paths`/`outDir` in the parent resolve against the **parent's** location. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`files`** — an explicit allowlist of files. No globs. Best for tiny projects; otherwise use `include`. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`include`** — glob patterns (`"src/**/*"`). If omitted, defaults to everything under the config dir (minus `exclude`). `*`/`?`/`**` supported; patterns without an extension match `.ts/.tsx/.d.ts` (and `.js/.jsx` when `allowJs`). [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`exclude`** — globs removed from `include` (defaults to `node_modules`, `bower_components`, `jspm_packages`, and `outDir`). `exclude` only filters `include`; it does **not** stop a file pulled in by an `import` or a `/// <reference>`. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`references`** — array of `{ "path": "../pkg" }` for **project references** (composite builds). *Deep coverage → `typescript-project-references-monorepo`.* [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- `strict` is a **bundle switch**. Setting `"strict": true` turns on all eight family members at once; [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- you can then re-disable any single one (`"strict": true, "strictNullChecks": false`) — the explicit [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- flag overrides the bundle. The **eight `strict`-family flags**: [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- > The exact membership of the `strict` family is these eight per the TSConfig reference. Newer TS [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- > lines have floated additional `strict`-gated checks; verify against the reference for your version [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- > before relying on one beyond these eight. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **Standalone checks** (NOT enabled by `strict` — opt in individually): [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- The **`@tsconfig/strictest`** preset enables the full set above (plus `noUnusedLocals`, [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- `noUnusedParameters`, `noImplicitReturns`, etc.) for green-field projects that can afford it. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- These four options are interdependent — set them as a group, not piecemeal. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`module`** — the module format `tsc` *emits* and the import syntax it understands: [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- `"commonjs"` — `require`/`module.exports` output. Legacy Node / CJS packages. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- `"node16"` / `"nodenext"` — emit format is chosen **per file** from the nearest `package.json` `"type"` (and `.mts`/`.cts` extension). The correct choice for code that runs in modern Node. `nodenext` tracks the latest Node behavior; `node16` pins to the Node 16 semantics. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- `"esnext"` / `"es2015"`/`"es2020"`/`"es2022"` — pure ESM output at the stated level. Use for code a bundler will consume, or pure-ESM libraries. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- `"preserve"` (TS 5.4) — leave imports/`import()` exactly as written, no rewriting. Implies `moduleResolution: bundler`. The modern "I'm handing this to a bundler" choice. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- (Deprecated/legacy: `amd`, `umd`, `system`, `none`.) [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`moduleResolution`** — *how* a specifier maps to a file: [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- `"node10"` (the option formerly named `"node"`) — classic Node CJS resolution. No `exports`/`imports` field support. Legacy only. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- `"node16"` / `"nodenext"` — modern Node resolution honoring `package.json` `"exports"`/`"imports"`, conditional exports, and `.mts`/`.cts`. Pair with `module: node16`/`nodenext`. **Required** for correctly typing dual-format packages. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- `"bundler"` (TS 5.0) — models esbuild/Vite/webpack/Parcel: extensionless imports allowed (like CJS) but prefers `import` conditions in `exports` (like ESM). For app code consumed by a bundler. **Not for published libraries** — it hides resolution problems your consumers (who may not bundle) would hit; ship with `node16`/`nodenext` instead. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- `"classic"` — pre-Node TS resolution. Effectively never use it. *(Resolution **algorithm** internals + `exports`/`imports` mechanics → `nodejs-module-resolution`.)* [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`target`** — the ECMAScript version `tsc` downlevels syntax to (e.g. `es2015`…`es2023`, `esnext`). [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- Drives the default `lib` and the default `module`. Through 5.x the default is `ES5`; pick at least [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- `es2022` for modern runtimes (top-level await, class fields, `Error.cause`). [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`lib`** — which built-in type declarations to include (e.g. `["es2022", "dom", "dom.iterable"]`). [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- Omitting it derives a set from `target`. Set it explicitly to control DOM availability: include `dom` [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- for browser code, omit it for pure Node/server code so `document`/`window` don't type-check. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **Path mapping & related:** [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`baseUrl`** — base directory for resolving **bare** specifiers. (Deprecated in TS 6.0; prefer `paths` without it, or package `imports`.) [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`paths`** — remap import specifiers to locations, e.g. `{ "@app/*": ["./src/*"] }`. **`tsc` and editors honor these for type-checking only — they do not rewrite emitted paths.** A bundler, `tsc-alias`, or `package.json` `"imports"` must make them work at runtime. Node's native runner ignores `paths`. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`rootDir`** — the input root that mirrors into `outDir` (controls output folder structure). `rootDirs` merges multiple virtual roots into one. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`outDir`** — where emitted `.js`/`.d.ts` go. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`resolveJsonModule`** — allow `import data from "./x.json"` with an inferred type. Requires a `module` that supports it (most do except some legacy modes). [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`allowImportingTsExtensions`** (5.0) — permit `import "./x.ts"` (explicit TS extension). Only allowed with `noEmit` **or** `emitDeclarationOnly` (since `tsc` can't emit a `.ts` import). Needed for Node's native type-stripping workflow. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`moduleDetection`** — `"auto"` (default; a file with any `import`/`export`, or under `module: node16`/`nodenext` with `"type":"module"`, is a module), `"force"` (treat **every** file as a module — recommended to avoid global-scope surprises), `"legacy"`. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`resolvePackageJsonExports` / `resolvePackageJsonImports`** — consult the `package.json` `"exports"`/`"imports"` fields. Default **`true`** under `node16`/`nodenext`/`bundler`. *(Field mechanics → `nodejs-module-resolution`.)* [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`declaration`** — emit `.d.ts` files. **Mandatory for a published library.** Defaults `true` when `composite` is on, else `false`. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`declarationMap`** — emit `.d.ts.map` so consumers' "go to definition" jumps to your `.ts` source, not the `.d.ts`. Ship for libraries with source. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`sourceMap`** — emit `.js.map` for runtime debugging. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`noEmit`** — type-check only, produce no files. The standard setting when a **bundler** (or Node's strip-types) does the actual transpile and `tsc` is the type gate. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`isolatedModules`** — guarantee every file can be transpiled **alone**, without cross-file type info (which is exactly how esbuild/swc/Babel/Node-strip operate). It bans constructs needing whole-program knowledge — re-exporting a type without `export type`, `const enum`, certain namespace patterns. Turn it on whenever a single-file transpiler is in the pipeline. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`verbatimModuleSyntax`** (5.0) — leave any import/export **without** a `type` modifier exactly as written, and **drop** anything with `type`. Replaces the deprecated `importsNotUsedAsValues` + `preserveValueImports`. Makes value-vs-type imports explicit and prevents accidental elision — pair it with `isolatedModules`/`erasableSyntaxOnly`. Caveat: it won't rewrite ESM syntax to `require`, so don't combine it with `module: commonjs` if you write `import`/`export`. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`esModuleInterop`** — generate interop helpers so `import express from "express"` works against a CJS module without a real default export. Implies `allowSyntheticDefaultImports`. Effectively always-on in modern configs (and undisablable in TS 6.0). [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`allowSyntheticDefaultImports`** — allow default-style imports from modules lacking a default export, for **type-checking** only (no emit change). Implied by `esModuleInterop`. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`erasableSyntaxOnly`** (5.8) — error on TS constructs that **emit runtime code**: `enum`, `namespace` with runtime members, parameter properties (`constructor(private x)`), `import =`. Mirrors exactly what Node's native type-stripping refuses, so the editor catches the mismatch instead of a runtime crash. Pair with `verbatimModuleSyntax`. *(Node runtime side → `nodejs-typescript-and-runtime-features`.)* [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`allowJs`** — let `.js`/`.jsx` files into the program (imported by, or alongside, `.ts`). Needed for incremental migration and for emitting from a JS codebase. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`checkJs`** — type-check those `.js` files (using JSDoc annotations). Per-file opt-in/out via `// @ts-check` / `// @ts-nocheck`. Requires `allowJs`. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`jsx`** — JSX transform: `"preserve"` (emit `.jsx`, leave JSX for a bundler), `"react"` (classic `React.createElement`), `"react-jsx"` (the automatic runtime — no `import React` needed; **the modern default for React 17+**), `"react-jsxdev"`, `"react-native"`. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`jsxImportSource`** (4.1) — the module the automatic runtime imports `jsx`/`jsxs` from (default `"react"`); set to `"preact"`, `"@emotion/react"`, etc. Only meaningful with `jsx: react-jsx`/`react-jsxdev`. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- TypeScript **6.0** (released March 2026) is the **last JavaScript-based release** before the Go-based [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **TS 7.0** ("native"). Per the official handbook release notes it **changes compiler defaults** — [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- relevant to this skill: [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- `strict` now defaults **`true`** (was `false`). The notes are explicit: *"If you were relying on the previous default of `false`, you'll need to explicitly set `"strict": false` in your `tsconfig.json`."* [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- `module` defaults **`esnext`** (ESM is now the dominant format). [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- `target` defaults to the **most recent supported ECMAScript spec** — a floating target, currently **`es2025`**. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- `types` defaults **`[]`** (no longer auto-pulls every installed `@types` package — declare what you need). [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- `rootDir` defaults to the **directory containing `tsconfig.json`**. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- `noUncheckedSideEffectImports` defaults `true` (already true on the 5.6+ reference); `libReplacement` now defaults `false` for performance. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- It also adds `--stableTypeOrdering` (to diff 6.0 vs 7.0 output) and **deprecates/removes** legacy [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- surface (`target: es5` + `--downlevelIteration`, `moduleResolution: node10`/`classic`, [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- `module: amd/umd/system/none`, `--outFile`, `baseUrl`). **Practical takeaway:** explicitly set [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- `strict`, `target`, `module`, and `lib` in your config so behavior is identical across 5.x and 6.0 [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- instead of relying on defaults that shifted. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`tsc --init`** — scaffold a commented `tsconfig.json`. The generated defaults have grown stricter over versions; treat the output as a starting point, not gospel — prune comments and pin the four module/target options. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`@tsconfig/bases`** — official community base configs you `extends`: `@tsconfig/node20`, `@tsconfig/node22`, `@tsconfig/strictest`, `@tsconfig/recommended`, framework bases (`@tsconfig/vite-react`, etc.). Inherit one and override the few project-specific keys. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`tsc --showConfig`** — print the fully-resolved config (after `extends` merging and defaults). The fastest way to answer "what is actually in effect here?" [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`tsc --explainFiles` / `--listFilesOnly`** — show why each file is in the program (which `include`/`import`/`reference` pulled it in). Use when `include`/`exclude` isn't behaving. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`tsc --noEmit`** — the type-check gate to run in CI when a bundler or Node strip-types does the real build. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`tsc-alias` / bundler `resolve.alias`** — make `paths` work at runtime (since `tsc` doesn't rewrite them). [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **Inherit, don't hand-roll.** Start from `@tsconfig/node22` (or a framework base) via `extends`, then override only what's project-specific. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **Set the module quartet together** by runtime target: Node → `module: nodenext` + `moduleResolution: nodenext`; bundler/web → `module: preserve` (implies `bundler`) + `noEmit`; library → `module: nodenext` (or `esnext`) + `declaration: true`. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **Turn on `strict`** (default in 6.0) and, for new code, the high-value standalone checks `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` + `noImplicitOverride`. Add `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`/`@tsconfig/strictest` only if the team will pay the friction. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **Pin `target` and `lib` explicitly** (e.g. `es2022`; `["es2022"]` server vs `["es2022","dom","dom.iterable"]` web) so the 6.0 default flips don't silently change behavior. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **If a single-file transpiler is in the pipeline** (esbuild/swc/Vite/Node strip-types), set `isolatedModules: true` + `verbatimModuleSyntax: true` (+ `erasableSyntaxOnly` for the native-Node path). [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **Verify with `tsc --showConfig`** and a `tsc --noEmit` run before trusting the file. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **Node app (TS 5.x/6.0, transpiled by `tsc`):** [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "extends": "@tsconfig/node22/tsconfig.json", [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "module": "nodenext", [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "moduleResolution": "nodenext", [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true, [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "noImplicitOverride": true, [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "esModuleInterop": true, [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "isolatedModules": true, [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "verbatimModuleSyntax": true, [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "resolveJsonModule": true, [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "moduleDetection": "force", [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "skipLibCheck": true, [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "include": ["src/**/*"], [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "exclude": ["dist", "node_modules"] [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **Bundler / web app (Vite/esbuild/webpack do the transpile; `tsc` is the type gate):** [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "module": "preserve", [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "lib": ["es2022", "dom", "dom.iterable"], [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true, [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "esModuleInterop": true, [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "isolatedModules": true, [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "verbatimModuleSyntax": true, [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "resolveJsonModule": true, [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "moduleDetection": "force", [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "skipLibCheck": true, [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "allowImportingTsExtensions": true, [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "paths": { "@/*": ["./src/*"] } [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **Published library (dual-friendly types, source-mapped declarations):** [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "extends": "@tsconfig/node20/tsconfig.json", [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "module": "nodenext", [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "moduleResolution": "nodenext", [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "declarationMap": true, [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "isolatedModules": true, [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "verbatimModuleSyntax": true, [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "exclude": ["**/*.test.ts"] [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **Node native type-stripping (zero build; `tsc --noEmit` only validates):** [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "module": "nodenext", [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "erasableSyntaxOnly": true, [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "verbatimModuleSyntax": true, [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "rewriteRelativeImportExtensions": true, [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- "allowImportingTsExtensions": true [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- (*Native-runtime behavior itself → `nodejs-typescript-and-runtime-features`.*) [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **Mixing module modes.** `module: esnext` with `moduleResolution: node10` (or `bundler` with `module: commonjs`) gives wrong resolution/emit. Keep `module`/`moduleResolution` consistent with the runtime. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`moduleResolution: bundler` in a published package.** It validates only the bundler case and hides breakage for consumers using plain Node resolution. Libraries → `node16`/`nodenext`. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **Expecting `paths` to work at runtime.** `tsc` never rewrites them; without a bundler/`tsc-alias`/package `imports`, the emitted JS has unresolved bare specifiers. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **Leaving `target: ES5` (5.x default) unset on a modern runtime** — bloated downlevel output and missing lib types. Always pin `target`. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`enum`/`namespace`/parameter-properties under `isolatedModules` or a strip-types runtime** — they need whole-program emit; use `erasableSyntaxOnly` to catch them at author time. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`skipLibCheck` everywhere as a crutch** — it's a performance win, but it can mask genuine conflicts between `@types` packages; don't reach for it to silence a real type error. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **Re-exporting a type without `export type` when `isolatedModules`/`verbatimModuleSyntax` is on** — a single-file transpiler can't tell it's type-only and may emit a broken value import. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **Relying on TS 6.0's default flips.** Be explicit about `strict`/`target`/`module`/`lib` so a 5.x and a 6.0 toolchain produce identical results. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **"Cannot use import statement outside a module" / wrong require-vs-import emit** → `module`/`moduleResolution` don't match the runtime; switch to `nodenext` and check the package's `"type"`. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`paths` import fails at runtime** (works in editor) → expected; wire `tsc-alias`, a bundler alias, or `package.json` `"imports"`. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **"This import path can only be used with allowImportingTsExtensions"** → you imported `./x.ts`; set `allowImportingTsExtensions: true` (and `noEmit`/`emitDeclarationOnly`). [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **"`X` is declared but never used" / unexpected unused errors** → a `@tsconfig/strictest` base enabled `noUnusedLocals`/`noUnusedParameters`; relax or prefix with `_`. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **`enum`/parameter-property errors under a no-emit setup** → `erasableSyntaxOnly` is on (or the runtime strips types); rewrite to erasable constructs. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **Config changes seem ignored** → run `tsc --showConfig`; an `extends` parent or an editor pinning a different `tsconfig` is overriding you. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **A file you expected isn't compiled** → it's outside `files`/`include` or hit `exclude`; `exclude` can't remove a file reached via `import`. Use `tsc --explainFiles`. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **New type errors after a TS upgrade** → `strict` may gate additional checks in the new line (and 6.0 flips defaults); pin versions and read that release's notes. [src: typescript-compiler-config]
- **DOM globals (`document`, `window`) missing or unexpectedly present** → set `lib` explicitly (include/exclude `dom`). [src: typescript-compiler-config]

- <!-- Provenance: reference under the `lang-js-ts` hub. Mirrored from ~/.claude/skills/lang-js-ts/references/typescript-declaration-files.md by scripts/persist-spoke.mjs. --> [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- A `lang-js-ts` hub reference for **producing and shipping TypeScript type information**: how `.d.ts` [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- files are emitted, how to hand-author ambient declarations and augment other people's types, and how [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- to distribute types from an npm package so downstream consumers (and `tsc`, `attw`, editors) resolve [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- them correctly across ESM and CJS. [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- A `.d.ts` is **types only** — no runtime code, no JS output. It is the contract `tsc` reads when it [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- can't see a library's source. Scope discipline: declaration **emit** compiler options live here (not in [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- `typescript-compiler-config`); the **runtime** resolution algorithm that finds the file lives in [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- `nodejs-module-resolution`; the **bundler** that produces the file lives in [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- `nodejs-build-tooling-bundlers`; advanced **type operators** used inside a `.d.ts` live in [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- `typescript-advanced-types`. [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- There are two ways a `.d.ts` comes into existence: **emitted** by the compiler from `.ts` source [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- (`declaration: true`), or **hand-authored** as an ambient declaration for code TypeScript can't analyze [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- (plain JS libs, globals injected by a `<script>`, env vars). Distribution is the third axis: a package [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- points consumers at its types via the `types` field and the `exports` map, or — if it ships no types — [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- the community publishes them under `@types/*` via DefinitelyTyped. [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- **Version anchors (memorize — these drive "does my TS have X" questions):** [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- With `declaration: true`, `tsc` emits a `.d.ts` next to each `.js` it produces. The four knobs: [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- // tsconfig.json — library that emits its own types [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- "declarationMap": true, [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- "emitDeclarationOnly": false, [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- "module": "nodenext", [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- "moduleResolution": "nodenext" [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- **Why explicit return types help emit (this is load-bearing).** When a function lacks an annotated [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- return type, the emitter must *infer* the type and write it into the `.d.ts`. Inference can be slow on [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- complex code, and worse, it can produce a declaration that **references a symbol the consumer can't [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- name** — TS then errors with `TS2742` ("inferred type cannot be named without a reference to …") or [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- `TS4082` ("default export of the module has or is using private name …"). Annotating the public surface [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- (exported function/method return types, exported `const` types) makes emit a near-mechanical copy and [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- sidesteps the un-nameable-symbol class of failures entirely. This is exactly what isolated declarations [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- `isolatedDeclarations: true` forces the public API to be **explicitly typed enough that a `.d.ts` can be [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- generated from a single file without consulting any other file**. That one-in/one-out property lets [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- non-`tsc` tools (oxc, swc, esbuild's experimental path) emit declarations **in parallel, per file**, [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- which `tsc`'s whole-program declaration emit can't do. [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- **Requires `declaration: true` (or `composite: true`)** — it's a stricter mode *of* declaration emit, [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- so the compiler errors if neither is set. (`isolatedModules` is a recommended companion for the same [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- "per-file" philosophy, but it is **not** the enforced prerequisite — `declaration`/`composite` is.) [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- **What it enforces (representative error: `TS9007`, "Function must have an explicit return type [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- annotation with --isolatedDeclarations"; the `TS900x`/`TS903x` family covers the other [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- inference-blocking cases):** [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- Every exported function / arrow / function-expression assigned to an exported binding needs an [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- explicit return type. [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- Exported `let`/`const`/`var` need an annotation or a trivially-inferable literal initializer. [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- Public and protected class members (fields, accessors, method return types) need annotations. [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- Constructs whose emitted type can't be computed locally are rejected (e.g. spreading a value whose [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- type comes from another file, computed property keys whose type needs inference). [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- // FAILS isolatedDeclarations [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- export function load(name) { return readJson(name); }   // TS9007: needs : Config [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- export const PORT = process.env.PORT ?? 3000;            // ok (literal-ish), but annotate to be safe [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- export function load(name: string): Config { return readJson(name); } [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- export const PORT: number = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000); [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- The single most important authoring fact: **a `.d.ts` with any top-level `import` or `export` is a [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- *module* — its declarations are scoped, not global.** A `.d.ts` with **no** top-level `import`/`export` [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- is a *script*: every `declare`d name lands in the **global scope**. `moduleDetection` is always `auto` [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- for `.d.ts`, so you cannot force this with config — it's purely structural. [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- // global.d.ts — SCRIPT (no top-level import/export) → adds to global scope [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- declare const APP_VERSION: string; [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- declare function gtag(...args: unknown[]): void; [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- interface Window {            // merges into the built-in lib Window (see merging below) [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- myWidget?: { open(): void }; [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- // ambient module declaration — for an untyped JS package or a non-code import [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- declare module "untyped-lib" { [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- export function doThing(x: number): string; [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- export default function (): void; [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- declare module "*.svg" {       // asset import (bundler magic) [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- To put global types in a file that *is* a module (has imports/exports), wrap them in `declare global`: [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- import type { Logger } from "./logger.js";   // this import makes the file a module [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- interface Window { logger: Logger } [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- var __DEV__: boolean;        // `var`, not `let/const`, to declare a global variable [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- export {};                     // ensures module-ness if there were no other export [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- **Triple-slash directives** (must be at the very top, before any statement): [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- /// <reference types="node" />          // depend on another @types package's globals [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- /// <reference lib="es2022.array" />    // pull in a specific built-in lib slice [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- /// <reference path="./other.d.ts" />   // legacy file include — AVOID in published types [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- In **published** declaration files, use `/// <reference types="..." />` to declare a dependency on [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- another package's types; **do not** use `/// <reference path="..." />` (the TS team explicitly flags it [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- as a red flag — it bakes in a relative file layout). Prefer real `import`s where the file is a module. [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- TypeScript **merges** multiple declarations of the same name in the same scope. This is the mechanism [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- behind extending types you don't own. [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- **Interface merging** — same-named interfaces combine their members: [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- interface Box { height: number; } [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- interface Box { width: number; }      // Box now has BOTH height and width [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- **Namespace + function/class/enum merging** — a `namespace` merges with a same-named function, class, or [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- enum, letting you hang static-like members off a callable/constructable: [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- function buildLabel(name: string): string { return buildLabel.prefix + name; } [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- namespace buildLabel { export let prefix = "Hello, "; }   // buildLabel.prefix is typed [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- **Module augmentation** — re-open another package's module from **a file that is itself a module** and [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- `declare module "their-pkg"`. The augmenting declarations merge into the original; you cannot add [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- *new top-level* exports this way, only augment existing shapes. [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- // augment a third-party module's interface [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- import "express";                                  // make this file a module + load the target [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- declare module "express" { [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- interface Request { userId?: string; }           // adds req.userId everywhere [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- **Augmenting globals from inside a module** uses `declare global`. The two canonical Node patterns: [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- // 1. Strongly type process.env  (NodeJS.ProcessEnv is itself an interface you merge into) [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- interface ProcessEnv { [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- DATABASE_URL: string; [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- NODE_ENV: "development" | "production" | "test"; [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- // 2. Add a property to the DOM Window [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- interface Window { dataLayer: unknown[]; } [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- **Bundled (most common):** emit `.d.ts` with your build and point at the entry declaration. [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- "main": "./dist/index.js", [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- "types": "./dist/index.d.ts"   // "typings" is an exact synonym [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- **With an `exports` map (modern, and `node16`/`nodenext` resolution requires it):** add a `types` [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- condition. **It MUST appear first in each condition block** — TypeScript reads conditions top-to-bottom [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- and stops at the first match, so a `types` placed after `import`/`require`/`default` is silently [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- "types": "./dist/index.d.mts",   // types BEFORE the runtime target [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- "default": "./dist/index.mjs" [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- "types": "./dist/index.d.cts", [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- "default": "./dist/index.cjs" [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- "./package.json": "./package.json" [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- **Dual-package types (the gotcha):** when you ship both ESM and CJS, a *single* `index.d.ts` is wrong if [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- your package is `"type": "module"` — under `require`, the consumer's compiler sees the `.d.ts` as ESM [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- syntax describing a CJS file. Ship **two** declaration files: `.d.mts` for the `import` condition and [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- `.d.cts` for the `require` condition (or `index.d.ts` + `index.d.cts`). This is precisely what [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- `@arethetypeswrong/cli` flags as **"Masquerading as CJS/ESM."** [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- **`typesVersions`** — serve different declarations to older TypeScript versions, or remap subpaths: [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- "types": "./index.d.ts", [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- ">=4.0": { "*": ["ts4.0/*"] },          // TS ≥4.0 reads ./ts4.0/*.d.ts [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- "<4.0":  { "index.d.ts": ["index.v3.d.ts"] } [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- **UMD global (`export as namespace`)** — for a library usable both as a module and as a `<script>` global: [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- // index.d.ts for a UMD library "myLib" [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- export as namespace myLib;     // exposes global `myLib` when loaded via <script> [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- export function greet(name: string): string; [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- export interface Options { loud?: boolean } [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- `export as namespace id` is **only legal in a `.d.ts`** that also has other top-level exports; placing it [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- in a `.ts` errors with `TS1315`. It only takes effect when the file enters compilation via a [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- triple-slash reference or as a top-level input — it's a no-op when the package is `import`ed. [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- **`tsc`** — `tsc --emitDeclarationOnly` (types-only build), `tsc -b` (project references; needs [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- `composite: true`, which implies `declaration: true`). [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- **`@arethetypeswrong/cli` (`attw`)** — `attw --pack .` or `attw <tarball>` validates that published [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- types resolve under every module/condition combination. Flags "Masquerading as CJS/ESM," [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- "Fallback Condition," "No types," "missing `package.json` `exports`." Run in CI before publish. [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- **`tsd`** — type-level test runner (uses `expect-type` under the hood). Write `*.test-d.ts` files with [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- `expectType<T>(value)` and `expectError(...)`; `tsd` runs the compiler and asserts. Configure via a [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- `tsd` block in `package.json`. [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- **Vitest type testing** — alternative to `tsd`: `*.test-d.ts` with `expectTypeOf(x).toEqualTypeOf<T>()` [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- or the simpler `assertType<T>(x)`; gated behind `typecheck` config (statically analyzed, never run). [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- **`@types/*` + DefinitelyTyped (DT)** — the community type registry, auto-published to the `@types` [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- npm org from the DT monorepo. [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- **Emit vs. hand-author.** If you own the `.ts` source, prefer **emitted** `.d.ts` (`declaration: [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- true`) — never hand-maintain types that duplicate your source. Hand-author only for untyped JS deps, [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- ambient globals, or non-code imports. [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- **Annotate the public surface** (exported return types, exported `const` types). Consider turning on [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- `isolatedDeclarations: true` to *enforce* it and unlock parallel/third-party d.ts emit. [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- **Decide global vs. module per file** by the top-level import/export rule; reach for `declare global` [src: typescript-declaration-files]
- only inside module files; reach for `declare module "x"` to augment a dependency. [src: typescript-declaration-files]

- A `lang-js-ts` reference for driving the **`typescript` npm package as a library** — parsing source to [src: typescript-compiler-api]
- an AST, type-checking through the `TypeChecker`, rewriting code with **custom transformers** built on [src: typescript-compiler-api]
- the modern `ts.factory` node API, hosting the **Language Service**, and the **ts-morph** wrapper that [src: typescript-compiler-api]
- makes all of it ergonomic. This is the engine behind linters, codemods, code generators, doc tools, [src: typescript-compiler-api]
- and editor plugins. For the type *system* and `tsconfig` defer to `typescript-expert.md` / [src: typescript-compiler-api]
- `typescript-compiler-config`; for *running* `.ts` (type stripping, tsx, ts-node) defer to [src: typescript-compiler-api]
- `nodejs-typescript-and-runtime-features.md`. [src: typescript-compiler-api]
- The compiler ships one public module (`import * as ts from "typescript"`) exposing the same pipeline [src: typescript-compiler-api]
- `tsc` uses: a **scanner/parser** turns text into an immutable **AST** (`ts.SourceFile` of `ts.Node`s); [src: typescript-compiler-api]
- a **binder** + **`TypeChecker`** resolve symbols and types; **transformers** rewrite the tree; a [src: typescript-compiler-api]
- **printer/emitter** writes `.js`/`.d.ts`. You opt into as much of that as you need — a one-file [src: typescript-compiler-api]
- syntactic codemod uses only the parser; a type-aware lint rule needs a full `Program` + checker. [src: typescript-compiler-api]
- **The single most important framing fact — Strada vs Corsa:** everything in this skill is the [src: typescript-compiler-api]
- **"Strada"** API, the original JavaScript/TypeScript-based compiler. **TS 6.0 (2026-03-23) is the [src: typescript-compiler-api]
- final JS-based release.** **TS 7.0 "Corsa"** is a ground-up Go port (≈10× faster) that **does *not* [src: typescript-compiler-api]
- support the Strada compiler API** — a replacement programmatic API is in progress and not stable as [src: typescript-compiler-api]
- of mid-2026. So any tool you write against this surface targets **TS ≤ 6.x**. `ts-morph` wraps Strada [src: typescript-compiler-api]
- too, so it shares that ceiling. Plan migrations accordingly; don't assume your transformer/LS plugin [src: typescript-compiler-api]
- **Version anchors (memorize — these drive most "does this API exist" questions):** [src: typescript-compiler-api]

- **Standalone:** `ts.transform(sourceOrNodes, [transformer], options?)` → `TransformationResult`; [src: typescript-compiler-api]

- The **Language Service** (`ts.createLanguageService(host, registry?)`) is the *incremental, editor* [src: typescript-compiler-api]
- half of the compiler: it answers completions, quick-info (hover), diagnostics, go-to-definition, [src: typescript-compiler-api]

- <!-- Provenance: reference under the `lang-js-ts` hub. Mirrored from ~/.claude/skills/lang-js-ts/references/typescript-decorators.md by scripts/persist-spoke.mjs. --> [src: typescript-decorators]
- A `lang-js-ts` hub reference for the **two distinct decorator systems** TypeScript ships. They share the `@expr` syntax and nothing else: different semantics, different signatures, mutually incompatible emit. The single most important fact: **the `experimentalDecorators` compiler flag toggles the whole semantics** — flag absent ⇒ TC39 Stage 3 *standard* decorators (TS 5.0+); flag present ⇒ *legacy* experimental decorators (TS 1.5-era proposal). For the type system defer to `typescript-expert.md`; for advanced type operators `typescript-advanced-types.md`; for tsconfig `typescript-compiler-config.md`; for *why* decorators can't run under Node's strip-only TS execution `nodejs-typescript-and-runtime-features.md`. [src: typescript-decorators]
- Standard decorators are functions called at class-definition time with a uniform `(value, context)` signature; they can replace the decorated value or hook initializers, and they emit plain ES (no `reflect-metadata` dependency). Legacy decorators use kind-specific signatures (`target`, `propertyKey`, `descriptor`/`parameterIndex`), support **parameter decorators** (which Stage 3 still lacks), and — paired with `emitDecoratorMetadata` — feed runtime type info to the dependency-injection ecosystem (Angular, NestJS, TypeORM, class-validator). That DI dependency is exactly why those frameworks **cannot** migrate to standard decorators automatically. [src: typescript-decorators]
- **Version anchors (memorize — they drive "does my TS support X" questions):** [src: typescript-decorators]
- **Before TS 5.0**, decorators *required* `"experimentalDecorators": true`; there was no standard option, so a decorator without the flag was an error. [src: typescript-decorators]
- **TS 5.0+**: `experimentalDecorators` **present/true** ⇒ legacy semantics + legacy type-checking + legacy emit (`__decorate`/`__metadata` helpers). **Absent/false** ⇒ standard Stage 3 semantics + emit. [src: typescript-decorators]
- They are **not interoperable.** A function written for one signature throws or mis-types under the other. The TS 5.0 notes state the new proposal is "incompatible with `--experimentalDecorators`… and `--emitDecoratorMetadata`… and parameter decorators." You pick one system per project (effectively per `tsconfig`). [src: typescript-decorators]
- Every standard decorator is `(value, context) => replacement | void`. `value` is the thing being decorated (a method/getter/setter function, the class constructor, the `{get,set}` pair for an auto-accessor, or **`undefined` for a plain field**). `context` is a per-kind object: [src: typescript-decorators]
- **What each kind may return:** [src: typescript-decorators]
- A non-conforming return throws (e.g. a method decorator returning a non-function). [src: typescript-decorators]
- // Standard method decorator (TS 5.0+, NO experimentalDecorators) — fully typed [src: typescript-decorators]
- function logged<This, Args extends any[], Return>( [src: typescript-decorators]
- target: (this: This, ...args: Args) => Return, [src: typescript-decorators]
- context: ClassMethodDecoratorContext<This, (this: This, ...args: Args) => Return> [src: typescript-decorators]
- const name = String(context.name); [src: typescript-decorators]
- return function (this: This, ...args: Args): Return { [src: typescript-decorators]
- console.log(`-> ${name}`); [src: typescript-decorators]
- const result = target.call(this, ...args); [src: typescript-decorators]
- console.log(`<- ${name}`); [src: typescript-decorators]
- // Field decorator: value is UNDEFINED; you return an initializer mutator. [src: typescript-decorators]
- function double(_value: undefined, ctx: ClassFieldDecoratorContext<unknown, number>) { [src: typescript-decorators]
- if (ctx.static || ctx.private) throw new Error("public instance only"); [src: typescript-decorators]
- return (initial: number) => initial * 2;   // runs per-instance against the initializer [src: typescript-decorators]
