- Spoke of the **consumer-finance** family (the personal-money side of the broader [src: personal-banking]
- **`consumer-credit-and-debt`** hub). This skill covers where you keep money: [src: personal-banking]
- deposit accounts, the insurance behind them, the fees that erode them, and how to [src: personal-banking]
- pick and safely use a bank or credit union. It covers scam *prevention* and what [src: personal-banking]
- the reimbursement rules are (Section 8), but not borrowing, investing, or the [src: personal-banking]
- step-by-step *recovery* after fraud or identity theft. See the cross-references [src: personal-banking]
- -- [src: personal-banking]
- **HYSA vs MMA.** Both are deposit accounts (insured, variable rate). MMAs add [src: personal-banking]
- limited transactional access (checks/debit). Neither is a *money market fund*, [src: personal-banking]
- which is an **investment** (not deposit-insured). That last point is a common and [src: personal-banking]
- **CDs** trade liquidity for a locked rate. A **CD ladder** (staggered maturities) [src: personal-banking]
- balances rate and access. Watch for **auto-renewal** at maturity; there's a short [src: personal-banking]
- grace period (often ~7-10 days) to withdraw penalty-free. [src: personal-banking]
- **"Withdrawal limits."** Federal **Regulation D's** 6-per-month limit on savings [src: personal-banking]
- transfers was **suspended in 2020 and remains optional**, but many banks still [src: personal-banking]
- enforce a limit by their own policy. Check the account's terms. [src: personal-banking]
- A higher **APY** beats a low one mechanically: on $10,000, the gap between 0.40% [src: personal-banking]
- and 4.0% is roughly **$360/year**. For an emergency fund, an HYSA is usually the [src: personal-banking]
- -- [src: personal-banking]
- **Truth in Savings (TISA), implemented by Regulation DD (12 CFR 1030)**, exists so [src: personal-banking]
- you can comparison-shop deposit accounts on uniform terms. (For credit unions the [src: personal-banking]
- parallel rule is **NCUA's Truth in Savings, 12 CFR 707**, same substance.) [src: personal-banking]
- **APY (annual percentage yield)** is the standardized number for comparing [src: personal-banking]
- accounts. It bakes in the interest rate **and compounding frequency** over a [src: personal-banking]
- 365-day period, so two accounts are directly comparable. **Always compare APY, [src: personal-banking]
- not the nominal "interest rate."** [src: personal-banking]
- An ad that states a return **must** state it as an **"annual percentage yield"** [src: personal-banking]
- using that term. That's a Reg DD requirement, not marketing courtesy. [src: personal-banking]
- Banks must disclose fees, the rate, the APY, and other terms **before you open** [src: personal-banking]
- A change that **lowers the APY or otherwise hurts you** requires **≥30 days' [src: personal-banking]
- advance notice** (with limited exceptions, e.g., variable rates tied to an index). [src: personal-banking]
- **Watch the asterisks:** intro/teaser APYs, balance tiers (the headline rate may [src: personal-banking]
- apply only above a threshold, or only *up to* a cap), and required activity [src: personal-banking]
- (direct deposit, debit transactions) to earn the top rate. [src: personal-banking]
- -- [src: personal-banking]
- Functionally similar for everyday banking. Credit unions frequently offer higher [src: personal-banking]
- savings APYs and lower/zero fees because profits return to members; large banks [src: personal-banking]
- often win on ATM networks, branch density, and app polish. **Insurance protection [src: personal-banking]
- is equivalent**: $250k per the same ownership-category rules (Section 4). Many [src: personal-banking]
- people use both (e.g., a credit union for savings, a big bank for a slick app). [src: personal-banking]
- -- [src: personal-banking]
- Both agencies are backed by the **full faith and credit of the US government** and [src: personal-banking]
- provide **identical** coverage mechanics. **FDIC** insures **banks**; **NCUA** [src: personal-banking]
- (through the **National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund, NCUSIF**) insures [src: personal-banking]
- **federally insured credit unions**. At a credit union, deposits are called [src: personal-banking]
- **"shares,"** so it's "share insurance," but the math is the same. [src: personal-banking]
- > **$250,000 per depositor, per insured institution, for each account ownership [src: personal-banking]
- Three multipliers expand coverage: **more depositors**, **more institutions**, and [src: personal-banking]
- **more ownership categories**. Deposits at two *separately chartered* institutions [src: personal-banking]
- are insured separately. (Note: an online "brand" and its parent may be the **same [src: personal-banking]
- charter**, so verify with **FDIC BankFind** / **NCUA Research a Credit Union** [src: personal-banking]
- before assuming you've doubled coverage.) [src: personal-banking]
- **Spread across institutions**, $250k each at separate charters. [src: personal-banking]
- **Use different ownership categories** at one bank, e.g., a single account [src: personal-banking]
- ($250k) + your half of a joint account ($250k) + an IRA ($250k) are insured [src: personal-banking]
- separately, so one couple can cover well over $1M at a single bank. [src: personal-banking]
- **Name beneficiaries** on trust/POD accounts (up to 5 → up to $1.25M per owner). [src: personal-banking]
- **Sweep / network programs** (e.g., IntraFi/ICS, CDARS) spread large balances [src: personal-banking]
- across many banks to keep each slice under $250k, but understand how the [src: personal-banking]
- program is structured before relying on it. [src: personal-banking]
- **Use the official calculators:** FDIC **EDIE** and the **NCUA Share Insurance [src: personal-banking]
- Estimator** compute your exact coverage. [src: personal-banking]
- Insurance covers **deposits** if the **insured institution fails**. Full stop. [src: personal-banking]
- It does **not** cover: [src: personal-banking]
- **Investments**: stocks, bonds, mutual funds, **money market mutual funds**, [src: personal-banking]
- annuities, life insurance, Treasury/municipal securities, even if bought *through* [src: personal-banking]
- **Crypto assets.** [src: personal-banking]
- **Safe-deposit box contents.** [src: personal-banking]
- **Fraud, theft, or scams** you fall victim to (Sections 8-9). [src: personal-banking]
- **The failure or bankruptcy of a nonbank company / fintech** (Section 6). [src: personal-banking]
- -- [src: personal-banking]
- Banking is far cheaper than it looks if you read the fee schedule: [src: personal-banking]
- **Monthly maintenance fee** is almost always **waivable**: maintain a minimum [src: personal-banking]
- balance, set up qualifying **direct deposit**, link accounts, or pick a free [src: personal-banking]
- account (most online banks and many credit unions charge $0). [src: personal-banking]
- **Overdraft / NSF fees**: the big ones; Section 7. [src: personal-banking]
- **Out-of-network ATM fees**: both the ATM owner and your bank may charge; some [src: personal-banking]
- banks/credit unions rebate them or belong to **surcharge-free networks** (Allpoint, [src: personal-banking]
- **Wire transfer fees**, **paper-statement fees**, **early CD-withdrawal penalties**, [src: personal-banking]
- **excessive-withdrawal**, **foreign-transaction**, **dormancy/inactivity**, and [src: personal-banking]
- **account-closing** fees. [src: personal-banking]
- **Tactics:** read the **Truth in Savings disclosure / fee schedule** before [src: personal-banking]
- opening; choose a free or fee-waivable account; keep enough to clear any minimum; [src: personal-banking]
- **opt out of overdraft coverage** (Section 7); use in-network ATMs; and **ask** — [src: personal-banking]
- banks routinely waive a fee on request, especially a first occurrence. [src: personal-banking]
- -- [src: personal-banking]
- **Online banks** (e.g., the direct-banking arm of a chartered bank) are usually [src: personal-banking]
- **themselves FDIC-insured banks**. Lower overhead funds higher HYSA rates. Safe [src: personal-banking]
- **Neobanks / fintech apps** are frequently **NOT banks.** A fintech is a tech [src: personal-banking]
- company that *partners* with one or more chartered banks to hold your money. [src: personal-banking]
- > **A fintech app is not itself a bank.** Your money is FDIC-insured only **after** [src: personal-banking]
- > the fintech actually places it at an insured bank **and** accurate [src: personal-banking]
- > ledgers/records exist to identify your share ("**pass-through insurance**"). [src: personal-banking]
- **FDIC insurance protects against the failure of the *bank*, not the failure of a [src: personal-banking]
- *nonbank* company.** In the **2024 collapse of Synapse** (a banking-as-a-service [src: personal-banking]
- middleware firm), end customers of fintech apps were told their funds were [src: personal-banking]
- "FDIC-insured," but when Synapse went bankrupt, **reconciliation broke down**: [src: personal-banking]
- ledgers didn't match what was actually at the partner banks, and consumers were [src: personal-banking]
- **locked out of their money for months**, with some never fully repaid. FDIC [src: personal-banking]
- insurance never triggered, because **no bank had failed**, the *nonbank middleware* [src: personal-banking]
- failed, which deposit insurance does not cover. [src: personal-banking]
- Find out **which actual FDIC-insured bank(s)** hold the money, and verify them on [src: personal-banking]
- **FDIC BankFind**. If the app can't tell you, treat that as a red flag. [src: personal-banking]
- Read the disclosures to confirm **pass-through** eligibility and that you are the [src: personal-banking]
- recognized owner of record. [src: personal-banking]
- Note any **partner-bank concentration**: if a fintech sweeps your funds to a bank [src: personal-banking]
- where you already hold deposits, the **$250k limit is shared**, not stacked. [src: personal-banking]
- Be wary of apps that advertise insurance loosely or request suspicious permissions. [src: personal-banking]
- FDIC's **2024 proposed "custodial deposit accounts" recordkeeping rule** aims to [src: personal-banking]
- force exactly this ledger accuracy. As of 2026 its status is **uncertain [src: personal-banking]
- (proposed, not finalized)** — verify before relying on it. [src: personal-banking]
- -- [src: personal-banking]
- **Overdraft fee**: bank **pays** a transaction that exceeds your balance and [src: personal-banking]
- charges you (historically ~$30-35 each). [src: personal-banking]
- **NSF (non-sufficient funds) fee**: bank **declines/returns** the item and still [src: personal-banking]
- charges you. (Many large banks **eliminated NSF fees** in 2022-2024.) [src: personal-banking]
- > For **one-time debit-card and ATM transactions**, a bank **may not charge an [src: personal-banking]
- > overdraft fee unless you have affirmatively opted in** ("opt-in"/"affirmative [src: personal-banking]
- If you **never opted in**, those transactions are simply **declined** at no cost, [src: personal-banking]
- usually the right setting for most people. [src: personal-banking]
- The opt-in rule **does not** automatically cover **checks and recurring ACH/bill [src: personal-banking]
- payments** (e.g., your electric bill); those can still overdraw and trigger a fee [src: personal-banking]
- regardless of opt-in. Linking a savings account or a small line of credit as [src: personal-banking]
- **overdraft protection** is a cheaper backstop than per-item fees. [src: personal-banking]
- **CFPB Circular 2024-05** warned that charging these fees **without provable opt-in [src: personal-banking]
- consent** can violate the law, so if you were charged and never opted in, [src: personal-banking]
- The CFPB finalized a rule (**Dec 2024**) that would have forced the **largest [src: personal-banking]
- institutions (>$10 billion in assets)** to either cap overdraft at a **benchmark fee [src: personal-banking]
- (~$5)**, charge a **breakeven fee** covering only cost, or treat overdraft as [src: personal-banking]
- **credit under Truth in Lending (Reg Z)**, effective **Oct 1, 2025**. [src: personal-banking]
- > **That rule was repealed.** Congress used the **Congressional Review Act** to [src: personal-banking]
- > overturn it; the resolution (**S.J.Res. 18 → Public Law 119-10**) was signed in [src: personal-banking]
- > **2025**, so the rule **never took effect.** Large banks may continue charging [src: personal-banking]
- > overdraft fees without that cap. The **Reg E opt-in protection (above) still [src: personal-banking]
- > stands.** Because the CRA bars a "substantially similar" rule, don't expect a [src: personal-banking]
- > federal overdraft *price cap* soon. **Verify the current regulatory state before [src: personal-banking]
- > Predatory framing of overdraft as a credit product, and payday/high-cost [src: personal-banking]
- > alternatives, are out of scope; see **predatory-lending-and-high-cost-credit**. [src: personal-banking]
- -- [src: personal-banking]
- > **If a fraudster makes a transfer from your account without your authorization, [src: personal-banking]
- > that's an "unauthorized EFT" and Reg E protects you. But if YOU were *tricked into [src: personal-banking]
- > sending the money yourself* (an "authorized" payment), the law generally does NOT [src: personal-banking]
- > require the bank to refund you.** [src: personal-banking]
- This is the core trap of **Zelle/wire scams** (fake "your account is compromised, [src: personal-banking]
- move your money" calls; romance scams; fake invoices). Because **you** initiated the [src: personal-banking]
- transfer, banks have historically treated it as authorized and **declined [src: personal-banking]
- reimbursement**, and wires/Zelle are **irreversible**. [src: personal-banking]
- **Unauthorized vs. authorized is the whole game.** Reg E (12 CFR 1005) limits your [src: personal-banking]
- liability for **unauthorized** EFTs, especially if you report within **60 days** of [src: personal-banking]
- the statement. Fraudulently *induced* payments you sent yourself fall in a contested [src: personal-banking]
- gap. The **CFPB has pressed banks (and sued some) over Zelle fraud handling**, and [src: personal-banking]
- some networks/banks now reimburse certain **imposter** scams, but **don't count on [src: personal-banking]
- **Defense:** treat Zelle and wires like **handing over cash**. Verify the recipient [src: personal-banking]
- through an independent channel. No legitimate bank, agency, or company will tell you [src: personal-banking]
- to "move money to a safe account"; that instruction is itself the scam. [src: personal-banking]
- If hit: **contact your bank immediately** (speed can matter for a wire recall), [src: personal-banking]
- file with the **CFPB** and **FTC (ReportFraud.ftc.gov)**, and report to local police. [src: personal-banking]
- -- [src: personal-banking]
- **ChexSystems** is a **consumer reporting agency** (governed by the **FCRA**) that [src: personal-banking]
- banks use to screen checking-account applicants. A history of **unpaid negative [src: personal-banking]
- balances, bounced checks, or fraud** can land you there and get an application [src: personal-banking]
- **Your FCRA rights:** you're entitled to a **free report** (the bank that denied you [src: personal-banking]
- must tell you which agency it used), and you can **dispute inaccurate information**, [src: personal-banking]
- the agency must **investigate for free** and correct errors. Negative records [src: personal-banking]
- generally age off after **5 years** (ChexSystems' own retention window, shorter [src: personal-banking]
- than the FCRA's general 7-year limit for most negative items). [src: personal-banking]
- **Second-chance accounts** are checking accounts/prepaid products (offered by many [src: personal-banking]
- banks and credit unions) designed for people with a damaged ChexSystems record, [src: personal-banking]
- typically **no overdraft** (so no overdraft fees), sometimes a small monthly fee, [src: personal-banking]
- often graduating to a standard account. Some institutions require clearing old [src: personal-banking]
- unpaid balances first. [src: personal-banking]
- -- [src: personal-banking]
- **Joint accounts**: any owner can withdraw the **full balance**; each owner is [src: personal-banking]
- liable; both gain the deposit-insurance benefit (Section 4). Convenient for couples [src: personal-banking]
- but carries trust and (on death/divorce) estate/ownership implications. [src: personal-banking]
- **Account security**: enable **MFA**, set transaction **alerts**, never share [src: personal-banking]
- one-time codes (a bank will never ask for them), and beware "your account is [src: personal-banking]
- compromised" calls (Section 8). *Recovering* from a takeover or identity theft → [src: personal-banking]
- **identity-theft-and-credit-fraud**. [src: personal-banking]
- **Switching banks**: open the new account first, then **move recurring direct [src: personal-banking]
- deposits and autopays**, run both in parallel until everything migrates, then close [src: personal-banking]
- the old account in writing and **keep the closing confirmation** (avoids dormancy [src: personal-banking]
- fees and surprise overdrafts on a forgotten autopay). [src: personal-banking]
- **Unclaimed property**: dormant/abandoned accounts are eventually **escheated** to [src: personal-banking]
- the **state**. You can reclaim them for free via your state treasurer or [src: personal-banking]
- **MissingMoney.com** (the multi-state NAUPA search). Watch for **fake "asset [src: personal-banking]
- recovery" fee** scams. [src: personal-banking]
- **Beneficiaries / POD**: adding a **payable-on-death** beneficiary lets funds pass [src: personal-banking]
- outside probate **and** can raise deposit-insurance coverage (Section 4). [src: personal-banking]

- -- [src: personal-income-taxes]
- A US individual return (**Form 1040**) flows top to bottom: [src: personal-income-taxes]
- **Gross income** — wages (W-2 box 1), self-employment, interest, dividends, [src: personal-income-taxes]
- capital gains, retirement distributions, etc. [src: personal-income-taxes]
- **− Above-the-line adjustments** (Schedule 1) → **Adjusted Gross Income (AGI)**. [src: personal-income-taxes]
- AGI is the pivotal number; most phase-outs key off AGI or *modified* AGI (MAGI). [src: personal-income-taxes]
- **− Standard deduction OR itemized deductions** (Schedule A) → **taxable income**. [src: personal-income-taxes]
- **Apply the tax brackets** to taxable income → **tax before credits**. [src: personal-income-taxes]
- **− Tax credits** (some refundable, some not) → **tax after credits**. [src: personal-income-taxes]
- **− Payments** (withholding from W-2/1099, estimated payments) → **refund or balance due**. [src: personal-income-taxes]
- > **TCJA note:** Most of the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act individual structure was [src: personal-income-taxes]
- > set to *sunset* after TY2025. **OBBBA made the TCJA rate brackets and the [src: personal-income-taxes]
- > larger standard deduction PERMANENT** and added new (some temporary) deductions. [src: personal-income-taxes]
- > The "2025→2026 sunset cliff" people feared **did not happen** — but several [src: personal-income-taxes]
- > OBBBA add-ons (senior deduction, tips/overtime deductions) are **temporary [src: personal-income-taxes]
- > (≈TY2025–2028)**, so a *different* uncertainty now applies. Verify any [src: personal-income-taxes]
- > OBBBA-specific figure at irs.gov. [src: personal-income-taxes]
- -- [src: personal-income-taxes]
- Status is generally fixed by your situation on **Dec 31**. [src: personal-income-taxes]
- -- [src: personal-income-taxes]
- The US uses **7 marginal brackets** (10/12/22/24/32/35/37%). Your **marginal [src: personal-income-taxes]
- rate** is the rate on your *last* dollar; your **effective rate** is total tax ÷ [src: personal-income-taxes]
- taxable income (always lower). A raise into a higher bracket only taxes the [src: personal-income-taxes]
- *portion* above the threshold — it never lowers your take-home. [src: personal-income-taxes]
- > **Worked example (TY2025, Single, $60,000 taxable income):** 10% on the first [src: personal-income-taxes]
- > $11,925 + 12% from $11,925 to $48,475 + 22% on the last $11,525 = **≈$8,114 [src: personal-income-taxes]
- > tax → marginal rate 22%, effective rate ≈13.5%.** [src: personal-income-taxes]
- *(HoH, MFS, QSS thresholds differ — see the IRS releases linked below.)* [src: personal-income-taxes]
- -- [src: personal-income-taxes]
- Take the **larger** of the two. Most filers (since TCJA nearly doubled the [src: personal-income-taxes]
- standard deduction) take the **standard**. [src: personal-income-taxes]
- > ⚠️ **OBBBA retroactively RAISED the TY2025 standard deduction** above the [src: personal-income-taxes]
- > originally-announced Oct-2024 figures. The numbers below are the [src: personal-income-taxes]

- Your employer withholds tax from each paycheck based on the **Form W-4** you file. [src: personal-income-taxes]
- The **redesigned W-4 (post-2020) eliminated "allowances"** (they were tied to [src: personal-income-taxes]
- personal exemptions, which TCJA zeroed out). It's now a 5-step form: filing [src: personal-income-taxes]
- status (Step 1), multiple-jobs/working-spouse (Step 2), dependents/credits [src: personal-income-taxes]
- (Step 3), other income / deductions / **extra withholding 4(c)** (Step 4), [src: personal-income-taxes]
- A **big refund ≠ winning** — it means you over-withheld and gave the [src: personal-income-taxes]
- government an interest-free loan all year. **Owing a lot** can trigger an [src: personal-income-taxes]
- underpayment penalty. The goal is to land near **$0**. [src: personal-income-taxes]
- Tune withholding with the **IRS Tax Withholding Estimator** [src: personal-income-taxes]
- (irs.gov/individuals/tax-withholding-estimator), which outputs a pre-filled W-4. [src: personal-income-taxes]

- **Liability (Bodily Injury / Property Damage) — the foundation.** [src: personal-insurance]
- Pays for injuries and property damage you cause to others. Nearly every state requires [src: personal-insurance]
- a minimum, but the mandated minimums are often dangerously low (e.g., $25,000/$50,000/ [src: personal-insurance]
- $25,000 in many states as of 2026 — verify current minimums with your state DOI before [src: personal-insurance]
- relying on any specific figure). Liability does *not* pay for your own injuries or [src: personal-insurance]
- damage to your own car. [src: personal-insurance]
- Limits are written as three numbers: [src: personal-insurance]
- Liability experts and consumer advocates generally recommend limits well above the state [src: personal-insurance]
- minimum — your assets and future wages can be at risk if a judgment exceeds your [src: personal-insurance]
- coverage. The Insurance Information Institute (iii.org) recommends buying at least as [src: personal-insurance]
- much liability as your net worth. (Verify current guidance at iii.org; as of 2026.) [src: personal-insurance]
- **Uninsured / Underinsured Motorist (UM/UIM).** [src: personal-insurance]
- Pays for your injuries (and in some states, property damage) when the at-fault driver [src: personal-insurance]
- has no insurance (UM) or insufficient insurance (UIM). Many states require UM coverage; [src: personal-insurance]
- **North Carolina requires both UM and UIM** at limits matching your liability (verify [src: personal-insurance]
- current NC requirement at ncdoi.gov — as of 2026). Even where optional, UM/UIM is [src: personal-insurance]
- generally considered high-value protection given the share of uninsured drivers (the [src: personal-insurance]
- Insurance Research Council estimates roughly 1 in 7 U.S. drivers was uninsured as of [src: personal-insurance]
- recent studies; verify current figures at insuranceresearch.org). [src: personal-insurance]
- Pays to repair or replace your vehicle after a collision (hitting another car, an [src: personal-insurance]
- object, or a rollover), regardless of fault. Does not cover theft or weather damage. [src: personal-insurance]
- Lenders and lessors typically require collision. Generally not cost-effective on older [src: personal-insurance]
- low-value vehicles (rough rule of thumb: if the annual premium + deductible exceeds the [src: personal-insurance]
- car's value, reconsider — not financial advice; consult your agent). [src: personal-insurance]
- Pays for non-collision losses: theft, fire, flooding, hail, animal strikes, vandalism. [src: personal-insurance]
- Often paired with collision ("full coverage" colloquially = liability + collision + [src: personal-insurance]
- comprehensive). Lenders and lessors typically require comprehensive too. [src: personal-insurance]
- **Med-Pay (Medical Payments) and PIP (Personal Injury Protection).** [src: personal-insurance]
- Both cover medical bills for you and passengers regardless of who caused the accident. [src: personal-insurance]
- PIP, required in "no-fault" states (FL, MI, NY, PA, and others — verify current list), [src: personal-insurance]
- also covers lost wages and other expenses. Med-pay is narrower. North Carolina is a [src: personal-insurance]
- **tort state** (not no-fault) and does not require PIP; it offers med-pay as an [src: personal-insurance]
- optional add-on (verify at ncdoi.gov). [src: personal-insurance]
- The deductible is what you pay out of pocket before insurance pays. Higher deductibles [src: personal-insurance]
- → lower premiums. Common deductibles: $250, $500, $1,000. Choose a deductible you [src: personal-insurance]
- could actually afford to pay after a loss. Separate deductibles typically apply to [src: personal-insurance]
- collision and comprehensive. [src: personal-insurance]
- Insurers use a combination of factors; permissible factors vary by state. Common rating [src: personal-insurance]
- factors (verify current permissibility in your state): [src: personal-insurance]
- **Credit-based insurance scores:** insurers use a score derived from credit report data [src: personal-insurance]
- (separate from a FICO credit score) as a predictive rating factor in most states. It is [src: personal-insurance]
- NOT the same number as your FICO score. If you want to understand the credit data [src: personal-insurance]
- underpinning your insurance score, the mechanics of credit reports belong in [src: personal-insurance]
- `credit-reports-and-scores`, not here. [src: personal-insurance]
- **Safe Driver Incentive Plan (SDIP):** NC uses a mandatory rating plan that assigns [src: personal-insurance]
- points for at-fault accidents and convictions, raising premiums. [src: personal-insurance]
- **NC minimum liability (as of 2026 — VERIFY):** NC law requires minimum liability of [src: personal-insurance]
- 30/60/25 and UM/UIM at matching limits. *These figures are frequently cited as of [src: personal-insurance]
- 2025; NC raised its minimums effective July 1, 2025 from 30/60/25 from 30/60/25 — [src: personal-insurance]
- verify the exact current requirement at ncdoi.gov before advising anyone.* [src: personal-insurance]
- **NC Rate Bureau:** premiums in NC are set through the NC Rate Bureau system; insurers [src: personal-insurance]
- can apply for deviations. Shopping still matters. [src: personal-insurance]
- -- [src: personal-insurance]
- The **HO-3 (Special Form)** is the most common homeowners policy (verify terminology [src: personal-insurance]
- with NAIC and ISO forms, as forms vary by insurer). It has four main coverages: [src: personal-insurance]
- **Open-peril (all-risk) on the dwelling (HO-3):** covers any cause of loss NOT [src: personal-insurance]
- listed as an exclusion. More protection for the structure. [src: personal-insurance]
- **Named-peril on personal property (HO-3 default):** covers only perils explicitly [src: personal-insurance]
- listed (fire, theft, windstorm, hail, vandalism, etc.). An **HO-5** policy extends [src: personal-insurance]
- open-peril to personal property too. [src: personal-insurance]
- For a 10-year-old roof, the ACV payout after depreciation can be a fraction of what a [src: personal-insurance]
- new roof actually costs. A **replacement cost value endorsement** on personal property [src: personal-insurance]
- is usually worth the small additional premium. Verify your policy's valuation basis. [src: personal-insurance]
- **Flood** — standard homeowners policy DOES NOT cover flood. Flood coverage is [src: personal-insurance]
- available through the **National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP)** or private flood [src: personal-insurance]
- insurers. Many homeowners in flood-prone areas are unaware of this gap until they [src: personal-insurance]
- file a claim. (FEMA manages the NFIP; see floodsmart.gov.) [src: personal-insurance]
- **Earthquake** — standard policy does not cover earthquake. Separate earthquake [src: personal-insurance]
- policy or endorsement required. [src: personal-insurance]
- **Sewer backup / water seepage** — often excluded; endorsement available. [src: personal-insurance]
- **Mold** — limited or excluded; some remediation coverage if caused by a covered [src: personal-insurance]
- **Normal wear and tear / maintenance failures** — not covered. [src: personal-insurance]
- **Business property / home-based business liability** — typically limited; [src: personal-insurance]
- commercial policy or endorsement needed. [src: personal-insurance]
- **High-value items** (jewelry, art, collectibles, firearms above a sublimit) — require [src: personal-insurance]
- a **scheduled personal property endorsement (floater)**. [src: personal-insurance]
- A common and serious mistake: insuring the home for its **market value** rather than [src: personal-insurance]
- its **rebuild cost**. In high-cost-of-labor markets, the rebuild cost often exceeds [src: personal-insurance]
- the sale price. Consult an agent who uses a replacement-cost estimator tool; rebuild [src: personal-insurance]
- costs are updated annually. **Inflation Guard** endorsements auto-adjust the dwelling [src: personal-insurance]
- limit over time. (Source: III.org consumer guides; verify current guidance.) [src: personal-insurance]
- -- [src: personal-insurance]
- The **HO-4** renters policy covers the **tenant's** personal property (not the building [src: personal-insurance]
- structure) and their personal liability. The landlord's policy covers the building but [src: personal-insurance]
- NOT the tenant's belongings or liability. [src: personal-insurance]
- **Cost:** typically $15–30/month for $30,000 of personal property and $100,000 of [src: personal-insurance]
- liability (as of 2026 — verify current rates; varies by city, building, credit score, [src: personal-insurance]
- and coverage level). One of the highest-value-per-dollar personal finance products. [src: personal-insurance]
- **Liability:** a visitor slipping in your apartment and suing you is covered. Without [src: personal-insurance]
- renters insurance, that liability falls on you personally. [src: personal-insurance]
- **Displacement:** if a fire makes your building uninhabitable, ALE covers your [src: personal-insurance]
- temporary housing — your landlord has no obligation to provide it. [src: personal-insurance]
- **Myth:** "My landlord's insurance covers my stuff." The landlord's policy covers the [src: personal-insurance]
- structure, not tenants' property. [src: personal-insurance]
- -- [src: personal-insurance]
- An **umbrella policy** (also called "personal excess liability") provides an extra layer [src: personal-insurance]
- of liability coverage above the limits of your auto and homeowners (or renters) policies. [src: personal-insurance]
- Typically sold in $1 million increments. [src: personal-insurance]
- **When it pays:** after your primary policy's liability limit is exhausted, the umbrella [src: personal-insurance]
- kicks in for covered claims — including bodily injury, property damage, personal injury [src: personal-insurance]
- (defamation, false arrest in some policies), and some incidents not covered by underlying [src: personal-insurance]
- **Typical requirements:** insurers usually require minimum underlying limits (e.g., [src: personal-insurance]
- $300,000 auto liability, $300,000 homeowners liability) before selling an umbrella. [src: personal-insurance]
- Umbrella does NOT cover: your own property damage, workers compensation, intentional [src: personal-insurance]
- acts, business liability (use a commercial umbrella). [src: personal-insurance]
- -- [src: personal-insurance]
- Life insurance replaces income and covers financial obligations for dependents if you [src: personal-insurance]
- die. The need is strongest when others rely on your income. [src: personal-insurance]
- **The "whole life as investment" concern:** whole life and universal life policies [src: personal-insurance]
- accumulate cash value, but internal returns are typically far lower than a comparable [src: personal-insurance]
- term + invest-the-difference strategy for most consumers. Consumer advocates (including [src: personal-insurance]
- the III and many fee-only financial planners) frequently flag aggressive whole-life [src: personal-insurance]
- pitches as a consumer-protection issue. This skill does not make investment [src: personal-insurance]
- recommendations; route investment comparison questions to `investing-and-retirement`. [src: personal-insurance]
- Common rough guidelines include 10–12× annual income, or DIME (Debt + Income [src: personal-insurance]
- replacement + Mortgage + Education for children). These are rough heuristics; actual [src: personal-insurance]
- need depends on your specific debts, dependents, savings, and other income sources. [src: personal-insurance]
- A **fee-only financial planner** (no sales commission) can provide an analysis. (Verify [src: personal-insurance]
- fee-only planners via NAPFA.org or CFP Board at cfp.net.) [src: personal-insurance]
- -- [src: personal-insurance]
- Statistically, a working adult is significantly more likely to experience a disabling [src: personal-insurance]
- illness or injury during their career than to die during that period. Yet disability [src: personal-insurance]
- insurance is far less commonly purchased than life insurance. The Social Security [src: personal-insurance]
- Administration's own data indicates roughly 1 in 4 20-year-olds will become disabled [src: personal-insurance]
- before retirement age (verify current SSA statistics at ssa.gov). [src: personal-insurance]
- **Own-occupation vs any-occupation definition:** the definition of "disability" is [src: personal-insurance]
- critical. **Own-occupation** pays if you can't perform your specific occupation [src: personal-insurance]
- (stronger). **Any-occupation** pays only if you can't perform any gainful occupation [src: personal-insurance]
- (weaker; harder to qualify). Most employer group LTD policies shift to any-occupation [src: personal-insurance]
- California, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island, and Hawaii require employers to provide [src: personal-insurance]
- short-term disability insurance (verify current list and benefit rules with your state's [src: personal-insurance]
- labor department; as of 2026). Most other states have no mandate; employer provides it [src: personal-insurance]
- voluntarily or not at all. [src: personal-insurance]
- SSDI is a federal benefit for workers with a sufficient earnings record who become [src: personal-insurance]
- disabled. The definition of disability is strict (inability to perform any substantial [src: personal-insurance]
- gainful activity) and the approval process is lengthy. It is not a substitute for [src: personal-insurance]
- adequate private disability coverage during working years. (More at ssa.gov.) [src: personal-insurance]
- -- [src: personal-insurance]
- The **declarations page** is the summary sheet attached to your policy — the most [src: personal-insurance]
- important page to locate and review. It contains: [src: personal-insurance]
- Named insured(s) and mailing address [src: personal-insurance]
- Policy number and period (effective / expiration dates) [src: personal-insurance]
- Covered property or insured vehicle(s) [src: personal-insurance]
- Coverage types and **limits** [src: personal-insurance]
- **Deductibles** for each coverage [src: personal-insurance]
- Listed **endorsements** (riders) attached [src: personal-insurance]
- Annual/installment premium [src: personal-insurance]
- Lienholder or mortgagee (if required by lender) [src: personal-insurance]
- Review the dec page annually at renewal to confirm limits are still adequate and no [src: personal-insurance]
- coverage was dropped. [src: personal-insurance]
- **Report promptly.** Most policies require prompt notice of a loss. Delays can [src: personal-insurance]
- complicate or void a claim. [src: personal-insurance]
- **Document the loss.** Photographs, police reports (auto/theft), receipts, and an [src: personal-insurance]
- inventory of damaged property are essential. [src: personal-insurance]
- **Cooperate with the adjuster.** An insurer sends a claims adjuster to assess the [src: personal-insurance]
- loss. Get any repair estimates they use in writing. [src: personal-insurance]
- **Deductible applies.** You pay the deductible; insurer pays the covered loss above [src: personal-insurance]
- it. For ACV policies, depreciation is deducted too. [src: personal-insurance]
- **Appeal a denial.** If a claim is denied, request the denial in writing with the [src: personal-insurance]
- specific policy provision cited. You can dispute through the insurer's internal [src: personal-insurance]
- process, hire a **public adjuster**, or file a complaint with your state DOI. [src: personal-insurance]
- **NC DOI complaint:** ncdoi.gov → Consumer Services. [src: personal-insurance]
- Filing a claim — even a not-at-fault auto claim — can raise your premium at renewal. [src: personal-insurance]
- Insurers use **CLUE (Comprehensive Loss Underwriting Exchange)** reports, maintained [src: personal-insurance]
- by LexisNexis, which contain your claims history for up to 7 years. Homeowners may [src: personal-insurance]
- also want to consider whether a small loss is worth filing vs paying out-of-pocket to [src: personal-insurance]
- avoid a premium increase. This is a judgment call, not a blanket rule — consult your [src: personal-insurance]
- **Compare at least 3 quotes** — premiums for identical coverage can vary 30–50% [src: personal-insurance]
- by insurer for the same driver and property (III.org data; verify current guidance). [src: personal-insurance]
- **Use an independent agent** who can quote multiple carriers, vs a captive agent [src: personal-insurance]
- (represents one insurer). Both can be excellent; independence expands options. [src: personal-insurance]
- **Bundle home and auto** — most insurers offer a multi-policy discount (typically [src: personal-insurance]
- 5–15%; verify with insurer). [src: personal-insurance]
- **Avoid underinsurance by checking your limits annually.** Inflation raises rebuild [src: personal-insurance]
- costs, replacement costs for electronics, and medical cost trends. [src: personal-insurance]
- **Verify your insurer's financial stability** — check AM Best ratings (ambest.com) [src: personal-insurance]
- or Standard & Poor's. An insurer that can't pay claims is not cheap insurance. [src: personal-insurance]

- -- [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- You almost never pay the "sticker" price of care. A plan splits cost between you [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- and the insurer through a few interlocking levers. Learn these six and you can [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Premium** — the fixed monthly amount you pay to *have* the plan, whether or [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- not you use it. A premium is not a cap on anything; it buys the contract. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Deductible** — what you pay **out of pocket first**, each plan year, before [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- the insurer starts paying its share for most services. A $2,000 deductible [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- means you cover the first $2,000 of covered care. (Some services — often [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- preventive care, sometimes a few copay'd visits — are covered *before* the [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Copay (copayment)** — a **fixed dollar** amount for a specific service [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- (e.g., $30 for a primary-care visit, $15 for a generic drug). Predictable. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Coinsurance** — your **percentage share** of a covered service *after* the [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- deductible (e.g., you pay 20%, the plan pays 80% of the allowed amount). [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Out-of-pocket maximum (OOP max)** — **the single most important number for [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- worst-case protection.** It is the most you can pay in a plan year for covered, [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- in-network services (deductible + copays + coinsurance all count toward it; [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **premiums do not**). Once you hit it, the plan pays **100%** of covered [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- in-network care for the rest of the year. A low premium with a high OOP max is [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- a bet you won't get sick; the OOP max is what bankrupts people who lose that bet. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- > **Mental model:** premium = the cost of *having* coverage; deductible/copay/ [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- > coinsurance = the cost of *using* it; OOP max = the ceiling on how bad a year [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- > can get. A "cheap" plan usually just moves money from the premium into the [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- > deductible and OOP max. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- Plans contract with a **network** of doctors/hospitals at negotiated rates. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- Going **out of network** can mean paying full freight or having it not count [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- toward your OOP max. The four common structures (as of 2026): [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- Always confirm your doctors and hospitals are **in network for the specific [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- plan** — networks differ even between plans from the same insurer. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Formulary** — the plan's list of covered drugs, sorted into **tiers** [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- (generic → preferred brand → non-preferred → specialty), each with its own [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- cost share. A drug off-formulary may not be covered at all. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Prior authorization (PA)** — the insurer must approve certain drugs, [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- procedures, or imaging **before** you get them, or they won't pay. Build in [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- time; a denied PA is appealable (see Part 5). [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **EOB (Explanation of Benefits)** — **not a bill.** It's the statement the [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- insurer sends after a claim showing what was billed, what the plan allowed, [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- what it paid, and what you may owe. Compare the EOB to the provider's actual [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- bill before paying — mismatches and the bills themselves are a [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **`medical-debt-and-billing`** topic. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- -- [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- Most people get coverage from **one** of these sources. Work top-down; the first [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- match is usually your best/cheapest option. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Employer-sponsored insurance (ESI / group plan)** — offered by your or a [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- family member's employer; the employer typically pays a large share of the [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- premium, and your contribution is usually pre-tax. **Usually the best deal if [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- offered**, because of the employer subsidy. Enrollment is at hire, during the [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- employer's annual open enrollment, or after a **qualifying life event**. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- *Caveat:* if the employer's offer is "affordable" by IRS rules, it generally [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **disqualifies you from marketplace premium tax credits.** [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Medicare** — if you're 65+ or qualify by disability/ESRD/ALS → **Part 3.** [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Medicaid / CHIP** — if your income is low → **Part 4.** [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **ACA Marketplace (healthcare.gov or your state exchange)** — the default for [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- the self-employed, those without an employer offer, early retirees, etc. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **COBRA** — a *bridge*, not a destination, when you lose an employer plan [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- (see end of this Part). [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Metal tiers** set how the plan splits cost (all cover the same essential [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- benefits): **Bronze** (low premium, high OOP — pairs with an HSA if HSA-eligible), [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Silver** (moderate; **the only tier that unlocks cost-sharing reductions**), [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Gold** (higher premium, lower OOP), **Platinum** (highest premium, lowest OOP). [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- Pick by *expected use*, not premium alone: heavy/predictable care → Gold/Platinum; [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- healthy + savings cushion → Bronze; **anyone who qualifies for CSRs → Silver.** [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Premium tax credit (PTC) / APTC** — a subsidy that lowers your monthly [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- premium, based on household size and **estimated annual income.** Taken in [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- advance it's the **APTC** (Advance Premium Tax Credit); you **reconcile** it on [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- your tax return (**Form 8962**) against actual income — underestimate income and [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- you may **repay** part of it. (The income-estimate and reconciliation mechanics [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- cross-ref **`personal-income-taxes`**.) [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Cost-sharing reductions (CSRs / "extra savings")** — a *separate* discount [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- (on top of the PTC) that lowers your **deductible, copays, and coinsurance** for [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- lower-income enrollees — **but only if you enroll in a Silver plan.** If you [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- qualify for CSRs, a Silver plan is usually the right answer even when Bronze is [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **🚩 2026 POLICY VOLATILITY — verify before relying.** The **enhanced premium [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- tax credits** (the temporarily larger ARPA/IRA subsidies that, among other [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- things, removed the old "subsidy cliff" and capped premiums as a % of income [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- above 400% FPL) **expired December 31, 2025.** As of 2026, the law reverts to [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- the **pre-2021 structure**: PTCs generally only for **100–400% of the federal [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- poverty level (FPL)**, and the **400% FPL "subsidy cliff" returns** — a dollar [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- of income over the line can cost thousands in lost subsidy, hitting **older, [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- middle-income** enrollees hardest. Whether Congress extends/changes this is [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- unsettled — **check current rules at healthcare.gov before assuming subsidy [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- amounts or the cliff's status.** [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Open Enrollment (OEP)** — the annual window to enroll/switch. For plan-year [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- 2026 on healthcare.gov it ran **~Nov 1, 2025 – Jan 15, 2026** (enroll by ~Dec 15 [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- for a Jan 1 start; state exchanges vary). Dates shift year to year — confirm. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Special Enrollment Period (SEP)** — a window *outside* OEP triggered by a [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **qualifying life event**: losing other coverage (incl. job loss, aging off a [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- parent's plan at 26), moving, marriage, birth/adoption, etc. SEPs are usually [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- ~60 days from the event. Losing CSRs can itself trigger an SEP. **Not every life [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- change qualifies** — e.g., a raise that pushes you over a subsidy threshold, or [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- voluntarily dropping coverage, generally does **not** open a marketplace SEP; if [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- no SEP applies you wait for the next OEP. Confirm your event qualifies at [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- When you lose an employer plan (job loss, hours cut, divorce, etc.), **COBRA** [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- lets you keep the *same* plan temporarily — but you now pay the **full premium + [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- up to a 2% admin fee** (i.e., the part the employer used to cover too), so it's [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- often expensive. Key facts (as of 2026): you generally get **60 days** to elect [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- after coverage ends or the election notice (whichever is later); standard [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- duration is **up to 18 months** (extendable to 29 with an SSA disability [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- determination, or 36 for certain dependent events). **Compare COBRA against a [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- marketplace plan** — job loss is an SEP, and a subsidized marketplace plan is [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- frequently cheaper than unsubsidized COBRA. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- -- [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- A **High-Deductible Health Plan (HDHP)** is a plan whose deductible/OOP limits [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- meet IRS thresholds; pairing it with a **Health Savings Account (HSA)** is the [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- only way to get an HSA. **You must be enrolled in a qualifying HDHP and have no [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- disqualifying other coverage to contribute** — a **general-purpose FSA** [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- (yours *or* a spouse's) and enrollment in **Medicare** both block HSA [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- contributions; a limited-purpose (dental/vision) FSA does not. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **The HSA "triple tax advantage":** (1) contributions are **pre-tax / [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- deductible**, (2) growth is **tax-free**, (3) withdrawals for **qualified medical [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- expenses are tax-free.** The HSA is **yours and portable** (unlike most FSAs), [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **rolls over** year to year, and after age 65 acts like an IRA for non-medical [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- withdrawals (taxed as income, no penalty). [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **IRS limits & thresholds (tax year 2026 — verify at irs.gov):** [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- > **Catch-up is per eligible individual, not per family.** Each spouse 55+ gets [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- > their own $1,000 catch-up, but it must go into **that spouse's own HSA** — a [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- > couple can't pool both catch-ups in one account. So a family where both spouses [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- > are 55+ can contribute $8,750 + $1,000 + $1,000, but only by **each opening an HSA.** [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- > **HSA vs FSA (quick contrast):** an **FSA** is employer-owned, generally [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- > **"use it or lose it"** (limited carryover), **not portable**, and doesn't [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- > require an HDHP; an **HSA** is **portable, rolls over, invests, and requires an [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- > HDHP.** A **limited-purpose FSA** (dental/vision) can coexist with an HSA. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- > **Cross-ref:** the **HSA tax mechanics** — reporting contributions/distributions [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- > on **Form 8889**, the above-the-line deduction, and reconciliation — live in [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- > **`personal-income-taxes`**, not here. This skill covers the *coverage* side [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- > (eligibility, the HDHP pairing, the limits). [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- -- [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Medicaid** is joint federal-state coverage for low-income people; **eligibility, [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- names, and benefits vary by state.** Under the ACA, states can **expand** Medicaid [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- to nearly all adults under **138% of the federal poverty level (FPL)**; some [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- states have not. **CHIP** covers children in families earning a bit too much for [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- Medicaid. Medicaid enrollment is **year-round** (no open-enrollment window). [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **🟢 North Carolina expanded Medicaid — live since December 1, 2023.** NC now [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- covers adults **ages 19–64 up to ~138% FPL** (roughly **$1,800/month for a single [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- person**, **~$3,000–$3,065/month for a family of three** — figures change [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- annually). This closed NC's old "coverage gap." Verify eligibility and current [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- income limits at **[medicaid.ncdhhs.gov](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov)**. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- If a healthcare.gov application finds you (or your kids) likely Medicaid/CHIP- [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- eligible, it routes you to the state agency — you generally can't take a [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- marketplace subsidy instead. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- -- [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Medicare** is federal coverage for people **65+** (and certain people under 65 [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- with disability, ESRD, or ALS). Two ways to assemble it: [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Part A — Hospital insurance.** Inpatient hospital, skilled nursing, hospice. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Usually premium-free** if you/spouse paid Medicare taxes ~10 years. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Part B — Medical insurance.** Doctors, outpatient, preventive, durable [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- equipment. **Has a monthly premium** (standard **$202.90/month in 2026**; [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- higher earners pay an income surcharge — IRMAA). [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Part C — Medicare Advantage (MA).** A **private** all-in-one alternative that [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- bundles A + B (usually + D), often with extra benefits, but with **networks** [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- and **prior auth**. You pick *either* Original Medicare (A+B) *or* Advantage. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Part D — Prescription drug coverage.** Private plans; standalone (with [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- Original Medicare) or built into an Advantage plan. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Two routes:** **(A)** Original Medicare (Part A + B) + usually a **Part D** drug [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- plan + a **Medigap** supplement; or **(B)** a **Medicare Advantage (Part C)** plan. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Medigap (Medicare Supplement)** — standardized **private** policies (plans [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- labeled by letter) that cover Original Medicare's out-of-pocket gaps [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- (coinsurance/deductibles). **Works only with Original Medicare**, not Advantage. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Enrollment periods & penalties (as of 2026 — verify at medicare.gov):** [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Initial Enrollment Period (IEP):** a **7-month** window around your 65th [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- birthday (the 3 months before, your birthday month, and the 3 months after). [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **General Enrollment Period (GEP):** **Jan 1 – Mar 31** each year, if you missed [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Medigap Open Enrollment:** a **6-month** window starting the month you're 65 [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **and** enrolled in Part B — your best (guaranteed-issue) shot to buy Medigap. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **⚠️ Late-enrollment penalties are usually permanent:** [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Part B:** **+10% for each full 12 months** you could have had it but didn't [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- — added to your premium **for as long as you have Part B.** [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Part D:** **1% × the national base premium ($38.99 in 2026) × the number of [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- full uncovered months** — added for as long as you have Part D. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Part A** (only if you must *buy* it): up to **+10%**, for twice the number [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- of years you delayed. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Special Enrollment Periods** can let you delay penalty-free if you had [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **creditable coverage** (e.g., from an active employer plan). [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- -- [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Estimate your year:** routine + any known surgeries/meds/pregnancy. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Compare total expected cost = premium × 12 + expected cost-sharing**, then [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **stress-test against the OOP max** for a bad-year scenario. Don't shop on [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Check the network** for *your* doctors/hospitals and the **formulary** for [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- *your* drugs — on the specific plan. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Apply any subsidies:** if PTC-eligible, see real net premiums; **if [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- CSR-eligible, look hard at Silver.** [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **HSA angle:** want to save tax-advantaged for healthcare and can absorb a [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- high deductible? An **HDHP + HSA** may win (Part 3). [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- Read the **Summary of Benefits and Coverage (SBC)** — a standardized one-pager [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- every plan must provide, with example cost scenarios. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- If a plan denies a claim or a prior authorization, you have **rights** (ACA-era [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- protections, as of 2026): [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Read the denial** — it must state the reason and how to appeal. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **Internal appeal** — you ask the insurer to reconsider. There's a filing [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- deadline (commonly **within 180 days** of the denial) and a window for the [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- insurer to respond; **urgent/expedited** review exists when delay endangers [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- health. Submit supporting documentation (doctor's letter, records). [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **External review** — if the internal appeal fails, you can take it to an [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **independent third party** whose decision the insurer **must follow.** There's [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- a deadline to request it after the final internal denial, with **standard** and [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- **expedited** tracks. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- Keep a paper trail; your **state insurance department** and the marketplace can [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- help, and **expedited** paths exist for urgent care needs. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- > Exact appeal/external-review **deadlines and decision timelines vary by plan and [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- > state and have specific day-counts** — confirm yours on the denial letter and at [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- > **[healthcare.gov/appeal-insurance-company-decision](https://www.healthcare.gov/appeal-insurance-company-decision/)**. [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- > Note: disputes over the **bill/balance** (vs the coverage *denial*) — including [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]
- > surprise-billing and the **No Surprises Act** — are a **`medical-debt-and-billing`** [src: health-insurance-and-coverage]

- **payer-specific, provider-specific, and state-law-dependent.** Content is [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **current as of 2026** and may be stale by the time you read it. The regulatory [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- landscape around medical debt and credit reporting has changed rapidly since 2022 [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- and remains contested; **verify all figures and current rules** against the [src: medical-debt-and-billing]

- charity-care applications and payment plans [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- -- [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- An **Explanation of Benefits (EOB)** is a statement from your **health insurer**, [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- not a bill. It explains what a claim was billed for, what the insurer paid, what [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- was adjusted (contractual discount), and what you supposedly owe as [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- patient responsibility (deductible, co-pay, coinsurance). It is not a bill, [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- but it is the key document for catching billing errors. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- A **medical bill** comes from the **provider** (hospital, physician group, lab, [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- imaging center). It states what the provider is asking you to pay, which should [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- match the patient-responsibility column on the EOB if the provider is in-network. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- If the numbers diverge, that is a flag worth investigating. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- > Verify: as of 2026, insurers are required under the ACA to provide EOBs for [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- > all covered benefits. The exact format varies by plan. Request a paper or [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- > PDF copy if the portal version is hard to read. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- You have the right to request an **itemized statement** from any provider — a [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- line-by-line list of every service, supply, and medication billed, with the [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- corresponding billing codes (CPT codes, HCPCS codes, revenue codes for hospital [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Call the provider's billing department; ask for "an itemized bill" or "itemized [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- statement" in writing (email or certified mail creates a record). [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Many providers are required by state law or by Medicare/Medicaid conditions of [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- participation to provide itemized bills. Federal No Surprises Act regulations [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- also reinforce these rights for uninsured patients. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Compare each line item against your EOB. Flag any service, date, or code that [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- does not appear in your EOB or that you do not recognize. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- -- [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Medical billing errors are extremely common. A 2021 Medical Billing Advocates of [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- America survey (verify; as of 2026) estimated billing errors in a substantial [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- majority of hospital bills. Identify errors before paying. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **Get the itemized bill and your EOB first.** [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **Identify the specific line item** and the suspected error (code, date, amount). [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **Call the provider's billing department.** Ask them to explain the charge and [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- to review the error. Document the date, representative's name, and outcome. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **Submit a written dispute** if the call does not resolve it — certified mail [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- or email with read receipt. State the specific charge, the error, and what [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- correction you expect. Keep copies of everything. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **Contact your insurer.** If the error is on the insurer's processing (wrong [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- adjustment, incorrect benefit applied), file an appeal or billing inquiry with [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- the insurer through the process in your plan documents. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **Escalate if needed.** State insurance departments can take complaints about [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- insurers. The CFPB and CMS take complaints about No Surprises Act violations. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Medical billing advocates (patient advocates, consumer assistance programs) can [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- help for a fee or free through nonprofit programs. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- -- [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- The **No Surprises Act (NSA)** — enacted as part of the Consolidated [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Appropriations Act, 2021 (Public Law 116-260) and effective for plan years [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- beginning January 1, 2022 — protects patients from most **surprise [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- out-of-network bills** in two main contexts. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- > Verify: NSA implementation rules have been the subject of ongoing rulemaking [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- > and litigation (verify cms.gov for current status; as of 2026). [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- For **emergency services** at a hospital, freestanding emergency department, or [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- urgent care center that accepts direct payment from an insurer: [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Insurers must cover emergency services without requiring prior authorization, [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- regardless of whether the facility or provider is in-network. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **You cannot be balance billed** by out-of-network emergency providers above [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- your in-network cost-sharing (deductible, coinsurance, co-pay) for emergency [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- services covered by your plan. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- The provider must use your in-network cost-sharing amounts. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- For **non-emergency care** at an **in-network hospital or ambulatory surgical [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- If you receive care from an out-of-network provider (e.g., an out-of-network [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- anesthesiologist or assistant surgeon you did not choose), **you cannot be [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- balance billed** unless you gave informed, written consent and the provider gave [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- you a proper notice and consent form at least 72 hours before the procedure. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- The consent waiver is not valid for certain situations (when no in-network [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- provider was available for the service). [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Non-emergency and emergency **air ambulance services** from out-of-network [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- providers: balance billing is prohibited in most cases (ground ambulance was [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- excluded from NSA but may be covered under state law — verify). [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- If you are **uninsured or self-pay** (paying out-of-pocket, not through [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **Providers must give you a Good Faith Estimate (GFE)** before a scheduled [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- service (or upon request) — including expected charges for the primary service [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- and any services expected to be provided by the same facility. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- The GFE must be provided at least 1 business day before a scheduled service [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- (or as soon as possible for urgent care). [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- If your final bill exceeds the GFE by **more than $400**, you can initiate the [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **patient-provider dispute resolution process** (PPDRP) through the federal [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- portal within 120 days of the bill date. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- CMS provides the dispute portal at: cms.gov/nosurprises [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- (verify availability; as of 2026) [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Report NSA violations at cms.gov/nosurprises or by calling 1-800-MEDICARE. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]

- **IRS §501(r)** (added by the Affordable Care Act, effective for tax years [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- beginning after March 23, 2010) imposes four key requirements on [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **tax-exempt (501(c)(3)) nonprofit hospitals** — which are the majority of [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- US community hospitals: [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- > For-profit hospitals and physician-owned facilities are NOT subject to §501(r) [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- > but may have their own financial assistance programs. State law may impose [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- > similar requirements; verify your state. As of 2026, verify IRS §501(r) [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- > regulations at irs.gov. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Eligibility criteria vary by hospital, but **income-based thresholds** are most [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Many nonprofit hospitals are required by their FAP to provide **free or [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- discounted care** to patients at or below a percentage of the Federal Poverty [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Level (FPL) — commonly 200%–400% FPL for discounted care, with free care at [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- 100%–200% FPL or lower. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Asset tests, residency requirements, and insurance status requirements vary. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- The FAP must be publicly available; download it from the hospital's website [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **Typical income thresholds** (illustrative; verify the specific hospital's FAP): [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- > FPL amounts are updated annually by HHS. Verify current FPL figures at [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- > aspe.hhs.gov or hhs.gov. As of 2026, verify. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **Download the hospital's FAP** from their website or request it at the billing [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- or admissions office. Confirm the hospital is nonprofit (check their website, [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- IRS Tax Exempt Organization Search at apps.irs.gov/app/eos/). [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **Complete the application.** Most require: proof of income (recent tax return, [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- W-2s, pay stubs), proof of expenses or hardship (bank statements, other debt), [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- and household size documentation. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **Apply as early as possible.** §501(r)(6) requires the hospital to make [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- reasonable efforts before taking extraordinary collection actions (reporting to [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- credit bureaus, suing you, placing a lien), but starting early avoids the risk [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- of those actions occurring before your application is processed. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **Apply retroactively if needed.** Most hospitals accept retroactive [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- applications for past bills, sometimes up to a year or more after service. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- The ACA and IRS guidance contemplate this; verify the hospital's FAP for [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- its retroactive window. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **Appeal a denial.** The FAP must describe the appeals process. Escalate to the [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- hospital's patient advocate or social worker if needed. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **Get help.** Hospital social workers and patient financial counselors can [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- assist with applications at no charge. Nonprofit patient advocacy organizations [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- also assist (verify: Patient Advocate Foundation at patientadvocate.org). [src: medical-debt-and-billing]

- The correct order is: [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Verify the bill against the EOB and itemized statement (Section 2). [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Apply for charity care / financial assistance if you are a low- or [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- moderate-income patient or facing hardship (Section 4). Do this before paying [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- or negotiating — charity care produces the best financial outcome if you [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Negotiate the remaining balance after any charity-care discount. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Arrange a payment plan on whatever remains. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Do **not** pay a large medical bill from a nonprofit hospital without first [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- checking charity-care eligibility. Many patients who qualify never apply. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Hospitals and providers routinely offer **cash-pay discounts** (also called [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- "prompt-pay discounts" or "self-pay rates") to patients paying out-of-pocket. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- These discounts reflect the fact that collecting from a self-pay patient is [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- simpler than billing through an insurer. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **Typical range:** 20%–50% off the chargemaster billed amount for uninsured or [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- self-pay patients. For in-network patients with insurance, the insurer's [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- contracted rate already reflects a similar discount — ask the billing office [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- what your "self-pay rate" would be versus filing through insurance. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **How to ask:** Call the billing department and ask: "Do you offer a self-pay [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- or cash-pay discount, or a prompt-pay discount for paying in full within 30 [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- days?" State that you are comparing to your insurance patient responsibility. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Always confirm any discount offer in writing before paying. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- If you cannot pay the balance in full: [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **Negotiate an interest-free payment plan.** Nonprofit hospitals are generally [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- required by their FAP (and encouraged by IRS §501(r)) to offer interest-free [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- payment plans to financially distressed patients. For-profit providers may also [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Ask explicitly: "Can I get an interest-free payment plan?" [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Get the plan terms in writing, including the monthly amount, the total balance, [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- whether interest accrues, and what happens if you miss a payment. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Confirm the plan amount is one you can realistically pay. A missed payment can [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- void the plan and send the account to collections. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **Do not put a medical bill on a credit card — especially a medical credit card [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- (e.g., CareCredit, Scratchpay) — without fully understanding the terms.** [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **Better alternatives in order of preference:** [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Charity care / FAP application (free or deep discount) [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Direct interest-free payment plan with the hospital [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Negotiated lump-sum discount [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- If none work, consult a nonprofit NFCC credit counselor before using any [src: medical-debt-and-billing]

- > state as of 2026 is: the rule was vacated. The voluntary bureau changes from [src: medical-debt-and-billing]

- **Unpaid medical collections over $500 and older than 12 months** may still [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- appear on credit reports and affect scores under some scoring models. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **Paid medical collections** are generally not reported (per the voluntary [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **Under $500 medical collections** are generally not reported (per the voluntary [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- **How much medical debt hurts your score** depends on the scoring model: [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- FICO 9 and VantageScore 4.0 weight medical collections less than older models; [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- FICO 8 (widely used) treats medical collections similarly to other collections. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Route scoring-model details to `credit-reports-and-scores`. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Verify the amount — if it is under $500, the bureau should have removed it [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- voluntarily; dispute it if it appears. [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
- Verify it is unpaid — if it is paid, dispute it per the voluntary removal [src: medical-debt-and-billing]
