- Every method below is a way to run the same three-step loop. Get the loop right [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- first; the method is just packaging. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **Know your income** — total monthly **take-home (net) pay**, not gross. Use [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- pay stubs. (See §6 if income is irregular.) [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **Track your spending** — log where money actually goes for at least a few [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- weeks before trusting any budget. Most people underestimate discretionary [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- spending until they see it. Start small (one week of receipts or one checking [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- account) if it feels overwhelming. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **Plan and adjust** — assign the income to categories, compare plan vs. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- actual at month-end, and adjust. Income minus expenses should be **≥ 0**; if [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- it's negative you're spending more than you make and need to cut, earn more, [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- A budget is simply a written plan for the money you expect each month. Its job [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- is to make sure money covers obligations *and* leaves room to save. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- -- [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- These are not exclusive. A common, durable combination: **pay-yourself-first** [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- to automate savings off the top, run the rest as a **zero-based** plan, and use [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **envelopes** only on the one or two categories that tend to overspend. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- -- [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **Pick a capture method you'll actually keep up with:** a notebook/journal, a [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- receipts-in-a-folder review at week's end, a spreadsheet, or an app that [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- auto-imports transactions. Consistency beats sophistication. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **Categorize** (housing, utilities, groceries, transportation, dining, [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- entertainment, etc.) so you can see patterns, then compare to your plan. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- The CFPB publishes free, no-login **Spending Tracker** and **Budget [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- Worksheet** tools (see References) that do this on paper or PDF. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- Review **plan vs. actual monthly**. The point of tracking isn't guilt — it's [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- finding the one or two categories where small changes free up real money. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- -- [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- Vague goals ("save more") fail. Make each goal **SMART**: **S**pecific, [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **M**easurable, **A**chievable, **R**elevant, **T**ime-bound — e.g., "save [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- $1,200 for a starter emergency fund by saving $100/month for 12 months." [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- The federal **Financial Literacy and Education Commission (FLEC)** frames money [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- management around the **MyMoney Five** (a useful checklist behind any budget): [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **EARN** — understand pay and benefits. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **SAVE & INVEST** — start early, even in small amounts. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **PROTECT** — emergency savings + appropriate insurance. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **SPEND** — get value; comparison-shop big purchases. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **BORROW** — credit can enable purchases but interest is a cost. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- (Investing and insurance are only *named* here; their mechanics live in sibling [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- skills — see the SKIP list.) [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- A **sinking fund** is a planned savings bucket for a **known, irregular, [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- non-monthly expense** — car registration, holidays, annual insurance premiums, [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- a replacement laptop. Divide the expected cost by months until due and save that [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- slice each month. This converts "surprise" expenses into ordinary line items and [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- is the single best defense against raiding the emergency fund for things that [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- weren't actually emergencies. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- -- [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- The cushion that keeps a job loss, car repair, or medical bill from becoming [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- credit-card debt. This is the **PROTECT** piece of any budget. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **How much:** the common rule of thumb is **3-6 months of essential expenses** [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- (housing, utilities, food, insurance, minimum debt payments, transportation) — [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- not 3-6 months of *income*. CFPB itself sets no fixed dollar figure and [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- stresses that **even a small amount provides security**; a widely used [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **starter goal is $500-$1,000** (or one month of expenses) before building [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- toward the full 3-6 months. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- Lean toward the **higher end (6+ months)** with variable/self-employed [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- income, a single income supporting dependents, or specialized job markets; [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- the **lower end** is reasonable with very stable dual incomes. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **Where to keep it:** somewhere **safe and liquid but slightly inconvenient** [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- to spend — separate from your everyday checking. A **high-yield savings [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- account (HYSA)** or money market account at a bank or credit union is the [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- typical home (account mechanics, APY, and FDIC/NCUA insurance live in the [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **personal-banking** sibling). The emergency fund is **not** an investment — [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- don't put it in stocks where it can drop right when you need it. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **Starting when money is tight:** manage **cash-flow timing** (align bill due [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- dates to paydays; many billers will move a due date), and **capture [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- windfalls** — route all or part of a tax refund, bonus, or cash gift straight [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- -- [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- Gig work, commissions, tips, seasonal or self-employment income break the [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- fixed-paycheck assumption. The fix is to **budget on a conservative baseline and [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **Find a baseline.** Average net income over the last 6-12 months, or — safer [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- — **budget to your lowest recent month** so essentials are always covered. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **Cover essentials first.** Rank fixed/essential costs; the baseline must [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- cover those before any discretionary spending. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **Use a buffer / "income-smoothing" account.** In good months, park the [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- surplus above baseline; in lean months, top up to baseline from it. This [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- evens out the lumps. (This buffer is *separate* from the emergency fund.) [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **Make savings a percentage, not a flat dollar amount,** so it scales with a [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- big month instead of getting skipped in a small one. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **Set aside taxes** if self-employed (no employer withholding) — the tax-form [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- mechanics belong to a tax skill, but the *budgeting* habit is to quarantine a [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- percentage of every payment immediately. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- -- [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- Automation removes willpower from the equation and operationalizes [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **pay-yourself-first**: [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **Automatic recurring transfers** from checking to savings, timed just after [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- payday (even $25-$50 per paycheck compounds into a real fund). [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **Split direct deposit:** ask your employer to route a fixed amount or [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- percentage of each paycheck straight into savings so it never lands in [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **Auto-escalate:** raise the transfer amount when income rises or a debt is [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- paid off, so freed-up cash is redirected rather than absorbed by lifestyle. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **Automate sinking-fund contributions** the same way, one transfer per bucket [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- (or one bucket with a tracking spreadsheet). [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- -- [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- Two structured ways to attack multiple debts. In **both**, you pay **minimums on [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- everything** and throw **every extra dollar at one target debt**; when it's [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- gone, you **roll that freed-up payment onto the next** (the "snowball" rolling [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- effect). They differ only in **which debt is the target**: [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **Which to pick:** the avalanche is mathematically optimal, but the *best plan [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- is the one you'll actually finish*. If motivation is the bottleneck, the [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- snowball's early wins are worth a little extra interest. A hybrid (knock out one [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- tiny balance for a quick win, then switch to avalanche) is common. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- > **Scope line:** this is about *paying off debt you can afford to pay*. If a [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- > debt is in collections, charged off, or you're considering settling for less [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- > than owed (and the 1099-C tax hit), see [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- > **`charge-offs-collections-and-debt-resolution`**. If a collector is [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- > contacting or suing you, see **`debt-collectors-and-fdcpa-rights`**. A formal [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- > **debt management plan (DMP)** through a counselor is covered in §10. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- -- [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **The post-Mint shift:** Intuit's free **Mint** app — long the default [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- free aggregator — was **shut down in early 2024** (Intuit steered users to [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- Credit Karma, which lacks Mint's budgeting tools), pushing users to [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- alternatives. The current landscape is a mix of [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **subscription apps** (e.g., zero-based/envelope-style and aggregator tools), [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **free bank/credit-union built-in budgeting dashboards**, **spreadsheets**, [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- and **paper/PDF worksheets**. This skill stays **tool-neutral** — pick by [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- method fit and privacy comfort, not brand. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **Pick by the method you'll run:** want every dollar assigned → a zero-based [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- app or template; want hard category limits → an envelope/cash-stuffing app; [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- just want awareness → an aggregator or your bank's dashboard or a tracker [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **Privacy matters with aggregators.** Apps that link to your accounts pull [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- sensitive transaction data; the **CFPB has flagged that many financial apps [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- collect and share user data with third parties** (data brokers, advertisers). [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- Read the data-sharing terms, prefer providers with clear limits, and note [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- that a spreadsheet or paper system shares nothing. (The CFPB's own free tools [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- don't collect what you enter.) [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **You don't need an app at all.** A spreadsheet or the free CFPB Budget [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- Worksheet + Spending Tracker runs every method above. [src: budgeting-and-saving]

- Budgeting help is widely available at no cost — you should not pay an up-front [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- fee for basic budgeting or counseling: [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **Nonprofit credit counseling.** Member agencies of the **National Foundation [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- for Credit Counseling (NFCC)** offer a **free initial counseling session**: a [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- certified counselor reviews your full budget and debts and builds an action [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- plan. If credit-card debt is the problem, they can set up a **debt management [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- plan (DMP)** — you make **one monthly payment** to the agency, which [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- distributes it to creditors, typically paying off cards over **3-5 years**, [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- often at reduced rates. Choose an **NFCC-accredited** agency. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **Financial coaching.** Free/low-cost coaching is offered through many [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- nonprofits, employers (financial-wellness benefits), credit unions, [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- libraries, and military programs. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **Federal resources.** **MyMoney.gov** (the FLEC portal) and the **CFPB** [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- publish free, vendor-neutral guides, worksheets, and the *Your Money, Your [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- Goals* toolkit. **AnnualCreditReport.com** for free credit reports relates to [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- the credit-score siblings, not budgeting. [src: budgeting-and-saving]
- **Avoid "debt relief" or "credit repair" outfits that demand large up-front [src: budgeting-and-saving]

- category; legitimate nonprofit counseling starts free. [src: budgeting-and-saving]

- <!-- Provenance: standalone skill. Mirrored from ~/.claude/skills/investing-and-retirement/SKILL.md by scripts/persist-spoke.mjs. --> [src: investing-and-retirement]
- > **Framing (read first).** This is **general educational information, NOT investment, tax, or financial advice, and NOT a recommendation to buy or sell any security.** All investing carries risk, including loss of principal; past performance does not guarantee future results. Contribution limits, income thresholds, and Social Security rules **change every year** — every dollar figure here is stated **as of 2026** (sourced from IRS Notice 2025-67 and SSA). Verify against the primary sources in *References* before relying on anything, and for your own situation consult a licensed **fee-only fiduciary** advisor and/or a tax professional. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Where this sits.** Spoke of the **consumer-finance** family; the **`consumer-finance`** hub is the anchor. The sibling **`consumer-credit-and-debt`** hub owns credit/debt routing. This skill owns the *investing + retirement-savings* layer. It states the **tax treatment** of accounts but hands off tax-form depth to `personal-income-taxes`, deposit accounts/CDs to `personal-banking`, and life-insurance-as-"investment" to `personal-insurance` (see cross-references at the end). [src: investing-and-retirement]
- This skill is deliberately **boring**: the evidence favors low-cost, diversified, long-horizon investing over stock-picking and market-timing. It will not give hot tips. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- -- [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Risk and return are linked.** As potential return rises, so does risk. The SEC's plain-English rule: *there is no such thing as a high, guaranteed return.* If someone promises one, that is a fraud red flag (Part 5), not an opportunity. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Compounding rewards time.** Returns earn returns, so starting earlier matters more than starting bigger; a long time horizon is the single biggest advantage a small investor has. *Illustration (hypothetical, not a projected return):* at a 7% annual return, money roughly doubles about every 10 years (the "rule of 72": 72 ÷ 7 ≈ 10), so a dollar invested at 25 has far more doubling cycles left than the same dollar invested at 45. Investor.gov's Compound Interest Calculator runs your own numbers. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Diversification: don't put all your eggs in one basket.** Spreading money across many investments so one loss is cushioned by others reduces the risk tied to any single holding. A broad index fund diversifies in one purchase. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Asset allocation** is how you split money among **stocks, bonds, and cash**, and it is the biggest driver of your risk/return mix. The right mix depends on your **risk tolerance** and **time horizon**, not on predictions: a longer horizon typically means more stock, and nearing the goal typically means more bonds/cash. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Rebalance** periodically back to your target mix instead of chasing winners (for example, once a year, or when a holding drifts well past its target weight). [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Dollar-cost averaging (DCA).** Investing a fixed amount on a regular schedule (e.g., every paycheck) buys more shares when prices are low and fewer when high, and removes the temptation to time entry. This is how most 401(k) contributions already work. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Don't try to time the market.** Staying invested through ups and downs has historically beaten trying to guess tops and bottoms. Time *in* the market beats *timing* the market. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Costs are the one thing you control** (see Part 4). Low cost compounds in your favor. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Time horizon → allocation (illustrative, not advice):** money needed within ~1–3 years generally should not be in the stock market at all (that is a `personal-banking` savings/CD question); money you won't touch for decades (retirement) can tolerate more stock and more short-term volatility. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- -- [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Mutual fund vs ETF (FINRA):** both bundle many securities and charge an annual expense ratio. Key differences: ETFs trade throughout the day at market price; traditional mutual funds transact once daily at NAV. Index versions of either are typically the cheapest. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Active vs passive:** an **actively managed** fund pays a manager to try to beat a benchmark; an **index (passive)** fund just matches it cheaply. Because higher fees are a permanent handicap (Part 4), low-cost index funds are the evidence-based default for most long-term investors. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- -- [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **The core tax distinction — Traditional vs Roth (applies to both 401(k)/403(b) and IRA):** [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Traditional** = **pre-tax in, taxed out.** Contributions may reduce taxable income now; withdrawals in retirement are taxed as ordinary income. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Roth** = **after-tax in, tax-free out.** No deduction now; qualified withdrawals (and growth) come out tax-free later. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- Rough rule of thumb (not advice): Roth tends to favor those who expect a **higher** tax rate later; Traditional favors those who expect a **lower** rate later. Many people split. *The tax-form mechanics live in `personal-income-taxes`.* [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **403(b)** is the nonprofit/public-school/government analog of the **401(k)**; they behave similarly. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Employer match = free money.** If an employer matches contributions, contributing at least enough to capture the **full match** is the highest-priority step in almost any plan. Not doing so leaves guaranteed compensation on the table. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Vesting:** the match may **vest** over time, either **cliff** (0% until a set date, then 100% at once) or **graded** (a rising percentage each year). You keep only the employer portion you're vested in if you leave; your own contributions are always 100% yours. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Fees matter even here:** under ERISA, plan **fiduciaries** must keep plan costs *reasonable* and disclose fees; you can usually pick the lowest-cost index/target-date option in the menu (Part 4, DOL). [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Traditional IRA** vs **Roth IRA** follow the tax split above. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Roth IRAs have income limits**; direct contributions phase out at higher incomes. Traditional-IRA *deductibility* phases out if you (or a spouse) are covered by a workplace plan. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Backdoor Roth:** high earners above the Roth income limit may contribute to a (nondeductible) Traditional IRA and then **convert** it to Roth. It is a legal, IRS-acknowledged workaround, but the **pro-rata rule** (the IRS taxes a conversion proportionally across *all* your pre-tax and after-tax IRA money, so existing pre-tax IRA balances make part of the conversion taxable) can create a surprise tax bill. This is a **see-a-tax-pro** maneuver (`personal-income-taxes`). [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **SEP-IRA:** employer (or self-employed person) funds a Traditional IRA in the employee's name; high contribution ceiling, simple. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **SIMPLE IRA:** for small businesses with no other plan; employer + employee contributions, lighter administration and lower limits than a 401(k). [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **2026 IRA income phase-outs (verify; thresholds shift yearly):** Roth direct-contribution phase-out **$153,000–$168,000** (single/HoH) and **$242,000–$252,000** (married filing jointly). Above the top of the range, direct Roth contributions aren't allowed (hence the backdoor route). [src: investing-and-retirement]
- > **Boring priority order most educators suggest (not advice):** (1) contribute enough to **get the full employer match**; (2) pay down high-interest debt / hold an emergency fund (→ `budgeting-and-saving`, `consumer-credit-and-debt`); (3) max an **IRA** (Roth or Traditional); (4) go back and max the **401(k)**; (5) taxable brokerage after that. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- -- [src: investing-and-retirement]
- An **expense ratio** is the fund's annual operating cost as a **percentage of assets** (covers management, administrative, and 12b-1 fees). It is deducted from returns automatically, so you never see a bill, which is exactly why people ignore it. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Loads** (front-end/back-end sales charges) and **transaction fees** are *separate from* the expense ratio. Avoid loads when a no-load index equivalent exists. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **FINRA's illustration:** a fund charging 1.85% must out-perform a 0.75% fund by **more than a full percentage point every year** just to tie. Over decades, a seemingly small fee gap compounds into a large chunk of your ending balance. Fees are a permanent headwind; low cost is a permanent tailwind. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Tools:** the **FINRA Fund Analyzer** compares the lifetime fee drag of specific funds; Investor.gov's **Compound Interest Calculator** shows the upside of compounding. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **In a 401(k):** ERISA requires fee disclosure and that fiduciaries keep total plan costs reasonable (DOL). Use that disclosure to pick the cheapest broad-market or target-date option in the menu. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Bottom line:** you can't control returns, but you *can* control costs, and cost is one of the few reliable predictors of long-run net performance. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- -- [src: investing-and-retirement]
- Treat these as **stop signs**. Any one of them warrants walking away and verifying independently. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **"Guaranteed" or "risk-free" high returns.** The #1 tell. Every real investment carries risk; guaranteed high return = fraud. Compare any promised yield against returns on well-known market indexes; wildly higher = wildly riskier or fake. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **"Phantom riches" / "can't miss" / "huge upside, no risk"** pitches. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Pressure & urgency:** "limited spots," "act today," artificial deadlines. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Overly consistent returns** that never dip regardless of the market (a classic **Ponzi** signature: new investors' money pays earlier investors, and it collapses when inflows stop). [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Unregistered products / unlicensed sellers**, or trouble getting paid out or getting straight answers. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Affinity fraud:** the fraudster is (or pretends to be) a member of your religious, ethnic, professional, military, or community group and leans on that trust. *Never* invest solely because someone "like you" vouches for it; verify anyway. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Crypto / social-media scam awareness:** the same red flags apply to crypto "opportunities," DMs, and "finfluencer" tips; guaranteed-return crypto and "send funds to unlock your gains" are scams. If you've already lost money or had identity/data compromised, see the broader recovery angle in **`identity-theft-and-credit-fraud`**, and report to the SEC/FTC. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Always verify before you wire a dollar:** [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **FINRA BrokerCheck** (brokercheck.finra.org) — license, registration, and disciplinary history of a broker or firm. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **SEC IAPD / Form ADV** (adviserinfo.sec.gov) — registration and disclosures for investment advisers. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- Confirm the *product* and the *person* are registered; "check out everything no matter how trustworthy the person seems" (SEC). [src: investing-and-retirement]
- -- [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Full Retirement Age (FRA)** is **67** for anyone born **1960 or later** (it phased up from 66). FRA is when you get your *full* (unreduced) benefit. You choose when to start, between 62 and 70: [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **The tradeoff:** claiming early means more checks, each smaller; delaying means fewer checks, each larger (and a larger base for survivor benefits and cost-of-living adjustments). The "right" age depends on health, longevity expectations, other income, and spousal/survivor considerations. Run SSA's own calculators against your earnings record; this is a planning decision, not a one-size answer. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- -- [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Robo-advisor (digital/internet adviser):** software builds and rebalances a low-cost, diversified portfolio (often index ETFs) from your goals and risk tolerance; cheap, hands-off, and good for straightforward needs. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Human investment professionals (FINRA):** be aware that **"financial advisor," "financial planner," "wealth manager," "financial consultant"** are often **generic job titles, not credentials or licenses.** Ask what they're actually registered as (broker / investment adviser representative) and how they're paid. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Fee-only fiduciary vs commission:** [src: investing-and-retirement]
- A **fiduciary** is held to act in *your* best interest. A **fee-only** advisor is paid **only by you** (flat, hourly, or % of assets under management) and earns **no commissions**, minimizing the conflict where a product is sold because it pays the seller. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **Commission/transaction-based** compensation can create incentives to sell higher-cost products. Always ask: *"Are you a fiduciary, 100% of the time, and how exactly are you paid?"* [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **How to vet anyone before hiring (do this every time):** [src: investing-and-retirement]
- **FINRA BrokerCheck** for brokers/firms; **SEC IAPD / Form ADV** for advisers. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- Check licenses, registration, and **disciplinary history / complaints**. [src: investing-and-retirement]
- Decode **professional designations**; some are rigorous, some are marketing (FINRA's designation lookup explains each). [src: investing-and-retirement]
- Get fees **in writing** and understand every layer (advisory fee *plus* the funds' expense ratios). [src: investing-and-retirement]

- > **Educational legal information only; NOT legal advice.** Estate law is **state-specific and fact-specific**, and NC statutes change. Everything here is **as of 2026** and describes **North Carolina** law for an individual; another state's rules differ. Statute citations are to the **NC General Statutes (G.S.)**; verify the current text at [ncleg.gov](https://www.ncleg.gov) and the process at the [NC Judicial Branch](https://www.nccourts.gov). For your own plan, a contested estate, a blended family, sizable or out-of-state assets, a special-needs beneficiary, or any tax question, **consult a NC-licensed estate-planning attorney.** This skill is a spoke of the **consumer-finance** family; the **`consumer-finance`** hub is the anchor, and the sibling **`consumer-credit-and-debt`** hub owns credit/debt — so route debts-after-death and NC creditor questions to its **`north-carolina-credit-and-debt-law`** spoke. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- This skill is **knowledge**: explain the core documents, how NC intestacy and probate work, and where to verify. It is not a form-filling or legal-drafting engine; point people to a licensed attorney or the official AOC forms. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- Use this skill for the **core estate-planning documents and NC probate**. The description's `SKIP:` clause is abbreviated for length; the full deferral set is here. Each carve-out names the seam precisely, because the topics share vocabulary: [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- -- [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- A complete basic NC estate plan is usually **four documents**, not just a will: [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Last Will and Testament.** Directs who gets your property, names your **executor** (personal representative), and (critically) **names a guardian for minor children**. Takes effect only at death and only after it is **probated**. Does *not* avoid probate and does *not* control beneficiary-designation or jointly-titled assets (see below). [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Durable (Financial) Power of Attorney.** Lets an **agent** manage your money/property **while you are alive but incapacitated**. NC = the **Uniform Power of Attorney Act, G.S. Chapter 32C**. Dies with you (then the will/executor takes over). [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Health-Care Power of Attorney.** Names an agent to make **medical** decisions if you cannot. NC statutory form: **G.S. 32A-25.1** (Chapter 32A, Article 3). [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Living Will / Advance Directive ("Declaration of a Desire for a Natural Death").** Your wishes about life-prolonging measures at end of life. NC = **Right to a Natural Death, G.S. 90-321** (Chapter 90, Article 23). Often paired with a **HIPAA authorization** so providers may share records with the people you name. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- Supporting pieces: up-to-date **beneficiary designations** (retirement/life insurance), correct **account titling** (joint, POD/TOD), and a **digital-assets** plan (below). [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- -- [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Who may make one (G.S. 31-1):** any person **18 or older** and of **sound mind**. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Attested written will, the standard will (G.S. 31-3.3):** a written will **signed by the testator** and **attested by at least two competent witnesses**, who sign **in the testator's presence** (they need not sign in each other's presence). Best practice: a witness should be **disinterested** (not a beneficiary). [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Self-proving affidavit (G.S. 31-11.6):** a notarized affidavit by the testator and witnesses, executed with the will (or later). It lets the will be **probated without locating the witnesses** after death, a major convenience. **Strongly recommended.** [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Holographic will (G.S. 31-3.4):** a will **entirely in the testator's own handwriting**, with the testator's signature (or name written by the testator), found among valuable papers/effects after death. **No witnesses required**, but it is harder to probate (extra proof under G.S. 28A-2A-9) and easy to get wrong; a properly witnessed, self-proved attested will is far safer. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **What a will does / does NOT do:** [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Does:** distribute *probate* assets, name the **executor**, name a **guardian** for minor children, can create a **testamentary trust**. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Does NOT:** control assets that pass by **beneficiary designation, POD/TOD, or survivorship titling**; avoid probate; take effect before death; or transfer anything until it is **probated** before the Clerk of Superior Court. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **The executor (personal representative):** the person you name to gather assets, give creditor notice, pay valid debts and taxes, and distribute what remains, all under the Clerk's supervision (NC estate administration = **G.S. Chapter 28A**). Name a backup. If there is no will, the court appoints an **administrator**. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **You cannot fully disinherit a spouse (the elective share, G.S. 30-3.1):** even a valid will leaving a spouse little or nothing can be overridden. A surviving spouse may instead claim an **elective share** of the decedent's **Total Net Assets**, on a sliding scale by length of marriage: **15%** (married < 5 years), **25%** (5 to < 10), **33%** (10 to < 15), **50%** (15+ years), reduced by what already passes to the spouse (calculation under G.S. 30-3.4). The claim is filed with the Clerk **within 6 months** of letters being issued. (You generally *can* disinherit an adult child; NC does not protect children the way it protects a spouse.) [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- -- [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- "Intestate" = no valid will. State law (not your wishes) then dictates who inherits. NC shares (**G.S. 29-14**, **G.S. 29-15**; figures **as of 2026, verify**): [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Surviving spouse's share** depends on who else survives: [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- Whatever the spouse does **not** take passes to children/descendants (per G.S. 29-15/29-16). **No spouse and no descendants** → up the family tree to parents, then siblings, then more remote kin. **Unmarried partners, stepchildren, and friends inherit nothing under intestacy**; only a will (or beneficiary designations/trust) can provide for them. This is the single best reason to have a will. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- -- [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- A huge share of wealth passes **outside** the will and is **not** controlled by it: [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Retirement accounts** (401(k), IRA), **life insurance**, and annuities pass to the **named beneficiary** on the account, regardless of what the will says. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Payable-on-Death (POD)** bank accounts and **Transfer-on-Death (TOD)** brokerage accounts pass to the named person. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Joint accounts / property with right of survivorship** pass to the surviving owner. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Consequences:** a stale designation (an ex-spouse, a predeceased parent) controls over your current will. **Review beneficiary forms after every major life event** (marriage, divorce, birth, death). Naming a **minor** directly, or your **estate**, can backfire, so ask an attorney about a trust or custodial arrangement. These assets also **skip probate**, which is part of why they matter. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- -- [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- A **revocable living trust** is created during life; you move assets into it and typically serve as your own trustee, naming a **successor trustee** to take over at incapacity or death. Assets **titled in the trust avoid probate** and pass privately per the trust terms. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Trust vs will — the trade-off:** [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **A will** is simpler and cheaper to create, but its probate assets go through the **public** probate process. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **A revocable trust** can **avoid probate**, ease management at **incapacity**, keep terms **private**, and help with **out-of-state real estate**, but only for assets you actually **retitle into it** (an unfunded trust does nothing); it also costs more up front and does **not** reduce income or estate tax by itself. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Is it worth it in NC?** NC probate is relatively **clerk-driven and moderate-cost**, and small/spousal estates have streamlined paths (below), so a trust is **not automatic** for everyone. It tends to pay off with real estate in multiple states, a desire for privacy, planning for incapacity, or more complex family situations. Even with a trust you still need a **"pour-over" will**, a financial POA, and health-care documents. Decide with a NC attorney. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- -- [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- A **power of attorney** lets your **agent** act on your behalf for **property and financial** matters. In NC: [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **"Durable"** is the default: under the modern Act a POA is durable (it **survives your incapacity**) **unless** it expressly says otherwise (**G.S. 32C-1-104**). Durability is the whole point; a non-durable POA ends exactly when you'd need it most. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Execution (G.S. 32C-1-105):** sign before a **notary** (acknowledged). To bind real estate, **record** it with the county Register of Deeds. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Statutory short form:** NC provides a fill-in form at **G.S. 32C-3-301**. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- A POA **ends at death**; after that the **will/executor** governs. Choose an agent you trust completely; the agent owes you **fiduciary duties**. (For elder financial-exploitation concerns, CFPB has consumer guidance; see References.) [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- -- [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- Two complementary documents: [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Health-Care Power of Attorney (G.S. 32A-25.1 statutory form):** names a **health-care agent** to make medical decisions when you **cannot speak for yourself**; broader and more flexible than a living will because a person adapts to circumstances. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Living Will / "Declaration of a Desire for a Natural Death" (G.S. 90-321):** states whether you want **life-prolonging measures** withheld/withdrawn in specified end-of-life conditions. NC's form may be **combined with** the health-care POA. Both require **signing, qualified witnesses, and notarization** under their statutes. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- Add a **HIPAA authorization** so providers can release records to your agent/family. Give copies to your agent, doctor, and hospital; NC also has an **Advance Health Care Directive Registry** (NC Secretary of State). [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- -- [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- In NC the **elected Clerk of Superior Court** in each county acts as the **probate judge**; estate administration is governed by **G.S. Chapter 28A**. A will **has no legal effect until probated**. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Full administration (rough arc):** [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- The person named executor applies to the Clerk (forms in the **AOC-E** series, e.g., **AOC-E-201**) and qualifies; the Clerk issues **Letters** (Testamentary, or of Administration if no will). [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- The personal representative **inventories** assets, **gives notice to creditors**, **pays valid debts and taxes**, then **distributes** the remainder and files a **final account**. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Creditor claims (G.S. 28A-19-3, G.S. 28A-14-1):** the personal representative publishes/mails notice giving creditors a deadline **at least three months out**; most claims **not presented by the deadline (or within 90 days of a mailed notice, if later) are forever barred**. This is why probate takes months. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Streamlined paths (figures as of 2026, verify):** [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Small-estate collection by affidavit (G.S. 28A-25-1):** if the decedent's **personal property** (net of liens) is **≤ $20,000** (or **≤ $30,000 where the sole heir is the surviving spouse**), an heir/creditor can collect by **affidavit 30 days after death**, skipping full administration. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Summary administration (G.S. 28A-28):** when the **surviving spouse is the sole beneficiary/heir**, the spouse can petition to take the estate while assuming the decedent's debts. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Year's Allowance (G.S. 30-15):** a surviving spouse is entitled to a **$60,000** support allowance (and an allowance may be claimed for each dependent child), paid ahead of most claims and **exempt from the decedent's creditors**. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **No NC estate or inheritance tax** (below), but the estate may still owe the decedent's final **income taxes**. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- -- [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- If both parents die while a child is a minor, the **court appoints a guardian**. Your **will is where you nominate** the guardian of the **person** (who raises the child) and can address the guardian of the **estate** (who manages the child's money); NC guardianship sits in **G.S. Chapter 35A**. The court isn't strictly bound but gives your nomination great weight. Pair it with a way to **hold the child's money** (a testamentary trust or UTMA custodianship via **G.S. Chapter 33A**) so a young adult doesn't receive a lump sum outright. Naming a guardian is often the most important reason a young parent makes a will. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- -- [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- NC has adopted the **Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act (G.S. Chapter 36F)**, which governs whether your **fiduciary** (executor, agent, trustee, guardian) can access email, photos, cloud files, and online accounts. **Order of control:** a provider's **online tool** (e.g., a "legacy contact" / inactive-account manager) **wins first**; absent that, your **will/trust/POA** directions control; absent both, the provider's terms of service apply. **Action:** set legacy-contact tools where offered, and have your will/POA **expressly grant** digital-asset authority. Keep credentials in a secure manager, not listed in the will itself (the will becomes a public record once probated). [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- -- [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **North Carolina has NO estate tax and NO inheritance tax** (both repealed effective **Jan 1, 2013**). NC heirs do **not** pay a state death tax. *(Inherited assets can still generate later income, e.g. distributions from an inherited IRA, which is income-tax, not death-tax; see `personal-income-taxes` and `investing-and-retirement`.)* [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Federal estate tax** applies only to very large estates. **As of 2026** the exemption is **$15 million per person** (~$30 million per married couple), **made permanent by the 2025 law (OBBBA)**, indexed for inflation, with a top **40%** rate on the excess; estates over the threshold file **IRS Form 706**. **The vast majority of estates owe no federal estate tax.** Spouses also get **portability** of an unused exemption and an unlimited **marital deduction**. **Figures change; verify at irs.gov.** [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- -- [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **Reasonable DIY candidates:** a young, healthy person with simple assets and a clear plan: a statutory health-care POA, a financial POA, and a straightforward witnessed-and-self-proved will. NC's statutory forms exist precisely for this. Even then, get **execution right** (signature + two witnesses + notarized self-proving affidavit), or the will can fail. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- **See a NC-licensed attorney when:** you have a **blended family**, **minor or special-needs** beneficiaries, **business interests**, **out-of-state real estate**, a sizable estate, **any trust**, you want to **avoid probate**, you're **disinheriting** someone (remember the spousal **elective share**, G.S. 30-3.1, above), or there's potential **conflict**. The cost of a small mistake (an invalid will, a stale beneficiary, an unfunded trust) usually dwarfs the cost of advice. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- -- [src: estate-planning-and-wills]
- > NC statutes change; always confirm the current section text. All G.S. citations below resolve at `ncleg.gov`. [src: estate-planning-and-wills]

- The discipline of designing multi-lesson courses and curricula: the layer between learning science (mechanisms of how people learn) and single-tutorial craft (how to write one how-to guide). This skill covers process models, curriculum architecture tools, objective-writing frameworks, and course-format decisions for technical and engineering training contexts. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Boundary contracts:** [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Learning science mechanisms (cognitive load, retrieval practice, spacing, deliberate practice) → **applied-psychology** [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Tutorial / how-to / reference writing craft → **technical-writing-craft** [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Certification exam design and psychometrics → **assessment-certification-design** [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Training delivery craft, facilitation, live lab instruction → **technical-training-delivery** [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Program evaluation, ROI, Kirkpatrick → not yet a separate skill; out of scope here [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Teaching troubleshooting as a pedagogy → **teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning** [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Typical invocation outputs:** when asked to design a course from scratch, produce a course design document (TO/EO hierarchy, scope-and-sequence, format decision, prerequisite map). When asked to audit an existing course, produce an alignment audit table (ILO verb | TLA description | AT type | match Y/N) plus a findings list. When asked for a lesson plan, produce a Gagné event map for the module. Format adapts to the scope of the request; ask for clarification only when the target audience and learning objective are both absent. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]

- -- [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Three process models dominate instructional design practice. They differ on sequencing, iteration, documentation, and stakeholder involvement — not on underlying learning science. Choose based on content stability, timeline, documentation requirements, and team structure. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- ADDIE (Analysis–Design–Development–Implementation–Evaluation) originated in 1975 at Florida State University under U.S. Army contract. It functions as a **meta-framework** describing what must happen in any instructional design project without prescribing how to do it. Most other models are recognizable as ADDIE variants. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Analysis** — identify the instructional problem, learner characteristics, existing skill gaps, delivery constraints [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Design** — map learning objectives to assessment strategies; select instructional approach [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Development** — create content assets (modules, simulations, facilitator guides); pilot test [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Implementation** — deliver instruction; train facilitators [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Evaluation** — formative (ongoing quality checks within phases) + summative (outcome assessment post-delivery) [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- The "ADDIE is a waterfall" characterization is partially a myth: the model never prohibited iteration or mid-phase revision; that rigidity was an implementation choice, not a structural constraint. Contemporary ADDIE explicitly accommodates rapid prototyping as formative feedback within phases. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Best fit for technical/engineering training:** compliance-mandated curricula, safety certification, regulatory onboarding, content with a long shelf-life, contexts requiring documentation trails. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Weakest fit:** fast-changing technical content (new platform releases, agile workflows); tight timelines. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- -- [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Introduced by Michael Allen (Allen Interactions) in *Leaving ADDIE for SAM* (Allen & Sites, ASTD Press, 2012), explicitly as a response to waterfall-ADDIE dynamics. Draws from agile software development, prioritizing rapid prototyping and continuous stakeholder feedback over upfront planning. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **SAM1** (smaller projects): Preparation (rapid info gathering + "Savvy Start" brainstorm) → Iterative Design (rapid prototyping + stakeholder review) → Iterative Development (alpha/beta/gold with embedded testing) [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **SAM2** (larger projects): same core with added project management scaffolding [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Core differentiator:** produce something usable at every stage so stakeholders interact with real artifacts, not abstract specs. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Best fit:** evolving technical content; eLearning for new tooling; agile development contexts; tight timelines. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Weakest fit:** certification-track programs requiring audit trails, regulatory compliance documentation, or large-scale replicability. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- -- [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Published by Walter Dick and Lou Carey in *The Systematic Design of Instruction* (1978). A fully elaborated ten-component procedural model grounded in systems theory: instructor, learners, materials, delivery, activities, and environment are treated as interdependent components of a coherent system. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Ten components (abbreviated):** Identify instructional goals → conduct instructional analysis → analyze learners and contexts → write performance objectives → develop assessment instruments → develop instructional strategy → develop/select materials → design and conduct formative evaluation (1:1, small group, field trial) → revise instruction → design summative evaluation. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Components 1–9 are explicitly iterative and parallel; formative evaluation feeds back into earlier steps continuously. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Best fit:** complex competency-based programs; technical certification requiring rigorous performance-objective alignment; blended learning with multiple modalities. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Weakest fit:** small-scale or time-constrained projects; teams without dedicated instructional design expertise. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- -- [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- -- [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Understanding by Design (UbD) — Wiggins & McTighe (ASCD, 1998) — inverts conventional planning: define what students must ultimately *do* first, then design evidence of that performance, and only then plan instruction. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Stage 1 — Desired Results:** Establish specific measurable learning objectives and, deeper, "enduring understandings" (transferable big ideas expressed as declarative sentences, e.g., "Systems have emergent properties their components do not") and "essential questions" (open-ended, recurring, thought-provoking questions that anchor the course). The six **facets of understanding** — explain, interpret, apply, have perspective, empathize, have self-knowledge — inform what evidence of understanding looks like. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Stage 2 — Acceptable Evidence:** Determine *how* learners will demonstrate understanding before designing any instruction. Distinguishes performance tasks (authentic applications) from other evidence (quizzes, reflections). Sequencing this before Stage 3 prevents "teaching to the activity." [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Stage 3 — Learning Plan:** Design instruction last, in service of Stage 2 evidence requirements. The WHERETO heuristic guides design: **W**here and Why, **H**ook, **E**quip and Explore, **R**ethink and Revise, **E**valuate, **T**ailor, **O**rganize. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Scaling UbD to curriculum:** the backward design logic applies recursively — program-level transfer goals are established first, then courses are designed to build toward them, then units within courses. McTighe and Wiggins explicitly frame UbD as a "unit-planning process" that scales to full curriculum design. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Requires upfront commitment to fixed objectives, which can crowd out emergent or personalized learning pathways [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Highly dependent on the designer's disciplinary grasp — if you cannot distinguish enduring understandings from topic coverage, the output is misaligned curricula [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Expensive to adopt institutionally — working backward against content-first instincts requires significant professional development [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- -- [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Scope** defines breadth and depth of coverage. **Sequence** determines the order of content presentation, ensuring learning is cumulative and builds systematically. A well-designed scope and sequence ensures prerequisite skills appear before courses that require them. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- A curriculum is a directed acyclic graph (DAG): courses are nodes, prerequisite relationships are directed edges. Three structural roles emerge from this framing: [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Hub courses** — connect many subsequent topics; single point of failure if poorly taught [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Bridge courses** — connect otherwise isolated clusters [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Source courses** — foundational material with no prerequisites but many dependents [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Mapping the prerequisite graph explicitly surfaces structural bottlenecks before the curriculum is built. A hub course whose prerequisites are unclear or inconsistently enforced creates cascade failures in all downstream courses. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- A curriculum map is a visual matrix: courses vs. learning outcomes, marked at Introduction / Reinforcement / Mastery (I/R/M) levels. It verifies that critical competencies are: [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Introduced early in the sequence [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Reinforced across multiple courses [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Demonstrated at mastery level before program completion [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Missing or misplaced coverage is visible as matrix gaps. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- -- [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Chunking** groups content into manageable units grounded in working memory limits. Practical guidance: target 1–3 learning objectives per module; end each chunk with a practice activity (knowledge check, scenario, reflection) to facilitate transfer to long-term memory. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Sequencing approaches for technical content:** [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Standard pattern for technical/engineering content:** Declarative (what it is) → Procedural (how to do it) → Situated (when and why to apply it). [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Key failure mode:** over-loading declarative knowledge before procedural application — the "front-loaded lecture" where learners process concepts they cannot yet connect to practice. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- -- [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Robert F. Mager's *Preparing Instructional Objectives* (1962) established behavioral objectives as a design tool. The ABCD expansion makes all four design elements explicit: [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Each component constrains a downstream decision. Once Condition is fixed ("without reference materials"), instructional practice must mirror that constraint. Once Degree is fixed ("with no more than one error"), the rubric writes itself. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Well-formed technical example:** *Given access to the Atlas UI and current index configurations [C], database administrators [A] will identify the three indexes most likely causing collection scan warnings [B] by selecting all three correctly from a provided list of ten candidates [D].* [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Conditions opener patterns:** *Given a…* / *Without reference to…* / *Using the standard operating procedure…* / *Given access to the cluster dashboard…* [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Not every objective requires all four components spelled out. Explicitly state Condition when the performance constraint differs from daily work context; explicitly state Degree when a pass/fail line must be drawn for certification or safety-critical outcomes. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- -- [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Bloom's Revised Taxonomy (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001) is, for course designers, a **verb selection and objective leveling tool** — use it when writing learning objectives and sequencing lessons, not as a theory of cognition (that belongs in applied-psychology). The 2001 revision replaced nouns with action verbs, making it directly actionable for objective writing. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Taxonomy as a dependency chain:** a learner who cannot *remember* configuration syntax cannot *apply* it; one who cannot *analyze* a failure trace cannot *evaluate* whether an architectural change is warranted. This chain is a curriculum pacing heuristic. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Sequencing rule:** lesson-level verbs must be at or below the course-level verb's Bloom's level — never higher. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Verb table for technical training:** [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Common design defect:** training assessments test at Remember or Understand when the job demands Apply or Analyze. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Assessment alignment note:** objective-to-assessment alignment (ILO verb → AT demand) is covered in Section 8 (Constructive Alignment). Psychometrics, item writing, and IRT analysis belong in assessment-certification-design. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- -- [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Terminal Objective (TO):** the capstone performance the learner must achieve by module/course end. One TO per module scope is a practical limit (5–9 TOs per full course). TOs describe outcomes, not activities. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Enabling Objectives (EOs):** prerequisite sub-skills derived by asking recursively: "What must the learner already be able to do to achieve this?" The result is a directed graph of prerequisites — not a flat list. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Design payoff:** once the hierarchy is drawn, the instructional sequence is largely determined. EOs that are prerequisites for other EOs come first; EOs with no dependents can be taught in any order; the TO is assessed last. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Derivation method (subordinate skills analysis):** Start with the TO. Ask "What must they know/do to achieve this?" for each answer. Continue recursively. Validate the resulting graph with subject-matter experts. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Worked example — Atlas slow-query diagnosis:** [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- TO: Given a production Atlas cluster with a 24-hour slow-query log, identify the [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- three highest-impact missing indexes (all three correct, without assistance). [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- EOs (prerequisite chain): [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- EO1: Recall the components of an explain plan output (Remember) [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- EO2: Describe conditions under which a collection scan occurs (Understand) [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- EO3: Interpret IXSCAN vs COLLSCAN in an explain plan (Understand → Apply) [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- EO4: Compare candidate index strategies for a given query shape (Analyze) [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- └── requires EO1, EO2, EO3 [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- TO: Identify the three highest-impact missing indexes (Analyze/Evaluate) [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- EO1–EO3 have no dependencies on each other and can be taught in any order. EO4 requires EO1–EO3 before it can be practiced. The TO is assessed only after EO4 is demonstrated. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- -- [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- John Biggs' constructive alignment (1996) coordinates three components so they address the same learning agenda: [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Design sequence:** ILO first → TLA that practices the ILO verb → AT that measures the same verb under the ILO conditions. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Backwash mechanism:** learners tend to learn what they believe will be assessed. A misaligned course (objective says *analyze*, assessment tests *recall*) produces learners who study for recall and never practice analysis. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Alignment audit:** map ILO verbs → TLA activities → AT demands. Mismatches at cognitive demand levels are the primary finding. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Limitations:** When mandated top-down as a quality-assurance tool, constructive alignment can become a paperwork exercise disconnected from actual learning; it specifies the architecture but offers limited guidance on which specific TLAs to select. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- -- [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Robert Gagné's framework pairs nine external instructional events with internal cognitive processes. Operates as both a **lesson design scaffold** and a **lesson audit tool**. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Three-phase structure:** Preparation (Events 1–3) → Acquisition (Events 4–6) → Transfer (Events 7–9). [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Most commonly skipped — and an anti-pattern when absent:** Event 9 (Retention and Transfer). The framework provides a structural reminder to design for transfer, not just comprehension; skipping it is listed as an explicit anti-pattern in Section 12. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Sequence guidance:** for short modules, several events can be compressed into a single activity. Events should not be permanently omitted; if an event is absent, the designer should document an explicit reason. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Key limitation:** the framework does not include a motivation principle; Keller's ARCS model (Attention, Relevance, Confidence, Satisfaction) was developed explicitly to fill this gap. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- -- [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- M. David Merrill (2002) synthesized five invariant principles from a review of major ID theories. All five are **simultaneously necessary** — no single principle is sufficient without the others. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Pebble-in-the-Pond model:** Merrill's practical design process radiates outward from a real-world problem: design problem sequences first, then component skills, then demonstrations and practice, then integration activities, then assessments — in that order. Inverts the conventional outline-first approach. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Design reorientation:** the first question shifts from "What content must I cover?" to "What real-world problem must learners be able to solve?" [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Limitations:** resource-intensive to implement; presupposes design autonomy to restructure course around problem sequences (not always available in institutional/compliance contexts); less explicit about *how* to select specific activities than *what* principles to honor. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- -- [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Course format is an architectural decision that determines which learning activities are feasible and what learner behaviors the design can depend on. ILT = Instructor-Led Training (synchronous, cohort-based delivery). [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Design principle for blended:** use self-paced for declarative knowledge and easily codified procedural knowledge; reserve synchronous for situated knowledge and procedural content requiring real-time instructor correction. [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- -- [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- -- [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **When to use which process model:** [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Stable content, compliance required, documentation trail needed → **ADDIE** [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Fast-changing content, agile context, tight timeline, iterative stakeholder feedback → **SAM** [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Complex competency-based program, rigorous performance-objective alignment, blended learning → **Dick & Carey** [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Typical course design deliverables:** [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Course design document** — TO/EO hierarchy, scope-and-sequence, format decision, assessment strategy, prerequisite map [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Module blueprint** — objectives (ABCD), Gagné event mapping, activity type per objective, alignment audit table [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Alignment audit table** — ILO verb | TLA description | AT type | match? (Y/N) [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Prerequisite graph** — DAG diagram with hub/bridge/source roles labeled [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- *Design from scratch:* start with transfer goals → TO/EO hierarchy → process model selection → scope-and-sequence → module blueprints [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- *Audit an existing course:* run the alignment audit table; flag ILO/TLA/AT mismatches; apply Gagné event check per module; compare against Merrill's five principles [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- *Single-module design:* write the TO first; derive EOs via subordinate skills analysis; map Gagné events; confirm format matches stakes [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Objective quality checklist:** [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Link: [ ] Written from learner's perspective (not "the lesson will cover") [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Link: [ ] Behavior verb is observable (not vague state verbs) [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Link: [ ] Condition specified when it differs from daily work context [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Link: [ ] Degree stated when a pass/fail line is required [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Link: [ ] Bloom's level matches actual job performance demand [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Alignment audit steps:** [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- List all ILO verbs [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- For each, identify the TLA that practices that verb [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- For each, identify the AT that requires that verb [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Flag any ILO with no TLA and/or no AT → gap in the design [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- **Curriculum architecture checklist:** [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]
- Link: [ ] Transfer goals defined at program level before course design begins [src: instructional-design-course-architecture]

- Covers the full lifecycle from job task analysis through psychometric validation, cut-score setting, [src: assessment-certification-design]
- exam security, and digital credential issuance. Grounded in AERA/APA/NCME Standards, NCCA/ICE [src: assessment-certification-design]
