- Every defensible certification program follows this sequence: [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Job Task Analysis (JTA) [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Test Blueprint / Content Outline [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Item Development (MCQ + PBA) [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Item Review (Editorial + Sensitivity + SME) [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Field Testing / Pretesting [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Psychometric Analysis (CTT + IRT) [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Standard-Setting (Cut Score) [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Exam Delivery + Security [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Ongoing Validity / Reliability Studies [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Recertification / Credential Maintenance [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Skipping any step creates a defensibility gap under accreditation review. NCCA Standard 14 requires [src: assessment-certification-design]
- documented JTA linkage to every content domain in the blueprint. [src: assessment-certification-design]
- The blueprint (also called a table of specifications or content outline) is the governing document [src: assessment-certification-design]
- for all item development. It must be empirically traceable to the JTA. [src: assessment-certification-design]
- **Blueprint architecture rules (CEDMA guidance):** [src: assessment-certification-design]
- No more than 7 major content domains and 20–22 total objectives [src: assessment-certification-design]
- No single objective should be assessed by only one item (minimum 3–4 items per objective) [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Weight domains proportionally to JTA frequency × importance ratings [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Freeze the blueprint before item development begins; mid-cycle revisions invalidate items [src: assessment-certification-design]
- **Cognitive level distribution by certification tier:** [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Biggs's constructive alignment principle: intended learning outcomes define assessment tasks; tasks [src: assessment-certification-design]
- define instructional activities — not the reverse.[^biggs1999] The scenario-removal test: if a candidate can [src: assessment-certification-design]
- cover the scenario and answer from the stem alone, the item is testing recall, not reasoning, [src: assessment-certification-design]
- regardless of blueprint labeling.[^cedma] [src: assessment-certification-design]
- See `references/item-writing-and-psychometrics.md` for full distractor analysis tables. [src: assessment-certification-design]
- **Well-formed stem rules:** [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Complete problem statement in the stem; candidates should not need to read options to understand the question [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Use positive phrasing; reserve EXCEPT/NOT stems for cases where the negative is the exact professional skill being tested [src: assessment-certification-design]
- One clear question per stem (no double-barreled constructions) [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Avoid window-dressing text that adds length without adding discriminating information [src: assessment-certification-design]
- **Distractor design rules:** [src: assessment-certification-design]
- All distractors must be plausible to a candidate lacking the target knowledge [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Options must be parallel in grammatical form and similar in length [src: assessment-certification-design]
- A nonfunctional distractor (selected by <5% of examinees) degrades item discrimination; flag for revision after each administration [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Never use "all of the above" (rewards partial knowledge) or "none of the above" (unless an exact answer is required, e.g., mathematical calculations) [src: assessment-certification-design]
- **Six flaw categories to eliminate:** [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Structured faculty training + peer review reduces total item flaw rates from ~67% to ~21% within [src: assessment-certification-design]
- three years (longitudinal medical education data).[^pmc3809311] [src: assessment-certification-design]
- PBAs assess execution, not knowledge recall. Action-verb alignment rule: [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Blueprint verbs "configure," "demonstrate," "troubleshoot" → hands-on lab / PBA items [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Blueprint verbs "explain," "identify," "describe" → MCQ or scenario-based items [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Mixing these creates construct-irrelevant variance [src: assessment-certification-design]
- **Six-step PBA design process:** [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Ground each task in a specific JTA task statement [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Define scoring criteria (success outcomes) before designing the environment [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Engage SMEs during design, not as final reviewers only [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Build scoring rubrics concurrently with task design (not post-hoc) [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Validate each task against actual job performance data [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Plan ongoing maintenance (tools and duties evolve) [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Scoring must accommodate alternative solution paths (multiple valid command sequences achieving the [src: assessment-certification-design]
- same correct outcome). Partial-credit rubrics for directionally correct but incomplete solutions. [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Run after every exam administration to flag items for revision or retirement. [src: assessment-certification-design]
- **Key statistics and interpretation thresholds:** [src: assessment-certification-design]
- **CTT limitation:** all statistics are sample-dependent. The same item's p-value differs across [src: assessment-certification-design]
- cohorts with different mean ability.[^ctt-sampledev] This drives the migration to IRT for large-scale programs. [src: assessment-certification-design]
- IRT models the probability of a correct response as a function of latent ability (θ) and item [src: assessment-certification-design]
- parameters. The key advantage for credentialing: **parameter invariance** — item difficulty does [src: assessment-certification-design]
- not depend on who was tested; person ability does not depend on which items were answered. [src: assessment-certification-design]
- **Model selection guide:** [src: assessment-certification-design]
- **Key IRT concepts:** [src: assessment-certification-design]
- **Item Characteristic Curve (ICC):** plots P(correct) vs. θ; inflection point = b, slope ∝ a, lower asymptote = c [src: assessment-certification-design]
- **Item Information Function:** I(θ) = a²·P(θ)·Q(θ); items contribute maximum information at θ ≈ b [src: assessment-certification-design]
- **Test Information Function (TIF):** sum of item information functions; enables assembling forms with maximum precision at the cut score [src: assessment-certification-design]
- **Conditional SEM:** SEM(θ) = 1/√I(θ); unlike CTT's global SEM, CSEM varies and is typically largest at the cut score — must be reported for pass/fail decision accuracy [src: assessment-certification-design]
- **IRT assumptions to verify:** [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Unidimensionality (one dominant latent trait; use confirmatory factor analysis) [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Local independence (items not correlated after conditioning on θ; case vignette testlets violate this) [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Model fit (fit statistics for each item; misfit → revise or remove) [src: assessment-certification-design]
- **Test equating:** when multiple exam forms must be compared fairly, IRT true-score equating with [src: assessment-certification-design]
- a Non-Equivalent groups with Anchor Test (NEAT) design is the standard. Anchor item drift (items [src: assessment-certification-design]
- that change difficulty between forms due to exposure or coaching) is the primary equating threat. [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Pre-equating embeds new items as unscored pilots and calibrates them to the existing scale before [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Cut scores must be defensible, documented, and tied to a defined performance standard — [src: assessment-certification-design]
- "minimally competent candidate." The standard-setting study is a separate formal process. [src: assessment-certification-design]
- **Method comparison:** [src: assessment-certification-design]
- **Standard-setting best practices:** [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Train panelists on the definition of "minimally competent" before ratings (not after) [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Run multiple rounds; show panelists inter-rater disagreement statistics and allow discussion [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Document all panelist credentials, training procedures, and final decisions for accreditation [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Apply SEM at the cut score to define a "borderline zone" for decision accuracy analysis [src: assessment-certification-design]
- **ANSI/ISO 17024:2012** — The international standard for personnel certification bodies. Key [src: assessment-certification-design]
- requirements: impartiality (governance separation between certification and training arms), [src: assessment-certification-design]
- documented examination development, reliability and validity evidence, and a competence-based [src: assessment-certification-design]
- appeal process. Required for programs with international recognition ambitions. [src: assessment-certification-design]
- **NCCA Standards (National Commission for Certifying Agencies)** — The US-specific accreditation [src: assessment-certification-design]
- benchmark administered by ICE (Institute for Credentialing Excellence). 21 Standards organized [src: assessment-certification-design]
- around: governance, JTA, exam development, psychometric soundness, security, candidate policies, [src: assessment-certification-design]
- and recertification. NCCA accreditation signals program quality to employers and regulators. [src: assessment-certification-design]
- **Role separation requirement (both standards):** The governance body that awards credentials must [src: assessment-certification-design]
- be structurally independent from any body that provides preparation or training. Conflict-of-interest [src: assessment-certification-design]
- management policies must be documented and enforced. [src: assessment-certification-design]
- **Recertification / Maintenance of Certification (MOC):** [src: assessment-certification-design]
- CE-based: earn continuing education credits per cycle (most common) [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Point-based: accumulate points across CE, professional activities, contributions [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Re-examination: pass the current exam version at renewal [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Practice requirements: document ongoing professional activity [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Choice depends on domain velocity — fast-moving technical domains favor re-examination or [src: assessment-certification-design]
- point-based systems that include currency-of-practice requirements. [src: assessment-certification-design]
- **Item exposure control:** [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Sympson-Hetter (SH) procedure: assigns probabilistic exposure caps via simulation; prevents [src: assessment-certification-design]
- overexposure in CAT; two-stage SH (2023) adds minimum exposure floor to prevent underexposure [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Item bank rotation: partition banks into sub-banks and rotate active pools; most effective for [src: assessment-certification-design]
- multi-timezone global testing [src: assessment-certification-design]
- Field test items (beta items): embedded unscored items that collect psychometric data without [src: assessment-certification-design]
- affecting candidate score; rotate to operational after calibration [src: assessment-certification-design]

- <!-- Provenance: standalone skill. Mirrored from ~/.claude/skills/teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning/SKILL.md by scripts/persist-spoke.mjs. --> [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Expert reference for designing instruction and developing learner competency in **troubleshooting and diagnostic reasoning** — the pedagogy of fault-finding, not fault-finding itself. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- When this skill is invoked, responses should take the form appropriate to the request: [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- *H-D = hypothetico-deductive. Dual-process theory (System 1 fast/non-analytic vs. System 2 slow/analytic) explains this shift — see Core Concept 6. For the psychological mechanisms of expertise and learning, see applied-psychology.* [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- -- [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- When a running program is underperforming, map symptoms to instructional root causes before redesigning: [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- -- [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Collins, Brown & Newman (1989) provide the foundational framework. The six methods apply directly to teaching diagnosis: [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Modeling**: The expert diagnoses a live or simulated fault while making reasoning visible. In troubleshooting, this requires externalizing normally invisible processes: "I'm seeing high CPU and slow queries together — that pattern makes me think either a missing index or lock contention before I look at anything else." Think-aloud protocol is the vehicle. Without externalization, novices only see the *actions*, not the *reasoning strategy* that chose those actions. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Coaching**: The instructor observes the learner in the act of diagnosing and provides contingent, just-in-time feedback. Coaching in diagnostic contexts includes: [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Ask the learner to state their hypothesis before running any test [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Probe what evidence would falsify the current hypothesis [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Interrupt random-action patterns by returning to the hypothesis-first discipline [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Guard against premature closure on the first plausible explanation [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Scaffolding**: Reducing task complexity so the learner can engage with the diagnostic reasoning without being overwhelmed by system complexity. Scaffolding instruments for troubleshooting: simplified system models, fault-isolation guides, pre-populated hypothesis lists, structured troubleshooting worksheets. A key principle: *scaffolding must be contingent* — it must respond to where the learner actually is, not be a fixed template applied to everyone. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Fading**: Removing scaffolds as competence grows. In troubleshooting training: guide-based fault isolation → structured worksheet → open-ended diagnosis. The expertise reversal effect (Kalyuga) warns that scaffolds left too long become harmful for advancing learners — they create extraneous cognitive load rather than reducing it. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Articulation**: Having learners explicitly state their reasoning — "what do you know, what do you think, why?" Articulation forces the learner to surface tacit reasoning and exposes gaps invisible to the instructor. Techniques: verbal think-aloud, written diagnostic reasoning logs, structured debrief ("what made you suspect X before you tested it?"). [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Reflection**: Comparing one's own diagnostic process to an expert's. In practice: post-case debrief with expert trace side-by-side; asking "where did your path diverge from the expert's and why?". Reflection accelerates schema development because it highlights the *structural features* of cases rather than surface features. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Exploration**: Encouraging learners to generate their own diagnostic approaches, vary parameters, and build their own fault taxonomy. This is the autonomy phase — not free-for-all, but purposeful exploration of the problem space beyond the taught cases. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- -- [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Jonassen & Hung (2006) identified the core failure mode of traditional troubleshooting instruction: teaching procedures without system understanding produces technicians who can follow guides but cannot transfer to novel faults. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Effective troubleshooting requires a **multi-layered conceptual model** of the system: [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Topographic knowledge**: What components exist; how they are physically/logically connected. Learners need this map before they can reason about where a fault could originate. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Functional knowledge**: What each component does; how components interact; causal flow through the system. This is the prerequisite for hypothesis generation — you can only hypothesize causes you understand. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Strategic knowledge**: How experts reason about this class of systems — which fault hypotheses to eliminate first (split-half strategy), which observations rule out whole subsystems, what "normal" looks like at each measurement point. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Procedural knowledge**: The steps for performing diagnostic tests. This is often *over-taught* at the expense of the above — HYDRIVE's field evaluation showed that novice and expert technicians had similar procedural knowledge but radically different strategic knowledge. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Instructional implication**: System/conceptual model instruction must precede case-based practice. A learner who cannot reason about *why* a symptom implicates a subsystem cannot benefit from observing an expert diagnose it. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Causal reasoning as a bridge**: Learners must develop causal chains — "if component X fails, what are the observable consequences downstream?" Teaching from failure effects backward to causes (consequence-to-fault mapping) produces better transfer than teaching from component knowledge forward. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- -- [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Kapur (2008, 2014, 2015) demonstrated that having learners struggle with a problem *before* instruction is more effective for deep learning than instruction-first. The mechanism is **activation and differentiation of prior knowledge** — learners who have attempted to solve the problem attend differently to the expert solution because they have generated contrast cases to compare against. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **The two-phase Productive Failure design**: [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- *PF Generation phase*: Learners work on a complex novel fault with no scaffolding. They will typically fail to find the canonical solution. The failure is *productive* because it activates relevant prior knowledge, forces attention to critical conceptual features, and creates a knowledge deficit the learner is motivated to fill. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- *PF Consolidation phase*: Expert consolidates the learner-generated solutions — showing what each attempt got right, what it missed, and why the canonical approach is superior. This comparison-based consolidation builds deeper schemas than explanation alone. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **VanLehn's impasse-driven learning** (2003): Learning events concentrate at *impasses* — moments when the learner's current approach fails and no next step is available. Providing the answer before the learner reaches impasse eliminates this learning opportunity. Implication for coaching: resist the urge to intervene before the learner is genuinely stuck. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Design principles for troubleshooting Productive Failure**: [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Cases must be complex enough to challenge but not frustrate (require prior knowledge to engage with) [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Multiple plausible diagnostic paths should exist [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Phase 1 group work amplifies effect — learners generate a richer diversity of attempts [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Phase 2 must systematically compare learner attempts to the expert approach, not just present the answer [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- -- [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Research on expert-novice differences in technical troubleshooting (Johnson 1988; Rasmussen 1974, 1993) reveals: [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **How experts differ from novices in fault diagnosis**: [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Experts chunk symptoms into higher-order patterns; novices process each symptom individually [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Experts use constraint-seeking strategies (tests that eliminate whole subsystems at once); novices use hypothesis-scanning (test one fault at a time) [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Experts maintain a fault model of the system state and update it with each test; novices lose track of what has been eliminated [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Expert pattern recognition in familiar domains is fast and non-analytic (System 1); novel problems force a switch to hypothetico-deductive reasoning (System 2) [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Experts selectively seek information with a strategy; novices collect broadly without prioritization [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Instructional implications**: [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Teach the *strategy* layer explicitly: split-half strategy, working from most-likely to least-likely, eliminating subsystems before components [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Use process tracing (think-aloud, diagnostic logs) to reveal the strategy being used, not just the outcome [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Design cases that cannot be solved by memorized procedures — force strategic reasoning [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Build fault schemas explicitly: give learners frameworks for organizing symptoms by subsystem, not just checklists [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **The HYDRIVE lesson** (Gitomer, Steinberg, Mislevy): HYDRIVE was an intelligent tutoring system for F-15 hydraulic systems troubleshooting. The ITS that taught strategic and system knowledge outperformed procedure-focused tutoring precisely on novel problems — the ones that matter most in real operations. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- -- [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- For the cognitive load theory mechanisms underlying this section (working memory limits, intrinsic vs. extraneous load, schema formation), see applied-psychology. Below are the instructional applications specific to troubleshooting: [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Full worked examples** are optimal for novices because they free working memory for observing the reasoning structure rather than searching for a solution. For troubleshooting, a worked example is an annotated expert trace: symptom → hypothesis generated → test chosen → result → hypothesis updated → repeat. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Faded worked examples** (Renkl, Atkinson, Sweller): Gradually remove steps from the expert trace, starting from the *last* steps (backward fading). The learner completes increasingly larger portions of the diagnosis. This is more effective than alternating full examples with full problems because it maintains coherence of the diagnostic chain. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Expertise reversal effect**: As learners gain expertise, full worked examples become redundant and impose extraneous load. The fading schedule must adapt to the learner — not be fixed by session count. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Application to troubleshooting curriculum design**: [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- First cases: complete expert trace with full annotation [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Next cases: expert trace with final steps removed ("what do you test next and why?") [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Later cases: expert trace with most steps removed — learner drives with only the initial symptom and the ability to request hints [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Final cases: independent diagnosis; worked trace available only after learner commits to an answer [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Van Gog et al. (2006) confirmed in electrical circuit troubleshooting: novices learn more from studying worked examples than solving equivalent problems; the advantage inverts as expertise grows. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- -- [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Medical diagnostic reasoning education is the most developed field for teaching diagnosis. Its methods transfer directly to technical troubleshooting. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Illness scripts** (Schmidt & Boshuizen; Charlin et al.): Expert clinicians organize disease knowledge into *illness scripts* — mental representations binding enabling conditions (risk factors, context), fault (pathophysiology), and consequences (signs, symptoms, test findings). Novice knowledge is fragmented; expert knowledge is bundled into retrievable, comparable scripts. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Teaching with illness scripts**: [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Teach learners to *construct* fault scripts for each failure mode (not just memorize symptoms) [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Use case variation to *elaborate* scripts — same fault in different contexts [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Use *contrast cases* — two faults with overlapping symptoms — to force script differentiation [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Script-based reading: guide learners to organize new information by script structure, not linear chapter order [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Dual-process theory**: System 1 (fast, pattern-based, non-analytic) vs. System 2 (slow, hypothetico-deductive, analytic). Expert performance is not just more System 1 — it is *appropriate calibration*: using pattern recognition for familiar fault profiles, switching to analytic reasoning for novel or ambiguous presentations. This is distinct from System 1/2 as a psychology of cognition (see applied-psychology); here the focus is on teaching learners *when to switch systems*. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Key-feature problems** (Norman & Feightner 1995): Assessment format that focuses on critical decision steps rather than encyclopedic recall. A key-feature problem presents a realistic fault scenario and asks only 2–3 questions targeting the decisions that actually determine diagnostic success. Directly applicable to IT/SRE troubleshooting assessment. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- -- [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Simulation and controlled chaos injection are *pedagogical* vehicles when designed with learning objectives and structured debriefs — not just evaluation or operational exercises. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **What makes simulation-based troubleshooting learning effective**: [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Fidelity sufficient to activate relevant schemas (not perfect realism — realism is expensive and often unnecessary) [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Controllable fault injection — instructors set the fault type and observe learner behavior [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Safe failure — learners make diagnostic errors without real consequences [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Structured debrief immediately after — this is where learning consolidates [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Game days as structured learning events** (not just operational tests): [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- *Pre-brief*: establish learning objectives, not just operational goals [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- *Scenario design*: choose fault types that expose known gaps in learner mental models [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- *Observation protocol*: track time to hypothesis, tests chosen, when learner calls for help [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- *Debrief structure*: compare learner trace to expert trace; discuss the *reasoning*, not just the answer [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **ITS lessons (HYDRIVE, SHERLOCK, ITADS)**: Intelligent tutoring systems for troubleshooting that proved most effective combined simulation (realistic fault environment) with adaptive coaching (just-in-time hints keyed to the learner's current strategy) and after-action review. HYDRIVE (Gitomer, Steinberg & Mislevy) targeted F-15 hydraulics; SHERLOCK (Lesgold et al.) targeted avionics test stations; ITADS (Ramachandran et al., 2018) targeted US Navy IT network troubleshooting. All three outperformed procedure-only instruction on transfer problems. Full citations in `references/teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning.md`. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Fire drills as learning**: Netflix/Amazon game days work pedagogically because: (1) they create authentic impasses in a safe context, (2) team members see collective and individual gaps they would not discover through procedures alone, (3) structured post-mortems force articulation and reflection. Design fire-drills with the cognitive apprenticeship loop: expert narrates what they're thinking during the drill; debrief elicits comparison; next drill removes one scaffold. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- -- [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- *This section covers domain-specific diagnostic assessment instruments (key-feature problems, script concordance, scenario rubrics). For certification exam psychometrics, IRT, cut scores, or item bank design, see assessment-certification-design.* [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Key-Feature Examinations**: Case scenario + 2–3 questions targeting only the critical decision steps. Scoring keys accept multiple correct responses (reflecting realistic diagnostic flexibility). High content validity; resists rote memorization. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Script Concordance Test (SCT)**: Presents partial fault scenario with new evidence and asks how that evidence changes the probability of a given hypothesis. Scores learner responses against an expert panel. Measures *diagnostic reasoning process*, not just endpoint accuracy. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Scenario-based rubrics**: Rubrics that assess the reasoning process — hypothesis generation quality, efficiency of test selection, appropriate updating of hypotheses with evidence, recognition of red flags. Rubric domains aligned with the Diagnostic Competency framework (Daniel et al.): information gathering, hypothesis generation, problem representation, differential generation, leading diagnosis, justification, management. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Process tracing as formative assessment**: Think-aloud protocols, diagnostic logs, and simulation traces reveal the strategy the learner is using — visible to the instructor and to the learner during reflection. More diagnostic (appropriately) than outcome scores alone. [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- **Common assessment pitfalls for troubleshooting**: [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Assessing only the correct answer, not the reasoning path [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Using cases solvable by procedure-following without reasoning [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Testing in conditions too different from training (context specificity) [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- Over-reliance on self-report without behavioral evidence [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]
- -- [src: teaching-troubleshooting-diagnostic-reasoning]

- Reference for measuring training and enablement program effectiveness across the full evaluation stack — from post-workshop smile sheets to executive ROI reports and cross-system xAPI analytics. [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- See `references/learning-measurement-context.md` for the full deep-reference with worked examples, decision tables, and vendor comparisons. [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- Three frameworks dominate training program evaluation. They are complementary, not competing: [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- **When to use each:** Kirkpatrick levels 1–4 apply to any formal training; New World Kirkpatrick adds the pre-design planning discipline; Phillips Level 5 is appropriate for 5–10% of programs — those that are high-cost, strategically critical, and directly tied to measurable business KPIs. [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- Measures whether participants found training favorable, engaging, and relevant. Relevance is the most predictive sub-component. [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- **Limitation:** A 2009 study (n=335) found no statistically significant correlation between Level 1 scores and Level 3 behavior change. Alliger & Janak (1989) found the Level 1→Level 2 causal link produced only r=.23. [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- Measures acquisition of knowledge, skills, attitude, confidence, and commitment (5 components per the New World Model). [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- Measures whether participants apply what they learned on the job. Most organizations skip formal Level 3 evaluation — Kennedy et al. (2013) found 40%+ report it is not required by management. [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- Measures whether targeted organizational outcomes occurred. Requires pre-established KPI baselines and isolation methodology. [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- L1/L2 = L&D accountability; L3/L4 = shared accountability between L&D, managers, and the business. [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- Post-training reinforcement systems management must provide: coaching, job aids, work review, recognition. [TENTATIVE: ~85% vs ~15% application figures are from Kirkpatrick-affiliated sources — treat as directional.] [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- Short-term observations signaling whether critical behaviors are on track to produce results. [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- Plan evaluation in reverse: L4 KPI → L3 behaviors → L2 objectives → L1 design. [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- BCR  = Program Benefits / Program Costs [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- ROI% = [(Benefits − Costs) / Costs] × 100 [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- Isolation methods (descending reliability): control group → trend-line → forecasting model → manager estimates → participant estimates. [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- Apply to ~5–10% of programs: high-cost, strategically critical, tied to measurable KPI, with a viable isolation method. [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- xAPI adoption ~17% (verified-as-of: 2026-06-16) despite 10+ years. SCORM still dominant at 81.7%. [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- Baldwin & Ford (1988): transfer depends on trainee characteristics, training design, and work environment. Supervisor support is the single strongest driver (ρ=.51, *Human Factors* 2019). [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- LTSI (Holton, Bates & Ruona, 2000): 16-factor validated instrument for diagnosing transfer barriers. [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- Three audiences: Executive (ROI, time-to-proficiency), Manager (behavior change, team completion), L&D ops (engagement analytics). [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- Top metrics: time-to-productivity, 30/60/90-day retention, manager reinforcement score, application rate, completion rate (process only — not performance). [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- **Skip evaluation** for cohorts under ~20 or one-time deliveries where overhead exceeds value. [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- **Retrospective evaluation**: use trend-line data, untrained comparison cohort, or SME estimates with documented confidence reduction. [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- **ROI report structure**: Executive summary → Methodology → Financial detail → Intangibles → Sensitivity analysis. [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- **xAPI/LRS privacy**: anonymize actor IDs for PII; GDPR applies in EU; FERPA applies to educational institutions. [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- High-cost / strategic program? [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- ├── Yes → Levels 1–4; Level 5 if isolation feasible; plan backward [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- └── No  → Levels 1–2; add L3 if behavior change is the goal [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- Can you isolate the effect? [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- ├── Control group → Level 5 ROI defensible [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- ├── Trend-line    → Level 5 plausible with caveats [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- ├── Estimates     → Level 4 + conservative estimate [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- └── No            → Level 4 direction + intangibles only [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- ├── Native xAPI authoring → cmi5 if LMS supports it, else SCORM [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- ├── Mobile/offline/cross-platform → xAPI + LRS; plan data governance [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- ├── Simple completion+score → SCORM 1.2 [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- └── Government/regulated → xAPI (IEEE/ISO status matters for RFPs) [src: learning-measurement-evaluation]
- **Domain:** Educational applications of generative AI (2024-2026) — lens is EDUCATION, not LLM engineering. [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- **Verified-as-of:** 2026-06-16 [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- > **Scope limits.** This skill covers what AI does *for learners and designers*, not how AI works internally. For LLM/agent architecture, RAG, prompting technique, or model training, see the `ai-*` skill family. For ADDIE/SAM/course design with no AI component, see `instructional-design-course-architecture`. For psychometric mechanics (IRT, Angoff, DIF), see `assessment-certification-design`. For human trust calibration and cognitive bias in AI adoption (without a learning-outcome angle), see `applied-psychology`. [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- **Evidence confidence key:** [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- **Fact** — 3+ independent sources agree; treat as established finding. [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- **Qualified** — 2 sources, or 1 strong RCT with known limits; use with stated caveats. [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- **Tentative** — single study or preprint; directional signal only. [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- 84% of instructional designers reported using ChatGPT in their work by late 2024. Named commercial tools: Articulate AI Assist, Coursebox, Synthesia, Mindsmith, iSpring AI, ThingLink Scenario Builder. [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- HITL (human-in-the-loop) is the dominant recommended model. Five-stage lifecycle: Strategy & Analysis → AI-Assisted Drafting → SME/ID Expert Refinement → Governance Review → Continuous Feedback Loop. [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- ADDIE/SAM augmentation with AI: Analysis (survey summarization), Design (objective generation), Development (rapid prototyping), Implementation (comms drafting), Evaluation (performance analysis). ARCHED Framework (AAAI 2025 preprint): multi-agent ID with 4.43/5 expert rating (Tentative — single preprint). [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- Bloom (1984): one-on-one tutoring raised performance ~2 sigma. VanLehn 2011 meta-analysis (54 comparisons): pre-LLM ITS d=0.76 vs. no tutoring (Fact — peer-reviewed, accessed via 2015 secondary review). K-12 ITS meta-analysis 2025: g=0.271. [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- Major LLM-based ITS: Khanmigo (40+ districts, mixed outcomes), LearnLM UK RCT +5.5pp on novel problems (Qualified — preprint, Google-authored), MATHia/Carnegie Learning, GPT-4 ITS ~80% error diagnosis accuracy. [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- **Bastani et al. (Fact):** Unrestricted AI: +48% practice, -17% exam. Guardrailed GPT tutor: on par with or above control. The tool is not the problem; unconstrained use is. [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- Socratic patterns: separate system-prompt personas, finite-state slot structure (MWPTutor), RAG-based course grounding, daily usage caps + metacognitive reflection, explicit fallibility disclosure. [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- AIG: psychometric evaluations absent in most papers (systematic review, 60 papers). Automation bias degrades item quality. Lexical overlap cueing bias. AI detection tools: ~70% effectiveness (2024) — insufficient for enforcement. [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- AI-resistant formats (Strong evidence): oral exams/live follow-up, audience-tailored assessments, observational assessments, reflection on live events. Moderate: debate/panel, portfolio with process docs, timed in-person. [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- Platforms: Duolingo Max (ML+LLM, limited independent replication), Century Tech (55+ countries), ALEKS (most-studied in HE math). Meta-analysis of 25 studies: 59% show performance gains (Qualified — heterogeneous platforms and outcomes; directional support only). [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- SSP-MMC spaced repetition: 15-20% reduction in unnecessary reviews, ~10-15% retention improvement. Corporate L&D: FERPA does not apply; employee data governed by employment contracts and state privacy law. For xAPI/LRS architecture, see `learning-measurement-evaluation`. [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- GenAI acts as an **amplifier of existing advantage**, not an equalizer (Lau et al. 2024, ACM ICER). Strong novice programmers benefit; weak programmers experience compounded metacognitive failures and false confidence. [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- Anthropic RCT (2026, n=52): AI users averaged 50% on comprehension tests vs. 67% for manual coders. Mitigation: structured integration with compare → reflect → revisit scaffolding. [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- Disconfirming: Codex/Copilot 2023 study found no retention loss; harm is tool- and task-specific. Bastani guardrailed condition: students on par with or above control. [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- **Hallucination:** >50% of student detection attempts rely on intuition. Mitigate with RAG grounding and explicit fallibility warnings. [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- **FERPA/COPPA:** 42% of US districts lack DPAs with AI vendors. FTC finalized COPPA opt-in amendments January 2025. [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- Governance checklist: (1) DPA required; (2) explicit student consent; (3) vendor data-use prohibition; (4) data minimization; (5) periodic audits; (6) AI explainability for grading — rubric-aligned rationale per student, not a black-box score. [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- **Equity:** GenAI amplifies existing advantages. Community colleges cannot afford enterprise contracts. Device/connectivity gaps remain primary bottleneck. [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- Deploying LLM tutor without guardrails — unrestricted access harms novice learners [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- Treating AI-generated MCQs as ready-to-use — automation bias; psychometric review required [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- Assuming AI equalizes access — amplifier-not-equalizer finding is consistent [src: genai-education-instructional-design]
- FERPA compliance assumed from vendor claims — 42% of districts lack DPAs [src: genai-education-instructional-design]

- The front door for **active trading and how financial markets actually work** for a US retail participant. This skill does two jobs: [src: trading-and-investing]
- **Foundation** — it carries the shared overview every trading sub-topic builds on: the asset classes, the market participants, primary vs secondary markets, how an order travels from your broker to the market, market sessions and hours, the core investing-vs-trading distinction, and the risk/regulatory backbone. Deep treatments live in `references/` (loaded on demand). [src: trading-and-investing]
- **Hub / router** — it routes specific questions down to the family's spokes (see the routing table for the original 17-spoke plan, and the Foundation references table below for all 44 reference files as built). The spokes are the *intended* family; as each is built it owns its depth and this hub just points to it. [src: trading-and-investing]
- > **Educational information only — NOT financial, investment, tax, or legal advice, and NOT a recommendation to buy, sell, or hold anything.** All securities and trading carry **risk of loss**; you can lose money, and with leverage you can lose **more than you put in**. Past performance does not guarantee future results. **The large majority of active retail/day traders underperform a simple index or lose money** (see `references/investing-vs-trading.md`). Rules, products, tax treatment, and the vendor landscape change — every volatile claim here is stamped **as of 2026**; verify current facts with the primary regulator (SEC/Investor.gov, FINRA, CFTC, SIPC) before acting. For a personal decision, consult a licensed professional. [src: trading-and-investing]
- This family is the **active** side: markets, instruments, execution, trading styles, and the risks of trading. Its sibling **`investing-and-retirement`** (in the consumer-finance family) owns the **passive, long-term, retirement** side — low-cost index buy-and-hold, 401(k)/403(b)/IRA/Roth mechanics and contribution limits, employer match and vesting, dollar-cost averaging for retirement, Social Security claiming, target-date defaults, and choosing a robo-advisor or fee-only fiduciary. [src: trading-and-investing]
- "How do I start investing for retirement / which account / is this fund's expense ratio good / should I do a backdoor Roth / when do I claim Social Security" → **`investing-and-retirement`**. [src: trading-and-investing]
- "How do markets work / how do I trade X / what's a limit order / is day trading worth it / how does margin work / what is options-/futures-/forex-/crypto-trading" → **this family**. [src: trading-and-investing]
- The two overlap on shared vocabulary (diversification, asset allocation, ETFs vs mutual funds, fees). When the *intent* is long-term passive wealth-building, defer to `investing-and-retirement`; when the intent is understanding markets or actively trading, stay here. `portfolio-theory-and-asset-allocation` (a spoke here) covers the *theory* (MPT, efficient frontier, factor models, rebalancing math); `investing-and-retirement` covers the *consumer how-to*. [src: trading-and-investing]

[src: trading-and-investing]
- The shared foundation is split into focused references so a spoke can cross-reference one without pulling the whole hub: [src: trading-and-investing]
- When answering directly from this foundation: (1) for any advice-seeking question, **lead with the educational-only / not-advice framing** and that trading carries risk of loss; (2) **cite the primary regulator** (SEC/Investor.gov, FINRA, CFTC, SIPC) for load-bearing facts, and stamp volatile facts *as of 2026* with a "verify current" pointer; (3) when the question belongs to a spoke whose **reference file exists** in the Foundation references table above, `Read` its `references/<slug>.md` and answer from it — if a standalone installed skill also exists for that spoke, the standalone skill takes precedence; if the Read fails or the reference is silent on the specific question, degrade to foundation depth; (4) when the question belongs to a spoke **not yet in the Foundation references table**, first check the available-skills list for a standalone installed skill of that spoke's slug — if found, invoke it; otherwise name the destination spoke and answer at foundation depth; (5) when a query spans two spokes, identify the **primary spoke** (the one that owns the action) and answer from it, citing the secondary spoke for supplementary detail. Keep US-centric, flagging where a fact (T+1, PDT, SIPC, Reg NMS, CFTC caps) is US-only. [src: trading-and-investing]
- Everything downstream runs through a **brokerage account** opened with a broker-dealer (after identity verification, funded from a bank). The one account choice that gates the rest is **cash vs margin**: a **cash account** trades only settled funds (no borrowing); a **margin account** lets the broker **lend you money** against the account as collateral — which is what enables short selling and triggers the margin and Pattern-Day-Trader rules in `references/trading-risks-and-protections.md`. Account *type* (individual/joint/retirement-wrapper) sits on top of that; a retirement-wrapper account points to the passive sibling, `investing-and-retirement`. [src: trading-and-investing]
- A **retail participant** buys and sells **instruments** (equities, bonds, FX, commodities, crypto, pooled funds like ETFs/mutual funds, and derivatives) through a **broker-dealer**, which routes the order to an **execution venue** (an exchange like NYSE/Nasdaq, a wholesaler/market maker, or an ATS); the trade then **clears** through a central counterparty (NSCC for US equities, OCC for listed options) and **settles** the next business day (**T+1**, as of 2026). The issuer raises money only once, in the **primary market** (an IPO or new issue); everything after is the **secondary market**, where investors trade among themselves and prices are discovered. **Investing** means holding for the long term to build wealth through compounding; **trading** means buying and selling frequently to profit from price moves — and the evidence is strong that **most active retail traders underperform or lose money**, so trading capital should be money you can afford to lose. Markets are regulated (SEC, FINRA, CFTC) and your *brokerage account* is protected against broker failure by **SIPC** — but **nothing protects you against market losses**. [src: trading-and-investing]
- **`as of 2026` volatile claims to re-verify** (detail in the references) — one line each, highest-stakes first: [src: trading-and-investing]
- **Pattern Day Trader rule is being replaced** (highest-stakes): FINRA amended Rule 4210 to drop the $25k/PDT designation for a new **intraday-margin** framework, **effective June 4, 2026** (transition through Oct 20, 2027). Most third-party sites still describe the legacy $25k rule — verify your broker's *current* policy. [src: trading-and-investing]
- **Settlement is T+1** (since May 28, 2024); **SIPC** limits are **$500k / $250k cash** — both change, verify at the regulator. [src: trading-and-investing]
- **Spot Bitcoin ETFs** (approved Jan 2024) and **spot Ether ETFs** (Jul 2024) exist and have grown large. [src: trading-and-investing]
- **Nasdaq 23-hour trading** was SEC-approved (Apr 10, 2026), launch targeted H2 2026; **CME launched 24/7 crypto futures** (May 29, 2026). [src: trading-and-investing]
- US retail **forex leverage** is capped (~50:1 majors / ~20:1 others) by CFTC/NFA; **$0 stock/ETF commissions** are standard; capital-gains breakpoints change yearly. [src: trading-and-investing]
- **Commodities routing.** Commodities are an asset class in the foundation, but there is **no dedicated commodities spoke** — route commodity *futures* depth to `derivatives-futures-and-swaps` and commodity *ETP/ETF* depth to `stock-and-equity-trading`. [src: trading-and-investing]

The consumer-finance family's `personal-income-taxes` owns ordinary individual filing. Keep deep tax out of the foundation — it states only the short-vs-long-term-gains distinction at a high level. [src: trading-and-investing]

- **Blockchain seam.** Trader-side DeFi (executing swaps on DEXs, managing liquidity positions, MEV defense, perp DEX trading, bridge mechanics for moving assets) is owned here in `defi-and-onchain-trading`. Protocol mechanics, cryptoeconomics, and the academic/research layer (AMM math derivation, MEV supply-chain/PBS theory, tokenomics, consensus) → `blockchain` / `blockchain-economics`. [src: trading-and-investing]

[src: trading-and-investing]

Other major markets (LSE, Euronext, Tokyo, Hong Kong, Shanghai) run their own hours, regulators, settlement cycles, and tax regimes; the foundation flags where the US specifics (T+1, PDT, SIPC, Reg NMS, CFTC leverage caps) are US-only and would differ abroad. - <!-- Provenance: standalone skill. Mirrored from ~/.claude/skills/human-performance-technology/SKILL.md by scripts/persist-spoke.mjs. --> [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Quick orientation:** HPT is the discipline UPSTREAM of instructional design. It asks "is training the right intervention?" before any course is designed. This skill covers the full diagnostic and intervention-selection toolkit: the ISPI model, Gilbert's BEM, Mager-Pipe flowchart, Rummler-Brache, performance support (EPSS/DAPs), Five Moments of Need, and job aid design. [src: human-performance-technology]
- > **The foundational HPT claim:** "If you pit a good performer against a bad system, the system will win almost every time." — Rummler & Brache, *Improving Performance* (1990). About 80% of performance improvement opportunities are environmental, not individual (a practitioner estimate — see §2 for the calibration caveat). Training is the solution to a *knowledge/skill gap specifically* — not a performance gap generically. [src: human-performance-technology]
- *Volatile claims — the DAP/EPSS vendor landscape in §6 and the market/effectiveness figures throughout — were **verified-as-of 2026-06-16**. The durable models (§§1–5, 7–11) are stable HPT canon (Gilbert 1978; Mager & Pipe 1970; Rummler & Brache 1990; Gery 1991).* [src: human-performance-technology]
- -- [src: human-performance-technology]
- -- [src: human-performance-technology]
- Human Performance Technology (HPT) is ISPI's (International Society for Performance Improvement) systematic, systemic, results-oriented framework. The ISPI model (Deterline & Rosenberg, 1992; updated 2000) is "the most representative and frequently utilized process model in the HPT field" (ERIC/TechTrends, 2017).[^1] [src: human-performance-technology]
- **The fundamental distinction from instructional design:** "HPT models allow for a much broader range of interventions to a given performance problem, which often include non-instructional interventions as well as those that involve instruction or training." (Morrison, Ross, Kalman & Kemp, 2013, cited in jwkline.com).[^2] The HPT model determines *whether* training or other interventions are effective — training is one output, never the assumed starting point. [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Phase 1 — Performance Analysis (Need or Opportunity)** [src: human-performance-technology]
- Three sub-analyses run together: [src: human-performance-technology]
- *Organizational analysis:* vision, mission, goals, strategies — the business context [src: human-performance-technology]
- *Environmental analysis:* external and internal realities shaping actual performance [src: human-performance-technology]
- *Gap analysis:* actual performance vs. desired performance; if actual = desired, no intervention needed [src: human-performance-technology]
- Output: a quantified performance gap statement with business rationale. [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Phase 2 — Cause Analysis** [src: human-performance-technology]
- Why does the gap exist? Uses Gilbert's BEM (see §2) to categorize causes: [src: human-performance-technology]
- *Environmental support factors:* data/information/feedback; resources/tools; consequences/incentives [src: human-performance-technology]
- *Individual behavior factors:* knowledge/skills; individual capacity; motivation/expectations [src: human-performance-technology]
- Technique: fishbone diagram applied to each BEM cell. Output: a statement of *why* performance is not happening — before any intervention is selected. [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Phase 3 — Intervention Selection, Design, and Development** [src: human-performance-technology]
- Interventions are drawn from a broad taxonomy (see §4). Training is one category of seven. The rule: "Training should only be applied in those instances where no other cheaper and less timely intervention will work." (Robinson & Robinson, 1995, as cited by multiple HPT references).[^3] [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Phase 4 — Intervention Implementation and Change Management** [src: human-performance-technology]
- Four components: the intervention itself, organizational change, leadership engagement, individuals affected. [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Phase 5 — Evaluation** [src: human-performance-technology]
- Three tiers run in parallel with all prior phases: [src: human-performance-technology]
- *Formative:* evaluates each phase as it runs [src: human-performance-technology]
- *Summative:* reaction, competence, job transfer, organizational impact, ROI [src: human-performance-technology]
- *Confirmative/meta:* validates the process, captures lessons learned [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Empirical note:** A content analysis of 30 actual HPT business cases (ERIC/TechTrends, 2017) found practitioners compress or adapt the model in practice — actual performance analysis processes differ from the sequential model. A "refined performance analysis process" based on actual practice has been proposed.[^1] [src: human-performance-technology]
- -- [src: human-performance-technology]
- Thomas Gilbert published *Human Competence: Engineering Worthy Performance* (1978). The BEM is his Third Leisurely Theorem, grounded in two prior theorems: [src: human-performance-technology]
- **First Theorem (Worthy Performance):** W = A/B — human competence is the ratio of valuable accomplishments (A) to costly behavior (B). Optimize the ratio, not the activity. [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Second Theorem (Exemplary Performer Analysis):** Potential to Improve Performance (PIP) = W(exemplary) ÷ W(typical). The gap between typical and exemplary performers represents the addressable opportunity — and the exemplary performer's behaviors reveal the environmental conditions that enable good performance. [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Environmental factors (management's responsibility — fix these first):** [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Individual factors (performer's repertory — fix only after environment is addressed):** [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Diagnostic sequence:** E1 → E2 → E3 → I1 → I2 → I3 (Data first, Motives last). [src: human-performance-technology]
- Rationale: "Environmental factors such as information, resources, and incentives are usually more cost-effective to fix than individual factors... Even if we were to successfully change individual factors, performance will most likely not improve if environmental factors remain unresolved." (Chevalier, "Updating the Behavior Engineering Model", *Performance Improvement*).[^4] [src: human-performance-technology]
- Rummler-Brache practitioner estimate: "about 80 percent of performance improvement opportunities reside in the environment," with 15–20% in skills/knowledge and fewer than 1% in individual capacity (rummlerbrache.com).[^5] **Calibration caveat:** this 80/20 split is grounded in Rummler & Brache's consulting *experience*, not controlled empirical research (Clark, citing Christensen & Wallace, 2012).[^20] Treat it as a strong, directionally robust practitioner heuristic — not a measured statistic; the ratio shifts toward skills/knowledge for highly autonomous or novel-problem work. [src: human-performance-technology]
- Training's BEM position: Knowledge (I1) is the *fourth* cell to check — after three environmental cells. The BEM structurally makes training a later consideration, not a first response. [src: human-performance-technology]
- Gilbert asserted that improving environmental motivation "can usually obliterate all evidence of defective motives." He dismissed non-monetary incentives as ineffective, citing no supporting research (PerriKennedy.com, 2012). Modern organizational psychology — self-determination theory, engagement research — contradicts this; organizations can influence intrinsic motivation through environmental design. Structural support for the BEM's factor relationships is stronger than support for Gilbert's motivational sequencing.[^6] [src: human-performance-technology]
- -- [src: human-performance-technology]
- Robert Mager and Peter Pipe's *Analyzing Performance Problems* (1970; 3rd ed. 1997) is a decision flowchart for diagnosing any performance discrepancy. It "validates the importance of examining and attacking the 'non-training' solutions that arise first instead of creating costly and in many cases un-needed learning solutions." (GSU HPT Manual).[^7] [src: human-performance-technology]
- **The pivotal question:** "Could they do it if their life depended on it?" — Yes means it's NOT a skill deficiency; it's an environmental, motivational, or feedback problem. Only a "no" routes to training. [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Non-training "fast fixes" (Steps 3–4):** Remove negative consequences for performing correctly; add positive consequences; provide clear standards and feedback; remove obstacles; simplify the task or provide decision support. These are Gilbert's E-cells restated as actionable fixes. [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Criticism:** The Mager-Pipe model is "a bit too simple for complex problems because a yes/no answer is often not enough." Many problems have multiple causes requiring multiple interventions. The flowchart is a diagnostic starting point, not a complete solution tool. (Rothwell, Hohne & King, 2013).[^8] [src: human-performance-technology]
- -- [src: human-performance-technology]
- Geary Rummler and Alan Brache's *Improving Performance: How to Manage the White Space on the Organization Chart* (Jossey-Bass, 1990) extends Gilbert's BEM upward from the job/performer level to process and organizational levels. [src: human-performance-technology]
- **The "white space" concept:** Performance failures frequently occur at process handoffs between departments. These cannot be fixed by individual training or job redesign — they require process-level intervention. This is Rummler-Brache's distinctive contribution beyond Gilbert. [src: human-performance-technology]
- **The principle:** "The majority of managers simply do not understand the variables that influence performance. They are not aware of the 'performance levers' that they should be pulling." (Rummler & Brache, 1990).[^5] [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Intersection with HPT:** Rummler-Brache operates at Process and Organization levels; Gilbert's BEM operates at the Job/Performer level. Together they form the complete HPT diagnostic stack. When BEM analysis finds no individual-level cause, the problem is likely at the process or organizational level — requiring a Rummler-Brache intervention, not training. [src: human-performance-technology]
- -- [src: human-performance-technology]
- Once cause analysis is complete, interventions are selected from this full spectrum: [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Key principle:** Training should be "the solution of last resort among solutions of equal effectiveness — the most expensive option, the hardest to change." (ATD, 2017).[^9] When multiple intervention types address the same gap, prefer the cheapest and fastest to change first. [src: human-performance-technology]
- -- [src: human-performance-technology]
- "An orchestrated set of technology-enabled services that provide on-demand access to integrated information, guidance, advice, assistance, training, and tools to enable high-level job performance with a minimum of support from other people." — *Electronic Performance Support Systems* (Gery Performance Press, 1991).[^10] [src: human-performance-technology]
- Gery's vision was **day-one performance** — workers perform effectively from the first day because an expert system replaces lengthy apprenticeship. [src: human-performance-technology]
- Empirical finding: Higher integration produces better performance outcomes, attitudes, and system use. Any level of EPSS support outperforms no support (Altalib, *Performance Improvement Quarterly*, 2005).[^11] [src: human-performance-technology]
- The term "EPSS" faded in the 2000s into knowledge management and e-learning silos. Gartner named the category in 2019 (initially "Digital Adoption Solutions," now **Digital Adoption Platforms (DAPs)**). The modern DAP market: [src: human-performance-technology]
- **WalkMe** (SAP): Enterprise-leading DAP; extrinsic model; DeepUI AI adapts to application changes automatically. A WalkMe-commissioned Forrester Total Economic Impact study (2020) reported a **368% three-year ROI** for a composite organization (sub-3-month payback, ~$20.0M present-value benefits) driven by reduced training/onboarding time and fewer support tickets[^21] — a vendor-sponsored figure, so treat it as directional, not independent evidence; resolves adoption friction at point of use. [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Whatfix**: spans both Gery types — intrinsic embedded step-by-step Flows *and* extrinsic Smart Tips overlays (so it appears as the extrinsic example above); plus AI Agents, ScreenSense contextual guidance; SCORM-compliant; includes Mirror sandbox simulation for pre-go-live readiness. [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Pendo**: Analytics-first; designed for SaaS product activation (customer-facing) rather than enterprise ERP workflows. [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Conversational AI agents** (Continu Eddy, CGS Cicero Coach): Chatbot-embedded in Slack/Teams; resolve 85%+ of routine policy/procedure queries via LLM + knowledge base, implementing Gery's extrinsic EPSS in conversational form. [src: human-performance-technology]
- **AI evolution:** "Generative AI produces quality text, images, audio, and video via natural language prompts, further fulfilling performance support promises. However, the potential of enterprise performance-centeredness remains unrealized in the AI-integrated workplace." (Dickelman & Christensen, EPSS Central).[^12] *See genai-education-instructional-design for AI-EPSS platform engineering.* [src: human-performance-technology]
- -- [src: human-performance-technology]
- Conrad Gottfredson and Bob Mosher formalized this framework (2011 book; Learning Guild article 2012). It maps when learning and performance support are needed in relation to the work workflow. [src: human-performance-technology]
- Traditional L&D addresses only Moments 1 and 2. Moments 3, 4, and 5 — Apply, Solve, Change — occur entirely in the workflow and require **performance support (EPSS/DAP)**, not formal training. When organizations shift to performance-first design using 5MoN: training time is reduced approximately by half; time to competency is also reduced by approximately half. (5momentsofneed.com, 2020–2023).[^13] [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Moment 5 (Change) is the most neglected and most costly:** Once skills are automatic behaviors, replacing them requires sustained workflow performance support over time — formal training alone cannot accomplish this unlearning/relearning. [src: human-performance-technology]
- The 5MoN methodology produces exactly two output types: [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Targeted Training** — for Moments 1 and 2 (takes learners out of the workflow) [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Digital Coach (EPSS)** — for Moments 3, 4, and 5 (embedded in the workflow) [src: human-performance-technology]
- Design sequence is reversed: start with Apply (Moment 3), then work backward to determine what training is actually necessary. [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Misapplication warning:** Organizations frequently claim to "do 5MoN" by chunking eLearning into micropieces. Mosher explicitly calls this insufficient — true workflow learning eliminates the transfer phase entirely; microchunking still requires the learner to stop working. (Apply Synergies, 2024).[^14] [src: human-performance-technology]
- -- [src: human-performance-technology]
- Job aids are any artifacts that direct or guide work performance, reducing recall burden and minimizing errors during task execution (ATD / Klein).[^15] [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Use a job aid (not training) when:** [src: human-performance-technology]
- Task is infrequent (less than monthly) — memorization is waste [src: human-performance-technology]
- Task has strict sequential steps that must be followed exactly [src: human-performance-technology]
- Information changes frequently — a course would be obsolete at launch [src: human-performance-technology]
- High consequence if done wrong — support reduces error rate [src: human-performance-technology]
- Cognitive load reduction matters more than building durable memory [src: human-performance-technology]
- Many procedural steps — "if a process has thirty steps but only happens once a quarter, memorization is a waste of resources" (Sherpa Intelligence, 2026).[^16] [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Do NOT use a job aid when:** [src: human-performance-technology]
- Task requires rapid, fluid performance (frequent use demands automation) [src: human-performance-technology]
- Job aid use would damage credibility (e.g., medical professional in emergency) [src: human-performance-technology]
- Novel situations predominate — judgment replaces procedure [src: human-performance-technology]
- Performer lacks prerequisite skills needed to use the aid [src: human-performance-technology]
- "Guidance with job aids should always be the choice, unless barriers exist. Job aids generally cost less to develop than instruction, are easier to revise when performance requirements change, reduce the time to achieve on-the-job performance, and are not subject to forgetting." (Barry Boothby, HPT Treasures).[^4] [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Design principles:** one task per job aid; brevity (keywords over sentences); visual design (icons, white space, contrast); point-of-use design (matches the physical/digital environment where the task occurs); test with actual performers before deployment. [src: human-performance-technology]
- -- [src: human-performance-technology]
- Josh Bersin articulated this concept in 2018, synthesizing Gery's EPSS and Gottfredson's 5MoN with modern platform realities. [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Key empirical anchor:** The average employee has only **24 minutes per week** for formal learning (Bersin by Deloitte, 2015, 700+ organizations). Approximately **50% of all learning interactions** from O'Reilly's technical community are "in the moment of need" technical support (Bersin, 2018).[^17] [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Just-in-time vs. just-in-case:** [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Platform pattern:** Learning experience platforms (LXPs) plugged into productivity tools (Office 365, Salesforce, Slack) recommend microlearning based on tasks being performed — implementing Gery's intrinsic/extrinsic EPSS in modern SaaS infrastructure. [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Academic validation:** Chacko & Cox (2025, *Industrial and Organizational Psychology*, Cambridge University Press) provides peer-reviewed support for the just-in-time microlearning framework.[^17] [src: human-performance-technology]
- -- [src: human-performance-technology]
- The Robinson model (*Performance Consulting: Moving Beyond Training*, 1995/2015) defines the shift from training order-taker to performance partner. The central argument: training programs "focus on developing excellent learning experiences, while failing to ensure that the newly acquired skills are transferred to the job." (ERIC abstract, ED382791).[^3] [src: human-performance-technology]
- **The diagnostic sequence a performance consultant follows:** [src: human-performance-technology]
- Name the business outcome — not the learning need. "What's the business problem we're solving?" [src: human-performance-technology]
- Conduct performance analysis — desired vs. actual state and the measurable gap. [src: human-performance-technology]
- Conduct cause analysis (BEM cells) — before prescribing anything. [src: human-performance-technology]
- Apply the tacit/codified knowledge split (see §11 Limitations). [src: human-performance-technology]
- Apply the frequency/consequence test. [src: human-performance-technology]
- Select and blend: train for foundational skill, support for procedural reference. [src: human-performance-technology]
- **The "order-taker" pattern:** A client says "I want a training program because of increased customer dissatisfaction." The performance consultant recognizes this as a business problem with an assumed-training solution, pulls back to cause analysis, and may discover the cause is unclear expectations, not skill gaps. (Dana Robinson, ATD interview, 2015).[^3] [src: human-performance-technology]
- **US organizations spend $175 billion annually on training initiatives "yet often have little to show for it. One reason is that people jump to solutions before they identify the causes."** — Robinson, Robinson & Handshaw (3rd ed., 2015). [src: human-performance-technology]
- -- [src: human-performance-technology]
- HPT performs best on **codified knowledge** (procedures, checklists, reference data) and underperforms on **tacit knowledge** (clinical judgment, adaptive expertise, complex troubleshooting). [src: human-performance-technology]
- Edmondson et al. (Harvard Business School, 2002) studied minimally invasive cardiac surgery adoption across hospitals. Performance improvement via codified knowledge accelerated predictably — later adopters benefited from documented learnings. Performance improvement via tacit knowledge varied significantly and unpredictably across organizations. Conclusion: tacit-knowledge-dependent performance improvement requires "intense communication among past and future users, perhaps involving moving people around so that new users can work closely with more experienced users." A job aid cannot substitute for this.[^18] [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Implication:** When the operative performance driver is tacit/adaptive expertise, the HPT default toward performance support is wrong — investment in training, mentorship, and deliberate practice is required. [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Time-consuming:** Full performance analysis, cause analysis, and intervention design require significant data collection and stakeholder involvement, slowing implementation. [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Expertise required:** Not all organizations have trained HPT practitioners; the model's quality depends on the depth of the cause analysis. [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Systems overemphasis:** HPT's environmental focus can miss personal/attitudinal barriers — individual accountability matters when environmental factors are adequate. (247Teach, 2024).[^19] [src: human-performance-technology]
- **Knowledge-worker limitation:** HPT models designed for procedural work need adaptation for knowledge workers whose performance is driven by complex problem-solving, not procedures. Systems thinking (Senge, Checkland) is a corrective. (Korean academic analysis).[^19] [src: human-performance-technology]
- "Training without reinforcement becomes entertainment... Many programs are built backward: start with content, build the experience, then 'add later' objectives. The harder work — diagnosing the real drivers of performance — gets skipped. Without diagnosis, training becomes content delivery." (*Training Industry*, Feb 2026).[^16] [src: human-performance-technology]
- The mature HPT position: **blend training and performance support** rather than replace one with the other — train for foundational understanding, support for complex procedural reference and workflow reinforcement. [src: human-performance-technology]
